So they're the reverse of what the audience sees." He said it without any edge, the way you'd tell someone which door stuck. Priya crossed to the other side, and this time her entrance worked, and Andrew wrote SL in the margin of his script with a hand that was not quite steady.

He found Ms. Okafor at lunch and told her, half apology and half accusation, that nobody had explained any of it. "Nobody explained debate theory to you either," she said. "You read it, you lost rounds, you figured it out." That was true. His first year he had run a case about obsolete constitutional doctrine, some argument about obsolescent clauses that a senior had handed him, and he had defended it without understanding a word of it until he lost to a girl who simply asked him what the standard was. Losing had taught him more than winning ever did. He went back to the theater with a legal pad and began, for the first time in his life, to write down what he did not know.

The rehearsal that afternoon went badly and then went well. He blocked the whole first scene, drawing boxes on the pad, and when Dani froze in her monologue he almost fed her the line, and then didn't. Instead he called a break, sat on the edge of the stage beside her, and asked what the character wanted. "To be heard," Dani said, so quietly he almost missed it. "Then walk toward him while you say it," Andrew said. "Stage right, two steps." She looked at him to check, and he nodded, and she crossed and delivered the line to Marcus's face, and it was the first true moment of the day. Something in Andrew's chest went hot and clean, the way it did after a round he knew he had won on the merits, though this was better, because it wasn't his.

By evening he had found the two ways of thinking and could not get them apart. Debate had trained him to hold positions he did not hold, to argue a side to its limit and then drop it the second the bell rang. Directing wanted the opposite: a conviction about the scene that he had to keep pressing toward, take after take, without a bell to release him. Yet the arguing had a use here too. When Priya wanted her character to lie and Marcus wanted her to tell the truth, Andrew made them swap sides and defend each other's choice, and out of that argument came a third thing, a compromise that was better than either and that he could not have planned. He still did not know whether he was a person who could commit to one truth long enough to build anything on it. He knew he had blocked eleven pages and the entrance directions were all correct.

At eight o'clock Ms. Okafor looked in from the hallway. "You're missing your own round," she said. Andrew checked the time, and he did feel it, a pull toward the pairing sheets and the fluorescent rooms where he was good at things. But Dani was running her monologue again, unprompted, and Priya had moved a chair without being told.

"I'll take the loss," he said, and turned back to the stage. "From the top. Priya, enter stage left."

The mirrors in Grandmother's house were covered with sheets, and Arianna kept catching herself looking for her reflection anyway, finding only white cloth and the dim shape of the hallway behind it. She had arrived the night before the burial, straight from packing her dorm room into three boxes, and now the boxes sat in the trunk of her car outside while she sat on a low wooden stool in the living room, which was what her grandfather had told her to do. "We sit shiva now," he had said. "After the burial, seven days. The word means seven." Then he had gone into the kitchen and not come out for an hour.

The problem was orientation. Her college ran a mandatory advising session on Thursday, which was day three, three hours away by train, and her mother had offered a noncommittal shrug when Arianna asked whether she should go. "It's your education," her mother said, which was the kind of answer that handed the decision back to you like a plate you didn't order. Arianna had spent the whole year sharpening herself into someone practical, someone who could argue that grief was a chemical state and mourning a technology for managing it, a small private rationalism she'd built from philosophy podcasts and her own refusal to cry at the hospital. By that logic she should go to orientation. By that logic the stools and the covered mirrors were mechanisms too, just older ones, and she could take or leave them.

People came all afternoon. They brought casseroles and coffee cakes and plastic containers of things nobody would ever finish, and they said "I'm sorry" and then stood in the kitchen talking about parking. Around four the doorbell rang and it was Priya, from her calculus class, holding a paper bag with both hands like it might bolt. "I didn't know what to bring," Priya said. "My mom said food, but my mom also said don't ask questions, which was helpful."

"Food is right," Arianna said. "You can put it on the counter with the other twelve coffee cakes."

Priya set down the bag, which contained, it turned out, another coffee cake, and they both laughed at that, quietly, and then Priya sat down next to her on the couch and didn't say anything for a while, which Arianna understood was the correct thing, though she hadn't known it was correct until someone did it.

Her grandfather came out of the kitchen eventually and lowered himself onto a stool and told a story about Grandmother insisting on renting the same lake cabin eleven summers in a row, and how he had tried to extenuate the expense with a spreadsheet, and how she had looked at the spreadsheet and then at him and said, "Some things you don't get to make smaller." Everyone in the room nodded, and Arianna felt something shift in her chest that she did not want to examine yet, because examining things was how she made them smaller, and maybe that was the point of the stools, of sitting low, of seven whole days in a house with the mirrors covered: you didn't get to make it smaller, you had to sit inside the actual size of it.

That night she asked her uncle to drive her to the train station in the morning. She had reasoned it through, or told herself she had, but at the station she stood on the platform with her ticket in her hand and watched the board flip from ON TIME to DELAYED, and then to DELAYED again, forty minutes, and she thought about her grandfather alone on his stool while the house emptied out, and she thought about Grandmother's spreadsheet, and she walked back to the parking lot before the train came. Her uncle raised an eyebrow. "Changed your mind," she said, and he drove her back without comment, which was its own kind of mercy.

On day seven, the last day, Priya came by again with a bag of clementines because she'd decided coffee cakes were a failed genre. The house was loud with cousins and the smell of the brisket Aunt Renata had insisted on cooking even though everyone said they weren't hungry, and everyone ate it anyway. Somebody uncovered one mirror and left the others for later, and Arianna caught her reflection in the hallway, blurry and unfamiliar, older somehow, or maybe just less arranged. Her grandfather found her standing there.

"So," he said. "You missed your advising session. You'll have to make it up."

"I emailed them," she said. "I told them I was sitting shiva. Seven days, starts after the burial. The girl at the office said, 'What's shiva?' and I said, 'It means seven,' and she said, 'That's not an explanation,' and I said, 'I know.'"

Her grandfather laughed, a real one, the first since the funeral. "And what did you tell her instead?"

"That I'd explain everything Thursday," Arianna said, "when I'm back on campus." She peeled a clementine, split it, and handed him half through the doorway.

Elizabeth had forty minutes before her mother's headlights swept the parking lot, and the exam was at eight the next morning. She sat on the coping at the top of the quarter pipe with her review book open on her knees, working the same problem for the third time: two charged plates, a point between them, compute the field strength. The numbers kept sliding away from her, the way the park slid into shadow once the sun dropped behind the equipment shed.

Marcus wanted to film something before the light died entirely. He had a channel, ninety-three subscribers, and a plan involving his little brother's skateboard and a bucket of water he'd carried from the bathroom in a jaundiced old mop pail. "Five minutes," he said, holding up his phone sideways. "I need the drop test."

"Drop test," she repeated, not looking up.

He produced two hacky sacks from his hoodie pocket. "Dev says if you throw one out sideways and just let go of the other one, the thrown one takes longer to land. Dev owes me a dollar if he's wrong."

"They hit at the same time," Elizabeth said, and then heard herself say it, and frowned at the sentence as though someone else had left it on her page. She knew it the way she knew her own locker combination, without being able to say when she'd learned it.

"Prove it." Dev had come up the ramp without his board, chewing a straw, and there was the dollar, held out flat between two fingers like a card trick. Marcus set his phone on the ledge, propped against a skate left on its side, and started recording.

They used the top of the concrete picnic table, which put the drop at roughly waist height. Marcus held one hacky sack at the table's edge and Dev crouched with his arm extended, the second sack in his hand, ready to fling it horizontally the instant Marcus let his fall. Elizabeth stood back by the fun box with her book still open, half of her attention on the variable E and half on the two boys arranging themselves in the fading light.

"Listen for the sounds," Dev said. "Both hits. One-two and you win, one and then a gap and I win."

They ran it three times. The first was botched, Dev threw early; the second was clean, two taps so close together they overlapped into a single knock against the concrete; the third, Marcus insisted on doing himself, holding both sacks, dropping one straight down while flicking the other sideways over the table's edge, and again the taps landed together, a doubled click like a single syllable. Dev paid the dollar without ceremony, folding it into Marcus's palm and immediately demanding a rematch, best of five, different table.

Elizabeth looked down at her problem and felt the two halves of her evening titrate into each other, the memorized fact and the empty grid on her page, until the concentration of one in the other changed the whole thing. Between the plates, the field was what it was at the point; it did not care how the charge had gotten there, only where it was, and her mistake had been carrying a distance from the wrong side of the diagram. She erased two lines and rewrote them, and the answer arrived with the flat certainty of those two overlapping taps.

She checked her phone. Twelve minutes before her mother. Marcus was still filming, Dev was out another dollar, and the light had gone copper along the coping. She closed the book without checking the answer again, because she was done being jaundiced about it, done treating her own work like it came from antiquity, some dead relic she was obliged to memorize rather than something she had watched happen on a picnic table.

"Hey," Marcus called, phone still sideways. "That thing you said. Same time, no matter what. Put it in the video?"

She zipped her bag. "If you split the dollar."

"Two-fifty each," Dev said, already counting.

Behind them, the sprinklers hissed on across the soccer field, and her mother's headlights turned in at the gate.

The cultural center smelled of cempasúchil before Jackson even reached the door, the orange marigolds crowded in buckets along the entryway, their scent thick enough to lean on. His mother carried the framed photograph wrapped in a dish towel, the way she carried things she considered breakable in more than the obvious sense. His grandfather had been gone since March, and tonight, the first of November, the family would set his picture on the ofrenda for the first time.

Inside, the hall had been transformed by folding tables draped in white and purple paper, each one holding somebody's dead. Jackson moved past altars crowded with sugar skulls and clay dishes and old letters, trying not to read too closely, though it was hard not to. A woman was arranging pan de muerto in a careful spiral. Two kids argued over whose grandmother's candles were crooked.

"Where do you want him?" his mother asked. She had chosen a spot near the window, where the afternoon light came in slanted and gold. The family altar, she explained to his younger cousin, was called an ofrenda, and theirs would be modest this year because they were still learning. His aunt unpacked a bag of tangerines and set them out in a fan, because Grandfather had eaten tangerines every winter of his life, peeling them in one unbroken ribbon and dropping the peel into his shirt pocket like a man saving it for later.

Jackson had brought his own offering, and it was the wrong one, and he knew it was the wrong one before he even took it out of his backpack. A bottle of hot sauce, the ghost pepper kind he and his grandfather had dared each other over two summers ago, the kind that had catalyzed a whole evening of gasping and milk-drinking and laughing until his grandfather had to sit down on the porch step. He had thought of it in the car and been proud of it. Now, next to the tangerines and the photograph and the crossed marillas of orange flowers, it looked like a joke at a funeral.

"No," he said out loud, mostly to himself, and put the bottle back in the bag.

His aunt noticed. She was the one in the family who kept the calendar of obligations, who knew whose birthday fell on which saint's day, who could recite the chronology of every divorce and reconciliation without malice. She looked at the backpack, then at his face, and did not ask what was in it. Instead she picked up a marigold from the pile of stems and held it out.

"You know why these, mijo?" she asked. "The color and the smell. They guide the souls home. That's what my mother told me, for the first and second of November, when the dead come back." She was not lecturing; she was handing him a flower while she said it, already turning back to straighten the photograph so that his grandfather's eyes faced the room. "You have to make a path."

Jackson knelt and began laying the stems. His mother wanted them in a vase; his aunt wanted them scattered from the door to the table, so the scent would lead someone in. He did both, a small cluster at the base of the ofrenda and then a loose line of petals across the floor, unsure which version his grandfather would have found less ridiculous. Probably he would have found both ridiculous, and then he would have eaten a tangerine and stayed anyway, because he had never once left a room his wife had decorated while she was still standing in it.

Later, when the hall had filled and a small band was tuning guitars near the stage, Jackson took the hot sauce bottle back out. He set it beside the tangerines, cap off, the way you'd leave a drink for someone expected. A girl about his age stopped at their table, looked at the photograph, looked at the bottle, and smiled like she understood something. He didn't ask her what. He was still working out what he himself understood, whether he believed any of it literally, whether belief was even the right instrument for a task like this, or whether laying a scented path for a dead man was simply a way of saying that the dead man was still, in some stubborn accounting, owed a place to arrive. His grandfather would have called the whole thing very epicurean, all this food left out for people who couldn't eat it, and then he would have taken a tangerine from the altar and eaten it himself, right there, winking.

The band started playing. Jackson's mother reached over and turned the photograph a quarter inch, toward the marigolds, toward the door.

Victor spread the two books across his grandfather's card table, one propped against the other like feuding relatives at a holiday dinner. Outside, the sprinkler ticked across the brown lawn of the retirement community, and the smell of his grandfather's coffee, half cocoa, half regret, drifted from the kitchen. The assignment was due in September, his first week at college: compare two historians' explanations of the Cold War and decide which the evidence actually supported. He had picked Gaddis and a revisionist named Kolko because they seemed to disagree about everything, and now, four days before deadline, he realized he could not even say what counted as evidence.

"Grandpa, who started the Cold War?" he called.

His grandfather shuffled in with two cups and set one down near Victor's elbow, on a coaster, always on a coaster. "The Soviets," he said. "Obviously. They wanted to subjugate Eastern Europe, and they did."

"That's what Gaddis says. Kind of. But Kolko says the United States wanted markets and used the atomic bomb as blackmail." Victor tapped the page where Kolko had called American policy economic expansion dressed up as defense. "So which is it?"

His grandfather lowered himself into the chair across the table. "I lived through part of it. Does that count as evidence?"

Victor considered this seriously, pencil hovering. "It counts as something. Kolko would call it a confounder. You were raised on one story, so your memory is shaped by the story." He regretted it immediately; it sounded like he was calling his grandfather brainwashed. But his grandfather only laughed, a dry creak like the screen door.

"Read me the part you're stuck on."

Victor read aloud, the bit where Gaddis argued that Stalin's ideology made confrontation unavoidable, and then the Kolko passage arguing that American leaders inflated the Soviet threat to justify their own ambitions. Both cited the same events. The Yalta conference, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin blockade. Same facts, opposite arrows.

"That's the thing about historians," his grandfather said. He turned his cup slowly on its coaster. "You know who Thiers was? Adolphe Thiers. There's a statue of him in Paris, or there was. I saw it on leave, back in the fifties." He squinted at the ceiling. "He ran France later. But before that, he wrote the History of the French Revolution. Published from 1823 to 1827, three volumes, while the memory was still warm. And in it he praised the moderates, men like Mirabeau and Lafayette, and condemned the radicals, especially Robespierre."

"So?"

"So he wasn't lying. He wasn't stupid. He was a moderate himself, writing about a revolution where moderates got eaten. His position was inside the book." His grandfather leaned forward, forearms on the table. "You're trying to find the historian with no position. There isn't one. The question is whether the position bends the evidence or the evidence bends the position."

Victor wrote that down, then crossed out "position bends evidence" because it sounded cleverer than he understood it to be. He pulled the books back and tried the thing he had been avoiding: testing each claim against something outside both books. The telegram from Moscow that Stalin sent about Berlin, which Kolko quoted partially and Gaddis quoted at greater length, and which, when Victor found the full text online in the room where his grandfather's dial-up wheezed like an asthmatic dog, said something neither historian had said it said. Not the opposite. Something murkier. Stalin had been conciliatory and threatening in the same paragraph, which refused to support either clean story.

He worked until the sprinkler stopped and the lawn went quiet. His grandfather watched the evening news with the sound low, glancing over now and then. Victor filled eleven pages of a legal pad, crossed out eight of them, and discovered that Gaddis held up better on Soviet actions in Eastern Europe and worse on American motives, which Gaddis treated as innocent where the record showed them mixed. Neither explanation proved tenable on its own. The honest paper, he realized, would say that.

At ten his grandfather brought in a plate of sandwiches and found Victor staring at the pad.

"Well?" his grandfather asked. "Who started it?"

"I don't know yet. Both of them, probably, in different ways, and I can't make the proportions exact." Victor rubbed his eyes. "Is that an acceptable answer for a college paper?"

His grandfather set down the plate and picked up the pad, reading Victor's scrawled margin note, the one that said: Thiers problem. Check who benefits from the telling.

"You know," his grandfather said, "that's the first honest thing anyone in this family has written about history." He put the pad down and tapped the sandwich plate. "Eat. You can't weigh the world on an empty stomach."

Victor took a sandwich and pulled the pad back toward him, writing at the top of a fresh page: unfinished.

The county library smelled of carpet cleaner and old paper, and by four o'clock the afternoon light came through the tall windows in long bars that Hunter kept walking through on his way between shelves. He had four books spread across a study table, two of them fat histories of the Cold War, one slim, and one his grandfather had pressed on him at dinner last Sunday, saying that a man named Gaddis had settled the whole question decades ago. The question, apparently, was whose fault the Cold War was, and Hunter's history teacher had asked the class to take one side by Friday, with evidence. Hunter did not want a side. He wanted the thing itself, whatever it was, the way you want to see the bottom of a pool before you jump.

The first historian, the one his grandfather liked, wrote as if the answer were obvious. Stalin wanted security and got paranoia, or wanted paranoia and got security; either way, the Soviet Union moved first and moved hard, and the West merely reacted. The second historian spread the blame thinner, almost elegantly, like butter taken too far and tearing the bread. Both of them cited the same events, which was what unsettled Hunter most. The same speeches, the same summits, bent to opposite purposes, as though the facts were wet clay and each writer had a different thumb.

His reverie broke when Priya dropped her bag on the other end of the table and started unpacking highlighters with the seriousness of a surgeon laying out instruments. She was in his class and had chosen the other side, the one that put more weight on American actions, and they had agreed, in a loose and wary way, to work in the same room without helping each other.

"Did you get to the Churchill thing," she said, not quite a question.

"There's a Churchill thing in both books."

"Both books quote the speech," Priya said. "But the historian I'm reading says it was in Missouri, and yours says it was in England. One of them is wrong, or they're both being sloppy." She slid her book across, and Hunter slid his back, and the two sentences sat there like witnesses giving slightly different addresses for the same house. One thing they agreed on: the year, 1946, and the month, March.

Hunter went to the reference desk, where a laminated card listed the databases, and then to a terminal in the corner whose fan rattled like a small animal in the wall. He typed the sentence he half remembered from the books, the one about the curtain. The database returned a transcript, and there it was: Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946. A small college town in the middle of the country, not London, not Westminster, nothing grand. He sat back. It should not have mattered so much, the where, but it did, because the British historian had placed the speech in the wrong country and then built half a paragraph on that imagined setting, calling it a homecoming delivered to a war-weary London crowd. Hunter wrote the details on an index card in his small, careful hand: Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946, the speech where Churchill said an iron curtain had descended across Europe. He underlined nothing. Underlining felt like taking sides.

He carried the card back to the table and set it between Priya's book and his own, neutral territory. "The one who got the venue wrong also got the argument wrong," he said. "Or maybe he wanted the argument and then found the venue." He was thinking out loud, and he could hear how unsure it sounded. The American historian, the one his grandfather called definitive, had used the speech the other way, as proof of a clear-eyed warning the West ignored at its peril. But if the same speech could serve both masters, then the speech was not proof of anything except that a former prime minister, putative prophet or retired politician depending on who you read, had been invited to a small college in Missouri and said something memorable. Hunter found that he did not know what it proved, and that not knowing felt like standing on a floor that was, at last, solid, because at least he could see it.

Priya turned the card over, as if the date might be printed twice with a correction on the back. "So I can't use my guy for this part," she said. "He quotes it right, but he quotes it the way you quote scripture, like the words did the work instead of the tanks."

"Mine does it too," Hunter said. "He just does it in the other direction." He pulled a fresh sheet of paper and ruled two columns, then a third narrow one down the middle, and labeled them. In the first column he wrote what the evidence actually showed, the things both historians had to admit. In the second he wrote what each claimed the evidence meant, side by side, so the claims could look at each other. The third column he left almost empty, and at the top he wrote one word: unsolved. He would turn that in on Friday, he decided, not as a failure but as the honest shape of the thing, and he would argue not for one side but for the difference between what happened and what the tellers of it wanted.

The lights over the stacks clicked to half brightness, the library's signal that evening had started without them. Priya capped her last highlighter and leaned over to read his columns. "You're going to get marked down for that middle one," she said.

"Probably," Hunter said, and slid the iron curtain card to the top of the page, where the facts could keep watch.

Jessica spread the print across the picnic table and pinned its corners with rocks from her mother's garden border. The Two Fridas looked up at her, two women seated hand in hand on a bench, one in a white European dress, one in a Tehuana dress the color of deep water. Her assignment sheet, folded twice in her back pocket, asked for a formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism, and it forbade biography, a rule she'd already read four times because it seemed to want something from her she couldn't yet name.

Her neighbor Marcus came through the gap in the fence without knocking, which was the arrangement between their houses. He carried a battered shoebox of seed packets, because what Marcus wanted that summer was a cutting garden along the fence line, dahlias and zinnias, something he could photograph and sell at the farmers market by August. He set the box down at the far end of the table, out of the painting's light, and asked what she was doing.

"Learning to critique a painting before Tuesday," Jessica said. "I have to talk about it for ten minutes and I've never done this before." She pointed at the two figures. "There's a heart in each of them, and the European one has cut a vein with surgical scissors, and the blood spills onto her white skirt in these deliberate red drops. I can describe that. What I can't do is say what it means without just telling the class a story about her life, and we're not allowed to lean on biography."

Marcus leaned over the print, careful of the rocks. He was quieter than usual, and Jessica suspected the seed money was thinner than he'd admitted, but she didn't ask. Instead she made herself begin the exercise her teacher had suggested, naming what she actually saw. The left Frida sat slightly forward, the right Frida slightly back, and the stormy sky behind them was divided, she noticed, by nothing at all; the horizon line cut across both women equally, holding them in one field of paint. The two hearts were joined by a thin red thread, held at its midpoint by the small Frida's hand.

"So the composition says they're one person," she said slowly, "even while the colour says they're opposites. Warm side, cold side. But the thread is the same red as the blood, so the connection is also the wound." Marcus said that was the kind of sentence you could photograph, meaning it as a compliment, and she wrote it down.

Then he tapped the bottom corner of the print. "What's this number?" Beside a name she couldn't pronounce and a museum she'd never visited, the small caption read 1939. Jessica turned to her laptop, which she'd carried out on a cutting board like a tray, and looked up the date properly, because until that moment she had been treating the painting as timeless, a self-portrait of a divided self floating outside history. What she found stopped her with her hand still on the trackpad. Kahlo had painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera, and they had remarried the following year.

"That changes the blood," Jessica said. "I was going to call it a painting about being two people, and I still think it is, but it's also about a specific year. The cut vein, the storm, the white dress like a wedding dress that's also a shroud. She painted the wound while it was open, and then a year later she went back." She heard how it sounded and corrected herself. "I don't know that she went back because of the painting. I only know the dates. I have to be careful not to build a story the paint doesn't support."

Marcus had begun sorting his seed packets into rows while she talked, and now he interposed a jalapeno envelope between two flower packets with a faint frown. "I like it better your first way," he said, a little querulous, the way he got when his grandfather criticized the garden plan. "Just two selves, one heart. The date stuff makes it about a man." Jessica considered that. It was a fair objection. She had spent an hour on the formal analysis precisely to avoid reducing the work to gossip, and now the date threatened to drag Diego into every drop of red paint.

"That's the thing, though," she said. "It can be both. The formal stuff, the split composition, the colour opposition, the thread, that's how she made the feeling visible. The date tells me the feeling had a history, that it wasn't some abstract condition she invented for the canvas. If I only do the first part it's solipsism, like the painting exists in a sealed room. If I only do the second part I'm just reading her diary out loud." She pulled the assignment sheet from her pocket and smoothed it flat beside the print. "Maybe the rule against biography is really a rule against using biography instead of looking. Maybe I can use it after I've looked."

Marcus shrugged, satisfied or at least willing to be, and went to fill the watering can. Jessica sat down on the bench beside the table and read her own notes over once, then crossed out the sentence about opposites and rewrote it in the margin in small letters: the colour divides them, the thread insists they are one. She looked up at the actual sky over the actual fence, which was clear and ordinary and going gold at the edge, and then back down at the painted one, still stormy after all these years, and she left both sentences where they were. Behind her, water hissed into the dry soil by the fence, and Marcus called out, "If these come up, you get the first bloom."

The registration page asked for her date of birth before it asked for anything else, which Kaylee decided was either sensible or insulting, depending on how she felt about being reduced to three numbers before being asked her name. She typed it in anyway. February 14, 2007. "Valentine's baby," her grandmother liked to announce to strangers, as though it were a credential.

"You're actually doing it," her brother Danny said from the doorway, holding a bowl of cereal he had clearly resuscitated from some earlier hour, the milk gone grey at the edges.

"I'm registering. It's not the vote yet." She kept her eyes on the screen. "The vote is in October."

"Same thing." He leaned over her shoulder, breathing cereal fumes onto the keyboard. "Who are you voting for?"

"I don't know. That's the entire point of registering now, so I have time to figure it out." She angled her body between him and the monitor, a move she had perfected around age nine and never abandoned.

When the confirmation screen appeared, it informed her that her voter information card would arrive by mail, and beneath that, in small print, it welcomed her as one of Canada's newest electors. She sat back. Something about the phrase got her. Newest electors, plural, as though a whole cohort of people born in early 2007 were arriving at the same door at the same moment, all of them eighteen and none of them sure of anything.

She texted her grandfather, who answered everything, usually at length. Do you know how long 18 year olds could vote in Canada? His reply came in pieces: a thumbs up, then "since 1970," then "before that you had to be 21," then a voice memo she didn't open. Fifty-five years, she thought. Her mother had been born in 1972, into a country where an eighteen-year-old could vote but where most eighteen-year-olds apparently didn't, or didn't in the numbers that made anyone nervous. Kaylee tried to imagine her grandfather at twenty, ineligible, reading about an election he couldn't touch. She couldn't picture him young. She could barely picture him without a lawn to complain about.

At dinner, her mother asked how the registration had gone, and Kaylee mentioned the 1970 thing, and Danny, predictably, said, "That's it? That's basically yesterday."

"That's before Mom was born," Kaylee said.

"Basically yesterday," Danny said again, with the authority of someone who had recently learned that history existed.

"1970," her mother said, tasting the year. "People my age were the first babies of it. The first eighteen-year-olds who could vote." She passed the potatoes. "My father says he voted for the first time in 1972 and it was the most important thing he ever did, and also that he can't remember who he voted for, which I find very honest."

Later, alone in her room, Kaylee made a list. Not of candidates, but of what she actually wanted, which kept sliding sideways into what she thought she should want, and what her grandfather wanted, and what a viral post had wanted earlier that week before fact-checkers dismantled it for what her civics teacher would have called, with evident relish, chicanery. The post had claimed a candidate had said something she demonstrably hadn't; the correction reached one-tenth as many people. Kaylee had almost believed it for an afternoon. She wasn't proud of the afternoon.

Her grandfather's voice memo, when she finally played it, was four minutes long and mostly tangential, involving a story about a snowstorm and a polling station in a church basement, and then, near the end, his voice dropped into the register he used for things that mattered. "The vote isn't a verdict on who you are," he said. "It's just the entry fee. You pay it so you're inside the room where the arguing happens." Kaylee played it twice, then opened her notes app and wrote inside the room, which she suspected she would misinterpret later, the way she was already misinterpreting half of what she'd ever been told.

In October, the card came in the mail, her name printed in a font that seemed designed to inspire confidence in institutions. She carried it to the kitchen table, where Danny grabbed it and held it up like a trophy. "One vote," he said. "Gonna cancel out exactly one annoying person somewhere. Statistically, probably a guy named Gary."

"It doesn't work like that," Kaylee said.

"It absolutely works like that. Ask Gary."

She took the card back and set it on the counter, squared with the edge, where it stayed all week, face up, her name and her polling station and the date, saying nothing definitive about anything. On election night she would sit right here with her laptop open, but that was a problem for a future Kaylee. For now she opened the fridge, considered the leftovers, and called out, "Danny, is this soup still good or are we going to resuscitate it?"

The black box theatre smelled of dust and old paint, and Alexandra had claimed it for every free period of the past week. Her one-act, which she had also written, was scheduled for the spring showcase, and between now and then she had two actors, a bench, and the growing suspicion that she did not know what she was doing. She had watched Mr. Delgado direct the fall musical from the back of the house, taking notes on how he moved bodies through space, and she had assumed the knowledge would transfer. It did not. On Tuesday she had told Marcus to cross downstage left and he had walked into a chair.

The problem, she decided by Thursday, was that she was moving her actors the way she moved words on a page, one at a time, wherever they seemed to fit. At lunch she spread her script across a cafeteria table, and Priya from her drama class sat down across from her with a napkin and a pen. Priya had gone to drama camp the summer before and talked about it the way other people talked about foreign countries.

"You're trying to block without knowing where your climax is," Priya said. She drew a triangle on the napkin, then bisected it with a rising and falling line. "Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid, exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution. In his book on drama technique. Eighteen sixty-three."

"That old?" Alexandra said.

"Older than the building." Priya tapped a point near the top of the triangle. "Your climax lives here. Find it first, then block toward it."

Alexandra studied the napkin. Her play was about two sisters who meet at a riverbank to divide their dead mother's belongings, and she had written eleven pages of quiet conversation because quiet was what she trusted. She found the moment where the older sister reveals she had already sold the mother's house weeks before, and marked it. Then she drew her own pyramid in the margin of the script, a small neat slope, and set the reveal at the peak. Underneath she wrote: everything before must rise toward this. It was a mechanical thing to do to something she had made out of feeling, and she did it anyway.

That afternoon she ran the scene like an experiment. She placed the bench upstage right, near the painted backdrop of the riparian shoreline she'd begged the art class to make, reeds and a strip of water. The sisters began far apart, one at each edge of the playing space, and Alexandra blocked them moving inward along the rising action, a step closer each time a secret surfaced, so that by the time the house was sold they were nearly touching. Then, in the falling action, she sent them apart again, not to where they had started but to a middle distance, close enough to speak, too far to touch. It worked. She could feel it working, the geometry doing something the words alone had not.

Except that Marcus, who played the younger sister's silent boyfriend for all of six lines, kept watching from the doorway, and on Friday he finally said what his face had been saying for two days. "They're moving like chess pieces. It's clean. It's dead."

She wanted to defend the pyramid. She wanted to say that structure was not the enemy of feeling, that a river needs banks or it's just a flood. But she had also seen it herself, the moment in Wednesday's run when Nadia, playing the older sister, abandoned her mark to pick up a scarf that had slipped from the props box, and the small unscripted gesture had been the most alive second of the entire rehearsal. Alexandra had said nothing about it at the time. She had underlined the mark in her script instead.

She spent the weekend trying to metabolize the contradiction. On Saturday she walked the actual creek path behind her house, the one the play's riverbank was borrowed from, and found she could not hold both ideas in her head at once. Freytag's pyramid was true; the sisters' slow approach and withdrawal was the best thing she had made. Marcus was also true; the approach was legible as approach, it looked planned, and looking planned was a kind of lie. Two true things, refusing to fit.

On Monday she ran the scene a third way, which was not a compromise so much as a surrender she had thought her way into. She kept the pyramid as the floor plan, the deep map, the rise and the peak and the fall, and she told her actors what it was. "The shape's mine," she said. "The steps are yours. Break the marks whenever the moment asks you to. I'll fix the lights around whatever you do." Nadia grinned. Marcus stopped leaning in the doorway.

The run that followed was rougher and better. Nadia picked up the scarf again, this time on purpose, and carried it to the top of the rising action instead of her assigned mark, and Alexandra watched the reveal land in a place she had never planned, three feet from where the pyramid said it should be, and it was still, unmistakably, the climax. The shape held. The actors were not inside the shape; they were leaning against it, pushing at it, and the pushing was what made it visible.

Afterward Priya came to watch the last ten minutes and sat with the napkin pyramid folded in her pocket. "So which one won?" she asked in the aisle, meaning structure or freedom, and Alexandra found she could not say, could only say that she had stopped needing them to fight. There was no rapprochement exactly, no tidy treaty; there was a truce she re-negotiated at every rehearsal, and some nights the actors would keep every mark and the scene would be cold, and some nights they would wander and she would lose the ending in the reeds, and both failures taught her something she could not yet name.

She turned back to the stage, where Nadia was still holding the scarf, standing in her wrong place, exactly right.

"From the top," Alexandra said. "And this time, Nadia, take your time coming in."

Hunter got the job on a Tuesday, at Ray's Family Market, four blocks from his house. Mr. Kessler, the owner, wrote $7.25 on a yellow sticky note and slid it across the counter. "That's starting pay," he said. "Bagging, carts, stock on Sundays. You can start Thursday." Hunter said thank you and put the note in his pocket. It stayed there through dinner, through the dishes, through the game he half-watched with his father, who only said, "A job's a job," when Hunter mentioned the number.

Dez lived two streets over and had also just gotten a job, at a supermarket in Fairmont, across the river. Fairmont was in a different state, twenty minutes by bridge, and Dez's cousin worked there and had gotten him in. On Saturday they sat on the tailgate of Dez's brother's truck in the driveway, phones out, comparing their first paychecks on the banking app.

"Twelve ten," Dez said, turning his screen around.

Hunter looked at his own deposit. Seven twenty-five times twenty-six hours. He did it twice, as though the app might have dropped something. "Same job," he said. "Same everything. You bag, I bag."

"Welcome to Fairmont," Dez said, grinning, but Hunter wasn't grinning, and after a minute Dez wasn't either.

They argued about it the way they argued about everything, which meant they didn't. Dez said the answer was obvious: cross the bridge, apply at his store, stop working for a man paying 2009 prices. Hunter said his mother knew Mr. Kessler, and the store was four blocks away, and he didn't have a car. Dez said his brother could drive him. Hunter said his brother already did enough driving him places. The argument reached the detente their arguments always reached, both of them on the tailgate, neither moving, and then Dez's brother came out and told them to quit sitting on his truck.

That night Hunter looked it up himself. He had planned to ask his economics teacher, but school was out, and anyway he didn't like asking people things when he could find them. He found a government page, plain white, small text, and read it twice to be sure. "The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009," he said out loud, alone in his room, to hear it in a voice. Below that, the page said many states and cities set a higher minimum. He clicked the map. His state was gray, the federal number. Across the river, Fairmont's state was a darker shade.

He sat with that for a while. The bridge was twenty minutes. His mother had gotten him the interview at Ray's by mentioning his name to Mr. Kessler at church, and she'd been pleased in a quiet way he didn't want to undo. But twenty-six hours at $7.25 was $188.50, and the same twenty-six hours across the river was $314.60, and he was trying to save for books in the fall, the fall being college, which was now eight weeks away and costing more every time he thought about it.

He thought about Mr. Kessler, too, who was saturnine at the register but had once driven Hunter's mother home when her car wouldn't start, and who presumably hadn't raised the wage because, as far as Hunter could tell, he didn't have to. Hunter tried to hold both of these at once: that Kessler was decent in the ways he was decent, and that decency and the number on the sticky note were separate things. He couldn't get them to fit together cleanly, and he decided that might be fine.

On Sunday, Hunter bagged groceries for four hours. Around noon a woman came through with two small kids and WIC checks, and the register rejected one of the items, a specific cereal, and she stood there while Kessler voided things and the line built behind her. She didn't beseech anyone, didn't explain herself, just swapped the box for the right one and kept her eyes on the belt. Hunter bagged the new box. He'd been there four hours and his feet already hurt, and he kept doing the math in his head anyway, multiplying the ache by the hours by the rate.

At the end of his shift, he asked Kessler if he could talk to him for a second. Kessler came out from behind the register, arms folded, waiting, and Hunter said he'd gotten another offer across the river and wanted to know if there was any room on the rate. Kessler looked at him for a long moment, then at the schedule taped by the time clock.

"You start college in the fall," Kessler said. It wasn't a question. "You'll leave anyway."

"August eighteenth," Hunter said.

Kessler unfolded his arms and rubbed his jaw. "I can do eight. That's what I can do." He said it flatly, like a price on a receipt, and Hunter understood it was the ceiling and that there was no ceremony attached to it. He also understood, standing there, that eight was not twelve-ten, and that a man across a bridge he'd never crossed was willing to pay him five dollars more an hour for the same work, and that neither of those facts made Kessler a liar, exactly.

He said he'd think about it, and walked home in the heat with the sun going down behind Ray's sign. When he got to the driveway, Dez was sitting on the front steps of Hunter's house, phone in hand, screen already loaded to the Fairmont supermarket's application page, turned toward the street like an offering. "You can put my cousin down as a referral," Dez said. "Line three."

Annabelle had five days to learn to argue about carbon taxes for five minutes in French, and her grandmother's kitchen table had become the debate hall. The table was maple, older than her mother, and it smelled faintly of the clove cigarettes her grandfather had given up a decade before he died. Her grandmother set down two cups of tisane and slid into the chair opposite her, palms flat on the wood like a judge about to call a session to order.

"Encore," her grandmother said. "Dès le début."

Annabelle began, and fell apart almost immediately. The word for tax escaped her the way a cat slips under a fence, present one moment and gone the next. She stopped. In the silence she could hear the refrigerator ticking, and behind it the small humiliation of a girl who had won her school's English debate finals in the spring and now could not produce a single noun.

Her grandmother did not correct her. She folded her hands and waited, which was somehow worse.

"I don't have it," Annabelle said in English. "The word. La, the thing the government makes people pay, for carbon." She gestured, drawing a rectangle in the air, then pointing at the window toward the invisible government.

"Ah." Her grandmother tapped her own temple once. "C'est de la circonlocution. When you cannot find a word, you describe it instead of stopping. It keeps you talking. A speaker who talks around a missing word, we say she uses circumlocution. It is a real strategy, not cheating."

"It sounds like drowning politely."

"It sounds like a debater," her grandmother said. "The judges cannot mark you down for a word they never noticed was missing."

So Annabelle tried again. She acclimated to the rhythm of it slowly, the way she had once acclimated to the cold water of the lake at her aunt's cabin, by degrees and without dignity. When "pollution" vanished, she said "the smoke that cities breathe." When "economy" deserted her, she said "the money that moves between everyone" and kept going, and her grandmother lifted one eyebrow a millimeter, which in her language was applause.

The problem was not only vocabulary. The problem was that Annabelle did not actually know what she believed about a carbon tax. Her debate coach had assigned her the opposing side, the bellicose one, the side that attacks, and she was good at attacking. But her grandmother, she had learned over the summer, had worked thirty years as a hospital administrator and thought about policy the way a gardener thinks about weather, with patience and resentment in equal measure. Over dinner on the second night her grandmother had said, in English, "The tax works only if poor families get the rebate back. Otherwise it is just a fine for being born without money." Annabelle had argued back, coach-style, listing the studies, and her grandmother had waved her off and gone to wash the lettuce.

On the fourth day, Annabelle stood at the sink drying dishes while her grandmother washed them, and tried out a position in French, haltingly, talking around every third word. She said that the tax could be a good tool and also a cruel one, that it depended on the rebate, that she would defend the policy only with that condition attached. The water ran. Her grandmother handed her a wet plate and did not say anything for a long time.

"That is not what your coach asked you to argue," she said finally.

"I know. I'm supposed to destroy the tax, not fix it."

"Then you must decide whether you are a person who argues what she is told, or a person who argues what she has decided." Her grandmother rinsed a fork and set it in the rack with great care, as if setting down the question itself. "Both are honest. Only one is yours."

Annabelle did not sleep well that night. She lay in the guest room under a quilt pieced from her grandfather's old shirts and rehearsed both speeches against the ceiling. The attack speech was easier and stronger; it had statistics in it like flares, and it would win. The other speech had a hole in the middle where her certainty should have been. She could admit, in it, that she did not know whether the rebate would actually reach the families who needed it, that this was the part the studies disagreed about, that she was arguing for a version of the tax that might not exist yet. That was either honesty or weakness, and lying awake she could not tell which, and by morning she still could not.

The day of the trial run, her grandmother cleared the table, set the kitchen timer to five minutes, and stood at the end of the room with her reading glasses pushed up into her hair. Annabelle took a breath and began in French, slow and then steadier, the attack rising in her throat and the other argument rising underneath it. Halfway through, the word for "rebate" abandoned her completely, and she did not stop. "The money," she said, in French, "that the government gives back, to the families, the poor ones, so the tax does not fall only on them," and her grandmother's mouth curved, and the timer ticked on.

"Time," her grandmother said, when it rang. She took off her glasses, looked at her granddaughter across the maple table, and asked, "Which speech was that?"

Annabelle was still catching her breath. "Both," she said. "I don't know yet if that's allowed."

Her grandmother turned the timer over in her hands, considering it, then wound it again and set it back to five. "Then tell me the parts you are still unsure of," she said. "Start now."

The assignment was due at eleven fifty-nine, and Sienna had until then to submit a Book class with private fields, getter methods, and a test file proving it all worked. She'd brought her laptop to Grandma Ruth's house because her own internet was down and Mom had said a change of scenery would do her good. Now she sat at the kitchen table between a bowl of walnuts and a jigsaw puzzle missing its edge pieces, watching forty red compiler errors crawl up her screen like ants finding spilled sugar.

"Still fighting with it?" Grandma asked, setting down two mugs of tea. She had her diurnal rituals so firmly fixed that Sienna could have set a clock by them: tea at four, crossword at four-thirty, the porch from five until the light failed. Today the schedule made a kind of cage around the deadline, and Sienna found it oddly steadying, the way the world kept its ordinary shape while her code refused to.

"Forty errors," Sienna said. "All the same error, which is somehow worse."

She scrolled to the first one. Her test file had a line that said assertEquals("Beloved", b.title) and the compiler complained it couldn't see title, that the field was private. She'd written private String title in her Book class herself, the way the assignment sheet told her to, without really pausing over what the word committed her to. Apparently it committed her to a lot. She tried a different line, tried to set b.title directly, and got the same complaint. She looked at the two files side by side, the test and the class, and began to understand what she'd built: a field marked private could be read or changed only by code inside the same class. Her test file was a different class. It lived outside the wall, knocking.

"So the wall is real," she said aloud.

"Wall?" Grandma settled into the chair across from her with the crossword and a pencil she refused to sharpen.

"Nothing. Talking to my program." But she kept turning it over, because she'd started the afternoon with two ideas that now refused to sit together. One was that private was a hassle, a rule from the assignment sheet designed to trip people up. The other, older one, came from Grandpa's old shed talk about how a well-made thing keeps its insides where you can't reach them, how you don't poke the wiring in a radio, you turn the knob. She'd half-listened back then. Now she introspected, as her English teacher would say, on which idea was actually hers, and found the second one had more weight. If anyone could scribble on the fields from anywhere, the class couldn't promise anything about its own contents. The wall wasn't a hassle. It was the promise.

The trouble was practical: her test still couldn't read anything. She stared at the assignment sheet again and found the phrase she'd skimmed past, getter methods, and then a line near the bottom: "your test should call public methods only." She'd been so sure the test was the important file that she'd treated the class like paperwork. She typed public String getTitle() into Book, returned the field, and changed her test line to assertEquals("Beloved", b.getTitle()). The red error there vanished. She added getters for author and pages, fixed each test line, and watched the errors fall from forty to eleven to three to none.

Grandpa came in from the porch at some point and read over her shoulder, which he did without apology. "Forty mistakes this morning," he said. "How many now?"

"Zero. It runs." She hit the test button and the little green bar filled, and she felt a ridiculous pride in it, a bar the width of her thumb.

"Runs correctly?"

"Runs and passes." She hesitated, because honesty seemed owed to the green bar. "Mostly I'm trusting it. I tested three things. There are probably ways it breaks that I haven't thought of, and I won't know which until they happen." It was a travesty to call a program finished just because a deadline said so, but it was also eleven fifteen, and she submitted anyway, watched the confirmation page load, and closed the laptop on a screen still showing the green.

Grandpa put a walnut half on the table in front of her like a medal. "So what did you build, exactly?"

"A class that keeps its own secrets," she said, "and decides what to tell."

Grandma looked up from the crossword. "I'd like to meet her."

The kitchen table had been cleared of everything except the launcher, a meter stick, a roll of masking tape, and a bag of marbles that Vanessa's little brother kept trying to steal. The regional engineering fair was in forty hours, and the fair's judges awarded points for hitting a target eleven meters away with a projectile fired at a set angle. Every other team would bring a launcher. Only the teams that could explain their own numbers would advance.

Vanessa had spent the evening doing what her textbook demanded: dichotomize the motion, treat the horizontal and vertical components as separate problems linked only by time. The marble left the barrel at eight meters per second, tilted at forty degrees, so the horizontal piece was a steady 6.13 meters per second and the vertical piece started at 5.14, rose, decelerated, fell. She worked the vertical equation for the time of flight, carried that time across to the horizontal equation, and got a range of just over five meters on paper. Then she set the launcher on the kitchen tile, aligned it with the tape line she had stuck to the floor, and fired.

The marble hit the floor at four and a half meters. She measured it twice. She fired again, and again, and marked each landing spot with a small pencil tick on a strip of painter's tape, because her mother had already objected to pencil marks on the tile. Four ticks clustered tightly, all short of the calculation, all short by roughly the same margin. She checked her arithmetic, found nothing, and checked it again with her calculator upside down for no reason she could defend.

Her brother Marcus came in for a snack at nine and stood over the tape marks with a plastic cup of apple juice. "You missed."

"I didn't miss. There's no target yet. It landed short of where the math says it should land."

"Then the math is wrong."

"The math is not wrong." She said it with more force than she felt, and he shrugged and went to the living room, where her mother was watching something with the volume low. Vanessa sat back down. The launcher was a project she had inherited in a sense: her physics teacher had announced the fair three weeks ago, and her lab partner, Priya, had done the building while Vanessa had done the deriving. Priya was asleep by now, or studying for the calc exam they both had on Monday, and Vanessa had agreed to handle the trajectory model. The agreement had seemed fair at the time. Now the model and the machine were telling different stories, and she had until Saturday morning to reconcile them.

She tried a different angle, thirty-five degrees, recalculated, refired. Short again, by a comparable fraction. She tried the marble her father had brought home from a trade show, slightly lighter than the others, and it landed shorter still. At ten thirty she drew the parabola from her equations on graph paper, then plotted her four tick marks below the point where the parabola met the floor, and stared at the gap between the curve and the dots. In class, the problems always ended with the marble landing exactly on the parabola, because the problems were about the parabola. The textbook had a footnote she half remembered, something she had skipped because footnotes were a disincentive to finishing problem sets on time. She got the book from her backpack and found it, small type at the bottom of the page: the calculations ignored air resistance, and real projectiles did not.

She read the sentence three times. The problems in the book assumed the marble flew through nothing, through a vacuum, and her kitchen was full of air. The gap on her graph was not an error in her algebra. It was the difference between the clean world of the equations and the tiled, air-filled world where the marbles actually flew. A thrown or launched ball would land shorter than the calculation predicted, because the calculation had never promised anything about air.

Her mother appeared in the doorway in her robe, dour about the hour but holding a mug of tea, which she set down beside the graph paper without comment. Vanessa explained anyway, fast, pointing at the parabola and then at the tick marks. "The math assumes no air. The air is real. So it lands short, every time, by about this much."

"So add the this much."

"It's not a constant this much. It changes with the speed and the angle and probably the marble." Vanessa looked at the ticks again. "I can't derive that. Nobody in our class can derive that. There's a whole drag equation and it's not in our book."

"Then what will you tell the judges?"

Vanessa turned to a fresh page. She could not make the model match the machine exactly, but she could make the model honest. She would present the clean calculation, then present her measured landings, then state the difference plainly: air resistance slows real projectiles, so a real ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts. She would show the graph with the parabola and the ticks and let the judges see the gap. If they asked why the gap had the size it had, she would say she didn't know yet, and that this was the next problem. Some teams would hide the discrepancy or fudge the launch angle to compensate. She wrote a note to adjust the launcher's angle by trial until the marble covered eleven meters, then wrote a second note beside it: do not pretend the adjustment is part of the theory.

She texted Priya a photo of the graph, the parabola and the four ticks, with the message: we land short of the math, it's the air, I'll explain on the bus. Priya's reply came as a single question mark, then, a minute later: ok good, I knew the launcher wasn't crooked.

Vanessa fired the last marble of the night at forty degrees and watched it thump down short of the tick cluster, half a tile's width short of the rest, and she picked it up and turned it under the kitchen light looking for the reason. She set it aside in its own spot on the counter, labeled with a torn piece of tape, and turned off the light over the table.

"How late are you planning to do this?" her mother asked from the hallway.

"Until Saturday," Vanessa said, and clicked the launcher empty to check the spring.

I am not a competitive person, which is why I let Dara talk me into the race in the first place. That's what I told myself on the walk to the coding club, the January dark pressing against the classroom windows when I got there, and it was almost true. Really I wanted to lose. Losing to Dara in front of people would prove something I needed proven: that I was here to learn, not to win, and a person like that could afford to lose.

Mr. Okafor's room still had the antiquated desktops along the back wall, the ones nobody used since the laptops cart arrived, but the club met here anyway because it was the only room with the good whiteboards. I claimed a seat near the middle and opened my laptop on a half-finished file called WordList.java. Dara dropped into the chair beside me and spun a marker like a baton.

"New project," she said. "Dictionary lookup. Whoever finds a target word in the club's word list faster wins. I'll go front to back. You do your weird halving thing."

"It's not weird. It's called binary search." That was the whole of my authority on the subject, a name and a rumor.

"Fine," she said. "I'll do it the normal way."

Theo, who kept the club's data files on a drive shaped like a rubber duck, announced that the list had a million entries, sorted, and he proposed to commandeer the projector so everyone could watch our screens magnified and merciless. A million sounded infinite to me. I imagined the evening ending with Dara somewhere in the C's and me apologizing.

But first, homework review. Mr. Okafor had asked us to build a Java class with private fields and getter methods, and to test it, and I had done this at my kitchen table with a confusion I hadn't admitted to anyone. The confusion was this: why hide the data? If the whole point of a WordEntry class was to hand out its word and its definition, why wrap them in private and make callers go through getWord() like a customs gate? It seemed ceremonial. It seemed like something invented to give tests something to check.

My test file was a small embarrassment. I had written one test that constructed an entry and one that didn't. "That's not testing," Theo said, leaning over, "that's attendance." So I wrote a real one: build an entry, call getWord(), assert it equaled what I'd put in, try to change the field directly and watch the compiler refuse. The refusal was the interesting part. I had expected to resent it and instead felt something closer to relief, the way you feel when a railing turns out to be solid. Dara, whose own class had public fields everywhere, watched my error message scroll up and frowned at it like it had insulted her family.

"Private just means you have to knock," I said, and immediately worried it sounded smug.

"It means extra typing," Dara said, but she opened her file and started changing her fields to private anyway, jaw set, typing getters with the aggression of someone losing an argument she'd started.

Then the race. Theo loaded the million-entry list into both our programs and picked the target: "perspicacity." He wrote it on the whiteboard in his terrible handwriting so we wouldn't claim spelling errors later. Dara started at index zero, her counter ticking on the big screen, one, two, three, a march into a desert. I halved. Take the middle of the list, compare, throw away half the world, take the middle of what's left. The screen made it look casual, my index leaping like a skipped stone, and my counter climbed in a way I didn't believe: single digits, then twelve, then it stopped.

Seventeen.

Dara was at forty thousand and somewhere deep in the B's. She kept going for a while out of dignity, then closed the lid of her laptop, which on the projector looked like a curtain falling.

"Twenty," Theo said, reading off something on his own screen. "Halving a million twenty times leaves a single item. So a search like yours never needs more than twenty comparisons." He said it flatly, the way he said everything, and I sat with the number. At most twenty, out of a million. Dara would have needed, in the worst case, the whole million, or half of it on average, I didn't know which and it didn't matter against twenty.

Here is what I told Dara on the bus afterward, and I want to be honest that I made it sound more finished than it was. I said the class exercise and the race were the same lesson: you accept a constraint, the private field or the sorted list, and the constraint pays you back, order at the door, speed at the counter. I said the railing and the railing's solidity were one thing. Dara listened with her forehead against the window and said, "So hide the data and halve the world. Great slogan. Doesn't tell me what to do when the list isn't sorted."

I opened my mouth and found nothing in it. Because that was the part I hadn't worked out, and the part I'd skipped in my kitchen-table sulk, and the part my neat speech on the bus had papered over. The getters guard the door only if everyone agrees to use the door. Binary search buys its twenty comparisons only if the million entries are already in order, and sorting a million of anything is its own expensive question, one nobody had asked me and I hadn't asked myself. I had been congratulating myself on not being competitive, and then on losing gracefully, and now on winning gracefully, and somewhere in that chain I had stopped checking what I actually knew.

"Theo," I said, texting him from the bus, "how long does it take to sort the list before we can search it?"

Three dots appeared, stopped, appeared again. Dara watched me watch the screen.

"Ask him if the sort's worth it for one search," she said, "or only if you're searching all night."

The dots kept pulsing, and I typed, deleted, typed again, while outside the window the streetlights came on one at a time, in order, all the way down the hill.

The porch screen at his grandfather's house had a torn corner, and Matthew kept noticing it the way you notice a wrong note in a scale, half listening while he laid his sketchbook pages across the table. Ten drawings, all of them of hands. His grandmother's hands shelling peas, his grandfather's hands on a radio dial, his own hands drawn blind, without looking, in the margins of chemistry homework last spring. The college application wanted a portfolio of ten works around a single theme, plus an artist's statement, and the deadline sat eleven days out like weather on the horizon.

"You've spread yourself all over my table," his grandfather said, setting down two glasses of iced tea. He was a taciturn man who mostly spoke in observations rather than questions, so Matthew answered anyway.

"It's a portfolio. Ten pieces, one theme. I picked hands because everyone in this house has interesting ones." He slid a drawing toward his grandfather, the one of the hands on the radio dial. His grandfather studied it long enough that Matthew began to ruminate on whether he'd chosen badly, whether hands were too obvious, whether the admissions people had seen a hundred portfolios of hands and sighed at every one.

His grandmother came out with her own sketchbook, a fat canvas thing with a rubber band holding it shut. She had gone back to drawing at sixty-eight, taking a class at the community center, and she sat down and opened it to a page of loose clippings. "I've been collecting this," she said. "For my show at the library."

Matthew leaned over. It was a photocopy of a page from some guide for artists, with two paragraphs marked in yellow. "Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement," he read aloud, "a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words."

"That's what my teacher says," his grandmother said. "The short one goes on the little card next to the picture on the wall. The long one goes in the application or the file." She tapped the photocopy. "I wrote my short one first and it was terrible. Two hundred words of nothing. Then I wrote the long one, and when I went back, the short one came out true."

Matthew sat with that. He had been treating the statement as a single hoop to jump through, one paragraph he could polish and send everywhere, and the idea that it might come in two sizes, doing two different jobs, rearranged something in his thinking. The wall card and the application were different rooms. A person standing in front of a drawing read differently than a person sitting at a desk with a stack of folders.

"Can I borrow this?" he asked.

"It's yours. I have the book inside."

He read the marked paragraphs again, then turned to a blank page and started on the long version, because his grandmother had done it in that order and because he suddenly had too much to say for fifty words anyway. He wrote about his grandfather's hands, how they had rebuilt the porch railing two summers ago, how the drawings were partly about work and partly about the fact that hands tell on people, that you can read a life in the knuckles. He wrote about drawing his own hands blind, how the lines went wrong in honest ways. Somewhere in the middle of it he stopped performing for an imaginary admissions officer and started describing what he had actually done, and the difference, though he couldn't have named it, showed up on the page as plainer sentences.

Then he counted backward. He tried to compress the long version and got it to about 140 words, which was still too many, and stared at the torn screen while he thought. His grandfather went in for more ice. His grandmother drew the porch itself, the swing and its shadow, working without comment, and Matthew watched her hand move and understood that she was doing in front of him the very thing his portfolio was about. He cut adjectives. He cut the sentence about honesty, since the drawings were right there to make that argument themselves. He got down to 92 words, counted twice, and read it under his breath.

"Say it out loud," his grandmother said without looking up.

He did. It was six sentences. It said the theme was hands, that hands record work and age and attention, and that ten drawings let him look closely at three pairs of them, his included. It sounded like him, he thought, or close enough.

His grandfather came back out with the ice and sat listening to the screen door bang shut behind him. "Which pair is hardest to draw?" he asked.

"Mine," Matthew said. "I keep wanting to make them better than they are."

His grandfather considered the drawing of his own hands on the radio dial, the knuckles Matthew had shaded heavier than they needed, and pushed the glass of tea closer to his grandson's elbow. "Draw them again, then," he said. "You've got eleven days."

Matthew turned to a clean page, held out his left hand in the slant of afternoon light, and began.

The garage smelled of cut grass and the cold metal of his father's old workbench, and Joseph sat on an upturned milk crate with his grandmother's guitar across his knees, playing the opening of "Wish You Were Here" for the ninth time that afternoon. He had it clean now. Every note landed where he aimed it, and the familiar chords rolled out warm and easy, and he was about to start it a tenth time when his sister Priya came through the side door carrying her violin case and a bag of chips she was clearly not intending to share.

"You're playing the same thing again," she said, settling onto the porch cooler they'd dragged in years ago and never returned. "I could hear it through the wall. Twice. Maybe more."

"It sounds good."

"It did sound good. The first six times." She opened the chips, extruding one from the bag with the careful fingers of someone rationing a limited supply, and pointed it at the sheet music leaning against the paint cans. "What's that thing you keep skipping?"

He followed her finger. Two bars, mid-page, where the tablature turned into a stretch his left hand simply could not make. He'd been flipping past them for two weeks, the way you drive around a blocked street, and he had developed a quiet taxonomy of excuses: his hands were small, the guitar had high action, the song was better without that section anyway. He said none of this. He played the two bars, and they collapsed, strings buzzing, the fourth fret abandoned somewhere in the middle of the reach.

Priya winced on his behalf, which was somehow worse than laughing. "My teacher did that to me Tuesday," she said. "I played the first page of my piece and she stopped me before I even got to finish it. She said playing through what you already know feels great and teaches you nothing, and then she assigned me four measures. Four. Out of three pages."

"That's brutal."

"It's called deliberate practice," Priya said, and stole a chip. "You work on the specific thing you're bad at, with a goal, and she's sitting right there telling me the instant I get it wrong. I hated every minute of it. Also I got those four measures better in one day than the rest of the piece got in a month." She brushed salt off her skirt, circumspect, deciding whether to say the next part. "I want to play the whole piece at the spring recital. The actual whole thing. If I keep only replaying the part I love, I'll stand up there and play thirty beautiful seconds and then die."

Joseph looked at the two bars again. Somewhere in the back of his mind he had known, for two weeks, exactly what he was doing, and it stung a little that it took his little sister eating chips in a garage to make the knowledge loud. He set a goal, since Priya's teacher apparently demanded one: the stretch, clean, five times in a row. He didn't have a teacher, so he made Priya the feedback. "Count my attempts," he said. "Tell me when it's wrong. Don't be nice."

"I'm never nice," she said, and put the chips down, which for her was an act of real sacrifice.

He played the two bars slowly, wrong. She said "one, wrong" in the flat voice of a lifeguard. He adjusted his thumb behind the neck, curled his fingers, tried again; a buzz on the fourth string, "two, wrong." The sixth attempt rang clear, and she said "one" in the counting-good voice, and he felt something absurdly bright open in his chest. On the third clean repetition his hand cramped and he had to shake it out, and Priya slid the chip bag across the floor to him without being asked, because she had been watching his face go white with concentration and knew what that cost.

They worked like that for forty minutes, her calling attempts, him failing the fifth clean repetition twice and starting the count over while the light through the garage door went from yellow to amber. When he finally got five in a row, she applauded by slapping the cooler lid, and he played the whole passage from the top, and this time the blocked street opened and the melody walked straight through.

"It still needs speed," he said, listening to himself.

"It needs a lot of things," Priya said. "You're going to have to do that whole ugly business again tomorrow, and the day after, and probably for weeks. I don't know if I'll be free to count every time."

He nodded. He didn't know either; that was the part nobody had a method for. But he propped the sheet music open to the page anyway, weighted it with a wrench so morning-Joseph couldn't turn past it, and Priya picked her violin back up and played her four measures into the rafters, slow and deliberate and already better than Tuesday.

"One more time," she said.

Connor had two hours before the pharmacy closed and one night before he had to stand in front of a sophomore health class and explain things he was not entirely sure he understood himself. The peer education program had assigned him the unit on consent, contraception and testing, and Mr. Reyes had said, "You'll do fine, you just have to know it cold," which was exactly the problem. He did not know it cold. He knew it the way he knew the bus schedule, well enough to ride it, not well enough to drive.

He stood in aisle four with his phone out, comparing the shelf against his notes. Condoms were locked behind plastic, which meant he had to press a button and wait for someone to come unlock the case, and while he waited he practiced his first line under his breath.
