Consent is a yes you can give freely, and can take back. The words felt like someone else's coat. He had learned them in a training where the facilitator had tried to inculcate the idea through roleplay, and the roleplay had been awkward in a way that made the idea feel smaller than it was.

"You're the peer ed kid," said a voice behind him. Maya from his civics class was standing there in her work polo, name tag crooked, holding a clipboard. "Reyes sent me an email. You're presenting fourth period tomorrow, and I'm supposed to be your backup if you freeze."

"I'm not going to freeze."

"Okay." She did not look convinced. She glanced at the locked case, then at his notes. "Since you're here, can I ask you something? Off the record. Not as your backup."

A pharmacist came and unlocked the case without a word, and Connor bought a box he did not need, just so he would have something in his hands. In the parking lot Maya sat on the curb and told him, in a flat hurried voice, that she had an appointment at the clinic across town at eight tomorrow morning, before school, and that she had been reading about options all week and the reading only confused her more. "I have to decide there," she said. "They said decide at the appointment or wait a month for the next opening. And my mom works at the school, so waiting means her finding out before I do it."

"What are the options?"

"Pill, shot, implant, IUD thing. The nurse on the phone said something I wrote down." She pulled out her phone and showed him a photo of her own scribbled notes. Under implant and hormonal IUD she had written less than 1 in 100 a year, and next to the pill a number that was much worse, and then a question mark.

Connor looked at the question mark for a long moment. The training binder had a chart, he remembered, and he had skimmed it, but the numbers had slid past him because they were all just numbers. Now, sitting on a curb with someone who had to choose in sixteen hours, he saw what the chart had actually been saying. "Okay," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "The pill fails more not because it's weaker, but because it's a pill. You have to remember it every single day, and people are people. The implant and the hormonal IUD fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on daily use. They just work, sitting there. It's not about the hormone being stronger. It's about not trusting memory."

Maya was writing this down. "So the smart choice is the one I don't have to think about."

"That's not a rule I can give you," Connor said. "That's the thing I keep running into with this whole presentation. I can tell you the numbers, and the numbers are real, I'm not doubting them. But which one is right for you depends on stuff I can't know. Needles. Your period. Whatever else." He rubbed the box of condoms with his thumb. "That's the part that made the training feel dishonest. They wanted me to hand out certainty."

"You could say that part," Maya said. "To the sophomores. The part where you don't know."

The light over the pharmacy door flickered on, that early melancholic blue of autumn evenings, and Maya stood and brushed off her jeans. She said she would text him after the appointment if he wanted to know how it went, and he said he did want that, genuinely, and then asked if she would still be his backup at fourth period. She said yes, but that if he froze she was going to do more than stand there, she was going to talk, and he told her that was the deal anyway.

That night he rewrote his outline on the back of a receipt. Under consent he wrote: it's about volition, a yes that is actually chosen, and you have to say what that means out loud even though it's uncomfortable. Under contraception he drew a crude copy of Maya's question mark. Under testing he wrote the clinic's address and the walk-in hours, because the nurse had given those to Maya too, and Maya had read them aloud to him like they were directions to somewhere ordinary. He practiced the whole thing once in his kitchen, to the refrigerator, and got through it without stopping.

At 7:52 the next morning his phone buzzed. It was a photo of a clinic waiting room, beige chairs and a fish tank, and beneath it Maya had typed: going in, tell the sophomores the truth. Connor put the phone in his pocket, picked up the box of condoms and the receipt and the marker he'd borrowed from his mother's drawer, and walked toward the school with the sun still low behind him and the outline already softening where his thumb had smudged the ink.

Sophie had claimed the corner table by the periodicals on Tuesday because it was farthest from the children's room, and by Thursday she had spread across it entirely: the case packet from Mr. Ruiz's constitutional law elective, two highlighters gone pale, and a legal pad ruled into two columns labeled FOR and AGAINST like she expected the arguments to fight each other without her.

"You're going to have to argue the school's side," Nadia said, dropping her backpack on the FOR column. "That's the whole assignment. Both sides. Mr. Ruiz wants you to lose to yourself on purpose."

"I know that. That's the problem." Sophie tapped the packet. Tinker v. Des Moines was settled, obviously, but the packet went further: a hypothetical extension where a student group had hung a banner reading CONDEMN THE COMPACT from a rail along the riverwalk, city-owned riparian land adjacent to school property, and the city had cut it down in the night. The mock court would hear arguments on whether the banner was school speech, public speech, or something in between, and Sophie had been assigned to argue both positions in sequence, an arrangement Mr. Ruiz called a dialectic, as though the two of her were supposed to arrive at a synthesis by Thursday.

Nadia, meanwhile, had a petition of her own, which was that Sophie write it. She had been trying to file a formal complaint against the vending machine in the student lounge for two weeks, on the grounds that it took her dollar and gave nothing back, and she believed Sophie's new legal powers could be turned to this purpose.

"You can't sue a vending machine," Sophie said.

"Students sue schools. Schools own vending machines. Interpolate."

"That's not what interpolate means. You can't interpolate a lawsuit."

"You're the lawyer." Nadia pulled the packet toward her and frowned at the fact sheet. "Okay, so. Your government. The president. If your congress decides they hate him, what happens?"

"Nothing, basically. He stays."

"For how long?"

"His term. The whole fixed term. He's elected separately from the legislature, so they can't get rid of him just for disagreeing with them." Sophie said it the way she'd say the date, and then heard herself saying it, because Nadia was already shaking her head.

"Where I'm from, prime minister, parliament, one election. They vote no confidence on a Tuesday, he's packing by Friday. Your president could be fighting with everyone and still sit there for years."

"Years," Sophie agreed, and something about the shape of that, a leader insulated from disagreement by design, made her look back at her two columns. The FOR column said the banner stayed because unpopular speech was the point of the First Amendment, the school's authority stopped where the riverbank began, and riparian land was public forum land by tradition. The AGAINST column said the school had sponsored the riverwalk cleanup, so the banner was school speech wearing a borrowed coat, and schools could discipline that. The columns were equally good. She had assumed that meant she hadn't worked hard enough.

A toddler escaped the children's room trailing a puppet fish, and the librarian, a large man named Gerald whom Sophie had watched shush a table of law students into submission, intercepted the boy with the gravity of a bailiff. The boy pointed the fish at Sophie's case packet and said, "Guilty," and was carried off.

"See, even the fish has a ruling," Nadia said.

Sophie laughed, then stopped laughing. Because the fish was right, in a way: somebody had to rule, and the ruling wouldn't come from the arguments agreeing with each other. In Nadia's system, the disagreement itself was the mechanism; losing confidence meant losing power. In Sophie's, the disagreement was weather. The president stood out in it. And maybe, she thought, that was actually the strongest version of the AGAINST column, not that the students deserved punishment but that the school, like a president, had to be able to hold an unpopular position for a fixed term without the argument of the moment dissolving it. She wrote that down, then wrote under it: but students are not presidents, and underlined it twice, and did not have an answer.

She worked until the lights dimmed for closing, then past it, interpolating Nadia's question into her closing statement for both sides, so that each argument ended by conceding what the other one proved. It felt less like winning and more like standing in the middle of a river with the water going both ways.

Friday, the mock court convened in the library's meeting room, because the classroom was being waxed. Gerald had been drafted as a justice and wore his shushing finger like a gavel. Sophie stood, arranged her notes, and began, "May it please the court," and got four sentences into the school's side, the side she had privately come to distrust, delivering it with a conviction that surprised her, before Mr. Ruiz leaned over to Gerald and whispered something. Gerald rapped the table.

"Ms. Okafor. The assignment sheet says you're arguing for the students first. You've prepared the rebuttal as the opener." A pause. "Which is against you, apparently. You argued it very well."

From the second row, Nadia raised her hand and said, "Your Honor, I'd like the record to show I predicted this."

The note from Principal Vaughn waited in David's inbox like a splinter he could not stop touching. He had opened it four times during sixth period, and now, in the library's back corner where the newspaper staff kept two mismatched desks, he opened it a fifth time. The Clarion had planned an editorial endorsing Marcus Oyelaran for student council president on a platform of reallocating the activities fund, which happened to be the fund that paid for the Principal's annual leadership retreat. "I'd ask you to reconsider running that piece," Vaughn had written, insouciant enough to add a smiley face, as though reconsideration were a small favor between friends.

David printed the editorial anyway and left it in the tray, then walked to the circulation desk to clear his head. Behind the counter, Ms. Ferreira was stamping returns, and he asked, almost idly, whether the library kept the Los Angeles Times on microfilm or if he needed the databases. "Databases," she said, not looking up. "You looking for something?" He said maybe. He didn't say that a senior named Priya had mentioned something in the newsroom two weeks ago, half-gossip, half-warning: that even the big papers had owners, and owners sometimes said no.

He found it in fifteen minutes. In October 2024, the Los Angeles Times had not endorsed a presidential candidate. That part he learned first, from the archived editorial page, a strange blank where a recommendation should have been. Then, piecing together the reporting that followed, he learned the rest: the paper's owner had blocked the editorial board's plans, and the paper's own journalists wrote about it openly. Several members of the editorial board resigned in protest. He sat back in the chair with its cracked vinyl armrests and read the names of the people who had quit. Ordinary names. People who had decided that a blank page was worse than no job.

Priya found him there, dropped her backpack on the table. "Vaughn got to you too?" she said. He showed her the principal's email, and she made a sound between a laugh and something harder. "So what are you going to do, run it and get shut down, or fold like cheap laundry?" David turned the monitor toward her. "Read this," he said. She read, and her face changed the way faces do when a small local problem turns out to have ancestors.

They argued about it until the library closed at eight. Priya's position was simple: print the endorsement, make Vaughn censor them in writing, and thereby prove the point more loudly than any editorial could. David kept coming back to the resignations. "Those people quit," he said, "and the paper still ran, and the owner still owned it. They didn't win. They just refused to pretend." Priya said refusing wasn't nothing. He wasn't sure. He had been editor for a year and had inured himself to small compromises, the softened headline, the quote cut to spare a teacher's feelings, each one defensible, each one making the next easier. Somewhere in that accumulation, he thought, a paper stops being a paper, though he could not say exactly when the change happened, which bothered him more than the principal did.

The solution he arrived at was uglier and more honest than either of their positions. On Thursday the Clarion ran its election issue with the endorsement of Marcus exactly as drafted, but above it, on the same page, an editor's note, unsigned because David had insisted it be his byline alone: "An administrator asked us to reconsider this editorial. We are printing it, and printing the fact that we were asked not to." He knew the note was itself a kind of leverage, a move in a game he claimed to stand apart from, and he let that contradiction sit in him unresolved rather than paper over it.

Vaughn summoned him Friday morning. The office was warm and smelled of coffee, and the principal did not shout. He called the editor's note "unfortunate framing," and David recognized the maneuver, the careful dysphemism, an endorsement becoming "that piece," a threat becoming a request, a censor becoming a concerned administrator. "You know I fund that paper," Vaughn said, mild as milk. "I know," David said. "It's in the budget." Neither of them mentioned the retreat. The silence stretched until Vaughn waved him out, which David understood was not a victory, only a postponement.

He walked back through the hall past the trophy case, and in the glass he could see the library doors at the far end, the place where he had found, in a fifty-year-old paper's small collapse, both a warning and a permission. He still didn't know whether the board members who resigned had done the right thing or merely the clean thing, whether quitting was courage or abandonment, and he suspected he would not know until he stood where they had stood. For now the paper was out, Marcus's name in bold, the note beneath it, and Priya was taping a copy of the page to the newsroom door as he came in. "There's your blank page," she said. "Full."

The gym smelled like rubber and cold concrete, and Laurence had the clipboard against her knees because the bleachers were too high to write on. Around her the junior team ran suicides, sneakers squeaking, and Coach Ferreira sat two rows down with her arms crossed, watching no one in particular. Laurence was supposed to hand her a training week by Friday. That was the deal: she wanted to be captain, and the coach had said, "Then show me you can build a week, not just survive one."

She had drafted it Sunday night at the kitchen table. Monday sprints, Tuesday weights, Wednesday sprints again, Thursday match play, Friday weights, Saturday scrimmage, Sunday more sprints, because Sunday was when everyone else slacked. She'd been proud of the density of it, the way the days pressed together like folded steel.

"That's a schedule for machines," said Priya, flopping onto the bleachers beside her after the suicides, hair stuck to her forehead. Priya had been injured in October, a hamstring that tore because nobody had warmed up properly in the rain, and she'd come back in January slower and warier. "You put me in that week and I'm done by Thursday."

"You're the fittest one we have."

"My hamstring doesn't care how fit I am." Priya pulled the clipboard toward her, scanned it, and Laurence let her, which was itself a concession. "Where's the rest?"

"Rest is for people who don't want it enough."

Priya looked at her for a long second. "You sound like an autocrat," she said, and handed the clipboard back. "Like a small one. A gym autocrat."

Laurence laughed before she could stop herself, and then didn't apologize for it, and then didn't take the line out of the plan either.

After practice she stayed behind, ostensibly to collect cones. Actually she went to the office alcove where the coach kept her binders, shelves of them, spines labeled by season. She wasn't sneaking, she told herself; she was doing research. In the binder marked with last year's dates she found week-by-week sheets, and each sheet had a word typed at the top that she'd never seen before: microcycle.

"You're in my binders," Ferreira said from the doorway. She didn't sound angry.

"What's a microcycle?"

"Come here." Ferreira pulled a sheet out, one week on a single page, hard days and easy days laid out like weather. "In periodized training, a season gets divided into cycles. The microcycle is the smallest one. It usually lasts about one week." She tapped the page. "That's what you're writing. You're not writing seven days. You're writing one unit."

Laurence looked at the sheet. There was a rest day in it, an actual blank day, and two of the days were marked "activation," which when she flipped back she found meant warm-ups counted as content, not as an apology before the real work. The week was shaped. It had a top and a slope down.

She rewrote the plan that night at the kitchen table, the same table, the same pen. Monday hard, Tuesday easy, Wednesday hardest, Thursday technical with long warm-ups, Friday moderate, Saturday scrimmage, Sunday nothing. Sunday nothing. It looked lazy. It looked like a document written by someone altruistic, someone concerned with other people's hamstrings, and she sat with her discomfort about that until she understood it wasn't discomfort about them. It was discomfort about letting go of the version of herself that believed effort meant stacking.

She also kept one thing. Monday sprints stayed, first thing, no negotiation, because she had decided she was allowed to be a little bit of a tyrant about Mondays specifically.

Friday she handed the clipboard to Ferreira in the gym, under the far basket while the juniors ran their warm-up laps. The coach read it slowly, the way she read everything, and Laurence stood with her hands behind her back and admitted to herself she could not tell from the woman's face whether this was passing or failing.

"Microcycle," Ferreira said finally.

"I found it in your binder. I hope that's okay."

"That's what binders are for." Ferreira closed the clipboard. "Captain's announced Monday."

Laurence nodded and went to set up the cones, arranging them in the pattern for the warm-up drill, and it was only halfway through the second line of cones that she registered what the coach had said. She turned around. Ferreira was already walking toward the juniors, and Priya was jogging over from the storage room with the ball bag, calling out, "Coach, who's the new captain, then?" And Ferreira pointed at Priya, without breaking stride, and said, "Her hamstring approved the week, so she's got my vote, but the team votes Monday."

Laurence stood between the cones with her hand still raised from placing one, and started laughing, and put the cone down.

The morning smelled of wet asphalt and coffee, and Alexander carried both into the community hall like contraband. He was eighteen years and twenty-three days old, and this was his first federal election, a fact he had mentioned to his grandmother so many times in the last month that she had started answering the phone with "Yes, Alexander, I know, you're voting." She had died in March. Since then nobody eulogized her better than Alexander himself did, quietly, on walks, in the shower, composing sentences he would never say out loud. He had promised her this vote the way other people promise their grandparents graduation photos.

The hall had been a badminton court in some earlier life; the lines were still visible under the folding tables, and volunteers in laminated lanyards moved along them like players in a slow rally. Alexander joined the short line and rehearsed what he would say. His father's voice was in one ear, his civics seminar in the other. His father, who had voted the same way for thirty years and called it chess, believed a vote was a tool, something you aimed at the least bad outcome. His teacher, Ms. Okonjo, believed a vote was a statement, a small public philosophy. Alexander had spent the election period unable to decide whether he was a chess player or a philosopher, and this morning the question had a deadline.

"Name," said the woman at the table. Her badge said DIANE. She had a pen behind each ear, which Alexander found quietly wonderful.

"Alexander Petrou. Uh, this is my first time." He handed over his driver's licence with the self-consciousness of a man presenting a passport at a border he wasn't sure he had the right to cross.

Diane typed, frowned, typed again. "You're not on the voters list."

The floor seemed to tilt toward him. He had assumed the list was like a class roster, something the world kept for you automatically. "I never got anything in the mail," he said. "I moved for school in September. I figured I was, I don't know, in the system."

"Are you still resident here? In this riding?"

"Yes. My parents' address. I'm home this weekend." He had come home specifically to vote, had argued with himself about which ballot he belonged on, and now it appeared he belonged on none.

"Then you can register here, today," Diane said. "At your assigned polling place. Just need ID with that address, or a piece of mail and something with your name on it."

Alexander stared at her. He had spent three weeks certain that forgetting to register meant forfeiting the whole thing, that democracy had a paperwork wall and he had walked into it face first. The discovery sat in him strangely, half relief and half embarrassment at his own certainty. How many other walls had he imagined? He caught himself wondering, with genuine curiosity, what else he believed wrongly about how the country worked, and whether everyone carried around a private, inaccurate epistemology like a second wallet.

He emptied his pockets onto the table: licence, a bank card, a crumpled hydro bill from his father's stack at home. Diane flattened the bill with the heel of her hand. "This works." She wrote his name onto a form, printed a voter registration certificate, and directed him to table four, where another volunteer crossed his name off with a satisfying stroke of purple ink. The whole thing had taken six minutes. Six minutes to be invented as a voter.

The ballot was smaller than he expected, a slip of paper the size of a receipt, as though something so consequential should weigh more. Behind the cardboard screen, he read the names top to bottom twice. His father's candidate was third, his teacher's was first, and between them sat the question he had carried since March. What was a vote for, exactly? A lever, or a sentence about who you were? He noticed that his hand was hovering and that he was smiling at his own hand, this absurd, trembling machine that had to decide alone now that both his advisors were gone. His grandmother would have told him to stop thinking and mark something. She had also, once, driven an hour to deliver a winter coat to an indigent man she'd read about in the paper, without ever voting differently from her husband, so the two of them had cancelled each other out for forty years, and she had seemed fine with that arithmetic.

He marked the ballot. He would not tell his father which box, and he would tell Ms. Okonjo only that he had voted, and he still did not know whether he had played chess or written a sentence, and he suspected he would not know for years, maybe not ever, maybe the not-knowing was the actual adult condition that everyone had been too polite to mention. The pencil had no eraser, which struck him as either an oversight or a philosophy.

He fed the ballot into the box, listened to the soft click of it landing among the others, and stood for a moment with his empty hands. Outside, the rain had stopped. A man at the next table was arguing cheerfully with a volunteer about the polling place assignment, waving a letter, and the volunteer was saying, gently, "You can sort it out right here today."

Alexander took one of the pencils from the little cup by the door. Nobody stopped him.

Maria sat in the corner booth of the Cedar Fork with her hands folded on the table, waiting for the manager. The restaurant smelled like onions and floor cleaner. She had a folder on her lap with one page in it, a page she had rewritten three times since Tuesday. On the page was a single sentence: "Tell me about a time you handled conflict in a group."

Her brother Dev had told her interviews were rigged toward people who could talk about themselves, and that the only fair way to fight that was preparation. He'd printed something off the internet and slid it across the kitchen table. "It's called STAR," he said, chewing a piece of toast. "Situation, Task, Action, Result." He hadn't explained further; he was seventeen and believed explanations were a form of condescension. She'd read the printout herself, twice, then folded it into the folder.

The story she had chosen was the chemistry project from last spring. Priya, Marco, and a fourth kid named Elliot whom nobody had wanted, had been assigned a presentation on water treatment. Elliot had turned out to be bellicose about nearly everything: fonts, slide order, whether the word "flocculation" was too hard for the class. He'd shouted at Priya in the library until a librarian came over, and after that the group had stopped meeting together, meeting instead in pairs, in fragments, in the hallway before class.

The manager came out at four minutes past two, carrying a paper cup. She was shorter than Maria expected, with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair. "Maria? I'm Ruth. You applied for the Saturday host position." She sat down across from her, set the cup aside, and opened a small notebook. "First job?" "Yes." "That's fine. Everyone here had one." She clicked a pen. "Tell me about a time you worked with a group and something went wrong."

Maria's rehearsed sentence dissolved. What came out instead was the truth: that the project had gone wrong slowly, in the way things do, that nobody could name the day it failed. She heard herself talking about the library, about Elliot's voice, about Priya leaving the table. Ruth kept writing. Maria thought, with the clarity of panic, that she was telling this badly, in the wrong order, and then she thought about the folded page.

She put her hand flat on the folder but didn't open it. "Let me start over. There's a way to tell these, I practiced it. Situation, task, action, result." She laid it out. The situation: four students, one grade, three weeks. The task: her piece was the research, but she'd also taken on getting the group to function at all, because someone had to. The action: instead of holding a group meeting, which had already exploded once, she went to each person separately, one lunch period at a time, and asked what they needed from the others. Marco wanted Elliot to stop rewriting his slides. Priya wanted an apology, or at least an acknowledgment. Elliot, it turned out, had been sure from the start that the others were going to cut him out, and had decided to be loud before he could be quiet.

Ruth looked up. "And the result?" "We split the presentation into four solo sections so nobody touched anybody else's work. We got an A minus." Maria paused. "It wasn't really solved. It was more like an arbitration nobody agreed to. I made a ruling and they accepted it because nobody wanted another library scene. I still don't know if that was the right thing or just the thing that worked." Ruth stopped writing. She took a slow drink from the cup and studied Maria over the rim.

"You didn't put that on your application," she said. "The part about not knowing." "I didn't think it helped." "Here's what I know after eleven years of this. On Saturdays I have two servers who've filed complaints against each other twice. I've settled it twice. My way of settling it is I underwrite whatever truce they make, meaning if it falls apart on a Saturday night, it falls apart on me. I need someone at the door who can read a room before it goes loud." She closed the notebook. "Can you start this Saturday at ten?"

Maria said yes before she had finished deciding whether she meant it. Ruth stood, then stopped, hand on the back of the booth. "One thing. When you split the presentation into four parts, did the class notice it was four separate projects wearing one title?" "The teacher did," Maria said. "She wrote on the rubric, 'Functioning apart is not the same as functioning together.'" Ruth laughed once, a short sound, and pushed her glasses down onto her nose.

On her way out, Maria passed the two servers, a tall woman and a younger man, setting tables on opposite sides of the room without looking at each other. She recognized the geometry of it, the careful distances, the pairs meeting in fragments. She stopped at the door, then turned back toward the host stand, where the Saturday chart was taped with names in two different inks, and began reading it.

Brooklyn signed her name on the volunteer sheet at the St. Vincent food bank and noticed, beneath it, a column headed "Hours." Behind her, a boy from her school, Dev, was already filling his in.

"You've got thirty-eight written down," she said, looking over his shoulder. "I have zero."

"Deadline's Friday," Dev said. "Graduation's in June, but the school wants the paperwork in before the diploma meeting." He capped his pen. "Forty hours of community involvement, or you don't get the Ontario Secondary School Diploma. I've been putting it off since grade nine."

Brooklyn had known about the requirement for years the way she knew about the periodic table, as a fact that lived in school and never followed her home. Now it had followed her to a church basement that smelled of cardboard and dish soap, where pallets of canned corn stood against one wall and a woman named Ruth was sorting bread with quick, practiced hands.

"Brooklyn, was it?" Ruth said. "You're on the bread table. Check dates, pull anything green or furry, and don't agonize over it. The compost doesn't judge."

She worked through the morning. A man came in with his daughter, maybe four years old, and took a box of rice, two cartons of eggs, a bag of apples that had gone soft on one side. Brooklyn watched him thank Ruth twice, once at the counter and once at the door, as if the first time hadn't been enough. The girl waved at nobody in particular.

In grade ten, Brooklyn remembered, her civics teacher had asked who was volunteering and why, and a girl named Priya had said she tutored immigrant kids in math because her grandmother had been helped that way forty years ago. Another girl had said she did shoreline cleanup because it looked good on applications. The teacher had written both reasons on the board and asked the class which was better, and the class had argued until the bell, and nothing was decided. Brooklyn had said nothing. She had wanted a reason that fit entirely on one line, and she had never found one.

Today she had come, honestly, because of the deadline. Her guidance counselor had flagged her file in April: forty hours still outstanding, and Ontario high school students could not earn the diploma without them. Brooklyn had resented the errand all the way here, resenting most the possibility that she was the kind of person who only showed up when a certificate was held hostage. But by noon she had learned the bread table, and where the dated milk went, and that Ruth had volunteered here eleven years and still got the sorting bins confused on Mondays.

Dev, meanwhile, was intransigent about the scanner. A new inventory app had been installed on the food bank's single tablet, and Ruth wanted the cans logged digitally. Dev insisted the paper list was faster and refused, politely but completely, to switch over. "Two hours I have left to log," he said. "I'm not spending them learning software."

Brooklyn took the tablet herself. The app turned out to be simple, three taps per item, and within twenty minutes she had catalogued a shelf that would have taken Dev an hour by hand. Her arriving late and under compulsion had, in a small way, catalyzed the change; she had no loyalty to the old system, no stake in being right.

"You didn't have to do that," Dev said, watching her.

"I know. It was faster, that's all."

But driving the whole thing home, later, was a confusion she couldn't sort: whether the mandatory hours corrupted the giving or simply got people through the door who would never otherwise have come. The boy at the counter with his daughter didn't know or care why she'd sorted his apples. The soft spot was cut away either way.

Ruth called a lunch break at twelve thirty and put out sandwiches for the volunteers. She sat down across from Brooklyn and peeled an orange in one long spiral, the kind of thing a person learns from doing it ten thousand times.

"Why'd you start so late?" Ruth asked. "Most kids your age bank their hours in grade nine."

"Honestly? It was something I had to do for the diploma. Forty hours, or no graduation." Brooklyn pulled the crust off her sandwich. "That's the whole reason I'm here. I keep thinking that makes it not count."

Ruth considered this while she chewed. "Some people who start for the paper stay for the work. Some who start noble quit in a month. The reason you walked in is the least interesting thing about you by the time you walk out." She pushed half the orange across the table.

Brooklyn took it. She didn't know yet, she admitted to herself, which kind she would turn out to be, and there was no way to find out except to keep coming back after the form was signed. Two hours remained on her sheet. After that, the counting stopped and she would learn what she did when nothing was being measured.

At the end of the shift she wrote "2" in the hours column, capped Dev's pen, and looked up at Ruth sorting bread for the afternoon crowd.

"Same time next Saturday?" she said.

The community theatre smelled of dust and burned coffee, and the stage was smaller than Aaron's bedroom, which he kept forgetting when he drew his blocking diagrams on graph paper. He had been given the one-act because nobody else wanted it, a forty-minute play about two brothers arguing over a dead father's watch, and he had spent two weeks drawing arrows that meant nothing once actual humans stood where the arrows pointed.

The trouble was Marcus. Marcus played the older brother with a kind of pugnacious energy that Aaron had first mistaken for talent and now recognized as a habit of charging across the stage whenever he forgot his lines, as if movement could stand in for memory. Every time Marcus crossed, Priya, who played the younger brother's wife and had the only quiet scene in the play, ended up with her back half-turned or her body swallowed behind Marcus's shoulder, invisible from the folding chairs that passed for an audience.

"You're blocking me out again," Priya said on the fourth night, not unkindly, which somehow made it worse.

"I'm acting," said Marcus.

"You're a wall," said Priya. "You're a wall that walks."

Aaron sat in the third row with his graph paper and tried to see the stage the way an audience would, as a flat picture rather than a room. He had read somewhere that theatre was a two-dimensional art pretending to be three-dimensional, and he hadn't understood it until now, watching Marcus erase Priya every time he moved. He rubbed out an arrow and drew another, and then, sitting very still, he drew a second, smaller arrow next to Priya's mark, a small adjustment rather than a new position. When Marcus crossed left, Priya needed to shift right, just slightly, to keep both of them in the picture.

"Okay," he said, standing. "Marcus, do your cross again. Priya, when he moves, you move too. Just a half step, opposite direction."

They ran it. Marcus swept left with the dead father's watch in his fist; Priya drifted right, unhurried, and the stage, which had been collapsing all week into a single stubborn column of one actor, opened into two visible people. From the folding chairs it looked almost intentional.

"There's a word for that," said Dolores, the volunteer stage manager, who was seventy and had been threading her way to the coffee pot. She paused by the fourth row. "Countering."

"Countering," Aaron repeated, and wrote it down.

Dolores went on to the coffee pot, and that was all she said about it, which Aaron appreciated more than he could have said. He worked the principle through the rest of the scene himself, calling out adjustments, wrong twice before he was right: once he moved Priya so far she faced the wall, once he moved her into the doorframe. By nine o'clock the cross and the counter ran clean, and Priya, who had privately seemed ready to quit on Tuesday, was smiling at Marcus as though he were a scene partner instead of an obstacle.

That night Aaron lay on his bed and composed a message to his older sister, Maya, who was doing her second year at a conservatory and would, he knew, mock him for the graph paper if he didn't get ahead of the mockery. "I used to think directing meant telling people where to stand," he typed, "like furniture arrangement. Tonight I learned it's more like that thing where you watch a flock of birds on a nature documentary and every bird is adjusting to every other bird, except the birds have lines and one of them keeps forgetting his. Also the word 'countering' is now the most important word in my life. A seventy-year-old woman told it to me and then walked away, which I think is how wisdom is supposed to arrive. I still don't know if I'm directing this play or just preventing disasters in sequence. Possibly those are the same job. Don't answer that." He sent it before he could edit it into something cooler, and Maya replied only with a bird emoji and the sentence "The disasters ARE the job," which he read three times and decided not to interpret.

Opening night was a Friday, and the audience was thirty-one people, four of whom were there for the free coffee. Aaron stood in the wings with his graph paper rolled in his fist like a bad idea he couldn't put down, because the play was no longer on the paper; it was out there, happening. Marcus did his big cross in the second scene, the one with the watch, and Priya countered him, a half step right, smooth as a bird adjusting on a wire, and from the wings Aaron could see both of their faces at once, lit and turned to the house. Something in him that had been clenched for two weeks let go.

Afterward, in the lobby with its folding tables and its plate of abandoned cookies, Marcus found him. Marcus, who had never once apologized for anything, who had once argued for fifteen minutes that a missed entrance was the lighting designer's fault, stood holding a paper cup and looking at his shoes.

"I watched the video Dolores took," Marcus said. "Of Tuesday's run. I couldn't see Priya at all and it was my fault. Every time." He looked up. "How do I fix it, the crossing thing? Do I cross less? Do I cross on her lines instead of mine?"

Aaron opened his mouth to answer and found he didn't have one yet. Cross less and the scene went flat; cross more and it was a chessboard with pieces nobody could see. There was some balance in there he hadn't found, and he suspected he wouldn't find it tonight, or maybe before the run ended, which was in six performances.

"Run it with me tomorrow," Aaron said. "You cross, I'll counter, and we'll see what it looks like from the house."

Marcus nodded, drained his coffee, and glanced at the cookie plate.

"Take the oat ones," Aaron said.

The Herreraons' basement smelled like salsa and radiator dust, and by halftime Payton had claimed the corner of the couch closest to the mini-fridge, because that was where the good seat was and because Mrs. Herreron kept drifting past it, and Payton had noticed she was looking for a place to sit down.

"Jax is on fire," Derek said from the floor, pointing his pizza crust at the screen. "Eight straight points. You don't guard a man like that. You pray."

"He's not on fire," said Marcus, Derek's older brother, home from his first semester of college and apparently determined to prove it. "The hot hand is an illusion. There's a famous study. Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky. They looked at the streaks and found nothing."

"They found the Sixers," Derek said.

"They found that a made shot doesn't make the next one more likely. It's coin flips. People see patterns that aren't there."

Payton had been quiet through most of this, half watching the game and half watching Mrs. Herreron finally settle into the folding chair Derek had dragged over for her without saying anything about it. But the argument snagged on something. Her statistics teacher had made them read a paper in October, one of those things she'd assumed she'd forget, except that she hadn't, and now it was surfacing the way a name surfaces at the second introduction.

"That study's been challenged," she said.

Both brothers turned. On the screen, Jax rose for a three and missed, and Derek groaned as though she'd personally knocked the ball away.

"Challenged how?" Marcus said.

"Two thousand eighteen. Miller and Sanjurjo. They reanalyzed it." She was reaching now, pulling it up out of memory, and she was aware of the risk of reaching wrong in front of a room. "They found a flaw in the statistics. A statistical flaw. And they found evidence of streak shooting. Actual streaks."

"So which is it?" Derek demanded. "Fire or no fire?"

"I didn't say it was one or the other."

"You said the hot hand was real."

"I said the study was flawed." Payton felt her face warm, and she also noticed that Mrs. Herreron had leaned forward, interested, her paper cup of cider held in both hands. That was worth more than winning. Still, she didn't back off. "Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky called the hot hand an illusion, and for thirty years everybody believed them. Then somebody checked the math again."

Marcus had his phone out. "Miller and Sanjurjo," he read, half to himself. Payton watched his expression move from dismissal to something more careful, the way a person checks a price and finds it lower than expected. "Huh."

"Huh what?" Derek said.

"Huh, she's right."

"You're just saying that because she's the only one here who can do your homework."

"I'm saying it because I'm reading it." Marcus turned the screen toward Derek, and Derek squinted at it with the concentration of a man being asked to translate a language he'd only ever spoken.

The game came back from a timeout. Mr. Herreron appeared at the top of the stairs with a second tray of wings, having clearly decided the first tray had been expropriated by the teenagers before it ever reached the table, and Derek intercepted it at the bottom step with an apology that was mostly chewing.

"Bring those here," Mrs. Herreron said, patting the arm of her chair, and Derek brought them, and Payton moved her feet so the tray could rest between them.

"This is a hedonistic spread," Marcus announced, surveying the wings, the queso, the seven-layer dip going cold at the edges.

"It's the playoffs," his father said, as if that explained a philosophy of life, which in this house it did.

In the third quarter Jax scored six straight again, and the basement erupted, and Derek pointed at Payton across the chaos of standing bodies. "Hot hand. Say it. Say I'm right."

"I can't say that," she called back over the noise. But she was grinning, and she stood up too, because Jax was pulling up from the corner and there was no sitting through this. "The 2018 paper found evidence of streak shooting. That's all I can give you."

"That's everything!"

"It's not everything. The first study still exists. They're both sitting there. I don't get to pick one just because it's loud in here."

Derek laughed at that, a real laugh, and even Marcus cracked, and Mrs. Herreron reached up and tugged the hem of Payton's sleeve without saying anything, just once, the way you'd touch a sleeve to say stay.

Jax missed the next two shots and hit the one after. Derek threw his hands up as though the universe were mocking him personally. Marcus held up his phone again, as if it were a ruling. Payton sat back down between the wings and the woman who wanted them, and watched the fourth quarter decide nothing yet, all of it still possible, the scoreboard holding both arguments open at once.

"Next commercial," she said, "somebody's getting my numbers."

The flyer had been taped to the gym door since September, curling at one corner: Build a School, Summer in Kestari, two weeks, applications due Friday. Chase stood in front of it with his phone out, taking a picture, when Priya came up behind him with her own reasons for being there.

"You're applying," she said. It wasn't a question. Priya had been saving for the trip since sophomore year, working Saturdays at her uncle's pharmacy, and she'd told anyone who'd listen that her application essay would be about global citizenship. What she hadn't counted on was the new requirement, printed in small type at the bottom of the flyer: applicants had to submit a one-page analysis of why the destination country needed classrooms. No analysis, no interview.

They ended up in the library during lunch, laptops open. The program's information packet linked to two countries, Kestari and a place called Valden, each with a chart labeled population pyramid. Chase had expected something Egyptian, all triangles and mystery. What he got were two bar graphs turned on their sides, age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top, males on the left, females on the right.

"Which one are we supposed to pick?" Priya asked, tapping the screen. Kestari's chart flared outward at the bottom, wide as a church bell, then tapered to almost nothing at the top. Valden's was the opposite, a narrow base widening into a heavy, blocky crown. Chase turned his notebook sideways and sketched both shapes. "Okay," he said slowly, "so Kestari has a ton of people at the bottom. Young people. The bars are widest for the little kids." He counted the age brackets with his pen. "A pyramid with a wide base and a narrow top means a high birth rate and a young population."

"So?"

"So they're going to need schools. Teachers, classrooms, the whole thing. Look at Valden, it's practically upside down. Nobody's having kids, everybody's old." Priya pulled up Valden's government page and found an article about converting a primary school into a residential care facility, and they sat there for a second without saying anything, the implication settling between them: the same shape that made a country build schools could make another country close them.

Chase started drafting his analysis that night, but the drafting went badly. He kept thinking about his grandmother, who had spent last spring convalescing at Riverside after her hip surgery, and how the ward had been full, the hallway lined with wheelchairs, a nurse telling his mother they were short-staffed again. He'd thought of it as bad luck at the time. Now it looked like a pattern you could read off a graph, the way Valden's shape predicted it, and the thought made him uneasy in a way he couldn't quite name, a low-grade malaise that had nothing to do with the essay and everything to do with what his own country's pyramid must look like underneath the numbers.

The next day he found Priya in the chemistry lab before class. "I wrote it," he said, "but I cut the last paragraph." He'd drafted a conclusion arguing that building schools in Kestari was obviously the right priority, more futures, more potential. Reading it back, it sounded like a person who had never met anyone over seventy. His grandmother had spent her convalescence teaching him gin rummy and telling him about the flood of '87; her value wasn't in her future productivity. He had tried to hold both ideas, the graph's arithmetic and that memory, in the same paragraph, and the paragraph had refused.

"So what's your position?" Priya asked, not looking up from her titration. She had her own problem: her essay draft was all feeling and no evidence, and she knew it, and she needed what Chase had figured out about the shapes. He slid his notebook across the bench, the two sketches side by side, Kestari wide at the base and Valden narrow. "Kestari needs the classrooms. That part's clear, the data says so, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't." He paused, watching the burette drip pink into her flask. "But which country needs more, schools or nursing homes, that's a different question than which matters more, and I don't think the graph can answer the second one. I'm going to write that I'm sure about the first part and not sure about the rest."

Priya copied the sketches without asking, which was fair, since he'd shown them to her. "They might not like uncertainty in an application," she said. "They want conviction. Nascent philanthropists, all of them." Chase laughed, and the bell rang, and he gathered his notebook, the drawings still wet where Priya's sleeve had smudged them, Kestari's wide base blurred into Valden's narrow one at the spine of the page.

The kitchen table had been Samantha's since eight that morning, and by noon it was a landscape of highlighters, torn notebook pages, and her mother's anatomy textbook, borrowed without asking. Her placement exam was in two days. If she scored well, she'd skip the intro biology lecture and go straight into the second-semester course, which mattered only because it would free a slot for the poetry seminar she actually wanted. So she sat there, rehearsing the central dogma out loud, because the test had an oral component and she could not yet say the words in order without stumbling.

"DNA gets copied into RNA," she said to the room. "Transcription. Then the RNA gets read three letters at a time, and each three letters makes one amino acid, and the amino acids chain up into a protein. Translation."

"Who are you talking to?" Her brother Danny stood in the doorway with a peanut butter sandwich, thirteen and incorrigibly curious about anything that looked like suffering.

"Myself. Go away."

"You sound lugubrious," he said, which was their father's word, deployed whenever one of them moped. "Like a funeral for a science."

"It's not a funeral." But she was saying it wrong somehow, and she knew it. She could recite the steps and still not hold them together, the way you could know every word of a poem in a language you didn't speak. She flapped a hand at the chair opposite her. "Sit. Be an audience."

He sat, chewing, and she started over. "Okay. In the nucleus, an enzyme unzips the DNA, and it builds a messenger RNA strand off one template. That's transcription. The mRNA travels out to a ribosome, and transfer RNAs bring amino acids that match the codons, three bases at a time. The ribosome stitches them together." She paused. "That's it. That's translation."

"Okay," Danny said, in a tone that adjudicated nothing. "So why is it called the Krebs cycle?"

She blinked. "What?"

"Mom's book. That page you keep flipping past. It says Krebs cycle. Why does it have a guy's name on it if it's just, like, how cells work?"

Samantha turned the book toward herself. There it was, a wheel of reactions, citrate at the top, and she had been skipping it because the exam outline said it was covered in the second-semester course, the one she was trying to test into. She read the caption twice. "It says Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937," she said slowly. "And Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it." She looked up. "Sixteen years later. He figured it out and then waited sixteen years."

"So why only Krebs? What about Johnson?"

The caption didn't say. Danny leaned over the book, leaving a smudge of peanut butter near the margin, and Samantha felt something shift, small and unwelcome. She had been treating the whole subject as a machine that had always existed, facts the way water exists, and now the machine had builders in it, and the builders had been people who got prizes or didn't, and one of them had apparently vanished from the name.

"I don't know," she said. "Maybe he died. Maybe he did less of it. Maybe it's unfair."

"You always say life's not fair like that's an answer."

"That's not an answer, it's a weather report." She pulled the book back and stared at the wheel again, and the question she'd been circling all morning came back with a different weight. She had wanted to memorize the mechanism. Now she wanted to tell it, actually tell it, the way you'd tell how something was found. "Okay. New version. Listen and tell me if you follow."

Danny nodded, sandwich suspended.

"Everything in you is built from instructions, and the instructions stay locked in the nucleus, like an original document you don't want smudged. So the cell copies the part it needs. Transcription makes the copy, and the copy is messenger RNA, and it goes out through a pore to a ribosome, which is basically a factory sitting in the cytoplasm. The ribosome reads the copy in threes. Translation. Each three-letter word calls for one amino acid, and the amino acids get linked in that order, and the order makes the protein, and the protein is hemoglobin or an enzyme or keratin, whatever the cell ordered." She stopped. "And the enzymes that do all of it, including the ones in that cycle on the page, they're proteins that were made the same way, by other instructions. It's all built out of itself."

Danny frowned. "So who built the first one?"

"I don't know that either." She heard her own surprise at how little it bothered her. For two days she had wanted certainty, clean steps, a mechanism she could recite like a train schedule. Now the honest version had a seam running through it, names and dates and gaps, and it felt truer in her mouth than the recitation had. She would learn the rest of the gaps in the second semester. That was, she realized, the whole reason to take it.

"So did I pass?" Danny asked. "As an audience?"

"You were terrible. You ate through the second half."

He grinned and closed the book on her finger, gently, and slid the whole thing toward his side of the table.

Isaac had taped the diagram to the refrigerator door so he would see it every time he went for water, which was often, because the kitchen was the only room in the house with decent light since his father had started sleeping through the afternoons. The diagram showed a long, wavering strand labeled mRNA and a lumpy shape sitting on it like a bead on a wire. He'd redrawn it twice. Both times the lumpy shape came out looking like a potato, and both times his sister Dara had laughed at it.

"You're going to fail," she said now, from the table, where she was ostensibly doing her own homework but mostly watching him.

"I'm not going to fail." He uncapped a marker and held it over the paper without writing anything. The placement exam was in nine days, the one that would let him skip the intro biology lecture his schedule couldn't hold, and the packet the college had mailed described transcription and translation in a prose so dense it read like a legal contract. He'd underlined a sentence about RNA polymerase and then un-underlined it, because underlining had started to feel like a ritual rather than understanding.

"Explain it to me, then," Dara said. She was fourteen and relentless. "You always say if you can explain something you actually know it."

He could feel the moment stretch. Their father's furlough had entered its eleventh week, and the house had gone quiet in a way that made any conversation sound louder than it was, so that even Dara's challenge seemed to hang in the air. He sat down across from her and pulled the diagram between them.

"Okay. First part, transcription. The cell copies a gene. DNA stays in the nucleus like a reference copy at a library, the kind you can't check out. The copy that travels is mRNA, messenger RNA." He tapped the wavering strand. "It carries the instructions out to where the protein gets built."

"That part I get. It's the second part that's garbage." She rotated the diagram toward herself, squinting at the potato. "What is this thing?"

He had written "ribosome" beneath it in small letters, and he looked at those letters and realized that although he had copied them faithfully, he had never once managed to say out loud what the ribosome did. In the packet it was a sentence he'd read maybe thirty times: something about movement, something about joining. He knew it moved along the mRNA, and he knew the words amino acid and peptide bond were in there somewhere, but when he tried to assemble them they scattered like beads dropped on a floor.

"Give me a second."

"Nine seconds," Dara said, and started counting.

He looked past her at the window, where their mother's wind chimes moved without sound. In his mind he tried to picture the potato, the strand, the small units waiting. His grandmother used to restring her broken necklaces at this table, and he could still see her hands, a saucer of loose amber beads beside her, her thumb pressing each one down onto the thread in order. She had a pattern laid out on a paper towel, little pencil marks, and she never looked up, just moved along the marks and pressed bead after bead onto the string until the necklace was whole.

"Stop counting." He took the marker and, on the back of the diagram, drew a thread with pencil marks on it and a thumb above the first mark. "It's like this. Somebody restringing a necklace. The paper towel with the pencil marks is the mRNA, the pattern. The beads are amino acids, the building blocks. The person threading, the thing doing the work, that's the ribosome, the potato." He drew a bead going onto the thread, then another. "It moves along the pattern, and as it goes, it joins the amino acids together with peptide bonds, one after another, building the whole protein chain." He looked up. "That's translation. That's the whole thing."

Dara studied the drawing, her mouth slightly open, and he understood that he had just performed the exact test he'd set himself, because she had known nothing an hour ago and now she was nodding.

"Wait," she said slowly. "So the protein is the necklace."

"The protein is the necklace."

She picked up the marker and added a clasp to the end of his thread. "Grandma would like that you used her beads."

He almost laughed, and then didn't, because the reason he needed to skip the intro lecture, the reason the schedule mattered at all, was the scholarship condition he hadn't told either of them about yet, the one requiring him to hold a campus job from the first week. He put the cap back on the marker.

"Nine days," Dara said.

"Nine days." He taped the necklace drawing to the refrigerator beside the potato, over the note from the plant about his father's insurance paperwork, and went to fill his glass again.

Tristan had been sitting at the corner table of the coffee shop for two hours with one cold flat white and a laptop open to the UCAS application. Six courses sat in his list. The system allowed only five. He had read the page four times, hoping the number would change, and it had not.

Nadia slid into the seat across from him, uninvited, carrying a green tea she barely touched. She had her own list folded into the pocket of her denim jacket, and she pulled it out and flattened it against the table so he could see that hers had five lines, five course codes, no hesitation.

"How did you cut yours?" he asked.

"I didn't cut anything. I never had a sixth." She tapped his screen. "Five courses maximum. That's the whole allowance. And it doesn't rank them, you know. The list is unordered. No order of preference. They just sit there, all equal."

"So the sixth one is just gone?"

"The sixth one never existed, officially." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she said it.

The sixth course was mathematics at a university three hundred miles north. The other five were all within an hour of his mother's flat: two economics, one statistics, one joint honours, one engineering with a foundation year. He had built the list the way you build a wall, each choice braced against the others so nothing could fall. He wanted to subsume the whole decision under a single principle, and the principle he had chosen was proximity. His mother's shifts had been cut in October. Nobody had said out loud what that meant for the spring, and nobody needed to.

"I could drop the foundation year one," he said. "The engineering. That's the weakest."

"You said it was the safety."

"Safe and weak aren't opposites."

"Fine. Drop the one far away, then." Nadia said it while looking at the window, at a man struggling with an umbrella that had turned inside out. She had wanted him to apply north since September, and she had never once said so directly, which was its own kind of statement. Anxiety about choices was endemic this term; half their year had it, teachers kept saying so in assemblies. But hers ran quieter than most, and it surfaced mainly as opinions about other people's decisions.

"It's not that far," Tristan said. "Four hours by train."

"Then keep it."

He looked at the screen for a while. The five-course limit was not a moral test, he told himself, and yet it behaved like one, forcing a ranking onto a system that officially refused ranking. He could keep the wall of five nearby courses, or he could trade one brick for something he actually wanted and let the structure carry a gap. Both were defensible. He could not make both true at once, and no amount of reasoning would make the sixth slot appear.

He deleted the foundation year course. The list rebalanced itself, five items, four of them close and one far, all listed flat and equal, no preference shown anywhere on the page, which was either a mercy or an erasure. He pressed submit before he could reconsider, and the confirmation banner came up green.

"There," Nadia said. "Done."

"Not done. Now we wait."

"Then you can start drinking your coffee like a person." She pushed it toward him. He lifted the cup. It was cold, and he drank it anyway.

The bell over the door of Kessler's Corner Store rang twice before Nicholas noticed it, once for the woman buying lottery tickets and once for nobody, just the wind. He had spread his homework across two bags of sunflower seeds near the register end of the counter, where Mr. Kessler let him sit on weeknights, and he was staring at a graph he had drawn for the fourth time.

The problem was from math club. Yesterday, in Room 214, Priya and Marcus had squared off over the area trapped between a line and a parabola, and their answers had come out different, and different not by a sign flip but by some stranger wrongness, as though two shapes had been measured and one of them belonged to a different problem entirely. Ms. Okafor, whom the whole club half-ironically lionized, had refused to settle it. "Figure out who's wrong and why," she had said, and left early for a department meeting, and the club had dissolved into argument and then into the hallway.

Nicholas worked Saturdays here, sweeping and restocking, and tonight he had stayed past closing to think, because at home there was only the apartment's noise and here there was the refrigerator's hum and the glossy poster by the ice cream case, a nature scene of a river winding through forest, captioned with words like riparian and biome, which the store's supplier had printed to make the store look wholesome. He looked at the poster now the way he looked at the graph. A river had banks. The water lay between an upper bank and a lower one. If you wanted to know how much water, you did not measure the banks separately and add them up.

He wrote the line's equation above the parabola's on his paper. Between the two crossing points, the line sat on top; the parabola curled beneath it like a cupped hand. Priya, he remembered, had integrated the parabola minus the line, because she liked reading her equations left to right in the order they'd been printed in the problem. Marcus had done the reverse. On the interval between the crossings, one function was upper and one was lower, and the area was the integral of the upper function minus the lower function, taken across that whole stretch. Nicholas said it to himself in almost those words, quietly, and Mr. Kessler, locking the cigarette cabinet, glanced over.

"Talking to yourself now."

"Finding area," Nicholas said. "Between curves. You take the top one minus the bottom one over the whole stretch between where they cross. Priya flipped it."

"So she's wrong."

"She's wrong," Nicholas said, but he slowed on it, because Priya was not wrong the way a person is wrong about a fact. She was wrong the way a person is wrong about a direction, and directions could be stood in. He remembered her face when the numbers disagreed, the flat refusal to be embarrassed, the way she had said "one of us measured something real and one of us didn't." He had admired that more than Marcus's quick answer, which had been right and smug at once. Marcus had computed first and thought second, and Priya had thought first and computed into a mirror.

The bell rang again. Nicholas looked up and Priya herself came in, still in her track warmups, hair wet from the gym, hunting the fridge for the lime soda she liked. She saw his papers fanned across the counter and came over without asking.

"Please tell me you solved it," she said. "It kept me up."

"The line is above the parabola between the crossings," Nicholas said. "So the area is the upper minus the lower, integrated over that interval. You did it the other way around. You didn't get a different shape. You got the same shape counted as if the ground were the ceiling."

Priya pulled the paper toward her and read his work, chewing the inside of her cheek. "Same two curves," she said. "Same crossings. And Marcus just happened to write his in the right order."

"He got the right number. But he couldn't say why the order mattered. He just said 'top minus bottom' like it was a rule someone told him."

"And you can?"

Nicholas looked at the poster by the ice cream case, the river lying between its two banks, filling exactly the space the land allowed. "I think so," he said. "But I want to check the case where the curves cross in the middle of the interval, because then which one is upper switches partway through, and I don't know yet whether you split it into pieces or something else happens. That part I haven't got."

Priya sat down on the stool Mr. Kessler kept for slow afternoons and uncapped her soda. "So you're saying Marcus is right and also can't be trusted, and I'm wrong and also kind of right."

"I'm saying the top minus the bottom is what's true, and everything else is us arguing about who deserves credit for a river," Nicholas said, and nodded at the poster. Priya looked at it, laughed once, and pulled a fresh sheet of paper out of his binder.

"Draw the switching case," she said. "I'll do the algebra."

On Monday Mr. Okafor announced that the ten-minute plays would be staged Friday night in the black box theater, which gave Amelia four days to finish a draft, hear it read, and revise it. The assignment required a moment from her own life, and she had chosen the night last spring when her father sat in the parked car outside the driver's license office and told her he was moving to Phoenix in June. She had written seven pages over the weekend, working at the kitchen table until one in the morning, and she believed the script was finished.

Tuesday, Mr. Okafor collected the pages and assigned casts. A junior named Dante got the part of the father, and a quiet girl from her economics class, Priya, got the part of Amelia-as-character, called simply Girl. When Amelia asked what happened next, Dante said, "Table read tomorrow, right? Where we all sit and read the script out loud so we can hear how the dialogue sounds before we do any staging." Mr. Okafor nodded and said to bring pencils. Amelia said she didn't need to change anything, and Dante looked at her the way people look at a homeowner describing a house they have only seen from the street.

The table read was Wednesday, fourth period, in the drama room with its racks of costumes and its smell of dust and hairspray. Eleven students sat around a rectangle of folding tables pushed together. Amelia took the seat nearest the window so she could watch the parking lot instead of the readers. Priya's voice was smaller than she expected, and the first two pages went fine. Then Dante read the line Amelia had been proudest of, the one where the father says, "I have impugned my own integrity by staying silent this long," and the room went still in the wrong way. Nobody laughed. It was worse than laughing. A boy named Marcus looked down at his copy of the parking map he was supposed to hold as a prop and turned the page too early, twice.

Amelia kept her eyes on a gray sedan outside until Dante reached the end of the scene. Her father had never talked like that. Her father had said, "I should have told you before I signed the lease," and then he had apologized for the lease, not for himself, and she had understood in that moment that his apology was ductile, something she could bend into whatever shape she needed for the next three years if she wanted to. She had written the stiff sentence because the truth sounded too small, like a city ordinance posted on a chain-link fence, technically correct and unread.

"Can we stop," she said. Mr. Okafor lifted his hand and the readers stopped. "Page four," Amelia said. "Cross out the line about integrity. He just says he should have told her before he signed the lease." Dante asked whether that wasn't blaming the lease instead of himself, and Amelia said that was the point, that was exactly what he had done, and Dante wrote it in the margin. Priya asked whether the Girl character would let that pass, and Amelia said she had, out loud, she had said "okay" and turned up the radio, and the radio had been playing a song she still could not hear in grocery stores.

They read the last three pages. The smaller lines held better than the polished ones. When Priya said "okay" and Marcus, unprompted, made a small turning motion with his hand as if adjusting a volume knob, Amelia wrote volume knob in the margin and underlined it. Mr. Okafor said they had twenty minutes left and told each writer to take notes on what their ears had caught. Amelia wrote until her hand cramped. Some of the script was true and some of it was a better-shaped version of true, and she could not always tell from the page which was which. At the table she could hear the difference, though she could not have said what the difference was made of.

Thursday night she retyped the play in her room, cutting four lines and adding two. She left the ending where the Girl says "okay" and the lights go down on the radio playing. She did not add a scene where the Girl forgives him or a scene where she doesn't, because she had not decided, three years later, on Friday mornings when his number came up on her phone, whether the deciding was finished.

Friday at six, the black box theater filled with forty folding chairs. Priya sat on a wooden bench that was supposed to be the front seat of a car, and Marcus stood behind a music stand holding a boom box that was not plugged in. Dante sat in a chair beside the bench with his copy of the script on his knees. Amelia stood at the light board in the back. The house went dark and she pushed the slider up halfway, the way she had practiced, and Priya said the first line.

The museum's French Revolution wing smelled like dust and radiator heat, and Jordan had been standing in front of a diorama of the storming of the Bastille for ten minutes without writing anything. His essay was due Monday. Not a report on the Revolution, his teacher had said, but a historiographical essay: an essay about the historians, about how views of 1789 had shifted since 1800, and why. He had three pages of quotations from Carlyle and Aulard and Simon Schama, and no idea what any of it added up to.

He moved to a glass case holding a small printing press, the label explaining that pamphlets had spread revolutionary ideas faster than the authorities could suppress them. That was the kind of detail his paper was full of, and the kind his teacher kept crossing out. This is about events, not historians, she had written in the margin of his draft, in green ink. He needed perspectives, arguments, revisions. He needed, apparently, to care about who had told the story and what they wanted.

His grandfather had offered to pick him up at four, which gave Jordan two hours. He sat on a bench beneath a portrait of some deputy in a grandiose collar and opened his notebook. The early writers after 1800 had mostly mourned or celebrated, depending on which side their families had been on. Later, Marxists read the Revolution as a bourgeois seizure of power. Later still, revisionists questioned whether anything so tidy had happened at all. He wrote the sentences and they felt like inventory, a warehouse of opinions with no one inside them.

At four his grandfather was early, waiting in the lobby with his coat still buttoned. On the drive home he asked what Jordan had found, and Jordan admitted the problem: every historian seemed certain, and they all disagreed. His grandfather laughed and said that was the point, that he'd written a paper like that himself once, in 1960, his second year of college.

"You wrote about historians?" Jordan asked.

"About the Cold War. There was a book the year before, 1959, William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy. Started the whole revisionist school." His grandfather changed lanes, unhurried. "Williams argued that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War."

Jordan stared at him. "An American blamed the United States?"

"That's what the book said."

"Was he right?"

His grandfather didn't answer for a long moment. "People argued about it for twenty years. Some of them still do."

When they got to the house, Jordan followed him inside, essay forgotten. The book itself was gone, sold in a move decades ago, but his grandfather remembered the fight it started in his seminar, how half the room thought Williams had committed treason against history and the other half thought he'd finally told the truth. Jordan sat at the kitchen table taking notes on a napkin. What struck him was not who was right. It was that Williams had looked at the same documents everyone else had, the same speeches and cables, and seen something different, and that the difference had lasted, had forced every historian after him to say where they stood.

That night he spread his sources across his desk. The Marxists had a framework, the revisionists had a corrective, the early memoirists had their wounds. He began a new draft arguing that each generation's account of the Revolution told him as much about the generation as about the Revolution, and that the honest move was not to pick a winner but to say plainly what each view revealed and concealed. He could see, dimly, where this left him: with an essay that ended in uncertainty. His teacher might call that a failure to conclude. He kept typing anyway.

At one in the morning his cursor sat blinking after the last sentence, which was about how the historiography had no ending, only revisions. He read it twice. Then he opened his phone and texted his grandfather: was there ever a book that settled it? He waited, watching the screen. The reply came as a photo, the napkin from the kitchen table, on which his grandfather had written a single word, underlined twice. Jordan leaned closer to make it out.

Thomas had until eight o'clock, which was when his mother would drive Marisol home and when, by unspoken agreement, the physics quiz would stop being something he could still prepare for. It was Tuesday evening in the backyard, the grass still giving off the smell of the rain that had come through at four, and the only light came from the kitchen window and a citronella candle his father insisted worked. Thomas had the textbook open on the dry part of the picnic table, a bag of tennis balls at his feet, and the strong suspicion that projectile motion was about to ruin his grade.

He was trying to expiate a semester of doing just enough, the homework copied half-understood, the labs passed off as group work. His father had used the word once, lightly, about his own year off after high school, and Thomas had looked it up and found it heavier than his father had made it sound, all that guilt worked off through effort. Anyway, tonight he was throwing tennis balls at the fence and writing down where they landed.

The rule he kept circling was that the horizontal and vertical motions didn't interfere. The ball went sideways at a constant rate, the way a puck on ice would, while at the same time it fell the way anything falls, faster and faster, and you solved them separately and only married the two answers at the end through time. It felt like a lie until he tested it. He tossed one ball gently and one hard, marked the landing spots with his heel in the soft ground by the fence, and found that both hit within a hand's width of the same moment, thud, thud, almost together. The hard-thrown one had simply gone farther before the ground caught it. He wrote it down, the pencil wet where the grass had brushed it.

Marisol arrived at six-thirty, cutting through the gate with her phone in her hand and a plastic binder under her arm. She also had a history outline due tomorrow, a five-paragraph thing on Iran as a theocracy, which she claimed she could write in her head while walking, and she said this in the slightly disaffected voice she had been using all spring, the one that said school was a performance she was tired of giving. But she sat down at the picnic table anyway, which Thomas took as the real signal. She was worried about the quiz too, though she'd never have said so plainly.

"Look at this," she said, tilting the phone at him. It was a photo she'd taken of her older brother's diagram from when he took the class, two parallel plates, one marked positive and one marked negative, with arrows drawn between them pointing from the negative plate toward the positive one. Her brother had gotten an A, she said, so the diagram had to be right. "I've been staring at it for an hour and I can't make it match the textbook."

Thomas squinted at it in the candlelight, then carried it closer to the kitchen window so he could see. He was supposed to know this; the quiz covered it after the projectile problems. He thought about the tennis balls, about how you had to ask what a thing would actually do rather than what a tidy picture suggested. There was a way to check the diagram that didn't depend on trusting anybody's arrows.
