Elizabeth copied the call number from the spine when he set it down. She carried the Manual to her table and opened it, expecting bureaucracy, and found instead a kind of architecture. The footnotes were not decoration; they were a second argument running beneath the first, a quiet ledger of debts. Each note said: I learned this here, from this person, on this page, and you may go check. She thought of Mr. Okafor's red line, and of her uncle, and of DeShaun, and understood suddenly that an argument was not a fist. It was a claim standing on the record of what it owed.

She worked until the overhead lights clicked to their evening half. First she drafted a thesis she could actually defend: that transfer to adult court, whatever its logic for violent offenses, should require a judge's individual finding rather than automatic prosecution by statute, because DeShaun's case had turned on a mandatory statute and a judge who said, on the record, that his hands were tied. Then the footnotes, numbered, each one a small confession of source. When she reached for the case citation she found she could not remember whether the statute came from 2016 or 2018, and she wrote both possibilities on the pad and left a note to herself: check. The uncertainty did not feel like failure. It felt like honesty with a number attached.

She tried to explain this to Tomas on the way out, proselytizing a little, she admitted, the way anyone does after a conversion. "It's like the syntax of trust," she said. "Where the note goes, and what comes first, and what you admit you don't know. It's not sectarian, it's not one side's ritual. It belongs to whoever uses it honestly."

"You're describing paperwork," Tomas said, holding the door.

But walking home under the stripped maples, carrying the bag with eleven days of work in it, Elizabeth kept thinking about the ledger underneath, about 1906, about all the dead people who had argued in notes and been checked and been right or been corrected. And she thought again of the afternoon she stayed home, thirteen years old, obedient, sure that following a rule was the same as supporting a person. At the corner of Bergen and Sixth she stopped, took out her phone, and dialed the number for the county records office, the one she had found in the library's database but been afraid to use.

"Records division," a voice said. "We closed at five."

"Tomorrow, then," Elizabeth said, and put the phone away, and the manual, checked out in her name, sat in the bag on her hip, already three days overdue.

Mia had shared the video during first period without watching it twice: a flooded street, a woman clinging to a doorframe, water the color of milk chocolate, and a caption that said it had happened that morning in a city three states away. By lunch, forty-one people had shared it from her page alone, and Priya was sitting across from her in the cafeteria holding her phone like evidence in a trial.

"Look at this," Priya said, sliding the phone across the table. "Reverse image search. The same clip is from four years ago. Different flood. Different country." She said it quietly, the way you say something when you don't want the whole table to hear that your friend is the problem.

Mia wanted to defend herself, and she hated that the first thing she reached for was an excuse rather than a question. The video had felt true. The woman's face had felt true. But feeling true and being true were apparently two different currencies, and she had been spending one as though it were the other. Down the table, Devon and Marcus were arguing about computer science homework, their voices rising over the clatter of trays. "It's sequel," Devon insisted. "Everyone says sequel." Marcus shook his head with the sullen certainty of someone who believed he was the only serious person in the room. "You spell it out. S-Q-L. That's the whole point."

"It was first called SEQUEL," said a sophomore named Elena, without looking up from her laptop. She was someone Mia had never spoken to, pale and precise, the kind of person who kept her opinions filed rather than loose. "SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and it was first called SEQUEL." She closed the laptop halfway, reconsidering, as if she had said more than she intended. Devon and Marcus stared at her, then at each other, and neither conceded, which struck Mia as its own small lesson about how facts arrive and how rarely they settle anything.

Later, in the library during her free period, Mia opened the search engine's image page and dragged Priya's screenshot into the box. The results loaded slowly. She watched the spinner rotate and thought about how the woman in the video would never know that her worst day was being recaptioned for strangers, that her fear had become a kind of raw material. When the matches appeared, they went back years: a news article, a humanitarian site, a blog post that had transliterated the original caption into English badly enough that the woman's name had become something it wasn't. Mia checked the date on the news article twice, then a third time, because she did not trust herself to be the one doing the checking.

She was still looking at the screen when Mr. Okafor, the vice principal, sat down two seats away and opened a folder. She recognized the paper inside before he said anything: a printed screenshot of her post, forwarded by a parent who had called the school in a panic because she had family in the city named in the caption. "Do you know how many calls we got?" he asked. Mia said she didn't. "Nine. Nine families scared for no reason." He did not raise his voice, which somehow made it worse, and she understood that her complicity was not something she could uninstall with a delete button, because the sharing had already done its work, and the work was out in the world wearing her name.

She took down the post. She typed a correction, deleted it, typed it again, and finally posted something short: the video was old, the flood was in another country, she was sorry for the scare. Some people thanked her. Someone replied with a single laughing emoji. Someone else said she was covering something up, and she watched that reply collect likes faster than her correction had, which felt like watching water rise in a street she recognized.

Walking home, she found Priya at the corner by the convenience store, waiting as though she had known Mia would come this way. "You didn't have to post the correction," Priya said. "Nobody does that." Mia said she wasn't sure it had helped. Priya pulled out her phone and showed her a different video, brand new, flooding a street that looked almost exactly like the first one, captioned with a city and a date. "So," Priya said, holding it between them. "Before I share this one. Show me what you do."

The seminar room on the third floor of Hollis Hall had one window that faced the parking lot, which struck Jeremy as either poor planning or an accident of prophecy. Twelve students sat around a table with the professor, who had assigned them a city council transcript from a town called Fenwick, where the council had spent four hours arguing about whether to raise the downtown parking fee from two dollars to three. Jeremy had read it twice on the bus, twice more at his desk, and had underlined so many passages that the underlining had stopped meaning anything.

"Who wants to open," Dr. Okonkwo said, not quite making it a question.

Priya opened. She had prepared, which was her way of saying she had prepared. "The fee is too low," she said. "Three dollars still wouldn't cover the maintenance, and the overflow parking spills into the Elm Street neighborhood, so residents can't park in front of their own houses. The fee should be five."

Marcus countered that five dollars would push commuters to the mall on the highway, which would kill the downtown businesses, which would shrink the tax base, which would, he implied, eventually cause the heat death of Fenwick. A girl whose name Jeremy kept forgetting argued for a sliding scale by income. Someone else proposed validation stickers for local shops. The debate had the shape of an archipelago: eleven separate islands of argument, a thin channel of civility between each, no bridge anywhere.

Jeremy had not prepared a position. What he had was a memory, from the night before, of his roommate Dev scrolling past a meme and saying, "Oh, that's the Meadows thing," and refusing to elaborate because his show was starting. Jeremy had typed the name into the library database at midnight and found a 1997 essay about leverage points. He had read it in the common room under a diaphanous curtain of moths swarming the porch light, and certain sentences had rearranged the furniture in his head without asking.

He raised his hand, mostly to stop Priya from parametrizing the fee schedule any further. "Can I ask whether we're solving the right thing?"

"That's not a real objection," Priya said. "Everything is the right thing if you care about it."

"Sure. But the council spent four hours on the fee. Nobody asked why the city is organized so everyone drives downtown alone and leaves at five." He was aware his voice had gone up, and lowered it. "There's this essay. Donella Meadows, 1997, on leverage points. She argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much. Changing a system's goals, or the paradigm underneath it, changes the most."

Dr. Okonkwo's eyebrows did something small and interested, which Jeremy chose to read as encouragement.

"So the fee is a number," he went on. "We could fight about two dollars or three or five forever, and Meadows would say we're turning a dial that barely moves anything. If Fenwick actually wanted fewer cars downtown, the goal would have to change. Or the paradigm. The whole picture of what the street is for."

Marcus leaned back. "That's convenient. Your essay says the thing you want to argue can't be costed out."

"It's not my essay."

"It's also unfalsifiable," the girl whose name was, Jeremy now remembered, Talia, said pleasantly. "You can't run the experiment twice."

This was, Jeremy had to admit, true, and he said so, which in his experience of seminars was a tactical error, because admitting things invited more of them. Priya asked whether a paradigm was just a word people used when they didn't want to do math. Dr. Okonkwo asked whether Meadows herself had said anything about how paradigms get changed, and Jeremy had to say he'd gotten to the last section at two in the morning and remembered only the part about paradigms changing all the time anyway, in societies, without anyone planning it, which was either hopeful or terrifying depending on the century.

The problem, as Jeremy framed it for himself on the walk back across the quad, was that he believed two things at once. He believed Meadows, that the fee debate was a hall of small mirrors, and he believed Priya, that the residents of Elm Street needed relief this year and the fee was the lever actually attached to the machine. He had spent the seminar trying to get the two ideas to sit in the same chair, and they had refused, and he had ended by proposing, out loud, almost by accident, that Fenwick raise the fee to three and put the revenue toward a downtown where the fee itself could eventually shrink, which Marcus called incoherent and Talia called the only honest position anyone had taken all morning and Priya called a cop-out. He did not know which of them was right. He suspected that not knowing was, for the moment, the most accurate thing he had.

The parking lot below the seminar window had been nearly empty all morning, and Jeremy noticed, as they filed out, that it was nearly full. Somewhere a bell rang the hour. He stopped at the railing, took out his phone, and, instead of opening anything, just photographed the lot, rows of cars baking in the October sun.

"For the paradigm," Talia said, passing behind him.

He looked at the photo. "I was going to say for the fee."

"Same picture," she said, and walked on toward the science building, leaving him holding the rail and the phone and, for once, both of them.

The dryer hummed like it was withholding an opinion, and Liam spread the two leases across the folding table as if they were maps of the same country drawn by enemies. His mother's laundry spun in the machine behind him, three loads of it, because she had taken the double shift and he had taken the keys. He was sixteen and about to have opinions about rent.

The first lease was for a basement apartment near campus, six hundred a month plus hydro, which the landlord's daughter, Priya from his physics class, had estimated at forty in a bad winter month. The second was a shared room above the bakery, five fifty, utilities included, but with a clause near the end demanding first and last month's rent plus a damage deposit of eight hundred dollars. He read it twice, then a third time, because eight hundred was not a number you could produce by feeling optimistic about it.

"This is more than the rent," he said to Priya, who had come along partly to help and partly because her own laundry was frankly ancient and her mother trusted Liam's mother's machines more than their own. She set her coffee on the table, dangerously close to clause fourteen.

"My cousin got hit with one of those last year," she said. "Turned out they can't even do that here. In Ontario a landlord can take a rent deposit, but only up to one month's rent, or one rent period if you pay more often, and a damage deposit they can't charge at all."

"Called what? A damage deposit?"

"That's what it says. They're not allowed."

Liam sat with that. He had assumed, the way he assumed about taxes and lane changes, that the paperwork knew what it was doing. The idea that a printed clause could simply not be allowed felt like finding out the referee was also a player. He took out his phone, checked, and the provincial page said the same thing Priya had, in the same unhurried way laws have of being obvious once you find them. He felt briefly powerful, then less so, because knowing it was not allowed did not tell him what to say to a man who controlled a room he wanted.

Last summer flashed back to him uninvited: his uncle arguing with a contractor on the porch, waving a invoice for indemnity he insisted he'd never agreed to, and finally saying, "Fine, take it, but I'm never calling you again." His uncle had paid to keep the peace and lost the peace anyway. Liam had watched from the steps and thought it was about money. He understood now it had been about which losses you could live with.

"So do I tell him the clause is illegal," Liam said, "and risk him giving the room to someone quieter, or do I pay it and hate myself monthly?"

"Neither of those is a math answer," Priya said. "You've done the math. That's the easy part." She was right; the totals were done, the bakery room cheaper even before the eight hundred, the basement cheaper after it if he stayed two years, which he could not promise anyone, least of all himself. The comparison was clean and the decision was not, and he had not expected those to be different things.

He folded his mother's towels, matching corners with more attention than towels required, because his hands needed a task while the rest of him worked. He would ask the landlord, politely, whether they could adjust the deposit to what was actually allowed, and he would keep the basement lease folded in his back pocket as the second life, the one where he paid more for hydro and less for hope. Whichever way it went, something would be given up, and he could not yet say which something he would mind less. He stacked the last towel, and Priya asked if the dryer had always made that sound, and they both stood listening to it knock, once, twice, like a small animal with a question of its own.

The rental truck followed them the whole way, and Morgan kept checking the side mirror to make sure it was still Dad behind the wheel and not some stranger hauling her boxes to a town she had agreed to only twice out loud. In the passenger seat, her grandmother sat with a road atlas open on her knees even though the phone was navigating, because she liked to know where she was in a way the phone never told her.

"You could have flown ahead with your mother," her grandmother said. "This is forty hours of road for a girl your age."

"I wanted to drive." Morgan had her own reason, though she had not said it in the car. Priya and Denae were meeting her at the pancake place on Route 9 at noon, one last breakfast before the truck got too far east to turn around. That was the plan. The plan had a hole in it, which was that after the pancakes there was nothing but four hundred more miles.

Grandma Ruth had her own want, and it had to do with the boxes in the truck. She was moving into the new house with them, giving up the apartment she had kept alone for nineteen years, and twice this morning she had asked whether the movers had wrapped her writing desk. She wanted, Morgan understood, to be the one who decided what got brought and what got left, and she was doing it by making lists on the back of a grocery receipt.

They stopped at the pancake place for fifty minutes. Priya was late and Denae was early and they split a short stack three ways, and Denae made a joke about Morgan's new town that started funny and turned vitriolic halfway through, about the people there, the kind of people who would love her, the kind who had never met her. Morgan laughed at the first half and then stopped laughing and said, "You don't know them either." Nobody said anything for a while after that. Priya took a photo of the three of them at the table, and it came out blurry, and she said she'd take another one, and then didn't.

The night before, they had all sat on Denae's garage roof, the way they had since seventh grade, and Priya had said the thing Morgan was now thinking about in the car. "It's not like we'll be strangers," Priya had said. "We'll text every day." And Denae had said, "No, we won't, we'll mean to," and it had sounded harsh but Morgan had known it was the more honest sentence. Friendship, she was beginning to see, was not only a feeling. It was a set of conditions, some of which nobody chose.

She had learned the actual evidence for that in June, killing time in the library while her mother packed dishes. She had been reading about college, about how to make friends in a place where nobody knew her, and she found a study from 1950 by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter, and Kurt Back, done in student housing. The students had all been assigned their rooms more or less at random, which was what made it a study rather than an accident. The researchers found that people living closer together were more likely to become friends. People whose doors were near a shared stairway became friends more often too, because the stairway made them pass each other. Morgan read it twice. It wasn't shallow, she decided, or if it was, it was the shallow part of something real. You could love someone and never see them, and the love would sit there like a letter nobody opened.

"There's a stairwell apartment," Grandma Ruth said around dinnertime, somewhere in Ohio. "In the new house. Your father gave me the room by the back stairs."

"That's the Festinger room," Morgan said.

Grandma Ruth looked over. "The what?"

"Nothing. A study. People near the stairs make more friends. From 1950. Festinger, Schachter, and somebody named Back." She paused. "You'll be the popular one."

"I was planning on it," her grandmother said, and made a note on the grocery receipt.

Morgan texted Priya from a gas station outside Zanesville: ask Denae if she's still mad. Priya wrote back that Denae wasn't mad, she was just Denae, and then sent the blurry photo after all. Morgan looked at it under the fluorescent awning, three faces smeared by motion, and set it as her lock screen anyway. She did not know yet whether the study meant she should stop grieving the old friends or start forgiving the new ones in advance, or whether it meant nothing a person could act on at all. Probably, she thought, she would find out in September, and probably by accident, the way the students in the housing had. The truck's headlights swung into the lot behind them, and her father got out stretching his arms, holding the keys up so she could see them glint under the lights.

Sophia's grandmother had always bought her tomatoes from the third stall on the left, the one with the crooked hand-painted sign, and so Sophia went there first, even though the tomatoes at the entrance looked just as good and were fifty cents cheaper a basket. The market had been going since seven and by ten the asphalt was giving back heat in slow waves. She held the list her mother had texted against the wind and worked down it: tomatoes, bread, a wedge of cheese, eggs from the Hsu farm if they still had any.

She was making dinner tonight, the whole thing, because her parents had driven to her aunt's to help move furniture and wouldn't be back until late, and because her brother Danny had asked her to, which he never did. He was leaving for basic training in three weeks and had requested one specific meal, their grandmother's pasta with fresh tomatoes and the slow-scrambled eggs she used to fold in at the end. Sophia had said yes before she understood what she was agreeing to, which was a kind of cooking that depended on a woman who had died in March.

The Hsus had eggs. She bought two dozen, more than she needed, because their carton was cold to the touch and it made her feel competent to plan ahead. Then she stood too long at a table of honey and jam, texting a friend about dorm assignments, and then longer still arguing pleasantly with the cheese man about whether pecorino or the cheaper local sheep's cheese was closer to what an Abruzzese grandmother would use. He gave her a taste of both. She bought the local one, then walked three stalls and turned around and bought a small piece of the pecorino too, because she could not decide, and because undecided felt, this summer, like its own small malaise she couldn't name.

It was past noon when she got home. She put the bags on the counter and stood in the kitchen with the door open behind her, letting the screen door bang the way her grandmother used to when her hands were full. The eggs sat in their bag. The cheese sat in its paper. The tomatoes, at least, she set out on the windowsill, because that was what her grandmother did, and the image of them there, fat and red against the glass, steadied her.

She cooked for two hours. The sauce took longer than the recipe card said, because the recipe card assumed you already knew things, assumed you knew that the garlic should barely color and that the tomatoes would give up their water if you just refused to hurry them. The eggs she scrambled on the lowest flame, stirring in figure eights, and when she folded them into the finished pasta the whole kitchen smelled like being eleven years old. Danny ate two plates and kept saying the word exactly, as in, this is exactly it, and their younger sister Lucy ate one plate and then asked if she could take the rest to her friend's house tomorrow because her friend's mother worked nights and never cooked.

So there were leftovers, a big steel bowl of them, and it was Lucy's question that made Sophia look at the clock. Four hours, she realized, since she'd left the market with the eggs, and the eggs had spent that time in a bag, then in the car, then on the counter while she cooked. She'd read something once, in the food safety unit of a class she'd half slept through, and now she dug through her phone to find it. Perishable food shouldn't sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours. She read it twice. And one hour, the page said, if it's above 90 degrees out. She checked the weather app. Ninety-four.

"Where are the eggs?" she asked, and her voice came out sharper than she meant.

Danny, nonchalant, feet up on a chair, pointed at the counter. "Right there. Why?"

Sophia stood very still, holding the phone, doing the arithmetic. The eggs had been out at least four hours in a kitchen that had to be eighty-five, maybe more, with the oven running. The cooked pasta was newer, but it had been sitting out while they ate, and it was nowhere near the fridge. She thought of her grandmother, who left things out all day and waved off worry, and of her mother, who refrigerated butter. Two people she loved, two completely opposite instincts, and neither of them had ever stated a rule. She was tired of inheriting positions without reasons.

"The eggs are done," she said. "I can't use them. They've been in the danger zone way too long. The pasta I can save if I move it now, it's only been out about an hour, but the raw eggs are out." She heard herself and worried she sounded like a pamphlet, but Lucy was already looking at the bowl with narrowed eyes.

"So we can't give any to Kayla tomorrow?"

"We can give her the pasta. If it goes in the fridge right now." Sophia carried the bowl to the refrigerator, and the cold air on her wrists felt like arriving somewhere. She came back and scraped the eggs into the trash, all two dozen, the carton that had felt so reassuringly cold at eight in the morning. It was only money, she told herself, and then stopped telling herself things, because the loss was real and pretending otherwise was its own kind of dishonesty.

"You could've asked me," Danny said. "I know that stuff. We get it drilled into us. Two hours, one if it's hot out, above 90." He said it without any accusation, just handing her the fact the way you'd hand someone a tool they were already reaching for.

"You could've mentioned it four hours ago," she said, and he laughed, and she laughed, and then she went back to the recipe card and turned it over and wrote on the back, in her grandmother's old pencil stub, what she had learned, so that next time the knowledge would be in the family and not just in her phone. At the bottom she added the shopping order for a second attempt at the eggs, and under it a note to buy a cooler for the drive home from the market.

Then she texted her mother: pasta safe, eggs a loss, will contextualize later. And after a minute she picked up the pencil again and crossed that out and wrote, more simply, it's a long story, I'll tell you when you're home. She put the tomatoes back on the windowsill, the ones she hadn't cooked, and set one in the center of the sill where the light would find it in the morning.

Colton arrived at fifth period with the essay prompt already folded into his back pocket, though he had written nothing but a single underlined sentence: Who do you trust in Wuthering Heights, and why? He had read the whole novel in nine days, mostly on the bus, and somewhere around chapter nine he had begun to feel that the story kept catching in a filter, the way pond water looks different through a dirty jar.

Ms. Reyes had pushed the desks into a circle, which Colton hated, because circles demanded speech. She asked who narrated the book, and Drew Oliphant said Catherine, which was wrong, and then Priya said Heathcliff, which was also wrong, and then the room went quiet in the way rooms do when everyone is waiting for someone else to be wrong in a more interesting fashion.

"It's the housekeeper," Colton said, surprising himself. "Nelly Dean. Most of the book is her telling the story to this visitor, Lockwood. He's renting a house from Heathcliff, he gets sick, and while he's stuck there she tells him everything. So it's not like a normal narrator. Everything gets to us through both of them."

Priya leaned forward. "But wait. Didn't Nelly hate some of those people? Does that change how she tells it?" She had a pencil behind her ear and a paperback bristling with pink tabs. "Like, when she describes Catherine, is she describing Catherine or describing her own grudge?"

Colton opened his book to a page he had dog-eared without admitting it to himself. He had marked the spot where Nelly admits she warned Heathcliff about Hindley's plan to separate him from Catherine, an intervention that had consequences Nelly then narrated as though she had merely been a bystander. "She says she was only giving information," he said slowly, "but she chose which information. She's in the story and telling the story at the same time."

"That's an unreliable narrator," Priya said.

The phrase landed in Colton strangely, because he recognized the shape of it from somewhere outside the classroom. Last spring he had sat in his grandfather's kitchen while the old man explained, overCards and coffee, why Colton's mother didn't speak to her brother, and Colton had listened and believed every word, and only later, at Thanksgiving, heard his uncle's version of the same year, which matched his grandfather's in dates and almost nothing else. Neither man had lied, he thought now. Each had simply been the housekeeper of his own account, arranging the furniture of the past so that he stood in the most defensible corner of the room.

He said none of this aloud, but the inchoate idea pressed at him for the rest of the discussion. Drew argued that Lockwood was the bigger problem, a vain city man misreading everyone he met, and Colton found he could not entirely disagree, which unsettled him more than disagreement would have. If both narrators distorted, then the reader was left triangulating, and what he wanted, what the essay demanded, was a verdict. Trust or don't trust. He had assumed analysis meant sharpening a question until it cut one way.

After the bell he stayed behind, pretending to organize a binder that needed no organizing. Ms. Reyes asked if he had a question. He said not exactly, then asked it anyway: whether an essay could argue that you trust Nelly about some things and not others, that she might be accurate about weather and dishonest about motives, and whether that counted as an answer or just a refusal to choose.

She smiled and said the prompt asked who he trusted, not how much.

On the bus home he opened his notebook under the fogged window and wrote the word "scale" at the top of the page. Trust, he was beginning to think, was not a door you opened or kept shut; it was something with sentience of its own, an attention you paid in increments, adjusting as the evidence adjusted. He could not say that in an essay, or not in those words. But he could take the scene where Nelly watches Catherine through a keyhole and Heathcliff watches through the same keyhole, hearing two people he loves say two incompatible things about him, and he could ask what Nelly chose to keep, and what Lockwood chose to laugh at, and where the reader's own keyhole had been all along. He underlined a line of dialogue in the chapter, closed the book, and watched the houses slide past, each one holding, he supposed, somebody's version of the truth.

He got off two stops early and texted his mother: ask Uncle Ray about Thanksgiving 2016. Then he stood at the crosswalk, thumb still over the send button, and waited for the light.

The lemonade stand had cost Brooklyn eleven dollars in lumber, four in lemons, and one argument with her mother about whether a card table covered with a bedsheet counted as a business expense. She set it up at the corner of Maple and Third, three blocks from the high school, because that was where the afternoon foot traffic was: juniors cutting across to the gas station for slushies, which she regarded as her true competition, however artificial their coloring.

Her first customer was Mr. Okafor, who worked at the bank downtown and stopped by every Tuesday on his walk. He had his phone in his hand, tuned to the news, and while Brooklyn poured he held it up absentmindedly, so that she caught the announcer saying something about the Fed raising rates. She'd heard the phrase a dozen times and never once pinned it down.

"Which rate?" she asked. "Like a mortgage rate?"

Mr. Okafor lowered the phone. "The federal funds rate," he said. "That's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." He took his cup, paid her a dollar seventy-five, and added that the radio would keep saying rates all week and mean that one thing, mostly. Then he walked on, leaving Brooklyn with the strange feeling of having been handed a fact like a coin, small and exact and heavier than it looked.

The second complication arrived at four o'clock, on a bicycle, wearing sunglasses. Devon lived two streets over and had opened his own stand on Saturday, selling iced tea and lemonade both, undercutting her by twenty-five cents. He rode past slowly, the way people ride past when they want to be seen riding past, and called out that he hoped she'd had a good week, which did not presage a good week for either of them.

She sat with her pitcher and did the arithmetic she'd been avoiding. She could make twelve cups an hour. Devon, from what she'd observed through the fence, could make maybe nine, and his lemonade was weaker. But his cookies, which he baked the night before, were better than anything she could produce, and she knew it, because her one attempt had yielded something her brother described as a geological event. Her mother, in a rare moment of interference, had suggested she just buy Devon's cookies and sell them alongside her lemonade, an idea Brooklyn had dismissed as specious, since it seemed to concede the whole market to him. Now, watching him coast down the hill toward his own table, she turned it over again.

It wasn't concession, she realized, or not exactly. It was the thing Mr. Alvarez kept circling in econ without ever quite landing on: two people both gain from trading even when one of them is better at everything, if each does the thing they're comparatively best at. She was faster at lemonade and terrible at cookies; Devon was slower at lemonade and very good at cookies. If she gave up cookies entirely and he gave up lemonade, they'd have more of both between them than if they each did everything badly at half speed. She'd understood it as a diagram in a textbook, arrows between two boxes labeled countries. It was different standing in the grass with a pitcher, understanding that the diagram was also about her, on a Tuesday, on Maple Street.

She walked over on Wednesday with a proposal, which she had written on an index card because she suspected Devon of arguing with anything spoken. Two dollars per dozen cookies from him, sold at her stand with her lemonade, both of them promoted as a set. He read the card twice, took off his sunglasses, and said the obvious thing, which was that her lemonade was better than his, so why should he stop making his own.

"Because your cookies are worth more than your lemonade," she said. "Every hour you spend squeezing lemons is an hour you're not baking. And I can't bake at all, so every hour I spend failing at it is an hour I'm not making the thing people actually come to me for." He looked at his table, at the three unsold cups sweating in the sun, and she watched him run the same arithmetic she had, at his own speed.

They agreed to a one-week trial, sealed with no handshake, only Devon riding home to bake. Brooklyn walked back to her stand, took out the index card, and added a line at the bottom, a question for Mr. Alvarez: if two kids at card tables both gain from this, is that the whole story, or just the story that's convenient to tell? She was aware that she had fitted the theory to her own interests as smoothly as anyone fits anything, and that her newly discovered enthusiasm for trade deserved some skepticism, the same discernment she'd applied to her mother's suggestion. She didn't have that worked out yet.

Mr. Okafor came by on Thursday, asked for the usual, and nodded at the plate of cookies beside her pitcher. "New supplier," Brooklyn said. He raised an eyebrow, and she found herself explaining, cups versus cookies, hours versus hours, while the ice shifted and settled in the pitcher behind her. "It's comparative advantage," she said, and then, because he still looked amused, "which until this week I thought was about countries." He paid, thanked her, and said he'd take two cookies. She put them in a napkin and watched him go, already calculating what Thursday's totals might presage for Friday's order.

The community centre rented its music room by the hour, and on Thursdays at four it belonged to whoever arrived first. Naomi arrived first, because she had walked the twenty minutes from school with the score in her bag and a pencil sharpened to a dangerous point, and because the alternative was her house, where her mother was packing boxes for the move to her aunt's and did not want help.

She spread the Mozart on the upright piano's lid: the first movement of the K. 333 sonata, photocopies so pale the staves looked like the ghost of staves. Mr. Okoye, who ran the Thursday sessions, had given them a task that sounded simple and was not. Mark the exposition, the development, the recapitulation. Show where each begins. He had said, in his garrulous way, that the form was not a box the music went into but something the music kept almost leaving and returning to, and then he had been called away to the front desk, where a woman was arguing about a badminton booking, and he had not come back.

Theo came in at ten past, shaking rain off his jacket. He was seventeen, took piano seriously in the way that made other people nervous, and had a habit of saying bromides like trust the music that Naomi privately filed under things people say instead of thinking. He pulled up the other bench without asking. "You've already started."

"I've been staring at it for ten minutes. Starting is generous." She had bracketed the first theme in pencil and then rubbed it out twice. The opening eight bars kept pulling at her. They ended, and yet they didn't; the sound arrived somewhere and stood there, leaning.

Theo dropped his bag and played the opening, and at the eighth bar he lifted his hands deliberately, so the sound stopped exactly there. The room held the absence of the next phrase like a held breath. "There," he said. "That's a half cadence. The phrase ends on the V chord, so it sounds unfinished. Your ear expects another phrase to follow." He said it as if reporting the weather, and Naomi wrote V in the margin, and then, underneath, unfinished.

"Play it again," she said, "but keep going into bar nine." He did, and the second phrase arrived like an answer that had been waiting to be asked. She felt something settle that she could not yet name, which annoyed her, because she preferred to name things before she trusted them. Her chemistry teacher liked to say you couldn't manage what you couldn't operationalize, and Naomi had carried the phrase around until it felt like a tool she could apply anywhere: break the thing into marks you could actually make. Pencil marks. Roman numerals. Brackets. If she could mark the form, she would own it.

But the marking fought her. The exposition was supposed to end at the repeat sign, and it did, only the second theme had already started dissolving into things that belonged, she thought, to the development, wobbles and dark turnings that arrived before their appointed hour. She drew the bracket, then extended it, then rubbed the extension out. "It's not clean," she said. "Mr. Okoye said it wouldn't be."

"So mark where you think it starts and argue from there." Theo was playing the passage again, quietly, his foot off the pedal so the notes came out dry. He ended at the eighth bar again, on purpose this time, and looked at her, and she understood he was showing her something a second time not to teach it but because he liked the waiting it made. Maybe that was the whole reason people loved this music, she thought, and maybe that was also why her mother had left the packing until the last week: some part of a person prefers the unresolved chord, the phrase that demands its answer, to the answer itself.

She wrote a small question mark next to the development, then softened it to a wavering line. Her position, if she had to give one, was that the form was real and the edges were real and the edges were also where the music lived, and she could hold the first half of that and only gesture at the second. Mr. Okoye came back at last, hair damp from the front-desk argument, and asked what they had found. Naomi turned the score toward him. "Exposition, development, recapitulation," she said, and put her pencil on the eighth bar, where the half cadence waited for whatever came next. "Start here."

The party had spilled from the Kowalskis' kitchen onto the lawn, and someone had propped the screen door open with a brick so the music could follow everyone outside. Mathis stood near the folding table with the sheet cake, his mortarboard under one arm, and listened to the tinny march coming from a phone propped against a pitcher of lemonade. It was the same processional they had walked to that afternoon, slowed and flattened by the little speaker, and his cousin Theo was conducting it with a breadstick.

"Best part of the whole day," Theo said. "The walking-in song. Very dignified. Very British."

"Pomp and Circumstance," said Priya, from the class below Mathis's, still holding her plate. "I looked it up once because my mother plays it every June and cries. It's by Elgar."

Mathis had assumed the title meant nothing more than ceremony, that "pomp and circumstance" was simply a fancy phrase for trumpets and gowns. He was about to say so when Dana came around the corner of the house with her cup and stopped, head tilted, the way she did in English seminar when a line of Shakespeare rang a bell somewhere behind her eyes.

"Wait," Dana said. "We studied that. It's Othello. The phrase comes from the play. Othello says it, right at the end, when he's giving up everything: the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war. Elgar took his title from that." She recited it again, quietly, as if testing the weight of it. "Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."

Theo lowered the breadstick. "So our walking-in song is about war?"

"About losing it, sort of," Dana said. "Othello's farewell speech. He's undoing his whole life in it."

The march kept playing, bright and patient, while the cake sweated in the heat. Mathis felt the odd double exposure of it: the tune that had made his grandmother dab her eyes in the gymnasium, and underneath it a general stripping off his sword and his history. He wanted to say something clever, to preempt Theo's next joke, but instead he found himself holding both ideas at once and not being able to drop either one.

The summer before, Mrs. Andaya had taught them the word synecdoche, the part standing for the whole, and had made them find examples all semester until it became a private habit. Now he watched the gowns on the lawn, the sash of a girl dancing badly by the fence, the stolen faculty hood Mr. Brandt had worn backwards, and thought that the costume was the same trick: one garment carrying four years. Elgar had done it with a phrase. He lifted a piece of Othello's ruin and made it stand for beginnings, and now every June, ten thousand gymnasiums played a broken soldier's farewell while parents wept for reasons they would have called happy.

"That's depressing," Theo decided. "I'm going to eat more cake."

"It's not depressing," Priya said. "It's beautiful. It means the ceremony knows something."

Mathis's father was across the lawn talking to Mr. Kowalski about the scholarship fund, the one that paid the deposit for students whose families couldn't, the fund that kept the school from quietly losing its indigent kids between June and September. His father had put money in it every year since Mathis started, quietly, the check written in the kitchen with the same pen used for grocery lists. Mathis had never asked why. Tomorrow his own deposit was due, and his father had already told him not to worry about it.

He crossed the lawn to Dana, who was watching Theo and Priya argue about whether the song could be reclaimed for hope or whether it would always carry Othello underneath, the way a river carries what was dumped upstream.

"Here's what I can't decide," Mathis said. "Whether Elgar was being ironic or whether he meant it straight. Whether it's a joke on all of us, or whether he thought graduating was a kind of glorious war and the phrase fits."

"Maybe he didn't decide either," Dana said. "Maybe that's why it lasts."

The phone by the lemonade looped the march again, and someone turned it up. Theo resumed conducting, grander now, and Priya saluted him with her fork. Mathis put on his mortarboard, crooked, the way it had sat all afternoon, and walked over to the folding table for a second piece of cake.

"Save me the corner piece," Dana called after him. "The one with the most frosting. Consider it my graduation gift."

"That's my piece," Mathis said, and cut it anyway.

Mya's one-act had a narrator problem, and she had known it since Tuesday. The black box theater smelled like dust and radiator paint, and her three actors sat on stacking chairs in the crepuscular light that leaked through the half-shuttered doors, waiting for her to tell them where to stand.

"Same question as before," Marcus said. He played her brother, sort of. "When I'm talking to the audience, where is everybody else? Frozen? Gone? What?"

"Let me try something," Mya said, though she did not have the something yet. She moved Priya, who played her mother, downstage left, and Marcus up to the lip of the stage, and she said, "Stay there, don't move," and then she just looked at it. The frozen tableau behind the speaking actor looked bad, like a wax museum. She scratched it in her notebook and told them to take five.

She had written the one-act about the year her father left, and she had defended it fiercely at auditions when Deshawn asked whether it was too close, whether she could be trusted to direct her own past. "I'm not on trial," she'd told him. "Nobody has to exculpate me." But privately she suspected he was right about one thing: the script kept trying to prove that everyone had behaved badly except her. That was not directing. That was lawyering.

In the library at lunch she found Deshawn at a table with a battered anthology open to The Glass Menagerie. "Is that for Okafor's class?" she asked, sitting down without waiting for an answer.

"Memorizing Tom's opening speech." He tapped the page. "You should read the intro. Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie a memory play. It was first staged in Chicago in 1944, and it's narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family." He said it lightly, the way he recited facts he liked, and went back to his lines.

Mya read the speech over his shoulder. Tom telling the audience the play is memory, that it is sentimental, not realistic, that in memory things don't move the way they should. She read it twice, and something in her chest went quiet, like a room when the refrigerator shuts off. She had been staging her past as if it were a news report, blocking every entrance and exit to match what actually happened, and it kept refusing to work because the actual events were not the point. The point was that she was the one remembering them, and memory is soft, guilty, and unfair, and you have to admit that out loud or the whole thing curdles into self-defense.

After school she taped a new mark on the floor, a chalk-white X far stage right. "Marcus, this is your island," she said. "When you step on it, the past goes dim. The lights on everyone else drop to half. You're the only one who's real, because you're the one telling it."

"So I'm Tom," Marcus said.

"You're me," Mya said, and Priya laughed before she could stop herself. "No, it's not a joke. I'm not acting in it, so I'm borrowing his body. When I step out, the memory is allowed to be wrong. You can look at your mother and love her and blame her in the same breath, and the audience doesn't get to decide which one wins." She ran the dinner scene that way, Marcus stepping off his island into the half-light, correcting his own memory mid-sentence, saying, "That's not how she said it. She said it quieter," and saying it again quieter, and Priya answering as if she hadn't heard him, locked inside the remembered moment. It was the first thing in three rehearsals that had made the hair on Mya's arms stand up.

There was still the ending, which she had not solved. Deshawn found her after rehearsal stacking chairs and asked how the memory thing was going, whether it had fixed everything. "It fixed the middle," she said. "The ending is still a hostage situation. I want my mother to be forgiven, and the scene wants her to be forgiven, but I don't know yet if those are the same thing, and I won't know until I stage it wrong at least twice." He asked what she'd do if it stayed wrong, and she said she'd stage the not-knowing, because that was also true, and he said that sounded like a dodge, and she said maybe, and wrote it in her notebook anyway.

On Friday the lights were better than the words. Priya stood in the half-dark holding an invisible dish, and Marcus stepped onto his island and told the empty seats, "I left too. Nobody talks about that part," and the shuttered doors leaked their last stripe of daylight across his shoes. Mya, sitting in the back row with her notebook open on her knees, underlined the line twice, then crossed out the ending she'd planned and left the space blank for Monday.

Isabelle had told herself, on the bus downtown, that she did not care whether Ms. Okafor liked her theme. This was not quite true, but she kept it in place the way you keep a bookmark in a page you mean to return to. She carried her ten sketchbooks stacked against her chest, and the gallery door was heavier than she expected, so that she entered the Saturday critique group slightly out of breath and slightly late.

The group met in the back room of the Meridian, where the walls held a touring print collection and the floor held eight folding chairs. Ms. Okafor, who ran the teen portfolio program, had one rule: bring a theme, not a pile. "A portfolio of ten pieces around one idea," she said each week, as if repeating it might make it true for all of them. Isabelle's idea was wounds. She had nine pieces about wounds and one about her grandmother's hands, and she had written an artist's statement claiming the hands were also a wound, which she privately suspected was a lie.

A boy named Theo, who was applying to the same schools, went first. He had brought a print of Kahlo's The Broken Column because he wanted to argue with it. "In it, nails pierce her face and body while tears run down her cheeks," he said, "yet she looks straight at the viewer. Every time I meet her eyes I want to apologize and look away." He turned to the room. "That's a flaw. The tears do the feeling for you, and then the stare dares you to react, and I don't like being dared."

Isabelle, who had spent three weeks staring at a reproduction of that painting, said nothing at first. She did not want to preempt him with her own reading, or perhaps she did, and the wanting was the problem. She smoothed the edge of her top sketchbook instead.

When her turn came, she laid out the nine wound pieces in a grid on the floor: the stitched apple, the cracked blue bowl, the self-portrait with the bandaged forearm that she'd told everyone was about her cousin, though it was about her. Ms. Okafor walked the grid slowly, hands behind her back, and Isabelle noticed that she walked around it twice, and that the second circuit was slower.

"In every piece," Ms. Okafor said, "the damage faces outward. You've made the viewer the one who flinches. But there's no stratum underneath, nothing that shows me what the wounding sits on top of. It's surface all the way down." She stopped at the tenth piece, the grandmother's hands, folded in lamplight. "And this one is the only honest thing here, which is probably why it doesn't fit."

Isabelle heard that as a compliment at first, the way you hear rain as restful until you remember the window is open. She looked at the hands again. Her grandmother had been obdurate about the move to the care home, refusing for months, gripping the doorframe of the house on Delancey while her son explained and explained. The drawing showed the hands folded, at peace, and Isabelle had drawn them that way because it was easier than drawing the doorframe.

She took the statement out of her bag and unfolded it. Ten pieces about wounds, it said, exploring how damage is carried. Theo leaned over from his chair. "But the hands aren't wounded," he said. "They're just old." He said it without malice, which was somehow worse, because it left her nothing to argue against.

"That's the problem," Isabelle said. She heard her own voice go flat. "The Kahlo you showed us. She's pierced and crying and she still looks straight out. I keep doing the opposite. I look at the wound and refuse to look at whoever's looking at me." She picked up the grandmother drawing and held it, then set it down again, in the center of the grid, where it broke the pattern entirely. "I think my theme isn't wounds. I don't know what it is yet. Maybe it's who's allowed to watch."

Ms. Okafor said nothing for a moment, which Isabelle chose to read as permission. She took out a pen, turned the statement over to its blank side, and at the top wrote the word watching. Underneath it she wrote a question she could not yet answer, and then, because the group was waiting and the afternoon light had moved across the prints on the wall, she began to read the nine pieces again, one by one, starting with the apple.

The screen door banged behind Chase before he remembered to close it softly, and his grandmother looked up from her crossword without complaint, as she always did. He set his laptop on the kitchen table beside the bowl of tomatoes she was sorting, one hand still warm from the walk from the bus stop, and opened the document he had been fighting all week. The assignment was due in nine days, for the freshman seminar he would not even start until September, a placement essay the college had mailed with unsettling confidence: apply a critical lens to a passage from a classic novel. He had chosen Jane Eyre, the chapter where Rochester's wedding is interrupted and Bertha Mason is dragged into the light, mostly because it was the one classic he had actually finished.

The trouble was that he had two lenses and only one essay. His annotated copy of the novel was bristling with pink tabs for the feminist reading, blue for the Marxist one, and the margins had become a small civil war. The pink notes said that Bertha existed only as a plot device, a woman whose entire ontology was reduced to a growl in an attic so that Jane could have a conscience and a plot. The blue notes said the whole marriage was an economy, that Rochester wanted to expropriate Jane's youth and legitimacy the way his family had expropriated Bertha's fortune thirty years before, and that the novel never once blushed at this.

"What's the face for?" his grandmother asked. She had a pencil behind her ear and another in her hand, and the morning light came through the lace curtain in a fine grid across the table.

"I wrote this sentence," Chase said. He turned the laptop toward her. "Rochester is an unreliable narrator, and the novel asks us to notice it."

She read it, tapping the pencil once against her teeth. "Where did you get that phrase, unreliable narrator?"

"Everyone says it. It's all over the internet. It's basically the first thing anyone learns about the book."

"Mm," she said, and slid the laptop back, and returned to seven across, which was some word for a kind of pigeon. Chase sat with the small cold feeling of having been found out without knowing for what. Her "mm" was not disapproval; it was the sound she made when something needed looking up.

He went looking himself. He typed the phrase into the library database with the tomatoes smelling sharp and green from the bowl, and the result surprised him: the term had not drifted down from ancient Greece or been coined by some Victorian man with side-whiskers. It was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth, in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction. Sixty-some years old, younger than his grandmother. He said it out loud before he could stop himself. "It's from 1961. Wayne C. Booth. The Rhetoric of Fiction."

"Wayne C. Booth coined it," his grandmother said, filling in her square. "The Rhetoric of Fiction, 1961." She said it the way she recited phone numbers, a fact held flat in the hand, and then she was quiet again, which was her way of letting him keep it.

The fact sat strangely with him. The phrase felt like a law of nature, and it was younger than the Formica table. It made him wonder what else in his pink-and-blue margins was younger than it pretended to be, and that thought folded itself into the larger problem, which was that he had been treating his two lenses as rivals when they might be witnesses to the same scene. If Jane told the story, and Jane was shaped by money she did not acknowledge and by a marriage market she thought she had transcended, then the unreliability was not a trick Rochester played. It was the water Jane swam in. The feminist reading asked who got to be a person in the story; the Marxist reading asked who got paid. Both of them, he saw now, were asking about the same wedding morning, from opposite ends of the same attic stairs.

He typed a new sentence, deleted it, typed it again. Rochester does not only conceal Bertha; the novel expropriates her, taking her fortune in its backstory and her humanity in its plot, so that Jane's moral victory can be purchased at a price Jane never counts. He read it over and hated and liked it at once, which he suspected was the correct condition for a first draft. What stayed uncertain was the part he could not wedge into either lens: whether Jane, a fiction shaped by a woman writing for money under a male pen name, was unreliable in the way Booth meant or in some other way the term did not yet cover. He left a note in the margin to think about it in September, when there would presumably be a seminar table and other people's faces to watch while he tried out the sentence aloud.

His grandmother rose to put water on for tea, and outside a mourning dove started up its low questioning note from the fence, and Chase closed the laptop on the pink and blue tabs both. "Nine across," she said. "Six letters, 'untrustworthy.'"

"Try unreliable," he said.

The mock election ballot had been sitting in Claire's binder for three days, folded once, then folded again, until the creases wore the paper thin. Her eighteenth birthday had fallen on a Tuesday in October, and the county's special election on the school levy was exactly six days later, which meant that for the first time in her life the county clerk's record of her would change from a name in a file to a name on a roll. Mr. Okafor had announced it to the class almost casually, the way he announced everything, and then assigned them to research voter turnout around the world and present a comparison on Friday.

"Australia," said Priya, from two rows over, on Thursday night in the emptying classroom where a few of them had stayed to finish their posters. "I found this and I keep rereading it because I thought it was a typo. Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and if you don't vote without a valid reason you can be fined."

"Wait, fined?" Claire put her marker down. "For not voting? Like a parking ticket?"

"Like a parking ticket for democracy," Priya said, and laughed, though her poster was entirely serious, bar graphs of turnout climbing after 1925 like a staircase.

Marcus, who had been slouched near the window drawing a skull in the margin of his notes, sat up a little. "That's insane. You can't make people vote. That defeats the whole point. The point is that you get to choose, including choosing nothing." He was repeating something his father said at dinner, Claire suspected, the way he always did, but she had argued with his father's opinions often enough that it hardly mattered whose they were.

"Choosing nothing is still a choice," Priya said. "It's just a choice someone else pays for." She smoothed a piece of tape across her graph. "You don't get fined if you have a valid reason. They're not dragging people to polls in chains."

Claire found herself not taking either side, which was unusual, because she generally took sides the way other people took stairs, quickly and without looking down. Her mother, who had staffed phone banks in every election since Claire could remember, treated voting as a duty so basic it barely needed language, like breathing or yielding at a stop sign. Her brother Theo, twenty-two and recently desensitized by an overload of political ads to the point where he claimed not to believe in any of it, had told her over text that her one vote was a raindrop and the raindrop should stay home. She had never doubted her mother. But she had also never had to think about it, and thinking about it now felt like picking up a familiar object and noticing its weight for the first time.

"Here's what I can't figure out," she said, pulling her folded ballot out of the binder and unfolding it on the desk between them, creases and all. "Marcus is right that forcing a choice seems to contaminate the choice. But Priya's graph is right that everyone's there. And the levy." She tapped the mock ballot. "This one's for a fake election for practice. But next Tuesday there's a real one, and it decides whether the schools get the money, and half the town will stay home because it's a Tuesday in November and it's raining and the ads have made everyone numb. My brother's not voting because he thinks his vote is nothing. Someone in Sydney who thinks the same thing has to show up anyway, or pay."

"Or pay," Marcus repeated, and frowned at his skull. "That's the part that gets me. Money. It's a quagmire, honestly. You fine people into participating and what do you get? People marking a ballot at random just to avoid twenty dollars?"

"We don't know it's twenty dollars," Priya said. "The article doesn't say the amount."

"That's worse," Marcus said. "An incipient police state that won't even tell you the fine." But he was grinning a little now, and Claire saw the shift happen, the way you see weather change over water. "Okay, but. If everyone has to come, then the candidates have to talk to everyone. Not just the people who already agree with them. That's something."

Claire looked down at the mock ballot, at the two names printed there for treasurer of a student government that met during lunch on Wednesdays, and felt the small absurdity of it. She was eighteen. In six days she would stand in the fire station on Route 9 behind a curtain that smelled like pencil shavings, and she still could not say whether freedom meant the right to abstain or the obligation to show up. Probably the answer was in there somewhere between the two, in the part she couldn't yet see. She believed in showing up. She also believed that belief shouldn't be compelled, and she could not make those two beliefs stop arguing, and she suspected she wasn't supposed to.

"So are you voting Tuesday?" Priya asked her, capping the markers, gathering poster tubes. The hallway had gone quiet; the janitor's cart squeaked somewhere far off.

"I don't know about the fine," Claire said, folding the mock ballot back along its worn creases. "But nobody here has to make me." She slid it into her binder, zipped her bag, and turned off the lamp over her desk.

The open house on Marsden Street was Blake's idea before it was his mother's, which surprised them both. He had seen the listing at eleven the night before, a flat above a shuttered bakery with a letting agent's name he didn't recognise, and by morning he had talked her into driving over, mostly because he wanted to see what £725 a month actually looked like when it stood in front of you as a room. The agent, a man named Dev with a lanyard and a folding table, was halfway through telling a young woman about the deposit when Blake and his mother came up the stairs.

"Two months up front," Dev was saying. "That's the deposit, plus your first month's rent in advance. Standard practice."

The woman, who introduced herself to nobody in particular as Priya, had a folder of printouts under her arm. She was maybe twenty-two, twenty-three, with the particular tiredness of someone who had viewed six flats this week. "Two months," she repeated, in a voice that suggested she had heard this number before and disliked it more each time.

"That's right." Dev had begun to pontificate about landlords needing security, about people who damaged properties, about the market being what it was, and Blake could see Priya's attention sliding off him the way his own did when a teacher covered material he already knew was beside the point.

She opened her folder. "The flat's £900 a month," she said. "That's under fifty thousand a year. So the deposit can't be two months. It's capped at five weeks' rent. I checked last night, the Tenant Fees Act 2019." She said it plainly, not triumphantly, the way you'd read out a bus timetable.

Dev's mouth opened and then reconsidered. Behind him, another couple had paused at the folding table, listening. "Five weeks," he said slowly, as if weighing a stone in his hand. "Right. Let me just call the office."

Blake drifted toward the kitchen while Dev stepped onto the landing with his phone. His mother followed, running her finger along the windowsill the way she did in every property they entered, an audit she performed without thinking. Blake had been doing the arithmetic since the listing: £725 a month, a deposit of five weeks, which meant five sevenths of a month's rent, which meant roughly £518. He did it again on his phone to be sure. And then the other number, the one that had brought him here in the first place: his mother's mention, three weeks ago and half a glass of wine into the evening, that she'd never owned, that she'd been paying other people's mortgages for twenty years.

"Mum," he said quietly, "if we put our rent money toward a deposit instead, what would that even take?"

She didn't stop looking at the windowsill. "A down payment, you mean. Different thing from a deposit, though everyone mixes them up. You pay a deposit to borrow a flat. A down payment buys you a stake in one." She turned around. "Ten percent, usually, for a first-time buyer with a mortgage. On a small place around here, that's fifteen, eighteen thousand."

Blake let the number sit. He had £2,400 saved from two summers of shelf-stacking, which had previously felt like a lot of money and now felt like a paragraph of a much longer book. "So the landlord's been collecting our rent for years," he said, "and that's been paying off his mortgage, and at the end we have nothing."

"That's the arrangement," his mother said. "It's not a betrayal. It's just what rent is." But she said it while looking at the little garden through the kitchen window, a strip of concrete with a stubborn rosemary bush in a pot, and Blake understood that explaining a thing and accepting it were not the same act.

On the landing, Dev came back in with the flattened posture of a man overruled by his own office. "Five weeks it is," he said to Priya. "I'll amend the paperwork. In advance, that's the first month's rent still, but the deposit comes down." Priya nodded and wrote the numbers in her folder, and Blake watched her do it, this small correction of a system by one person with a printout, and felt something adjust in his chest that he couldn't yet name.

He thought about his grandfather, who lived with a kind of grandiose asceticism, refusing heating in winter and calling it character while filling the house with enormous ornate furniture nobody could sit on. Saving money and wasting it, all at once, in the name of a story he told himself. Blake suspected the housing market had a bit of that in it too, people spending enormous sums to feel a certain way about themselves, landlords and tenants both.

Outside, Priya was on the steps, and Blake caught up with her before he'd decided to. "That thing you said, about five weeks," he said. "Would you send me where you found it? I'm trying to work all this out and I don't know anyone who's done it."

She looked at him, sixteen and earnest in his school coat, and something in her expression softened. "I'll send the link," she said. "Half the battle is knowing the rules exist. The other half I haven't worked out yet." She pulled her folder tight under her arm and started down the street toward the bus stop, and Blake stood on the steps with his mother's car keys in his hand, adding five weeks and ten percent and £2,400 together in his head, and then took out his phone and made a note of the number he got.

The funeral home closed at noon, and it was already ten, so Anthony's mother drove faster than she usually did, both hands on the wheel, the interstate unspooling in long gray ribbons toward the town where his grandmother had lived and, six days ago, had not. In the back seat Anthony held the eulogy in his lap, three paragraphs he had rewritten four times, and beside him his little cousin Marisol played a game on a tablet with the sound off, which he was grateful for.

He had not cried yet. That was the problem he kept circling back to, the way his grandmother used to circle a crossword clue before filling it in pencil. On Monday, two days after the phone call, he had gone to school, taken a calculus quiz, and laughed at something Danny said at lunch, a real laugh, loud enough that people turned. Then he had felt like a criminal. His mother had cried at the kitchen table on Sunday, and his aunt had cried at the airport, and Anthony had sat among all that weeping like a stone in a stream, wondering what was wrong with him.

"Say the part about the loquat tree again," Marisol said, not looking up from her screen. "For the eulogy."

"Grandma planted it the year I was born." He read it to her quietly. His voice sounded normal to him, which also felt like evidence against himself.

His mother glanced in the mirror. "You don't have to read it if it's too much, honey. Your uncle can."

"It's not too much." It wasn't, and that was the thing that frightened him. He had assumed grief worked like a staircase, that everyone climbed the same stairs in order, and that his failure to reach the first one meant he was skipping the whole structure, building a house with no foundation. Somewhere in him he believed that if he didn't break down now, he would break down later, worse, at some inconvenient and devastating time, like a delayed bill.

At a red light outside the county line, he took out his phone and searched the thing he'd been afraid to search: is it normal not to cry after a grandparent dies. The first results were junk, but one was an interview with a psychologist, George Bonanno, who had studied bereaved people for years. Anthony read it twice. Bonanno had found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss. He read it a third time, slowly, the way his grandmother read the fine print on sweepstakes entries.

"Put that away, we're almost there," his mother said, but her voice had no urgency in it, so he read one more line and then put the phone face down on his knee.

The fact rearranged something in him, quietly, the way furniture gets moved in a room you know well. All those afternoons in his grandmother's kitchen, she had never once demanded that he feel a particular thing. When his dog died at eleven, she had said some people cry and some people plant something, and he had planted beans, and she had watered them when he forgot. He had thought she was being easygoing. Now he thought maybe she had known something the staircase people didn't, something he could hold alongside his worry instead of instead of it. He was still uncertain. It was possible he was resilient and it was possible he was numb, and he could not yet tell the difference, and maybe the difference was not even his to diagnose. He would find out by living through the next hours, not by deciding in advance what they should look like.

His grandmother had been a nurse for forty years, and she had kept her old diagnostic manuals on the shelf beside the cookbooks. Once, when he was thirteen, she had explained the word etiology to him over boiled eggs: the cause of a thing, the why behind the what. He had loved the word and never had occasion to use it until now. There was no etiology for how a person grieves, he thought, or rather there were too many, one for every person, which amounted to the same thing as none. Marisol leaned her head against his shoulder, and he let it stay there.

The parking lot of the funeral home was half full, his uncle's truck already there, the front doors propped open with a rubber wedge despite the cold. Anthony folded the eulogy into his jacket pocket. Before they got out, he said, mostly to the windshield, "Did you know resilience is common? That there aren't mandatory stages?" His mother turned around fully, and after a moment she said, "No," and then, softer, "That's good to know." He opened the door and the cold came in around his ankles, and across the lot his grandmother's sister was standing under the bare loquat tree they had driven two hours to be near, waving at them with both hands.

Hayden had been carrying the folded printout in his blazer pocket for three days, and by graduation morning the paper had gone soft at the creases, the way money does.

The hallway outside the gym smelled of floor wax and carnations. He stood at his locker for the last time, turning the dial out of habit even though the locker was already empty, and Dana from his econ class stopped beside him with her cap mashed flat under one arm.

"You're still on about the wages thing," she said. It wasn't a question. Dana had spent the year building a spreadsheet of every scholarship in the state, and she wanted his essay in the class anthology because it had made their teacher, Mr. Ruiz, actually sit down.

"My uncle said it at dinner Friday," Hayden said. "He works at the community college. He told me workers twenty-five and older with a high school diploma earned eight ninety-nine a week, median, in 2023, and people without one earned seven oh eight." He recited it the way he'd recited it to himself in the shower, in the car, in the dark before sleep. "He said, that's your present, kid. That's what the paper's worth."

"That's not what the paper's worth," Dana said, but she didn't say what it was worth, and he noticed that.

The problem was that Hayden had written his exit essay, the one Mr. Ruiz had read aloud in April, about how a diploma measured nothing, how the whole ceremony was theater, a kind of polite nihilism dressed in robes. He'd been proud of the anger in it. Now the anger had a number attached, a small one, a hundred and ninety-one dollars a week, and the number refused to be romantic. He tried to transcribe the essay's argument into his notebook on the bench by the trophy case, to see whether it survived contact with what his uncle had said, and found that his own sentences looked petulant to him, a boy throwing his cap at the floor because the floor existed.

"Ruiz wants to read your name wrong," Dana said, watching him write. "He told me. He's been practicing."

"He won't read it wrong. It's two syllables."

"He reads everything wrong. He called me Dana with a hard E for a month." She fixed her cap on her head, crooked on purpose, because Dana wanted the yearbook photographer to catch it, wanted one image from the day that hadn't been arranged by adults. "My mother wants the cap straight. My whole family's coming straight-ward today. I'm the crooked element."

He laughed, and then the doors opened and the gym swallowed them, and the ceremony went the way ceremonies go, long and warm and strange. Mr. Ruiz did read his name wrong, "Hay-den" like two separate words, and Hayden walked the length of the gym with his hand out for a diploma case that turned out to be empty, a holder, the real one to be mailed in July after the office confirmed his detention hours had been served. He held it up anyway. His mother stood up in the third row and took a picture, and later he found the picture showed the case's emptiness clearly, the little window with nothing behind it, and he understood that his uncle's numbers and his own essay had both been about this case, one saying it was worth eight ninety-nine a week and the other saying it was worth nothing, and both of them talking about a piece of cardboard that hadn't even arrived.

Afterward, in the hallway, the one from that morning, now scattered with programs and a dropped carnation, his uncle found him. Uncle Marcel had the community college lanyard still on, though it was Saturday.

"So," Marcel said. "You got the eight ninety-nine version or the seven oh eight version?"

"Neither yet," Hayden said. "They mail it."

Marcel grinned, then didn't. "You know I wasn't trying to put a price on it. I was trying to say it matters. There's a difference."

"I know," Hayden said, and found that he did, mostly. What he couldn't say, what stayed uncertain even as he reached for it, was whether the diploma mattered because of the money or the money because of the diploma, or whether both of those were smaller than something his essay had been circling without landing on. He had spent a year learning to argue one side of things. Nobody had taught him how to hold two true sentences at once.

Dana appeared with her cap still crooked, holding her phone at arm's length. "The photographer got it," she said. "Look. My grandmother is frowning at me in the background and my mom is mid-yell. It's perfect. It's the only real picture anyone took today." She turned the screen toward Hayden and his uncle together, two witnesses, as if the picture needed certifying.

Hayden looked at it, the crooked cap, the frowning grandmother, the half-open gym doors behind them all, and thought that this was what he'd write next, if he wrote anything. Not that nothing mattered. Not that anything could be priced.

"So what's it going to be, kid," Marcel said, clapping him on the shoulder. "College or the seven oh eight?"

"College," Hayden said, and then, because the hallway was almost empty and the honest thing was easier out loud, "I don't know what for."

Marcel pulled the lanyard over his head and dropped it in Hayden's blazer pocket, right on top of the soft folded number. "Hold onto that too," he said. "It's worth exactly nothing a week."

The kitchen thermometer, the cheap dial kind that had lived beside the stove since before Edouard could remember, read thirty-four degrees Celsius, and the chocolate refused to cooperate. He had the notebook open on the counter, the one with TEMPERING written on the first page in his own careful hand, and above that word a grid of temperatures he had copied from a video: melt to forty-five, cool to twenty-seven, bring back up to thirty-one and a half, hold, hold, hold. The problem was that his kitchen was already hotter than the chocolate was supposed to get at the end.
