That afternoon James rode his bike the six blocks to Miller Street, mostly because he didn't want to go home and admit the day had confused him. The pantry occupied the basement of a church, and there was, in fact, a line out the door. He watched a woman with two kids choose between pasta and rice with the seriousness of someone balancing a ledger, and a teenage girl from his own school, he realized with a small shock, signing in at a clipboard table. He looked away before she could see him, then felt ashamed of looking away, then made himself look back. She was gone.

Back in the warehouse on Monday, he had volunteered to come again, he found himself defending the warehouse against Wendell's complaining, which had turned political. Wendell had decided that the whole system was a scam run by people who liked feeling generous, and he made a speech about politicians, using the word populist twice, once as a compliment and once as an insult, in a way that seemed to James to cancel itself out. "You can't impugn Rosa's motives just because the system's ugly," James said, surprising himself with the firmness of it. "The food got here. It'll get there. Somebody has to move the boxes."

"Look at you," Wendell said, but he said it quietly, and he went back to sorting.

James didn't think he had solved anything. The girl from his school had seen him at a pantry and he hadn't said hello; he had spent a whole day working hard for people he would never see, and it was good work or it was easy work or it was both; the line at Miller Street and the silence of the warehouse were the same fact in two rooms, and he could hold them together without pretending one canceled the other. What he could not yet decide was whether that was enough, or whether enough was even the right question, or whether questions like that were just another way of standing outside. He finished the pallet, tore down the empty boxes, and stacked the flattened cardboard against the wall until Rosa called from the office that the truck was early. He picked up the box cutter and went to meet it.

The garage smelled of motor oil and cold metal, and Mia had spread her chemistry homework across her grandfather's workbench, weighting the pages with a wrench and a jar of screws. She had come to his house for the weekend to recuperate from a week of exams, or that was what she'd told her mother, though mostly she wanted the quiet. The quiet was not cooperating. On the page in front of her, an equilibrium problem sat like a locked door: a reaction at equilibrium, the temperature raised, and the question of which way the system would shift.

She understood shifting fine when the changes were concentrations. Add product, the reaction ate some of it back; remove reactant, the reaction made more. That part felt like a seesaw, like common sense. But temperature was different. Temperature wasn't a substance. It wasn't on either side of the arrow, and her teacher's phrase "the system opposes the change" kept sliding off her mind without catching on anything.

Her grandfather was at the far end of the garage, stripping a bicycle wheel with a rag, and he had said almost nothing since she sat down, which was one of the reasons she liked working here. He let problems stay problems. At home her father would have leaned over her shoulder within two minutes and started guessing, and guessing out loud was worse than silence.

She copied the equation onto a scrap of sandpaper, the only paper left in her bag. Nitrogen and hydrogen on the left, ammonia on the right, the double arrows of equilibrium drawn between them. Below it she'd written, in her own handwriting, "exothermic," because the textbook had said so, and then a question mark so fierce she'd torn the paper slightly with the pen. The forward reaction released heat. So where did the heat go? It came out of the reaction, so it came out the right side, like the ammonia. Like a product.

She sat with that for a moment, then wrote the word heat on the right side of the equation, after the ammonia, in lowercase, almost apologetically. Nitrogen plus hydrogen gives ammonia plus heat. It looked wrong, like graffiti on a textbook, but it also looked like something. She raised the temperature. If heat was on the right, then raising the temperature was like adding product, and the system would oppose her by shifting left, consuming nitrogen and hydrogen, undoing ammonia. She checked the answer in the back of the book and the letters came up correct. She pressed the pen down so hard the sandpaper dented.

"Did you figure it out?" her grandfather asked, not turning around.

"I think so. I wrote heat into the equation, like it's a product. Then everything got easy." She held up the scrap. "If it were endothermic instead, heat would go on the other side. As a reactant. You'd treat it like something the reaction takes in and uses up."

He set down the rag and came over, adjusting his glasses to look at the sandpaper. He had never taken chemistry, she was fairly sure, but he studied her handwriting the way he studied a bicycle chain, patiently, without pretending to expertise he didn't have. "So hot weather would be like adding fuel," he said slowly. "For that kind."

"Sort of backwards from that, actually, but yes, it changes the direction." She heard the hedge in her own voice and decided to keep it there rather than smooth it over. There was still a question she couldn't answer, and she didn't want to hide it under confidence she hadn't earned. She didn't know why temperature behaved like a substance when it wasn't one. The trick worked; she had watched it work; and she could feel the outline of something underneath that she hadn't reached. Maybe the why came next year, in college, or maybe it came from no one, the way most understanding seemed to arrive at her, sideways and unannounced.

"It's like apportionment," her grandfather said, tapping the double arrows. "You move something in, and the balance moves somewhere else to pay for it." He meant it loosely, she thought, the way he used words he'd collected from decades of invoices and hardware catalogs, but the looseness helped. The system had a budget. Everything you added had to be paid for somewhere.

She copied the sandpaper version into her notebook, heat and all, and wrote a small margin note to herself: true, even if I can't say why yet. Outside, the afternoon had started turning that melancholic gray that came before October rain, and the light through the garage door's small window had gone the color of pencil lead. She gathered the screws back into their jar and put the wrench where it belonged, not because he'd asked but because the bench felt like a place that deserved order.

On Monday there would be a quiz, and she would probably get the exothermic ones right, and possibly the endothermic ones too, and possibly she would encounter some third kind that undid her. That was fine, or fine enough. She had one working tool and one open question, and for now, at seventeen, that seemed like an honest apportionment of what a person could know. She folded the scrap of sandpaper and put it in the pocket of her jacket.

"Supper at six," her grandfather said, picking up the wheel again. "Bring your notebook. I want to see those arrows."

Levi had the museum's third-floor gallery almost to himself on the Tuesday before school started, which was the point of coming. His backpack held two books on the French Revolution, a photocopied packet of excerpts, and a half-empty notebook with the words "HOW VIEWS CHANGED SINCE 1800" underlined twice at the top of a blank page. He stood in front of a case holding a cockade, its ribbon faded to the color of rust, and tried to imagine Burke looking at one of these and feeling the world come apart.

The assignment terrified him in a way he had not admitted to anyone. His older sister, Devi, had told him that a historiographical essay was not about what happened but about how historians had argued, and the distinction, which had sounded simple in her kitchen, kept dissolving when he tried to write. He had Burke's reaction, Carlyle's drama, the Marxist reading, the revisionists of the 1980s who said class had been the wrong lens all along. He had the facts. What he lacked was a way to hold them together without flattening them into a timeline with a moral at the end.

He moved along the cases slowly, because the gallery guard, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor whose badge he had read on previous visits, had once told him that slow looking was the whole trick of museums, and he had decided to believe her. "You're back," she said, coming over to straighten a label someone had knocked crooked. "Same bag, same frown."

"College essay," Levi said. "Sort of. It's about how people have seen the French Revolution differently since 1800, and I can't figure out if the historians are arguing about the Revolution or about themselves."

Mrs. Okafor considered the cockade case as if it might answer. "Maybe they're arguing about the present, using the past as the room to do it in." She pointed down the corridor. "There's a display on how museums change their own exhibits. Same idea, smaller scale. And the library room is open if you need to sit."

The library room, it turned out, was less a library than a reading alcove with a shelf of exhibition catalogs and a few donated books of history. Levi sat down anyway, mostly to have somewhere to put his despair, and texted Devi: "I have nine historians and no argument. Every time I line them up they cancel each other out."

Her reply came while he was still staring at a catalog called Revising the Revolution. "Stop trying to make them agree. Pick two who genuinely clash and build the essay on the seam between them. Also: look up what historians do in other fields when the big interpretation breaks. That's your model. It doesn't have to be France."

He almost put the phone down. Then he thought about what she had said, the seam rather than the summary, and began pulling catalogs off the shelf. The Cold War was not his subject, but a fat blue book had a prize sticker on its spine, and he opened it because the sticker said Bancroft, which Devi had once mentioned the way other people mentioned the Pulitzer. The book was Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, and its argument, compressed into the introduction, stopped him cold. Leffler had won the 1993 Bancroft Prize for maintaining that American leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world. Where other historians Levi had heard of, especially someone named Gaddis, saw defense and containment, Leffler saw the pursuit of preponderance itself, security achieved by standing above everyone else.

He read the introduction twice. What gripped him was not the Cold War at all but the shape of the disagreement: two historians, the same archive, opposite readings, and the argument was really about what the country was for. That was his seam. If historians of the Revolution had split the same way, then his essay was not a timeline but a set of running questions: who feared the crowd, who trusted it, and what present danger each historian was answering when he looked back at 1789.

He worked for two hours, filling pages, and at some point Mrs. Okafor brought him a cup of water without being asked, setting it on the far side of the table away from his notebook. "You looked like a man in the desert," she said. He thanked her and noticed that the afternoon light had shifted through the tall windows, and that the museum's diurnal rhythm was closing around him, guards rotating, voices thinning, the front desk cashing out.

By closing time he had a plan and a problem. The plan: pair the Marxist historians with the revisionists and show that the disagreement was about the present, not the past, using the Leffler model as his structuring idea without pretending the Cold War explained France. The problem: he did not actually know whether the Marxist reading was really dead after 1989 or whether the revisionists had overcorrected, and every time he tried to resolve it he circumscribed his own argument until it said nothing. He wrote in the margin of his notebook, "I don't know who is right. I know what each side was afraid of. Is that enough?" and, after a minute, added, "Maybe that's the essay."

He packed slowly. At the door Mrs. Okafor was logging the last visitors out, and she nodded at his bag. "Did you find your seam?"

"Maybe," Levi said. "I found a book about the Cold War instead of the French Revolution, and it told me how to write about the French Revolution. But half my historians still won't line up."

"Good," she said, and held the door for an elderly couple shuffling toward the exit. "The ones who line up too neatly are usually hiding something."

Jordan had told his mother the assignment was basically finished, which was true in the sense that a house is basically finished when the frame is up. He'd brought the folder to his grandmother's house for the long weekend because she had a real desk and because nobody at school would be around to ask him how it was going. The assignment asked for a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and he had chosen two papers about whether remote learning narrowed or widened achievement gaps. He had read both twice. He had opinions. What he did not have was any idea how to make the opinions sit next to each other on the page without one of them winning by default.

His grandmother set a mug of coffee beside the folder and said she was going to the garden and that he should not let the desk go to waste. He arranged the two articles side by side. The first, by a researcher named Achebe, argued that gaps widened, and it underpinned the claim with test scores from three districts. The second, by a Dr. Lindqvist, argued the data were too noisy to say anything yet, and Jordan had privately decided Lindqvist was just being a coward about it. Privately, and somewhat unfairly, because Lindqvist's tone was mild where Achebe's was acerbic, and Jordan had confused mildness with weakness before.

He wrote for an hour and a half. It went badly. Every paragraph he produced was a summary with a verdict stapled to the end, like Achebe says this, and he's right, and then Lindqvist says this, and he's wrong. He could feel the essay becoming a courtroom where he was judge, prosecutor and stenographer, and the verdict never changed no matter what the witnesses said, which suggested the courtroom was decorative. He deleted two pages. Then he ate a peach on the porch and told himself he was thinking, which was half true.

His grandmother came back with tomatoes and asked, not looking at him, whether the work was going well. "It's fine," he said. "It's basically done." She said that was good and put the tomatoes in the bowl with the peaches, and something about the way she did it, the older fruit to the top where he'd see it, made him feel caught, though she hadn't said anything catching. He went back to the desk and opened the folder again.

This time he tried the opposite of what he'd been doing. Instead of deciding who was right, he wrote down what each article assumed before it argued anything. Achebe assumed the test scores measured the thing that mattered. Lindqvist assumed that without knowing who had actually logged on during remote instruction, the scores could be measuring attendance rather than learning. Jordan sat back. The two men weren't disagreeing about the answer. They were disagreeing about what the question was even made of. He wrote a sentence that began "Where Achebe treats the scores as evidence, Lindqvist treats them as an artifact," and it was the first sentence all day he actually liked.

He kept going until dark, and somewhere in the rush he assembled his list of sources, which he typed up in the order he'd used them: Achebe first, then a school district report, then Lindqvist, then a statistics textbook. He sent the draft to Priya, who was in the writing club with him and who had agreed weeks ago to trade reviews over the weekend. Then he went down to the kitchen and told his grandmother, with more honesty than he'd managed at noon, that it had been going badly and now it was going better. She said the peaches were the ripe ones.

Priya called at nine. "Your argument part is good," she said, which he made her repeat. "Like actually good. But your sources list is wrong." He said it couldn't be wrong, it was just a list. She said she'd made the same mistake last year and lost points for it. "In Chicago, MLA, and APA, entries in the final list of sources are alphabetical by the author's surname," she said. "Not in the order you cited them." He looked at his page. Achebe, then the district report, then Lindqvist, then the textbook, exactly the order of use, exactly wrong. He told her the system was arbitrary and she said maybe, but it was the arbitrary system everyone used, and then she asked whether he really thought Lindqvist's position was weaker or just less fun to read.

That question sat in him while he reordered the list, Achebe first anyway by luck of the alphabet, then the district report under D, then Lindqvist, then the textbook under T. It occurred to him that alphabetical order didn't care who was right either. It didn't care about the order of ideas, or the order of anything. It was a convention, a flat surface the actual thinking had to sit on, and nobody confused the surface with the thinking. He wondered whether his earlier draft had made that exact confusion, treating the sequence in which he'd encountered the articles as if it were the structure of his judgment.

He wrote one more paragraph that night, at the desk with the lamp on and the window open to the sound of the garden. He put both positions together and then was honest about the seam: he wrote that his own reading leaned toward Lindqvist's caution, but that he could not rule out that this was because Achebe's tone had irritated him, and that the evidence Achebe presented was real evidence even if it was thinner than Achebe believed. He read the paragraph over twice. It did not conclude. It ended with a question he didn't answer, and for the first time all weekend that felt like strength rather than failure.

In the morning his grandmother asked if he'd finished, and he said mostly, and she raised an eyebrow at the difference between that and basically done. He laughed. He told her the list of sources at the end had to be alphabetical, and she said she didn't know that, and he said neither had he until yesterday. She poured him more coffee and said his grandfather had once written a whole thesis with the footnotes on cards spread across the kitchen floor, and that some things you learn late and some things you learn just in time.

He packed the folder, and Priya texted a picture of her own reordered list with the caption check yours twice, and he texted back a photo of his, Achebe, district, Lindqvist, textbook, all in a row. "Read it one more time on the train," she wrote. He said he would. He slid the articles into the folder with the final list on top.

Arianna had forty-one dollars, a market full of October, and a theory that if she planned the whole week's meals in advance she would stop buying the seven-dollar cheese croissant every time her roommate Dana said the word "brunch." The theory was untested. So was she. In three weeks she would be at college with a shared kitchen and a meal plan that covered dinner only, which meant five breakfasts and five lunches a week depended on whatever she could learn now, standing between a pumpkin stall and a man selling honey with his dog's face on the label.

She had made a list, which was a kind of victory. Onions, carrots, a sack of potatoes, dried lentils from the grain vendor who called everyone "friend" in a way that made her trust him less. At the tomato stand she hesitated over a bruised half-basket marked down to two dollars, and the vendor, a woman with soil in her knuckle creases, said, "Those are for sauce or soup. Can't eat them raw." Arianna took them. It felt like being let in on something, though she wasn't sure what.

The problem revealed itself slowly, the way a stain does. She had never cooked a meal before, exactly. Her mother made dinner the way other people took showers, privately and without commentary, and Arianna had absorbed nothing except that garlic went in everything and complaining did not. What she wanted, she realized on the bus home with potatoes rolling under the seat, was not one good dinner. It was a system. Something she could do on Sunday and then live off all week, the way Dana lived off one pedicure for a month. Dana had systems. Arianna had cheese croissants.

The community kitchen on Fuller Street ran a Sunday session where anyone could cook, and the woman at the desk said the lentil soup they were making that day was "the same idea you're describing, honey, we make forty servings and freeze them." Arianna had come intending only to watch, but watching lasted four minutes before a man named Renato handed her a wooden spoon and said, "Stir from the bottom, they settle," and after that she was staff.

The kitchen had a huge pot, wide as a truck tire, and Renato ladled the finished soup into containers while narrating his life to anyone within earshot. When Arianna asked whether she could just put a pot like that straight into the fridge, full, he looked at her with something between pity and delight. "You could," he said. "It'd sit warm in the middle for hours. That's why we split it into these shallow ones, it cools fast." He stacked the flat containers like bricks. Arianna wrote it on her list under "onions": shallow containers, not the deep pot. It was the first piece of information all day that felt like a tool rather than a fact.

Her own soup happened the following Sunday, in her mother's kitchen, while her mother was at work and her brother Theo narrated from a stool. Theo was fourteen and blase about nearly everything except the instant noodles he ate like a sycophant praising a king, groaning "so good" at the package before the water even boiled. When Arianna's soup was done, a genuine double batch with the bruised tomatoes cooked down into it, Theo watched her divide it into six flat containers, two inches deep each, and slide them onto the fridge shelf.

"Why not just put the pot in?" he said. "Like Mom does."

"Mom puts it on the counter with a dish towel over it, Theo. It sits there steaming all night." She had looked this up, or rather she had remembered Renato, which felt more reliable than looking things up. A deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours; she'd filed that away the way other people filed phone numbers. Theo shrugged and went back to his noodles, exculpated of all culinary responsibility by his age, or at least using it that way.

The week that followed was not a triumph so much as a series of small, survivable events. Monday's soup needed salt. Tuesday she burned the flatbread while reheating it and ate it anyway, charcoal edges and all, standing at the counter because dishes were already a negotiation she was losing. Wednesday Dana tried the soup, said "this is actually good" in the tone of someone announcing a lab result that had surprised her, and asked for the recipe, which Arianna recited from memory and realized, mid-recitation, she was making half of it up. She hadn't written anything down. She'd been so pleased with the list, the containers, the system, that she'd forgotten the part where the system needed to be repeatable.

Thursday she sat in the empty kitchen with her notebook and tried to reconstruct what she'd actually done, which was also, she supposed, the moment she combined her mother's wordless competence with Renato's loud, narrated method and got something third, something hers: plan the list, buy the marked-down tomatoes, cook double, split it shallow and fast, write it down. What stayed uncertain was everything else, whether Sunday cooking would survive homework and homesickness, whether Dana would keep eating it, whether five dollars of lentils could really carry a week. Friday she found Theo at the stove with one of her containers, and he said, without turning around, "There's one left after this, so."

The gray looked warm on the left side of the canvas and cool on the right, and Kaitlyn had mixed both patches from the same cup. She sat with her brush above the paper, checking the cup, checking the canvas, checking the cup again. Around her the craft shed smelled of cedar shavings and turpentine, and through the open door she could see the lake, flat and white at noon, and the dock where the younger campers were lined up for swim check. Mrs. Okafor had said the pieces were due on the porch by four o'clock Friday, hung and labeled, for the parents' visiting day. That gave Kaitlyn two afternoons, and she had spent the first one painting a sky that refused to be one color.

"Your gray is doing something weird," said Dana, leaning over from the next stool. Dana was painting a frog, which was not the assignment, but nobody had impugned her choice yet, least of all Kaitlyn, who admired people who could ignore instructions without visible anxiety.

"It's the same gray," Kaitlyn said. "I mixed it once. I've been using one cup."

"Then your eyes are broken." Dana held her own brush up like a thermometer. "Left side it looks like it wants to be brown. Right side it wants to be blue."

Kaitlyn laid a strip of the gray on a clean scrap of white paper, and there, alone, it was neither warm nor cool, just gray, a plain honest gray. She set the scrap beside the canvas, beside the orange she had laid down for a sunset below the sky, and beside the green she'd used for the far shore. Against the orange the gray bent warm. Against the green it bent cool. She moved the scrap back and forth like a card trick, watching the color slide, and felt the particular pleasure of a problem turning from an accident into a law. Something was happening that had rules, which meant something had written the rules down, somewhere, in a book, before she was born.

From her stool, Dana watched this happen with the patience of someone waiting for a kettle. She had known Kaitlyn for six weeks of canoe trips and dish duty, long enough to recognize the stillness that came over her when she stopped painting and started hunting. Dana herself worked the other way, piling paint on and hoping; but she liked watching Kaitlyn corner an idea, the way she liked watching the counselors try to fix the leaky craft-shed roof with a confidence neither of them had earned. Kaitlyn got up without a word and went to the shelf by the window where somebody's donated books were stacked between the jars of brushes, books with swollen covers and water stains shaped like continents.

The book she wanted was not there, but an older one was, a paint manual with a cracked spine, and in its index she found a line that stopped her: Chevreul, 1839. She read the page twice. The chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She said it under her breath, then out loud, because Dana was watching.

"The law of simultaneous contrast," Kaitlyn said. "That's what he called it. Complements. Orange and blue, green and red. The gray shifts toward whatever's opposite its neighbor."

"So your sky is a science experiment now."

"My sky was always a science experiment. I just didn't know I was running it."

She went back to the canvas with the scrap of gray still in her hand. The problem, once she understood it, got larger rather than smaller. If the gray changed depending on what touched it, then she could not paint a neutral sky at all; she could only paint a sky that behaved differently in every region, warm over the sunset, cool over the pines. Part of her wanted to fight that, to isolate the gray, to give every patch its own border of white so it would hold still. Another part of her, a newer part, wanted the opposite: to choose the neighbors on purpose, so the gray would turn warm exactly where she wanted warmth, without her ever dipping the brush in anything but the one cup. It seemed almost like cheating, and also like the most honest thing available, and she could not fully decide which, so she sat with both ideas while the swim-check line on the dock moved one camper at a time into the water and out again.

Mrs. Okafor came through at three to count finished pieces, tapping her clipboard against her palm. "Friday at four," she said, stopping at Kaitlyn's table. "Not Friday at five. Not Saturday morning while the cars are loading." She looked at the half-sky for a long moment. "What you have there is either unfinished or very subtle, and I can't tell which."

"Neither can I," Kaitlyn said, which was truer than she meant it to be.

On Friday she hung the painting with a label card that read, in her small careful hand, Kaitlyn, age 16, sky in one gray, and stood back beside Dana while the first parents came up the path. The gray lay warm and cool in bands above the sunset and above the painted shore, doing both things at once, and she watched a woman in a sun hat lean in close, tilt her head, and touch the canvas frame as if checking it for heat.

The receipt printer at Pemberton Hardware jammed whenever the air conditioning was off, so Alexis had learned to read the tape as it emerged, line by line, like a telegram. Pipe fitting, 6.49. Pipe fitting, 6.49. GST, 0.65. She was seventeen and had been working the counter since June, and it was the GST line that bothered her, because she could not make it come out right. Seven percent of 12.98 was 0.91, not 0.65, and either the machine was broken or she was.

She asked her uncle Ray at Sunday dinner, since he had owned a body shop since before she was born and claimed to know everything the government did to a person. "Seven percent," he said, with the certainty of a man who had not looked at a receipt in years. "It's the Goods and Services Tax. Came in when I was your age. Seven percent, and they swore it would never go up." Alexis wrote it in her phone under a note titled Things To Verify, which also contained the boiling point of castor oil and the name of the boy who had painted the mural behind the arena.

The following Thursday her father asked her to come along to the accountant's office, partly because he liked the company and partly because she was his witness now that her mother refused to attend anything involving the word remittance. Alexis brought the crumpled receipt in her jacket pocket. She also brought her own paycheque stub, her first from the hardware store, which she had examined on the bus until the numbers felt like a riddle: gross pay 612.00, then a staircase of subtractions, then net pay 549.33. Someone was taking money out before the money reached her, and the stub named them all in a small, patient font.

The accountant's office was above a florist's and smelled faintly of lilies and toner. Mr. Okafor had a desk with two monitors and a jar of liquorice allsorts he offered to visitors and never ate himself. He and Alexis's father went through the tax return like men walking a familiar field, checking fences. Employment income. Union dues. The deduction for the safety boots her father had bought in March, which reduced the income he was taxed on rather than the tax itself, a distinction Alexis found slippery until Mr. Okafor held up the boot receipt and said, "This makes your income smaller on paper. The tax man taxes the smaller number." Her father said that seemed fair, in the tone of a man who did not quite believe it.

Alexis had been waiting for a gap, and there was one while her father went downstairs to feed the parking meter with coins he counted like a gambler. She flattened the hardware receipt on the desk. "Can I ask something that isn't about us," she said. "The GST on this. It's five percent, isn't it. I checked the arithmetic four times." Mr. Okafor turned the receipt toward himself without hurry. "Five percent," he said. "It was seven when it started, on the first of January, 1991. It's been five percent since the first of January, 2008."

She absorbed this the way you absorb news that a relative has been remarried for years. Her uncle had been so sure. She thought of her math teacher, Mr. Delgado, who called a small proven fact a lemma, a stepping stone you built on your way to the theorem you actually wanted, and she thought that uncle Ray's seven percent had been a lemma built on sand. "So my uncle's wrong," she said. "Not wrong about his whole life," said Mr. Okafor. "Just behind it by a while." He pulled a liquorice allsort from the jar, looked at it, and put it back.

From where he sat, Marcus Okafor could see the girl doing arithmetic in her head, her lips moving slightly, the way his daughter did when calculating whether she could afford both the sneakers and the concert. He had learned, over nineteen tax seasons, that the ones who asked about the GST line at seventeen either became accountants or became the kind of citizens who read their mail, and both were fine outcomes. Her father came back up the stairs with a sullen expression about the meter, having fed it four dollars for forty minutes, and the return resumed.

But Alexis kept returning to her paycheque stub, which she unfolded now and laid beside the receipt. "So the GST is me paying tax when I spend," she said slowly, "and these are tax taken out when I earn. Both at once. I'm taxed going in and coming out." Mr. Okafor considered whether to correct her and decided she had earned the simplification. "More or less," he said. "Though the return exists because we guess wrong in both directions. Sometimes you've paid too much through the year and they owe you. Sometimes not." Alexis looked at the stub's patient little font, at the deductions that had been taken from her as though she were an established person with obligations, and felt something complicated that she did not yet have a word for. Pride, possibly. Or indignation. They sat close together.

Her father signed the return in three places, each signature smaller than the last, as though the pen itself were being taxed. "Will we get money back?" Alexis asked. "We'll see," her father said, which was his answer to everything from refunds to weather.

On the bus home, Alexis texted her uncle: it's 5 percent now, it changed in 2008, it started at 7 in 1991. Three dots appeared, hovered, and vanished. She put the phone away and took out the receipt one more time, running her thumb over the small grey line, GST 0.65, correct and certain and printed twice because the machine had jammed.

Ms. Ruiz had a clock on her wall that ticked too loudly for a room where people were supposed to say private things, and Naomi had decided, over four visits, that she hated it. She sat with her hands folded on the folder of printouts, waiting to be told, one more time, what she already knew.

"Your list is all reach schools," Ms. Ruiz said, turning the paper toward her. "Where's the safety?"

"She'll say the state school," Naomi said, meaning her mother, though her mother wasn't in the room. "She calls it the fallback, which is her word for failure."

"That's not what it means to her," Ms. Ruiz said, mild, and Naomi thought, you've met her twice, you don't get to translate her. But she only shrugged, because arguing took energy she was saving for the wait, which had begun to feel like a job in itself. Every morning she checked the portal of the faraway school, the one in the city with the studio art program, and every morning the status read the same two words, and she had trained herself to look away before the words could arrange themselves into a verdict.

The night before, she and her mother had sat at the kitchen computer until nearly one. The state deadline was the next day, and her mother had printed the instructions and read them aloud in her careful, slow way, the way she read anything official, as if the government might be listening for mistakes. The form was called the FAFSA, her mother said, tapping the screen, and it was how you applied for federal financial aid, the Pell Grants and the federal loans. Naomi had assumed the loans were the whole point, that the form was basically a debt application dressed in a cheerful acronym, a bureaucratic dysphemism if she'd ever heard one, though she kept that to herself. Then her mother's finger moved down the page. The states used it too, she read, and the colleges, for their own aid. Their own money, Naomi said slowly, money we haven't even applied for yet, and her mother said, well, that's what it says, and for a while neither of them spoke, just the furnace cycling on in the basement.

"Choleric" was the word Ms. Ruiz had used in October, not about Naomi but about the father in the novel they'd ended up discussing when Naomi came in claiming it was about course registration. She'd meant the character, but Naomi had taken it home and tried it on her mother and found it almost fit, her mother's quick flare over the electric bill, over the guidance office's voicemail, over the word "fallback." Almost fit. This morning her mother had driven her to school early so they could finish the form's last page in the car, phone hotspot on, both of them hunched over the small screen, and when Naomi hit submit her mother had put a hand flat on the dashboard, not a victory gesture, just steadying, and said, "Okay. Okay. Now they know we exist."

The trouble was that Naomi had spent months thinking about college as a problem you could parametrize, like the curves in calculus: set the variables, tuition and distance and prestige, plot the points, find the feasible region. Her mother lived inside a different math entirely, one where you applied everywhere the form reached and let the money tell you where home would be. For a long time Naomi had filed her mother's method under the heading of giving up, and she was honest enough, sitting under the ticking clock, to admit the filing had been wrong, or at least premature, which in her experience was the same thing as wrong but softer to hold.

"So what do you want from me today," Ms. Ruiz asked. "You've submitted everything. There's nothing left to do but wait."

"I want you to tell me the waiting means something," Naomi said. "That checking the portal helps. That it's not just a slot machine."

Ms. Ruiz didn't answer right away, which Naomi disliked and also trusted. Outside, someone's class change filled the hallway with noise, then emptied it.

"My mom wants me to add the state school," Naomi said. "I told her it was a fallback. She got quiet. She does that instead of fighting."

"Is that what it is to you?"

Naomi looked at the folder, at the printouts her mother had made at the library because their printer was out of ink, the pages still warm when she'd slid them across the table. "It's money we could actually get," she said. "It's a place with a real studio. I don't know if that's settling or if I was being proud and calling it standards."

Ms. Ruiz slid a blank add form across the desk and set a pen on top of it. "You don't have to decide what it means today."

Naomi picked up the pen and wrote the state school's name, her letters smaller than usual, careful, and then she looked up and asked, "Can I use your phone? My mom's at work, and she'll want to know before I lose my nerve."

" Dial nine for outside," Ms. Ruiz said, and turned back to her computer as Naomi started pressing the buttons.

Sofia had volunteered to run the peer health table at the pharmacy on Saturday mornings because the alternative was a second shift shelving shampoo, and the pharmacist, Mrs. Okafor, had said the table counted as community service, which Sofia needed for her scholarship application. The table itself was a folding card table between the cough drops and the photo counter, and her job was to hand out flyers about the teen clinic two bus stops away and answer questions, even though she had only been trained once, in a conference room with bad coffee, by a nurse who talked fast.

The training was supposed to have a second session, on consent and contraception and testing, but it had been cancelled twice, and Mrs. Okafor had told her, do your best, you're not diagnosing anything, you're pointing at a door. That had felt like enough until a girl from her chemistry class, Dana, appeared in front of the table at nine-forty with her hands in her hoodie pocket, looking at the vitamins behind Sofia's head.

"I need to ask something but you can't tell anyone," Dana said.

Sofia came around the table, which was a gesture she had learned from the nurse, get on the same side of the thing, though she was aware of how it might look, two girls whispering between the antacids. Dana's question came out in pieces. She had been with a boy from the archipelago of magnet schools across the county, someone Sofia vaguely knew, someone with a reputation she did not fully trust, and the condom had broken, and now she wanted to get tested but her mother read the mail, and her mother read the insurance statements, and her mother would need to sign.

"Does she, though," Sofia said, and realized as she said it that she did not know.

The fact surfaced slowly, from a folded pamphlet in the box under the table, the one with the small print she had skipped during the single training. All 50 states and Washington, DC, let minors consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections themselves, without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age. Sofia read it twice with the pamphlet tilted away from the photo counter, where a man was waiting for his blood pressure pills. She told Dana the shape of it, that no form was coming home, no signature required, that she could walk into the clinic Monday. Dana asked what the minimum age was in their state, and Sofia had to say she didn't know that part, and that the clinic would. Dana nodded, wrote the address on her wrist in pen, and bought a pack of hair ties so it would look like she had a reason to have been at the pharmacy, which Sofia thought was a strange and careful kind of planning.

It was the consent part Sofia had not prepared for, and it kept coming up. A boy from the middle school stopped by to take a flyer because his friends dared him to, and Sofia found herself saying, it means yes, and it means you can change a yes, and it has to be a yes you actually said, not one somebody decided for you. She was transliterating, really, taking what the nurse had said in her fast conference-room voice and putting it letter by letter into ordinary words, and she could feel the places where the translation was thin. A girl asked whether the pill made you gain weight and Sofia said some kinds can, and you can switch kinds, and the clinic helps you do that, and she heard herself sounding almost like a person who knew things, which was itself a kind of warning she decided to notice rather than ignore.

By eleven she had explained condoms to two boys who were too embarrassed to hold still, walked one woman toward the emergency contraception shelf with the flatness Mrs. Okafor had modeled for her, and given out the clinic's number nine times. When Mrs. Okafor passed with a cart of deodorant, she paused and said, "You're better at this than the last one," and Sofia said "than the last what," and Mrs. Okafor said "than the last volunteer, obviously," and rolled the cart on.

At noon Dana came back. She was holding a receipt and a pharmacy bag with a toothbrush in it, and she said her cousin had driven her to the clinic on a Saturday hunch, and they had been open, and the intake nurse had not asked for a single parental thing. "I signed my own name on my own line," Dana said, as though the line itself were the discovery. Then she leaned in and said, "I told them you sent me, and they asked if you'd want to train the next peer group. They said you already know the law." Sofia looked at the pamphlet still in her hand, at the paragraph she had read to one person, once. "Tell them I know one paragraph," she said.

Dana zipped her hoodie and walked out past the photo counter, and Mrs. Okafor set a second folding table against the wall beside the first one.

The queue at the phone store moved slowly enough that Samantha had time to read the posters twice. One promised a free phone with a two-year plan, the word free set in type so confident it seemed to presage a world where nothing was paid for, ever. She clutched the paper sleeve of her broken handset, which had died in a puddle outside her internship two days before, and rehearsed what she would say: she needed something cheap, something that would last until September, when college began and everything was supposed to become clearer.

"Next." The clerk was younger than Samantha expected, maybe twenty, with the patient ascetic air of someone who had explained the same three plans a thousand times and had stopped expecting anyone to understand them. He slid a folder across the counter and uncapped a pen. "Just need your signature here, here, and initials there. It's the standard agreement."

"Can I read it?" she asked.

He blinked, then recovered. "Sure. Nobody does, but sure." He stepped away to help a man comparing screen protectors, and Samantha bent over the pages. The first was dense with language she half recognized from movies: terms and conditions, liability, limitation thereof, the company shall not be held responsible. Further down, the word consent appeared in a paragraph about data sharing, and she realized she was being asked to agree to things she had not known existed an hour ago.

Her phone buzzed, which was impossible, and she flinched before remembering the clerk's loaner on the counter. It was her friend Dana, and the message brought the old argument back whole: Marcus still hadn't paid the fifty dollars he'd promised for a month of calculus tutoring in the spring. Dana insisted a deal was a deal. Marcus had laughed and said, "It's not like we signed anything," and Samantha had let it go because finals were coming and the money felt somehow unimportant next to the physics exam. Now, reading a document whose entire power seemed to live in a signature, she wondered what exactly a signature did.

The man at the screen protector counter was speaking loudly into his own phone, and she caught fragments without meaning to. "No, look, I'm telling you, there's no contract there. A contract needs an offer, an acceptance, and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange." Samantha's eyes lifted from the page. "You offered to pay him, he tutored you, that's the something of value from each side," the man said. "The writing doesn't matter. Tell him that."

She looked back down at the folder. The free phone, she now saw, was folded into the plan as a monthly credit; the plan itself cost more per month than the cheaper one without a phone. The free thing was the expensive thing wearing a costume. And the early termination fee, buried two pages in under a heading about liability, was two hundred dollars. She thought of Marcus's fifty dollars and felt an odd double movement in herself: she had been on his side because he was funny and the debt was informal, and she was on the store's side because the folder was formal, and both positions had rested on the same lazy assumption, that seriousness lived in paperwork. Apparently it did not. Apparently Dana had been right for a reason Samantha hadn't understood until a stranger's phone call drifted over a counter.

"Ready?" the clerk had returned.

"Almost." She read the termination clause a second time, slowly, letting the sentence about the two hundred dollars sit in her like a bruise she was choosing to accept or not accept. College was four years, not two. The plan would hold her longer than the phone would survive; screens met puddles, her whole recent history proved that. But her mother had wired her three hundred dollars that morning, the last gift before the declared end of parental subsidies, and the idea of losing two hundred of it to a broken screen in October felt genuinely deleterious, not abstractly but in meals.

"Question," she said. "If I take the smaller plan and buy the phone outright, is that the same total?"

He tapped his screen, and his eyebrows moved a millimeter, which from him was practically astonishment. "It's forty dollars less. But you'd pay the phone up front today."

"Then that one." She signed the shorter form, once, where the arrow indicated, and her signature came out smaller than she expected, as though her hand understood before she did that this was the version she meant. She slid the pen back and pocketed the loaner. Outside, she stopped on the curb and texted Dana: "You were right about Marcus. Tell him it counts even without a signature. I'll explain tonight."

"Explain what?" Dana wrote back.

"The thing somebody said in line at the phone store," Samantha typed, then deleted it, then wrote, "His fifty dollars. I'm collecting it, and he's paying it."

The museum was nearly empty on weekday afternoons, which was exactly why Felix came. He had a physics placement exam on Monday that would decide whether he started college in the introductory section or one level up, and his bedroom had stopped being a place where thinking happened. Here, at the ballistics exhibit, a small brass cannon fired a ball across a dark chamber once every eight seconds, and a strobe light froze it into a string of pearl-bright positions against a gridded wall. Felix had his notebook open on the railing, and he was losing to the problem.

He kept trying to compute the whole arc at once, one velocity, one angle, everything tangled together, and the numbers collapsed every time. On the fourth shot he stopped writing and simply watched the strobe. The horizontal spacing between the pearls was even. Every single image, the same distance across. The vertical spacing, though, widened going down, ball images spreading apart like a dropped handful of coins. He wrote that in the margin, then drew two small axes, and something loosened. Nothing pulls the ball sideways, he thought, so across it just keeps whatever it started with. Up and down is where the gravity gets to act, alone, on its own clean problem. The motion wasn't one thing. It was two, stacked.

A boy of maybe ten arrived at the railing with a half-eaten pretzel and an expression that augured poorly for Felix's concentration. The boy's name, announced unprompted, was Deshawn, and he wanted to know why the ball went farther when the cannon tilted up but not when it tilted up too far.

"Forty-five degrees," Felix said, and then, because that would mean nothing, "watch the even spacing. When you tilt it, you trade across for up. Too steep and you have tons of up, which gravity just eats, and barely any across." He angled his notebook so Deshawn could see the two axes. "You have to split it. That's the trick. That's the whole trick."

"Split every throw?" Deshawn said. "Like my dad throws footballs?"

"Every one," Felix said. "Rockets, spitballs, everything."

Deshawn nodded with the gravity of someone being inducted into a secret, then wandered off toward the electricity hall, and Felix, surprisingly, missed him. He worked the problem again with the split, and the pearls lined up with his arithmetic almost exactly. The gap he couldn't close was small, and he suspected his strobe timing, not his physics, which was a feeling so unfamiliar it took him a moment to recognize it as confidence.

He found Deshawn ten minutes later at the Van de Graaff exhibit, where a docent named Renata was demonstrating field effects, and Deshawn was looking worried that the machine's crackle would hurt him. Renata noticed too. She crouched to his height and said the dome was loud the way thunder is loud, and that she would hold his hand the whole time if he wanted to touch the field meter's wand. He did want. She kept her word.

The wand read out the electric field strength at different distances from the dome, numbers on a small screen. Renata asked the small crowd to guess which nearby speck of dust, floating in the air, would feel the bigger push: the speck carrying a small charge or the speck carrying twice that charge, both sitting in the same field. Someone said it made no difference. Deshawn, with total intransigence, said the small one, because it was lighter.

"Field's the same for both," Felix said slowly, working it aloud, watching the screen. "The force on a charge in a field is the charge times the field strength, F equals q E. Same field, double the charge, double the force." Renata glanced at him, checking, and he nodded to say he'd stand behind that. Deshawn squinted at the floating specks as though they had personally deceived him.

"So the dust with more charge gets pushed harder," Renata said, "just like that, straight from the field." She let Deshawn move the wand and watch the field numbers climb as he neared the dome, his fear apparently filed away under matters already handled.

Walking out past the ballistics chamber, Felix stopped at the railing one last time. The cannon fired. The strobe caught the ball mid-air, pearls strung even across, spreading down, and he copied the spacing into his notebook without doing a single calculation. Deshawn's father probably threw better footballs than Felix ever would, but that was fine. He had what he'd come for, and he wrote at the bottom of the page, underlining it twice, "split it first, always."

"Forty-five degrees," said Deshawn, appearing at his elbow with the last of the pretzel.

"Forty-five degrees," Felix agreed.

Carter had exactly one day left before his driving test, and the cones at the far end of the school parking lot were waiting for him like a verdict. His mother had left the car keys on the kitchen counter beside a note that said only "5pm," which was when she got home and when, by prior arrangement, the test would already be behind him. So the afternoon was his, and the empty lot with its faded lines was his, and the recalcitrant cone at the corner of his imaginary parking space refused, on his first three attempts, to remain upright.

"You're turning the wheel too early," said Priya from the curb, where she sat cross-legged with a chemistry textbook she was visibly not reading. She had agreed to come on the condition that Carter drive her to her debate tournament on Saturday, win or lose, license or no license. "You keep cutting it before your back wheel is even with the cone."

"I know what I'm doing," Carter said, which was untrue in a way they both understood. He had watched four videos that morning, each ascribing slightly different timing to the same set of motions, so that the advice had begun to cancel itself out. One instructor swore by the two o'clock method; another called that an oversimplification and recommended watching the rear tire. Carter had tried to apportion his trust between them, giving each video half his confidence, and the result was a parking job that would have flattened a mailbox.

He backed up, reset, and tried again, this time counting aloud. The car slid in close to the curb on the fourth attempt, close enough that Priya stood and walked over to eyeball it. "Maybe eighteen inches," she said. "That's passing distance." She tapped the roof twice, the way his mother did, and Carter felt something loosen in his chest. It was not joy exactly. It was more like the feeling of a proof coming out, the answer arriving after the work rather than before it.

But the parking lot was the easy part, and they both knew the test ended with a short drive, and the drive included the on ramp to Route 9. So at four o'clock, with the sun going low and orange across the windshields of the teacher lot, Carter signaled, checked his mirrors, and pulled out of the school drive toward the highway. Priya came with him because she refused to let him face the ramp alone, and also, she admitted, because her tournament was Saturday and she intended to arrive in a vehicle, not on two buses.

The ramp climbed and curved, and the merge lane shortened faster than the videos had suggested it would. Carter checked the side mirror, saw nothing, and began to drift left. Priya made a sound, a short inhale, and Carter glanced over his shoulder through the rear passenger window and there it was: a gray sedan sitting beside him, close enough that he could see the driver's mouth moving, the driver talking to someone Carter could not see. He straightened the wheel and stayed in his lane until the sedan passed and the road behind him emptied.

"Mirrors," Carter said, when they had pulled into a gas station and stopped, both of his hands still on the wheel. "Mirrors leave blind spots, right there beside the car." He turned in his seat and looked at the space where the sedan had been, then at the mirror that had shown him nothing. "I looked. I actually looked, and it wasn't there."

"That's why you turn your head," Priya said. "My dad calls it the shoulder check. He made me practice it forty times before he'd let me near his car." She checked her phone, saw three messages from her debate partner about rebuttal evidence, and typed a quick reply. "So you look twice now. Mirror, then shoulder. Both, every time."

Carter nodded slowly. The two views of driving he had been trying to reconcile all week, the videos that treated it as a system of rules and his mother's way of treating it as a matter of habit and feel, were not actually opposed. The rule was the shoulder check; the habit was doing it until it was as automatic as breathing. What he still did not know, and could not know until the examiner slid into the passenger seat tomorrow morning, was whether a half day of practice was enough to make a habit out of anything. He started the car, checked the mirror, and turned his head anyway.

"Okay," he said. "Once more around the block, then your turn to buy the gas station coffee."

"Deal," said Priya. "But if you pass tomorrow, I'm picking the music on Saturday."

Nicolas had a list on his phone and a mission in his pocket, and the mission was this: cook dinner for his family before his mother got home at seven, and cook it well, because tonight was the night he proved he could be trusted with the kitchen. The farmers' market occupied two rows of white tents in the gravel lot by the river, and the morning smelled like roasted chiles and wet lettuce. At five thousand feet above the sea, the town sat high enough that the light came down thin and bright, and Nicolas felt efficient just standing in it.

The trouble began, as troubles do, with memory. He wanted to make the pasta dish from the family's camping trip last month, the one his father had requested twice since. But that trip had produced a pot of noodles that were, in his sister Priya's verdict, "crunchy in a way pasta should never consent to be." He had boiled them for exactly the time on the box. Everyone had teased him for a full twenty minutes. Priya had announced she was drafting a formal complaint. Nicolas had told her she'd need a subpoena if she wanted him to testify about the water. He had laughed about it, then and now, but something about it still snagged, like a fact with a burr on it.

At the tomato stand, a girl about his age was arranging heirlooms with the seriousness of a museum curator. She was effusive about everything, every variety, every grower, every irrigation method, so much so that Nicolas briefly wondered if she was being paid by the adjective. "The Purple Cherokees," she said, holding one up like a jewel, "are the sweetest thing at this market, and I will defend that position against all rivals." He bought four.

"Can I ask you something weird," he said, bagging them. "You've lived here your whole life, right? Does pasta take longer to cook up here?"

"Pasta, rice, beans, eggs, everything boiled," she said. "The water boils cooler at this altitude. Around ninety-five degrees Celsius at five thousand feet, instead of a hundred. So things just take longer."

He stared at her. "The box said nine minutes."

"The box lives at sea level," she said, and turned to greet another customer, leaving Nicolas holding his tomatoes and his whole ruined alibi. It wasn't his fault. Or it was partly his fault, in the way that not knowing things is a kind of fault you can fix by finding out. On the camping trip, he had stood at the stove feeling like a failure while the altitude quietly sabotaged him, and Priya's complaint had been, technically, dismissed.

He stopped at the herb stand and then, because he was on a roll, at the egg stand, where the vendor's metal cashbox gave him a shock sharp enough to make him yelp. "Dry mountain air," the vendor said, not looking up. "It'll ionize everything you touch by October. Hair, sweaters, doorknobs. You get used to it or you get used to apologizing to cats." Nicolas rubbed his thumb and decided he would do neither, and also that he loved this market, where even the static electricity came with commentary.

At home he laid out his ingredients like evidence for a trial he now intended to win. Priya drifted into the kitchen around six, ostensibly for a glass of water, actually to supervise. "Is it the pasta again," she said. "Should I alert the authorities."

"The authorities have been consulted," Nicolas said. "The water boils at ninety-five degrees Celsius here, not a hundred, because of the altitude. So it's going to take longer, and I'm building that in. Eleven minutes, twelve, whatever it needs."

Priya leaned against the counter, watching him salt the water with the new confidence of a man who understood his enemy. "So you're saying the camping pasta wasn't your fault."

"I'm saying the mountain did it," Nicolas said. "I was an innocent bystander."

"You were the one holding the spoon."

"I was an innocent bystander holding a spoon, in a jurisdiction with compromised boiling." He stirred the sauce, tasting, adjusting, and Priya stole a piece of tomato off the cutting board and pronounced it, grudgingly, excellent.

He tasted a noodle at nine minutes, another at eleven, and at twelve and a half they gave, finally, in the way they were supposed to, soft all the way through without going limp. He fished one out for Priya without being asked. She chewed it slowly, like a judge who had been wrong before and knew the cost of ruling too fast. Their mother's car pulled into the driveway. Priya swallowed, looked at the pot, looked at him, and said, "Withdraw the complaint. Mostly."

Ryan had told his father he would handle dinner, and his father had said fine, in the flat voice he had been using since March, since the plant cut its second shift and the house went quiet in the middle of the day. So Ryan stood in the kitchen on Sunday afternoon with flour on his forearms and a plan he had not entirely thought through: homemade bread, the kind his grandmother used to make, soup from a carton, a table that looked like somebody had tended it.

The recipe said to mix flour, water, yeast and salt, then knead for eight minutes. Eight minutes felt like a very long time when your hands kept sticking and the dough kept tearing, so he had stopped at maybe five, maybe less, shaped it into a round, and set it near the window to rise. His sister Delia came through for a glass of water and watched him hover over it. "You're staring at bread," she said. "It's not going to do tricks." But it did rise, slowly, a pale dome under a damp towel, and when he slashed the top with a knife and put it in the oven he felt something in his chest unclench for the first time in weeks.

The loaf came out looking right, golden and cracked along the cut, and it sounded hollow when he knocked on it, which the recipe said was good. But when he sawed off the end piece, the crumb was dense and close, almost crumbly, nothing like the open, springy interior of his grandmother's loaves. He pressed a piece between his fingers and it compressed and stayed compressed. He ate it anyway, standing at the counter, and it tasted like flour and salt and failure in roughly equal parts.

His father drifted in around five, saturnine as he'd been all spring, and looked at the loaf without comment. "It's the first one," Ryan said, more sharply than he meant, and his father held up both hands, palms out, the gesture of a man declining a fight he hadn't started. Delia, who could not bear a silence, said, "It's actually not bad with butter," which was kind of her and also a bit of a prevaricate, since she had eaten one piece and made a face at it when she thought no one was watching.

That night Ryan sat at the kitchen table with his phone and a library book Delia had brought home on a whim, a fat one about bread, its dust jacket long gone. He had assumed bread was mostly luck, or a talent some people had, but the book kept insisting on process. He read one sentence three times. "Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water," he said aloud, mostly to the empty room, "and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier." Delia, passing through in pajamas, repeated "gliadin" twice as though tasting it, then said he'd better not become one of those people with a starter in the fridge named after a dead poet, and went upstairs.

So the crumbly loaf had been his fault in a way he could name. Five minutes of kneading had not been enough to build whatever glutenin and gliadin built when water got involved, and the network inside his dough had stayed weak, and the bread had come out dense because there was nothing strong enough inside it to hold it open. He didn't know whether that was the whole story, whether the water had been off or the yeast tired, and the book admitted that bread kept its own accounts. But the kneading part was something he could control, and he decided that was worth more than knowing everything.

He started the second loaf at seven the next morning, before anyone else was up. This time he set a timer and kneaded the full eight minutes, then kept going, folding the dough over itself, pushing with the heel of his hand, turning the bowl a quarter turn, over and over, until his shoulders burned and the dough stopped tearing and began to stretch, smooth as an earlobe, a veneer of satin on its surface where the shaggy roughness had been. It was strange to think that the change was happening at a level he couldn't see, proteins linking hands underwater, and stranger still that his tired arms were the instrument of it.

The second loaf rose higher and faster, as though the dough had been waiting for permission. When it came out of the oven at noon, his father was at the table with the job listings spread in front of him, and Delia was eating cereal, and Ryan set the loaf down on a rack without a word. He let it cool as long as he could stand, which was not entirely, and cut it. The crumb tore open, soft and full of irregular holes, and when he pulled a piece it stretched before it gave.

"Chewy," Delia said, with her mouth full, in a tone that suggested she was surprised to be issuing a compliment. His father put down the listings, tore a piece from the heel, and chewed it slowly, looking at the window, and then at his son's flour-dusted shirt, and then back at the window. "Save me another slice," he said. "I'll take it with the soup tonight."

The cones in the driving school lot were orange and scuffed, and Kate had backed between them eleven times before Mr. Reyes said anything at all. He sat in the passenger seat with his clipboard against his knee, the window cracked to let the August heat escape in slow degrees. On the twelfth attempt she came in too wide, corrected too late, and ended with her rear tire resting against the curb like an apology.

"You're looking at the cones," he said. "Look where you want the car to be."

She tried again. The car slid in on a smooth arc, and when she straightened the wheel and looked up, the cone behind her was close enough to touch through the rear window, and the one ahead had a hand's width of clearance. Mr. Reyes made a small mark on his clipboard that could have meant anything.

Kate had a reason for being here that went beyond the ordinary one. Her mother was moving at the end of the month to an apartment across the river, closer to the hospital where she'd taken the night shifts, and Kate would be staying in the old house with her father on the weeks he wasn't traveling. The two addresses were forty minutes apart by two buses and one transfer, and the transfer never came on time. A license would emancipate her from the bus schedule entirely, from waiting under a shelter with a broken panel, from arriving places already tired. She had explained none of this to Mr. Reyes. He knew only what the clipboard said.

Between parking runs, while another student took the car, Kate sat on the metal bench at the edge of the lot with her math homework on her knees. The chapter was on induction, and the book kept using a word she'd had to look up twice: lemma, a smaller result you proved first, on your way to the thing you actually wanted. She liked that there was a word for it. Almost everything in her life at the moment felt like a lemma, a preliminary step whose only meaning was that it came before something else.

That afternoon her mother had texted her a phone number and a question about the new apartment. Her mother was at work and couldn't call the landlord, so it had fallen to Kate, who was sitting in the driving school office with the landline and a scrap of paper. When the landlord picked up, he was eating something, and he set it down.

"I can do the rent," Kate said, "but I'm trying to figure out the electric bill. Do you know what the last tenant used?"

"Six hundred kilowatt-hours a month, give or take," he said. "That's a pretty normal month there. Electricity gets billed by the kilowatt-hour, so you can work it out yourself if you know the rate."

"What's the rate?"

"Fifteen cents a kilowatt-hour, out there."

Kate wrote the numbers down. On the paper, under the scrap of the lemma she'd copied out at the bench, she multiplied six hundred by fifteen and got ninety dollars, and then, remembering something the landlord had muttered about service fees, she asked whether anything else got added on.

"There's fixed monthly charges from the utility, whatever those are," he said. "The ninety is just the usage part. Before those."

She thanked him and hung up. Ninety dollars, plus whatever the fixed charges turned out to be, on top of rent, out of a night-shift paycheck. She sat with that number for a moment. It was not catastrophic, and it was not nothing, and she could not decide which it was more of, because the fixed charges were still unknown and she had learned this year not to round unknowns in either direction.

Back in the car, it was highway merging, which Mr. Reyes said was where students failed who had passed everything else. The on-ramp rose and curved, and the traffic in the right lane came on at highway speed, and Kate's hands were damp on the wheel. She signaled, checked the mirror, checked it again, and then made the error Mr. Reyes had warned her about on paper and never yet in person: she slowed instead of speeding up, hunting for a gap so perfect that it would never arrive. A truck bore down, flashing its lights, and she had to ride the shoulder for a hundred yards before an opening came.

"Braking on a ramp," Mr. Reyes said calmly, as they came back around for another try. "It's a pernicious habit. It feels careful, and it's the most dangerous thing you can do up there."

"But what if there's no gap?"

"There's always a gap if you're going the speed of the traffic. You're asking the highway to accommodate you. Don't. Arrive at the speed it's already going, and the gap makes itself."

She thought about that on the second run. It ran against something in her, the same something that had made her creep between the cones with inches to spare, the belief that safety came from minimizing your presence, from taking up exactly the room you were given and no more. But the merge required the opposite: to meet the traffic at its own speed, to claim a space. Somewhere in the two ideas there was a middle she couldn't yet name, a way of being careful that didn't mean shrinking.

The second merge was not perfect. She came on a little fast, corrected, and slid into the lane a half-length behind a blue hatchback whose driver never even looked at her, which was somehow the point. On the way back down the off-ramp, Mr. Reyes made another mark on the clipboard, the same mark as before, she thought, though she couldn't be sure.

"One more week of this," he said, "then we book the test."

That evening she texted her mother the number, ninety dollars a month for the electricity usage before the fixed charges, six hundred kilowatt-hours at fifteen cents, and asked if that changed anything. The reply took an hour to come. While she waited, she carried her math book to the kitchen table and worked through the lemma again, proving the small thing first, the preliminary thing, the thing you needed before you could need the rest. Her mother's answer arrived at last, and it was only three words long, and Kate read it twice before she set the phone face-down beside the book and picked up her pencil. "It'll work."

The theory room above the concert hall smelled of radiator dust and old coffee, and Logan spread his staff paper across the table just as the piano downstairs began the afternoon rehearsal. He had sixteen blank bars to fill by Friday, a melody with chord changes written in standard notation, and so far he had four bars he liked and twelve he was faking.

His friend Dev slid into the chair across from him and pulled the sheet over without asking. "Bar three's good. The rest is you avoiding bar three."

"It's development," Logan said.

"It's wandering." Dev tapped the empty measures. "You've got a D minor seven going nowhere and then this G that sounds like you got bored."

That was accurate, which annoyed Logan, because he had spent two evenings on the G. He took the sheet back and played the four good bars on his phone keyboard, then the rest, and heard it the way Dev must have heard it: a sentence that started and then cleared its throat for eight bars. The rehearsal downstairs broke off mid-phrase and started again, and he listened to the pianist play the same passage twice, the second time slower, the way you'd repeat something to make sure it was true.

He tried a new approach. Instead of inventing bars five through sixteen, he wrote a return: bar one's melody, brought back over a different chord, then under the original chord, the way the rehearsal downstairs kept circling its opening theme. When he played it for Dev, Dev shrugged in a way that was equivocal, half nod and half wince, and Logan made him point to the wince. It was bar fourteen. The melody had come home, the chords had settled onto the tonic, and then there were two more bars on the page that did nothing but repeat the final chord like a guest who did not realize the party had ended.

"So end at fourteen," Dev said.

"I need sixteen. The assignment is sixteen bars." Logan stared at the last two measures. The problem was not that he lacked notes; it was that he lacked a reason for them. Everything before bar fourteen had a job. These two bars were after the job was done.

Downstairs the rehearsal reached its ending, and then, after what Logan had assumed was the ending, the piano kept going for another phrase, brief and firm, hammering the home key twice and landing hard on the tonic. Logan stopped writing. He listened to the whole thing again in his head. The melody had ended, resolved, and then this extra bit had come after and made the ending feel finished rather than merely over.

He leaned over the railing by the stairs and caught the rehearsal assistant, a conservatory student named Petra, coming up with a thermos. "That last part," he said. "After the piece ends. What is that?"

"A coda," Petra said. "Optional closing section. Comes after the recapitulation, reinforces the home key, brings the movement to an end." She stepped past him, then paused. "You can also skip it."

Back at the table, he wrote the word in pencil above his final two bars and then tried to make the bars earn it. Not a repetition of the ending, but a reinforcement: the tonic chord voiced lower, the melody's first three notes descending instead of rising, a quiet echo rather than an announcement. He played it for Dev without saying anything first. Dev listened all the way through, which he rarely did.

"That's it," Dev said. "The last two bars sound like they mean to be there."

Logan erased the pencil word and wrote it again more neatly. He was aware of a small, dishonest impulse to explain to Dev what he had done, to frame the coda as a plan he'd had from the start, and he let the impulse pass without acting on it, though he could not exactly exculpate himself either, since he had already half-opened his mouth before deciding not to. Some things you just didn't do, and that was the whole of it.

At the piano that evening, in the empty hall after the rehearsal crew had gone, he played the sixteen bars through at tempo. Bars one to four still worked. Five through thirteen still wandered a little, and he heard it plainly now, without Dev needing to say so. The return at fourteen landed. The coda landed after it. He played the whole thing a second time and then, because Petra had said it was optional, he played it once more ending at fourteen, no coda, to hear the difference.

Both endings were defensible. The one without the coda stopped like a held breath; the one with it settled like a door closing on a soft latch. He sat with his hands on the keys and could not decide which was truer, and he thought that might be the actual thing he was learning, though he would not have said it that way to anyone. He wrote "with coda" in the corner of the page, then looked at it, then left it.

He packed his sheet music, checked the practice room was empty, and let himself out through the stage door into the parking lot, still humming the last three notes.

Kaitlyn had told herself the plan so many times that afternoon that it had started to feel like a memory instead of a choice: meet Marcus at the fountain by the food court at four, wander the mall, eat pretzels, and be home by seven because her mother, who trusted her exactly as far as the parking lot, would be waiting in the car. She had also told herself that she looked calm, which was true only if you didn't count her hands.

She got there early, which she did not do, and stood outside the aquarium shop watching a tank of clownfish weave through anemones. A plaque said the arrangement was called mutualism, both creatures getting something from the deal. That was the thing about Marcus, she'd decided. They were good for each other. He'd helped her monetize the vintage-clothing account she ran by suggesting she photograph the good jackets flat-laid on white, and sales had doubled. She was good for him too, though she couldn't have said how, exactly, and decided not to examine it.

"You're already here," Marcus said, arriving at 4:02 with his skateboard under his arm like a coat rack had followed him in from the sidewalk. "I was going to be the early one."
