"I was passing," she said, which was a lie, since the mall was a forty-minute bus ride from her house and she had tried on three shirts before noon.

They walked. That was the whole activity, walking, and it turned out to be enough. They went into the bookstore and read each other the worst lines from romance novels in the aisles. They rated the smell of every candle in the home store, and Marcus gave one called Seaside Dawn a four because, he said, the real thing at the littoral edge where the tide pulled back smelled more like salt and rotting kelp, and she believed him, because he actually went to the shore and paid attention to it, which seemed like a reason to like someone more than any shirt she'd tried on that morning.

By the time they bought the pretzels, she had revised her account of the evening several times, and each version was more confident than the last. In the current draft, they were already basically together, and the only remaining question was how the night would end, which she had also drafted. He'd walk her to her mother's car. Something would happen at the door, probably, or maybe just outside the mall doors where the evening light came through the glass all long and gold.

Then, on the walk toward the exit, he slowed down near the fountain and said, "Hey, can I say something weird."

"Is it about the pretzel? Because I know I got cinnamon sugar on your sleeve."

"No. It's that I told my brother this was a date, and you told Priya it was hanging out, and I don't actually know which one we're doing, and either one is fine, but I'd rather know than guess." He turned the bracelet on his wrist twice around his finger, the way he did when he'd decided something.

Kaitlyn stood very still next to the fountain, where the coins of a hundred other wishes sat green underwater. She had said it was hanging out to Priya. She had said it to protect herself, in case it went badly, so she could claim nothing had been at stake, and only now, with the evidence in the open, did that look less like protection and more like a locked door. "It was a date," she said. "I said the other thing because I was scared you'd say it wasn't."

"Okay," Marcus said. "Good." And he smiled in a way that took the whole architecture of her drafted evening apart, gently, like taking out a pin.

They walked out through the big glass doors into the gold light she had predicted, and near the bench by the crosswalk he stopped again. "So I was going to maybe kiss you goodnight, and I told myself I would, but I think I'd rather just say goodnight instead. Is that okay? You can change your mind about stuff too, that's the whole point, you can even say yes and then take it back."

"Yeah," she said. "That's okay. You can take it back."

Her mother's car was idling under the lamp at the far end of the lot. Kaitlyn found that she was not disappointed, or not the way the drafted versions of her had been. Something had been offered and something had been declined and both of those things had been survivable, which was a kind of mutualism too, if she was honest, though she still didn't know what he got out of the arrangement, and might not for a while.

"Same time next Saturday," Marcus said, stepping back, skateboard up under his arm. "Actual date. You can wear the third shirt, the one you almost picked."

"You don't know about the shirts."

"Priya knows about the shirts," he said, and walked off toward his bus while she stood there deciding whether to be furious at Priya or text her the entire evening immediately. She chose the second one, thumb already flying, and behind her the mall doors sighed open and shut on the smell of cinnamon sugar and cold salt air.

The envelope had been in the bottom of Sophia's backpack since Tuesday, and by Friday morning she still had not opened it. It was thin, institutional, the kind that extruded envelopes by the thousand from some office on the second floor of the humanities building, and everyone in the economics elective knew what it probably was. Ms. Ferreira had announced on Monday that the summer research stipend decisions had gone out. Sophia had applied in October for the two-year track, the one that paid a hundred dollars more in the second summer but nothing the first. She had chosen it deliberately, back in October, and had felt principled about it, the way you feel principled about things that are far away.

At lunch Marcus slid his tray across from hers without asking, which was how they always sat. He was eating with the grim discipline of an ascetic, plain rice, plain chicken, because he was saving for a camera lens, and he wanted to talk about the study the psych students were running in the library for course credit. "It's those questions about money," he said. "Would you rather have fifty now or a hundred in a year. Then they ask you again with years added on. It took ten minutes and I got a granola bar."

"And you said?"

"Fifty now, obviously. I'm not waiting a year for anything." He shoveled rice. "Except the weird part is, for the far ones I picked the hundred. A hundred in six years over fifty in five. Six years, man. Who cares." He said the researcher had a word for it, something clinical, and Sophia said she didn't want to know the word yet, and he shrugged and moved on to the lens, which was $340, which was why he was eating like a monk and why he had, last week, sold his concert ticket to Devon for $50 cash.

That was the offer on the table, actually, still technically on the table. Devon had a job now and wanted to buy the ticket back, and he had told Sophia, because she'd been saving for the same summer program's materials fee, that he'd front her the money today. Fifty dollars, today, for the sketch supplies she'd need if she got the one-year track. Or she could hold out, decline Devon, wait on the envelope, and if it was the two-year track take the larger amount later. She had watched herself in October pick the patient option without even hesitating. She had also, this morning, watched her hand start toward texting Devon yes before she put the phone face down on the lab table.

She opened the envelope fifth period, in the stairwell by the chemistry rooms where nobody went. The air smelled like the tar the roofers had been heating all week, and below her, through the door, she could hear Mr. Okonkwo's voice droning through molarity. She slid her thumb under the flap.

Two-year track. Confirmed. $100 the second summer, nothing the first. She read it twice. Then she stood very still, because a fact she had been refusing to look at all week was suddenly standing in front of her with its hands out. She had chosen the hundred, waiting two whole years for it, and it had cost her nothing to choose, because six years or five years or two years versus one, the distance made the patience easy. But today, with Devon's fifty dollars real and immediate, her whole body had leaned toward it. Same girl. Same arithmetic. Two different answers depending on how close the money stood.

She found Marcus after last bell by the vending machines, feeding quarters into the slot with his rice-survivor expression. "That word," she said. "From the study." He looked at her, then at the machine as it clunked and withheld his chips. "Present bias," he said, and hit the glass with the flat of his hand. "That's what they called it."

Sophia leaned against the machine. She told him the whole shape of it, the two-year stipend, the October version of herself who had been so serene about waiting, the fifty dollars she'd nearly taken this morning because it was today and her sketch paper was today and the fee was due Monday. "The far choice I made like it was nothing," she said. "The near one, I couldn't even feel my own principles." She didn't pretend it was solved. She still needed supplies by Monday, and the patient track still paid nothing for a year, and no insight changed either of those facts. What she had was smaller: she could see the seam now, where her October self and her Friday self disagreed, and she could refuse to pretend they were the same person by accident.

Marcus retrieved his chips at last, handed them to her without ceremony, and told her Devon was still in the weight room if she wanted the fifty. Sophia took out her phone. She typed a message to Devon, deleted it, typed another. Then she put the phone away and walked down the hall toward the art room, because Mrs. Lantz kept a cabinet of donated supplies that nobody had inventoried since September, and she wanted to see what was in it before she decided anything. The door was locked, but the art room had a second entrance through the kiln room, and the kiln room door was always open. She pushed through it into the warm clay-smelling dark, her hand finding the light switch by feel.

The line outside the food bank reached the corner of the parking lot before the doors opened at ten. Eva stood behind a folding table stacked with canned tomatoes and wondered whether she should have chosen a Saturday, when she imagined the volunteers would outnumber the visitors. A woman in a lanyard named Priya handed her a clipboard and said, "You take names and household sizes, I bag." The first man through the door gave his name in a voice so quiet Eva had to lean over the table.

By eleven her handwriting had gone small and cramped. A boy from her school, Daniel, came through with his younger sister, and they both pretended not to recognize each other, which was a courtesy she understood and accepted. He counted for a household of four. After he left, Priya glanced at the line still folded along the wall and said, "It's a Tuesday. You'd think a Tuesday would be slower."

Eva looked it up on her phone during her break, crouched beside the milk cooler. Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 had recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. She read the sentence twice. A record for a single month. She had expected the number to be large, but not a record, and she had not expected the record to be now, in an ordinary month with no holiday and no crisis she could name. She sat with the milk sweating against her knee and felt the fact ferment in her, slow and sour, changing shape the longer she held it.

Her mother had sent her here with an injunction she had repeated at the door: be useful, stay quiet, don't stare. Her civics teacher, on the other hand, had spent a unit on structural causes, poverty as a design flaw rather than a personal one, and had told them that charity could soothe the conscience without fixing anything. Eva had written that in an essay and gotten an A. Standing at the table, she found the two positions did not fit together the way they had on paper. Handing a man a bag of rice was not nothing. It was also not enough, and both of those things were true at once, and she could not make them into one sentence.

At noon a volunteer named Gerald, older and obdurate about procedure, refused a woman a second bag of formula because the sheet said one per household per visit. The woman said her sister and the baby were waiting in the car and were a separate household. Gerald said the sheet didn't say that. Priya came over and put her hand flat on the clipboard and said, "Write it as two households. I'll initial it." Gerald's jaw worked, but he stepped back, and Eva wrote the second entry while the woman held her sister's ID against the table edge to keep it steady.

Eva discovered that she had opinions about the clipboard. Rules existed so the supply lasted, and the supply had to last, because there were 2.2 million visits in a single month and this was only one food bank on one Tuesday. But the rules were written somewhere else, by people who had not seen the sister waiting in the car. Priya's initials were a small, local correction, the kind Eva's teacher would probably call a bandage. Eva was not sure the teacher was wrong. She was also not sure that mattered to the woman walking out with the formula, whose problem today was not structural.

Daniel came back near closing because his sister had left her scarf on a chair. He stood at the table while Eva looked for it under the coat rack, and he said, "You can't tell anyone, right." It was not really a question. She found the scarf, gray with a hole at one end, and held it out.

"I won't," she said. She signed out on the volunteer sheet, wrote her hours, and noticed her hand was still cramped from the morning's names. Priya called from the doorway that Tuesday next week she should come early, before the line reaches the corner. Eva zipped her jacket and said, "I'll be here at nine thirty."

Jeremy had signed up to be a peer health educator mostly because the training counted for service hours and because Priya Raman had signed up too, and he was not proud of the arithmetic, but there it was. On the first Tuesday of training, Ms. Okafor handed out a plastic bin of demonstration kits and told them they would learn to explain consent, contraception, and clinic testing well enough to teach it to freshmen. "You will be asked questions you cannot answer," she said. "Practice saying 'I don't know, but I know who does.'" That sentence alone felt worth the whole hour.

The second Tuesday was held in the empty seminar room with the good chairs, and a nurse from the county clinic came with a rolling suitcase that clattered like a fish cart. Her name was Dee. She spread out brochures in fans, burnishing each one flat with the heel of her hand as though the creases were personal insults. Then she had them pair off and role-play. Jeremy drew Marcus Wei, who folded his arms and announced, in the voice of a difficult freshman, "I feel fine, so why would I go get tested for anything?"

Jeremy opened his mouth and closed it. He had been about to say something about being responsible, which he understood instantly would sound like a poster. Dee drifted over, not to rescue him, just to listen with her arms crossed. "Here's the thing," Jeremy tried instead. "You could still have something." Marcus, staying in character, said feeling fine was proof enough for him. Jeremy faltered, and Dee crouched beside their chairs. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms at all," she said. "Testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one." Then she straightened up and walked away, leaving the sentence sitting between them like a coin someone had dropped.

Marcus broke character. "Wait, seriously? None?" Jeremy shrugged, but the fact had already rearranged something in his head, the way a hallway looks different after you learn there's a room behind the wall. He thought of his cousin Daniel, who two years ago had sworn up and down that he was clean because he felt clean, the way people swear a car is fine because it starts. Daniel had ended up at a clinic anyway, in March, for reasons nobody in the family would state out loud at Thanksgiving. Jeremy had been fifteen and had not asked a single question.

The role-play went on. Priya, across the room, was handling her freshman with a kind of brisk comedy, miming a condom package instructions leaflet like a flight attendant, and Jeremy laughed despite himself. When it was his turn to play the reluctant student, he made himself truly obnoxious, drawling, "But I feel amazing," until Priya's partner, Sasha, laughed so hard she had to put her head on the table. Dee let the noise run itself out. "Good," she said. "If you can survive this room, you can survive a freshman who thinks he's immortal."

At the end, Ms. Okafor asked each of them to say one thing they would carry into the presentations. Priya said something about the clinic's walk-in hours. Marcus said, to Jeremy's surprise, "The no symptoms thing. That one's going to stick with people." Jeremy had been planning to say something more abstract, about listening before informing, which he privately suspected was an encapsulation of everything he'd absorbed in two Tuesdays, but the word felt too polished for the room, so he abandoned it at the last second and said, "Say 'I don't know, but I know who does.' It actually works." Ms. Okafor nodded like she'd already known that.

Walking out, he caught up with Marcus by the water fountain. "You argued pretty hard in there," Jeremy said. "For a fake freshman." Marcus drank for a long time. "My brother," he said finally, "spent a year feeling fine." He didn't add anything, and Jeremy didn't ask, because some things you leave where they're set down. The hallway smelled like floor wax and somebody's microwaved lunch, and outside the windows the November light had gone the color of dishwater, capricious enough that it might storm or might turn gold within the hour.

Jeremy thought about Daniel again, on the bus home, and about how he'd never once said the word clinic in that house, and about whether honesty was a duty you owed family or a presumption. He didn't land anywhere. He took out his notebook and wrote, "feeling fine is not proof," and underlined it twice, then added a question mark, because he was seventeen and had learned just enough to know that certainty was usually somebody else's confidence borrowed without permission.

The following Tuesday, Ms. Okafor scheduled the first real presentation for December, ninth graders, forty minutes, no co-teacher. She asked for a volunteer. Priya's hand went up fast as a shutter. Jeremy's went up a half second later, and he kept it there.

Rose found the violin in her grandmother's hallway closet, behind a box of winter coats, and carried it to the kitchen table the way you carry something that might still be alive. Her grandmother looked up from the sink, dried her hands, and said only, "The E string is flat. It's been flat since 1987."

She had played clarinet for six years, sight-read anything put in front of her, and had assumed that reading notes was what playing an instrument meant. But the violin had no holes for her fingers, no keys, no map. Her grandmother tuned it for her, placed her fingers on the strings one afternoon, and then did something Rose didn't expect: she hummed a phrase from an old folk song and said, "Now play that back." When Rose asked for the sheet music, her grandmother laughed. "I never had any. There wasn't any in the house."

The problem arrived on Saturday in the form of Birdie, nine years old, who lived two farms over and took the bus to the house every week for a lesson her grandmother gave for nothing. Rose thought that was altruistic of her, though she also suspected her grandmother simply liked the company. Birdie could play. That was the humiliating part. She set her small violin under her chin and produced a clean, singing "Go Tell Aunt Rhody" while Rose stood in the doorway holding the sheet music she had transcribed the night before, her version of being prepared.

"You read it off the paper," Birdie said afterward, squinting at Rose's pages. "What are all those flags for?" She genuinely didn't know. She could play a dozen songs and could not name a single note on the staff. Rose felt something twist that wasn't quite contempt and wasn't quite envy, some hybrid she couldn't file. She had spent years building a system of reading, and here was a child who bypassed it entirely, the way, Rose thought and then stopped thinking, a toddler talks long before anyone hands it an alphabet.

She cornered her grandmother at the kitchen table that evening, the fact sheets spread out. "How does she do that without reading?"

"It's how she was taught. The Suzuki method. Shinichi Suzuki, the Japanese violinist. He started children playing by ear before they ever read music, the way they learn to speak before they learn to read."

"Then she's missing half of it," Rose said.

"Or you are."

They did not settle it. Rose went to bed angry in the clean, useless way that keeps you awake counting ceiling cracks. In the morning she found Birdie on the porch steps sawing through "Twinkle, Twinkle" and sat down beside her with the transcript. "Trade," Rose said. "You teach me the song by ear. I teach you the notes." Birdie considered this with the gravity of a customs officer. "You have to promise not to abrogate," she said, and Rose, who had taught her that word two days earlier from a crossword, promised not to abrogate.

The lesson was harder than either expected. Birdie could not understand why Rose kept stopping to look down at fingers that wouldn't obey, and Rose could not understand how Birdie's hands knew where to go without ever asking permission. "You just hear where it goes," Birdie said, and when Rose snapped that that wasn't an answer, Birdie played the next phrase wrong on purpose, so slowly that Rose could hear the right note arriving before Birdie's finger landed on it. Rose copied the correction. Then copied it again. On the fourth try the phrase came out whole, and she had not looked at the paper once.

Her grandmother came out with lemonade and the mail, and set down a postcard from the clinic reminding her that her allergy shots were due. "Antigens," she said vaguely, reading it, "little troublemakers they inject so your body learns the tune." Rose thought about that longer than the postcard deserved. A small dose of the thing that hurts, given on purpose, so the system learns to answer it.

She didn't conclude anything tidy. Some days she still believed reading was the spine of music and Birdie was a trick pony; other days, playing "Aunt Rhody" in the dark barn with her eyes shut, she believed the opposite. She decided she was allowed to hold both. On the last night of the visit she played the folk song through, twice, no music stand, and her grandmother called from the kitchen, "The E string's still flat."

"I know," Rose called back. "I like it now."

Gavin stood in his mother's kitchen on the last Sunday of August, five days before he left for college, with a legal pad on the counter and a pen that kept dying. She had handed him the pad that morning and said if he was going to refuse the meal plan, he had to prove he could do this, and she wanted to see a full week by tonight. Not intentions. A list, a budget, a cooking plan, all before she drove him to the train station at seven.

He started the way he started most things, by writing headings and admiring them. Monday. Tuesday. Then he got stuck, because he realized he did not know how many meals a week actually contained. Twenty-one sounded hedonistic and impossible, like something from a banquet, but skipping breakfast was how he had lived for years and his mother would circle it in red if she saw it. He texted his cousin Dana, who had survived two years of apartment life on rice and stubbornness.

Her reply came as a long message he read aloud to the empty kitchen. "Batch cook on Sunday, one big pot, portion it out, and get a food thermometer, the instant-read kind. Mine saved me twice. Leftovers aren't a vibe, they're a temperature." He read the last line twice. He had been imagining leftovers as a matter of smell and confidence, the way his father reheated chili from 1998 on pure faith. Dana made it sound like math.

The deadline tightened around lunchtime when his mother came through in her coat, car keys already out. "I'm doing the shopping run at four," she said, not unkindly. "If your list is done, you come and buy it yourself. If it isn't, I'll buy what I think you need." He heard the offer inside the threat, that she would feed him either way, and it made him want the other thing more. He called Dana from the pantry while he inventoried.

"Rice, chicken thighs, two kinds of beans, onions, whatever vegetable is on sale," she recited, the sound of her own chopping undulate... he smiled and corrected himself under his breath; her voice undulated with the rhythm of the knife, rising and dipping. "Cook it all at once, portion it into containers, fridge for four days, freezer for the rest. And when you reheat, check the middle with the thermometer." He asked her what number he was looking for. "The USDA says 74 degrees Celsius," she said. "That's 165 Fahrenheit." He wrote both on his hand, because the pen had died again.

At the store he learned that planning and shopping were separate humiliations. The chicken cost more than his spreadsheet claimed it would, and the sale vegetable was cabbage, which he bought out of principle and without a single idea for it. In the checkout line an older man ahead of him muttered something about prices never coming down no matter what the news said, a word Gavin half caught, stagflation, and filed away to look up later. His mother watched him count out the total in bills and said nothing, which was its own kind of help.

The cooking itself filled the kitchen with steam and took two hours longer than the plan said. He cubed the chicken badly, wept over the onions, and discovered that cabbage, shredded and fried with the beans, was actually good, which felt like a small and private victory over the whole concept of planning. By six he had nine containers cooling in rows on the counter, and a thermometer in his pocket that he had not yet used.

He used it at ten to seven, reheating a test portion of rice and chicken in the microwave, the train now an hour away. He stuck the probe into the center of the pile and watched the number climb and stall at 61 Celsius. Under. He stirred the portion, put it back in, and tried again. 74 on the display, 165 on the small secondary line, and he stood there holding the thing like it was proof of something. He still did not know if he would actually eat this way in October, when the novelty wore off and midterms ate his Sundays, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that question open on the pad, in the margin, unanswered.

His mother honked from the driveway at seven. Gavin grabbed his bag, then went back for the thermometer and the container of rice and chicken still warm in his hand, and carried both out to the car. "You can test it when we stop," he said. "It hit 74 in the middle."

Lucas arrived at the community center twenty minutes early, notebook against his chest, because Ms. Ferreira had offered the only extra credit she offered all semester: attend the town hall on the county charter question and transcribe the public comments verbatim for the school paper. He found a folding chair near the back, third row, where he could see both the podium and the exit. The room smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and a fan in the corner turned its head slowly, like it was deciding whom to blame.

The meeting opened with the Pledge, then a budget item about the firehouse roof, then the charter amendment itself. When the moderator called for questions, a woman at the microphone said the whole thing felt rigged, like some foreign parliament where nobody votes for anything directly. Lucas's pencil stopped. He was supposed to be neutral, a transcription machine, but his own government class was swimming in his head, and he wanted, suddenly and badly, to be the one who answered her.

He got his chance in the lobby afterward, at a folding table where volunteers handed out voter registration forms. A girl from the college, tabling for a civic engagement club, had been explaining something to an older man in a gravel trucker cap, and Lucas drifted close enough to hear. "So they got a king over there," the man said, "and a prime minister under him? What's the king for, then, decoration?"

"Basically," the girl said. "In a lot of parliamentary systems the head of state is separate from the head of government. The monarch or the ceremonial president does the ribbon cuttings and the prime minister actually runs things." She tapped her stack of forms square. "In the United States our president is both."

Lucas had written a paper two weeks ago claiming the opposite, that a prime minister was just a president with a British accent, and Ms. Ferreira had marked it with a single question mark that he had not followed up on. The question mark had been sitting in his folder since, half shame and half splinter. Now the splinter moved. He waited until the gravel man took his form and left, then stepped up to the table.

"I got that backwards on a paper," he said. "I said the prime minister and the king were the same office in different centuries."

The girl laughed, not unkindly. "Half my intro class did too, first week."

"Is there a way to test which I actually understand," Lucas asked, "besides writing it again and hoping?" He explained about the town hall, the transcript, the woman who thought anything parliamentary was rigged. He asked whether he could quote the exchange at her table. She said that depended on its veracity, which he should check somewhere better than a folding table, and slid a thin blue textbook across it. "Chapter four. Borrow it, bring it back to the next meeting."

He sat on the curb outside with the book while the parking lot emptied, headlights sweeping the brick face of the firehouse. Chapter four laid the two systems side by side, and what struck him was not the diagram but the removal part: a parliament could withdraw its confidence and the head of government was gone, sometimes inside a week, while here a president served out the term unless the whole cumbersome machinery of impeachment turned over. One made it easy to fire the boss and hard to know who'd be next; the other made the boss nearly immovable and the succession perfectly predictable. He had always assumed predictability was the obvious good. Now he wasn't sure which he'd choose if the choice were his, and the not-sure felt less like failure than like the room had gotten bigger.

Inside, the cleanup crew was stacking chairs, and Ms. Ferreira was zipping her bag by the door. She saw the blue book on his knees. "You followed the question mark," she said.

"I got it wrong first," Lucas said. "Then a girl at the registration table, she's from the college, she set me straight, and I'm not done deciding which system I'd actually defend." He stood. "The woman who called it rigged, in there. Part of what bothered her is that in the parliamentary version you never vote for the head of government directly, and part of what bothers me about our version is the opposite. I can argue both sides now. That's new."

Ms. Ferreira looked at him for a long moment, the fan still turning its slow head behind her. "Then write that," she said, "the both-sides version, with the transcript attached," and held the door open.

Outside, the October air had gone cold and the last car's exhaust hung white under the streetlight. Lucas tucked the blue book under his arm where he wouldn't drop it, took out his phone, and typed a note to himself: return book, next meeting. Then, underneath, still standing in the emptying lot, he added a second line and read it back to himself aloud: "Ask her name."

Blake found the box in his grandfather's study on the second morning of the visit, wedged between a set of encyclopedias nobody had opened since the nineties and a photograph of soldiers posing in front of a canvas tent. The box held his grandfather's old college papers, and on top, yellowed and soft at the corners, was an essay titled "Atomic Diplomacy and the Revisionist Case." Blake sat down on the carpet with it before he had decided to.

His grandfather found him there an hour later, holding the essay under the window light. "That was a long time ago," his grandfather said. "A professor made us argue a position we didn't hold. I got the side that lost, more or less." He set a mug of coffee on the desk, within Blake's reach but not offered, which Blake understood as an offer anyway.

The argument was this: that the atomic bombs dropped on Japan were not only about ending the war. Blake read the paragraph twice. The paper cited a historian named Gar Alperovitz, who had argued in a book called Atomic Diplomacy, published in 1965, that the bombs were used partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. Not instead of ending the war. Partly. Blake kept coming back to that word, because his friend Dominic had shouted something like this at the war memorial on the school trip in April, and Blake had shouted back, and neither of them had known enough to know who was right.

He had said to Dominic, at the memorial, under the long wall of names, that the bombings were the last act of World War II, and Dominic had said they were the first act of the Cold War, and they had argued until the teacher moved them to opposite ends of the group. Blake had gone home angry in the specific way that meant he knew he had been arguing from nothing. He had wanted, since then, to be the kind of person who had actually read things, though the wanting had inured him mostly to scrolling summaries on his phone at midnight rather than to any real study. He recognized that now, sitting on his grandfather's carpet with the primary source of a fifty-year-old term paper.

"Did you believe it?" Blake asked. "When you wrote it."

His grandfather moved a stack of mail off the chair and sat. "Belief is a strong word for a nineteen-year-old with a due date. I believed the sources, where they were honest. I distrusted the ones that were tidy." He nodded at the pages in Blake's hands. "The trouble with that argument is it can explain too much. If you already think the diplomats were monsters, everything looks like a weapon aimed at Moscow. And if you think your country was always good, nothing does."

Blake looked at the margin notes, cramped pencil in his grandfather's younger handwriting. Next to one paragraph the note said only "check." He flipped to the bibliography, then back. The Alperovitz claim sat there with a page number, and beside it, another historian's rebuttal with its own page number, and his grandfather's "check" between them like a small flag planted in disputed ground.

That night Blake took his phone to the porch and texted Dominic instead of searching. The porch smelled of his grandfather's pipe tobacco, though nobody had smoked it in years, and the impecunious state of the house, the porch rail gone soft, the gutters pulled straight by hand each fall instead of replaced, meant the tobacco smell would probably outlast the house itself. He typed, "Ok so I found something. This guy Alperovitz argued in 1965 that the bombs were partly to intimidate the Soviets. Partly. Not instead of. I keep getting stuck on partly."

Dominic's reply came in three bubbles. The first said "so I was right." The second said "wait." The third said "partly is annoying though. If it's partly then it's both and we were both yelling about it at the memorial like idiots."

Blake thought about his grandfather saying tidy sources were the ones to distrust, and about how a person could want history to have an autocrat's clarity, one ruler deciding everything, one motive, one clean sentence you could carry to the top of a monument and shout. The truth seemed to be more like the margin note, a check in pencil beside two page numbers, an admission that you had to go read both.

"We weren't idiots," Blake typed. "We were just loud." He looked up at the yard going dark, then back down. "Want to read the book with me? I can get it from the library when I'm home Sunday. You take his side, I'll take the other one, and this time we actually finish it before we fight."

Dominic's answer was a single thumbs up, and then, a minute later: "bring the essay too. Tell your grandpa his handwriting is terrible."

Blake laughed, locked the phone, and carried his grandfather's mug inside to wash it.

The article was four paragraphs long, in Spanish, and Isabella had read the first paragraph six times before the words stopped sliding off her. She sat in the far corner of the school library where the carrels faced the window, her phone face down beside a dictionary she was trying not to open. The piece was from a Chilean paper: the port authority in Valparaíso wanted to expropriate a strip of hillside houses to widen a cargo corridor, and the city council had split over it. She had volunteered for this. Five minutes, in Spanish, in front of the whole class on Thursday, arguing one side and then summarizing the article aloud. Her teacher had said the word "B2" when she assigned it, and Isabella had nodded as if she knew what that meant.

She did not know what that meant. She copied the first sentence into her notebook, then underlined every verb she recognized. Queria. Expropiar. She looked up long enough to see Dana from her class slide into the opposite carrel, drop a binder, and start highlighting something with the concentration of a person performing concentration.

"Ask your phone," Dana said, without looking up.

"I'm not asking my phone."

"You asked your phone for the debate topic."

Isabella turned the phone over. The course outline was in her email, a PDF her teacher had sent in September, and she had never scrolled past the second page. She scrolled now. Under "Trimestre 3" it said, in English, that students at B2 level should be able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. She read it twice. It didn't say argue. It didn't say win. It said explain, and it wanted both sides, advantages and disadvantages, laid out.

"That's it?" Dana leaned across the aisle. "That's all B2 is?"

"That's what the outline says." She turned the screen so Dana could see it.

"So you don't need to beat Tomas. You just need to sound like you read the article."

Isabella pulled the screen back. She had been planning to beat Tomas. Tomas had spent a semester in Madrid and rolled his r's like a native, and she had spent a semester ordering the wrong sandwich at the deli on Fulton Street. She had planned to memorize a script so dense he couldn't get a word in.

She read the second paragraph again. The port handled more cargo than the rail line could carry; a city planner was quoted saying the throughput of the corridor had to double or the shipping companies would move to San Antonio. Throughput. Rendimiento. Even in English the word was a kind of wall. She wrote "throughput" in her notebook and drew an arrow to a house.

Because the third paragraph was the houses. Eleven of them. A woman named Rosa Herrera had lived in hers for forty years, and the compensation offer covered the market price and nothing else, and her street was the only one where the fishermen still repaired nets outside in the evenings. The reporter didn't editorialize. The reporter gave the planner his numbers and gave Rosa her sentence about nets, and then the article ended.

Isabella tried out the summary in a whisper. "El puerto quiere expropiar las casas." Her accent flattened every vowel. She tried it again, louder than she meant to, and a boy two carrels over looked up. She mouthed the rest. To widen the corridor. The throughput. The advantages. She stopped. What were the advantages? Jobs, she guessed, or the city not losing the shipping companies, and she wrote "ventajas" and then nothing under it, because the article hadn't said jobs. She had invented jobs. She crossed it out.

She sat with the crossed-out word for a while. The B2 line wanted advantages and disadvantages of various options, and the article gave her one option, widen and expropriate, and one alternative mentioned in half a sentence, let the companies leave. Rosa Herrera's nets were not an advantage or a disadvantage. Rosa Herrera's nets were a cost that didn't fit in the planner's column, and Isabella did not know whose job it was to say so. Maybe hers. Maybe that was what explaining a viewpoint meant, standing in the gap between the columns.

Dana was watching her. "You're making a face."

"I'm missing something. The article says the companies would go to San Antonio, but it doesn't say what happens to the workers here if they stay. So if I say that's a disadvantage, I'm making it up."

"So say you don't know."

"In Spanish?"

"That's the whole language. 'No se sabe.' That's three words."

Isabella laughed before she could stop it, and the librarian turned from her cart of returns. Isabella lowered her voice. "No se sabe," she said, trying it. The syllables sat more easily than the argument had.

She started over, whispering the summary from the top. The port wanted the houses. The corridor's throughput had to grow. The companies had another option, another port, another city. Rosa Herrera had forty years and a street and an offer that measured neither. "Por una parte," Isabella said, and then, more slowly, "por otra parte." On the one hand. On the other. The scales in the sentence felt honest, like the sentence knew it was leaving something out and was willing to say so. She wrote "no se sabe" at the bottom of her notes and starred it.

Thursday was two days away. Tomas would still roll his r's, and the class would still hear every flat vowel she produced, and she was not sanguine about winning. But the outline hadn't asked her to win. It had asked her to stand there with both hands open, advantages in one, disadvantages in the other, and admit which palm was empty. She read Rosa Herrera's sentence once more, closed the notebook, and slid the article between its pages, the side with the nets facing up.

Laurence found him at the third row of the bleachers, holding two cups of hot chocolate even though the game wouldn't start for twenty minutes, and she understood immediately that he had been worried about the same thing she had been worried about, which was having nothing to do with his hands. "I didn't know if you liked it," Dev said, offering one cup. "I guessed. Sugar's in the packet, not the cup, because I read once that people are particular." She took it. The night had that September smell of cut grass and cigarette smoke drifting from the parking lot, and the floodlights turned everyone's faces the same flat orange, which felt merciful, since it hid whatever her face was doing.

She had spent the drive here composing herself into someone blasé, a girl who watched football with mild amusement, who laughed at the right moments without investing anything, and the plan had already failed in the parking lot when she'd tripped on a chain and he'd caught her elbow and she'd said thank you twice, the second thank you quieter, as though the first had been a mistake. Now she sipped the hot chocolate and it was good, actually good, and she resented that, because it was harder to be cool about something good.

The marching band came out and scattered across the field like an archipelago, each cluster of brass and drums its own small island of noise. Dev leaned toward her to be heard over the drums. "You know my sister's in the clarinet section? Third row. She's been talking about this game for two weeks." He pointed, and there was a small wave from a girl in a green uniform, and Laurence waved back, and something about the wave, its unembarrassed eagerness, made her like him more, which she filed away as information she would examine later, alone.

By halftime she had accumulated a list of failures she kept without wanting to. She had misheard his joke about the referee and laughed two beats late. She had talked for what felt like four straight minutes about her intended major, urban studies, and had used the word "problematize" out loud, in a sentence, at a football game, and watched his expression go politely blank. When he'd asked whether she wanted a soft pretzel, she'd said "I'm good" in a tone that must have sounded like rejection of the entire category of pretzels, of shared food, possibly of him. The score was 21 to 14 and she could not have told you who was winning.

When the third quarter ended, Dev's phone buzzed and he looked at it too long. "My mom," he said. "She wants me home by eleven, she's, my grandpa's visiting and she wants the car in the driveway before he wakes up, he sleeps weird hours." He stood there holding the phone, not moving, and then he said, "I'm sorry. I know this is the worst possible timing. This was really..." He stopped, restarted. "I don't want to go."

Laurence walked him to the gate because it seemed like the thing a person would do, and the whole way she was composing the post-mortem: he couldn't even wait through the fourth quarter, he stood there struggling to say the date was anything at all. At the gate he turned around. "Can I be honest about something?" he said. "I've spent the entire game thinking you were bored. Like you came because your friend Priya said I was nice and now you're stuck here until the clock runs out. You kept looking at the field instead of at me, so I figured the field was more interesting, which, fair, but." He pushed his hands into his jacket pockets. "I kept trying to think of a way to ask if you were hating it without asking if you were hating it."

She stood there with her cup going cold in her hands. The field, the band, the whole roaring stadium was behind her, and she had been looking at it because looking at him was too much, and it had never once occurred to her that the direction of her eyes might have been read as a verdict on him. "I looked something up before tonight," she said. "Because I do that, I look things up, I looked up what to expect on first dates. There's this thing where after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them. And how much they enjoyed their company. Both of those, it's the whole finding." She heard herself speeding up and made herself slow down. "It's called the liking gap. People walk away from first conversations and the other person liked them more than they think. That's what the study said."

"So you're saying," Dev said, "that I've been sitting there thinking you hated me, and you've been sitting there thinking I hated you, and we were both, statistically." He laughed, and she laughed, and then he wasn't laughing anymore, he was saying, "Text me when you get home, okay, not because I'm worried, just because I want to know," and then he jogged toward the parking lot, one hand raised, and she stood at the gate in the floodlight noise and took out her phone and typed, before she could curate it, "I did not hate a single minute."

The cemetery sat on a hill above the mosque, which was either planning or happenstance, and Sophie had never decided which. Her grandmother lay under a plain stone near the rowan tree, and it was here, on the afternoon of the ninth day of Ramadan, that Sophie had come to rehearse. In her canvas bag she carried the small notebook where she had written the order of everything: the dates, the water, the maghrib prayer, the food, the tea. Her father had led the family's iftar for as long as she could remember, but this year his shoulder surgery had left his arm in a sling, and he had looked at her across the kitchen and said, "It's yours, Soph. Start to finish."

Start to finish meant the dates had to be ready at the exact moment the sun went down. Not a minute before, not after. She had learned that the hard way two years ago, when she was fifteen and put the dates out early and her little cousin Yusuf, who was seven and fasting his first half-days, had eaten one before the adhan sounded. Her grandmother had not scolded him. She had only looked at the empty space on the plate and then at Sophie, and the look had done all the scolding necessary. Sophie still turned the memory over, the way you keep testing a bruise. She could not decide whether she had failed Yusuf or whether Yusuf had simply been seven, and the wanting had been too much for a small body at sunset.

She sat cross-legged on the dry grass and laid out her supplies like a surgeon. The dates were the recalcitrant ones this year, a box of Medjool from the corner shop, half of them stuck together in a dense brown clump that refused to separate along its natural seams. She worked at them with her thumbnails, splitting the fruit open, easing out the pointed pits, and arranging the halves on her grandmother's favorite plate, the white one with the thin blue rim that she had smuggled out of the kitchen cabinet that morning.

"You're doing it here?" said a voice behind her. Aya had followed her up the hill, which Sophie had neither asked for nor minded. Aya was her cousin and her opposite: loud where Sophie was quiet, certain where Sophie calculated. She flopped down on the grass without ceremony and picked up one of the rejected pits, turning it in her fingers.

"I needed to think somewhere," Sophie said. "And I wanted to ask her."

"Grandma can't tell you the order of an iftar."

"She can, kind of. She did it for forty years." Sophie turned the notebook toward the stone so the pages faced her grandmother's name. "You break the fast with a date first. That's how it's done, the way the Prophet Muhammad did it. Then water, then prayer, then everything else."

"I know that," Aya said, though she said it more softly than she usually said anything.

"I know you know. I'm saying it out loud so it sticks." Sophie separated another date, and its skin tore a little, and she set that one aside for herself, the imperfect one, because she would eat last tonight, after everyone. She had decided that on the walk up the hill, halfway between the bus stop and the gate, and she was still not sure whether it was humility or performance, whether she was serving the family or auditioning for their approval, and she let the not-sure stand. Some things you could hold in both hands at once.

The sun was lowering itself behind the water tower on the far edge of town, and Sophie checked her phone against the paper prayer timetable she had folded into four, because her grandmother had never trusted a phone for this, and Sophie had begun to understand why. The screen said 7:41. The paper said 7:41. The sky said soon. Aya lay back with her hands behind her head and closed her eyes the way fasting people do in the last hour, conserving themselves, and Sophie counted the pitted dates one more time: thirteen for thirteen people, plus the torn one for her, plus one extra laid apart on the grass, in front of the stone.

"That one's for her," Sophie said, without being asked.

"You know she'd say don't waste good dates on the dead," Aya said, but her eyes had gone glassy, and she reached over and straightened the blue-rimmed plate so it sat square to the horizon. The light on the hill turned the color of weak tea, and somewhere below them a door opened and the sound of children spilling out of the mosque reached them faintly, like something fermenting under a lid, pressure building toward release.

At 7:40 Sophie stood, brushed the grass from her knees, and took one date from the plate and held it out to Aya, who took it and stood beside her, and they faced west together where the sun was going down over the water tower, and Sophie whispered, "Okay. Watch the sky. The second it touches the horizon, we eat."

Xavier arrived at the library twenty minutes before it opened, which was a kind of asceticism he practiced only during exam week, standing in the cold with his backpack straps gripped in both fists. Inside, he claimed the corner carrel by the window, the one with a wobbly leg he had learned to balance with a folded napkin, and laid out his assignment sheet: a comparison essay on how a parliamentary system chooses and removes a head of government, versus how a presidential one does it. Mr. Okafor had written a single comment in red ink at the bottom. "You have listed facts. Now take a position, and admit what you cannot settle."

The problem was that Xavier did not want to admit anything he could not settle. He liked the clean logic of the parliamentary column: the party that wins seats chooses the prime minister, and if the party withdraws confidence, the prime minister falls, sometimes within days, without any election at all. The presidential column was messier: a fixed term, a direct mandate, removal only through the cumbersome machinery of impeachment, which in his sources had rarely succeeded anywhere it had been genuinely attempted. He copied citations, underlined the word "fusion" where one textbook described the blending of executive and legislature, and felt the pleasing click of a system that seemed to hold together.

"Excuse me. Are you the guy who knows where the law books are?" A girl about his age stood at the edge of the carrel, holding a printed outline with the front page curling. Her name, from the badge on her debate binder, was Priya, and she was preparing a moot court argument against a school dress-code policy, along with two classmates who had scattered toward the computers. "We need the most famous line there is about student speech," she said. "Everyone says it exists, nobody remembers the case."

Xavier almost said he was busy. Then he found himself standing, because the assignment in front of him had begun to feel evanescent anyway, the facts thinning out the moment he tried to build a conclusion on them. He led Priya to the constitutional law shelf and they ran fingers along spines until he pulled a casebook with a battered index. She flipped pages while he read over her shoulder, and there it was, in the section on students and the First Amendment.

"Tinker v. Des Moines," Priya read aloud, slowly, getting each piece into her memory. "1969. The Supreme Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." She wrote it down twice, then a third time on her palm. Her teammate Marcus came back from the printers waving a copy and she made him recite the case name back to her, and he got the year wrong twice before he got it right. Xavier watched her insist, and something about her insistence rearranged his thinking more than the textbook had.

He returned to his carrel and looked at his two columns again. Priya's problem had a specific question, a famous line, a ruling, and she was building an argument out of them. His essay had no such spine. He had been trying to compare the systems as though one could be proved better, the way he might prove a math answer, and it occurred to him that political systems were not problems with solutions but arrangements with trade-offs. He took out a fresh sheet and began to contextualize the comparison: the parliamentary system made leaders accountable quickly but made governments unstable; the presidential system made governments stable but let an unpopular leader cling to a fixed term. Both columns were describing the same human difficulty from opposite directions.

He wrote for an hour, crossing out whole paragraphs, then a better hour in which he crossed out less. When he could not decide whether quick removal or fixed stability mattered more, he wrote that down instead of hiding it: that the answer depended on whether one feared disorder more than entrenchment, and that reasonable people in the sources disagreed. His pen slowed at that sentence, because admitting uncertainty felt like a failure, and then kept going, because it also felt, strangely, like the first honest sentence in the draft.

At the study table across the room, Priya's group had begun a practice round, Marcus standing to argue in a voice pitched too loud for the library, Priya leaning over her notes correcting him. A librarian drifted toward them with a look of mild warning, and Xavier watched Priya lower her voice without lowering her intensity, one hand flat on the page where the famous line sat.

On his way out, he stopped beside her. "Which case did you say it was?" he asked, testing her, and himself a little.

"Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969," she said. "Seven to two. Students don't shed their rights at the schoolhouse gate." She tapped the page twice and turned back to Marcus, already arguing again.

The used car lot sat behind the school like an archipelago of metal islands, and every afternoon David cut through it on his way home, slowing past the blue sedan with the faded FOR SALE sign in the window. He had two thousand dollars saved from three summers of mowing lawns, and his mother had promised, quietly, in the kitchen, that if he could cover half, she would help with the rest. The sedan was six thousand. The math felt possible in a way that made his chest tighten.

In geology that spring they had been forced to memorize rock types, and Mr. Okafor had passed around a chunk of obsidian, black and glassy, an igneous stone born from cooling lava. David had held it longer than he needed to. His grandfather had kept a chunk like it on his dresser, next to a savings passbook, and David remembered being nine, sitting on the bed's edge while the old man showed him the small deposits and the tiny sums the bank added each year, unearned, arriving like weather. "Money that sits still can grow," his grandfather had said, tapping the booklet, and David had believed it the way children believe things, without mechanism, without question.

Then the letter came. It was addressed to his mother, from the credit union, and she left it open on the counter while she made dinner, so David read it standing up, a spoon in his hand. The savings account had earned four percent last year; the balance, which had dipped after his father left, was climbing again, dollar by patient dollar. His mother watched him read it over his shoulder. "Grandpa would like that," she said, and handed him the carrots to peel.

At the dealership on Saturday, the salesman was a big, warm man named Ruiz who called David "young man" and his mother "ma'am" and brought them bottled water without being asked. The blue sedan was there, freshly washed. Six thousand dollars, Ruiz said, or they could finance it. He slid a paper across the desk: seventy-two months, one hundred and five a month. His mother's shoulders dropped a little with relief. David knew what her paycheck looked like; he knew one hundred and five was almost possible and one hundred and sixty was not.

"Or forty-eight months," Ruiz said, tapping another column, "but that's one thirty-five." David took the pen and added down both columns, twice, because the first answer seemed wrong. Forty-eight months at one thirty-five came to six thousand four hundred eighty. Seventy-two months at one hundred and five came to seven thousand five hundred sixty. He showed his mother the two totals. "The longer one has the smaller payment," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke, "but it costs more in the end. Like more than a thousand dollars more." Ruiz didn't argue. He looked at the paper, then at David, and something in his face shifted, less salesman, more uncle. "That's true," he said. "That's just how it works. At the same rate, more months means more interest over the life of the loan."

His mother was quiet in the car afterward. "We could do the four years," she said. "Tight, but maybe." Then, half a block on, the twist of the afternoon: Ruiz came jogging out of the lot with his jacket unbuttoned and caught them at the light. He handed David a card. "The sedan's owner trades with us," he said. "He'd probably take fifty-two hundred cash. No loan at all. I just thought somebody should mention it." He shrugged, embarrassed, and walked back before either of them could fully thank him.

David thought about it that night instead of homework. The cash offer would expropriate most of his savings in one gesture, the whole two thousand plus his mother's share, and the letter's patient four percent would have nothing left to work on. But no payment would arrive every month either, no stream of small subtractions, and his mother would keep her margins. He tried to hold both pictures at once: money growing because it sat still, and money spent because it moved something real into their driveway. He could not make the two pictures agree.

He texted his mother from bed: "We could pay cash and start saving again. Slower but no loan." She replied a minute later with a single thumbs up, then, after a longer pause: "Monday we offer 4900. If he says no, we do the 4 year loan. Deal?" David typed "deal," put the phone face down, and lay listening to the furnace tick. On Monday he would walk through the archipelago of cars one more time, and maybe drive one of them home.

The writing club met in the spartan back room of the public library, four folding tables pushed into a square, and Ava arrived first with her laptop and two printed articles, which she laid side by side like hands of cards. The question her professor had assigned was whether a river could legally be a person, and the two articles disagreed: one argued that granting rivers legal personhood empowered indigenous communities, the other that it was symbolic gesture, a way for governments to look virtuous while changing nothing. Her review draft was due in nine days, and she had written two pages she already suspected were dead on arrival.

Ms. Ferreira, the librarian who kept the club going, had left a note in her returned draft folder, but Ava hadn't opened it yet. She'd seen the envelope at breakfast, slid it under her laptop lid, and carried it around all day like a stone in her pocket.

Priya came in shaking rain off her jacket, then Marcus, then Dee, who was writing a novel about a haunted laundromat and never read anyone else's work but came anyway for the chairs. "Read yours," Priya said, dropping into the seat across from Ava. "You look like you're guarding a body."

"It's a review of two articles. Not exactly a thriller."

"Everything's a thriller if the stakes are real." Priya tapped the printed pages. "So what's your argument?"

Ava opened her laptop and read the first line of her draft. "Both articles agree that legal personhood for rivers is a significant development in environmental law."

Marcus winced. Dee looked up from her notebook for the first time all evening.

"Wait," Priya said. "Both articles agree. So what are you arguing?"

"That it's significant."

"Ava." Priya leaned forward. "A research paper's thesis has to be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, not a fact everyone already accepts. If nobody could disagree with you, there's no paper."

Ava had heard something like this in ninth grade and filed it away as one of those teacher rules, like margins. She looked at her two pages, which summarized each article politely and then said, in her closing paragraph, that the truth probably lay somewhere in between. Somewhere in between. She felt her ears go hot.

Flashback: last spring, in chemistry, she'd written a lab report whose conclusion stated that deposition occurs when a gas turns directly into a solid, and Mr. Okafor had circled it and written, correct, but so what? She'd been insulted for a week. Now, in the library's back room, the insult rearranged itself. The fact had been true and useless, because no one alive disputed it. She had spent her draft being correct in the same way.

She pulled out the envelope, finally, and slit it open with a car key. Ms. Ferreira's handwriting was small and even. Your draft is careful and fair to both authors. But a research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts. What is this paper actually arguing? Ava read it twice, then set it face down on the table.

"That bad?" Marcus said.

"It's the same thing you just said. Almost word for word." She laughed once, without much humor in it. "So what do I actually think? That's the problem. I don't know yet."

"So find out," Dee said, not looking up. "That's what the two articles are for. Put them in a room together and watch what happens."

Ava turned the articles toward each other, physically, so the first page of one faced the first page of the other. The author who supported river personhood had spent three years collecting testimony from Māori iwi whose river, the Whanganui, had been declared a legal person in 2017. The skeptic had never been to New Zealand; he had read the legislation and found the river's new rights narrow, its guardians underfunded. One measured the law by the dignity it restored, the other by the budget line attached to it. They weren't disagreeing about rivers at all, she realized. They were disagreeing about what evidence counts.

The library's overhead lights buzzed and dimmed for a second, the way they did before closing announcements, and everyone kept talking anyway, and Ava started typing in the dark of her screen. Priya moved her chair around the table to read over her shoulder. On the page, Ava wrote: The dispute between these authors is not about whether rivers should have rights but about what a law must do before it can be called meaningful, and I will argue that the skeptic's standard, though harsher, cannot account for the testimony the first author records. Then she stopped, cursor blinking, and said out loud, "But I might be wrong. The budget thing is real. The guardians can't sue without money."

"That's fine," Priya said. "Say that too."

The closing bell chimed through the building, twice, the sound it made when the doors were about to lock. Dee closed her notebook, Marcus stacked the chairs, and Ava kept typing, both articles open under her hands, the envelope with Ms. Ferreira's note pressed flat beneath the Whanganui one like a bookmark holding her place.

Megan had chosen the bowling alley for practical reasons, which she could admit to herself but not to Dana, who was standing at the shoe counter holding size eights like they were evidence in a trial. If the date failed, a bowling alley offered exits: the arcade, the vending machine, the parking lot. If it succeeded, there were twelve frames in which to find out which kind of success it might be.

They had already done the coffee shop, an hour of small talk that Megan had tried twice to resuscitate with questions about siblings and weather and whether the barista had tattooed the words on her forearm or just Sharpied them. Dana had answered everything carefully, in complete sentences, and asked her almost nothing back. So when the silence had stretched to the point of embarrassment, Megan had reached for the one thing she'd been saving, the thing she'd read about at two in the morning instead of sleeping.

"There's this study," she'd said, stirring a coffee she no longer wanted. "Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk."

Dana had looked at her over the rim of the cup. "Closer than small talk. That's a low bar."

"It's a measurable bar. That's the point."

"So you want to run a psychology experiment on me."

"I want to bowl," Megan had said, standing up, "and ask you hard questions while we do it. You can ask me back."

Now, in the third frame, they were on question nine, which was the first one that had made Dana stop mid-approach and stand at the line with the ball held low, thinking. "If I could change one thing about the way I was raised," Dana repeated, "then what." The ball went into the gutter and neither of them mentioned it.

"For a long time I would have said nothing," Dana said, sitting down. "My parents would like that answer. It's the perspicacious answer, the one that makes you sound like you've thought everything through and arrived at gratitude." Megan watched her lace and unlace the fingers of the borrowed shoes. "But there was a year my mother didn't speak to my uncle, and nobody told me why, and I learned to stop asking why. I'd change that. The not asking."

Megan wrote her own answer to the same question on the back of the score sheet, folded it, and slid it across the ball return, which was their agreed system: answer for answer, no commentary until both were in. She bowled a spare while Dana read it. There was a consonance between them, she thought, in the way they both wrote small and fast, like they were afraid of being caught at it.

By the eighth frame they had reached the twenties, the questions she had privately doubted anyone would answer honestly. "When did you last cry in front of another person," she asked, and Dana said, "At my grandfather's funeral, but only because everyone else was crying and I was afraid of what it meant that I wasn't." Megan had a list of things she was afraid it meant too, and she said so, and Dana nodded like this was the most normal thing anyone had ever told her at lane fourteen.

The problem, Megan was beginning to understand, was that the questions were working, and she couldn't tell whether that was the same as the evening working. If closeness could be produced by a procedure, thirty-six items in ascending order of exposure, then what exactly had she learned about Dana, and what had she merely manufactured? Her sister would say she was overthinking it, that the study only opened a door and you still had to walk through it yourself. But her sister hadn't watched Dana answer question twenty-eight, the one about dying, with a specificity that had made the arcade noise seem very far away.

She was still turning it over in the tenth frame, in the honest way that meant she didn't pretend to have settled it, when Dana rolled the last ball of the night and turned around before it reached the pins. "Question thirty-six," Dana said. "Of all the people in your family, whose death would you find most disturbing." Then, after a beat: "You don't have to answer that one. Pick your own. But I get to watch your face while you decide."

The ball hit the pocket and scattered all ten pins, and Megan pulled the folded score sheet out of her back pocket, unwrinkled it, and clicked the pen.

The guidance counsellor's office smelled like instant coffee and the lemon disinfectant they used on the desks between periods, and Hannah had been sitting in the orange chair for eleven minutes because Mrs. Okafor's door was shut and someone was crying in there, audibly, in the way of a person who wanted to be heard through the door.

She had come to drop Calculus. The form was already filled out, folded twice, warm from her pocket. The deadline was four o'clock today; after that she was locked in for the semester, and the semester average she needed for the scholarship was not something she intended to titrate against a unit on integrals. She had done the math. She was good at math, which was the annoying part.

Her phone buzzed. Dev again. can u cover sat? my shift. third time this month. Dev worked the front desk at the rec center with her, had worked it since September, and had developed a talent for discovering, always on a Saturday morning, some obligation that outranked the schedule. He was charming about it, effusive in his apologies, and Hannah had covered twice because the alternative was explaining to their supervisor, whose management style could generously be called autocratic, that Hannah's coworker was a mirage.

The crying in Mrs. Okafor's office stopped. The door opened and a junior Hannah vaguely knew came out with red eyes and a parking pass application, and Mrs. Okafor beckoned her in.

"So," said Mrs. Okafor, reaching for the drop slip before Hannah had fully unfolded it. "Tell me why."

"Calculus is going to wreck my average," Hannah said. "I can take it in college. It's one course. It doesn't matter that much."

Mrs. Okafor didn't answer right away. She was looking something up on her laptop, turning the screen slightly, the way she did when a student's file said something different from the student's mouth. "Your grade is an eighty-one," she said. "That's not wreckage."

"It's going to be a sixty by finals." Hannah sat back. "It's one decision. One semester."

While Mrs. Okafor typed, Hannah's eye drifted to the bulletin board, to a photocopied page pinned between a poster about sleep and a flyer for votech programs. It was a summary of some study, Dunedin, a place in New Zealand, it said, following a thousand people born in one year across their whole lives. An analysis from 2011 had found that children with lower self-control were more likely, as adults, to have poorer health, less wealth, and criminal convictions. Hannah read it twice. It did not say how. It didn't say what happened in between the children and the adults, whether anyone had intervened, whether a single dropped calculus course was the same species of thing at all.

Her phone buzzed against her thigh. Dev. please please

"I know what you're thinking," Hannah said to Mrs. Okafor, before the counsellor could say it. "That the small stuff adds up. There's a whole page about it on your board."

"I was thinking about parking," said Mrs. Okafor. "But go on."

"There was this analysis, 2011, of the Dunedin Study. Kids with lower self-control ended up worse off. Health, money, criminal record." She heard herself say it and felt the argument land on her own head like a dropped textbook. "But that's children. Over decades. I'm deciding about one class in one semester. That's different. That's a single, rational, contained decision."

"Is it," said Mrs. Okafor, in the tone of a woman who had filed this exact form four hundred times and could probably predict the date of the final in question.

Here was the thing Hannah could not get around: she liked hard things when she chose them, and she avoided things she hadn't chosen, and Calculus had been her idea until it stopped being fun. Dev, she suspected, was the same. Dev did not think of himself as a person who abandoned his shifts; he thought of himself as a person with extenuating circumstances, each one reasonable, each one single and contained. Whereas the study on the bulletin board said the single and contained decisions were possibly the whole mechanism, or possibly not, since it didn't say, and neither did Hannah.

She picked up her phone. no, she typed to Dev. your shift is your shift. Then she deleted it for something kinder: can't. also you should know the swap list is three people deep and Bev is counting.

"The slip," said Mrs. Okafor, holding out her hand.

Hannah looked at the form, still folded, still warm. Outside, someone's class change rang through the hallway speakers, and she calculated, in the way she calculated, that she had until three fifty.

She tore it in half, once, neatly, and put the pieces in her pocket.

"Wise," said Mrs. Okafor, reaching for her stamp.

"It's one semester," Hannah said. "Ask me in December."

"Ask yourself in thirty years," said Mrs. Okafor, stamping something that was not, after all, her drop slip, and handing her a pass back to class.

Mr. Okonkwo had divided the class into two benches, and Aidan had drawn the side defending algorithmic bail decisions, which was a problem because he had spent the whole weekend failing to write his opening argument.

"You're overthinking it," Marcus said, sliding into the seat beside him. "It's a debate. You argue whatever side you get."

"I know how debates work." Aidan pulled up his laptop. The classroom's old projector hummed above them, casting a torpid blue wash over the whiteboard, where Okonkwo had written only one word: NEUTRAL. "I just don't believe my side."

"So fake it."

The door opened and Priya came in early, the way she always did, carrying a folder of printed articles because she distrusted screens in arguments. She sat across the aisle and began arranging her pages. Aidan could see headlines upside down, and one of them had a word he recognized from somewhere, COMPAS, though he couldn't place it.

When the bell ended, Okonkwo clapped his hands once. "Computers should decide bail because they are neutral," he read from the board. "Bench one, you defend. Bench two, you dismantle. Five minutes to prepare."

Marcus leaned forward immediately. "Look, a judge has a bad morning, a fight with his wife, he's biased and doesn't even know it. An algorithm never had a bad morning. Same inputs, same outputs. That's your opener."

"That's fine," Aidan said, but he was watching Priya. She had flipped to a specific page and marked it with a yellow tab. He typed into his own laptop, not the debate prep document, just the search bar: COMPAS.

The results loaded and he read the first one twice. He looked up at the clock, which gave him three minutes.

"Bench one," Okonkwo called. "Your case."

Marcus stood. He gave the bad-morning-judge speech, then the part about consistency, then a line about how a tool that treats everyone the same is the definition of fairness. He sat down and nudged Aidan's elbow. "Your turn. Finish strong."

Aidan stood. "I had a second argument," he said. "I don't have it anymore."

"Take your time," Okonkwo said.

"In 2016, ProPublica investigated a risk tool called COMPAS, the kind used in bail decisions." He kept his eyes on Priya, who had stopped arranging her pages. "They found it misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants."

Nobody in the room moved. Someone at the back said, "Twice?"

"About twice the rate," Aidan said. "Same tool, same claim of neutrality." He turned toward his own bench. "I was going to argue that a computer has no volition, so it can't discriminate. But somebody chose the data. Somebody chose what to measure. The neutrality isn't in the machine. It's a claim people make about the machine." He sat down before he could soften any of it.

Marcus stared at him. "You just torched your own side."

"Yeah."

Priya stood slowly. She didn't gloat, which somehow made it worse. "I was going to use the same study," she said. "I spent Sunday deciding whether to say the word COMPAS out loud in this room." She didn't explain why that had been hard, and Aidan didn't ask, though he understood it had something to do with being the only student in the class who would ever have that hesitation.

"Then you agree with me," Marcus said to Aidan, "that the technology is fine and the data is bad? Fix the data, ship the tool."

"I don't know." Aidan heard how weak it sounded and kept going anyway. "Maybe. But we keep hearing that automation removes human judgment, and every example we've studied, the bail tool, the hiring filters, the school surveillance cameras Principal Reyes wants, replaces human judgment with somebody else's judgment, baked in and hidden. At least a judge can be questioned. A score just gets printed."

Okonkwo had been writing on the board through all of this. He underlined NEUTRAL, then crossed the word out, and the dry marker squeaked against the silence. "For Thursday," he said, "you'll each write a position statement. It must contain at least one thing you are still unsure about. I'll fail anything completely certain."

The room emptied in its usual noisy rush, but Priya waited by the door. She held out the yellow-tabbed article. "You should read the whole thing. My printer's dying anyway, so consider it a donation."

Aidan took the folder and slid it into his backpack without breaking it down, the paper stiff against his textbooks. Marcus was already in the hallway calling that he wasn't mad, exactly, but Aidan walked the other way, out toward the parking lot, where the district's new security cameras turned slowly on their mounts above the bike racks, tracking nothing in particular, recording it anyway.

Luca had until Friday to finish the drawing for his application portfolio, and the chair he'd chosen as his subject sat in the reading room of the public library like an accusation. He had picked it because it looked simple: wooden, straight-backed, older than anyone in the building. Three afternoons in a row he had sat cross-legged on the carpet with his sketchbook, and three afternoons the legs had come out wrong, the back slats leaning where they should have stood straight, the whole thing warping on the page like something seen through water.
