Maika sat cross-legged on her bed with the schedule from the ice rink spread in front of her and her phone propped against the pillow. Three shifts were open on Saturday: morning skate guard, afternoon birthday parties, and the evening public session. She could take only one, because her mother had already claimed the other hours for her uncle's moving day. She wrote all three at the top of a page, then began adding them up: morning, forty-two dollars; afternoon, fifty; evening, sixty plus a share of tips. One hundred fifty-two dollars, then, that Saturday was worth, and she was losing all of it to a truck full of her uncle's furniture.

The math bothered her in a way she couldn't place at first. She texted Jolie, who worked the concession stand and was doing the same accounting for her own weekend. Jolie replied with a photo of her own list, three columns, a total circled at the bottom. "i'm missing like 160" the message said. Maika stared at the number and felt the wrongness sharpen. They weren't both missing everything on their lists. If Jolie took the evening shift, she wasn't missing the morning, because she'd never been able to take the morning anyway. Something was being counted twice, or counted that had never existed to be lost.

She called her. Jolie answered on the second ring, chewing something. "You're adding all three," Maika said. "But you can only work one. You're not giving up three shifts. You're giving up the best one you didn't take." There was a pause, then the sound of a chip being finished. "My brother kept saying that word," Jolie said. "Opportunity cost. He says it's only the next-best one." Maika wrote the phrase on the page and underlined it, then crossed out two of her three numbers and circled the evening shift at sixty plus tips. If she took the morning instead, what she gave up was the evening, not the evening plus the afternoon plus the morning stacked into a turgid total that looked like a real loss and wasn't.

The choice itself didn't get easier. The evening shift ended at ten, which meant she'd miss Devi's going-away dinner, the one where everyone was bringing a dish and Devi's mother had asked specifically whether Maika would come. Maika had said probably, which both of them understood to mean no. The morning shift ended at noon. She could guard the ice from eight to noon, earn forty-two dollars, and be at Devi's table by six with a bowl of something. The evening was worth twenty more dollars and the tips. She sat with her back against the headboard and tried to make the two things comparable, which was like weighing water against an hour.

She tried to circumscribe the problem, to draw a line around what actually counted. The dinner wasn't the money she'd spend on it, and it wasn't even Devi exactly, since Devi would be at college in the fall either way and they'd already agreed to write. It was the table, she decided. The specific table with the specific people, on the last night those people would be in one room for at least a year. That was the next-best alternative to the evening shift, the single thing standing behind the door she didn't open. The afternoon birthday parties were nothing. They were a door she'd already walked past.

There was a small bathos in realizing this, like climbing a staircase that turns out to have one fewer step than expected. She had wanted the decision to feel large, and instead it had a flat, ordinary bottom: twenty dollars and tips against a dinner. She picked up her phone and typed the text to her supervisor, then set the phone face down on the quilt without sending it, and got up to look out the window at the parking lot, where her uncle's truck was already half loaded with boxes although it was only Thursday.

From the window she could see her mother carrying a lamp to the truck, setting it down on the asphalt, going back for another. Her mother moved in short decisive trips. On Saturday, Maika would be at the rink for one of the three shifts or at the dinner, and the other possibilities would not pile up anywhere, would not sit in a ledger waiting to be mourned. They would simply be the one next-best thing, and then gone.

She went back to the bed, picked up the phone, and sent the message. "Can I take Saturday morning?" She put the schedule in her desk drawer, then took it out again and folded it into her back pocket, and went downstairs to ask her mother what she should cook for Friday, since there wouldn't be time to make anything on Saturday.

The trail behind the reservoir looped for two miles through pine and birch, and Leo had chosen it because nobody walked it on weekday afternoons. He carried his phone in one hand, stopwatch running, and spoke to the trees.

"DNA is the master copy, right, and it stays in the nucleus like a reference book you can't check out. So the cell makes a photocopy of the one page it needs. That's transcription. An enzyme unzips the double helix, reads one strand, and builds a single strand of messenger RNA off it, letter by letter." He stumbled on a root and kept talking. "Then the messenger leaves the nucleus, and translation happens. A ribosome locks onto it and reads three letters at a time, and each three-letter word codes for one amino acid, and the amino acids get chained together, and the chain folds up, and that folded chain is a protein. That's it. That's the whole thing."

Eight minutes, and the trees had asked no follow-up questions. On Friday he would stand in front of a review panel for a summer fellowship and do this for real, and if he rambled or hedged, the fellowship would go to someone else. He stopped at the overlook where the water opened gray and flat, and that was where he found Dana, sitting on the guardrail with her backpack beside her, a blue ribbon of paper crushed in her fist.

"You're the guy who talks to trees," she said. She was a junior; he knew her from the science fair in the spring, where her model of enzyme kinetics had taken second place behind his presentation on gene expression. "I heard you from the switchback."

"I'm practicing an explanation. Transcription and translation."

"Of course you are." She smoothed the paper against her knee, and he could see it was a rejection letter, county-level competition, her fall research entry turned down. "They said my design lacked clarity of purpose. Whatever that means. I'm never doing it again."

Leo sat down on the rail a few feet from her. His heart had begun to palpitate, the way it did before he had to speak in front of anyone, and he was honest enough with himself to notice that talking to Dana counted. "Can I try the explanation on you? You already know most of it."

"I don't want a lesson."

"It's not a lesson. It's practice. You tell me if it makes sense." He waited until she shrugged, that minimal permission, and then he started over, slower this time, and Dana interrupted twice, once to say the photocopy image was confusing because a photocopy isn't single-stranded, and once to ask how the ribosome knew where to start. He had answers, but the answers changed as he gave them, and he found himself saying "I think" and "probably" and then correcting himself, because hedging in front of a panel was death, but pretending certainty where he hadn't earned it was worse. Somewhere in the middle of this he understood that the two things he was holding, clarity and honesty, were not the same value, and that every sentence was a small arbitration between them.

"You say 'the cell wants' a lot," Dana said. "Cells don't want anything."

"You're right. That's anthropomorphism. But it helps people follow."

"So use it, and then say you're using it."

He looked at her. That was it exactly, and it had taken a sixteen-year-old on a guardrail to say it. "Where'd you learn that?"

"From getting rejected." She held up the letter. "Clarity of purpose. I finally figured out what they meant. I never said what the project was for. I just showed that I could do it." She looked at the water instead of at him. "My mom said Krebs had a paper turned down once. I looked it up last night so I'd have something to be smug about."

"What paper?"

"The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle. He published it in Enzymologia instead." She said the names flatly, like reciting a spell. "He got the Nobel later, so, you know. Whatever."

Leo laughed, and it came out harsher than he meant. "That's supposed to comfort you? Nature is the journal. Everyone in the field reads it."

"That's the point. The people whose whole job is judging science got that one wrong. The system isn't an oracle, it's a panel. Panels are obdurate and panels are sometimes wrong and you go back to work anyway."

He turned that over while a merganser lifted off the reservoir, wings slapping the surface like applause from someone who didn't mean it. He had been treating Friday as a verdict on whether he was a scientist, and Dana had been treating her letter as a verdict on whether she was finished, and both of them, he thought, were confusing the judges for the truth. Though he couldn't prove the truth part. Maybe the panels were right about both of them. He held that possibility open the way he was learning to hold an uncertain step in an argument, not closing his hand around the nearest comfortable conclusion.

"Do the explanation again," Dana said. "From the top. But this time tell me what it's for."

"For?"

"You said it yourself. Clarity of purpose. Why should I care how DNA gets copied?"

He set the phone face down on the rail, took a breath, and began. "Every cell in your body carries the same two meters of DNA, and almost none of it is being read at any moment, and what gets read, and when, is the difference between a nerve cell and a skin cell. So the interesting question isn't the copying. It's the choosing." He heard his own voice change on the last sentence, and Dana was writing something on the back of her rejection letter.

"What are you writing?"

"An idea for spring," she said, and folded the paper into her pocket.

The flyer had promised snacks, which turned out to be a single tin of shortbread passed around a folding table in the common room of Maple Grove Seniors' Residence, where the basement food bank did its sorting on Saturdays. Vincent had signed up because his college application had demanded forty volunteer hours, his mother had demanded the application, and the hours had, mysteriously, never been logged. Now, with September looming and a form still blank, he sat between a woman named Dot who smelled of peppermint and a boy from his old school called Percy, who everyone agreed was insufferable but who could carry two boxes at once.

The work itself was simple enough that Vincent distrusted it. Cans and boxes came up from the donation bin in the loading dock, and the sorters checked labels, wiped dust, and stacked what was good on metal shelves while Percy narrated everything in a golf-announcer whisper. "Peaches, dented, risky. Rice, intact, a triumph. Beans, beans, the eternal beans." Vincent found the rhythm of it soothing, the small arithmetic of use versus waste, and he was stacking a row of tomato paste when he picked up a can of chickpeas, read the label, and dropped it straight into the discard bin with a flourish he privately found a little gratuitous.

Dot retrieved it before it hit the bottom. She held it up to the fluorescents, one eyebrow climbing toward her perm. "And what, may I ask, has this poor can done to you?"

"It's expired," Vincent said. "Well, past its date. Tenth of the month, and it's the sixteenth."

"Past its best before date," Dot said, and she said it the way his mother said "allegedly," with a whole courtroom behind it.

"Which means expired."

"Which means nothing of the sort. A best before date marks when the quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe. Sealed food past that date may still be safe." She set the can back on the shelf with the tenderness of someone returning a rescued kitten. "Six days, dear. The chickpeas have more life in them than I do."

Percy leaned across Vincent, delighted. "So all this time you've been executing perfectly good chickpeas?"

"I've been executing chickpeas that said so themselves, on the label, in writing." Vincent picked up another can, turned it over, and hesitated with his hand over the discard bin like a man pausing at a gallows. The trouble was that he had grown up in a house where the date on the milk was law, where his father poured out yogurt on the stroke of midnight like some dairy Cinderella, and Dot's claim, delivered with total confidence by a woman who had also just told him she was ninety-one and had outlived three optometrists, sat uneasily beside all that inherited certainty. He didn't want to believe things just because someone said them with authority. On the other hand, he had just believed the label with no authority at all except ink.

"You're doing philosophy," Percy observed, mouth full of shortbread. "There's a whole word for it. Epistemology. How you know what you know. My cousin took a course and now he can't order lunch."

"I'm not doing philosophy. I'm doing chickpeas." But it was true that he was standing there weighing sources: the printed date, which told him nothing he could verify, against Dot, whose information at least came with a mechanism he could test. So he tested it. He carried the can, plus two others past their dates, to the residence's front office, where a young woman named Camille was stapling a newsletter, and he asked to use the computer. Four minutes later he came back down the hallway at a pace that startled a man with a walker, holding his phone like a torch.

"She's right," he announced. "Whole thing. Quality, not safety. Sealed food past the date may still be safe to eat. There's a government page and everything."

"I could have told you that," Dot said.

"You did tell me that. I just didn't believe you, which I want to apologize for, because apparently I trust a can more than a person." He restacked the discarded chickpeas on the shelf, then retrieved the ones from the morning's earlier stack, feeling like a man releasing wrongly convicted prisoners. It didn't entirely assuage his unease; some part of him still wanted a bright line, a date after which the world was simple, and he suspected that part of him would keep whispering at the back of the fridge for years. He was going to college in three weeks to learn how to know things, and here he'd spent the morning finding out he'd been doing it wrong over legumes.

"What about the crackers?" Percy called from the next table, holding up a box. "Best before the second. Still good, or are we crackers-lawyers now?"

"Put them on the shelf," Vincent said, and then, because the morning had earned it, "and Percy, one more golf commentary and you're sorting the beans alone."

"The beans," Percy said solemnly, "are the eternal beans."

Sofia filled out the application in the truck, using the hood as a desk, and walked into Ferrante's Hardware at ten past nine on a Saturday in June. The store smelled of sawdust and WD-40, and a fan in the corner turned its head slowly from side to side like it was deciding whom to blame. Mr. Ferrante, who owned the store along with the small grocery next door, read her application twice, looked at her shoes, and said she could start Tuesday, stocking shelves and running the register when it got busy.

"Minimum wage, Saturdays and two afternoons," he said. "You turn seventeen in November, right?" She said she'd be seventeen in December. He wrote that down on a yellow pad and told her the stockroom was through the swinging door.

Tuesday she worked beside Deshawn, who was seventeen and had been there since April and who knew where everything was, including the strange things, the pipe threaders and the十六 different kinds of sandpaper. He talked the whole time, mostly about his brother's car, and when a woman came in asking for a fitting that didn't exist, he sold her two that together would do the same job. Sofia decided she wanted to be that good by August.

At noon Mr. Ferrante came through the swinging door with his keys in his hand. "Pilar called in," he said. "I need somebody on the slicer in the deli for the lunch rush." The deli was on the grocery side, behind the case of cheeses and cold cuts, and the slicer was a chrome machine with a circular blade the size of a dinner plate. Deshawn picked up the apron off the hook.

Sofia had been in her room Sunday night, half doing biology homework, half rehearsing her first day, and she remembered a worksheet from the spring about employment law, one column of jobs minors could not do. She had thought it was boring then, a list of prohibitions from some distant bureaucracy, and she had almost malign ed the whole unit as filler. Now she said, "Wait. Are you allowed? The thing about power-driven meat slicers." Deshawn stopped with the apron half over his head.

"I don't know," he said. "Mr. Ferrante asked me." She told him what she remembered, that it wasn't just this state or this store, it was federal, workers under eighteen, and it didn't matter whether it was a grocery store deli or a restaurant. Deshawn hung the apron back on the hook. He didn't look relieved; he looked like a person doing arithmetic he didn't like. "If I say no and I'm wrong, I'm the kid who wouldn't work," he said. "If I say yes and you're wrong, I'm the kid who sliced his hand."

They went looking for proof and found it taped inside the break room cabinet door, next to the schedule: a laminated notice from the Department of Labor, which said that under federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant. Deshawn read it out loud, twice, and took a photograph of it with his phone. Sofia felt a small settling in her chest, though she noticed she also felt something like foreboding, because the paper was the easy part and what came next was not.

Mr. Ferrante was not a cruel man. He took the phone, looked at the photo, and said, "Fine, Sofia, you're sixteen, Deshawn, you're seventeen, neither of you. Sofia, you're on register two in the grocery, Deshawn, come with me, we'll do it fast between customers." He did the slicing himself for the lunch rush, and Sofia watched him through the connecting doorway, taking half-pound orders of turkey with his shirt cuffs unbuttoned, and she thought about how the rule protected Deshawn and also protected Mr. Ferrante from himself, two interests she hadn't expected to line up. She still didn't know whether Mr. Ferrante had forgotten the rule or had counted on nobody saying anything, and she understood that she might never know, and that she would have to work for him anyway, or not, and decide that separately.

At the end of her shift she clocked out and found Deshawn restocking bolts in aisle four. "He's going to ask one of us again," she said. "Some Saturday when it's just us and the deli's busy." Deshawn tightened a wing nut onto a shelf bracket and said, "Then he'll get the same answer." He slid the drawer of ten-penny nails closed with his hip and went back to the front.

The cafe smelled of burnt espresso and wet umbrellas, and Victor spread his materials across the corner table as if laying out evidence for a trial nobody had asked to attend. There was his grandfather's copy of a style guide, its spine cracked and its margins penciled in a hand he almost recognized, and there was his rough draft, returned Thursday with three red circles around the same word. On the draft, Ms. Andaya had written "outdated, check current manual" beside each circle, and the circled word, three times, was "ibid."

"Grandpa's book says it's fine," Victor had told his mother that morning, and she had said, in the tone she used for weather, that manuals change, that his grandfather had typed his dissertation on a machine you had to hit. Victor had carried the old book to the cafe anyway, out of something between loyalty and stubbornness, because his grandfather had pressed it on him the last visit, saying the rules in it were the rules, that scholarship meant consistency. He had also carried his laptop, because he was seventeen and knew that consistency was not the same as being current, though he could not yet have said why both felt true.

His friend Devon slid into the opposite chair with a hot chocolate and no intention of working. "What's the word?"

"Ibid." Victor turned the draft around. "It means, like, same as the source right above it. My grandpa uses it everywhere."

"So what's the problem?"

"The problem is Ms. Andaya circled it like it was a typo." Victor opened the old guide to the tabbed page, where his grandfather had underlined a passage in blue pencil gone violet with age. The page prescribed "ibid." for repeated references. He read it twice, then closed the book and opened his laptop and typed, with the slight shame of a betrayal, "Chicago Manual of Style ibid."

What he found rearranged something in him, a small seismic shift, less an earthquake than the settling of a floor he'd thought was level. The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, had begun discouraging "ibid." in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title. Not because "ibid." was wrong, exactly; it was old, and it broke easily, and the new way repeated the author and a short title so a reader never had to hunt backward. He sat with that for a moment. His grandfather had not been careless. His grandfather had been careful in 1974.

"So is your grandpa's book garbage?" Devon asked, stirring his chocolate.

"No," Victor said, and heard how quickly it came out. "It's right about where to put the commas. It's right about footnotes going at the bottom. It's just wrong about this one thing, and only because the seventeenth edition came out in 2017 and started discouraging ibid. Now you're supposed to repeat the author and a short title instead." Saying it aloud like that, with the edition and the year and the direction of the change, made it solid, a fact he could stand on.

He began to collate the pieces: the draft, the old guide, the library's online copy of the current manual, his notes on the Ludlow Massacre, which was his actual argument, that the Colorado National Guard's actions in 1914 had been less a spontaneous escalation than a planned operation. That was the paper underneath the paper, the thing the citations existed to serve, and for an hour the footnote question had threatened to swallow it. Now he worked through the pages and replaced each "ibid." with Turco, The Ludlow Massacre, 112, and Klamforth, "Company Towns," 58, watching the draft become both more correct and more his. Somewhere in the middle of that his phone buzzed with a photograph from his mother: his grandfather asleep in his armchair, the twin of the style guide still on his shelf.

Victor looked at the photo for a while. He would call the old man on Sunday, and he did not know what he would say. That the guide had been the beginning of the trail, not the end of it? That learning the new rule had made him trust the old ones more, because a rule that admits of revision is a rule you can actually think with? He couldn't say any of that without it sounding like a speech, and anyway part of it was still uncertain to him, whether authority lives in the book or in the edition, whether his grandfather would feel retired or merely superseded. He marked the question in the margin of his notebook, next to a doodle of a footnote number climbing a page.

"Breaking news," Devon said. "Nerd finishes homework at nine p.m. on a Friday."

"Nearly." Victor was on the bibliography now, alphabetical, hanging indents, the author's name reversed and then given straight, and he typed his grandfather's old guide into the list of works consulted without deciding whether it belonged there. Under "additional sources," with a note beside it in his own shorthand: 17th ed., 2017, no more ibid. Then he closed the laptop, left the old book open on the table to the page his grandfather had underlined, and took a photograph of that, too, to send with the phone call he had not yet figured out how to make.

The kitchen at Marchetti's extruded steam from the pasta window in a steady ribbon, and Dylan stood beneath it in a borrowed apron that smelled of garlic and someone else's shift. He was seventeen, hired an hour ago at eleven dollars an hour, and already he had knocked over a bin of grated parmesan, swept it up, and been congratulated by the owner's daughter, Priya, for sweeping with commitment.

"Wash your hands like you mean it," she said. "Dad watches hands."

Mr. Marchetti watched everything from the pass, a squat man who moved slowly, as if conserving himself against the obsolescent equipment around him, the dented steamer, the slicer older than Dylan's parents. He had hired him on the strength of one question, asked over a Form I-9: "You here for the summer or for real?" Dylan had said for real, and it had felt true and also like a thing you say.

His first paycheck came two Fridays later, in a thin envelope Priya tossed him with a flick of her wrist like a card trick. Dylan read it leaning against the wait station, and his face fell before he could rearrange it. He counted hours on his fingers, quietly, then not quietly.

"Okay," he said. "I worked thirty-two hours. Thirty-two times eleven. That's three fifty-two. This says three thirty." He held the stub out as though it had personally wronged him. "Where'd twenty-two bucks go?"

"Tax," Priya said, stacking plates.

"What tax? I'm seventeen. Seventeen-year-olds are tax-exempt. That's a known fact."

"That is not a known fact." She took the stub from him and tapped a line. "See that? Social Security. Your employer withholds six point two percent of your wages for it."

Dylan stared at the line. "Six point two percent of everything?"

She shrugged. "Up to a yearly wage limit. Past that, it stops. Not a problem you'll have this year, dishwasher."

"So the government takes a cut of my dishwater." He did the math on a paper takeout menu, tongue between his teeth. "Six point two percent of three fifty-two, that's about twenty-one eighty. Plus whatever this other little guy is. Okay. Fine. It's not theft, it's arithmetic."

"Congratulations," Priya said. "You're an adult now. Your first adult feeling is disappointment at your paycheck."

That night he wrote to his older cousin Nadia, who was twenty-four and worked at a credit union in the city and answered family messages like a person doing a favor at gunpoint. He texted her a photo of the stub and a single question mark, then, because she demanded more, an actual message:

Dear Nadia, since you are the family's only financially literate member: Priya at work says my employer withholds 6.2 percent of my wages for Social Security, up to a yearly wage limit, and past that limit it stops. Is that real, or is she messing with me? Also is that money gone forever, or does it come back someday like some kind of annuity, paid out when I'm old? Please advise. Also hi. Your cousin, Dylan.

She replied at eleven, in her usual style, which was terse to the point of rudeness: "It's real. And yes, think of it as paying into something that pays back later, though don't build your retirement plan around a dishwashing job. Go to bed."

At work the next Saturday he found Priya restocking the soda cooler and told her, with the air of a man delivering a verdict, "I've confirmed your numbers with a professional."

"Your professional. The credit union one."

"She says hi."

"She's never met me."

"She says hi through me. It's a thing we do." He crouched to help her stack the two-liters. "Here's what I decided, though. I was mad, because it's my money and I earned it pushing plates around. But the money goes to people who already did their forty years of pushing plates around, and someday somebody's pushing plates around for me. That's if it all holds together. Nadia says don't build a retirement plan on it, and she's probably right, and I don't actually know what it'll look like in fifty years. So I've landed on: annoyed, but paying in anyway. Both at once."

"That's very mature of you," Priya said. "For a guy who told me Tuesday that seventeen-year-olds were tax-exempt."

"I said it with confidence. Confidence is different from being right. My dad taught me that."

Mr. Marchetti came around the corner with a tray of veal and paused long enough to look at the two of them crouched among the soda bottles. "In my country," he said, "you would not be texting and working at the same time."

"I'm working," Dylan said, holding up a two-liter in each hand as evidence.

"You're chatting," Mr. Marchetti said, but he was almost smiling. He set down the tray and pointed at the pasta window, where the steam extruded itself in its usual ribbon. "Water's boiling. Wednesday you learn the sauté station. Friday I'll teach you to slice prosciutto, and you will not cut yourself, because the slicer is older than my marriage and slower than my wife, God rest her patience."

Priya stood, dusting her knees. "He likes you," she said quietly. "He offered you the slicer. Marco worked here a year before the slicer."

Dylan carried the two two-liters to the wait station, set them down, and looked back at the old machine gleaming dully in the corner. Then he tied his apron tighter and went to find the boiling water.

The bus shelter on Carling Avenue smelled like wet gravel and old coffee, and Jackson stood under it with a folded page of G-test notes in his back pocket, running through the steps for the third time. Mirror, signal, shoulder check. Full stop at the line. His road test was at two o'clock, and his mother had left the Corolla in the lot by the pharmacy so he could practice parallel parking between two traffic cones she'd bought with the last of her patience. He had knocked one over four times that morning and cleared it twice, and both of those times he'd sat in the idling car with his hands on the wheel, grinning at nobody.

His grandfather was at the stop too, waiting for the 16 to his own appointment, and he was muttering at a letter he'd taken out of his jacket. "Petrov wants me to come in and sign," the old man said. "A new lease. One whole year, he says, or he can't promise the unit."

"Aren't you moving?" Jackson asked.

"Nowhere to move to. But I don't like signing things when I don't know what I'm agreeing to." He folded the letter along its worn creases. "Maybe I should take it to that woman at the church who reads contracts for people. Last time she did it, they gave her an honorarium, forty dollars in an envelope, and she tried to give it back."

Jackson had his phone out already, half for the transit app and half out of habit, and he typed his grandfather's situation into the search bar without deciding to. He expected a maze of landlord-tenant forms. Instead the answer surfaced plainly, on an official page, in a sentence he read twice: in Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month automatically, on the same terms. He read it aloud, slowly, holding the phone where his grandfather could see the blue-and-white page over his shoulder.

"So I say nothing," his grandfather said, "and it just keeps going?"

"That's what it says. Month to month, same terms. You don't have to sign anything."

The old man was quiet for a moment, refolding the letter into a smaller square. "Forty years I've been signing papers because someone with a desk told me to." Then he laughed, short and surprised, and put the letter back in his jacket. "You're useful today. What's all this driving you're doing, then? Cones in the parking lot?"

"Road test at two." Jackson showed him the notes, the cramped handwriting about merging. "That's the part that scares me. The on-ramp. Everyone says you have to get up to speed fast, but the ramp near the test centre is short and there's always a transport truck in the right lane."

His grandfather had driven trucks for thirty years and offered no wisdom at all, which Jackson understood to be its own kind of wisdom. "The highway doesn't care that you're nervous," the old man said finally. "You acclimate to it or you stay in the right lane forever." He watched the 16 appear at the far corner, its sign lit through the drizzle. "Both of those are allowed, mind you. But you already put down the cones in the lot, so I know which one you picked."

On the ride out, Jackson sat by the window and thought about the two things he was doing that day, giving his grandfather a fact that meant the man didn't have to sign, and taking a test that would put his own name on a licence. One was refusing a signature; the other was earning one. He couldn't make them line up cleanly. Maybe independence was just deciding case by case, and maybe he'd get the merge wrong anyway. The bus ran its diurnal route past the mall and the test centre, the same stops it made every day regardless of who was aboard, and he got off two blocks early so he could walk past the on-ramp and look at it.

From the sidewalk he watched the cars merging, how each one chose its gap, some smoothly, some with a wobble that straightened out. He walked to the pharmacy lot, moved the cones to the exact width the examiner would use, and got into the Corolla. He adjusted the mirror, and pulled out of the space to begin again.

Sophie had three bars of dark chocolate, a thermometer she'd borrowed from the chemistry classroom without asking, and a marble slab that was actually the underside of a serving tray from Dani's mother's kitchen. She laid them out on the counter like surgical instruments.

"You know this is just chocolate," Dani said, leaning on the fridge. "People eat it. They don't perform rituals on it."

"People eat bad chocolate," Sophie said. "Chocolate that's gray and streaky and bends instead of breaking. That's what happens if you don't temper it." She was repeating this like an aphorism she'd decided to live by, though she'd learned it from a video at midnight two days ago, and she didn't fully understand it yet. Something about crystals. Something about temperature windows, 115 degrees down to 80 and back up to 88, precise as a landing approach.

She chopped the chocolate into even pieces, which took longer than expected because her knife skills were theoretical, and melted two-thirds of it in a bowl over simmering water. The chocolate went glossy and loose. She stirred in the remaining third, the "seed," watching the thermometer creep down.

"Hand me the tray." She poured a puddle onto the cold marble and began working it with a spatula, spreading and scraping, spreading and scraping. Her wrist ached. The chocolate thickened by degrees, and just when it seemed on the verge of calcifying into a dull lump, she scraped it back into the warm bowl and stirred. The thermometer read 88. She dipped a knife blade and waited.

"Why are we whispering?" Dani whispered.

"I'm not whispering."

"You are. You've been whispering since the thermometer hit 90."

The chocolate on the knife set in about ninety seconds, and when Sophie bent it, it snapped, cleanly, with a sound like a small dry branch. It was shiny as a beetle's back. She actually bounced on her toes, which she would deny later. "Okay. Okay. Now we dip things." There were strawberries, and some pretzels, and one Oreo Dani had designated the test subject.

From Dani's perspective, the whole enterprise looked like a friend briefly possessed by a very calm demon. Sophie dipped with the focus of someone defusing something, coating each strawberry in a thin even sheet and setting it on waxed paper. The Oreo went under completely. It was a good afternoon, is what Dani would have said, until her older brother Marco came home from his shift at the garden center and opened the cupboard.

He pulled down a bag of orange candy melts, the kind he used for coating pretzels at Halloween, and stood eating them by the fistful while he watched Sophie work. "Why's yours so complicated?" he said. "I just melt these and dip. They harden right up on the counter. No thermometer, no slab, none of this."

Sophie stopped with a strawberry suspended over the bowl. "What are those?"

"Candy melts."

She took one from the bag and read the label, frowning. Palm kernel oil. Vegetable oil. She looked up palm kernel oil on her phone with chocolate-sticky fingers, then read for a while, then laughed, one short surprised note.

"What," Marco said.

"They're not really chocolate. That's compound, or coating chocolate. It replaces some or all of the cocoa butter with other fats, so it sets without tempering." She set the bag down between them like evidence. "But it doesn't have the same snap." She took one of his melts, broke it. It gave with a soft, slightly waxy bend, no sound at all. Then she took a shard of her own tempered shell and broke it next to his ear, so he could hear the crack.

"So mine's better," she said, and immediately felt the ground shift under her, because that wasn't the whole truth and she knew it. Marco's melts had cost four dollars and taken ten minutes. Sophie had spent an hour, used her mother's good chocolate, and seized a batch an hour ago when a drop of water got in the bowl and the whole thing went grainy and ruined. She held both broken pieces in her palm, hers bright and brittle, his matte and pliable, and could not rank them honestly. Ease was worth something. So was the snap. She didn't know yet how to weigh one against the other, and she suspected she'd be finding out for years, and not only about chocolate.

"Yours is prettier," Marco conceded, eating another melt. "Mine's done already, though."

"Mine's better," Sophie said again, but quieter, testing it.

Dani picked up the fully drowned Oreo, cracked it open, and offered half. "Test subject survived," she said. "Barely."

Brooke had claimed the carrel by the periodicals at three o'clock, and by five she had filled the whole table with folders, a laptop, and a stapler she'd taken from the supply shelf without asking. The application deadline was midnight. She opened the laptop, typed her legal name, and then sat looking at the question about her activities as though the screen might volunteer something first.

"You're going to burn out that outlet," a voice said. A boy from her civics class, Dev, stood at the end of the shelf holding a copy of an engineering magazine he clearly had no intention of reading. "They shut the Wi-Fi at nine now. Council cut the hours."

"I know when they shut the Wi-Fi."

He sat down across from her anyway, uninvited, and turned one of her folders to face himself. "You're doing all fourteen of these tonight?"

"Thirteen." She took the folder back. "Fourteen if the essay survives." She had written about her grandmother's garden, then about quitting piano, and both drafts had ended up saying nothing, careful paragraphs of nothing that any admissions reader would skim past. "It's the same essay going everywhere. Same form, everything. The Common App."

He squinted at her. "You think the college in Vermont wants what the one in Arizona wants?"

The question had been circling her all week, and she had kept swatting it away. "It's one application. It goes to all of them."

"Convenient," Dev said, and she heard the edge under the word, the accusation she'd been making to herself.

At the reference desk, because she refused to argue from memory, she asked the librarian on duty if there was anything on how college applications worked, history-wise, and was pointed to a shelf where an education handbook sat with a cracked spine. She read standing up. In 1975, the book said, the Common Application had been founded with 15 member colleges. She turned pages. More than 1,000 members now. Fifteen schools and a mimeographed form, and now the thing she was feeding her whole self into, one essay to stand for every version of her.

She carried the book back to the carrel. "Guess how many colleges it started with. Fifteen. It's over a thousand now."

"So they made it efficient."

"So they made it cheap to apply everywhere. Which means everyone applies everywhere, which means nobody's application means anything." She heard her own voice climb and lowered it. The woman two tables over looked up from her newspapers. Brooke pressed her palms flat on the table. "That's the argument, anyway. My dad makes it. Apply to fewer schools, mean it somewhere. My mom says the opposite, that it's a system and you use the system you're given, and being circumspect about it is how other people get your spot."

"And you?"

She had spent months refusing to introspect on the question because introspection felt like stalling, like one more draft of the garden essay. But the book was open in front of her, and the number, that original fifteen, had settled something loose in her. "I think they're both describing a real thing. The form makes you generic and it makes you possible. Both at once. I don't think it cancels out."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the answer I have." She closed the book. "My dad keeps saying find the one school, like it's a person. Like there's exactly one. He said it at dinner again last night, and I nodded, because it's a platitude, and platitudes are what he has instead of money." She hadn't meant to say the last part. Dev didn't say anything back, which she appreciated more than sympathy would have been worth.

She opened the laptop. The essay was still the piano one, four paragraphs about quitting and one paragraph pretending she'd learned something. She read it once, honestly, the way she'd been avoiding. Then she cut the last paragraph and wrote three sentences about the night she'd taken the garden essay and the piano essay and realized they were the same essay, both written for nobody in particular, and that she wanted, before any school answered her, to write one thing for somebody in particular even if that somebody was only her.

At nine the Wi-Fi died exactly as Dev had promised. She tethered to her phone, paid for the essay's last look with a warning about her data, and pressed submit at 9:41, thirteen applications gone into the dark, one held back. The one she'd kept was the small school her father had never heard of, the one she had visited alone on a bus in October and liked without being able to say why.

Dev leaned over to watch the confirmation screen load. "Now what?"

"Now we wait until March." She began stacking the folders, and her hands were not quite steady, and she kept stacking anyway.

The chemistry lab smelled of hot dust and somebody's abandoned instant noodles, and Katherine had claimed the corner bench because it was the only one where the radiator actually worked. She spread her revision notes across it like a general planning a campaign she expected to lose.

"You look morose," said Dev, dropping his bag on the stool opposite. He was only in the room because his frees coincided with hers, and because Mrs. Okafor had stopped chasing non-chemistry students out of the lab sometime around October.

"I look like someone doing equilibrium problems." She turned her notebook so he could see. Nitrogen plus hydrogen going to ammonia, arrows pointing both ways, a little rectangle of graph paper where her working had collapsed into cross-hatching. "The principle says if you change the conditions, the system shifts to oppose the change. So if I heat it, it shifts to take the heat back. It goes the wrong way. I can predict that part. I just can't make myself believe anyone cares."

Dev leaned over and read the page upside down, a skill he had refined across years of copying homework he had no intention of understanding. "Why would a factory choose a temperature that gives less product? That seems like the sort of thing a factory wouldn't do."

"That's exactly the question." Katherine sat back. "If making ammonia gives out heat, then low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium. Hot it, and the balance slides backward, away from what you want. The Haber process should be run in a freezer. Every textbook problem says so, and every textbook problem is three lines long."

"So what's the problem?"

She looked at him, and then at the radiator, which had begun its afternoon complaint, a ticking like a small animal trapped in the pipes. The heat was the point, she thought. Not the conclusion, but the choosing. "The problem is that the problems are lying by omission. There's a whole part of the world the exam doesn't want me to look at."

She went to the shelf where Mrs. Okafor kept the old reference books, the ones nobody signed out, and pulled down the industrial chemistry volume with the cracked spine. She read standing up, one hip against the bench, while Dev ate crisps with the refinement of a man feeding a furnace. What she found made her sit down slowly, the way you sit when a thing you already half-knew gets confirmed.

"They run it hot," she said. "Industrial plants. Hotter than the temperature that would give the most ammonia. On purpose."

"That's stupid."

"It's not stupid, it's the opposite of stupid. It's just not equilibrium." She tapped the page without showing it to him, guarding it like a card. "At low temperature you get the most ammonia sitting there in the balance, but the reaction is too slow when cold. Too slow to be anything. The yield is beautiful and nothing happens. You'd own a perfect amount of a substance you'd wait a geological age to collect."

Dev considered this with his mouth full. "So the factory wants speed, and the exam wants the maximum."

"And I have to hold both of them in my head at the same time and write down only one." She laughed, briefly, without much humour in it. "It problematizes the whole principle, honestly. Not the chemistry, the chemistry is fine. The teaching of it. It gives you a rule for the perfect balance and then grades you as if the perfect balance were the whole of engineering."

She began copying the diagram into her notes, the double arrow drawn with real care this time, and under it she wrote the temperature figures in her smallest hand. She was aware of a small private shift, the kind that no mark scheme would ever record: she had spent two years thinking of chemistry as a set of answers, and now she could see that some of its answers were answers to questions nobody actually asked. The equilibrium yield was true. The industrial temperature was also true. What stayed uncertain was which truth you were obliged to serve, and she suspected the honest answer was that you served whichever one was standing in front of you at the time.

Mrs. Okafor came through to collect the glassware, saw the open reference book, and raised an eyebrow at Katherine's notes.

"You do realise," she said, "that none of that is on the syllabus. On Thursday they will ask you one thing: which way does the equilibrium shift when you heat it."

"Backward," Katherine said. "Away from ammonia."

"Good. Write that."

Katherine wrote it. Then, underneath, in ordinary handwriting, not hidden but not advertised, she added: but they run it hot anyway.

Dev read it upside down and frowned. "Is that going to cost you marks?"

"Probably," she said, and put the pen down. "Do you want the rest of these crisps or not?"

The festival took over four blocks of Maple Street, and by six o'clock the whole neighborhood smelled of charcoal and charoset. Alexa's family claimed a stretch of curb near the stage where the rabbi's table had been set up for the public Seder, white cloth pinned against the wind. Her grandmother unwrapped the old Haggadah from a dish towel and smoothed it flat, the way she did every year, and Alexa noticed that the book had gone to the long table this time instead of to their own blanket. Her mother had volunteered it without asking. That was the first thing wrong with the evening.

The second thing was her cousin Dov, who was twelve and had the Four Questions. He had earned them the hard way: he was the youngest child present from any of the three families sharing the table, and the rabbi's own granddaughter, who was nine, had backed out that afternoon with a fever. Dov had been talking about the questions for a week, and now he stood behind the folding chairs with the photocopied page in his fist, saying nothing, going gray.

"You're on in twenty minutes," Alexa told him.

"I can't."

"You've known this since you were six."

"That was at Grandma's house." He crumpled the page partway and then smoothed it against his knee, as if the paper were the problem. "There's two hundred people out here."

She could have let it go. She wanted, honestly, to be at the front table herself, holding the Haggadah her grandmother's mother had carried out of Salonika, but the custom was the custom: the youngest child present asked the questions, beginning with the one everyone knew, "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Alexa had asked them herself at seven, in a voice so small her uncle had leaned in to hear, and she remembered the weight of it, all those adults waiting. There was something in that memory she still couldn't decide about, whether the tradition honored the youngest or simply used them, whether making a child carry the opening of the Seder problematized the whole idea of welcoming the stranger, or was exactly what welcoming meant.

"Okay," she said. "Stand up. Now."

He stood. A man selling fried dough shouted past them, choleric at his register, and Dov flinched, and Alexa put herself between the shout and her cousin.

"First line."

"Why is this night different..." He stopped. "Different from all other nights."

"Again. Louder than feels right. Out here everything eats your voice."

They ran it six times. She made him sing it to the traffic on Maple, to a woman waiting for the port-a-john, to a group of college kids who slowed down and listened, which was worse for Dov than any silence, and he knew it, and he got through it anyway. By the seventh run he was doing the sequence without the paper: the dipping twice, the reclining, the bitter herbs, the bread of affliction. His voice found a rhythm that belonged to him rather than to his fear.

Then her grandmother appeared at the front table, holding the old Haggadah up like a signal flag. "The rabbi wants the book for the reading," she called. "And the boy, when it's time. Where is the boy?"

Dov looked at Alexa. The lights on the stage came up, and the rabbi was already saying something about the order of the evening, about who asks and why, and two hundred people settled into their chairs.

"You're the youngest one here," Alexa said. "That's you. Go."

"The book," he said. "I can't read Grandma's. It's Ladino on one side."

"So don't read it. You know it. Sing it at the sky."

He walked up the middle of the aisle with the photocopy and then, at the table, folded it away in his pocket and took the old Haggadah from their grandmother, who held on one second longer than she needed to before letting go. The rabbi gestured for quiet. Dov put his hand flat on the page, and Alexa stood on her toes at the back of the crowd, and her mother's hand landed on her shoulder without a word.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?" Dov asked, and the whole street went quiet enough to hear the fryer hissing two blocks away, and then he went on to the second question, and then the third, and Alexa stopped counting and just listened.

The campaign office smelled of burnt coffee and wet cardboard, and Avery had been there for forty minutes before anyone asked who she was. She had written "student journalist" on her nametag in handwriting that suddenly looked young to her, so she pressed her thumb over the word whenever anyone glanced at her. Along one wall, volunteers worked phones in a low murmur, and above the copier someone had taped the new poll results on a sheet of butcher paper, the numbers fat and black: 58 percent.

Avery had come for the school paper. Her editor, Devon, had wanted the piece by Friday, and he had wanted it loud. "Lead cut in half, that's the story," he had texted her, and in her draft that was the lede, followed by the poll and a line about the margin of error, which she had written from memory: plus or minus 3 percent of 58 percent. It had sounded right when she typed it. It sounded right again when she read it on the bus. Now, standing in front of the butcher paper with her notebook open, she couldn't remember where she had learned it, and the not remembering sat in her stomach like a stone.

She copied the poll numbers down, then drifted toward the front desk, where a woman named Priya was stapling walk lists. Avery asked about the poll, and Priya pointed her toward a stack of printed memos bound with a rubber band. "Everything we're allowed to say is in there," Priya said, and went back to the stapler.

Avery carried the memo to a folding table by the window and read it in the gray light. The language was duller than she expected, all caveats and footnotes, but one line stopped her: the margin of error was expressed in percentage points. Plus or minus 3 points on a result of 58 percent meant a likely range of 55 to 61 percent. She read the line twice, then set the draft of her article beside it on the table.

She took out a pencil. In her draft, the margin of error was "3 percent of 58 percent," which would have been a sliver, barely more than one and a half. She looked from her notebook to the memo and back, and felt a slow, cold sense of foreboding spread through her, the kind that comes not from danger but from realizing how confidently you can be wrong. Her version had made the poll look nearly exact. The truth made it a wide band. Under her pencil, she drew the actual range, 55 to 61, and saw that everything Devon wanted to claim about momentum could dissolve inside it.

Devon answered on the second ring. "Tell me you have the numbers."

"I have them. But the margin of error part in my draft is wrong. It's points, not percent," she said. "Three points. So 58 could really be anywhere from 55 to 61."

There was a pause long enough that she could hear a television in his background. Then he said, "That's the same thing," in a tone she recognized, the petulant drawl he used when a fact got between him and a headline.

"It's not the same thing," she said. "One of them makes the race look decided. The other one makes it look like anything." She kept her voice level, the way the phone bank volunteers did, and watched rain start to dot the window beside her.

He argued for a while, then went quiet, then asked what she wanted to do. She told him she wanted to run the range, 55 to 61, plainly, and let the readers see how much room was in it, even if it made a softer story. She admitted she didn't know whether the lead had really been cut or not; the numbers didn't say, and she wasn't willing to pretend they did. Devon said he'd look at it, which was not yes, and hung up.

Avery gathered her things slowly. On her way out, Priya was taping a fresh sheet to the wall, a reminder about Saturday canvassing, and Avery stopped to read it though she didn't have to. Behind her, the phones kept up their murmuring, and someone laughed near the coffee machine. She put her notebook in her bag, zipped it, and pushed open the door into the rain.

Olivier sat at the kitchen table with the assignment sheet in front of him and the laptop open to a blank document. Ten minutes, one scene, drawn from his own life, staged for the class in two weeks. He had tried to parametrize the thing at first, listing possible subjects in columns, rating each for stakes and feasibility, but the list kept collapsing toward one entry he did not want to use. His sister Camille, who had come home from her first semester in November and now spent most afternoons in her room with the blinds tilted so the light fell in a single stripe across the floor.

Margot, fourteen, came in and put her chin on the back of his chair. "Is it about Camille?"

"It's not about anything yet."

"You should make it about Camille. And I should be in it." She pulled out the other chair and sat, which was her way of claiming territory. "I can cry on command. Watch."

"I'm not watching."

She dried her eyes with her wrist anyway. "If you put her in it and it's mean, that's chicanery. You'd be stealing her to get a grade."

He told her the assignment was autobiographical, not theft, and she said that was exactly what a thief would say, and then she went to the refrigerator and stood there with the door open, radiating grievance, until he told her to close it.

Later that night he typed a scene about the day Camille came home, then deleted it, then typed a version where the sister was called Bridget and had a different reason for everything, and that version was worse because it was vague where his memory was exact. The teacher had put The Glass Menagerie on the list of models, so he found the script online and read it straight through at the table, and when he went looking for why the play felt so sure of itself, one page after another, he found what he hadn't known. Tennessee Williams had based Laura, the fragile sister in The Glass Menagerie, on his own sister Rose. He read the sentence twice, then said it out loud to the empty kitchen, just to hear it. "Laura is Rose." The stage had a door and his family had a door and the same person had walked through both.

He sat with that for a while. It didn't tell him whether it was permitted. Williams had done it, and Williams's sister had spent her life in hospitals, and Olivier didn't know what Rose had thought of the play or whether anyone had asked her. What he had was the fact that the version people trusted most was the version closest to the real girl, glass animals and all, and the fact that he was afraid of the same closeness. He could keep hiding behind a renamed sister, and the scene would stay thin, a story about a girl shaped generally like grief. Or he could write Camille and let the class see her, which felt less like writing than like opening her door while she slept.

In the morning Margot found him at the table again, surrounded by printed pages with lines struck through. "Did you do it?" she asked.

"I started it. It's about her. The real her, not a fake sister with a fake problem."

Margot picked up a page and read the first lines with her lips moving. Her shoulders settled. "It's not mean," she said. "It's just sad."

"That's the same thing to some people."

"It's not, though." She put the page down and squared it against the edge of the table. "Can I still be in it? There could be a little sister. I wouldn't even have to cry. I could just stand in the doorway like I do."

He looked at her standing there in the actual doorway, hand on the frame, and then at the page where he had written the doorway in. "Fine," he said. "But you say the lines the way they're written."

"I always say lines the way they're written," said Margot, and came and sat down across from him to hear the whole thing.

The house smelled of cardamom and old paper, as it always had, and Alexis stood in the hallway holding the folded newspaper like a summons he had been waiting all summer to ignore. His grandfather had left it on the kitchen table that morning with a pencil resting across it, which in this house meant something. It had meant something for three weeks now, ever since Alexis arrived, and he had learned to read the small signals: the coffee set out at nine, the dictionary pulled from the shelf and left open, the chair turned toward the window where the light was best.

Today he could not pretend not to see it. He carried the paper to the porch, where his grandfather sat with his hat on his lap, and sat down across from him without asking permission, because asking would have made it a thing that could be refused.

"Vorwärts," his grandfather said, nodding at the front page. "One article. You read it, then you tell me what it says. In German or English, I don't care which."

"I don't speak German."

"You speak ten words and you have a dictionary. That is how everyone starts."

Alexis unfolded the paper. The article was short, maybe four paragraphs, about a bridge somewhere in the north, and the first thing he noticed, before he understood a single sentence, was the strangeness of the page itself. Half the words seemed to begin with capitals, not just the ones at the start of sentences or the names of towns. Words sat in the middle of lines with their first letters raised like flags. He counted them in the opening sentence and found five capitals in a stretch of text that should have had one.

"Why does everything start with a big letter?" he asked, and immediately regretted it, because his grandfather's face closed the way a drawer closes.

"Figure it out," his grandfather said. "You have the dictionary. You have the pencil."

So Alexis bent over the page and worked, and the morning went by. He looked up Brücke and found it meant bridge, and it was capitalized; he looked up the words around it and found that the ones in lowercase were doing things, going, standing, costing, while the capitalized ones were things themselves: the bridge, the city, the river, the year. He wrote the words in the margin in two columns, capitals in one, lowercase in the other, and sat back and looked at it. He tested it against the names, Hamburg, the minister's name, and against every small word he knew, und, in, der. The pattern held. German capitalized every noun, not only names, so that a reader's eye could pick the nouns out of a sentence at a glance, and the whole strange page suddenly made sense as a design, a system someone had built on purpose, like the grid of the garden behind the house.

"It's the nouns," he said. "They're all capitalized. Every single one. That's why the page looked like that."

His grandfather's expression was equivocal, half approval and half something Alexis could not name, and he said only, "So read."

Alexis read, slowly, halting over the second paragraph, where the article turned to a dispute about whether the bridge should be repaired or torn down, and the word Abbruch kept sliding away from him. The pace of the reading slowed until each sentence felt like wading. His grandfather sat perfectly still, hat still on his lap, and Alexis became aware, in the way you become aware of a sound only after it has gone on too long, that the old man was watching him with unusual concentration, more concentration than a bad reading of a newspaper article could possibly warrant.

He reached the third paragraph and stopped. There, beside a column of text, was a name in the byline that he had skimmed past at the top and now saw properly for the first time. It was his grandmother's name. His grandmother, who had died in March, who had written for newspapers in Hamburg for forty years, whose desk was still locked upstairs.

"That's Oma," Alexis said.

His grandfather looked out at the garden for a long moment. "Her last piece," he said. "They printed it in April. I have been trying to read it since. My eyes, they don't..." He set his hat down on the table, carefully, brim aligned with the edge. "I wanted to know what she said. The German is easy for me. The eyes are not. So you read it, and you tell me."

The porch was quiet enough that Alexis could hear the wasps in the eaves. He understood, then, the coffee at nine and the dictionary left open and all the folded newspapers, and he understood that his grandfather had not been teaching him German at all, or not only that, and the distinction mattered, though he could not have said exactly how. He thought of his mother saying that his grandfather was too proud to ask for anything, as if pride were a wall rather than a door, and of his own school arguments about whether anything could be true for one person and not another, the relativism his philosophy teacher kept pulling them back to. Sitting here, he felt that pull weaken. The article said what it said, in a language with rules, and a reader either got it right or didn't, and it was in no one's power to make the words mean something easier. Yet what the article meant to his grandfather would not be what it meant to him; that much stayed uncertain, and he decided he could hold both ideas at once without dropping either.

He read the last two paragraphs aloud, translating as he went, stumbling and correcting himself, and the article turned out to be short and dry, a small matter of a small bridge, and his grandmother had used it to write about the things a city owes its river. When Alexis finished, his grandfather took off his glasses and pressed the heel of his hand to one eye, and then the other, and was silent.

"That's what she said," he said at last. "That is exactly what she would say." He put his glasses back on and squared the newspaper on the table, folding it along its old creases. "Tomorrow, the second page. Bring the dictionary."

He stood, put on his hat, and walked down the porch steps toward the garden, and Alexis stayed where he was with his two columns of nouns still penciled in the margin, listening to the wasps in the eaves.

Landon had claimed the cooking duty at the campsite with the confidence of a boy who had watched exactly four cooking videos and internalized none of them. The family soup, his mother had decreed, was his contribution to the trip, and so he stood at the picnic table with a cutting board, a dull knife, and an onion the size of a softball, while his younger sister Marisa read a paperback in the folding chair beside him.

The first cut went badly in a way he had not anticipated. He halved the onion, began dicing, and within thirty seconds Marisa slammed her book shut, wiped her eyes with her sleeve, and announced, voice wobbling, "Something's attacking me."

"You're crying over an onion," Landon said. "That's genuinely pathetic."

"I'm not crying. My eyes are on fire."

"It's fine to cry," he said, magnanimous, dicing on. "I won't tell anyone at school that my sister weeps over produce."

She threw a pinecone at him. He ducked, laughing, and then the vapor reached his own eyes and the laughing stopped quite abruptly. He turned away from the table, blinking hard, and Marisa said, with terrible relish, "Oh, now who's crying over produce," and Landon, eyes streaming, said, "Neither of us is crying, that's the whole point," and then had to stop talking because his throat had closed around the word "point."

He walked to the cooler, splashed water on his face, and thought back to the summer before, when his grandfather had sat on the porch shelling peas and told him about his own father, a chemist who had kept a jar of something or other on the kitchen windowsill. Landon had been twelve and mostly interested in the popsicles, but he remembered one detail now with sudden clarity: the old man saying that onions were chemistry, that the tears were not sentiment but a reaction, and that anyone who mocked a person for crying at an onion was mocking science itself. Landon had not understood, and his grandfather's explanation had been long, prolix even, full of words that slid off a twelve-year-old like rain off a poncho.

Now, blinking at the cutting board, he took out his phone, held it at arm's length with one eye shut, and searched. It took him a minute of squinting through water to find it, and when he did, he read it aloud, half to Marisa and half to the sky. "Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear."

"Say that again," Marisa said.

"Syn-propanethial-S-oxide," Landon said, carefully, tasting the syllables like a foreign candy. "It's a vapor. It floats up off the cut cells and attacks your eyes. It's not emotion. It's not weakness. It is a chemical ambush."

"So we're both victims of chemistry," Marisa said.

"We are casualties of science," Landon said. "I take back everything I said." He considered this for a moment, holding the knife still against the board. There was something in it that interested him beyond the excuse for his stinging eyes: the way the same fact could make teasing seem both crueler and sillier at once. His instinct had been to mock; the truth said the mockery had no target, that Marisa's tears were as involuntary as a sneeze. But it also meant his apology was easy, purchased with a fact rather than with anything harder. He wasn't sure those two things balanced. He filed the question away, the way his mother filed receipts, somewhere retrievable.

He tried the folk remedies. He put on his sunglasses, which helped approximately nothing and made Marisa laugh so hard she had to leave the table. He chewed bread, which his mother swore by and which accomplished nothing except making him look like a hamster in distress. Finally he cut the rest of the onion underwater in the wash bin, and when no vapor reached anyone's eyes, he felt enfranchised by his own learning, a citizen of the republic of not weeping.

"This is my heuristic now," he told Marisa, pointing the knife at the bin. "Onion plus water equals dignity."

"You learned that an hour ago."

"All wisdom is recent if you live long enough," Landon said, which he thought was possibly profound, and poured the diced onion into the pot, where it hissed against the oil and filled the campsite with a smell so good that even Marisa, still sniffling, drifted back toward the fire.

Their mother came up from the lake, took one look at the table, the wash bin, the sunglasses lying in the dirt, and said, "Why is everyone's face swollen?"

"Chemistry, Mom," Marisa said. "Ask Landon. He's a citizen now."

Landon opened his mouth to explain, and the wind, obliging to the last, shifted direction off the cutting board where the onion skins still sat, and both of his eyes filled instantly with tears.

"Not crying," he said, wiping his face with the hem of his shirt. "Chemistry."

The kitchen smelled like burnt toast and solder, which meant Marcus had commandeer the entire first floor for his interview prep. Jason set his backpack down by the door and found his friend at the table with his grandfather, both of them adjusting their grips on each other's hands like they were tuning an instrument.

"Again," the old man said. "You're giving me a dead fish."

"It's a handshake, Grandpa. Not a hostage exchange."

"It's the first thing they'll judge you on. Jason, tell him."

Jason hesitated, because the thing he actually knew was more specific than that. "There was a study," he said. "Two thousand, led by a psychologist named William Chaplin. He found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions. That's it. That's the whole finding."

"There," the grandfather said. "Firm handshakes, favorable impressions. Science agrees with me."

"Correlation," Marcus muttered. "Not destiny."

Upstairs, the real work was waiting. Their robotics team had regionals in eleven days, and Marcus was the presenter, the one who had to explain their water-quality sensor to the judges in four minutes. He ran the demo for Jason and his grandfather, who had followed them up to reclaim his reading glasses, and Jason watched him lose the room in the first thirty seconds. He fiddled with the sample vial. He said "um" the way other people breathe. He ended with "so, yeah," which was the verbal equivalent of the dead fish.

"Well?" Marcus said, after. He was still holding the vial, and his knuckles had gone pale around it.

Jason knew what he was supposed to say, because Coach Ramirez kept saying it: be honest with your teammates. He also knew that last month, when he'd told Marcus the old arm design was "kind of a mess," Marcus hadn't spoken to him for two days. Those two approaches sat in him like two incompatible things, honesty on one side, the friendship on the other, and he could not find the hinge between them.

"It was fine," he said.

"Fine means bad," Marcus said. "You do this face."

"I don't do a face."

"You're doing it right now."

Marcus's grandfather, from the doorway, did not help by being facetious about it. "Perhaps the machine could shake hands with the judges," he offered. "Since it appears to be the only one here with a firm grip." Marcus threw a pillow at him and he retreated, laughing, down the stairs.

Jason pulled out his biology flashcards, mostly as something to do with his hands. Antigen, read the top one, and he stared at the word while he tried to think. An antigen was a thing the body recognized as foreign and responded to. That was the problem, he realized. His feedback kept arriving looking like an attack, so Marcus's whole system treated it as something to fight off. "Kind of a mess" wasn't information. It was a shapeless insult with no handle on it.

"Run it again," Jason said. "I want to time the opening."

"Seriously?"

"Thirty seconds to the demo, then you're talking. Go."

Marcus ran it again. Jason counted the filler words on his fingers, marked where the vial-fiddling started, watched where the explanation of the sensor's calibration actually landed, because it was good, sharper than anything the other teams would bring. When Marcus finished, Jason made himself start there.

"The calibration part, the ninety seconds in the middle, is the best thing you've done all season. It's clear, it's confident, and it's the part the judges will remember." Marcus's shoulders came down an inch. "The problem is everything before it. You said 'um' nine times in the first thirty seconds, and you picked up the vial before you told us what it was for, so we watched your hands instead of listening. If you just stand still for the first ten seconds, the 'um's stop."

Marcus looked at the vial in his hand, then set it deliberately on the desk. "Nine?"

"I counted."

"Creepy, but okay." He rubbed his palms on his jeans. "Again?"

They ran it four more times. By the third, the opening was clean, and by the fourth Marcus had stopped reaching for the vial entirely. His grandfather reappeared at the door with two glasses of lemonade and made them both shake his hand before he would surrender the drinks, and Marcus gripped hard enough to make the old man's eyebrows go up in approval.

"See," the grandfather said. "Favorable first impression."

"Correlation," Marcus said, but he was grinning. He turned back to the desk and squared his shoulders toward the imaginary judges. "Thirty seconds. Time me."

Jason raised his phone, thumb on the stopwatch. "Go."

The market opened at seven, and by half past, the tent behind the peach stand already smelled of warm cocoa. Charlotte had asked for the job two weeks earlier, after spending her savings on a thermometer and a slab of marble she could not really afford. Marisol, who ran the chocolate stall, had looked at the marble, then at her, and said Saturdays, be early, don't touch the tempering machine until you can do it by hand.

That was the arrangement: learn the old way first. The old way meant melting the chocolate to fifty degrees Celsius, cooling it on the marble with a scraper until it thickened and lost its shine, then warming it gently back to thirty-one, where it would set glossy and hard and snap when broken. Charlotte had done it four times now. Four times it had worked, more or less, though her snaps were still duller than Marisol's.

The problem that morning was the weather. Rain had come through overnight and left the air thick, and the tent's canvas held the dampness like a held breath. Marsol frowned at the hygrometer hanging from the center pole and moved the finished bonbons away from the open side. Charlotte, meanwhile, had a box of sample squares she had made the night before and kept in her refrigerator at home, because her mother's kitchen was the only cool place in their apartment. She had carried the box to the market in her backpack, packed against a cold gel pack, and she set it on the table between the cash box and the sign that said SAMPLES, TAKE ONE.

"Those were in the fridge," Marisol said. Not a question.

"For three hours. They were fine when I closed the box."

Marisol picked one up and turned it over. Where the night before there had been a shine like polished stone, there was now a dry, pale film, gritty when she dragged a fingertip across it. Charlotte felt something drop in her stomach. She took another square from the box and rubbed it with her thumb. The coating came away as a powder, and underneath the chocolate was still firm, still good, only gray.

She had wanted to show off. She had wanted Marisol to taste one and say something that acknowledged the snap, the shine, the weeks of scorched batches and gritty failures. Instead she stood there while a customer reached toward the samples and Marisol moved the box out of reach with one hand.

"The heat, right?" Charlotte said. "They got too warm in the bag?"

"No. Heat gives you fat bloom, streaky, oily-looking. This is different."

Charlotte looked at the powdered square again. Her mother had once left a chocolate bar in the fridge door for months and it had come out wearing the same dull white, and her mother had said it had gone bad and thrown it away, and Charlotte had said nothing because at twelve she had not known there was anything to know. Now she turned the fact over the way Marisol turned the bonbon. The fridge was cold. The market air was wet. The chocolate had come out of one into the other, and the wet air had touched its cold surface, and something on that surface had dissolved and then dried out again into rough little crystals. She held the square close to her mouth.

"Sugar bloom," she said.

Marisol nodded once and went back to piping.

Charlotte stood by the table and thought about her two weeks of work, which now looked like two different projects. There was the chocolate itself, which behaved according to rules you could learn and then trust: temperatures, seed crystals, the precise moment when the cooling mass stopped flowing like liquid and started moving like tar. And there was the air, which followed no schedule and owed her nothing, which could undo in an hour of humidity what five degrees of careful heating had built. She had been treating the craft as if precision alone were enough, and this morning it plainly was not, and she could not yet say where the line fell between controlling conditions and simply choosing better ones. She only knew the box should have stayed home, or come dry, or not come at all.

She threw the samples away behind the peach stand, where the pit bucket was, and came back and washed her hands. Marisol was scraping the tempered chocolate off the marble, folding it over itself, and she did not look up when she spoke.

"You want to watch or you want to do it?"

Charlotte took the scraper. The chocolate moved under it in a wide, even ribbon, cooling as it spread, and she kept her eyes on the surface, waiting for the shine to go flat.

Paige had never once been wrong about anything at a Super Bowl party, which was a thing she could say because nobody kept records. The rink's banquet room smelled of nacho cheese and skate oil, the TV bolted high above the rental counter, and the whole extended family had been herded in between periods of public skating because Aunt Renata refused to miss the game and Cousin Dex refused to miss the ice. Paige sat between the two loyalties with her chemistry textbook open on her knees, half watching the screen, half watching everything else, because that was what she was good at, noticing.
