Grandpa Walt planted himself in front of the television with a paper cup of coffee he would never admit was decaf. "You kids don't know what a Super Bowl is," he announced, which was how he began most sentences. "I remember the first one. I was there, matter of fact. Saw it with my own two eyes. Best day of my life, outside of marrying your grandmother."

Dex snorted without looking up from lacing his skates. "You were there, Grandpa?"

"In person. Front row, practically."

Paige did not verbalize her doubt, because she had learned that arguing with Grandpa Walt was like arguing with the Zamboni, but something snagged in her mind the way a skater's blade catches a rut. She pulled out her phone under the table, angling it away from Aunt Renata, who confiscated phones on principle.

The chemistry chapter, meanwhile, was staring up at her from her lap, all about polymers, and she let her eyes drift down to it while the search loaded. A polymer was just a chain, and a monomer was a single link, one small unit that seemed like nothing on its own until it repeated and connected and became something you couldn't snap with your hands. Families, she thought, were like that. One dinner, one argument, one Super Bowl party, none of it mattered much alone.

The page came up. The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles. She read it twice, then a third time, because a fact like that deserved a slow look. Grandpa Walt had been born, as far as she knew, in a small town in Ohio, and he had told the story of his one trip to California a hundred times, and in that story he was nineteen and it involved a girl named Carol and a broken-down Pontiac, and it had happened, by Paige's arithmetic, several years after 1967. Which meant he had been nowhere near Los Angeles that day. Or the Ohio math was wrong. Or the hundred tellings of the Pontiac story had drifted, the way stories drift, the way she herself might already be misremembering the Pontiac story right now, sitting here believing her own memory was a camera when really it was more like Grandpa's.

She looked up at him. He had gone quiet, watching the screen with his cup cradled in both hands, and there was something in his face she did not usually let herself see, because noticing was easier when you kept it shallow. He looked like a man at a window. He had a congenital heart thing, the family murmured, an arrhythmia he'd had since birth, and every year the game got a little louder around it.

Paige thought about the fact in her hand, small and hard and exact, one little monomer of the truth. She could march over and set it down in front of him. The first Super Bowl, she would say, was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles, and you were not there. It would be accurate. It would also be like throwing a puck at the window just to prove glass could break. Maybe he knew it was false and told it anyway, the way you keep a photograph of a place you've only imagined. Maybe he half knew. Maybe she was wrong about Ohio, wrong about the Pontiac, wrong about all of it, and the only thing she could be sure of was the sentence on her screen, and even certainty, she was starting to suspect, was just doubt that hadn't been tested yet.

Dex clattered onto the ice through the far door and fell almost immediately, waving cheerfully through the glass. Grandpa laughed, a real laugh, and pointed with his cup.

On the television a receiver caught the ball at the sideline and both teams reset, and Paige closed the phone and slid it into her pocket, the fact still sitting in her like something swallowed whole. She would keep it. She wasn't sure yet whether she'd ever use it, and that, at least, felt honest.

She stood, tucked the chemistry book under her arm, and walked toward the rink door to watch Dex fall again.

"There she goes," Grandpa called after her. "Write that down, Paigey. Your granddad saw the first one."

Edouard had been at the kitchen table for two hours, laptop open, the personal statement drafted and redrafted until the words had gone smooth and meaningless, like a stone handled too long. Amelie had sent him her old statement in the spring, back when he first mentioned applying, with a note that said: this got me five offers, steal whatever you want. He had stolen the structure, the opening anecdote about taking apart a radio, the closing paragraph that tied ambition to gratitude. Tonight he meant to paste it into the form and be finished.

His sister Colette sat across from him with her homework, which she was doing in a way that involved a great deal of drawing on her wrist. "You're still on that?" she said.

"Checking the character count." He scrolled through the portal to the section marked personal statement, ready to paste, and then stopped. There was no box. There were three of them, each with its own question above it, and a counter beneath each that read zero.

"Problem?" Colette said, without looking up.

"There's supposed to be one statement." He read the first question. Why do you want to study this subject? Then the second, about how he had prepared, and a third he had to read twice. "This isn't the form Amelie described."

"So message her."

She was in Lisbon, two hours ahead, but she answered on the second ring, her face pixelating against a hostel wall. "Edouard. It's late there."

"The form's changed. It's three questions now, not one statement. Did you know that?"

"No. When did they do that?" She looked genuinely thrown, and he found that almost worse than the problem itself, because Amelie was the person in the family who knew things. "Mine was just one long box. Four thousand characters, say something clever in the first line, that was the whole game."

"That's what I wrote." He turned the laptop so she could see the three empty boxes, the questions sitting above them like invigilators. "It says the change started with people applying for 2026 entry. That's me."

"Then your opening anecdote is dead," she said. "The radio thing was for a single narrative. Three questions want three answers." She paused, someone behind her laughing at something. "Look, the advice that mattered wasn't the structure anyway. It was: don't denigrate other subjects to make yours look better. Admissions people hate that."

"I never do that."

"You wrote 'unlike the vagueness of English.' I read your draft."

He closed the call not long after, telling her to enjoy Lisbon, and she said something about how the city was not nearly as hedonistic as their father claimed, and then he sat looking at the first question. Why did he want to study engineering? The honest answer had a shape he didn't like. Part of it was the radio, taken apart at eleven, the copper coil like a small brass nest. Part of it was that engineering was respectable, that their father approved of it, that it led somewhere with a salary. Part of it was simply that he was good at physics and had let the good narrow the choice the way a river narrows into a channel without deciding anything.

Colette had stopped drawing on herself and was watching him. "You look like you're arguing with someone."

"I'm deciding whether to lie."

"That seems easy."

"It's not lying lying. It's choosing which true thing to say." He thought of the boys at his school who talked about their fathers' firms, the placements arranged over dinners he would never attend, a small oligarchy of connections that no personal statement could compete with and that he was not supposed to resent. He could write around all that, or he could write the version where he admitted the radio was partly an escape from a bedroom he shared with Colette, where the preparation was a job at the garden centre and a library card and YouTube, and nothing that cost money.

He began typing into the first box. He wrote about the radio, then deleted the graceful part and left the clumsy part, which was that he had broken it permanently and learned more from that than from fixing anything. In the second box, about preparation, he listed the garden centre, the broken lawnmower engines, the maths he did for fun on the bus. The third question he answered in nine sentences, and none of them were clever.

When he finished, near midnight, Colette had gone to bed and the counters showed numbers well under the limits, so much space unused that it felt like leaving a room half-furnished. He read it once through and could not tell whether it was better than Amelie's version or only barer. He moved the cursor to submit, then stopped, and read the first line again.

"Why do I want this," he said to the empty kitchen, and typed one more sentence at the top of the first box.

"There," he said, and pressed the button.

Jake's mother had declared an amnesty on the refrigerator. Anything left in it by Sunday night would be thrown out without comment, without blame, and, she said, without a funeral. This was her way of telling him that if he wanted to eat next week, he had to figure out how, because she was working the night shift and his father still believed pasta was a food group.

So on Saturday morning he stood at the entrance of the farmers' market with a list he had written the night before, half in his handwriting and half in his friend Priya's. She had walked him through it over the phone: pick four dinners, make each one twice, cook everything on Sunday in one long stretch so the week took care of itself. Rice on Monday means rice on Thursday. Roast the squash, save half, buy the greens loose. He had argued with her about whether a person could actually eat the same soup twice in five days. She said he could and that she had receipts, metaphorically, and also that he should exhume whatever was at the bottom of his crisper drawer before he bought anything, because he was the sort of person who owned three bags of carrots without knowing it.

He did, in fact, own two bags of carrots, softened into something like regret, plus a lime and a bulb of garlic that had begun to sprout. He threw them out at home before coming, which felt like progress.

The market ran along the waterfront, and the stalls closest to the water sold what the vendor called littoral greens, kelp and sea beans and a salty spinach that grew where the tide reached. Jake bought a bag of the sea beans because Priya had put them on the list with a question mark, and because the vendor's dog was lying across the bags of arugula in a way that suggested the dog, at least, had strong feelings about the sea beans.

He was carrying a flat of eggs, the sea beans, three squash, and a lump of honeycomb he had not planned on when he found Priya at the chocolate stall. She lived above the bakery two streets over, and the chocolate vendor was her mother's friend, and Priya had an apartment with a kitchen and, more importantly, a broad stone counter by the window that stayed cold even in August.

"Come up," she said. "I'm tempering. You can watch. Or help. Or eat the failures."

"The failures are the best part," the vendor said, and sold Jake a slab of dark chocolate at what he suspected was not the real price.

Upstairs, Priya chopped the chocolate into small pieces and melted some of it in a bowl over a pot of water, and then she did something Jake did not expect. She poured the melted chocolate directly onto the cold stone counter and spread it flat with a scraper, working it back and forth, pushing it out and gathering it in, over and over.

"It's called tabling," she said, when he asked why she was bullying the chocolate. "You spread it on the stone and work it to cool it down."

"For how long?"

"Until it thickens a little and it's right. Then it goes back into the bowl with the rest."

She tested it by dabbing a bit on her lower lip, which Jake thought was unscientific and possibly the most scientific thing he had ever seen, since her lip was exactly the temperature a human was. Then she folded the cooled chocolate into the warm, and poured it into molds, and set them on the windowsill.

"You're doing your batch thing too, right?" she said. "That's why you're carrying a squash like a football."

He laid out his plan on her table while the chocolate set. Sunday he would roast all three squash at once and cook a pot of rice and the lentils, and the sea beans would go with the eggs on Tuesday, and the soup would happen Wednesday and also Friday, and Thursday was the wildcard, which in his system meant whatever he could make from whatever remained. He had learned this from two directions, he realized. His mother cooked by improvising from whatever the fridge offered, and it never lasted the week; Priya cooked like a general planning a campaign, and hers did. He was trying to hold both, to plan hard enough that the improvising had something to improvise with. What he could not figure out, even on paper, was whether Thursday-as-wildcard was freedom or just a failure he had scheduled in advance.

"The thing about Thursday," Priya said, "is you're going to buy something on the way home anyway. Nobody's wildcards stay empty."

"I could be disciplined."

"You brought honeycomb you didn't plan on."

"That was the dog," Jake said. "The dog made a case for it."

The molds on the windowsill had gone glossy and hard. Priya turned one out and broke it along the lines, and the pieces snapped clean, with a sound like a small dry branch. She handed him the end piece and kept the one with the little defect, the shallow bubble near the corner, which had always been her favorite and which she claimed tasted different, though they both knew it didn't.

The chocolate had the snap of something that had set up exactly right, and Jake ate it slowly, looking at his bags of squash and eggs and sea beans by the door, and at the stone counter with its faint brown residue of the work. He took out his phone and photographed the counter, in case it mattered later, in case his own kitchen and his own week turned out to need something like it.

"Same time next Saturday?" Priya said, already scraping the stone clean.

"Same time," he said, and picked up the squash like a football, and tucked it under his arm.

Sadie spread the photocopy across the kitchen table and weighted its corners with a mug and a jar of pens. The passage was from Jane Eyre, the scene where Mr. Rochester dresses as a gypsy fortune-teller to trick his guests, and the assignment, due at the end of her college's summer bridge program, required her to read it through a critical lens of her choosing. She had chosen feminism at eleven o'clock that morning, switched to Marxism by noon, and by two in the afternoon had written nothing except her name and a thesis she had crossed out so hard the paper tore.

Her younger brother, Owen, slid into the opposite chair with a peanut butter sandwich and no apparent awareness that she was working. He was fourteen and loud, but he also refilled her water glass without being asked whenever he got up, which was a kind of courtesy he would have denied under torture.

"Who's the gypsy," he said, chewing.

"A disguise. A man puts it on so he can manipulate a young woman into confessing her feelings."

"That's creepy."

"I know it's creepy. That's not the paper. The paper is about why it's creepy and to whom." She tapped her pen against the mug. "If I read it as a feminist, it's about Rochester controlling what Jane is allowed to know and feel. If I read it as a Marxist, it's about a rich man playing at being poor and exotic, borrowing a lower class like a costume, then going home to his estate. Both of them fit. That's the problem. They both fit so well I can't tell which one is the reading."

Owen considered this with the seriousness of someone who had recently discovered that teachers sometimes argue with each other about books. "Can't you do both?"

"That's called having no thesis." She pulled her laptop closer and opened her notes, which were a trenchant mess of quotations and accusations, every line capitalized at the guilty party: HE ALREADY KNOWS. HE ASKS ANYWAY. "Or it's called synthesis, which is what Dr. Okafor keeps saying she wants. A considered position. Honestly about what stays uncertain."

The screen door banged and their grandmother came in from the garden with a colander of tomatoes, her hands stained at the knuckles. She set one, small and split, beside Sadie's papers without comment, the way she always did, and Sadie ate it without comment, the way she always did, because it was how they told each other things.

"Whose idea was the cross-out," her grandmother asked, nodding at the torn page.

"Mine. All of it's mine. That's the whole problem with this assignment. There's no answer to check."

Her grandmother laughed and started sorting tomatoes by ripeness, discarding the ones the sun had begun to desiccate into a bowl for sauce. "In my day we were told what the book meant and we wrote it down. You get to mean it yourself. Harder."

It was Owen, surprisingly, who broke the logjam. He had gone quiet over the second half of his sandwich, reading the margins of her notes where she had scribbled comparisons to unreliable narrators, and he pointed at a line she'd copied from somewhere.

"What's this one? The Poe thing?"

"That's from discussion on Tuesday. We were on 'The Tell-Tale Heart,' Poe's story from 1843. The whole time he's describing how he murdered an old man, the narrator keeps insisting he is not mad. And this guy in my seminar, Danny, said the protests are the problem. The more he says he's sane, the more you doubt him. Nobody made him say it. He just keeps saying it." She realized she was talking faster. "What you claim about yourself can be the evidence against you."

"So what does Rochester claim about himself?"

Sadie looked at the passage. Rochester, in his fortune-teller costume, claims to read minds, claims to be outside the social order, claims it's all a game. "He says he's only playing," she said slowly. "He says it's harmless. He says he'll tell her the truth about another woman afterward, as if that cancels it." She started writing before she finished speaking, the sentences arriving in an order she hadn't planned. The feminist lens and the Marxist lens weren't competing explanations; they were two ways of naming the same confidence, the rich man's certainty that he is entitled to know a poor woman's secrets and that his performance, including his performance of harmlessness, will be forgiven.

She wrote for twenty minutes without stopping. When she surfaced, Owen had cleared his plate and her grandmother had left three more tomatoes by her elbow, and there was a paragraph at the end she was genuinely unsure about, about whether Jane's silence in the scene was submission or strategy, and she underlined a question mark beside it instead of pretending to be certain.

"Dinner's at six," her grandmother called from the stove. "Write your revolution, but leave room for soup."

Sadie saved the file twice, copied it to a thumb drive, and then, feeling like either a savant or a fraud and unable to decide which, read the uncertain paragraph aloud to the empty kitchen to hear how it sounded.

"It might be both," she told the tomatoes. "I'm allowed to say it might be both."

Owen, passing through with his headphones half on, said, "Then say it," and kept walking.

The bookshop had a back table reserved on Tuesdays for the summer reading circle, and Brianna had claimed the corner chair three weeks running before Mrs. Amaro finally asked her what she was doing there with a single paperback and a fistful of orange sticky notes. Brianna had shown her the cover, The Great Gatsby, and explained, with more confidence than she felt, that she was preparing for a first-year seminar that expected her to read the novel through a feminist or Marxist critical lens, whichever she could defend by September. Mrs. Amaro had squinted at the book, then at Brianna, and offered her a small honorarium, ten dollars a session plus trade credit, if she would lead an informal discussion for the shop's high school summer staff. Brianna had accepted before she understood what she had agreed to.

Now, on the first Tuesday of July, she sat with the novel open to the scene where Nick first visits the Buchanans' house, and across from her sat two teenagers who worked the register, Priya and Marcus, both holding copies they had clearly not opened. "So we just talk about it?" Marcus asked, spinning a pencil on its point. "We just talk about it," Brianna said, and realized as she said it that she had no idea how to make that true.

She had tried, the night before, to parametrize the problem, breaking the chapter into questions she could actually answer: who speaks, who is described, who gets money and who spends it, whose marriage is praised and whose is merely endured. But every question kept snagging on the same knot. Nick, the narrator, kept insisting on his own judgment, that he was inclined to reserve all judgments, that he was one of the few honest people he had ever known, and yet everything he described seemed to quarrel with everything he concluded. She had begun, almost superstitiously, to mark the spots.

"Here," she said, turning the book toward them. "Nick tells us Daisy's voice is full of money, like he's figured her out. But listen to what Daisy actually says on this page." Priya leaned over. Daisy tells the story of her daughter's birth, says she woke up and asked the nurse whether it was a boy or a girl, and that when the nurse said a girl Daisy turned her head away and wept, and said she hoped the girl would be a beautiful little fool. "That's not what a person full of money sounds like," Brianna said. "That's someone who knows exactly what being a girl in that house costs, and Nick walks right past it because her voice is prettier than her complaint."

Marcus had stopped spinning the pencil. "So the narrator's lying?"

"Not lying," Brianna said, though she was working this out as she spoke, watching her own hands arrange the sticky notes into a loose line down the table's edge. "Wrong, maybe, or motivated. Look what happens when I put these in order." She had marked, over the weekend, every place where another character contradicted Nick directly: Jordan catching him in a claim about being engaged back home; Gatsby correcting his own biography that Nick had repeated as fact; Tom, of all people, accurately naming Nick's pretense. And beneath those, the events themselves refusing to cooperate, the party guests behaving nothing like Nick's summary of them, the marriage neither charmed nor broken in the way he kept insisting. Readers usually catch an unreliable narrator exactly this way, she had read somewhere and now watched prove itself on her table, through contradictions, other characters' words or the events themselves not matching what the narrator claims. Stacked in orange, the pattern was almost embarrassingly visible.

"It's like tectonic plates," Priya said, and Brianna looked up, grateful. "Two things sliding against each other, and you only see the pressure where they catch."

"Exactly. So a feminist reading and a Marxist reading aren't different books," Brianna said, sliding one stack of notes on top of another. "They're two ways of measuring the same fault line. Nick keeps telling us the women are careless, the workers are invisible, and the story keeps showing us the opposite, that Daisy is calculating because calculation is all she's been given, that Wilson matters precisely because everyone, including Nick, declines to see him. The contradictions aren't noise. They're the argument."

They worked for another hour, and it stopped being her session at all. Priya argued that Daisy's fool line was a Marxist critique disguised as a mother's wish, that she understood her daughter's value would be assigned, not earned. Marcus argued back that this let Daisy off too easily, that plenty of people in that book saw clearly and chose comfort anyway, and that Nick's real unreliability was that he never chose anything. Brianna took notes on both and found she could not fully side with either, and said so, and was surprised that saying so felt less like defeat than like the beginning of an essay she might actually write.

When the shop emptied, Mrs. Amaro came back with two cups of tea and set one in front of Brianna. "Good crowd," she said. "You'll come back next week?"

"I'll come back," Brianna said. She began collecting the sticky notes, peeling them off the table one at a time, and Mrs. Amaro watched her with something that was almost a smile.

"You know," Mrs. Amaro said, "that book you were quoting from, the study guide with the yellow cover you had on your lap? I sold the last three copies in June. It was written by my daughter." She straightened the tea cups. "She never actually finished college."

Brianna looked down at the yellow book in her lap, with its confident margins, and slowly ran her thumb along the page where it had told her, in calm and certain prose, exactly how to spot a narrator who couldn't be trusted.

The bill had started as Alexa's homework, one page of careful clauses about letting sixteen-year-olds vote in municipal elections, and now it sat on the overhead projector while twenty-three classmates pretended to be the House of Commons. Ms. Okafor had divided the class with playing cards pulled from a shoebox: red for government, black for opposition, jokers for the Speaker's table. Alexa had drawn a red seven, which meant she was supposed to defend a bill she had written herself, a strange position, like being asked to argue for her own existence.

"First reading is just the introduction," Ms. Okafor had said on Monday, holding up the shoebox. "No debate. You publish the bill and it's on the record. The real work starts after that." She would not say more. She had a habit of answering questions by pointing at the procedure binder on the front desk, its plastic tabs labelled in fading marker, and telling them the rules lived there, not in her.

The debate began well enough. Priya, voluble as always, rose from the opposition benches to say that the bill was a plot to disenfranchise taxpayers by diluting their votes with teenagers who, in her words, "cannot yet be trusted to operate a slow cooker." The class laughed. Alexa stood to respond, and she was halfway through a point about school boards making decisions for people who could not vote for them when Marcus raised his hand and did not wait to be called.

"Point of order," he said, with the gravity of a man uncovering chicanery. "Clause two, subsection b. There's a comma after the word 'residency' that shouldn't be there. As written, it changes the meaning of the whole qualifications section." He held up his photocopy, which he had annotated in three colors of pen, as if the comma were a fingerprint at a crime scene. "How can we vote on a bill that says something it doesn't intend to say?"

For ten minutes the chamber argued about the comma. Someone moved to amend it. Someone else said the amendment itself needed a comma. Priya declared that if the drafting was sloppy, the thinking must be sloppy too, and Alexa felt the ground shifting under her, the whole debate sliding sideways into punctuation while the actual question, whether sixteen-year-olds deserved a say, sat untouched on the projector like a guest nobody had greeted.

She went to the binder. She hadn't planned to; her hand just reached for it while Marcus recited the comma rule from some style guide on his phone. Under the tab marked READINGS she found a paragraph about Westminster procedure, and she read it twice, and something in her went quiet and then loud. She stood.

"Speaker," she said. "This is the second reading. It's a debate and vote on the bill's general principles. The details get examined after, line by line, in committee. So the comma isn't before us yet." She looked at Marcus, whose pen was still hovering. "It's a bad comma. You're probably right about it. But it's not this debate."

Marcus frowned at his three colors. "So we just ignore that it's wrong?"

"No. We fix it later, where fixing belongs. Right now the question is whether the idea is worth fixing at all."

Priya stood, and for once she didn't speak immediately. "I still think you're handing the franchise to people who can't drive after nine," she said, "but fine. On principle, then." She sat down, and Alexa understood that this was Priya's version of a gift, and that Priya had wanted all along to argue the big argument, not the comma, that the comma had been Marcus's want, his three colors of proof that he was the smartest person in the room, and both of them had been briefly using the same lever.

The vote came. Fourteen hands for, nine against, the bill passing on its general principles, and Alexa wrote on the margin of her copy: second reading, principles; committee, details. It seemed strange to her that a parliament would split the work that way, and also strangely honest, an admission that ideas and their wording live in different rooms and must be visited separately. She wondered whether her own opinions worked the same way, whether she believed things in principle that she would quarrel with in the particulars. She thought of her brother, twenty-two, who hadn't voted in the last election because, he said, one ballot changed nothing, and she thought that in principle she disagreed with him, though she couldn't yet say exactly where her disagreement would break down into clauses.

The bell rang. Marcus stayed behind, sorting his pens. "Bring it to committee on Thursday," he said, not looking up. "I'll have the comma fixed by then. And subsection d is a mess too."

"Subsection d is fine," Alexa said.

"It's a mess," said Marcus, and clicked his pen twice.

The assignment sheet said seven days, and Clara had filled all seven. Sprints Monday, throws Tuesday, plyometrics Wednesday, and so on until Sunday, which she had labeled "active recovery" in handwriting that looked, even to her, like an apology. Coach Renner tapped the paper twice and slid it back across the desk. "Where's the rest?"

"That is the rest," Clara said. "I planned every day."

"Rest isn't what you do when you're not planning. It's what you plan so the planning works." He wrote nothing on the sheet, which was worse than a grade. "Warm-ups, too. Revise it. Thursday."

She took the sheet to the bleachers behind the gym, where Priya was sitting with a bag of frozen peas pressed to her elbow. Priya had been the best thrower in ninth grade and was now, by her own account, disaffected, a word she had started using after quitting the competitive squad. She still came to practices, still threw, but only for Clara's ragtag rec team, the one that existed because Ms. Okafor had signed the gym request out of pity.

"He maligns rest days," Priya said, nodding at the sheet. "He used to make us do ladders on Sundays."

"He's making me redo the whole plan."

"Let me see." Priya read it, peas shifting against her arm. "You have throws the day after plyometrics. You threw last Thursday, remember? Your elbow was wrecked and every javelin went flat."

Clara remembered differently, or wanted to. She remembered her wrist. Coach Renner had spent the whole session circling her saying "bend your wrist, bend your wrist," and she had bent it so conscientiously that she'd forgotten the field existed. The javelin had landed like something dropped from a window.

"Thursday," Priya said, "Nadia's sister ran the drills. She's doing a sports science degree. She kept saying the same thing until I wanted to throw a cone at her."

"What thing?"

"Something about a researcher. Wulf. She said Wulf found that learners improve faster focusing on the effect of a movement, the target, instead of their own body parts." Priya shrugged. "Sounds like fortune-cookie coaching."

Clara wrote it down anyway, on the back of the training plan, under an arrow that pointed nowhere yet.

Thursday she was on the track at six, before Renner even arrived, with Priya and two others from the rec team. She had taped paper plates to the fence at throwing height. "Don't think about your arm," she told Marcus, who had the worst elbow flare on the team and knew it. "Just hit the plate."

"Hit the plate," Marcus repeated, in the voice of someone humoring a person with a clipboard.

His first throw sailed wide. His second clipped the fence post. The third hit the plate dead center, and when he turned around his face was doing something complicated, half delight and half suspicion, as if he'd been tricked into competence. He didn't flare his elbow at all, Priya said, and Priya had spent three years watching his elbow flare like a settling pigeon.

"Say the Wulf thing again," Clara called to Priya. "For the plan."

"Learners improve faster with an external focus, the effect on the target, not the body parts." Priya delivered it flat, then ruined it by grinning. "Revisionist history. Next you'll tell me warm-ups matter."

But Renner had arrived somewhere during Marcus's third throw, and he was standing at the edge of the track with his coffee, watching. When Clara gathered her pages he came over and read the revised plan without asking. Tuesday and Friday were blank now except for the words REST, deliberate, capitalized, and a Monday warm-up block with dynamic mobility written as an actual progression, not a line item. He read it twice.

"The plates," he said.

"For external focus. The target, not the wrist."

"I know what it is." He handed the sheet back. "I coach the way I was coached." He said it like a confession that had cost him something, and then, more quietly, "My senior year my coach had me thinking about my shoulder so hard I couldn't feel the field."

He walked off toward the equipment shed. Priya raised the bag of peas in a small salute.

Clara sat on the low wall with her plan and a pen. She still didn't know how much of Thursday belonged to the plates and how much belonged to Marcus simply being tired of failing, or whether rest days were medicine or just permission, and the honest part of her suspected the answer changed by the person. She underlined REST twice, then wrote beside it: ask Marcus how the arm feels before deciding.

He was still at the fence, collecting the paper plates. She jogged over. "Same time Saturday?"

He folded a plate into quarters and put it in his pocket, like he intended to keep it. "Hit the fence post by the third flag?" he said. "I want to try something."

The whiteboard appeared on the first Monday of December, propped against the boards by the zamboni gate, and on it Dana the trainer had drawn four stick figures landing on one leg with their knees bent. Underneath she had written a schedule: single-leg hops, lateral holds, cutting drills, ten minutes before every practice, all season. Evan read it twice while lacing his skates. Behind him, Marcus Delgado read it once and said, to no one in particular, that they were a hockey team, not a yoga studio.

Marcus had a reason for his impatience. In February a junior scout from the conference was coming to watch the team's last stretch of games, and Marcus, who had waited two years for a starting spot on defense, counted every minute of ice time like a man counting money he was owed. Ten minutes of hopping in place was ten minutes gone from breakouts and power plays. The resentment did not fade after the first practice; it metastasized, spreading down the bench in low remarks, until even the quiet goalies were rolling their eyes during the balance holds.

Evan was less sure of his own position than he pretended to be. In his rhetoric seminar that term he had learned to name the parts of an argument, and he had noticed that both sides of the locker-room dispute ran mostly on pathos. Marcus had pride and urgency; Dana had authority and a whistle. Nobody had produced what his professor would have called logos, the actual reasoning, the evidence underneath the claim. So on Thursday, while the others shot pucks at empty nets, he drifted over to where Dana was coiling a jump rope near the whiteboard and asked her, plainly, why the routine was shaped the way it was.

She didn't lecture. She said Dana rarely lectured, which was part of why people trusted her, that she had run the same program at a club up north, and that they could talk after if he wanted the details, and then she blew her whistle for the hop series. He did the hops. He noticed, without deciding to, that the kid next to him, a sophomore named Peter, kept wobbling on the single-leg landings, knees collapsing inward every time he came down.

Afterward, in the corridor outside the weight room, Dana gave him the one thing he had asked for, in the flat tone of someone stating a schedule rather than making a case. The program trained balance, landing technique and cutting technique, she said, because warm-ups built on those things had been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. That was all she claimed for it, and the modesty of the claim was what made it land. No promises about performance, nothing about Marcus's scouts. Just that word, risk, and the quiet verb reduce.

Evan carried it back to the bench the next week, but not as ammunition. He found himself in an awkward middle position, which he could feel the team pressuring him to abandon. When Marcus complained again, Evan said only, "It lowers the chance of blowing out a knee," and Marcus said, "So does luck," and the discussion should have ended there, except that it didn't, because Peter went down in the Saturday game.

It was ugly and ordinary at once, the way injuries are. Peter cut hard to avoid a check, his skate caught a rut, and he folded onto the ice holding his leg, and the arena went very quiet, the way large cold rooms do. The trainer knelt with him; the game stopped; boreal light from the high windows lay in long pale bars across the scratched surface. Peter skated off with help, favoring the ankle, not the knee, and it turned out to be a sprain, two weeks, nothing structural. He would be fine. In the locker room afterward, no one said anything about the whiteboard, and the silence had more than one meaning, and Evan did not try to sort them out loud.

He sat tying his skates the next Monday, in the blue half-dark before the lights came fully up, and watched Marcus at the far end of the room. Marcus was the last one dressed, always, because he liked to walk out last, and today, when he stood, he stood a moment with his weight on one foot, testing his balance the way the routine had taught them, an idle private gesture that no one else saw. Evan laced his last eyelet, stood, and found his own wobble on the left leg, the one that had always been worse, still there. He steadied it, and skated out onto the fresh ice.

The stadium smelled like spilled beer and cold air, and Rosalie's grandfather had already claimed his seat in the second row of the club level, directly behind the glass, before anyone else in the family had found the right stairwell. It was Game Seven, and his team was down by one going into the third period. He had waited, he told anyone who would listen, forty-one years for a night like this.

The trouble started before the puck dropped. Her uncle Rick, who had come only because his sister, Rosalie's mother, had insisted, kept checking his phone and saying things like "wake me when it's over." He denigrated the whole sport at dinner beforehand, calling it men with sticks and no dental plan, and now he was doing it again in a low mutter that Grandpa could obviously hear. Rosalie's cousin Theo, who was facetious about almost everything, offered to sell Rick his seat for twenty dollars, which didn't help, though it made her mother laugh into her scarf.

On the jumbotron between whistles, a trivia question appeared: which trophy, first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America? Rosalie knew it before she finished reading. She had known it since she was eleven, since the summer after her grandmother died, when Grandpa sat her down at the kitchen table with the old encyclopedia and told her the whole thing himself. The Cup had been donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, he had said, tapping the page with two fingers, and first awarded in 1893, and nothing older still existed for any professional team on the continent. It was older than every player on the ice tonight, older than the arena, older than Rick.

"Stanley Cup," she said out loud, quietly, and Theo gave her a look of mock astonishment, and the screen confirmed it a moment later with a burst of confetti graphics.

What she hadn't known, until this evening, was that her grandfather had almost sold the tickets. Her mother confessed it in the concourse while they waited in line for hot chocolate. He'd had an offer, a good one, from a broker at his church, and he'd sat on it for a week, because the property tax bill had come and his pension, as he put it, was a rumor that kept not arriving. He had decided to keep them only that morning. Rosalie thought of last October, when he'd invited her to his birthday dinner and she'd stayed home instead to study for a calculus exam, telling herself the session mattered, that there would be other birthdays. She had gotten the grade she wanted. It had cost her nothing, apparently, except that now she counted things like that.

She carried the hot chocolate back down the stairs carefully, and it was somewhere around the eighth minute of the third that the game tied itself up, and then, with four minutes left, untied itself in the other direction. Grandpa was on his feet with his hands in the air, and Rick was on his feet too, though he would deny it later. Theo had his phone out, filming his grandfather filming the ice, a video of a video of a man watching the thing he'd waited four decades for.

Between the tying goal and the winning one, Rosalie found herself thinking about a lemma her math teacher kept returning to, some small proven statement that you accepted so that larger arguments could be built on top of it. She had never liked that word as a girl; it sounded like a disclaimer. But tonight the oldest fact she knew, a trophy donated by a governor general in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, was holding up a whole family in a cold building in the third period, and the fact seemed less like trivia than like a foundation, something to stand on while everything else wobbled. Whether that was a real thought or just the scoreboard talking, she couldn't have said.

When the horn sounded, Grandpa didn't cheer. He sat back down, put his hat over his heart, and stayed there while the arena detonated around him, streamers falling from the rafters onto the heads of people who hadn't waited forty-one years for anything. Rosalie sat down beside him and put her hand flat on the back of his neck, the way her grandmother used to. The players were lining up to shake hands, an old custom, and her grandfather watched every single one of them do it.

"He would have hated this," Theo said into the roar, meaning his own father, meaning Rick, who was crying a little and pretending it was the cold. Rosalie didn't answer. She was watching the tunnel, where a silver bowl older than everyone in the building was being wheeled out toward the ice on a padded cart, two men in gloves walking beside it the whole way.

Elizabeth arrived at the community kitchen on Delancey Street twenty minutes early, which was unusual for her, and stood at the door watching Mrs. Okafor's Saturday class arrange stainless steel bowls on the long counter. She had signed up because her college essay was due in eleven days and she had nothing to write about except grades, which she suspected was like submitting a résumé as a love letter. Her mother had said, learn something with your hands. Her father, who read the news aloud at breakfast like a man delivering verdicts, had said the whole country was becoming a plutocracy where even dessert was a luxury good, and that if she wanted to understand value she should learn to make things people wanted. She was not sure either of them was right, but here she was, tying an apron.

The first weeks were custards and bread, forgiving things. Chocolate was different. Mrs. Okafor handed out thermometers and said only that chocolate had opinions, and that they would find out what they were. On the board she had written a single number, 32, and beside it the word dark, and then, lower down and half erased, something Elizabeth could not read. Elizabeth copied the 32 into her notebook and underlined it twice.

She chose dark chocolate for her first attempt because dark seemed like the adult choice. She chopped it, melted it over the water bath, stirred, cooled it against the marble slab, watching the thermometer the way you watch a sleeping animal. When the mercury read 32 she poured the chocolate into the little molds Mrs. Okafor kept in a bin by the sink, bars shaped like leaves. She waited. In twenty minutes the dark bars had set with a gloss so deep it seemed to transfix the fluorescent light, holding it rather than reflecting it, and when she snapped one the sound was clean, like a knuckle cracking once.

The woman beside her, a nursing student named Priya who talked through everything she did, had chosen milk chocolate because her nephews refused anything darker. Priya melted, cooled, tested, and poured at 32, exactly as Elizabeth had, in the same molds, on the same counter, and the two of them stood over her tray like witnesses at a disaster that refused to occur. Nothing happened. The chocolate stayed soft and dull, thickening slowly into something that looked like candle wax left in a car. Priya touched it with one finger and left a print.

"It's not fair," Priya said. "I did everything you did."

Elizabeth wanted to say that fairness had nothing to do with it, that thermometers do not negotiate, but she had learned in the last month that this was the thing she liked about kitchens: complaining changed nothing except the mood. She scraped Priya's failed batch back into the bowl and started her own milk chocolate instead, because it seemed cowardly to hand over advice she had not tested. She melted it, cooled it on the slab, and watched the thermometer fall past 32, past 31. At 30 the chocolate on the spatula still looked greasy. She kept stirring. At 29 it suddenly did something she could only describe as deciding: it smoothed out, lost its grain, gathered itself around the spatula like silk. She poured it into the leaf molds quickly, before she could think of a reason to doubt it.

While the tray sat cooling, she went looking for the erased words on the board and found Mrs. Okafor's recipe binder open on the desk by the window. In the margin of a page headed milk, in pencil, in the same looping hand, was a note: milk chocolate works around 29 to 30 degrees, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter. Elizabeth read it three times. She felt something almost atavistic, the old satisfaction of finding food that had gone right, something older than grades or essays, and she also felt slightly cheated, because the answer had been sitting in a binder the whole time.

The bars set. Priya snapped one above her head like a celebration and ate half of it before speaking. "Same chocolate," she said, mouth full. "Same everything. It was the temperature."

"Milk fat softens the cocoa butter," Elizabeth said. "That's what the note says. So it needs to be cooler."

"Then why does the board only say dark?"

Elizabeth had wondered this herself, standing at the desk. She thought Mrs. Okafor erased things on purpose, the way she said chocolate had opinions instead of reciting numbers, and Elizabeth still could not decide whether that was a kindness or a cruelty. A person could waste a whole batch learning what a sentence would have told her. But she had also felt the milk chocolate change under her spatula at 29, had felt it in her wrist before she read it anywhere, and she did not think a sentence could have given her that. Maybe both things were true. She carried the tray back to the counter, set a finished bar in front of Priya, and lifted the second one toward the light.

"Snap it," Elizabeth said.

The truck smelled like cardboard and her father's coffee, and Maelie had been riding with her knees against the glove compartment since the state line. Behind them, in the stacked boxes marked MAELIE in her mother's handwriting, was most of what she owned, including the shoebox of notes Priya had passed her over four years of shared classes. Her father drove with the saturnine concentration of a man who believed the truck's mirrors were lying to him. Every few miles he said, "Still in the lane," to no one.

"I keep doing the math," Maelie said, somewhere past the second rest stop. "There was this study. Jeffrey Hall, 2018. He figured out that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together. I read it back in junior year for a psych paper and I didn't think about it again until last night."

Her father glanced over. "Two hundred hours. That's nothing. That's, what, a week."

"It's not nothing." She unrolled the window an inch and let the highway roar in. "I did it for Priya and me. First period, freshman year, through June. Lunch, the walks home, the weekends at her house, the summer her grandmother was sick and I basically lived there. It came out to over three thousand hours. Probably more, because I only counted the parts I could remember, and you forget hours, you don't remember them." She stopped, aware she had been talking too long, and put her hand flat on the shoebox between her feet.

Her father was quiet for half a mile. Then he said, "So you're saying you can't just do it again."

"I'm saying it's not a personality thing. It's not like I'm good at friends and this new town will recognize that. It's hours. It's sitting next to someone for a year and a half before anything counts." She had been trying to ruminating on this all morning, turning it over like a stone, and saying it out loud made it both smaller and heavier.

At the third rest stop, while her father inspected a tire with theatrical suspicion, Maelie sat on the truck's warm tailgate and opened Priya's last message, sent at six that morning.

Do NOT open the shoebox until you get there, it said. Rules. Also I calculated something. If we videochat every Sunday for three hours, that's 150 hours a year, so by the time we're 40 we'll have more hours than we do now, which honestly feels like a mutualism, like we're two organisms that keep each other alive. I looked that word up to make sure I was using it right. I was. Anyway. Your dad just passed a sign for a town called Bucyrus and I need you to confirm it's real.

She typed: Bucyrus is real. Saw the water tower. Then she added: I found the Hall study again. 200 hours. I keep thinking it means we're done, you and me. Banked. Like we passed some exam nobody can take away. Then I keep thinking it means nobody new gets to start for a really long time, and both feel true. She stared at that, deleted it, wrote it again, and sent it before she could delete it twice.

Priya's reply came as they pulled back onto the highway, and Maelie read it with her phone tilted so her father couldn't see, though he was fully occupied with a passing semi. Or, Priya wrote, it means the new people are already starting their hours today and you don't even know which ones they are yet. Also my mom says hi and also that your dad should stop for lunch, he gets saturnine when he's hungry, which I looked up, and yes I am on a vocabulary arc this morning, deal with it.

Maelie laughed out loud, which surprised her father so much he drifted half a lane and corrected himself with dignity. "Share with the class," he said.

"Later." She put the phone face down on the shoebox, on the two of them, and watched the fields run backward, or seem to, the way everything behind you does. Somewhere ahead was a town full of people who had already started, without knowing it, spending their hours on her. She slid the box closer with her heel.

"Hey," she said. "Can we stop at the first diner we see? I'm starving."

Her father checked the mirror, frowned at it, and took the exit.

The kennel room smelled of disinfectant and something faintly animal beneath it, and Logan had learned in three weeks of volunteering that this was the smell of a slow Saturday. He set his biology binder on the counter beside the scale, opened it to the diagram of a mitochondrion, and began filling the water dishes in the run while Dr. Patel's voice carried from exam room two, telling someone that the dog would be fine.

"You're studying cellular respiration," said Marisol, the technician, glancing at the binder as she passed with a stack of clean towels. She was the one who had shown him, on his first day, how to fold a towel so it stayed put under a cat's chin. "Glycolysis and all that."

"Glycolysis, then the Krebs cycle, then the electron transport chain," Logan said, mostly to himself, the way tracing the steps aloud made them stick. "Glucose gets broken down, and the mitochondria make ATP." He crouched to slide a bowl under the chain-link gate of run four, where a beagle named Gus lifted his head, decided Logan was not worth standing up for, and lowered it again.

"You say that like a recipe," Marisol said. "Glucose in, energy out."

"That's the problem. It's a recipe I can recite and not cook." He turned the page to his homework, which the red pen had marked wrong, and there it was: the example problem. A sequence of DNA bases, one letter changed from the textbook's original, and the question asked what would happen to the resulting protein. Logan had written that the protein would be damaged, or at least different, because a changed letter should change something. His answer had a slash through it and the word "recheck" beside it, and the recheck had only deepened the puzzle, because when he'd looked up the amino acid each codon specified, the changed letter gave the exact same amino acid as before.

Marisol set the towels down and looked at the page for a long moment. "What are they called again?" she said. "My niece had this last year." She frowned, then snapped her fingers. "Silent mutations," she said. "That's the word. Her whole class had to memorize it."

Logan copied the phrase into his margin, but the word didn't settle anything; it only named the strangeness. "So the DNA changed and nothing changed," he said. "The protein comes out exactly the same." He thought of his own life in the past year, his father's move to Phoenix, the way everyone kept telling him nothing essential had changed when everything visible had, and he set that thought aside because it was the kind of thing his English teacher would call a metaphor and he didn't need a metaphor, he needed the mechanism. Except the mechanism, or at least the part he was allowed to know, was just this: several codons could code for the same amino acid, so some single-base mutations changed nothing in the finished protein. The cell went on. The lineage of cells descended from it went on. Somewhere in Gus the beagle, Logan supposed, entire ancestries of cells carried altered letters and produced their proteins anyway, undamaged, indifferent.

"Bring the beagle," Dr. Patel called from the doorway, and Logan closed the binder, clipped the leash to Gus's collar, and walked him down the hall with the dog's shoulder brushing his knee at every second step. In exam room one, a woman sat with her hands folded too tightly in her lap, and Logan recognized the posture before he recognized her, the mother of the cat who'd been in two weeks ago with the lump.

"Good news," Dr. Patel was saying. "The biopsy came back, and it's benign. It's not what we feared." The woman's hands came apart, and she pressed one of them flat against her chest, and Logan stood very still by the door with Gus leaning warm against his leg. He was not sure what the biopsy had tested, exactly, but he understood the shape of what had happened: something had looked like an error, looked like damage, and the test had exonerated it. The cells were doing what cells were supposed to do.

He thought, and then tried to stop thinking, that it was like the homework problem. A change that changed nothing. Except that it wasn't, or wasn't quite, or he couldn't tell whether it was, and that distinction seemed suddenly to matter more than glycolysis. The mutation in his textbook was harmless because the protein was the same either way. The lump had been harmless because it was the same kind of tissue behaving the same way it always had. But a change could also be harmful while looking like nothing, or be harmless and still change something he had no test for, and Logan had no way, standing there with a borrowed beagle, to sort those cases into columns.

"Logan, Gus needs his weight recorded," Dr. Patel said, and Logan guided the dog onto the scale, steadied him with a hand on his ribs, and read the number out loud while the woman smiled at both of them with her hand still resting over her heart.

After the appointment, Marisol brought him a cup of coffee from the lobby machine, although she must have known from his age that she wasn't supposed to, and they stood at the counter while he wrote Gus's weight on the chart. "So did you figure out your homework?" she asked.

"I figured out the answer," Logan said. "I haven't figured out whether the answer is reassuring or terrifying." He looked at the binder, still open to the mitochondrion, the little folded inner membrane like a maze with glucose entering one end and ATP coming out the other, and he tapped the diagram with two fingers. "Every step in here goes one direction. Glucose to pyruvate, pyruvate to the cycle, electrons down the chain. Everything in the cell has to follow the steps." He paused. "Except apparently sometimes the instructions change and the cell can't even tell."

Marisol drank her coffee and considered that. "And you think that's terrifying."

"I think it's both," Logan said. "I think it's both and I can't make it be just one." He closed the binder, and Gus, hearing the sound, thumped his tail once against the floor of the run.

Megan arrived at the community garden a few minutes early, carrying a folding table under one arm and a crate of onions against her hip. The food bank shared a corner of the garden with compost bins and a shed whose door had been propped open with a broken spade since spring. She had signed up two weeks ago, mostly because her mother kept saying it would look good on scholarship applications, and partly because the garden was three blocks from home and she had walked past it a hundred times without once going in.

A woman in a sun hat waved her over. "You're the Saturday volunteer? I'm Dolores. You can sort at the long table. Soft produce one crate, firm another, and if anything smells noxious, really bad, it goes to compost, not to anyone's kitchen." Megan set down her load and began separating bruised tomatoes from sound ones, learning by feel which gave too easily under her thumb.

The sorting was simpler than she had expected, and she was faintly ashamed of that. She had imagined hunger as something she would confront directly, a line of faces she could help, and instead there were only onions, and a clipboard, and Dolores humming something from the seventies. A boy about her age, wiry, with soil under his nails, kept arriving with baskets of chard and zucchini from the far beds. He introduced himself as Tariq between trips and said he had been coming since he was fourteen.

Tariq was the one who mentioned the date. They were washing carrots at the outdoor tap, and Megan had said, half to herself, that she guessed food banks had been around forever, like libraries. "Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981," he said, wringing out a cloth. "That's it. That's the whole beginning." Megan stood with water running over her hands and thought about how recently that was, after her parents were born. Forty-some years, and before that, nothing of the kind, and now there was one in her own neighborhood, in a shed, beside a broken spade.

A man came up the path with an empty wheeled cart and a letter folded in his jacket pocket. While Dolores weighed his squash, he pulled the letter out and asked whether someone could read it to him, because he had left his glasses on the bus. Megan volunteered before she thought about it. The letter was from the city, confirming his appointment at the housing office, and it thanked him for his patience. He listened with his eyes on the zucchini, thanked her twice, and said his daughter used to read his mail before she moved to Calgary.

She washed the carrots more slowly after that. There was a version of volunteering, she understood, that was mostly about the volunteer, about a feeling of rectitude you could carry home and set on a shelf. She had wanted that feeling, and she could admit it now without trying to exculpate herself, without saying the sign-up sheet had been her mother's idea. But the letter had not been about her at all. It had been about an appointment on a Tuesday and a daughter in Calgary, and it had taken four minutes, and it had mattered more than the onions.

Still, the onions mattered too. When a girl of maybe nine came through with her grandmother and chose a bag of carrots, Megan felt a small, plain satisfaction in knowing those were the carrots she had washed, that they had been mud-wet an hour before. The two ideas did not settle into one another easily. One said you show up and you do small things and the small things are real. The other said the small things are stopgaps, that the country had run for over a century without food banks and had built them in 1981 and kept needing them more each year, which meant something upstream was wrong. She could not make those two truths hold hands, and she decided, for now, that she did not have to.

At closing, Dolores handed out paper cups of lemonade and asked Megan if she would come again next Saturday. Megan looked down the rows of beds, at the chard standing dark and ruffled in the late light, and at Tariq stacking crates with the unhurried competence of someone who had done it for years. "Same time?" she said. Dolores nodded and squeezed lemon into the cup. Megan drank it standing up, watching the shadow of the shed door swing slowly across the path.

Mr. Alvarez handed back the first drafts with the expression of a man returning borrowed umbrellas. "Daniel," he said, pausing at Daniel's desk, "you've summarized two articles. I asked you to weigh them. What do you actually think?" Daniel looked at his paper, at the two neat paragraphs, one on each article, and realized he did not know. Both concerned the same question, whether a school reading program raised comprehension scores, and both claimed to answer it. That was the assignment: compare, evaluate, decide which argument held more water. He had described both buckets and never touched the water.

At lunch he spread the articles across the table in the corner of the cafeteria, near the window where the radiator clanked like a small imprisoned animal. Article A, from a glossy education journal, reported a clear improvement across twelve schools. Article B, denser, from a smaller journal, found nothing at all, no effect, and spent its last section listing every way the first study might have gotten lucky. Priya slid into the seat across from him and stole a fry.

"Which one's right?" she asked, chewing.

"That's the whole problem. I found eleven other studies this weekend. Eleven. Every single one found the program worked."

Priya gesticulated at the pile with her stolen fry, as though the papers themselves were being unreasonable. "So it works. Write that."

But it bothered him, the way a word repeated too many times begins to sound invented. He said so, and she rolled her eyes with an insouciance that suggested she had never in her life been bothered by anything at eleven in the morning. "Everything agrees with everything," he said. "Since when does that happen?"

After last period he went to the library, which smelled of old laminate and the lemon cleaner the custodian used on the tables at three o'clock. He did not go looking for more studies. He went looking for the null one, Article B, because it was the only dissenting voice he had, and dissenting voices, his father liked to say at dinner, usually know something. He read its bibliography, which ran three pages, and noticed something odd: the authors kept citing themselves, earlier papers reporting failures to find effects. Failure after failure, in print, going back a decade. If they had a drawer full of these, where were everyone else's?

He followed one citation to a 1979 paper by a psychologist named Robert Rosenthal, found it in a database, and sat very still while the abstract loaded. The screen was slow; somewhere behind him a printer groaned through someone's chemistry lab. Rosenthal had given the thing a name. Studies with null results, the ones finding nothing, go unpublished, sitting in researchers' files, and so the published record ends up looking more positive than the actual evidence. Daniel read it twice. It was like being told that the parking lot outside was only the cars that hadn't broken down.

The next morning he found Priya at her locker, which she was decorating with a laminated photo of a capybara for reasons she declined to explain. "It's called the file drawer problem," he said. "Nineteen seventy-nine. This psychologist Rosenthal. The studies that find nothing never get published, so the record only shows the winners."

"So your eleven studies are the survivors."

"Which means I can't just count them. I have to count what's missing, and I can't, because it's missing." He heard how absurd it sounded and said it anyway.

Mr. Alvarez's fifth period was warm and smelled of whiteboard marker. When Daniel asked, during work time, whether he could write part of the review about the studies he couldn't find, Mr. Alvarez leaned back and said only, "Interesting instinct. What would you put in that section?" which was the teaching equivalent of handing someone a flashlight and pointing at a cave.

Daniel wrote it anyway, that night, at the kitchen table while his mother washed dishes and the window went from gray to black. He argued that Article B deserved more weight than a single study normally would, not because it was better designed, though it was, but because a null result that got published at all had climbed out of a drawer most null results never left. Article A's positive finding was real, and he said so; eleven other studies agreed with it, and he could not pretend they didn't. But he could no longer pretend they settled anything either. The honest position, he wrote, then crossed out "the honest position" because it sounded like a trophy, was that the evidence leaned toward the program working while the record itself leaned further than the evidence did. He sat back. The last sentence sat on the page, and after a while he underlined one word in his head, leaned, and left the pencil on the table.

At school the next day Priya read the draft standing in the hallway, capybara photo gleaming behind her. "So what's your final answer? Works or doesn't?"

"I'll tell you in ten years," Daniel said, and took it back.

The community theatre smelled of dust and old velvet, and Tyson had three weeks to learn how to direct. He'd been on stage since he was nine, mostly as townspeople and once as a horse, but the one-act festival needed a director and Mrs. Okafor had looked straight at him when she said so. His script was a twenty-minute piece by Priya, a sophomore who'd written it during the summer and refused to let anyone else hold the pages. That was the first problem, and it arrived before he could even begin blocking.

"No copies," Priya said, clutching her binder at the first rehearsal. "What if somebody takes one and puts it on at their school and says they wrote it? The showcase is in two weeks. Everyone will see it."

The cast stood around the folding tables looking at her, then at him, and Tyson understood that whatever he said next would decide whether he had a production or a mutiny. He wanted to say yes, fine, whatever, because he needed her script more than he needed to be right. But he also knew he couldn't block a play if the actors were memorizing from a single binder passed around like contraband.

He told her he'd look into it and drove home wondering what there was to look into. He'd assumed copyright meant forms, a fee, some office you visited, a certificate that arrived in the mail like a diploma. He searched that night, expecting to find a maze of paperwork, and instead found the answer sitting flat on the screen: a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it's written down. No registration required. He read it twice, then read it on a second site because it seemed too easy, and the second site said the same thing. He sat there feeling both relieved and strangely suspicious, the way you do when a door turns out to have been unlocked the whole time.

"It's protected already," he told Priya the next evening, before the actors came in. "As soon as you wrote it down. It's automatic. You don't have to register it." She frowned at him, and he added, "Here, look," and showed her the page on his phone. She read it slowly, her thumb hovering over the screen, and he watched her try to decide whether to trust a fact or her fear, which he realized was the same decision he'd been making all week about every note he gave the cast.

After that, rehearsals changed shape. Priya allowed copies, each one marked with her name, and Tyson could finally work. He learned that blocking was a language of small decisions: who crosses, who sits, who gets the light. He learned that Marisol, playing the daughter, wanted to stand the whole time and that the scene only worked when she sat, so he gave her a reason to sit, a chair she had to drag downstage, and the drag became the best moment of the play. When two actors argued about who should get the last line, he tried letting each of them have it on alternating nights, and the second actor's version was better, which surprised everyone including the actor.

What beguiled him most was how much directing resembled a conversation he wasn't having. He'd stand in the house, in the dark that smelled of friable old plaster flaking off the backstage wall, and imagine the audience's eyes as a kind of weather moving across the stage. He imagined them far away, somewhere flat and wide, an audience like a steppe, and the blocking as a path he was drawing for them to walk. He didn't say any of this out loud. Mrs. Okafor had told him that directors who explained their metaphors lost their actors.

On the night before the showcase, Priya found him taping down the spike marks for the chairs. "So if someone steals it," she said, crouching beside him, "I could still prove it's mine?" Tyson picked at the edge of the tape. There was a right answer, probably, something about drafts and dates and records, but he didn't actually know it, and the fact he'd found had told him only what he'd told her, nothing more. "I don't know everything about it," he said. "I just know you already own it. The rest I'd have to look up."

Priya nodded slowly, then pressed the tape down hard with her thumb, smoothing it flat. "Okay," she said. "Places tomorrow at six."

The rink had put the gold medal game on the big screen above the skate rental counter, and by the second period half the public skate had drifted into the lobby to watch. Henry sat on the boards with his skates still laced, his father beside him, his little cousin Priya cross-legged on a rubber mat with a paper flag she had drawn herself, blue and gold and black stripes she insisted matched their grandfather's village.

When the broadcast cut to a wide shot of the arena, the Olympic rings hung above the ice, and Priya held her flag up to the screen. "Which one is mine?" she asked. "Which ring is ours?"

Henry, who had spent a whole unit on Olympic history for a midterm he was still half proud of, said, "They're not anybody's. They're just the Olympic colors. Six of them. They picked them a long time ago because they looked good together." It came out more certain than he felt, the way things did when Priya asked him questions, but she accepted it and lowered her flag, and Henry's father gave him a look he recognized, the look that said an indictment was being prepared.

"You told her that like it was in a book," his father said during the intermission, while the Zamboni flooded the far sheet and Priya went to buy a hot chocolate. "I remember the rings from when I was her age. I always thought they meant the whole world was in them."

Henry shrugged. "They mean the Olympics."

"That's not what I said." His father was not angry; he almost never was. He just held on, patiently, the way he held on to the old songs and the old recipes, to the idea that if a symbol had lasted a hundred years it must be carrying something. "You can't look at those rings and think nobody thought about us."

Henry could and partly did, but he texted Marcus, who had done the same midterm and scored higher, mostly because Marcus checked things. Do the rings mean anything, he typed. Priya wants to know which one is ours.

They watched the third period start. On the glass behind the away net, a sticker version of the rings caught the arena light, five interlocking circles, blue, black, red, yellow, green, on white, and Henry found himself doing what Priya had done, holding an idea up against them, his grandfather's blue and gold stripes, and failing to make it fit cleanly. Gold and yellow argued in his head. His father leaned forward when the tying goal was scored and did not say anything, which for him was loud.

Marcus's message arrived between whistles. "Looked it up because you made me curious. Pierre de Coubertin designed the five rings in 1913. He chose the colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background. So technically the white counts. You owe me a milkshake." Henry read it twice. The last clause sat strangely with him, the fact that the emptiness around the rings was doing the same work as the colors, that something he would have called blank was included on purpose.

He showed his father the phone. His father read it, then read it again, and something in his face loosened. "So somebody did think about us," he said. "Whoever we were, back then."

"Every flag that existed then," Henry said. "That's the whole point. Not one ring per country. All of them in the colors together." He was aware he was half reciting, half arriving somewhere, and that the two felt different. His father's version and Marcus's version were not the same thing, one wanted the rings to hold a particular people, the other wanted them to hold everyone at once, and Henry could not make them stop rubbing against each other, though he noticed he did not want to give either one up.

"Priya," he called, and she came back with her hot chocolate, and he told her about Coubertin and 1913, plainly, without the fake certainty. "So your stripes have blue in them, and the rings have blue. And the white, the part that looks like nothing, that's yours too."

Priya studied the screen, then her flag, then him. "So which ring is mine?"

"None of them," Henry said. "All of them. I'm still working on that part."

She seemed to accept it, the way she accepted most of what he said, and turned back to the game, and Henry, watching the puck move through the neutral zone, thought about how he would have to decide eventually what he believed the symbols carried, or whether believing in them at all was something you could do honestly. Then his father stood up, shouting at a rebound, and Henry stood up with him, still holding his phone, and Priya lifted her paper flag over her head as the goal light went on.

Her father's car had a smell of pencil shavings and old coffee, and the instructor, a square woman named Mrs. Okafor, sat in the passenger seat and did not touch the key.

"Belt," she said.

Alexia had already put her hands on the wheel at ten and two, exactly as the booklet showed, and had adjusted the mirror, and had announced "checking mirrors" in the flat voice of someone checking mirrors. The belt had simply not occurred to her. She reached for it now, and the buckle clicked, and Mrs. Okafor turned the key as though nothing had happened, though Alexia suspected that something had, the way a first point is lost without anyone saying the score.

They pulled out of the gravel drive and onto the county road, which ran straight between soybean fields until it forgot itself near the creek. It was the second week of August, and her father was away on sabbatical, which was a word he used to mean a year in Tucson cataloguing lichens, and which her mother used to mean that someone else would have to teach Alexia to drive. Hence Mrs. Okafor, hence the insurance forms Alexia had signed in the kitchen, one clause of which promised to indemnify the driving school against anything Alexia did to a fence, a mailbox, or a passing cow. She had read it twice. It was the most adult thing she had ever signed.

"Relax your thumbs," Mrs. Okafor said. "You're strangling the wheel."

At the stop sign at Fenwick Road, Alexia stopped, checked both ways twice, and then sat there while a red-tailed hawk crossed the road at its leisure. She was thinking about the belt. Not the buckle, but the statistic printed in the margin of the driver's manual, next to a drawing of a skeleton wearing a shoulder harness like a pageant sash. Her friend Devi, who wanted to be an epidemiologist and said so at parties, had once recited it over cafeteria pizza: according to the CDC, wearing a seat belt cuts serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. Devi had called not wearing one "pernicious," which Alexia had looked up afterward, mostly to check whether Devi was using it correctly. She had been.

Half. Alexia turned onto Fenwick and accelerated to forty, then forty-five, then a cautious thirty-eight. Half was a strange number to hold in your head while steering. It was not a promise, the way her grandmother's prayers were promises, and it was not nothing, the way her cousin Ren treated every safety measure as an insult to his constitution. It was something in between, a probability, and she found she didn't know what to do with probabilities except carry them.

The summer she was eleven, before Ren had his motorcycle, her uncle had taken her and Ren out on this same road in his truck, and Ren had refused the belt on the grounds that he was eleven and free. Her uncle had refused to start the engine, and the two of them had sat in a parked truck in the August heat for forty minutes, both grinning, both certain the other would fold. Alexia, sweating in the back with her own belt on, had watched a spider build half a web on the windshield and had admired them both: her uncle for the principle, Ren for the stubbornness, though she understood even then that only one of them was going to grow up to be the sort of person who insisted.

"What's your speed?" Mrs. Okafor asked.

"Thirty-eight."

"Forty's fine here. You don't have to atone for the whole road."

Alexia eased up to forty.
