The creek came and went on the left, and the soybeans gave way to corn, and she understood something small and unsatisfying, which was that she agreed with her uncle and not with Ren, and also that she couldn't prove him right, exactly. Half. Not all, not none. Belt on, keys turn. That was the whole of her philosophy so far, and it seemed, for a first lesson, like enough.

"Turn here," Mrs. Okafor said. "Use your signal."

Alexia flicked the lever, checked the mirror, and made the widest turn of her life, both hands still on the wheel, the belt lying warm across her chest like a hand that had been there all along.

Katherine found the book on the bottom shelf of the public library, wedged between a broken atlas and something about composting. The spine said The Limits to Growth, and inside the cover a stamp gave the year, 1972. She had gone in for the town records, because Mr. Reyes's assignment was due Friday and her group had done nothing. Build a model, he had said. Show how the town's growth affects its water supply. Her group had produced one poster with a sad-looking lake drawn in marker.

"Can I check this out?" she asked at the desk. The librarian turned it over twice, as if it might be dead.

The book had been done for something called the Club of Rome, Katherine read on the bus, by a team at MIT. They had built a computer model, and the model linked five things: population, food, industry, pollution, resources. She read the sentence three times. The model had a name, World3, and the name appeared on every page like a character in a novel.

At school the next morning, Devon was waiting by her locker with his phone out. "Good news. My uncle says the developers got the variance approved. The Hathaway tract. Four hundred units."

"Four hundred." She was still holding the library book.

"Housing crisis, remember. People need places to live." He said it the way people say things they've decided not to think about. Devon's father sold insurance to the construction companies; Katherine had never held that against him until she noticed she was starting to.

In fifth period the group met in the corner of the classroom. Priya had printed aquifer maps, which was more than anyone expected. "The recharge zone runs right under the Hathaway tract," Priya said, tapping the paper. "More houses, more wells, more pavement. Rain doesn't soak in through pavement."

"So we draw a picture of pavement," Devon said. "Failing grade, guaranteed."

Katherine opened the book between them. "In 1972 these MIT people ran this whole world through a computer. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources, all linked. It was for the Club of Rome. The model was called World3."

"What did it say?" Priya asked.

"That's the part I'm still reading." That wasn't quite true. She had read the conclusions twice the night before, but saying them out loud felt like claiming something she hadn't earned yet. The MIT team had linked everything, and linking everything meant you couldn't pull one thread without the others moving. She didn't know yet what that meant for a town of eleven thousand with one aquifer.

That evening she went to her grandmother's house, because her grandmother had lived here when the reservoir was built and because her mother had said, twice, that Katherine should. Her grandmother was on the porch shelling peas.

"Did you know the reservoir almost didn't happen?" her grandmother said. "The farmers expostulated for a year. Letters to the paper, meetings at the grange. Then the drought came, and the letters stopped." She dropped peas into the bowl. "Everything here comes from that water. This town's whole lineage, you might say. Your grandfather's mill, the school, this house."

Katherine turned that over. She had been thinking of the water supply as one box on a poster and the growth as another box. But the book hadn't used boxes. It had used links, arrows that ran both ways. More industry drew more people, more people needed more food and more water, more of everything made more pollution, and pollution and resources pushed back on all of it. The town was small, but it wasn't separate. The developers needed buyers, the buyers needed jobs, the jobs were mostly at the distribution center out by the highway, and the highway had been built with federal money, which meant the growth was not exactly the town's own decision. Some of the pressure was extrinsic, she thought, coming from outside, like weather.

"You're quiet," her grandmother said.

"I'm working on something." Katherine picked up a pea pod and split it badly, crushing two peas.

On Thursday night the group met at Priya's kitchen table. Priya had made a spreadsheet: households, projected gallons per day, aquifer recharge rates she'd gotten from a county website. Devon had, unexpectedly, brought the sale price of the new units. "Two bedrooms starting at four hundred grand," he said. "My dad says half the buyers will commute to the city." He looked at Priya's numbers, then at his own, and for a second his face did something complicated. "Nobody making our town's wages can buy those."

Katherine spread the map, the spreadsheet, and the library book across the table. "Okay. So here's what I want to try. The MIT book linked things. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources. That was the whole world, but the idea works small. Watch." She drew the aquifer in pencil. She drew an arrow to the new development, an arrow back from pavement to runoff, an arrow from the distribution center to the jobs that justified the development, an arrow from the city's housing prices to the buyers. "Every line goes two ways. Pull here, something moves there."

They worked until eleven. Priya argued that recharge was the choke point; Devon argued that if they killed the development the jobs died too, and the town's school was already losing funding. They were both right, Katherine realized, which was the problem the book had been having since 1972.

On Friday Mr. Reyes walked the rows slowly. When he reached their table he stopped, put on his glasses, and read the web of arrows for a long time. "Where's this from?"

"A model called World3," Katherine said. "MIT. 1972. It was done for the Club of Rome. We shrank it."

He tapped the arrow between the distribution center and the buyers. "And this link. How confident are you in this one?"

"About sixty percent," Katherine said.

Devon exhaled through his teeth. Priya grinned. Mr. Reyes wrote something in his binder, and Katherine watched the pencil move, and did not look away.

The espresso machine had been hissing for two years before the tablet arrived, and Isla still thought of the tablet as a guest that had refused to leave. It decided who worked which shift, ranked the regulars by "loyalty score," and, as of Monday, flagged transactions it considered suspicious. Her manager, Dev, trusted it the way some people trusted weather reports more than the sky.

Mrs. Okafor came in at quarter past eight, which was itself seismic, because she had come at eight sharp every morning for a decade. Her coat was damp and one shoe was ruined. "The GPS took me down Hollow Creek Road," she said, setting her umbrella in the stand with its usual mannerism, handle turned outward, as though nothing had happened. "There were cones. A sign that said closed. But the voice kept saying left in two hundred feet, so I went left."

"You went around the cones?" Isla asked, already pouring the medium drip Mrs. Okafor never had to order.

"Between them, really. Very smoothly. Then the road stopped being a road." She said it lightly, but her hand shook a little on the cup. "The voice was so confident. It seemed wrong to disobey it."

Isla had a twenty-minute gap before the morning rush, so she stood by the pastry case with her phone and searched "why do people follow GPS onto closed roads." The top result was a short article with a name for it. She read it twice, then said it out loud, mostly to the croissants. "Automation bias. The tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct." The cones had been correct. The sign had been correct. Mrs. Okafor had a wet shoe anyway.

She was still holding that thought when Dana came in from the loading dock, waving her own phone. The tablet had rejected Dana's shift swap, the one Isla had approved on paper Sunday, because the system "detected an anomalous pattern of schedule manipulation." Dana had worked every one of those swapped shifts. She had the shifts' worth of dry hands and desiccated fingertips from the dish sprayer to prove it. Dev had looked at the paper schedule, looked at the tablet's red flag, and sided with the tablet. "It cross-references things we can't see," he'd said. Isla had pointed out that what they could see was Dana, standing there, having worked. Dev had tapped the screen gently, like patting a dog with a badge.

Now Isla counted on her fingers, out loud, so Dana could hear the tally: the cones Mrs. Okafor drove past, the paper schedule Dev overrode, and last month, the camera over the register that had auto-flagged the tip jar count and got Tomas written up for eleven dollars that turned out to be in the safe, exactly where he'd logged it. Three for the machines, zero for the contradicting information, which kept being correct and kept losing. She wasn't against the tablet. It caught actual theft sometimes; it scheduled around exams nobody remembered to mention; it never called in sick. But she noticed she had started believing it by default, the way Dev did, and that felt less like a decision than a slow leak.

She took the paper schedule and the tablet's rejection notice and laid both on the counter in front of Dev. "One of these is a machine that can't see Dana," she said. "The other is Dana's actual hours with my signature. You don't have to pick the paper. Just look at both before you pick." Dev picked up the paper, then put it down, then picked it up again, which for Dev was practically a conversion experience. He re-approved the swap with a note in the log. The tablet would probably flag it again by Thursday. Isla was honest enough, with herself anyway, to admit she didn't know what to do about that part, about systems that made you argue with them twice.

Mrs. Okafor finished her coffee and gathered the ruined shoe business into her coat like a folded map. At the door she paused. "Tomorrow I'm taking Ellsworth," she said. "It's six minutes longer and the voice hates it. Let it sulk."

Amy's bedroom had been colonized. Flashcards fanned across the duvet like playing cards after a losing hand, and her laptop balanced on a stack of library books that had nothing to do with biology, which she kept meaning to return and never did. In nine days she would take the placement exam that decided whether she started college in the regular intro sequence or in the accelerated one, and the accelerated one, her brother kept saying, would let her "amortize the misery of freshman year over fewer total credits." Whatever that meant. She was fairly sure he had used the word wrong, but he had said it with such confidence that she'd let it stand.

The problem was not effort. She had drawn the cell, the nucleus, the chromosomes, a fat pink squiggle she'd labeled DNA in handwriting that deteriorated as the night went on. The problem was that every time she read the textbook, the words slid past each other like magnets turned the wrong way. Transcription, translation, replication: three doors, and she kept walking into the wrong one.

Downstairs, her grandmother was watching a game show with the volume too loud, the way she did when she was waiting for someone to join her. Amy went down for water and found her instead, and got trapped for ten minutes by a contestant who could not name a single country beginning with N.

"You're studying," her grandmother said during the commercial. It wasn't a question.

"Trying to."

"In my day we memorized by writing things on our hands." She held up a palm, translucent and spotted, as if the answers might still be faintly visible there. "The nuns washed it off with soap and disappointment."

Amy laughed, and then, because she was stalling anyway, told her the thing that kept snagging her. "There's this part I keep getting wrong. How the DNA even opens up. It's a double thing, like a zipper, and something has to unzip it, and then everything else follows, but I can't hold the order in my head."

Her grandmother considered this with the seriousness of a woman judging a soufflé. "A zipper," she repeated. "Go get your jacket."

Two springs ago, before the exam had existed, before college had existed as anything other than a word adults used at parties, Amy had stood by the drainage pond behind the elementary school with Dex, who was trying to skip stones and failing at a level she considered almost artistic. He had unzipped his hoodie because it had gotten warm, and she had been reading for a class, and she had said, without planning to, "You know that's basically what an enzyme does to your DNA." He had held the zipper halfway, jacket sagging off one shoulder, and demanded to know what she was talking about, and she had told him: helicase, the unzipper, going down the strand. He had called it "the jacket enzyme" for the rest of the year and had once, in the middle of a boring assembly, whispered "helicase" at her so deadpan that she'd gotten a detention for laughing. That was the version she had understood, the pond version, the friend version. Not the textbook version. The textbook was intransigent; it insisted on its own order of presentation and would not meet her where she was.

Now she fetched the jacket. Her grandmother put on her reading glasses, which hung on a chain of tiny plastic pearls, and examined the zipper like a jeweler.

"So," Amy said slowly, something assembling itself, "before the DNA can be copied, this enzyme, helicase, has to unwind it. The helix, the double part. And it does that by breaking the hydrogen bonds. That's what holds the base pairs together, those bonds. That's the actual unzipping, not the fabric, the little fastenings." She worked the zipper down as she said it, tooth by tooth, and it was absurd, a seventy-year-old woman and a teenager unzipping a windbreaker in a living room while a game show contestant guessed Norway and was wrong, but the order finally sat still in her mind. Open first. Then copy. The bonds break, the pairs come apart, and only then can anything be read or duplicated.

"Good," her grandmother said. "Now put the thing back together and tell me the rest while you do it, because I want to know what the body does with all this copying, and because your grandfather is calling in six minutes and I like to be annoying before he calls."

So Amy zipped and unzipped and talked her way through it, transcription as a rough copy, the messenger carrying the message out of the nucleus, translation as the reading of that copy into amino acids, the chain of them folding into a protein, which was, she said, "basically the body manufacturing a worker for a specific job." Her grandmother kept interrupting with questions that were either brilliant or nonsensical, and Amy could not always tell which, which forced her to answer honestly. "I don't know why it's called that. I don't know if it's fast. I know the order now, and I know the unzipping, and the rest is still fuzzy." She had started the night believing she needed the whole system perfect before any of it counted, and somewhere between the zipper and Norway she had changed her mind: a wobbling partial understanding that could say "I don't know yet" was worth more than a confident blank.

Her brother wandered through mid-explanation, eating cereal from a mug. "You're describing hedonism," he said when she got to the part about the cell doing all this constantly, tirelessly, just to keep living.

"It is not hedonism. It's the opposite. It's like the least fun job in the body."

"Sounds exhausting and self-serving at the same time. That's hedonism with extra steps."

"Go amortize yourself," she said, and he saluted with the mug and left, and her grandmother laughed so hard she had to take off the reading glasses, and the phone began to ring, six minutes having passed exactly.

Amy zipped the jacket all the way to the collar, then down again, one last time, the little teeth separating with their soft rippled sound.

"Helicase," she said to no one in particular, and went upstairs to fail the flashcards differently, and better, than before.

Simon had written three pages about the day his father drove him to the hospital to see his grandmother, and by the second read-through in the empty auditorium he could see it was a lie. Not the facts, which were accurate, but the shape. The real scene, the one that kept surfacing at two in the morning, was smaller: his father in the parking garage, unable to find the ticket, saying nothing for eleven minutes while Simon held the stub and did not offer it.

Mr. Okafor's assignment hung on the board behind the stage: a ten-minute play drawn from your own life, staged by the end of the term. Simon had until Friday to hand in a draft, and he had spent the week avoiding the true scene because staging it meant admitting he had watched his father flounder and stayed quiet. He sat in the third row with his notebook open and wrote nothing.

Priya came in through the side door carrying the prompt book, a fat binder with a spiral spine that she had claimed as stage manager for the class productions. She dropped it on the front edge of the stage with a sound like a slammed encyclopedia.

"You're drafting," she said. It was not a question.

"I'm avoiding," Simon said.

"Same thing most days." She opened the binder to a page of diagrams, tiny stick figures with arrows, and began penciling something. Simon watched her work. During last month's showcase she had sat in the wings with that binder, and when Dev had frozen mid-scene and started toward the wrong side of the stage, Priya had flipped pages and held one up to him, and Dev had corrected himself without the audience catching it. Simon had assumed she was improvising, some quick stagecraft reflex. Now he could see the diagrams were dated, one per performance, each cross notated in pencil.

"That night Dev went left instead of right," Simon said. "You had it written down."

"Blocking," Priya said, not looking up. "The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book so it can be repeated the same way at every performance." She tapped a small arrow. "Dev argued about it afterward. Said he'd gone right all week. The notes said otherwise, and that settled it."

Simon looked at his blank page. Something about the idea worked on him, the notion that a moment could be fixed precisely enough to be repeated, that an argument about what had happened could be resolved by a record made at the time. His memory of the parking garage was the opposite: blurred at the edges, contested in his own head. His father remembered that day differently, had said so once, mildly, over dishes. You gave me the ticket right away, his father claimed. Simon remembered holding it. Two accounts of eleven minutes, no prompt book.

He began to write. The play would be two people in a car, one of them holding a small piece of paper, and neither of them saying what they meant to say. He worked for forty minutes, crossed out dialogue, wrote better dialogue. When Priya passed behind the seats collecting her bag, she read a line over his shoulder.

"That's the true one," she said. "The other pages were you reporting. This is you standing in the garage."

He stayed after she left. The auditorium lights hummed. He was aware of a fact he could not resolve: that he was transmuting his father into a character, and that the man who read the part on showcase night would say Simon's words in a register his father had never used, calm and articulate where his father had been irascible and then ashamed of it. The play would be true and not accurate. Or accurate and not true. He could not decide which charge mattered more, and he suspected the honest answer was that he would not know until someone else sat in the dark and watched.

In the back of his notebook, half a page of abandoned economics homework still showed, a list of vocabulary from the unit he had finished that morning: stagflation, inflation plus stagnation, a word for an economy that gets worse in two directions at once. He looked at it for a moment, then copied one of his staging notes beside it, an arrow and the word "holds."

On Friday he handed in the draft. Mr. Okafor assigned Priya as stage manager, and at the first blocking rehearsal she sat in the wings with the binder open, pencil ready, and said, "From the top, and this time I'm writing it down."

Sydney did not need this job, which was why she took an extra shift on a Saturday in July, standing behind the Lemon Squeeze in the food court, watching people carry bags from stores she could name but had never entered. She was saving for a laptop, or that was the version she told everyone, including herself. The truer version was that her college orientation packet had arrived with a note about an optional economics placement exam, and Sydney had decided, calmly and without any panic whatsoever, that she would rather be paid nine dollars an hour to review flashcards than sit at home being an autodidact with a highlighter.

Marcus arrived at four, which was his shift, though he liked to call it "the second act." He set down a crate of lemons on the counter, slightly out of breath, wearing the expression of a man who has done something clever and is waiting to be asked.

"Wholesale," he said. "From the produce market on Delancey. Half what the distributor charges. I looked it up."

"Delancey is across town," Sydney said. "How did you get there?"

"The bus."

Sydney flipped a flashcard. Raise interest rates. Below it, in her handwriting, borrowing gets more expensive. She held it up like a shield. "What's the bus fare?"

"Two fifty each way. But the lemons, Sydney. Half price."

She did the arithmetic on a napkin, mostly so she could keep her hands still and not show that she was delighted. Their distributor charged forty cents a lemon, delivered; the market charged twenty. A crate held a hundred. Marcus had saved twenty dollars and spent five on buses. She slid the napkin across.

"If it costs more to ship the good than the difference in what it costs to make it," she said, "the trade stops paying. That's why our distributor survives, by the way. Not because their lemons are better."

Marcus studied the napkin as though it might apologize. "So I rode a bus across town to lose five dollars."

"To lose five dollars with style," Sydney said. "That's called comparative advantage until the bus fare shows up."

He groaned and started juicing, and she went back to her flashcards, feeling extremely calm, the way you feel calm when you have reread the same card eleven times.

The problem, though Sydney would have denied having any problems, was the exam itself. Her flashcards said one thing; her mother said another. At dinner on Thursday her mother had heard the phrase "the Fed raises rates to fight inflation" on the radio and made a sound like a kettle. They vilify regular people, her mother had said, raising the rate on my card so I can't fix the car, and then they call it medicine. Sydney had argued back with the textbook line, that dear money cools spending, and her mother had looked at her the way you look at a parrot. Sydney had gone to her room and reread the paragraph and found, to her private irritation, that her mother was not exactly wrong, either.

So at the counter, while Marcus mopped, she tried it out loud, because saying things aloud was not the same as panic, it was pedagogy. "Okay. Pretzel guy. Why does raising interest rates slow inflation?"

Marcus, canny enough to sense a trap, said, "Because the radio says it does."

"Because when rates go up, borrowing costs more. People put off the car, the house, the expansion. Less buying means prices stop climbing so fast." She paused. "Also, my mom's credit card gets more expensive and her car stays broken, and the radio doesn't mention that part."

"That's two answers."

"It's one answer with a limp," Sydney said. "The card doesn't say what it costs or how long it takes. It just says the direction. I know the direction. I don't know the rest, and I think the exam just wants the direction."

Marcus squeezed a test lemon into a cup and handed it to her, ceremony intact. "Drink your economics."

The lemonade was actually good, sharper than their usual batch, and Sydney said so, and then immediately regretted it, because Marcus said, "See, worth the bus," and she had to point at the napkin again, and he had to concede that the tastiness was free and the five dollars was not. They agreed to keep the crate but sell the next batch at the regular price, and to call the whole thing tuition.

At closing, Sydney stacked her flashcards, squared them against the counter, and tucked the napkin with the arithmetic in among them, because it was the only card that had both directions on it, the savings and the fare, the cooling and the cost. Marcus held the door. Outside, the parking lot lights were coming on in a slow wave, and the bus to his side of town idled at the far curb, doors open, empty, five dollars a day just to keep running.

"There's my comparative advantage," Marcus said, and Sydney said, "Run, before the fare goes up."

The community studio smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee, and Megan had claimed the corner easel by the window because the light there made the photocopy of Frida Kahlo's "The Two Fridas" almost luminous. Her assignment was due Thursday: a formal analysis of color, composition, symbolism, three pages, no biography, no feelings about the unibrow, just the painting itself. She had circled the exposed heart, the artery snipped by the colonial Frida's own scissors, the storm-colored sky pressing down on both women's heads. On Tuesday she had written half a page and deleted it. The painting kept refusing to become an argument.

Across the table, Dara was taping her own paintings to the wall, phone raised, photographing each one for her portfolio site. She was applying to art schools in January and had decided, with the certainty of someone who had just read a forum thread, that posting her work online meant giving it away. "Once it's on the internet it's public domain," she said. "Anyone can take it. Some guy in another country could print my stuff on shirts and I couldn't do anything."

Megan frowned at her photocopy. "That doesn't sound right." She pulled out her phone and typed with her thumb while Dara kept taping. The studio's instructor, an older woman named Ruth who mostly wandered around refilling solvent jars, drifted past but said nothing, which was her way.

The search results were plain and strange at once. An artwork was protected by copyright automatically the moment it was created in a fixed form. A painting, a drawing, a photo of Dara's weird blue portraits: protected the second they existed. Registration was voluntary. Megan read further and found the catch, the part that would actually matter to Dara: you couldn't sue over a US work until you'd registered it. So the protection existed whether or not you did anything, but the door to the courtroom stayed locked until you paid for the key.

"It's protected the second you make it," Megan said. "The moment it exists in a fixed form, it's yours under copyright. Registration is voluntary, but you can't sue over a US work until you register."

Dara lowered her phone. "So my stuff isn't public domain at all?"

"No. But you'd have to register before you could take anyone to court."

Dara sat down hard on the paint-spattered stool, and Megan watched her redo the arithmetic of the whole evening: the portfolio, the posting, the imagined shirt thief now litigable, in theory, for a fee. Megan turned back to the Kahlo, and the two conversations braided together in her head. The red of the torn artery, the white of the European dress, the Tehuana skirt's deep green: color doing symbolic work she could name. Composition splitting one woman into two loyalties, an unresolved argument held in a single frame. Copyright did something similar, she thought, drawing a line around a made thing and saying: this belongs to its maker. Whether the line held in practice was a different question, and she let it sit unanswered.

Ruth paused behind her, coffee cup in hand, and looked at the photocopy. "Most students expatiate on her bus accident and stop at the first paragraph," she said. "You haven't."

"I keep wanting to and then deleting it," Megan admitted. "The assignment wants the painting, not the life." But she wasn't sure that was honest, either. She remembered her grandmother, who had come to this country with almost nothing and had painted saints on old fruit crates because canvas cost money she didn't have, and who would have called Kahlo's self-portraits vain if she'd seen them, in her reactionary way, suspicious of any painting that put the painter's own face above the subject's. Megan had inherited the crates and never hung them. Standing in this studio, she couldn't decide whether formal analysis was the most respectful way to look at a painting or the most indigent, a method for people who had nothing to give but their eyes.

She opened her notebook and began again. The left Frida, she wrote, holds the scissors herself; the bleeding is self-inflicted but the right Frida holds the tiny portrait of Diego, and the artery runs between them, so the composition makes dependency visible as a physical connection, red against white against the flat, cold sky. She wrote until the studio's overhead lights buzzed on against the darkening window, and Dara, at the wall, was still photographing, but slower now, tilting each painting with more care, as if the things she had made had quietly changed weight.

"Registration is voluntary," Dara said to no one in particular. "Huh."

Megan looked at the two Fridas, joined at the hands, neither one letting go.

Hudson had taped the ocean current map to the refrigerator because it was the only vertical surface his mother hadn't already claimed for grocery lists, and because he wanted to look at it until it stopped looking like spaghetti. His dad came through the kitchen with a mug, stopped, and tilted his head at the swirl of blue and orange arrows crawling up the Atlantic.

"That's the Gulf Stream," Hudson said. "It's why Ireland has palm trees and we have February."

His dad squinted. "Water goes north and gets warm how?"

"It's warm already. It carries heat from the tropics up past us, kind of like a radiator running through the wall of the planet." Hudson traced the current with one finger, from the Caribbean toward Iceland, then the branch that curled toward Norway. "It releases the heat as it goes. That's the whole essay, basically. The professor wants us to explain it from the map, not just name it."

His dad nodded slowly, in the way he nodded when he was deciding whether to ask the next question or let his son off the hook. He chose mercy and went to the porch, where his sister Priya was already arguing with her friend Marcus over a laptop. Hudson followed, because the porch was where the interesting noise was, and because Priya had texted him four times that afternoon in escalating capital letters.

"It's not either or," Priya was saying. "Stop being intransigent about this."

"I'm not being stubborn, I'm being right," Marcus said. "Methane is the big one. It traps way more heat than carbon dioxide, per molecule. That's just chemistry. If you care about the next few years, methane is what you cut first. You fix leaks, you fix the climate, boom."

"That's not how it works," Priya said. "CO2 is what everyone's talking about, so it must matter more."

"You're doing the thing where you decide what's true by counting headlines." Marcus turned and saw Hudson hovering by the door. "Hudson. Settle this. Which is worse, methane or carbon dioxide?"

Hudson almost said carbon dioxide, because that was the answer that felt like school. Then he remembered a paragraph from the reading he'd been skimming between current maps, something that had sat wrong with him until he'd read it twice. "Methane traps way more heat per molecule than CO2," he said slowly, watching Marcus start to grin. "But a methane molecule only stays in the atmosphere for about a decade on average. Carbon dioxide stays a lot longer. So they're both true, kind of. Methane hits harder but fades faster. CO2 is weaker but it doesn't leave."

Marcus's grin collapsed into something more careful. "Wait. So if we cut methane now, we get relief in the next few years, but if we only cut methane, the CO2 is still up there."

"Still up there for a long time," Hudson said. "Like, a lot longer."

Priya leaned back and looked at the ceiling of the porch, which was her posture for thinking. "So the methane people are right about the short term and the CO2 people are right about the long term, and everyone on the internet is just talking past each other because they're answering different questions without saying so."

"That's more or less the shape of it," Hudson said. He felt the strange satisfaction of two things he'd learned on different days clicking together, though he also felt the edge of what he didn't know. He didn't know, exactly, how much cutting methane leaks would actually slow warming in the next few years, or whether decade meant exactly ten years or an average with a lot of scatter. He said so. Marcus exhaled like a man robbed of a victory, but Priya wrote something in her notebook, which meant she'd believed him.

His dad came back through with the empty mug and paused at the door. "Your grandfather would have liked that," he said, apropos of nothing Hudson could trace. "He used to excoriate the newspaper for printing one side of everything. Said the truth was usually two things at once and nobody had the patience for it."

"That's not really a scientific principle," Hudson said.

"It's not a scientific one," his dad said, and went inside.

Later, with the porch emptied and the map glowing under the kitchen light, Hudson tried to write the Gulf Stream paragraph and found he kept writing around the methane argument instead. He thought about discernment, which a teacher had once defined for him as seeing what's actually there rather than what you expect, and he thought about how easy it was to hold a fact like the Gulf Stream warming Europe and never once ask what it didn't explain. The current map didn't tell you anything about the atmosphere. It didn't tell you why the heat stayed once it arrived. Two true things, and the gap between them.

Priya came in for water and stood beside him, reading over his shoulder. "You're stuck," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I'm trying to make the map do more than it does."

"Write what it does do," she said. "Then write what you'd need to know next." She filled her glass and, on her way out, straightened the map where it had begun to curl at one corner, pressing the tape flat with her thumb until it held.

The waiting room had four chairs and a fish tank with a single angelfish circling a plastic plant, and Lauren had memorized its route by the time her name was called. She was here for the second set of bloodwork. The first set had come back with something the receptionist wouldn't describe over the phone, only an "idiosyncrasy" in her clotting numbers, which was the word the nurse had used, the sort of word that meant nothing and therefore everything. Lauren wanted a clean result by Friday, because Friday was the deadline to confirm her spot on the summer research trip, three weeks on a boat studying pelagic birds off Cape Cod, the first thing she had ever wanted that required someone else's signature.

Her mother sat beside her with her coat folded over her knees. While they waited, Lauren's phone buzzed. A message from Dana, all capitals: HAVE YOU SEEN THIS. Below it, a link with a headline about an experiment that had proven Einstein wrong, particles traveling faster than light. Dana's next message read, physics is fake, everything they taught us is fake, and Lauren smiled at the screen the way you smile at a friend who is wrong with total confidence.

She looked up at the fish, then back down. Faster than light. She had a vague memory of her physics teacher mentioning it, but vaguely, and Dana's headline was new, or looked new. There was a poster in the doctor's hallway about not trusting medical advice from the internet, and Lauren thought about that while she typed OPERA neutrinos faster than light into the search bar, then deleted it and typed the headline itself, which was less leading, though she wasn't sure why that mattered yet.

The results assembled themselves slowly, the way silt coagulates at the bottom of a glass. In 2011, an experiment called OPERA had reported neutrinos that seemed to arrive faster than light. Seemed. Other labs had gone looking for the same thing and not found it. And in 2012, the OPERA result itself had been traced to a loose fibre-optic cable. Lauren read the sentence twice, then a third time. One cable. Other experiments, measuring again, had found the neutrinos moving at speeds consistent with light. So nothing had overturned anything; one team's anomaly had dissolved into a mechanical fault, and the checks that dissolved it were, she realized, the whole point. Nobody had believed the first number just because it was a number.

"Lauren," the nurse called, and she put the phone away.

They took her into the small room, and her blood pressure was fine, her pulse was fine, and the doctor came in with a folder and said the second panel had partially corrected the first. One marker was now normal. Another was still borderline, and there was a third test, a confirmatory one, that took ten days to process. Ten days. The trip left in twelve. Lauren did the arithmetic instantly and felt her stomach drop through the floor of the small room.

Her mother watched her daughter's face while the doctor talked, and what she saw there she recognized from the day Lauren had fallen off her bike at nine and stood up slowly, checking for damage before deciding whether to cry. The girl was doing that now, running some interior calculation about what she could still salvage. Her mother wanted to say that the trip would come again next summer, and knew exactly how that would land, as if next summer were a reasonable substitute for the only summer in which Lauren was seventeen and accepted and packed. So instead she said, "Can we do the blood draw today?" and watched her daughter's shoulders lower half an inch.

"Yes, today's fine," the doctor said, already writing the order, and then, almost as an aside, "I'd rather re-run it than trust one panel. That's how we get to something true in this business." Lauren nodded, and in the drawing chair, with the tourniquet biting her arm, she texted Dana back: it was OPERA in 2011, but in 2012 they traced it to a loose cable, and the other experiments matched light. One weird result isn't a discovery. Dana replied with a single eye-roll emoji and the words okay einstein, and Lauren laughed once, quietly, while the needle went in.

The vial filled dark and quick, and the nurse labeled it and set it in the rack with the others. Ten days, twelve until the boat. The angelfish was still circling its plastic plant when they passed back through the waiting room, tracing the same loop it had traced all morning, as if repetition were the only way it knew to be sure of anything. Lauren stopped at the window and looked out at the parking lot, then at her phone, at Dana's message still on the screen. "Book the trip," her mother said behind her. "We'll call them Friday."

The chocolate had to be told what to do, and it would only listen at certain temperatures. Madison stood at the steel counter with a thermometer in one hand and a bowl of melted couverture in the other, watching the numbers fall. Chef had said it once and walked away: melt it hot, cool it down, warm it just a little, and it will set with a shine and a snap. He hadn't said why. She liked that. It meant she got to find out.

At fifty-two degrees the chocolate was loose and glossy, almost lazy. She stirred in chopped chocolate a handful at a time, and the numbers crept down through the forties, the high thirties. Somewhere in the low thirties, if she moved at the right moment, the cocoa butter would form the crystals she wanted, the ones that behaved. She kept her wrist slow and circular so the surface undulated like something alive, and she wondered whether the chocolate knew the difference between being stirred and being hurried.

Behind her, Dex was arguing with someone on the phone by the walk-in. He'd brought in a stockpot of chili from home, leftovers from a batch-cook Sunday, and it had sat in the prep area since six in the morning. Now it was after two. When he hung up, Madison nodded at the pot.

"Was that out all night too?"

"At my place, yeah. I figured I'd bring it in and reheat it for family meal. It's fine, it's got to be fine. Chili's basically bulletproof."

Madison had believed that herself once. In her junior year she'd left a pot of soup on the stove overnight and eaten it the next day, and nothing had happened, and nothing had happened the time after that either, which was the problem with learning from nothing happening. It taught you the wrong lesson in a very convincing voice. She was still assembling what she actually trusted.

She looked up the range on her phone while the chocolate cooled, scrolling with her knuckle so she wouldn't touch the screen with wet fingers. Four to sixty degrees Celsius, it said, forty to one hundred forty Fahrenheit. The USDA called it the danger zone, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly. She read it twice.

"Dex. Four to sixty Celsius. Forty to one forty Fahrenheit. They call it the danger zone. That's the range where bacteria multiply fast. Your chili did a whole tour of it."

He came over and squinted at her screen. "Overnight, though. My apartment's cold."

"Your apartment's inside the danger zone, is what your apartment is." She turned the phone toward him so he could see the numbers himself. He read them, and she watched his face do the thing hers had done a minute before, the small recalibration of a person whose confidence has just been priced and found cheap. He picked up the stockpot, weighed it once in both hands like something being sentenced, and carried it to the dumpster out back. When he came in he washed his hands for a long time, saying nothing, which she took as the sound of a man changing his mind.

The chocolate had dropped to thirty while she wasn't watching. She panicked a little, then didn't. The margin was thinner than she'd thought but not gone. She warmed a corner of the bowl over the water bath, counterclockwise, ten seconds, checked, five more, and brought it up to thirty-one and held it there. On a scrap of parchment she poured a test strip and watched it set in the cool corner of the kitchen. It dried in a couple of minutes with a surface like a still lake, no streaks, no gray bloom. She broke off a piece and it snapped clean, a sound like a small decision.

Chef passed behind her without stopping. "That's tempered," he said, which from him was practically a speech. Madison noticed that she felt the compliment in her chest before she'd thought about it, some affective response arriving ahead of any reasoning, and she made a note of that too, the way she noted the temperature where the shine appeared. Her whole apprenticeship was turning into a collection of these small registers, what the material does, what the body does, and the strange space between.

Dex came back with the empty pot and leaned on the counter beside her. "So what am I supposed to do, take the temperature of my own kitchen?"

"Basically, yeah. Or just get it in the fridge inside two hours and stop arguing with the thermometer." She scraped the bowl down and began ladling the chocolate into the molds, tapping each one against the counter to chase out the bubbles. It would set shiny in the walk-in, and tomorrow she'd unmold it and the pieces would come out bright as tiles, and somewhere in that brightness was a fact about crystals she still couldn't fully picture, a structure she was taking on faith. The owner's son came through the kitchen then, checking invoices in his tailored apron, the family a small plutocracy in clogs, and Madison kept her eyes on the molds and kept working.

"You going to teach me that snap thing?" Dex asked.

"First lesson," she said, and tapped the last mold twice. "Nothing sits out overnight."

The burner's blue ring made the solution blush from pale pink to deep rose as Violet nudged the temperature up, and she leaned closer as if the flask might whisper its reasoning to her. Across the bench her lab partner, Desiree, was supposed to be recording times but was instead composing a message on her phone, thumb hovering, deleting, hovering again. The assignment was straightforward on paper: predict how heating would shift the equilibrium, then test the prediction. What Violet kept circling back to was the odd dignity of the idea, that a balanced system could be pushed and would answer, would rearrange itself to absorb the push, and she wanted to see it happen before she trusted it.

"Cobalt chloride," Desiree said, reading off the board without looking up from her phone. "Pink when it's hydrated, blue when it's not. Heat drives off water." She said it flatly, the way she recited things she intended to forget by June.

"You could just watch it," Violet said.

"I could also pass chemistry, which requires writing it down."

Last summer, before any of this, Violet had spent an August week making sandwiches in her grandmother's kitchen, and it came back to her now without being invited. Her grandmother had laid out a loaf of bread, a tower of turkey, a bowl of tomatoes sliced thin as coins, and Violet had kept assembling until the bread was gone and the turkey still stood there, absurd and unused, a monument to excess. Her grandmother had laughed at her bafflement. "The bread ran out first," she'd said, wiping her hands. "It's like what your teacher would call a limiting reactant. That's the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product you can make." Violet had thought it was just a kitchen joke until September, when Ms. Okonkwo said the same sentence almost word for word, and something in Violet's chest had tilted, the ordinary and the official folding into each other like two transparencies on a lightbox.

Now, with the flask warming in her hands, she wondered whether equilibrium had its own bread. She measured out two solutions, one rich in the starting material and one nearly spent, and ran them side by side in identical test tubes in the same warm bath. The rich tube bloomed blue from the bottom up, a slow intrusion, color climbing like weather. The spent tube stayed stubbornly pink no matter how long she held it under the heat. Heat was the same push in both, she thought, so why did one answer and the other stay silent? She turned the spent tube in her fingers and understood it the way you understand a locked door: everything she wanted to add was already used up. The starting material had run out first. It set the greatest amount of the blue product this little reaction could ever make, and no amount of heat could argue with that ceiling.

At the end of the period a folded page appeared in Violet's locker, because Desiree still wrote letters the way other people sent texts that vanished. Violet, the message began. You saw me typing in lab and you think it was about Marcus. It wasn't. I've been trying to write to my father in Houston telling him I'm not going to the college he picked, that I want the culinary program instead, and every draft I delete sounds like a betrayal and every one I keep sounds like an apology, and I refuse to apologize for it. You're the only person I know who watches a beaker like it's telling the truth. How do you know when to send a letter you can't take back? Violet read it twice by the water fountain, the paper going soft at the corners where her wet hands held it.

She found Desiree at the bus loop, backpack straps gripped in both fists. Violet started talking before she had fully decided to, the way the color had started climbing before the whole tube agreed. "I ran a reaction today where I added heat and nothing happened, because the thing that needed to be there first was already gone. And I ran another one where everything I added was still in there, waiting, and the heat moved it." She paused, not sure whether the analogy held or whether she was about to ruin it. "You're not out of options. You're out of his options. That's different. You get to decide what the limit is."

"That's the thing," Desiree said. "You sound so sure. Aren't you ever unsure?"

"All the time," Violet said. "I don't know if equilibrium is a balance or just a standoff that hasn't ended yet. I don't know if pushing a system helps it or just tells you where its edges are." She had been raised by a mother who tried to inculcate certainty like a religion, who called anyone who changed course an ideologue of convenience, and Violet had spent seventeen years assembling a quieter position out of parts that didn't fully agree with each other: notice first, decide second, admit what stayed unknown.

Desiree looked at the letter in her own hand, then held it out. The mailbox at the corner had its flag up, an incipient red signal against the gray afternoon, and the wind pulled one corner of the page loose from her fingers. "If I mail it," she said, "I can't take it back." Violet reached for the mailbox door and opened it, and they stood there together, the letter trembling between them.

The library's study room smelled like dry-erase marker and the cafeteria pizza Marcus had smuggled in behind the copy machine. Owen spread his sources across the table: two newspapers, a laptop with a dying battery, and the debate outline he was supposed to finish by Friday. The resolution was "A free press requires independent ownership," and Owen had drawn the negative, which meant he had to argue that rich owners could save newspapers instead of ruining them. His father, over rice and burnt chicken on Tuesday, had pounded the table about it. "Nobody buys a sinking ship out of charity," his father had said, while his mother said the ship was sinking anyway and somebody had to buy it, and his sister asked if she could be excused.

Owen had come to the library to find out which parent was right. He typed the name his father had dropped like a card on the table: Patrick Soon-Shiong, the biotech billionaire. The database loaded slowly, the way everything loaded when you had twenty minutes of Wi-Fi and a charger someone had already borrowed. The first result said Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for $500 million. Owen wrote that down. Then he kept reading and found the rest, the part his father hadn't mentioned: he also took on the pension obligations, the money owed to the paper's retired workers.

"Five hundred million," Marcus said, reading over his shoulder. "Plus pensions. That's like buying a house and also agreeing to pay the previous owner's mom's rent forever."

"That's the point, though," Owen said. "The pensions are the expensive part. Anybody could write a check for the building."

Marcus pulled a chair around and sat backward on it, arms folded across the backrest, which he did whenever he wanted to argue without admitting he wanted to argue. "So he's either a saint or a puppet master. Pick one, you have a debate to win."

The trouble was that Owen could see the shape of both arguments at once, and neither one fit inside the other. He found a story from after the sale, reporters describing the newsroom's fear that a billionaire's businesses, his drugs, his hospitals, his lawsuits, might quietly become untouchable in the paper's own pages. Then he found a story about editors pushing back on the owner over a planned endorsement, and the paper's editorial board overriding it. Both stories were in papers owned by other companies, which meant other owners, which meant the mirror went all the way down. Owen wrote a question mark in his margin and hated how accurate it was.

"You're spiraling," Marcus said. "It's a debate, not a religion. You just have to sound right for eight minutes."

"That's the problem with you," Owen said. "You think arguments are costumes." Marcus looked wounded, then stole a slice of the pizza, which was his way of accepting the insult.

Owen tried a different shelf, the periodicals, and found an old issue of the Los Angeles Times itself, printed months after the sale. He flipped to the business section and there it was, an article about one of Soon-Shiong's companies, written in the flat, unflattered tone of a paper covering somebody it could not afford to flatter. Or was the flatness itself the disguise? He held the page up to the light as though bias might be visible there, a watermark of ownership, and felt stupid doing it, and did it anyway.

His father had said, at dinner, "Money is never neutral." His mother had said, "Nothing is neutral, honey, that's not a standard, that's a mood." Owen had laughed then. Now, in the study room, he underlined his own outline, where he'd written that independence is a practice rather than a bank account, reporters who challenge their owner are independent the way a muscle is strong, by use, not by birth, and he wondered if that was an argument or a wish dressed in an argument's clothes. In English class they'd just finished a unit on existentialism, the idea that you are what you do, moment by moment, with no essence underneath to guarantee you. He'd thought it was depressing. Applied to a newspaper it was almost hopeful: no owner, however rich, could settle the question once, because the question came back with every story, every day, and had to be answered again by people who could choose badly or choose well.

He tried to suture the two halves of his outline together, the praise and the worry, and the line held, mostly. A newspaper saved by a billionaire is still a newspaper whose survival depends on one man's patience. A newspaper closed for lack of one is not independent either, it's gone. Somewhere between those sentences was his actual position, and it refused to sit still long enough for him to write it down cleanly, which he suspected meant it was the honest one.

Marcus leaned over and read the new paragraph. "So which side are you arguing Friday?"

"Mine," Owen said.

"That's not a side."

"Then I'll lose." Owen closed the laptop, slid the old Times into his backpack with the care of someone borrowing something he intended to return, and looked at the clock. His mother would want the whole story at dinner, and his father would push his rice around and say, "Nobody buys a sinking ship out of charity." Owen stood, chair scraping, and Marcus said, "Tell them I said hi," and Owen was already through the doors, out into the alluvial light of late afternoon, the low sun spreading gold across the parking lot like sediment, deciding on the drive home exactly which sentence he would open with.

The studio smelled of lemon polish and cold coffee, and the guitar lying across Sara's knees was not the nylon-string loaner she'd been using all spring. It was her grandfather's, a dreadnought with a sunburst finish gone amber at the edges, and it had spent eleven years in a closet in Paramus before her mother dug it out and said, take it, he'd want it played.

"Standard tuning," Mr. Okonkwo said, tapping the tuning pegs one by one. "From the lowest string to the highest, that's E, A, D, G, B, E." He plucked the fattest string and it wobbled flat, a sour moan, and he raised his eyebrows at her as if to say, your inheritance, your problem.

She had assumed the guitar would come to her ready. That was the first small insult of the afternoon: nothing arrives tuned. Her grandfather, she remembered suddenly, had sat on his porch in August with this same instrument across his belly, sweating through his shirt, turning a peg in tiny patient increments while the cicadas screamed. She had been nine and had asked why he kept doing the same thing over and over. "Because it drifts," he'd said. "Everything drifts, Saraleh." Then he'd played something Balkan-sounding and crooked, nothing like the chords she would later learn, and she had gone inside for ice, unimpressed.

Now she turned the lowest peg herself and watched Mr. Okonkwo's clip-on tuner, a little green-eyed parasite on the headstock. The needle swam left. Too low. She tightened, overshot, backed off. E. Then A, then D, each string a negotiation between her ear, which was mostly guesswork, and the needle, which was merciless. When she reached the fourth string and plucked, the tuner read F. She stared at it, plucked again, and Mr. Okonkwo laughed, actually laughed, the sound bouncing off the acoustic foam panels.

"Whoever restrung this put the G where a B ought to live," he said. "Or you've invented a new tuning. Groucho Marx had one, you know. Ask your grandfather."

"He's dead," Sara said, and then, because his face did the thing faces do, "eleven years. It's fine. Tell me about Groucho."

So she had to restring it, or at least detune and retune across the confusion, working out which string was which by listening down from the low E she'd already set: E, A, D, then G, then B, then the thin high E, and she said the sequence aloud like a spell, and Mr. Okonkwo made her say it again without looking at the tuner. Her fingertips hurt within twenty minutes, the old calluses from the loaner being the wrong kind, too soft in the wrong places. That was the arrangement with the guitar, apparently. It would let her learn it, but it charged interest.

Here was the thing she couldn't decide, and she told him so while she worked the B string up to pitch: part of her wanted the guitar tuned exactly, note-perfect, the way the tuner demanded, because that was the contract of music and because her grandfather had clearly believed in it, all that porch-side drifting-and-correcting. But another part of her kept thinking about his crooked Balkan tune, which had probably been out of tune by every objective measure and had still, in her memory, transfigured a hot boring afternoon into something she could still hear fourteen years later. Perfection versus that. She couldn't get them into the same sentence without cheating.

"It's not a plebiscite," Mr. Okonkwo said when she tried to frame it as two camps, the tuners and the drifters, and asked which side won. "You don't get to vote once and be done. You tune it every single time you pick it up. Every time. That's the whole job." He said it lightly, but she felt the weight land anyway, some of it unfair, some of it hers to carry.

By the end of the hour she had all six strings right, E to E, the way he'd said at the start, and she played an open chord, a clumsy C, and the sound was enormous in the little room, pelagic, like something deep surfacing. Mr. Okonkwo nodded once and started stacking his sheet music, which was how she knew the lesson was over and that it had gone well. She loosened the strings a quarter turn each, the way you're supposed to when you're done, and felt stupid about it, undoing the hour on purpose. At the door she stopped. "Is it cheating if I record myself saying it and listen on the bus? E, A, D, G, B, E." He looked up, considering. "It's cheating," he said, "if you never stop needing the recording."

Arianna had the thermometer in one hand and the marble slab wiped clean in front of her, and the chocolate, chopped into even pieces, sat in a steel bowl like something that distrusted her. She was leaving for college in nine days. The plan had seemed reasonable in June: learn to temper chocolate before she went, so that the last box she mailed to her grandmother would look like it came from a professional, shiny and snapping when you broke it, not the dull, streaked plaques her earlier attempts had produced. Her grandmother had stopped eating solid food in March, but she still held things, turned them over, judged their surfaces with her thumbs. Arianna wanted to give her something worth judging.

The method required precision and patience, two qualities she had in limited supply at eight in the morning. She melted the chocolate to forty-five degrees, then poured two-thirds of it onto the cold marble and worked it with a spatula, spreading and scraping, spreading and scraping, until it thickened and lost its gloss. That was the part that felt like failure even when it was the whole point. You cooled it down to twenty-seven, then rewarmed it gently to thirty-one, and if you had done it right, the cocoa butter formed the one stable crystal out of the six it could form, and the chocolate set with a shine and a clean break. She had read the temperatures so many times they had a liturgical rhythm. What she had not read carefully was anything about the second package in the freezer.

Her younger brother Theo came in barefoot, opened the freezer, and made a sound of accusation. He held up a container of their mother's beef stew, and across its surface were dry white patches, like frost that had decided to stay. "This is ruined," he said. "It looks malevolent. I'm not eating anything that looks like it's growing a skin on purpose." He set it on the counter next to her marble slab as if presenting evidence.

Arianna took it from him, mostly to get it away from her chocolate, and turned it over. She had read something about this, months ago, in one of her late-night spirals through food safety pages while her chemistry grade was dying. She cogitated on it, chewing the inside of her cheek, and then she had it. "It's freezer burn," she said. "Air dried out the surface. It happens to frozen food. It'll be tough and tasteless where those patches are, but it won't hurt you. It's not unsafe. It's just bad." Theo looked at her with the narrow eyes of someone whose sister had recently begun announcing facts. "You're sure," he said, and it was not a question so much as a dare, so she said, "Scrape the patches off and it'll still be stew," and put the container in the refrigerator to thaw, and turned back to her thermometer, which read twenty-nine and climbing.

She had overshot. The chocolate would have to go back to thirty-one, not a degree past it or the crystals she had coaxed into being would melt out and she would be back at the beginning, and her mother would be home in an hour, and the kitchen already smelled like a confectionery that had suffered a defeat. Theo watched her stir in tiny circles. "Why do you care this much," he said. "She can't even eat it." It was a fair question, and she resented how fair it was, and she answered it the way she answered most of his questions lately, with the truth split in half. "Because she can hold it," she said. "Because when I was nine she made me temper an egg custard and I curdled it and she ate it anyway."

What she did not say was that she had been doing a kind of revisionist accounting all summer, rereading their history together and finding that the version she had told her friends, the tyrant grandmother with the wooden spoon, left out almost everything worth keeping. The woman had taught her to salt water for vegetables, to listen for the change in the sound of simmering, to treat recipes as hypotheses. Somewhere in the last four years Arianna had stopped being a student in that kitchen and started being a defendant in it, and only the prospect of losing the kitchen entirely had shown her which role was the lie. But that was the half of the truth she kept, and she kept it while stirring.

She brought the chocolate to thirty-one, dipped the tip of a knife, and waited. Ninety seconds. The smear set dull and slightly tacky. Too warm still, or she had let moisture in, or the marble had been warmer than it felt. She stood there with the failed knife in her hand and thought about the stew, about how the air had gotten to it through some imperfect seal and dried out only the surface, ruined the texture and the taste, and left the thing underneath essentially itself. That was what the whole summer had felt like. That was what she was afraid college would do to her, if she let it, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she did not yet know whether she would let it.

She retempered from scratch. Melt, pour, spread, scrape, watch the gloss die, bring it back. The second knife smear set in under a minute with a dry, hard shine, and when she flexed the blade it snapped, cleanly, with a sound like a small door closing. She poured the remainder into the molds she had bought with her last paycheck, tapped out the bubbles, and slid them into the cool pantry rather than the refrigerator, because condensation was the enemy of the surface she had just won.

While the molds set, she scraped the white patches off the thawed stew and put the pot on to reheat, and Theo ate two bowls of it and admitted, grudgingly, that it tasted fine underneath. When the chocolate came out of the molds it caught the overhead light like something lacquered, and she wrapped four bars in the paper she had saved from a shop downtown, and Theo wrote the address on the box because her hands were shaking a little, and she did not tell him why. At the post office the clerk asked if there was anything perishable inside. "Chocolate," Arianna said. "Tempered. It'll hold."

The parking lot had been striped for graduation since Monday, and by Saturday afternoon the white lines were already flaking under two hundred folding chairs. Sofia stood beside her mother's Corolla in her gown, which was, according to the tag, "one size fits most," a maxim she intended to test by sitting down without splitting anything. She had the cap in one hand and her phone in the other, checking the time not because it mattered but because checking the time was something to do with her hands.

Marcus was leaning against the chain-link at the far edge of the lot, still in his work shirt from the warehouse, still holding the energy drink he'd been holding since junior year, it seemed. He had dropped out eighteen months ago, and they had not exactly stopped being friends so much as stopped being in the same building. She crossed the lot before she could decide whether to.

"So you did it," he said. "They let you walk."

"They let everyone walk. That's the whole point of the ceremony."

"Congratulations, I guess." He gesticulated with the can, a small ironic wave, and she noticed the ink on his forearm, a date she didn't recognize. "I've been putting in applications. Fourteen since March. I got one interview, at the tire place, and the guy asked if I had my diploma and I said I was working on the GED and he sort of nodded like that was a nice thing I'd said about the weather."

She wanted to say something useful. She was, in general, the person who said useful things; her friends had pointed this out often enough that it had stopped being a compliment. "I looked some of this up," she said, "for my econ paper. Last year, unemployment for people twenty-five and older with a high school diploma was 3.9 percent. Without one, 5.6."

"Where'd you find that?"

"Bureau of Labor Statistics. I had to cite everything, Mrs. Ahn was ruthless."

"So it's not that bad either way," Marcus said. "Sixteen people out of a hundred without a diploma, that's still a lot of jobs."

"Four point a half," she said. "Out of a hundred. Five point six." She heard herself doing the arithmetic out loud and stopped, but he had already shrugged, which was his way of filing things.

Her mother had a position on all this, delivered over the years with the confidence of someone who had once read half an article: school was the door, and without it you were outside knocking. Sofia had absorbed the position the way she'd absorbed the family recipes, without examination, and had repeated it in her college essay, "education as threshold," a phrase she now found slightly embarrassing. But the numbers she'd found herself were quieter than her mother's version. They said something smaller and harder to argue with, something about margins and odds rather than doors, and she hadn't fully worked out what she thought a margin obligated a person to do, or whether odds were the same thing as fairness.

There was a flashback she kept returning to, unbidden, at moments like this one. Sophomore year, before he'd stopped coming, Marcus had stayed after fifth period to help her jump the Corolla, because she'd left the lights on again, and he'd known exactly which terminal to clamp and in what order, and he'd explained it without making her feel stupid, which almost no one managed. "Red is positive," he'd said. "Dead battery first. It's not hard, people just like pretending it is." She had felt, that afternoon in the student lot with the hood propped and the November light going gray, that there were kinds of knowing she would never have, and that this was not a tragedy, just a fact with a shape.

"Hey," she said now. "The GED. Are you actually doing it?"

"Doing the practice tests. Math's fine. The essay part wants me to argue one side of something, which, you know me."

"I do know you." She laughed. "You'd argue both sides and fail for hedging."

"They should give extra credit for that," Marcus said. "Some of us can see the whole parking lot."

The PA crackled somewhere near the gym, the muffled voice telling seniors to line up. Sofia pulled at her gown, and a seam held, and she filed this under victories. She did not say the thing she had drafted, which was that the numbers meant he should finish, because the numbers did not exactly mean that; they meant his life would be one and a half someones harder in a way no one could point to on a calendar, and she could not honestly promise that a certificate would fix the tire place, or anything else. What she had instead was the memory of him explaining the jumper cables, patient, competent, undeservedly confident in her ability to turn a key.

"I'll sit with my phone on," she said, pulling on the cap. "Text me if the essay thing defeats you. I've written enough dishonest one-sided arguments for both of us."

"The ceremony's an hour," Marcus said. "That's a long time to keep a phone on."

"I'm graduating, not dying." She started toward the gym doors, gown flapping, one hand holding the cap down against a gust that came from nowhere, the way gusts in that lot always did.

The mock court had been assigned the city hall basement, in a room with fluorescent lights and a mural of the founding fathers that looked, in that light, slightly seasick. Clara arrived early to claim the long table nearest the outlet, because her laptop battery had been dying since Tuesday and she refused to buy a new one on principle, a principle she could not have explained to anyone, including herself.

The case was hypothetical but drawn from real life, which was the part her teacher had emphasized with grim cheerfulness. A speaker at a rally had told an angry crowd that certain people deserved what was coming to them, that the city would burn if justice failed, and then, quieter, that everyone knew what needed doing and it needed doing soon. Two hours later a warehouse had burned. The mock court had to decide whether the speech could constitutionally be punished, and Clara, who had drawn the swing vote, had spent the weekend avoiding the reading.

"Brandenburg versus Ohio," said Priya, sliding the handout across the table. "Nineteen sixty-nine. It's all there."

Clara read it twice. Advocating force could be punished, the handout said, only if it was directed to inciting imminent lawless action and was likely to produce such action. She read it a third time because the second reading had rearranged nothing in her head. It was the word imminent that snagged. Not soon. Not eventually. Imminent.

Her actual assignment, the one she'd been dreading for a month, was the closing argument of the comparative politics unit, staged that same afternoon in the council chamber upstairs. The prompt: which system better removes a dangerous head of government, the parliamentary way, where a vote of no confidence can bring a prime minister down in an afternoon, or the presidential way, where removal means impeachment, a long and public and usually failing surgery. She was meant to argue for one. Everyone was meant to argue for one. The whole unit valorized taking a side, and Clara had spent weeks suspecting that her real problem was that both sides were partly right.

In the basement, the petitioner's counsel argued first. He was a senior named Dominic who wore a blazer to school and pronounced "whereas" as though it were load-bearing. The speech, he said, was a fuse. The crowd was a bomb. She had to see it whole.

"It wasn't imminent," Clara said, before she had decided to say anything. "Two hours. He didn't name the warehouse. He didn't name a time at all."

"He told them what needed doing."

"He told them everyone knew what needed doing. That's different. That's the political speech we don't like, not the incitement we can punish." She pointed at the handout. "Both halves. Directed to inciting, and likely to produce it. That speech was directed to a mood."

Dominic said that was chicanery, dressing up a threat in vagueness so it could walk past the rule, and Clara said probably, yes, that was exactly what it was, and that the rule still stopped them at the door. She was aware that she had just argued for the protection of a speech she found noxious, and that she had done it without much internal struggle, and that this troubled her more than the ruling did. The other justices voted as she expected. When her turn came she said "no, not punishable under Brandenburg," and the vote was five to four, and the room exhaled the way rooms do when something has actually been at stake.

Upstairs, in the council chamber, the folding chairs were already full. Priya had taken the parliamentary side and Dominic the presidential, and Clara stood at the podium with two index cards she had rewritten during lunch. The no-confidence route, she said, was fast, but it made a leader's survival a matter of arithmetic, one bad week, one fractured coalition, and a country could lurch between prime ministers the way her laptop battery flickered between full and dead. Impeachment was slower, clogged with procedure, nearly impossible, and yet the difficulty was the point, or could be: removal was rare enough that everyone involved had to explain themselves for a very long time.

"But," she said, and here she left her cards, "I don't think speed and difficulty are really the values we're choosing between. This morning I had to decide whether a man's speech met the Brandenburg standard, and the whole time I kept thinking that the system was asking me to be certain about a crowd's future, and no system can ask that of anyone honestly." She looked at Priya, then at Dominic. "Parliamentary systems assume you can fix a mistake quickly. Presidential systems assume you should make mistakes rarely. Neither one assumes you might not know which is which until later, and that's the part I keep getting stuck on."

She folded her index cards in half and put them in her blazer pocket, where they would stay for three days, until her mother found them in the laundry and asked what "imminent lawless action" meant. Clara, from the kitchen, said, "I'll explain when the wash is done."

Anais had promised herself she would finish the portrait before Sunday, and now it was Friday afternoon and her grandmother's kitchen smelled of turpentine and toast. The portrait was of her grandmother at sixty, copied from a photograph she had found in the hallway drawer: her grandmother leaning on a gate in a yellow dress, squinting into some summer that had happened before Anais was born. She had it half done on the canvas propped against the salt jar, the left side tender and finished, the right side still raw pencil lines.

"I don't squint like that," her grandmother said, coming in with the shopping.

"You do. You do it at crossword clues."

"Nonsense. I look at things squarely. I'm a pragmatist." She set down the bags and studied the canvas for a long moment, and Anais could not tell whether the look was criticism or being moved, or both, which with her grandmother was often the case.

Anais was painting with the acrylics her uncle had left in the spare room years ago, tubes with names like Hooker's Green and Yellow Ochre, half of them crusted at the mouth. She had discovered on Wednesday that the paint thinned beautifully under the tap, that it moved like watercolor when she wanted it to, spreading in soft river deltas down the paper. That was how she had done the left side, all pale washes, and it looked like memory itself. She was proud of it in a way she did not say out loud.

But the right side wanted something else. In the photograph her grandmother's hands were gripping the gate, knuckles sharp, and every time Anais tried to wash them in like the rest, they dissolved into vagueness, into a grandmother-shaped blur. The hands needed to be solid. She wanted them opaque and stubborn, paint laid on thick, so that anyone looking would know those hands had held onto things.

She mixed a flesh tone in the jar lid and worked for an hour, then went out to the garden because Tom next door was calling something through the hedge about the wasps. She stayed longer than she meant to, arguing about whether the nest was theirs to remove or the council's, and when she came back the light had gone slanted and her brushes stood in the jar like little burnt trees. The bristles were stiff as matchsticks. She took one to the tap and ran hot water over it and bent it and the hairs snapped rather than softened, and when she tried to scrub the dried paint from the palette it sat there, glazed and insolent, refusing the water entirely.

She sat down on the kitchen floor, peevish, holding the ruined brush. So that was the arrangement: the paint was water-based while wet, it answered her completely, and then it dried, quickly, without ceremony, and after that it was water-resistant, past persuasion. She thought about her father, who had said at Christmas that painting was a lovely hobby but that she should think about something that would emancipate her, by which he seemed to mean a career that would let her leave. He had a washable kind of hope for her, one that rinsed out when it dried. She turned the brush over in her fingers. There was another jar in the spare room, and a bundle of new brushes still in their packet, and she thought she understood something, though she could not have said it in a sentence: that a thing could start soft and end permanent, and that this was not a betrayal of the softness but the whole point of it. Or possibly not. Possibly she was only justifying a mess.

She brought the fresh brushes down and unscrewed a new tube. The right side she would paint fast and thick, deciding each stroke before it left the bristle, because she would not get to reconsider it once it dried.
