The left side would stay as it was, pale and unfinished, water still implied in it. Her grandmother came in and stood at her shoulder.

"One half fog and one half fence post," her grandmother said. "Is that deliberate?"

"I don't know yet," said Anais, dipping the brush. "Ask me when it's dry."

Maelie laid the poster board flat on the picnic table, weighted its curling corners with her cleats, and wrote SEASON PLAN across the top in block letters she hoped would look like it belonged to someone with authority. She had volunteered for this at the last practice, mostly because nobody else would, and now she owned it: eight weeks of sessions for her little brother's team, the Bumblebees, a dozen nine-year-olds who had lost every game so far. Her father had signed the club's form that morning, the one that promised to indemnify the league against any claim arising from injury, and had handed it to her with a gravity he usually saved for tax documents. "You're the coach now," he said. "Try not to get sued."

The first week went badly in a way she hadn't predicted. She had done her research, sort of, scrolling forums at midnight and copying drills into a notebook, and she ran the Tuesday session with a whistle she'd found in the garage. Every time Teo took a shot, she corrected it. Chin up. Plant foot beside the ball. Follow through. Every pass, every trap, every turn, she called out the fix within two seconds, because that was what coaches did, she thought, and because silence felt like neglect. By Thursday the drills looked beautiful. The kids were crisp, obedient, precise, and she felt a flicker of pride she mentioned to her friend Dee over the fence while they watched Teo and the neighbor's boy, Ravi, kick a ball against the shed.

Saturday was the game. Within ten minutes, the Bumblebees fell apart. Teo froze on the ball, looked to the sideline before every touch, and passed straight to an opponent twice. Ravi, who had struck every corner of the shed two days earlier, sliced a simple shot into the parking lot. Maelie stood at the touchline saying nothing, because there was nothing to say fast enough, and she watched her brother's eyes keep flicking toward her, searching for a correction that wasn't coming, as though the words had been holding him up and someone had pulled them away.

She sat on the porch steps afterward with her notebook open to the blank page marked WEEK TWO. Teo came and dropped beside her, obstreperous for once in his silence, kicking at a pebble until it skittered off the step. "I don't know what I do wrong when you don't tell me," he said finally, and it came out like a confession, which was the part that unsettled her most. She had made him dependent on something that wouldn't exist during a game.

That night she went looking, not on the forums this time but through the sports science articles her school database could pull up, and she found a line about feedback given after every single attempt. It said such constant correction could make learners dependent on it, and that less frequent feedback often helped retention, meaning how well a skill stuck when nobody was talking. She read it three times, then texted Dee a photo of the paragraph. Dee called her within a minute. "We did this in psych," Dee said. "It's called the guidance hypothesis." Maelie wrote the words in the margin of her notebook and underlined them, once, and then sat looking at the fence until the porch light came on.

The hard part wasn't understanding it; the hard part was holding two true things at once. She still believed in correcting technique, because Teo's plant foot really was wrong, and she also believed, now, that her voice had been doing the work his own head should be doing, and she could not fully see how to give one without stealing the other. She was honest with herself about that gap. She did not fully know where correction ended and dependence began, and no article she found drew the line for her.

So she rebuilt the plan in the backyard on Sunday, crossing out half her notes and rewriting the rest. Warm-up first, every session, ten minutes of dynamic stretches because a pulled hamstring would end somebody's season and she had signed no form to indemnify herself against guilt. Then drills with feedback after only some attempts, not every one, so the kids had to feel their own errors and keep them. Then small games where she was allowed, by her own rule, to say almost nothing. And rest days, actual blank squares on the poster, because she'd read that recovery was where the body kept what the day had taught it. She gave the poster a border and a schedule and, at the bottom, the kind of lettering that suggested gravitas, and she believed maybe half of it would work.

Tuesday she ran it. During the shooting drill she bit her tongue after Teo's first attempt, counted three shots in silence, and spoke only on the fourth. "Plant foot," she said, and nothing else. He missed the next one badly, and she let the miss sit there in the grass between them, unexplained, and watched him set the ball down again on his own, moving his standing foot an inch to the side before she said a word.

The video arrived in the group chat at 9:47, and by 9:52 half of Alice's graduating class had shared it. It showed a warehouse full of spoiled food, a man's voice claiming the boxes were meant for flood victims in their own county, that officials had let it rot on purpose. By 9:55 the class president was calling for everyone to show up at the depot at ten tomorrow morning. Priya shoved her phone across the kitchen island toward Alice, who was sitting there with a mug going cold. "You're not even going to watch it?"

"Of course I'm going to watch it," Alice said. "That's the problem. It's so easy to watch it." She watched it twice. The warehouse looked familiar in the way all warehouses look familiar, and the voice had that urgent, wounded tone that made her thumb hover over the share arrow. Tomorrow at ten. Somebody from her mother's church group was already asking for a ride.

"My brother got lambasted last spring for reposting something fake," Priya said, pulling nachos out of the microwave. "Like, teachers went after him in the comments, and he still brings it up. I'm not sharing anything until someone checks it." She looked at Alice in a way that suggested Alice was now someone.

Alice set her phone face up on the counter. She had read something, months ago, in the moribund study guide folder she'd never deleted after AP Research ended. A method, four steps, named by some educator. She could remember the shape of it but not the words, which annoyed her, so she typed "SIFT method Mike Caulfield" into the search bar and waited while Priya's router groaned. The page loaded. She read it, then read it again.

"It's SIFT," she said, mostly to herself. "Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context."

"Is that a spell," Priya said, but she came around the island and leaned over Alice's shoulder.

Stop came first, which felt almost embarrassing, like being told to breathe. Alice put the phone down, took a sip of the cold tea, and asked herself whether she even knew where the clip had come from. A classmate had shared it from a classmate, and before that, an account with a fish emoji and a bio about "speaking truth." That was the whole provenance: a fish and a slogan. Investigating the source, as far as she could tell, meant admitting there wasn't one.

Find better coverage. She opened a second tab and searched for news about spoiled flood relief in their county. Nothing, from any outlet, including the scrappy local paper that had once run three paragraphs about her debate team. Then she widened the search, dropped the county name, kept the image. Trace claims to their original context. On a site she'd never heard of, a fact-check from three years ago showed the exact same footage, filmed in a different state, about a different storm, in a warehouse where the food had been quarantined for a recall, not withheld from anyone. The recall had made one small article and then vanished.

"So it's real footage doing a fake job," Priya said slowly. She had stopped eating. "That's worse than fake, somehow. Everyone will believe it because it looks true."

Alice sat with the two tabs open side by side, the old article and the new panic, the same boxes of rotting food serving two different stories. Some part of her understood why people would rather share it than check it; the checking had taken eleven minutes, and the outrage felt useful, felt like doing something. But the vigil at ten would be built on nothing, and her mother's church friends would stand in a parking lot holding signs about a warehouse that had never wronged them.

She typed a message to the group chat, deleted it, typed it again. What she settled on was the link to the fact-check and one line: "Please look at this before tomorrow." Then she put the phone in her pocket before she could see who was typing back, because she already knew. Someone would say the fact-checkers were in on it. Someone would say it didn't matter, the system still failed people somewhere. And underneath all of it, one question she couldn't answer even for herself: whether she had been searching for the truth or searching for permission to look away from a problem that probably existed somewhere, just not in that warehouse, not tomorrow, not like that.

Priya turned the video back on, watching the man's face with new attention. "He's so convincing," she said. "I would have shared it."

The staff lounge smelled like sunscreen and burnt popcorn, and Hailey had been rehearsing the same sentence for what felt like an interminable half hour. Her interview for junior waterfront director was in nine minutes, and the director, Marisol, was famous for questions that started with "Tell me about a time when." Hailey had never had a real job before. Camp was the closest thing, and camp was just lake water andcapture the flag.

"You look like you're defusing something," said Priya, dropping onto the couch beside her with a granola bar. Priya was seventeen and had already interviewed that morning, which made her, in Hailey's estimation, insufferably serene.

"Tell me about a time when you handled conflict," Hailey said. "Go on. Tell me."

Priya licked a crumb off her thumb. "I used the group project from last spring. Marisol ate it up. She said she doesn't care about job history, she cares about what you already did, because how you acted before is how you'll act again. Apparently there's a whole name for those questions. Behavioral interview questions. 'Tell me about a time when.' They're built on the idea that past behavior predicts future behavior." She shrugged. "So I told her about Dev having a meltdown about the slides and me not handling it well, actually, and she wrote something down and looked pleased. Camp people are weird."

Hailey stared at her. The problem she'd been chewing on all week suddenly rearranged itself. She'd been trying to sound like someone with experience instead of admitting she had exactly one experience that mattered, and it was sitting right there, waiting to be told.

The one experience was this: she and Marcus co-led the kayaking group, and Marcus explained everything wrong. Not dangerously wrong, just vague, which on the water amounted to the same thing. Kids dragged their paddles, tipped, cried. For two weeks Hailey had said "good job" and then quietly re-taught strokes behind his back, and the kids noticed, and Marcus noticed them noticing. She'd been, she could admit now, a coward with a smile on.

Marisol called her in. The office had a fan that ticked and a wall of confiscated slingshots. "Tell me about a time when you gave someone hard feedback," Marisol said, clicking her pen.

Hailey opened her mouth, and the sentence she'd rehearsed, the smooth one, evaporated. "Monday," she said instead. "This past Monday. My co-leader Marcus was explaining the sweep stroke, and it wasn't landing, and I'd been fixing it behind his back for two weeks, which was worse than saying nothing." She heard herself and kept going. "So Monday I took him aside before the session and told him two specific things. One, that our words were the same but our demos weren't, so the kids were copying me and ignoring him. Two, that I should have told him in week one instead of letting him look bad in front of eleven-year-olds."

Marisol's pen stopped clicking. "And?"

"And he was quiet for a second, then he said the eleven-year-olds had already told him, in kid words, that I was 'the real teacher.' We split the demos after that, he takes sweep, I take draw. Wednesday nobody tipped." Hailey exhaled. "That's it. That's the whole story. It's not a job, it's just camp."

"It's just camp," Marisol repeated, writing something, and Hailey couldn't tell if it was admiration or a note about kayaks.

From the dock that evening, Marcus watched Hailey march toward him with two paddles and the particular set of her jaw he'd learned to read over four summers. "Oh no," he said. "The feedback face."

"Shut up. I have notes." She handed him a paddle. "Your draw stroke demo on Wednesday, the one where you narrate while you do it, I timed it, you talk for like a full minute before your paddle touches water. Kids check out at about ten seconds. So: demo first, talk second. That's it. That's the whole note."

"Brutal," Marcus said, but he was grinning, and he took the paddle. "You know Marisol asked me the same question in my interview? About a time someone gave me hard feedback."

"She did not."

"She did. I used you. Monday, the lake, the whole thing." He stepped into the shallows. "Past behavior predicts future behavior, apparently, so I figured telling on you counted in my favor."

Hailey waded in after him, deciding she'd adjudicate whether that counted as a betrayal later, or possibly never. "If you tip tonight, I'm adding it to the notes."

"Demo first," Marcus called back, already talking, and his paddle, for once, hit the water before his voice did.

The line at First Meridian had six people in it and Lily counted them twice, because counting was easier than deciding. Her grandmother had claimed two chairs by the desk with the rope barrier, saving spots the way she saved spots at church, with her purse on one seat and her cane across the other. Lily sat down with the canvas bag in her lap and did not open it.

Marco was already at the desk, turning a statement sideways as though the numbers would rearrange themselves into something kinder. He was twenty-four, he had a wife and a baby on the way, and in three weeks he was supposed to close on a small house on Delancey Street. Lily had heard her grandmother on the phone all week, historicizing the whole affair, placing it in a long line of family milestones: Uncle Sal's storefront in 1974, her own first flat after the war, every relative who had ever signed anything at a bank with the whole family watching. "We are a polity of homeowners," she liked to say, though Lily suspected most polities did not hold meetings over cannoli.

"There's a charge here I don't understand," Marco said to the loan officer, a woman named Priya whose badge was pinned slightly crooked. He slid the paper across. "Every month, on top of the payment. Almost two hundred dollars."

Priya tapped the line. "You put five percent down," she said. "Below twenty, on a conventional mortgage, that carries private mortgage insurance."

"It protects the lender, not the buyer," Lily's grandmother said from the chairs, not unkindly, the way she might identify a bird. Marco looked at her, then back at Priya, who nodded once and reached for another form.

Lily sat very still. She was thinking about the apartment on Rankin Street, the one she and Dana had toured in April, third floor, a radiator that clanked like applause. The landlord wanted first month, last month, and a security deposit, which Dana had explained meant three rents upfront and none of it coming back if you broke anything. Eleven hundred a month, times three. Lily had done that math on the bus so many times the figures wore grooves. Rent, Dana said, was money you burned to keep warm; a mortgage was money you kept. Lily had found that neat and suspicious, the way slogans usually were.

The summer before, she had worked the counter at Corso's Deli, forty hours a week, and her grandmother had paid her under the table for painting the porch, and there had been the graduation cards, ten and twenty dollars folded into their little envelopes. She had kept it in a shoebox and then, when the shoebox felt childish, in a savings account with a passbook so thin it embarrassed her. This morning she had withdrawn all of it and put the envelope in the canvas bag, and she had told no one, not even Dana, what it was for. That was the thing she could not decide, and the teller line moved forward one person, and it did not help at all.

Priya was laying it out for Marco with a yellow highlighter. His closing costs had come in higher than the estimate, the seller had refused to cover the inspection repairs, and the five percent he had scraped together was suddenly, equivocally, not quite enough. Not a refusal. Not an approval. A number on a page that had moved. "If the down payment shrinks any further," Priya said, "the monthly insurance goes up. If it grows, the picture changes."

Lily stood up. She crossed the carpet that everyone in her family had crossed at one time or another, and she set the canvas bag on the edge of Marco's desk, and she took out the envelope. Thirty-one hundred dollars, mostly in twenties, the deli's smell still in the bills. "For the down payment," she said. Her voice came out steadier than she expected. "It's a gift. I signed something about that once, at the deli, when Mr. Corso's daughter bought the truck."

Marco stared at the envelope. Priya looked at Lily over her glasses and asked how old she was, and Lily said eighteen, and Priya said that was fine as long as there was a gift letter, and pulled a blank sheet toward her. "This gets you to about nine percent," she told Marco. "The insurance stays on, but it drops."

"Rent money," Lily said, mostly to herself. "I was going to use it for rent."

Her grandmother had come to stand behind them both, purse first. She looked at the envelope, then at Lily, for a long moment, and whatever she was calculating she kept to herself. Marco reached across and put his hand flat on the envelope, the way you steady something that might blow away.

"You sure?" he said.

Lily looked at the yellow lines on the page, at the house on Delancey Street that she had never seen, at the little crooked badge on Priya's blouse.

"Count it," she said.

Antoine found the book on the third shelf of his grandfather's study, wedged between a water-damaged atlas and a box of pipe cleaners no one had touched in decades. The French Revolution: A History, by Thomas Carlyle, published in 1837, if the title page could be believed. He had come to the house for a quiet weekend to draft his essay on how views of the Revolution had changed since 1800, and his laptop bag held six PDFs, two library books, and a stack of notes that read, dispiritingly, like the outlines of other people's arguments.

He should have left the volume alone. Instead he carried it to the kitchen table, where his grandfather was sorting mail with the concentration of a man defusing something.

"Is this yours?" Antoine asked.

"It was my father's." His grandfather squinted at the spine. "He was a connoisseur of gloom, Carlyle especially. Read passages aloud at dinner until my mother left the room." He went back to the mail, but Antoine noticed he kept glancing over, wanting, Antoine suspected, to be asked more than he was being asked.

The problem emerged within three pages. Carlyle did not write like the historians in Antoine's PDFs. He wrote like a man narrating a storm from inside it, giving whole chapters to single figures, to Mirabeau's face, to a coach arriving at Versailles. Where Antoine's modern sources discussed fiscal crises, class structures, and long-term forces, Carlyle seemed to care about whether particular people had chosen well or badly, as though the Revolution had turned on conscience. Antoine underlined a sentence, then another, then stopped underlining because he was underlining everything.

"You look querulous," his grandfather said at lunch. "That's the face your grandmother used to make at my father."

"I can't tell if this book is good history or just good writing."

"Read me some."

Antoine read a passage about the King's flight to Varennes, all thunder and moral weight. His grandfather listened with his fork down, which he never did, and when it ended he said, "He thinks people matter more than forces. That was his whole quarrel, I think. Individuals and their choices." He said it lightly, as if recalling a rival's position rather than reciting a fact, and then he ruined the moment by asking whether Antoine wanted the pipe cleaners.

That night Antoine sat with the essay outline on one side of the laptop and Carlyle on the other, and the two sides refused to ferment into anything. He tried drafting a paragraph claiming Carlyle was simply outdated, a pre-scientific dramatist superseded by structural analysis, and it came out smug. He tried the reverse, that Carlyle had grasped something the forces-people had lost, and that came out sentimental. Around midnight he deleted both and typed a single sentence at the top of a blank page: the question is not whether individuals or forces explain the Revolution, but what each way of explaining is for. He looked at it for a long time. It was not an answer. It might have been a hinge.

In the morning he found his grandfather in the study with a dust cloth, rearranging the shelf where the Carlyle had been, an activity that clearly required an audience. Antoine said he wanted to keep the book for the essay, and also, possibly, after.

"After the essay."

"After the essay. It's the first source I've actually wanted to read twice."

His grandfather straightened a row of atlases that did not need straightening. "You could quote him where he's wrong," he said. "My father hated that. Do that." He pulled a second book from the shelf, one Antoine hadn't noticed, a thin English edition of Tocqueville, and set it on the desk without comment, then stood there a moment as if deciding whether to say something further about his father, the dinners, the room his grandmother used to leave.

Antoine took the Tocqueville, sat down, and opened the Carlyle to the first page again.

Jeremy had the kitchen table to himself until five, which was the deal. His laptop sat open beside a plate of toast crumbs, and on the screen was his history teacher's assignment sheet: a research paper, eight pages, an argument, footnotes, a bibliography in Chicago style. He had written reports before, the kind where you gathered facts about the Panama Canal and stapled them together, but this was different. This wanted him to take a side and defend it.

His topic was whether mindfulness programs actually improved students' test scores. He had found a study, a good one, with two hundred students and a control group, and the results were statistically significant, p less than 0.05. His working thesis, typed at the top of the document in a font he already distrusted, read: "A 2019 study found mindfulness works, so schools should fund it." He stared at that sentence for a while, chewing the cap of a pen he wasn't using.

Denny came through the back door without knocking, holding a grocery bag his mother had sent over. "Your mom said you'd be doing homework. She also said you'd forget to eat." He set a container of soup on the counter and drifted toward the table, reading over Jeremy's shoulder the way only a friend since second grade could.

"Read this," Jeremy said. "The part in bold." He had bolded a line in his notes: Study is 95 percent likely to be right.

Denny squinted. "What's that mean? Like it's 95 percent true?"

"That's what I wrote, so, yeah."

"Then why'd you write it in bold like it's a problem?"

Jeremy scrolled to the study's results section and put his finger on a phrase. "It says significant, p less than 0.05. I thought that meant, like, 95 percent sure." He read further, lips moving slightly, and then sat back. "Hang on. It says the p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as these if there were truly no effect." He read it aloud again, slower. "It's not the probability that the hypothesis is true."

Denny pulled out the chair across from him. "So it's the chance of the numbers looking like that if the thing doesn't work."

"Right. If mindfulness did nothing, how likely is it you'd still see a difference this big." Jeremy opened a new document and started typing. "So it's not 95 percent likely to be right. It's five percent likely you'd see this by accident. That's not the same number doing the same job."

"So your whole bold sentence is wrong."

"My whole bold sentence is wrong." Jeremy laughed, a short, embarrassed sound, and deleted it. The screen looked emptier than he expected. He had been so pleased with that statistic, the way it seemed to end the argument before it started, and now it was just a door that opened onto a longer hallway. Weirdly, the wrongness invigorated him. He sat up straighter, pulled the study closer, and began building a note card, which his teacher had demonstrated with a sample about a genus of desert beetle, formatting the citation with a small superscript number and a corresponding footnote.

"Here's the thing though," he said, typing. "The study still counts. The effect is still there, statistically. I just can't claim more than it says."

"That sounds like a weaker paper."

"It's a more careful one." He wrote a new sentence: "While the evidence suggests a real effect, a single study cannot prove that mindfulness causes higher scores." Then he frowned at it. "Actually, my thesis can't just be schools should fund it. It has to be something like, the evidence justifies pilot programs, not district-wide mandates." He said it out loud twice, testing the weight of it, and Denny made a face like he'd bitten the soup.

"That's the most Jeremy sentence you've ever said. My brother would call that hedging."

"Your brother calls everything he disagrees with a straw man." Jeremy was writing now, fast, the footnote numbers stacking up along the margin like small flags. He had found a second study, smaller, that showed no effect at all, and instead of burying it he gave it its own paragraph and its own superscript, letting it stand there disagreeing with the first one in plain view. His teacher had written trenchant in red ink on his last essay, next to a paragraph she'd also called glib, and he'd looked up the first word and taken the second personally. He wanted both this time: sharp, but honest about what stayed uncertain.

At quarter to five his mother's car pulled into the driveway. Jeremy highlighted the line about the second study and dragged it up, then down, then left it where it was. Denny collected the empty soup container and paused at the door.

"You're not going to fix that part tonight?"

"No," Jeremy said. "I'm going to leave it messy and figure out tomorrow what I actually believe."

Mathis had agreed to coach the under-fifteens because Coach Rennie had asked him in the parking lot, holding a clipboard like a man handing over a deed, and because saying no to Coach Rennie felt like a moral failing rather than a scheduling choice. The boys could not pass. That was the whole problem, laid out plainly in the first twenty minutes: they hoofed the ball forward the way you'd shovel gravel, without pace on the pass, without checking their shoulders, and the move always died within three touches. So on Thursday night he sat at the track's concrete steps with a notebook and invented drills, two-touch triangles, a gate-passing game where you scored only by playing through a teammate's run, and at the end of the session he added a circuit of lunges and squat jumps, the kind of thing the senior team did, because strength was obviously part of it too.

"Hard session," said Ibrahim, the smallest one, on the walk to the gate. "Felt good though."

"Good," said Mathis, and wrote harder on his plan for Saturday.

Saturday, nine of fourteen showed up. Ibrahim arrived walking like a man navigating a ship's deck in weather, each step a negotiation. Two others limped behind him, and a boy called Fergus sat down on the track's infield and said, with some dignity, "I can't really get up."

They felt fine on Thursday, all of them. That was the part Mathis kept turning over while he jogged the track's outside lane to think. Fine that night, fine Friday morning, and then somewhere between Friday afternoon and this morning their legs had simply stopped answering. He texted his cousin Ellery, who did sports science, because he did not want to ask Coach Rennie and be told he'd nearly crippled the squad.

The reply came while Fergus was still negotiating with the grass. "That's normal. Delayed-onset muscle soreness. It peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it. So Thursday's session is landing on them now, basically." Mathis read it twice, then once more, and felt something between relief and accusation, both aimed at himself. He typed back "so it's not an injury?" and got a thumbs up, which absolved him of nothing, because Ellery had never seen the plan.

He jogged back in and gathered them on the touchline. "Delayed-onset muscle soreness," he said, holding up the phone like a subpoena. "Peaks 24 to 72 hours after a hard session, not right after. So this is Thursday arriving late, not Saturday's fault." Ibrahim looked at his own legs as though they'd kept a secret from him. "That's rubbish," he said, but without conviction.

They did the passing work anyway, the two-touch triangles, walking pace only, and here Mathis watched something he hadn't planned for. Fergus, unable to sprint, had to look up early, because he couldn't rely on his feet to fix a bad first touch, and his passes suddenly had a shape to them, angled into Ibrahim's run instead of at Ibrahim. The weakness in their passing, it turned out, was partly the weakness in their habits, and the sore legs had accidentally exposed it. Mathis stood at the center circle with his notebook and wrote nothing, because he wasn't sure yet which of the two things he'd learned.

Afterward Fergus's older sister drove up, and Fergus lowered himself into the passenger seat in stages, like furniture being moved. Through the window Mathis heard her ask who had run the session, and Fergus said, "Some senior guy," and then, as the car pulled out, something Mathis couldn't catch. He decided not to chase the car down the track to ask, though he did stand in the lane a while, holding the notebook against his hip.

That evening he emailed Coach Rennie the plan for Tuesday with a note: "Cut the jumps, keep the walking triangles, soreness apparently peaks 24 to 72 hours after the unfamiliar stuff, so I've spaced the loading." He read it over. It had the rectitude of a memo written by someone keen to seem in control of events he had mostly stumbled into, and he could hear the turbid, defensive tone underneath it, the sediment not quite settled. He sent it anyway.

Tuesday it rained, and only Ibrahim and Fergus came, the three of them under the floodlights with cones Mathis had to beg off the caretaker. They walked the triangles in the wet, passing, checking shoulders, and when Fergus played a first-time ball through a gate that Mathis hadn't even set up yet, just into space where Ibrahim would be, Mathis crouched by the cone and thought about how much of coaching was accident wearing the costume of intent. "Again," he said. "Same one."

Emily had the living room to herself until six, which gave her two hours to turn six weeks of her own life into ten minutes of theatre. The assignment for the community theatre's young playwrights' workshop said exactly that: a ten-minute play drawn from a moment from your own life, staged for an audience of strangers at the end of the month. She had chosen the night last spring when her father moved out, or rather the morning after, when she found her mother on the porch with his coffee mug, and neither of them said anything worth writing down, which was precisely the problem. Everything true about that morning had happened in the silences, and silence was the hardest thing to stage.

She typed the first draft at the coffee table, cross-legged, the laptop warm on her shins. Her mother's voice drifted from the kitchen, along with the smell of onions, and Emily kept flinching at it, at the ordinariness of the sound, because the play was set in a kitchen too and she had not decided whether that was honesty or theft. Her friend Dez was coming at four to read the other part, and after that Marcus, who acted in the theatre's mainstage shows, had agreed to do a cold read over the phone. Three readers, three opinions, and she was already exhausted by the arithmetic of them.

Dez arrived with a bag of chips and no tact, which was why Emily had asked her. "Okay," Dez said, dropping onto the couch and shaking crumbs off the script Emily had printed. "Who's who."

"You're my mom. I'm me."

"Great, typecasting." Dez squinted at the page. "There's a lot of this italic stuff. '(She sets the mug down too hard.)' Do I say that?"

"No, that's a stage direction. It's how the script tells you what happens but isn't spoken." Emily leaned over and pointed at the parentheses lower down. "They set them apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from the actual lines. Otherwise the whole page is just words running together and nobody knows what to say out loud."

"So if I see italics, I shut up and do it."

"Basically, yes."

They read it through, Dez's voice flat and unbothered in a way that made Emily's chest palpitate, because the words were so small on the page and so enormous in her memory, and hearing them in a bored teenager's monotone made them sound like nothing. When Dez reached "(She sets the mug down too hard)" she mimed setting down an invisible mug with an exaggerated bang, and Emily said "no, softer," and Dez said "then why does it say hard," and Emily did not have an answer.

That was the problem, actually, the whole problem, and she sat with it while Dez ate chips and texted someone. Her workshop instructor, Mr. Iyer, believed in restraint: write the action, he kept saying, and the feeling will carry itself. Her mother believed the opposite, in a way, believed that the truth needed a little veneer of politeness over it or nobody could live in the same house afterward, that you could love someone more by not saying the worst true thing. Emily had been treating those as two different doctrines. Now she wondered whether a stage direction was where they met: the mug set down hard, but the line delivered gently, the fact stated plainly and the manner softened. She could not tell if that was synthesis or just cowardice dressed up as craft.

Marcus called at five, and he wanted to read it cold, off a file she sent him, which meant he'd be looking at the formatting as she'd left it. She had a moment of doubt while the phone rang, some instinct she couldn't name, and then he was saying "Okay, page one, go."

He read beautifully, which made everything worse. He gave her mother a low, tired warmth that Emily had not written, and when he reached the porch he paused. "Then there's this line here, '(She keeps her back to her daughter.)', I'm not sure how to play that, is that the mom talking about herself in third person, like a Brecht thing?"

"No, that's a stage direction, you don't say it. I thought I formatted it."

"You did, it's in parentheses, I can see that now, but it's also on its own line between two spoken lines and I just barreled through it. Sorry. Happens at first read-throughs all the time." He cleared his throat. "Want me to take it again from the top of the page?"

They finished the read, and afterward Marcus said the play worked but the ending was too resolved, that the daughter forgave the mother too easily for ten minutes of stage time, and Emily said "she doesn't forgive her," and Marcus said "then write that," and hung up because his ride was there.

Dez had gone quiet somewhere in the middle of Marcus's read, which was unlike her. Before leaving she stood in the doorway with her jacket half on and said, "My parents split when I was eleven. Nobody set any mugs down. Nobody said anything at all. So the hard mug thing, that's actually a lot. Don't cut it."

After both of them were gone Emily sat back down at the coffee table. On her phone was a text from her mother, sent from the kitchen fifteen feet away: "Smells like you're burning something in here, come eat." And below it, from earlier that afternoon, a message she had half-written and never sent: "The play is about that morning. Is that okay." The cursor still blinked at the end of it. She looked at the kitchen doorway, at the steam and the onions and her mother's shape moving behind it, and she typed one more word, "please," and set the phone face down on the table.

Then she opened the laptop, found the last stage direction, the one after the final line, and deleted "(They hug.)" In its place she wrote "(She sets the mug down too hard.)" and, on the next line, italicized, "(Neither of them picks it up.)" The chips crumbs were still on the couch cushion. She left them there and went in to eat.

Kyle had been staring at the same diagram for eleven minutes when Marisol leaned across the lab bench and tapped the mitochondrion with her pencil.

"You're supposed to be labeling the inner membrane," she said. "Not having a religious experience."

He was having something, though he wouldn't have called it that. The worksheet showed glucose being broken down step by step, arrows shrinking it through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, until what remained poured into a spiral of proteins embedded in the folded membrane. At the end of the spiral sat a small mushroom-shaped structure, and the label read ATP synthase. Their teacher, Ms. Okafor, had drawn it on the board that morning and said only, "By Friday, each of you will be able to trace this pathway from start to finish and explain the last step. The last step is where most of you will stumble." The quiz was Friday. It was Tuesday, fifth period, and the radiator under the window ticked like a slow clock.

"The arrows go in a circle," Kyle said. "Look at it. Hydrogen ions come back through this thing, this synthase, and it turns, and then it makes ATP. But the worksheet doesn't say how turning makes anything."

"Maybe it just does," Marisol said. She was already filling in her own sheet, her handwriting small and certain. "Write what the diagram says and move on."

That was the difference between them, and Kyle knew it. Marisol wanted the right answer; Kyle wanted the reason underneath it. He used to think of his own habit as the better one, maybe even a grandiose way of thinking, as if he were the kind of person who saw deeper than everyone else. Lately it felt more like an indictment, something to be read aloud against him: Kyle cannot accept what he is given. His father said it at dinner last month, after Kyle had argued with an uncle about a news story for twenty minutes. "You can't just trust anything," his father had said. "Not a diagram, not an article, nothing."

He hadn't come back with an answer then. He was trying to come back with one now.

Ms. Okafor was at her desk grading quizzes from another class, a mug of tea cooling beside her. Kyle walked over with the worksheet and the classroom's battered laptop, which he'd carried back from the cart without asking, because the cart was open and asking took time. "Can I look something up?" he said. "The last step. The ATP synthase."

"Look it up," she said, not looking up. "That's what the internet is for. Cite it if you use it."

He typed the name into the search bar at the third lab table, near the window, where the afternoon light came through dusty and made the screen hard to read until he angled it away. The first results were diagrams like his. Then a headline caught him: two men, Paul Boyer and John Walker, had shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.

"They won a Nobel for this," he said out loud. Marisol looked over. "The last step. The part Ms. Okafor said we'd stumble on. Two guys worked it out and they gave them a Nobel Prize for it. Nineteen ninety-seven."

"So it's hard," Marisol said. "That's not news."

But it was news to Kyle, and it rearranged something in his thinking. He had assumed the worksheet left out the mechanism because the mechanism was simple, something a sentence could cover and the printer had skipped. Instead people had spent years on it, and a committee in Stockholm had judged the answer worth one of the highest honors there was. That meant the diagram wasn't withholding something small. It was withholding something enormous, simplified down to a mushroom shape and three arrows. His instinct to distrust the diagram had been right, and wrong at the same time: right that something was missing, wrong to think the missing thing was easy.

He read a little further, careful now, the way Marisuol would have been careful, checking the name and the year against a second page before writing anything down. Then he carried the laptop back to his own bench and picked up his pencil.

"Okay," he said. "Here's what I've got. Glucose gets broken down, the ions pile up on one side of the membrane, and they come back through ATP synthase, and that's what makes the ATP. The turning part, how the enzyme actually does it, that took decades. Boyer and Walker got the Nobel in 1997 for explaining it." He paused. "I don't fully get how it works. But I get what it does, and I get that the part I don't get is real and huge."

Marisol had stopped writing. "So for the quiz on Friday, we write the part we know."

"And I ask Ms. Okafor about the rest after class," Kyle said. "Not to argue with her. Just to ask."

The radiator ticked. Somewhere down the hall a door closed. Kyle wrote "ATP synthase, last step, Nobel Prize 1997, Boyer and Walker" in the margin of his worksheet, then drew a careful box around it, the pencil whispering against the paper.

Florence arrived at the park eleven minutes early, which she decided to think of as punctual rather than desperate. She sat on the bench by the duck pond, where she and Omar had agreed to meet, and set her phone face down on her knee so she would not look at it. Eleven minutes was long enough to reconsider everything: the shirt she had changed twice, the fact that she had said "see you Saturday" with an exclamation point, the deeper fact that she liked him more than she had planned to.

She knew something about liking, actually. In psychology last semester they had read about a 1999 study by Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh, who found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. Florence had found the study mildly sinister at the time. Someone could tilt their head the way you tilted yours and you would warm to them, and neither of you would ever know why. It had seemed like evidence that people were manipulable, that preference itself could be counterfeit. Now, waiting for a boy she wanted to like her honestly, she found the fact following her around like a stray.

He came up the path with two cups of slushie, one blue and one red, and handed her the blue without asking, because blue was what she always ordered at lunch. "I guessed," he said, and she thought that was a good sign, though she also thought, unhelpfully, that guessing right was a kind of data too.

They walked the loop around the pond. Omar talked about his little brother's obsession with magnet fishing, and Florence talked about the college essay she could not start, and somewhere near the willow trees she noticed that they had both leaned on their elbows along the railing, forearms angled the same way, chins on the same fist. He had done it after she had. She was almost sure he had done it after.

Here was the problem she could not adjudicate alone, standing there with her slushie going cold: if the study was right, the mimicry might be making her like him more, and if he was doing it on purpose, then some portion of what she felt had been engineered, and his culpability in that engineering was unknowable from the inside. She tested him. She shifted her weight to her left foot, and thirty seconds later, mid-sentence about magnet fishing, he shifted too.

"Did you just copy me?" she said.

"What?"

"I moved my foot and then you moved your foot."

Omar looked down at his feet as though they had betrayed him. "I don't think so. I mean, I wasn't watching your feet. Was I supposed to be watching your feet? Is that a thing?"

"It's a thing," Florence said. "There's this study, Chartrand and Bargh, 1999. People liked a partner more when the partner mimicked them, and nobody even noticed it happening. So now I can't tell if I like you or if I like the mirroring."

Omar laughed, a real laugh with a snort in it, and then stopped laughing when he saw she was serious. "Okay, but if neither person notices, then I didn't do it on purpose, so it's not fake. It's like a coincidence your body makes."

"That's one theory," she said, but she was turning it over. The study didn't say the liking was false; it said the liking grew without anyone catching it at work. Maybe that made it delusive, or maybe it made it like everything else that drew people together, posture and slushie flavors and the way someone snorts when they laugh, none of which anyone chose exactly. She had been treating unconscious influence as deleterious, a contaminant in an otherwise pure sample, but there was no pure sample. There was just this afternoon, this railing, this boy.

"Let's try it the other way," Omar said. "You copy me and I'll report my feelings." He draped one arm along the railing in an exaggerated slump, like a fainting Victorian, and Florence matched it, and they stood there slumped and solemn while a woman with a stroller gave them a wide look. Omar broke first. "Honestly? My feelings are that this is worse for my dignity than for my affection."

She still didn't know, walking back along the pond, whether what she felt was hers or partly something Chartrand and Bargh had measured in a lab in 1999. She suspected she would never fully know, and that not-knowing was going to have to be acceptable, the way she accepted that the ducks were probably judging her. Omar held out his hand near the gate, palm up, not grabbing, just offering, and after a second Florence took it.

The notice went up on Monday, tacked to the corkboard beside the lost-and-found bin: waterfront staff needed for the last four weeks of camp, applicants must be sixteen by June, interviews Friday at noon. Kaitlyn had been a CIT all summer, unpaid, hauling coolers and counting noses on the dock while the lifeguards sat in their tower and got paid to whistle. She wanted the tower. She wanted the tower so badly she had practiced her rescue breathing on a pillow the night before, timing herself, thirty compressions, thirty again.

But on Wednesday her phone buzzed at lunch. Marguerite, who ran the gift shop at the lake marina two towns over, needed someone for the rest of the season, starting Monday, eleven dollars an hour, cash tips on Saturdays. The camp job paid a stipend, a flat four hundred for four weeks, which worked out to less. Kaitlyn did the math twice on the back of a permission slip, then sat very still while a nine-year-old asked her to open his juice box.

"You already said yes to Marguerite?" Priya asked her that evening at the picnic tables, where the staff ate after the campers went home. Priya was seventeen and knew things the way she knew the periodic table, thoroughly and with citations.

"I said I'd come by tomorrow to fill out paperwork. She wants an answer before Saturday. But if I get the waterfront job Friday, and then the marina's better, I'd be quitting the camp job. I can't do that to them. They trained me. There's, like, four weeks left."

"So don't apply."

"Then if I don't get the marina paperwork done by Saturday, I have nothing."

Priya peeled the label off her water bottle in one long strip. "My cousin quit Kroger with a text message the night before her shift. No notice at all. She said it's called at-will. Most employment in the US is at-will, so the employer or the worker can end the job at any time, for any reason that isn't illegal. Kroger could've fired her that same way. Nobody's more wronged than anybody."

"That feels like a loophole," Kaitlyn said. "Like finding a rule that exonerates you before you've even done the thing."

"It's not a loophole if it's the whole road."

Kaitlyn didn't answer. Over by the fence, Mr. Deene, the program director, stood watching the empty swim area with his hands clasped behind him, saturnine in the long orange light, the way he always looked at the end of a day, as though tallying what had gone wrong. He had driven her to get her CPR card renewed himself, in his own car, and had waited in the parking lot reading a paperback. That was the problem with people. They kept doing things you'd have to remember later.

On Thursday she took her charges to the nature hut, where the quiet CIT, a college sophomore named Devon, was helping kids extract DNA from strawberries. Kaitlyn's least favorite camper, a boy named Oliver, mashed his strawberry with unusual violence and then peered into the bag. "So this is his genotype?" he asked, pointing at the goop. "The whole blueprint?"

"That's his DNA," Devon said. "The genotype's more like the instructions written in it. You can't see the instructions, only what they build."

Oliver squinted, unsatisfied, and went back to mashing. Kaitlyn stood there with a sudden clear picture of herself: instructions nobody could see, and a person built on top of them, and no way to know if the person matched. She believed she was loyal. She had a wallet card and a four-week record of punctual cooler-hauling to prove it. But the instructions, the ones you couldn't see, might just say take the eleven dollars an hour, and she'd never had them tested.

Friday at noon she sat across the picnic table from Mr. Deene, who had her file open even though there was almost nothing in it. He asked her the questions, she answered them, and then he said, "You'd start Monday. I have to tell you, though, if enrollment drops I cut staff the same week. It's the nature of the arrangement. Nothing personal, it's just how it works. I'd let you go with a day's notice if it came to that."

She looked at him. "So the camp could end it any time."

"That's the deal," he said, and closed the file. "I'd tell you the truth about that much."

He had not known he was doing it, but he had tipped the scale, or maybe he had only shown her where the scale already sat. The camp could cut her loose on a day's notice because that was the arrangement, ordinary and legal, and Priya's cousin could quit Kroger by text under the same arrangement, and neither one was a betrayal. Or both were, a little, and the arrangement just spread the small betrayals evenly so nobody had to carry one alone. She could not decide which way to see it. What she knew was that she would not be the only one at the picnic table with obligations.

"The waterfront's yours if you want it," Mr. Deene said. "I need an answer before the staff meeting at five."

"I know. I'll be back by four thirty."

She rode her bike the two miles to the marina with the permission-slip math folded in her pocket. Marguerite had her filling out the W-4 under the ceiling fan, then held out a pen for the schedule. "Monday through Saturday, nine to five. You're sure? I'm training you on the register and I don't get a second shot at the season."

"I'm sure about the job," Kaitlyn said. "I'm not sure about the money being the reason. Does that count?"

Marguerite considered her over the counter, the way she probably considered weather. "Counts more than the other kind," she said. "The sure ones quit by August."

At four twenty-five Kaitlyn stood at the edge of the staff meeting with the wind coming off the lake. Mr. Deene raised his eyebrows at her from the circle of folding chairs.

"I'm taking the marina job," she said. "And I'll finish out this week, today and tomorrow, the full days, so you're not short at the swim test." She held out her CPR card, since there was nothing else to give him. "I can't give you four weeks' notice. I'm sorry. I looked it up and I don't legally owe any, but that part I already knew before I looked."

Mr. Deene took the card, turned it over once, and handed it back. "Saturday, then," he said. "Bring the whistles back to the tower."

The travel agency occupied the ground floor of a building that had once been a bank, and Gabriel sat at the teller counter where his mother had arranged for him to help Mr. Adeyemi update the shop's wall maps before he left for university. The summer job was meant to be dull. Instead Mr. Adeyemi had installed a trial of mapping software on the back computer and told him, almost as an afterthought, that the city council had published flood risk data and that anyone could now lay it over a map of neighborhoods. Gabriel had assumed floods were a rural problem, something that happened to farms and river towns, and the assumption collapsed the first time he clicked the overlay button and watched the blue shading bloom across the eastern districts of the city he had lived in for eighteen years.

He learned the software the way he learned most things, by breaking it and starting over. Layers, he discovered, could be stacked like transparencies on an old projector: streets beneath parcels, parcels beneath the floodplain polygon, and above everything a census layer showing which blocks held the oldest housing. When he switched the layers on and off, the city changed its mind about itself. The same streets that looked ordinary under the street layer looked fragile under the flood layer, and the houses his aunt rented in Marshview sat squarely inside the deepest blue.

"You've been at that machine for three hours," Mr. Adeyemi said on the second Thursday, carrying two cups of tea though Gabriel drank coffee. "My customers think we've become an internet café."

"It's a GIS," Gabriel said. "A geographic information system. You put different kinds of data on one map and look at them together." He turned the monitor so the older man could see the blue and the census blocks overlapping. "This whole technology started in Canada. Roger Tomlinson led the development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s. First computerized one there ever was. They call him the father of GIS."

Mr. Adeyemi leaned in, reading the screen the way he read timetables, with a finger tracking the lines. "And this flood layer, is it a guess?"

"It's a model," Gabriel said, and then, because he had spent two evenings reading the council's methodology and half understanding it, "which means it's a guess with math behind it. A hundred-year flood, they call it, but the hundred years is an average, not a schedule. That part stays uncertain." It was the first time he had said anything like that aloud, the first time he had admitted that a system so precise on the screen could be imprecise about the world, and the admission sat oddly beside the pleasure the maps gave him.

He thought of his father, who had fixed plumbing for thirty years and distrusted anything on a screen that claimed to know a house better than a man standing in its basement. During his last year of school Gabriel had argued with him about exactly this, about some zoning map the city had mailed out, and his father had said that maps were drawn by people who had never gotten wet. Gabriel had been certain, then, that his father was simply behind the times. Now, toggling the layers, he found himself less certain of either position. The map showed Marshview flooded and his father's tools would show Marshview's cracked drainpipes, and neither one, alone, was the whole truth. The counterpoint between them was the point.

A woman came in that afternoon wanting a ferry ticket, and while Gabriel printed it she noticed the screen. She lived in Millbank, she said, high ground, and she wanted to know whether her sister's street in Marshview was in the blue. He showed her. She looked for a long time, then asked whether it meant her sister should sell, and Gabriel, who could have recited the flood probability and the median house age and the parcel values, said that he honestly did not know what it meant for one person's life. The map could say where the water would go. It could not say what her sister owed to a house she'd raised children in.

"She could ask about the buyout program," he offered. "The city has one for the deepest zones." It felt gratuitous to add, a fact offered to fill the silence, and he regretted it even as she wrote the number down, because he was not sure the program had ever actually paid anyone in Marshview, only that it existed somewhere in a PDF he had skimmed.

After she left, he turned the layers off one by one until only the plain street map remained, the kind Mr. Adeyemi sold to tourists, the kind Gabriel had folded and shelved all summer. Then he turned them back on. The blue crept over the eastern districts again, and over it the census blocks, and over everything the small red outlines of houses built before any of this had been mapped, before Tomlinson, before the council's models, before Gabriel. He dragged the cursor across Marshview and watched the parcel numbers flicker under his hand, and printed one of them, and folded the page into his back pocket to show his father.

The physics demonstration room on the second floor of the museum smelled like floor wax and old electricity, and Rose had claimed the ballistic table before anyone else could. It was a long metal runway with a launcher at one end and a carbon-paper sheet laid out on the floor beyond the edge, so that a marble fired off the end would land and leave a smudged gray mark wherever physics had decided to put it. Beside the table, a volunteer in a museum polo shirt watched with the expression of someone who had seen a hundred teenagers discover gravity that afternoon.

"You're supposed to predict first," he said. He was taciturn in the way of people who preferred machines to conversation, and he slid a clipboard toward her with the printed grid already on it. There was a girl from another school there too, a boy with a lanyard, a scatter of parents. Rose had come alone, on the bus, because the placement exam for the engineering program was in eleven days and she could not make the marble land where the equations said it should.

The problem was the launcher fired at an angle, and Rose kept treating the speed as one thing, firing it at herself, so to speak. She wrote and crossed out, wrote and crossed out. The other girl leaned over her shoulder.

"You split it," the girl said. "The sideways part never changes. It just goes straight at whatever speed it has sideways. Only the up-and-down part feels gravity." She tapped the grid. "Two problems wearing one coat."

Rose looked at the marble, the angle stamped on the launcher's protractor, and something rearranged itself behind her eyes. She multiplied by the cosine, wrote the horizontal speed as a constant, gave the vertical its own little equation with a minus sign in front of half of nine point eight. She marked the landing spot on the carbon paper with a pencil X. The volunteer released the spring. The marble struck two centimeters from her X, close enough that the boy with the lanyard said "whoa" without irony, and Rose felt a thin, almost embarrassing warmth climb her neck.

Eleven days, and a scholarship that would allay the part of the tuition her mother's job at the deposition office of the county courthouse could not cover, transcribing testimony eight hours a day with her wrists braced. Rose remembered being nine, sitting under her mother's desk among the boxes of taped statements, thinking that every word spoken in that building eventually lay down flat on paper, in lines, like the smudges on the carbon sheet. Her mother had wanted her to be a stenographer too. Steady, she had said. Numbers don't go to college, she had said, in the spring, before Rose's physics mark came back and she stopped saying it.

The volunteer was resetting the launcher when the other girl, whose name was Priya, asked about the next exhibit over, a glass case where a small metal ball hung between two brass plates and drifted sideways instead of falling straight. A placard gave the numbers. "Two parallel plates, 0.02 metres apart, 100 volts across them," Priya read aloud. "Five thousand volts per metre between them."

"That's it?" the boy said. "A hundred volts doesn't sound like much."

"Per metre," Rose said slowly. She was doing it on the clipboard margin, dividing, and the number that came out was the number on the placard, exactly. Then she thought of something and frowned. "Wait. If somebody put the distance in centimetres." She wrote it the wrong way, dividing 100 by 2 instead of 0.02, and got 50. Fifty against five thousand. "They'd get an answer a hundred times too small. Two centimetres instead of two hundredths of a metre." She looked up. "That's all it takes. You could do the whole method perfectly and still be off by a hundred."

Priya laughed, but not unkindly. "That's physics," she said. "Right and wrong at the same time."

The volunteer cleared his throat and pointed at the placard, which was already turning back toward the ball between the plates, but Rose wasn't really looking at it. She was thinking about the marble, the X in pencil, the two centimeters of miss. She had done the method right and still not hit the mark, and the two centimeters could have been air resistance or a stretched spring or her own handwriting, and she would not know which. The new way of splitting the motion had given her an answer that was almost true, and she found she could not decide whether that was a comfort or a warning. Eleven days from now there would be no carbon paper, no second launch, only the one answer she wrote down.

The room was emptying. Priya gathered her bag, asked which bus Rose took, and seemed pleased when the answer was the 14. They stood a moment by the ballistic table, where the fired marble had rolled into the corner and sat gleaming among its own gray smudges, a whole afternoon of attempts laid out flat.

"The vertical one," Rose said, mostly to herself, picking up the marble and weighing it in her palm. "That's the part that always comes back down."

Priya held the door, and the marble was cool and heavy in Rose's hand as she walked out still carrying it.

The Saturday market smelled of bruised peaches and cut herbs, and Stella moved through it with her grandmother's list folded into her back pocket, though she knew it by heart. Her mother had left that morning for a weekend conference, and the dinner, the first Stella would cook alone for all of them, had landed on her like a prize and like a weight. Her grandmother had made this chicken every Sunday of Stella's childhood, and Stella intended to make it tonight exactly, which was why she stood now in front of the poultry stall, watching a man in a canvas apron wrap two whole birds in butcher paper.

"You want the bigger one," her grandmother used to say, "because a small bird has no generosity in it." Stella had never known whether to ascribe that to experience or to some private doctrine her grandmother had invented and then believed, the way she believed in rinsing everything, twice, under running water. At the stall Stella chose the smaller bird, because there were only four of them now, and carried it in a paper bag against her hip like something newly alive. She caught herself checking the shape of it through the paper, half expecting sentience, half mocking herself for the thought, since a bird this cold and plucked was about as far from a creature as a package of anything.

Her brother Theo was waiting by the tomato crates, eating a sample plum with the guilty speed of someone who intended to take another. He was sixteen and had recently become the kind of person who read pamphlets in waiting rooms and repeated their contents at dinner. "Did you get the bird," he said, not a question, already walking. At home he followed her into the kitchen and leaned on the counter while she unpacked the bag, the peaches, the basil going limp already in their paper, the chicken sweating faintly in its wrapping.

Stella tore the paper away and turned on the faucet and held the bird under it, the way she had watched done a hundred times, cold water running over the pale skin while her grandmother's hands worked the joints and loosened whatever a joint holds. "Stop," Theo said, and he actually stepped forward and turned the faucet off himself, which was a thing he had no right to do and did anyway. "The CDC says not to wash raw chicken. The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the counters, everywhere around it."

"You're being doctrinaire," Stella said, because it was the word that came, and because she wanted a word bigger than his. She was still holding the wet bird over the sink, water dripping off it onto the steel. But Theo only stood there, waiting, and she remembered, unwillingly, a documentary he had made them all watch in March, and she understood that this was not a mood of his, that he had absorbed something and would not unbend from it, and that unbending, in him, was not quite the flaw she wanted it to be.

She set the bird on the cutting board, dry, and dried her own hands, and stood for a moment with her back to him. The problem was not the chicken. The problem was that her grandmother's hands were the first hands she had ever watched cook, and every motion of that cooking was a kind of inheritance, and now some pamphlet-sized fact had walked into the kitchen and told her the inheritance was wrong. She thought about arguing. She thought about saying that her grandmother had fed four generations on washed chicken and every one of them had survived to argue about it. She thought, too, that survival was not the same as proof, and that the arithmetic of germs was invisible and therefore could not be argued with by anecdotes, however beloved.

"It still has to taste like hers," she said finally. "That part isn't negotiable." Theo shrugged and went to wash the tomatoes, then paused, evidently running the same logic through his own doctrine, and wiped them with a damp cloth instead. Stella salted the bird inside and out, more salt than seemed decent, the way her grandmother had, and slid the lemon halves under the skin where they would steam the meat from above and below at once. Some of this, she knew, was gesture, a costume of fidelity. Some of it was real technique, and she could no longer entirely tell which was which, and she decided, for tonight, that she did not have to.

The oven ticked as it heated. Through the window she could see the market tents still up in the distance, white triangles against the hill, and she thought of her grandmother washing that first bird in this same sink, water splashing where Theo's elbows now rested, and she let the two of them sit in her mind together without forcing either one out. The chicken went into the oven at four, and Stella wrote nothing down, and Theo set the table without being asked, putting their mother's place at the head.

"Tell me again why you get the small bird," he said from the doorway.

"Because a big one has no generosity in it," Stella said, and wiped her hands on the towel, and did not tell him whether she believed it.

The community centre on Ashfield Road kept its pianos in a room that had once been a gymnasium, and the parquet still showed the ghost lines of a basketball key under the legs of the upright. Joseph arrived early on Tuesdays because the bus schedule left him no choice, and for twenty minutes he had the room to himself. He would sit at the piano with his workbook open to a page of blank staves and write nothing, which had become its own ritual.

The assignment was plain enough on paper: sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written in standard notation. Ms. Okafor had said the chords did not have to be adventurous, only honest, and Joseph liked that word applied to harmony, as though a C major triad could be a liar. He had a melody in his head, four notes that rose and then dropped a sixth, and he could hum it, but when he tried to write it down the rhythm kept dissolving, the way a dream does when you describe it out loud.

Marisol came at half past six, shaking rain off her jacket, and found him staring at the staves. She set down her coffee and pulled a pencil from her bag without being asked, the eraser chewed to a soft grey nub. "Bar lines first," she said. "Sixteen boxes. Draw the fences, then fill the field." He acceded, because arguing with her about method was a thing he had given up in September, and because the fences did help: within the boxes, his four notes found a home on beat one of bar one, whole and definite.

Ms. Okafor played recordings while they worked, and that evening it was a sonata with a first section that repeated its tunes politely, almost sweetly, and then a middle section that turned stormy. Joseph stopped writing. Something in the churn sounded familiar, three notes buried in the bass, then the same shape upside down in the treble. He leaned toward the speaker. "That's the opening tune," he said. "It's in there, isn't it? Broken up."

She looked at him over the rim of her coffee. "That's the development."

The word opened a door and Joseph walked through it alone, because she had already turned back to Marisol's workbook, and he liked it better that way. He listened again and again in his head, and then on his phone on the bus home, earbuds in, window streaked. The development took the exposition's themes and broke them into short fragments, and moved those fragments quickly through several keys, and that was why the section sounded restless, like someone pacing a small room. He tested the idea: he hummed his own four notes, chopped off the last one, and shoved the remaining three into a key he'd never written in, G minor, which made them sound melancholic and a little desperate, like relatives of the original who had fallen on hard times. There was a consanguinity between the two versions, a blood relation he could hear even when he could barely recognize the face.

The following Tuesday he brought in his sixteen bars, and they were no longer one melody but a family of them. Bars one through eight stated the tune over simple chords, F major with a D minor turn. Bars nine through twelve took the first three notes and ran them through three different keys, one bar each, no time to settle. Bars thirteen through sixteen brought the whole tune back, changed by the journey. Marisol read it over his shoulder while Ms. Okafor was helping Deni with his ledger lines. "Nine and ten feel like falling," Marisol said. "Is that on purpose?"

"Sort of," Joseph said. "I stole it from the sonata. The stormy part. The tune's in there if you listen for it, just cut into pieces and shoved around." He played bars nine and ten for her, then the original, then nine and ten again, and watched her face do the same thing his had done on the bus: confusion, then recognition, then a small laugh at herself for not hearing it sooner.

Ms. Okafor sat down at the upright and sight-read his page, pedal down, and the room filled. The fragments in the middle keys went by like fence posts from a train window. When she finished she did not say it was good or bad. She said, "Bar twelve, you never resolved the D minor. You land the return on the weak beat. Was that a choice?"

Joseph looked at bar twelve. He had written it at eleven at night, tired, and he honestly could not remember whether it was a choice or an accident, and he knew those were not the same thing even when they sounded identical. "I don't know yet," he said. "Can I leave it and find out next week?"

She handed back the page. Marisol was already playing bar twelve herself, then changing it, then playing his version again, her chewed pencil hovering over the staff.

Lea had said the blessing forty times in the back of her mother's car, and every time, at the same word, her voice thinned and the syllables collapsed into each other. Her grandmother had called on Tuesday and asked, in the tone she used for things already decided, whether Lea would make Kiddush on Friday night, the whole thing, for the whole table. "Your grandfather did it for forty years," her grandmother said. "It's time someone else held the cup."

Lea had said the word Kiddush back to her, uncertainly, and her grandmother had explained only this much: it was the blessing over the wine or grape juice that began Sabbath and festival meals, the words that marked the day as holy. Then she had hung up before Lea could ask why her, or why now, six weeks after the funeral.

Friday afternoon, the house filled the way it always did, which is to say past capacity, cousins orbiting the kitchen, her Uncle David claiming the armchair by the window. Lea carried the silver cup into the pantry to fill it, and found her grandfather's prayer book on the shelf where he had left it, its spine softened by decades of his thumb. The page was worn to a soft gray at exactly the place she needed. She stood among the jars of grape juice her grandmother had bought because Lea didn't drink wine, a courtesy no one had named aloud, and read the Hebrew slowly, her finger under each line, aware that she was doing something circumscribed by rules she only half knew, and that nobody had offered to fill in the other half.

Her little cousin Jonah found her there, drawn by the smell of the braided bread cooling on the counter. "What are you doing hiding," he said, which was not a question. He was nine and treated all rooms as his territory.

"Practicing."

"For what?"

"For tonight." She showed him the cup, which held a dark juice that looked, in that light, almost like the real thing. "There's a blessing that starts the meal. It's called Kiddush. It's over the wine or the juice, and it's what makes the day holy." Saying it to Jonah, she realized, was different from saying it to herself. He was listening the way children listen, with his whole face, and the words had to stand up straight.

"Can I hear it?"

"No," she said, and then, because his face began to fall, "It's not ready. If I practice it in front of you it'll use it up."

He accepted this, the way children accept all false economies, and went to find the bread.

At the table, her grandmother's good cloth was laid, and the candles had already been blessed by her mother, their light making the crowded room gentler than it was. Everyone found seats, and the noise lowered itself without being told to. Her grandmother poured the grape juice into the silver cup until it rose past the middle, which someone had once told Lea was required, though she no longer remembered who, and set it in front of her with both hands.

The room was quiet in the way rooms are quiet when they are waiting, and Lea understood that the silence was not duress, whatever it felt like. It was an invitation shaped like a test. She lifted the cup, and the weight of it surprised her, more than she had expected from practicing with a water glass in the car.

She began. The words she had drilled came out, and the word that always failed her did not fail her, and she could hear, in the strange acoustics of a full dining room, her own voice doing something it had never done in the back seat of the car. She was aware of her grandfather's absence as a shape in the room, an empty chair that was not empty tonight because Uncle David had been moved into it, and she held both of those facts together: that he was gone, and that the blessing did not stop being his, exactly, even as it passed through her. She did not know yet what she believed about any of it, the holiness, the day marked off from other days, and she let the not-knowing sit beside the words without pushing either one away.

When she finished, she drank, and the juice was sweeter than she had expected, and she passed the cup to her grandmother, who drank and passed it on. It went around the table hand to hand, cup after cup poured, everyone drinking, even Jonah, who made a face at the sweetness and then drank again. The meal began the way meals begin, in noise and the passing of plates, and nothing in the room announced that anything had changed, and yet something evanescent had happened and hung there anyway, refusing to be nothing.

After the soup, her grandmother leaned over and straightened the prayer book beside Lea's plate, which had slid crooked, and left her hand on it a moment. "Same time next month," she said. "You'll do the bread blessing too."

Lea looked at the book, at her grandmother's hand, at the candles burning low in their holders. "Teach me tomorrow," she said. "Before everyone leaves."

Julia spread the two leases across the kitchen table the way her mother used to spread tarot cards, corners squared, everything visible at once. She had told Dana she was good at this, had said it more than once, and Dana had believed her, which was the problem with being believed.

"Garfield Street is nine hundred a month," Dana said, tapping the first page. "Which is a hundred and ten less than the one on Willow."

"That's just rent." Julia pulled a legal pad toward her and wrote the number down anyway, because it felt like an accomplishment. Outside, the sprinkler next door chattered through its arc, and somewhere in the house her father was on a call, his voice rising and falling behind his office door.

The Garfield lease mentioned heat was not included. The Willow lease said it was. Julia sat back. She was eighteen and had never paid a utility bill in her life, though she had watched her mother do it, every Sunday night, a ritual of envelopes and small disbursements that Julia had pretended to find boring. Her mother had died in March, obdurate about the bills until the end, refusing help, refusing to explain. Julia had found the checkbook after, balanced to the penny, and had cried over the arithmetic of it, the neat carried digits.

"So what do we do?" Dana asked. "Just pick Garfield? A hundred and ten is a hundred and ten."

"We add it all up first." Julia was drawing columns now, and something in her chest loosened as the columns grew. "Rent, and then every recurring cost the tenant pays. Heat, electricity, water, internet, insurance. Everything that comes every month. Total monthly cost. That's how you compare them fairly."

"Where'd you learn that?"

"A book my mom left on the shelf. Personal finance, 1998. It smelled like her." Julia did not say that she had found the book in June and read it three times as if it were a letter.
