She did not say that last year she had advised her mother to renew a lease based on rent alone, that the building had switched to tenant-paid heat in the spring, that her mother had never once mentioned what the change cost. Julia had found the bills. She knew the number. She had not told anyone, not even Dana, that the advice had been hers.

They worked through it together, Dana reading figures off the lease riders while Julia wrote. Garfield: nine hundred rent, plus heat in winter that the current tenants estimated high, plus electricity, water, internet, renter's insurance. Willow: a thousand and ten, but heat was in the rent, water was in the rent, and only electricity, internet, and insurance landed on the tenant. When Julia added each column top to bottom, twice, the way her mother had taught her without either of them noticing it was teaching, the totals came out nearly even, and then, on the third check, Garfield came out higher. Fourteen dollars higher, and that was before winter.

"You're sure?" Dana leaned over the pad, and Julia could smell the chlorine still in her hair from the pool.

"I did it three times."

"Because you said you were bad at math in eleventh grade. You told Mr. Ferro you were bad at math."

"I was bad at math. This isn't math." It was true and it wasn't, and Julia held both of those in her mouth at once. What she had been bad at was being looked at while she worked. What she was good at, alone at this table, was numbers that underpinned a decision, columns that would hold weight. She turned the pad so Dana could see the arithmetic, every line visible, nothing squared away in a drawer.

"Then Willow," Dana said slowly, testing it. "The place that looked expensive is the cheap one."

"Cheaper. Not cheap." Julia looked at the two totals, fourteen dollars apart, and thought of winter in her mother's building, the radiator that clanked, the bill her mother had paid without comment while Julia advised her about rents. Fourteen dollars could reverse itself in a warm January or a cold one. She wrote both totals on the pad and did not cross either out. "There's a margin here we can't see yet. Utilities move. So we pick with that in the open."

Dana picked up the Garfield lease and folded it in half, then in half again, undecided, the paper thick in her hand. "Can we sleep on it?"

"We can sleep on it." Julia gathered the Willow pages but left the pad on the table, columns facing up, the two totals side by side, fourteen dollars apart. Behind the office door her father's call ended, and she heard his chair push back. He came out drying his hands on a dish towel and stopped at the table, reading the pad upside down the way he read everything.

"Which one's she leaning toward?" he asked Dana, nodding at Julia, and Dana said, "The one that costs more," and her father laughed once, short, before he saw Julia's face.

"What?" he said. "What is it?"

"Nothing," Julia said. "Read the columns."

He read them, right side up now, silent, his finger moving down each line the way her mother's had. When he finished he didn't laugh again. He sat down in her mother's chair and said, "Okay," and then, after a moment, "Which one was yours?"

"The Willow," Dana said. "But she says we should sleep on it."

Maxime arrived at the pool at six forty, before the lifeguards had finished unhooking the lane ropes, because Coach Reyes had told him that if he wanted to write his own training program he would have to see the pool empty first. He had a spiral notebook and a pencil he kept behind his ear like a carpenter. On the whiteboard by the office, someone had written lap swim 7-9 in blue marker, and beneath it, in different handwriting, GO MAXIME, which he suspected was his little sister, Noor, who had a key because she fed the filter fish in the office tank.

He wanted this program more than he had wanted anything since he'd made the county squad at fifteen. Two weeks ago he'd watched regionals from the bleachers, third alternate, and his father had put a hand on his shoulder and said nothing, which in their family's patrimony of silence was roughly a eulogy. So Maxime had drawn a grid on the first page of the notebook, seven columns, and filled Monday through Sunday with drills, kick sets, sprints, more drills, until his friend Dana had looked at it over lunch and gone morose in the particular way she did when she thought someone was about to ruin themselves.

"Where's the rest," she said.

"Rest is for people who aren't behind," Maxime said, and she had rolled her eyes so hard she had to steady her sandwich.

That had been Thursday. Now it was Saturday morning, and Noor was sitting cross-legged on the diving block with a book about sleep, of all things, because she was doing a school project on it and had sequestered herself at the pool where, she claimed, the hum of the pumps helped her think. She read aloud without being asked, which was her way of being useful. "In a 2011 Stanford study," she read, "basketball players who aimed for ten hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from seven point nine to eight point eight successful shots out of ten."

"That can't be right," Maxime said, treading water at the end of lane four. "Ten hours? Who has ten hours?"

"They aimed for it," Noor said. "In bed. Nightly." She turned the page as though the matter were settled.

He pulled himself out and sat dripping on the gutter, doing the arithmetic he could not stop doing lately. He practiced four hours a day. He also stayed up until two most nights, doing homework badly, watching videos of the Beijing final frame by frame, lying in the dark composing programs in his head. If the basketball players had gone from 7.9 to 8.8 out of ten just from being in bed, then the hours he spent planning at 2 a.m. were not hours in the bank. They were withdrawals. He wrote in the notebook, in the Saturday column where he had scheduled a fourth sprint set, the word SLEEP, then crossed it out because it looked stupid, then wrote it again smaller.

Dana arrived at nine with a thermos and her own agenda, which she announced immediately. "I need the shallow lane at four for the kids' lesson," she said. She had been trying for a month to get the rec department to let her run a beginners' class for the neighborhood kids, some of whom, she said, only knew how to jump in and hold their breath. "If you're writing the big fancy program, put it in the program. You have the coach's ear. I don't."

"I have the coach's elbow," Maxime said. "She gives me the whiteboard sometimes."

"Then write it on the whiteboard and photograph it. Guilt is a renewable resource."

He laughed, and then, because he was thinking about the grid, he pulled Dana down to sit on the wet concrete and showed her the page. "Tell me what's wrong with it," he said, "but the real thing, not the rest thing."

She looked at it for a long time, chewing the thermos cap. "There's no warm-up that isn't just swimming slower," she said finally. "You go from nothing to fifty-meter repeats like the water owes you money. And Saturday is insane, and Sunday is insane, and everything's insane. But the warm-up thing, that's the structural one."

He thought about the basketball players again, their free throws rising by almost a whole shot out of ten, and about how he had always believed the body was a machine you ran hotter and hotter. The study said nothing about why, and Noor's book said nothing more, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he did not know whether ten hours of bed would do anything at all for a swimmer, or whether it only worked on shooters, or whether it was one of those findings that evaporated when you tried to live inside it. But there was a version of his program where the drills were the same and the container around them was different, and he could not find a reason not to test it except vanity, which he did not think was a reason.

He erased the week with the side of his fist, which smeared, and started over. Monday, drills, after a real warm-up, ankle rotations and band work and eight easy laps. Wednesday, drills. Friday, drills, shorter. Sunday, nothing. In the margin he wrote 10 hrs in bed? with the question mark, because he refused to write it as a command when he did not yet believe it as one. Then, because Dana was still waiting, he took the blue marker and wrote beneath lap swim: 4 PM SHALLOW LANE, DANA'S KIDS' CLASS, and drew a sun around it so the lifeguards could not miss it.

"You didn't have to do the sun," Dana said, but she was smiling into her thermos.

At four o'clock he came back to watch, ostensibly to time his own easy laps, actually to see whether anyone showed up. Six kids came, two of them the twins from building C who had never been in water deeper than their bathtub, and Dana got in first and held out both hands, and the smaller twin took them and stepped off the edge into the shallow lane with her whole face scrunched like a person leaping off a cliff.

"Kick," Dana said. "Like you're mad at the water."

The kid kicked, and moved, and came up spitting and delighted, and Maxime wrote one more line in the notebook, and it said only: water temp 26, she'll need the shorter noodles.

The bookshop on Miller Street held its Thursday night club in the back corner, between the poetry shelves and a radiator that clanked every few minutes. Nolan had been coming for two months, since his senior year English teacher announced she was leaving and he wanted somewhere to keep arguing about books. Tonight the group was six people and the novel was Jane Eyre, and Nolan had promised himself he would say something that mattered.

He had marked a passage on page 271, where Jane returns to Thornfield and Rochester reminds her that he pays her wages, thirty pounds a year, and that she depends on him for everything. He had underlined it three times in pencil and then, ashamed of the pencil, tried to erase the extra lines. He wanted to say something about it. He had spent the weekend reading a photocopy of a critical essay that Ms. Andaya had left in his mailbox at school, and the essay's vocabulary sat in his head like borrowed furniture.

When Priya, who ran the shop, opened the floor, Nolan cleared his throat too loudly. "I want to try something," he said. "Not like an opinion exactly. More like a lens." He read the passage aloud, the wages, the dependence, the line where Rochester says he has bought her. "If you look at it through a Marxist lens," he said, "the romance is also a transaction. She's selling her labor. He owns the house."

"Sure," said Marcus, who was fifty and read everything with a pencil behind his ear. "But it's a love story. That's not nothing."

"I'm not saying it's nothing. I'm saying it's both." Nolan turned the essay over in his mind, trying to find a way to hold the two claims at once without dropping either.

Then Priya pulled a slim paperback off the shelf behind her, an old Penguin edition of The Communist Manifesto, its spine cracked white. "This might be your lens in its original form," she said, and found the page with her thumb. She read aloud: "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. That's how the first section opens. Marx and Engels, 1848." She looked up. "Does it fit the novel? Victorian England, a governess and her employer?"

The radiator clanked. Nolan thought about it. "Jane's not a factory worker," he said slowly. "She's educated, sort of gentry without money. So the class struggle in her case isn't barricades. It's that she can't marry Rochester without becoming his dependent, because her wages are nothing and his property is everything. The whole plot turns on that imbalance." He paused, aware that everyone was looking at him. "But here's what I can't settle. When she inherits money and comes back to him as an equal, is that the book fixing the class problem or just hiding it? One character getting lucky doesn't change the structure."

"That governess," Marcus said. "She's one woman, standing in for a whole class of them."

"Synecdoche," Nolan said, and was pleased that the word arrived on time. "The one standing for the many. The essay called it that." He had not expected to enjoy saying it. He had expected to feel like an impostor, the way he felt in the college writing sample he was supposed to mail by Friday. Instead the word did work that "symbol" would not have done.

Priya set the Manifesto on the table between the teacups. "The trouble with that lens," she said, "is it can flatten things. Love becomes wages, the person becomes a position. You reify them, turn living relations into dead objects, and then you've explained the book by killing it."

"Maybe that's the honest answer, though," Nolan said. "The lens shows you something real and it costs you something. Jane Eyre as a transaction, Jane Eyre as a love story. I can hold both. What I can't do is pick one and pretend the other isn't there." He heard his own voice go up at the end, like a question, and let it.

Marcus wrote something in his margin. Priya poured more tea. Outside the front window a bus went by, and its light crossed the poetry shelves and the faces around the table, and Nolan turned back to page 271 and read the passage aloud a second time, slower, listening for what he had missed the first time.

Dominic had the kitchen to himself by four o'clock, which was the only reason he had agreed to do it. His mother was on her second shift at the clinic, his father had taken the twins to a birthday party, and his grandmother was in the living room with the television turned to a panel show where one pundit after another explained the economy to nobody in particular. He had promised a proper dinner, not pasta from a box, and he had decided on breaded chicken with a homemade aioli, because a kid at school had brought some in a jar once and Dominic had thought about it for a week.

The recipe said to whisk one egg yolk with mustard and lemon, then add a cup of oil in a thin stream while whisking without stopping. He set the bowl on a damp towel so it would not skate across the counter, separated the yolk with the shells the way his grandmother had shown him years ago, and began. For a while it worked. The mixture turned pale and thick and he felt the particular smugness of someone watching a plan hold together. Then his elbow knocked the measuring cup and a quarter cup of oil went in at once, and the whole thing went thin and strange, oil floating in a yellowish liquid that refused to combine no matter how hard he whipped it.

He stood over the bowl, whisk in hand, doing the arithmetic of the evening. If the sauce was ruined he would fall back on butter, which was fine, which was what everyone expected anyway. He was still deciding when his grandmother came in for water and stopped beside him. She looked at the bowl and then at him. "Split," she said. He said yes, he had ruined it, he was sorry. She pulled a chair from the table and sat down.

"You started with the yolk?" she asked. He said he had, one yolk, exactly like the recipe. "And it broke when the oil came in too fast." She reached into the fridge, took out another egg, and handed it to him without standing up. "Clean bowl. Yolk in it, a spoon of the broken mess, whisk. Then the rest of the oil, slow." He asked what the second yolk could possibly do that the first one had not done, and she said, "Lecithin," as if that settled it. When he kept whisking without understanding, she added that the proteins in the yolk were emulsifiers too, and that was what held the oil in the water, tiny drops, kept apart so the sauce did not come apart.

He cracked the egg, dropped in a spoon of the curdled mixture, and whisked. It thickened almost immediately, faster than the first batch had, and he added the oil a few milliliters at a time, his wrist aching, watching the sauce climb the wires of the whisk in a slow gleam that seemed to burnish the steel itself. When it held, he stood back and looked at it. His grandmother drank her water and said it was the same with people, and he said probably, and she laughed at him for that.

While the chicken rested under foil, she stayed in the chair and grew querulous about the panel show, the pundits, the state of everything, and he listened with half his attention because the other half was still on the bowl. He had started the evening believing that a recipe was a set of instructions you followed and it worked or it didn't, and that his failure meant the dinner was over. Now he understood that the sauce had not failed so much as run out of its capacity, and that capacity could be added back in, one yolk at a time. But he was honest enough with himself to notice what he did not know: he could not have predicted the split, and he could not have said how much oil one yolk could hold before the next failure, and if his grandmother had not come in for water he would be melting butter.

The twins came home loud, his father behind them with cake, and they ate at the table with the aioli in a dish in the center, everyone dipping, nobody asking where it came from. His father said it was better than the store kind, and Dominic said he had almost thrown it out, and told the story of the second yolk. The twins wanted to know if they could break one on purpose next time and fix it, and he said he didn't see why not, though he wasn't sure they'd learn anything that way, since fixing a thing you'd broken on purpose was different from fixing a thing you needed.

Later, washing the dishes while his grandmother dried, he thought about telling her he had decided something, that he understood things now, and he decided against saying it out loud because it wasn't entirely true. He knew what he had seen. He knew the rescue worked. Whether the whole evening had been a success or a near miss depended on a question he couldn't answer, which was how much of the result was him and how much was the egg. His grandmother put the last bowl in the cabinet and turned off the light over the stove.

"Next time," she said, "use a bigger bowl."

I never cared about the tempering unit, which is why I signed up for it twice. That was a joke I told people, and like most of my jokes it worked because it was almost a lie. The truth was that last spring I had bombed the practical, left the room before the chocolate set, and never gone back to look at the dull, streaky results. Ms. Okoye had left them on the counter with my name card beside them for two days. I told everyone I'd forgotten. I told myself that too, and mostly it held.

The second time around, we had marble slabs, bench scrapers, thermometers, and a room that smelled like warm cocoa butter. I was paired with Nadia, who was morose that week over a rejected college application and stirred her chocolate like she was punishing it. What we were doing was called tabling: pouring two thirds of the chocolate onto cold marble, working it back and forth until it cooled and thickened, then returning it to the warm bowl. Ms. Okoye demonstrated once, said the words "form V crystals" without further comment, and left us to it. She believed, or claimed to believe, that we learned more from failure than from instruction, a philosophy I privately thought was convenient for someone paid to walk around with a clipboard.

My chocolate bloomed anyway. Gray stripes spread across my sample like weather. Nadia's, despite the punitive stirring, snapped clean and glossy, and she had the grace not to gloat, which somehow made it worse. I scraped my batch into the discard bowl and started over with the last of our couverture, and halfway through the tabling Nadia abandoned her slab to text someone, and I was alone with a thermometer reading a degree too high and a spoon going nowhere.

Here is where I have to be honest, since you'll hear it from Devi anyway. Devi had sent me a message that morning, and I hadn't answered it. She'd read it over my shoulder later and I let her believe I'd only just seen it, which is its own small accounting. The message said: "No marble slab at my house. I used the seeding method instead. Chopped up some leftover store-bought chocolate that was still tempered and stirred it into my melted chocolate. The melted part copies the crystals from the chopped part, form V, and sets shiny. Cheap Easter bunny, technically a hero."

So then there was Nadia, leaning over my shoulder, morose and curious at once, and there was Devi's message glowing on the counter. The choice in front of me was not really chocolate. I had spent a year dividing the world into people who followed the hard technique and people who took shortcuts, and I had put Devi in the second pile and myself in the first, and the whole dichotomy had been doing me no favors. It was, if I'm honest, less a way of thinking than a way of losing with dignity. My chocolate was currently demonstrating the dignity part.

I chopped a bar from the pantry shelf, checked the label, checked that it was glossy and snapped clean, and stirred the pieces into my too-warm bowl a few at a time until the thermometer came down. Nadia watched me do it. "Is that cheating?" she asked. "It's seeding," I said. "Tempered chocolate in, and the rest copies it." She said that seemed like less work, which from Nadia was litotes for admiration.

What I hadn't told Devi, and what I'd told Ms. Okoye at the start of term, was that I'd never even attempted the retest I'd promised myself. I'd said I forgot the practical, forgot the results, forgot the whole unit. Unreliable, my brother would say, meaning me. When the seeded chocolate came down to temperature, I dipped a knife tip and laid the strip on parchment, and we both stood there while Nadia's timer counted and my heart did something embarrassing.

The strip set in five minutes and snapped when I broke it, and the break was glossy at the edge, clean as anything off Nadia's slab. Devi texted again while I was holding the two pieces side by side: "Did you try it or are you still being a snob about your marble." I typed "maybe" and then deleted it and typed "it worked" and then deleted that too, because both were true and neither was the whole of it. Whether the tabling mattered more than the seeding, whether the technique was worth the year I'd spent guarding it, whether Devi would still want to talk to me if she knew how long I'd waited to answer her message, all of that stayed open on the counter with the parchment and the thermometer.

I put the two chocolate pieces in my pocket instead of eating them, which Nadia noticed and mercifully didn't comment on. Then I wrote "worked, sorry, call you tonight" and pressed send.

The bonfire was taller than Jeremy's uncle's house, which meant it was tall enough that the fire marshal, if such a person existed in this part of town, would have wept. Jeremy stood at the edge of the temple parking lot with his cousin Priya, who was explaining, with much gesticulating, exactly how the thing was going to collapse.

"It always leans north," she said, flapping her arm like a heron. "Every year. And every year my dad says it won't, and every year it does, and every year we move the aunties."

Jeremy had come because his mother had come, and because missing Holi at his aunt's temple was not an option that anyone had offered him. It was the night before the colors, the night of the fire itself, and the parking lot smelled like diesel and marigolds, which he decided was not a bad smell, just an honest one.

"I looked it up," he said. "The whole thing is astronomical. It's the full moon of Phalguna, usually in March. The fire's tonight, and the colors tomorrow morning, because the festival starts with the bonfire the night before."

Priya squinted at him. "Did you just learn my own religion off the internet?"

"Parts of it. I wanted to know why the date moves around."

"And what did the internet say about why the fire leans north?"

"That wasn't covered."

Her father overheard them, because her father overheard everything, and he arrived in the phlegmatic way he had, moving as though the crowd parted around him by prior arrangement. "It's called Holika Dahan," he said, and patted the woodpile like a horse he had trained. Then he went back to arguing with three men about the lean, which, Jeremy noted, leaned north.

Priya tugged Jeremy's sleeve. "Come on. If you're going to be an investigator, investigate."

She led him past the aunties on their folding chairs, past a boy trying to trade a laddu for a sparkler, to the temple's back hallway, where a bulletin board held a printout of the festival schedule. It was there, under a heading in both English and Hindi: Holika Dahan, full moon night, Phalguna. March, this year. Below it, a paragraph about Prahlad and the demon Holika, who could not be burned and who burned anyway, because protection, the paragraph said, does not belong to the one who misuses it.

"So it's a story about a fire that didn't do what it was supposed to," Jeremy said.

"It's a story about a fire that did what it was supposed to. You have it backwards."

"Fine. It's a story where the fire had a moral."

"That's not so strange. Your chemistry teacher has opinions about sodium."

He laughed, and then he didn't, because something in it snagged. He had spent the drive over rehearsing what he'd say if anyone asked, some version of I'm here for family, not for the metaphysics, which was a sentence he'd invented in the car and already regretted. But standing in the hallway with the schedule, he found he couldn't keep the two things apart so cleanly. The date was the full moon, that was physics. The fire was Holika, that was story. And the wood was leaning north, and the crowd was singing, and the whole thing was one event, not two, whatever he'd planned to say about it.

Outside, the singing had gotten louder. Priya grabbed his wrist. "It's starting. Watch the lean. Watch it."

The priest circled the pile with a lamp, and the men with the long poles set the base alight, and the flames took their time, the way big fires do, and then found the diesel and stopped taking their time. The heat arrived before the sound of the crowd. And the pile leaned. It leaned north, majestically, in flagrant disregard of her father's predictions, and a hundred phones went up, and somebody's uncle began gesticulating at the structure as though he could negotiate with it.

"North," Priya shouted over the roar. "Say it."

"North. I concede everything."

Her father appeared behind them, arms crossed, watching the pillar of sparks climb toward a sky where, if the smoke hadn't been in the way, the full moon would have been sitting right there, exactly on schedule, in its month, doing its ancient work. "The lean is traditional," he announced, without a hint of apology, and Priya made a noise like a kettle.

"Tomorrow," she told Jeremy, "you get the colors. Fair warning, I have three buckets and no mercy, and I know you didn't bring a white shirt on purpose."

"I didn't bring a white shirt because I'm not a fool."

"You'll stand out anyway," she said, and shoved a laddu into his hand, and pulled him back toward the fire before the aunties claimed all the good folding chairs.

The U-Haul followed them like a patient animal, and Hannah watched it in the side mirror until the highway curved and it swung out of view. Her father drove. Her mother sat turned halfway around in the passenger seat, holding a cooler shut with one hand because the latch had broken in Beaumont, or maybe before Beaumont; nobody had bothered to check. In the back seat, Hannah had her backpack, a shoebox of photographs, and the last text from Priya still glowing on her phone: "call me when you get there or sooner."

"Eleven point seven," her father said. He said it the way he announced gas prices, as though the number itself were the news.

"Eleven point seven what," Hannah said.

"Moves. A person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime. It's a Census Bureau estimate. They used 2007 survey data." He tapped the wheel twice, pleased with himself. "So this is what, number six for you? You're ahead of schedule."

"That's supposed to comfort me?"

"It's supposed to contextualize you." He glanced at the mirror to check on the truck again. "Most people do this. Most people do it a lot."

Hannah put the phone face-down on her knee. Ahead of schedule, like moving was an accomplishment you racked up, a merit badge for leaving. In her old town, Priya's mother had lived in the same house since she was four, and Priya used to say the house knew her, which Hannah had found funny and now found unbearable. Her own parents talked about relocation the way they talked about weather, something ductile enough to bend around, a thing that reshaped itself to whatever plans they made. She had gone along with it, mostly. She had let herself be persuaded. Her mother had cajoled her through March with milkshakes and promises about the new town having a real indie theater, and Hannah had let it work because resisting took energy she needed for finals.

They stopped for lunch at a diner outside Henderson, the kind with laminated menus and a waitress who called everyone "sweetheart" and meant it. Hannah's mother asked for a booth near the window and then, without being asked, ordered Hannah's fries the way she liked them, extra crispy, well done, whatever the kitchen would tolerate. It was a small thing. Hannah noticed it anyway and hated how much it mattered, that she was keeping score of kindnesses from people who were the reason she sat in this booth at all.

"Can I see your phone," her father said while they waited, and she handed it over because he wanted to look at the route, and instead he opened the browser and slid the phone back with the screen turned toward her. "I didn't make it up."

She read it. United States Census Bureau, based on 2007 survey data, a person could expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime. There it was, the same number, sitting in plain black text as if it were nothing. Eleven point seven. She thought of Priya's mother's house, of the 0.7 of a move, what that would even mean, standing in a doorway with one box, deciding. The number made the whole thing ordinary, and that was exactly what she couldn't decide how to feel about. Ordinary meant she wasn't singled out for punishment. Ordinary also meant nobody was going to stop it from happening again, and again, up to eleven and a fraction.

"You could have asked before you looked through my phone," she said, but without heat.

"You left it unlocked."

"That's not the same as yes."

He acknowledged this with a small tilt of his head, and the fries arrived, extra crispy, and her mother salted them before pushing the plate across, and outside the window the truck sat in the lot with their whole house inside it, compressed. Hannah ate slowly. Maybe the moves stacked up the way her dad said, one life distributed across a dozen towns, and you belonged to all of them a little. Maybe Priya was right that you belonged to one place completely or nowhere at all. Both felt true in her mouth at once, and she was tired of being told she had to pick.

Back in the car, with Henderson shrinking behind them, she picked up the phone and typed, "we are officially 3.7 moves ahead of nothing, i'll explain later, i love you." Then she leaned forward between the seats and said, "Mom, hold the cooler, I'll fix the latch at the next stop."

Her mother looked at her for a second before smiling. "There's a hair tie in the cup holder."

"Perfect," Hannah said, and reached for it.

The quarry filled with pale light by mid-afternoon, the cut walls of limestone catching the sun the way a bowl catches water. Sofia spread her notes on the flat top of a boulder and weighted the pages with smaller stones, because the wind off the water was insouciant about other people's work, flipping whatever it pleased. Dex sat cross-legged beside her with his laptop balanced on his knees, its screen dulled by the glare.

"Run it again," she said.

He pressed play on the animation she'd built for their Earth science presentation. Molecules drifted across the screen, and little arrows of infrared radiation rose from a cartoon ground, bounced off the drifting shapes, and came back down. She had drawn every frame herself in a notebook over three nights, then photographed and sequenced them. The point she wanted to make was simple in her head and impossible in her mouth: sunlight comes through, heat tries to leave, gases like carbon dioxide send part of it back. "It's not a wall," she kept saying to Dex. "It's more like the air remembers the warmth a little longer than it should."

Then he showed her the graph. It was the real one, the carbon dioxide record measured on a Hawaiian volcano across the last century, and she had seen it before in the textbook but never alone, never with time to run her finger along it. The line began low and level, wobbling faintly each year like something breathing. Then it bent. Then it climbed. The bend came in the same decades her grandmother was born, then her mother, then her, three generations stacked along a curve that did not care about any of them. She copied the shape onto a fresh page so she could carry it without a screen.

"So I found something," Dex said, and he hesitated, which was unlike him. In her draft, the one she'd already printed for the teacher, she had written a confident sentence: the Gulf Stream alone keeps Europe's winters mild. It had sounded authoritative. She had liked how it sounded. Dex turned the laptop toward her and read aloud from a study led by a researcher named Richard Seager, published in 2002. "He argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters."

"That can't be right," Sofia said. "Everyone says the Gulf Stream."

"I know. That's why I checked twice."

She sat with it. The quarry was quiet except for water dripping somewhere below the ledge, patient attrition wearing the rock down into something smoother, grain by grain, on a schedule no one kept. She thought about how a thing everyone says gets repeated until it hardens into fact, and how a graph does the opposite, keeps its soft shape, admits its wobble. Two ways of knowing, and she had been trusting the wrong one, or maybe trusting both and never checking where they disagreed.

"Say the Seager line again," she said. "Slowly." He said it, and she wrote it down word for word, then crossed out the sentence in her draft and wrote a new one with his pen, which was better than hers and she told him so. He shrugged, pleased.

That evening her grandmother sent her a message, the kind she typed with one finger on a phone with enormous letters:

Sofia, your mother says you are doing a talk about the air. When I was a girl in February the canal froze thick enough to walk on and the men played football on it. I have not seen it freeze like that again. I don't know if that means anything. But you like the numbers, so maybe you can tell me. Come Sunday if the bus is running. There is cake and it is the kind you like.

Sofia read it three times. Her grandmother's canal and the Hawaiian volcano had never met, and yet the wobbling line on the graph, that faint yearly breath, was winter and summer, was ice and thaw, was somewhere a canal freezing or not freezing. She could not say how much of the warming curve was the canal. She could say the curve was real, and that the old sentence about Europe needed correcting, and that correcting it felt less like losing than like being let in on something.

On Sunday she took the bus. She brought the page where she'd copied the graph by hand, and she set it on the kitchen table between the teapot and the cake, and put her finger on the low, level beginning. "This is your canal," she said.

Her grandmother leaned close, glasses down on her nose, and touched the climbing end of the line. "And this?"

"That's me," Sofia said, and cut her a slice of cake first.

Eli had been meaning to give Marcus the note for two days, and practice on Thursday was the last chance before the relay trial. He had commandeered the corner of the bleachers where the gym bags lived, sitting with his phone out, rereading a screenshot his older sister had sent him from a college psych course. In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise their essays when the teacher's critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them. His sister had added, "Works on roommates too." Eli didn't know if it worked on best friends you'd known since fourth grade, friends whose flyaway left elbow you'd watched ten thousand times.

The problem was simple and not simple. Marcus had started rushing his second exchange, and at the last meet it had cost them nearly half a second, which in a relay is an ocean. Half a second was the difference between qualifying and watching the sectional final from the folding chairs. Coach had said something vague about "cleaning up transitions," which told Marcus nothing and let him pretend the fault belonged to daylight or the official's whistle. Eli was the one who stood next to Marcus on the line. Eli was the one who could actually see it.

He tried it out in his head during the warmup laps. You're dropping your elbow early. True, specific, useless, because Marcus heard any correction the way he heard his mother about homework: something to be survived. Last season Eli had told him his start angle was off and Marcus had gone petulant for a week, doing the corrected angle with exaggerated slowness whenever he caught Eli watching, a performance of obedience that made them both feel small.

But Eli had also watched Coach Delgado fix a girl on the junior varsity, Priya, whose handoffs had been worse than Marcus's. Coach hadn't softened the criticism. She'd been blunt about the timing, and then she'd said, "I'm telling you because I think you can run with the varsity squad by October." Priya had stopped rolling her eyes at corrections after that. She'd started asking for them. Eli had assumed it was just Priya being mature, but the screenshot made him wonder if the sentence had done something, if belief wasn't a garnish but an ingredient.

Practice divided itself the way it always did, varsity on the near lane, everyone else drifting to the far one, a kind of speciation by stopwatch that Eli usually found funny and tonight found a little sad. He and Marcus were on the same side of it, for now. That was the whole point of telling him. If the elbow kept drifting, they'd end up on opposite sides of the gym, and Marcus would never believe it hadn't been said out of cruelty.

They ran the exchange four times before water break. On the fourth, Marcus rushed it again, the baton slapping into Eli's palm late and crooked, and Marcus's face did the thing it did, the wince he disguised as squinting at the scoreboard clock. Eli walked over with his bottle and made himself start before the silence got too heavy to cross.

"Your left elbow's flying open on the second exchange," Eli said. "You're losing the baton angle, and it's costing us like half a second." Marcus's jaw set, and Eli kept going, faster than he'd planned. "And I'm only saying it because I know you can run a clean exchange. You've done it. I think you're the best sprinter on this team when your form holds."

Marcus unscrewed his cap and drank for a long time. "Half a second," he said finally.

"Half a second."

"Fine. Watch the next one, then. Tell me if it's still ugly." They ran it again, and the elbow stayed tucked, and the baton landed in Eli's palm like it had been aimed there. It could have been the rest between reps. It could have been that Marcus was already tired of rushing. Eli didn't know, and he wasn't going to pretend he did; one clean pass wasn't a study. But at the end of practice Marcus lingered by the door instead of leaving first, and said, "Tomorrow, same thing. If I screw it up, tell me. Don't just tell Coach."

"Deal," Eli said, and picked up both their bags to carry them out.

Logan's father backed the sedan into the far corner of the Kmart lot, where the painted lines had faded to the color of old bone, and cut the engine. "Switch," he said, and got out into the November wind without another word, which was his way of pretending this was ordinary.

It was not ordinary. Logan had waited since August, when his mother had taken him to the licensing office for the permit test and then, at the last minute, refused to come inside. She sat in the car with the heater running while he stood in line beneath a poster he read four times because the line barely moved. The poster said that according to the CDC, drivers aged sixteen to nineteen had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. He had passed the test, walked out with the paper card in his fist, and slid into the passenger seat without mentioning the poster, and his mother had driven home on the far right of the road, both hands on the wheel, and said nothing either.

Now, four months later, his father tossed the keys across the roof of the car and Logan caught them against his chest. He adjusted the mirror too far, corrected it, adjusted it again. His father had already lowered the radio, which had been droning about inflation and stalled growth and something the commentator called stagflation, a word Logan filed away to look up later, though he gathered from context it meant prices climbing while the economy went nowhere, a kind of trap with no exit.

"Feet first," his father said. "Brake, then start it." Logan pressed the brake and the engine turned over and the whole car hummed around him like something alive that had merely been sleeping. He let off the brake too soon and they rolled an inch before he clamped down, and his father laughed, one short syllable, not unkind.

For half an hour it was only this: gas, brake, the wheel pulled in slow ovals around the empty cart corrals. Logan discovered that the car was parsimonious with information, telling him almost nothing until he asked with his hands and feet, and then telling him everything at once. His father said "wider" and "earlier" and once, quietly, "you're begging the wheel, don't beg it," and Logan understood that the machine could not be coaxed or beguiled into gentleness. It did exactly what he did, only larger.

"Pull up to that light pole and stop," his father said. "Then back around it." Logan lined up on the pole, checked the mirror his mother would have checked, and eased backward, and it was there, in the crooked slow arc of reverse, that the poster came back to him whole. Almost three times, per mile driven. He let the car stop and sat with his hands at ten and two.

"Dad," he said. "Did Mom see that poster at the DMV? The one about teen drivers." His father was quiet long enough that the ticking of the cooling engine became audible. "She stood outside last time because of it," he finally said. "August. You were inside taking the test and she was reading it through the window. She made me promise not to tell you."

Logan looked out at the empty lot, the cart corral, the light pole he had just circled without hitting. He thought of her silence on the drive home and had read it, all these months, as disappointment in him, and now he could not tell whether it had been fear instead, or whether the two were even separable. The numbers were the numbers. He was sixteen, and per mile he was more dangerous than his father, and no amount of care in this lot changed that yet; and still his mother had signed the permission slip, and still his father had driven him here, and both of those were also facts. "So she's been scared this whole time," Logan said, and it was not quite a question.

"She's been letting you drive anyway," his father said. "Same thing, sometimes." He pointed at the far end of the lot, where the empty spaces stretched out in long faded rows. "Take us down there. Full stop at the last line, and then home."

Logan checked the mirror, signaled out of habit into the emptiness, and pressed the gas.

The printer at the public library charged fifteen cents a page, and Juliette had four dollars in coins, counted twice, in the pocket of her jacket. She logged into the computer by the window and opened her application to Alder College, the school her cousin had gone to, the school with the quiet quadrangle she had visited once in October and thought about every night since. The screen said Early Decision deadline: November 1. Today was October 26.

"You're here again," said Marcus from the front desk as she passed him for more coins. He was a college sophomore on work-study, and he had watched her come in every afternoon that week. "What are you printing, a book?"

"Just forms." She set the quarters on the counter. "One form, a lot of times, because I keep changing it."

"Which school?"

"Alder."

"Early Decision?" He said it the way people name a diagnosis. "You know that's binding, right? If they take you and the financial aid is okay, you have to go. You have to pull all your other applications."

"I know it's binding." She hadn't, entirely, until Tuesday, when she had read the fine print on the agreement three times in a row at this same terminal. The sentence was plain: admitted with acceptable financial aid, she must enroll, and withdraw everywhere else. What the sentence did not say was what counted as acceptable, and that was the part her mother kept circling when Juliette read it to her in the kitchen.

Her mother had two positions and stated both at dinner. The first was that Alder was the place, that Juliette had lit up on that visit, that some things you recognize once and then spend years mistaking for something else. The second was that they had no idea what any school would actually cost them until the offers came, and offers came in the spring, and Alder's estimate was just an estimate. "You can't compare what you haven't seen," her mother said, sliding the salt across the table as though it were evidence. Her uncle, on the phone from Houston, had been more effusive about Alder, calling it an investment, a door, a family standard now that Kaya had gone, and Juliette had felt the pull of that praise and distrusted it in equal measure, because praise cost him nothing.

She printed the form anyway and carried it to the long table near the biography section, where Kaya herself sat across from her, home for the weekend, cracking open a thermos of coffee she was not supposed to have in the building. "So you're doing it," Kaya said.

"I printed the form. That's not the same as doing it."

"Then do it. It's Alder. It's basically yours with your grades."

"Nothing is basically anything." Juliette flattened the page with her palm. "If I apply regular, I hear in March, I get real offers from five schools, and I compare them. If I apply Early Decision, I hear in December, and if the aid is what they call acceptable, I go, and every other application is withdrawn. Done. Before I've seen a single other number." She heard her mother's cadence in her own voice and stopped.

"Kaya, did you apply early?"

"No. Regular. But I wasn't sure about Alder the way you are." Kaya wrapped both hands around the thermos. "That's the difference. You are sure. I watched you on that quad. You looked like you'd been issued a key."

Juliette looked down at the signature line. Two true things sat side by side in her, refusing to merge: that she wanted Alder with a specificity she could not generate for any other school, and that wanting something did not make it affordable, and binding meant betting the whole spring on one school's idea of acceptable. There was a version where she signed tonight and a version where she waited for the March offers, and she could not make either one the obvious one. Waiting felt prudent and also like a small betrayal; signing felt like conviction and also like complicity with a system that asked her to promise before it showed her the price. She noticed her pulse palpitating in her wrist, fast and shallow, the way it did before a race, and she pressed her thumb over it until it slowed.

The overhead lights clicked to half brightness, the library's signal for closing. Kaya capped the thermos. Marcus called out, "Fifteen minutes," from the desk, not unkindly. Juliette folded the form once, then twice, and put it in her jacket pocket, where it sat against the coins, the whole decision now the size of her palm. At the door, Kaya held it open and said, "Whatever you do, do it before the first, okay? Don't let it decide itself." Juliette stepped out into the parking lot and stood a moment under the streetlight, taking the paper out and unfolding it again.

The parking lot behind the closed hardware store had faded lines and one leaning light pole, and Savannah had chosen it because her mother would never think to look for her here. She sat in the driver's seat of the borrowed Corolla with her hands at ten and two, the way the pamphlet showed, while Mr. Okafor settled into the passenger seat and dropped a clipboard on his knee.

"I'm going to get my license before Labor Day," she said. "I have to. My brother's in a rehab place forty minutes out, and my mother works, and the visitation hours are two to four on Sundays." She had rehearsed the whole speech in the shower, and now it came out too fast, like she was afraid he would stop her.

Mr. Okafor buckled his seatbelt. "Turn the engine on first. Then we can litigate your Sunday plans."

She turned the key. The car shuddered awake under her, and she gripped the wheel harder than she needed to. For twenty minutes they did nothing but circles, wide lazy arcs around the light pole, her foot learning the small difference between the brake and the almost-brake. Twice she killed the engine and twice she restarted it without being told, and Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard both times, which she decided not to ask about.

"All right," he said finally. "Parking lot's done. We go on the road."

The road was a two-lane stretch behind the strip mall, empty enough at nine in the morning that she could hear her own pulse. She merged, sort of, and drove, and it was working, it was actually working, until she came up behind a delivery truck and realized she was close enough to read the phone number printed on its back doors. Her mother, who read contracts for a living and had once called Savannah's driving school contract "trenchant, in the way a dull knife is trenchant," would have said she was drafting a subpoena for a collision. Savannah eased off the gas but drifted forward again anyway, her foot convinced that closer meant safer, that if she could see the truck's mirrors the truck could see her.

"Don't slow down," Mr. Okafor said. "Just do something else. Watch the truck ahead of us. When it passes a fixed point, like that lamppost coming up, count seconds until we reach that same point."

"Why?"

"Try it. Out loud."

The truck's back bumper crossed the base of the lamppost. "One one-thousand, two one-thousand," she said, and her front bumper arrived at the same lamppost just after two. She checked the mirror. The gap between her and the truck looked enormous now, a whole polite room of empty pavement, and nothing bad had happened because of it. The truck hadn't escaped her. Nobody had honked. She tried it again at the next signpost, watching the truck pass the sign and counting, and got to three one-thousand before she reached it, and it still felt wrong, still felt like she was letting the world get ahead of her, but the wrongness was only in her foot, which kept wanting to close the gap like an apology.

"It's called the two-second rule," Mr. Okafor said, "in case anybody asks."

They drove to the end of the strip and back. Savannah held her count the whole way, at signs and mailboxes and a fire hydrant with a dented cap, and at a red light she sat with her hands still at ten and two and thought about her mother, who had spent the whole summer after Danny's arrest saying that if you loved people you stayed close to them, you stayed on their case, you did not let one inch open up between you. Savannah had believed her, had practically moved into Danny's room. But Danny had told her, the last visit, through plexiglass, that the inch was the only place he could breathe. She looked at the gap between her car and the truck idling ahead, counted it out of habit, three seconds, plenty, and thought that maybe you could hold on to people and still leave them room to move, though she couldn't have said where the holding stopped and the room began. That part she would have to work out the way she was working out the brake, by doing it and getting it wrong and doing it again.

"Same time Thursday," Mr. Okafor said when she parked, crooked but within the lines. "You'll count your way onto the highway."

"Thursday," she said. She was already planning the route to Danny's, every sign and lamppost along it, counting the seconds between her and everything ahead.

Samuel had the board across two sawhorses in his grandmother's backyard, sanding it down to bare wood by noon. It was a skateboard deck, old and water-stained, that he had bought for five dollars at a yard sale with the intention of turning it into something Dahlia could take to college in the fall. She left in eleven days. He had promised her a deck painted the exact orange of the sunset they had watched from the water tower the summer they were fifteen, that impossible color neither of them had been able to name afterward, though they had tried the whole walk home.

He started with cadmium yellow and added red a drop at a time on a chipped saucer. The first mixtures were promising, warm as toast, and then not warm enough, and then he added more red and it went tomato on him, then rust. He reached for white to lift it back toward light, and the orange dulled immediately, as though he had poured dust into it. He added more red, more yellow, more white, working the brush in small furious circles, and the saucer presented him with brown. Not sunset orange. Brown like the garden soil his grandmother turned over every April.

His grandmother came out with a glass of iced tea for each of them and stood at his shoulder, saying nothing for a while. The chickens muttered along the fence. An autochthonous stand of switchgrass grew up along the back wall, there before the house was, his grandmother claimed, and it moved in the small wind like it knew something.

"It's doing it again," Samuel said. "The brown. It's like it's waiting for me."

"Your grandfather called that color his nemesis," she said. "He painted the porch chairs every spring, and every spring he ended up with a bucket of brown." She tapped the saucer with one finger. "You're mixing everything together. It's subtractive. Every pigment absorbs some of the light, so when you pile them all up, they end up dark and muddy. Never white. The more you add, the less light gets out."

Samuel looked at the saucer. All afternoon he had been thinking of paint as something that added, that accumulated brightness the way words accumulated meaning, and the opposite had been true the entire time. Each pigment was taking something away from the light, quietly, without telling him. "So the sunset color isn't in the saucer at all," he said.

"It might be in the board," she said, and went back inside with her tea, leaving his untouched and sweating on the sawhorse.

He sat with that for a while. His fingers had inured themselves to the smell of turpentine over the summer, so that he barely noticed it anymore, and he noticed it now, sharp, as if his senses were waking up along with the rest of him. He washed the saucer and the brush under the spigot and started over. Instead of mixing, he kept the pigments separate: pure yellow, pure red, pure white, each in its own jar lid. He loaded the brush with two colors at once, barely touching, and drew them across the wood so the yellow dragged thin streaks of red behind it, the red breaking into the yellow like embers. Where the strokes crossed, the eye did the blending from a distance, at the length of a room, the length of a street.

He worked through the afternoon and into the blue hour, when the real sunset began over the roofline, and he held the board up beside it to compare. It was not the same. His orange was rougher, more stubborn, full of visible marks where the water tower sunset had been smooth and vast. But from across the yard, tilted a little, it caught the same temperature, the same refusal to settle into any single name, and he understood that the board would never be a copy of that evening, only a cousin of it, a thing made the opposite way, by keeping the colors apart and letting distance marry them. Whether Dahlia would see the sunset in it or just a nice orange, he could not know, and he found he was all right standing in that not-knowing, brush dripping yellow onto the grass.

He carried the board to the porch and set it on the rail to dry, then stood back from it, arms crossed, head tilted.

"Okay," he said to it. "Hold that."

The folding chair had her name on it, a strip of masking tape with CLAIRE V. in her principal's hurried print, and she sat down in the empty row of chairs an hour before anyone else would arrive. In her lap sat nine index cards, covered and recovered in her slanted handwriting, and the problem had not shrunk overnight. She could talk about resilience. She could talk about the future. Both options made her stomach turn, not because they were wrong but because they were borrowed, phrases worn smooth by every graduating class since the invention of folding chairs.

"Yo u up?" read the text from Dee, which was Dee's way of spelling "You're early." Claire texted back a photo of the chairs, the taped name, the white riser where the podium stood. "Coming," Dee wrote. "Don't abscond with my speech."

Dee was the salutatorian, a fact she had stopped pretending not to mind around March, when the final GPA had come down to a tenth of a point. She crossed the field now in the flat gray dress she'd argued about with her mother, carrying two coffees and her own cards, fewer than Claire's, held together with a rubber band. Her want was simple and she'd stated it plainly at lunch last week: she wanted to be funny. She'd spent three years being the smart one, the one teachers called on when no one else raised a hand, and she wanted, once, to make a whole stadium laugh on purpose.

"Read me the opening," Dee said, dropping into the chair beside her. Claire read it. Something about journeys and thresholds. Dee drank her coffee and said nothing, which in Dee's language was a verdict.

"I keep trying to write the ending," Claire said. "The goodbye part. And everything I write sounds like a greeting card ate a thesaurus. Like I'm performing erudition I don't actually have."

"So look it up. That's what you do." Dee tipped her chin at Claire's phone. "You're the one who found out the mascot was designed by a junior in 1974."

Claire already had the dictionary app open; that was the truth of it, she'd been typing before Dee finished the sentence. Valedictorian. She scrolled past the pronunciation, past the definition she knew, and found the etymology line near the bottom, small gray text under the entry.

"It comes from vale dicere," she read aloud. "Latin. It means 'to say farewell.' That's why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech. It's the whole job. I've been trying to write a speech about the future when the word itself is just asking me to say goodbye."

"Huh," Dee said, and stole one of Claire's index cards to write it down,vale dicere,in her rounder handwriting, and beneath it: "so it's not about being smart?"

The question sat between them longer than a question that size should. Because Claire had spent four years treating the title as a verdict, a number that proved something, and here was the word confessing that it had never been about that at all. It was about the leaving. The person with the highest grades had been assigned, by language itself, the task of standing up in front of everyone and admitting that this was over. She wasn't sure yet whether that was a relief or a heavier thing.

"So write the goodbye," Dee said. "Say what you'd actually miss. Not the building. Not the, like, hallowed halls."

"Marcus folding cheese pizza in half like a sandwich."

"The smell of the biology wing after the fetal pig unit."

They went on like that, trading specifics, and Claire wrote fast, filling a fresh card, then another. Somewhere in the middle of it she noticed the incipient ceremony assembling around them: a man on a ladder straightening the banner, the band hauling percussion up the riser steps, her grandmother's Buick pulling into the far lot, early the way her grandmother was early for everything, a woman who considered timeliness a form of love. Claire felt the strangest double pull, wanting the morning to stretch and wanting it over, and could not have said which wanting was stronger.

"Your turn to rehearse," she told Dee. "Show me funny."

Dee stood, cleared her throat at the empty stadium as if it were full, and delivered her opening line about the tenth of a point, a joke about how she'd asked the guidance office whether she could appeal it using attendance. The joke needed work. The delivery needed more work. But Dee grinned the whole way through, and somewhere out past center field a crow lifted off the goalpost and beat away over the treeline.

Claire looked down at her cards, the Latin copied twice in two hands. She still didn't know how to end the speech. She knew only that she would stand at that podium this afternoon and say farewell, in whatever clumsy words arrived, and that maybe the clumsiness was the point. She turned the taped chair around so the name faced her and said, quietly, "Vale."

Logan spread the data table across the kitchen table, pushing the fruit bowl aside to make room. The table listed the equilibrium constant for the same reaction at four temperatures, and he had been staring at it for ten minutes because the numbers were going the wrong way. He had expected them to climb as the temperature climbed. Instead, from 300 kelvin to 500, the K values fell, steadily, like a stairway descending into a basement he hadn't known was there.

His sister Delia came in with a mixing bowl under one arm and a bag of chocolate chips in her fist. "I need the oven at six," she said. "I'm making cookies for Kayla's going-away thing, and I need you to not be weird about the kitchen for one hour."

"I'm not even using the oven." He tapped his pencil against the table. "I'm using this table. Different appliance entirely."

"You're going to be sitting there muttering for an hour. You always mutter." She set the bowl down on the counter and began measuring flour with the concentration of someone defusing something. Delia was sixteen and treated every departure, every going-away party, every ending, as a seismic event that required baked goods to propitiate it. Logan had watched her do it for years, churning out brownies and lemon bars as if sugar could hold people in place.

He returned to the table. The assignment asked him to predict, using Le Chatelier's principle, which way the reaction would shift if he heated it. He knew the rule everyone recited: heat the system and the equilibrium shifts to use the heat up. What he kept missing was what that did to the constant itself. He copied the K values into his notebook in a column and looked at them until his eyes watered. Then he drew an arrow beside the column, pointing down, and wrote beside it: exothermic, so heat is like a product. He stopped. That was the part he'd had backwards all week.

"Move your elbow," Delia said, reaching past him for the vanilla. She cracked an egg one-handed, a move she had practiced until it worked.

"Say you have a reaction that gives off heat," Logan said, not looking up. "Exothermic. You raise the temperature."

"Is this going to be one of your lecture things?"

"You raise the temperature and the K actually drops." He turned the notebook so she could see the column. "Look. Four temperatures, and every time the temperature goes up, the constant goes down. And it's the opposite for a reaction that takes in heat. Endothermic. Raise the temperature and the K goes up. That's the whole thing I had wrong. I kept thinking K was fixed, like it was a property of the reaction. It moves."

Delia looked at the numbers for longer than he expected. "So the reaction changes its mind depending on how hot it is."

"Something like that." He pulled the sheet back toward himself. "For this one, heating it makes less product at equilibrium. If I wanted more product, I'd have to cool it, and even then I don't know how far, because the table doesn't tell me." That part bothered him, a low hum under the rest: the principle told him the direction, and the table told him the constants, and neither told him everything. He wrote that in the margin too, because it seemed honest.

Delia preheated the oven and began dropping dough onto a sheet, spacing the balls with a ruler's precision. "Kayla leaves Saturday," she said. "I keep thinking if I make the right thing, she'll come back more."

Logan watched her level off a scoop of dough, then looked down at his column of shrinking numbers. "Cooling helps," he said, "but it doesn't get you all the way."

"Everything all right at three fifty?" Delia asked, squinting at the oven display.

"Three fifty's fine," he said, and set his pencil across the page to hold his place.

Henry got the job the first week of June, which felt like a small miracle because he had assumed, all spring, that nobody would hire a sixteen-year-old who had never held anything resembling a position. The aquatic center hired him anyway, handed him a red whistle and a shirt two sizes too large, and put him in the tall chair by the deep end. He learned to watch the water the way his instructor had described it, in layers: the surface, where nothing was usually wrong, and beneath it, where everything could be.

By the middle of July he had stopped being nervous. He could spot an incipient panic from thirty feet away, a child whose strokes shortened and whose head bobbed a beat too fast, and he would slide down the ladder before the panic had a name. His mother said the job suited him. His father, who worked double shifts at the plant and considered rest a foreign country, said only, "Pick up hours when they offer them. You won't be sixteen forever."

So when the assistant manager, Dara, asked who could cover shifts during the county swim meet weekend, Henry raised his hand. He covered Marcus on Friday, covered two split shifts on Saturday, and came in Sunday for a birthday party of eleven eight-year-olds whose parents seemed to regard the lifeguard as a kind of rented conscience. By Sunday night his shoulders were sunburned and his legs ached from the ladder, and when he clocked out he counted the hours in his head and got forty-nine.

The paycheck came two Thursdays later. He read it standing at the mailbox in the wet heat, and the number was wrong, or rather it was wrong in a way that made it more right than he expected. The last several hours were paid at a higher rate than the rest, one and a half times what he usually made, as near as he could figure. He did the arithmetic twice on the back of a pool schedule he'd shoved in his back pocket. It checked out.

At work the next morning he found Dara at the front desk, sorting keys.

"Some of my hours were paid at a higher rate," he said. "Is that right?"

"Overtime," Dara said, not looking up. "Hours beyond forty in a workweek. One and a half times your regular rate. It's federal law for employees like us." She fished out a key, handed it to a man in a damp towel, and turned back. "Why, you didn't know?"

He hadn't. He had assumed that extra shifts meant extra money in a straight line, hour stacked on hour, and it had honestly never occurred to him that the law bent the line after forty. He felt something between gratitude and unease, the way he sometimes felt when a rule protected him for reasons he hadn't earned.

That afternoon, sitting in the tall chair, he thought about his father. His father spoke about the plant the way some people speak about the weather, as a thing that happened to him. Henry had heard him vilify management at dinner, then take a double the next day, and he had never understood how both could be true at once. Now he thought he saw it a little: his father worked the doubles because the money after forty was better money, and he resented that the better money existed only because the first forty had wrung him out. It was not hypocrisy. It was arithmetic with a wound in it.

Marcus climbed the ladder to relieve him at four. Marcus was nineteen, tanned, and indifferent to nearly everything except his car.

"You picked up the whole meet weekend," Marcus said, settling into the chair. "That's like a religious commitment. Lifeguard asceticism."

"It was forty-nine hours," Henry said.

"Saint Henry of the Deep End." Marcus blew the whistle at a kid running near the gutter, a short corrective blast. "I'd never do it. I did it one summer and stopped seeing my friends entirely. Money's money, but."

He said it lightly, the way people say things they mean more than they want to show. Henry looked at the water, which was calm, all layers of it, and considered that he had spent a weekend he would otherwise have spent with Eli and Sam at the creek, and that the check in his pocket had a number in it he liked, and that he could not yet tell which of those mattered more. He suspected the answer would change, and he suspected he would not always get to choose when.

Dara caught him at the gate as he left. "We need coverage again next weekend," she said. "Friday through Sunday. There's a meet."

Henry stood with his hand on the chain link, the whistle still warm in his pocket.

"Can I take just Friday?" he said. "Just the one day?"

Dara shrugged and wrote it on the clipboard. Behind her, the pool lay flat and bright, and a kid on the diving board was counting his toes in preparation for something reckless.

The decision was supposed to post at five o'clock, which meant Abigail spent seventh period in Mr. Okafor's Human Geography class with her phone face-down in her backpack and her heart rate somewhere near the ceiling. The room smelled like dry-erase marker and the oranges Marcus peeled every day without fail, dropping the rind in a slow pile beside his map of Central Asia. Mr. Okafor was drawing the Eurasian steppe on the board, a long flat grassland he shaded in green, and Abigail copied it into her notes without processing a single word.

Marcus leaned over during the worksheet. "You're writing steppe on top of Poland," he said.

"Am I."

"You've written it four times. Abigail."

She looked down. Four steppes, stacked like sedimentary layers across Eastern Europe, each one slightly crooked. She crossed them out. At five o'clock the portal would either show a word like congratulations or a word like regret, and everything she'd done for four years had already been boiled down to whichever one appeared, and no amount of knowing that was unreasonable made it stop being true.

"Hey," Marcus said, quieter. "Remember March."

"March," she said.

"When you took the SAT. You came out of that room looking like you'd seen a ghost. You told me the second math module was brutal."

She remembered it exactly. The testing room had been cold enough that her fingers slipped on the trackpad, and when the harder questions started stacking up, question after question she couldn't immediately untangle, she had been certain she was failing. She'd ridden home on the bus constructing an apology to her parents.

"And then I told you," Marcus said. "It's adaptive now. Since March of 2024, the SAT in the U.S. is digital, and it adapts. How you do on the first module of each section sets how hard the second module is. So if the second one felt impossible, that probably meant you'd earned the hard one. You did well enough on the first module that the test gave you the tough second." He tapped her worksheet. "And then your score came back and you screamed in the cafeteria and made a senior drop his pizza."

"I didn't make him drop it."

"You made him drop it."

She had gotten a 780 in math, a number no one could impugn, and she had felt, for about a week, like a person the world made sense to. Then she'd written her essays and hit submit and gone back to being a person checking her email eleven times a day. The adaptive test had at least been legible. Work hard on module one, receive module two, read the difficulty of your own future off the difficulty of your questions. Colleges were not adaptive. Colleges made you wait five weeks and then posted all decisions at the same hour on the same Friday, and gave you no module two at all.

The clock said 2:47. Mr. Okafor moved on to rain shadow deserts. Marcus went back to his worksheet, and the oranges sat in their rind pile, and someone's pencil case zipper went up and down three times in the back row.

At 3:31, in study hall, her phone buzzed once, face-up this time because she'd given up on dignity. An email from the admissions office. Not the decision, she realized after her stomach had already dropped; a notice that decisions would post at 5:00 as planned, with a link to the portal and a sentence thanking applicants for their patience. Abigail laughed out loud, alone at a library table, a short ugly bark that made the boy across from her look up from his flashcards.

At 5:04 she was home, on the floor of her room with the laptop actually on her lap, because sitting in a chair felt too casual for the occasion. The portal took forty seconds to load. The screen was pale and the fan hummed against her knees the whole time.

The word was "deferred." Not congratulations, not regret. We have not yet reached a final decision on your application, the letter said, and we will revisit it in the spring.

She sat there while the fan hummed. She had done well on the first module, she thought, and she had done well on the second, and the test had told her so with numbers, and this told her nothing except wait. There was no reading the difficulty of this off anything. Marcus texted a picture of the steppe worksheet with the word LOL under her four crooked crossings-out.

She typed back, "deferred," and then, before she could decide whether it was a joke, "the questions got harder. so I must be doing great."

From downstairs her mother called that dinner was in ten minutes. Abigail closed the laptop, and the room went quiet except for the fan winding down.

I had always been careful with lists, and this one was no exception: eleven colleges, ranked, with columns for average aid, distance from home, and whether they had a real Classics department, because I had decided, sometime in October, that I was going to be a polymath, a person who read Latin and coded in Python and could not be reduced to a single line on a resume. My brother Theo said that was just a fancy word for being unable to choose, but Theo was thirteen and believed this was a character flaw.

I sat at the kitchen computer because my laptop had died in November, and because the kitchen was where my mother was, wrapping candle orders for her holiday rush. The Common App glowed in front of me, seven of eleven applications done, and I told myself I did not care about the money part, which was, I understand now, the first thing I got wrong. I believed I had arranged everything so that finances were not the deciding factor. I had even told my college counselor, Ms. Okafor, that I refused to let money pick my school, as though refusing to look at something made it disappear.

"Which ones are left?" my mother asked, not looking up from her tissue paper.

"Carver, Halstead, Ryland, and Dupre," I said. "The good ones."

"The expensive ones," she said, mild, and I said, "Aid exists, Mom," in the voice I used when I wanted a subject closed. She let it close. That was her way; she noticed when I was gripping the mouse too hard and simply set a mug of tea at my elbow without comment.

Carver I submitted in ten minutes, my essay about translating Catullus at the laundromat already uploaded. Halstead took longer because Halstead wanted an extra paragraph on "intellectual curiosity," a phrase I found nearly meaningless. It was while fact-checking a statistic about Halstead's Classics department that I found the thread that unraveled everything: a forum post from a student saying that at some schools, applying for financial aid actually affected your chances of admission. I had assumed the opposite, obviously, because it would be monstrous otherwise, because money should not get to vote on your worth.

I clicked through to a table on a college data site and cross-checked it twice. Some colleges were need-blind, meaning they decided whom to admit without ever considering whether the applicant could afford to pay. Many others, and this was the part that made my ears go hot, were need-aware instead, which meant they did look. I checked the table against my list. Ryland and Dupre, my two remaining reaches, the ones I had been calling my dreams since September, were need-aware. Halstead, which I had just submitted with a financial aid application attached, was need-aware too.

"Mom," I said. "Do you know what need-blind means?"

She came over, hands still dusty with tissue paper, and read the screen. "No," she said. "Tell me."

"It means they admit you without looking at whether you can pay. Some schools do that. A lot of them don't." Saying it out loud, I heard how naive my earlier confidence had been, all that October certainty about not letting money decide, as if I had been the one in control. I had built my list on prestige and Latin and weather, and had never once checked this column, because checking it felt like admitting what we were, and I did not want our finances to be something that could stigmatize me even on paper. That was the second thing I got wrong, and it was worse than the first.

Theo wandered in, saw my face, and asked if somebody died. "Nobody died," I said. "I have to redo my list." And that, in the end, was what I did, though redoing is too tidy a word for it. I spent two hours at the kitchen table with the table printed out, my mother drying mugs beside me, moving Ryland and Dupre from the dream column to the honest column, where they stayed, because being need-aware did not make them villains and did not make me a charity case; it made them a risk I could see instead of one I couldn't. I added three need-blind schools I had dismissed as boring, and one of them, it turned out, had a scholar program for exactly the kind of unfocused, voracious reader I actually was, the kind Theo mocked. The worry that students like me, patching together aid, were somehow an underclass at the fancy schools, that this anxiety was endemic rather than particular to me, was a worry I could name now but not settle. I would not know until March whether any of it mattered.

At eleven, my mother went to bed and Theo left his half-finished algebra homework on the counter, a small surrender. I reopened the Common App, read my Catullus essay once more, and pressed submit on the first of the need-blind schools, then sat listening to the modem-shaped silence that follows.
