The last seat in the lab was by the window, and Camille had habituated to it over six weeks of sitting there, enough that when Mrs. Okafor reassigned the bench groups for the stoichiometry practical, she felt the rearrangement like a small ordinance, something decreed from above and not open to appeal. Her new bench had Priya, who annotated everything in three colors, and Marcus, who had a trenchant opinion on every topic and no patience for anyone else's. Camille wanted one thing from the practical: to leave with a grade good enough to hold her application to the summer research program, which required a B or better in the second semester. Her grade was sitting at a hair above a C.

The task sheet gave them a mass of reactant and asked for the moles of product. Camille read it twice, then a third time, the way you reread a text message hoping it will rearrange itself into sense. Marcus reached for the balance first. "You get the mass. I'll get the mass," he said, though the mass was already printed on the sheet, 4.90 grams of the reactant, and the weighing was only for verification.

"You have to go through the molar mass," Priya said, uncapping a blue pen. "Grams divided by grams per mole, then across the coefficients."

"I know what a mole is," Camille said, and discovered, saying it, that this was only half true. She knew it the way she knew the word for a country she had never visited. She wrote the molar mass of the reactant, 98.09, at the top of her page, then divided 4.90 by it, and the number that came out, 0.0500, sat on her paper looking back at her, small and exact, and she felt something loosen in her chest. One fiftieth of a mole. A countable thing, almost. She looked up the molar mass of the product, 100.46, multiplied, and got a theoretical yield, and then it was Priya's turn with the balance and the filtering flask, and the room filled with the smell of the hot plate warming.

It was while their precipitate was drying that Marcus, flipping ahead in his binder, started the argument. "Next unit," he said. "Equilibrium. Question. If the forward reaction is endothermic, and you warm it up, which way does it shift?"

"Toward the reactants," Priya said. "Heat's on the products' side, so adding it pushes back."

"That's backwards. Endothermic means the forward reaction absorbs heat. So heat it and it goes forward, toward the products."

Priya's pen stopped. "You're treating heat like a reactant. That's not what the question says."

"That's exactly what it says."

They both looked at Camille, the way people look at a third judge, and she wished they wouldn't, because she did not know. What she knew was the small clean chain she had just built, grams to moles, moles to moles, moles back to grams, and it annoyed her that the chain gave her nothing here. She thought about the hot plate in front of them, about their own reaction which had to be kept warm, and she thought about how the teacher had set out two sealed tubes at the front station with a sign that said observe, do not touch, one in an ice bath and one in warm water, both the same reaction, both changing color before their eyes.

"I don't know," she said. "But there's a way to find out that isn't arguing."

The tubes were at the front, and Camille was the one who walked up to them, Priya and Marcus trailing behind. The cold tube held a pale, nearly colorless liquid. The warm tube, the same reaction pushed only by temperature, held a deep, unmistakable blue, the blue of product. Mrs. Okafor had a card beside them with the balanced equation and a single phrase, forward reaction is endothermic, and Camille read it and read the two colors again, the cold faint and the warm saturated, and let the observation settle into the place where Marcus's claim had been standing.

"The products," she said. "If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. The warm tube's the one that went blue."

Marcus made a small sound of vindication. Priya crossed her arms, then uncrossed them, then leaned in to look, and Camille watched her do the thing that honest people do, which is to keep looking after they have stopped wanting the answer to be different. "Fine," Priya said. "But I still think my way of reasoning about it works for exothermic ones. There has to be some version where both framings agree."

"There probably is," Camille said. "I haven't gotten that far." She was aware of how much she hadn't gotten that far on, how the mole calculation had been the first thing all semester to feel like it belonged to her, and how the summer program committee would not care about tubes of blue liquid or about the moment Priya conceded. But when they got back to their bench, the precipitate had dried, and Camille put the filter paper on the balance and read the mass aloud, and Priya wrote it down, and Marcus divided it by the molar mass to compare against her theoretical yield. Their number was low, by about six percent, wet product or lost crystals, and Priya said they should note that, and Camille noted it.

At the end of the period she stayed behind to copy the two tubes into her notebook, the pale one and the blue one, drawing them side by side and writing underneath, warm goes toward the products, endothermic, forward. Mrs. Okafor passed behind her on her way to the ice bath and said, "Next week we do it with numbers."

"Good," Camille said, and kept writing.

The drive down from Silverton took an hour and a half, long enough for the last of her battery to bleed out somewhere past the reservoir, so Vanessa walked into the phone store holding a dead black rectangle instead of a phone. The town where she lived was small and montane, a shelf of houses pinned between two ridgelines, and the nearest store that sold anything was down here in the valley, in a strip mall between a nail salon and a credit union. Her phone was four years old. The battery had been dying by noon since spring, and yesterday it had shut itself off during her college interview, mid-sentence, while a woman on a screen in Denver waited for her to finish an answer about the book that had changed her life.

She had two hundred and twelve dollars, most of it from a summer bussing tables, sitting in an account at that credit union her grandmother had opened when Vanessa turned fifteen. The phone she wanted, the one with the camera good enough for the photography elective she'd been admitted to, cost seven hundred ninety-nine. A clerk named Deshawn, who kept a desiccated little cactus on the counter behind the register and clearly hadn't watered it in a year, slid a glossy card across the glass. Financing, he said. No money down, twenty-four payments, and she could walk out with the phone today. He smiled when he said today, the way people smile when they're handing you something.

Vanessa asked what the payments were. He turned the card over and pointed at a table of numbers, small ones at first, and she did what she did in math class, which was multiply. Twenty-four of this, plus an origination fee, plus a rate that got added because she was seventeen and had never borrowed anything and would need her mother to co-sign. The total came out to more than seven hundred ninety-nine. Not catastrophically more, but more, and when she asked why, Deshawn said, "That's the interest. That's how lending works. You're paying for the use of their money over time." He said it kindly, without any speech attached, and turned to help a man in a Carhartt jacket who was tapping a display phone with one finger like it might be fake.

While she waited she drifted next door, partly for something to do and partly because the credit union had a rack of pamphlets by the door and she was seventeen with two hundred and twelve dollars and a phone problem, which is to say she was in the mood to look at anything with numbers on it. A brochure about savings accounts for members under eighteen showed two options side by side. Both paid three percent. One compounded monthly, one yearly, and at the bottom, in faint gray print the size of ants, was the formula: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). Under it, a note the designer had probably been told to include and had done so as unobtrusively as possible: n is the number of times per year interest is added.

She borrowed a pen from the counter. She had no calculator, because her calculator was a dead phone, so she worked it out longhand on the back of a deposit slip, slowly, checking herself. Five hundred dollars, three percent, one year, annual compounding: five hundred times one point zero three, five hundred fifteen. Then the monthly one. Three percent divided by twelve, that tiny fraction, raised to the twelfth power. She multiplied it out digit by digit, and the answer was five hundred fifteen dollars and a bit of change. More than the other one. Not by much, a dollar and change on five hundred, but more, and the difference came from nothing except how often they added the interest. She sat with that for a second. The same rate, the same year, and the money that got touched twelve times came out slightly ahead.

So here was what she knew, standing between the two buildings. If she borrowed, seven hundred ninety-nine would quietly become more than seven hundred ninety-nine, the way water runs downhill, without her ever feeling it leave. If she saved, two hundred and twelve would become slightly more than two hundred and twelve, the way a plant grows, also without her feeling it. The two facts faced each other in her head like people on opposite benches, and she couldn't make them shake hands. One said walk out with the phone today. The other said the future version of her, the one in college, would be either slightly richer or slightly poorer depending on this afternoon, and that version of her was the one who needed the camera.

She went back into the phone store. Deshawn was free now, and she set her dead phone on the counter and asked what it would cost to just replace the battery. He turned it over, looked at the swelling along the back seam, and winced. Fifty-five dollars, and he could have it done in an hour. She heard herself say okay before she had fully decided, and then she stood at the counter sliding her card into the reader for the fifty-five, watching the little hourglass, and her stomach tightened because she was suddenly unsure, for no reason she could name, whether the two hundred and twelve was all still there, whether the overdraft from the book she'd ordered in August had ever actually cleared.

The screen read APPROVED. She let out a breath she hadn't noticed holding.

"The savings account," she said, while Deshawn pried the back off her phone, "the one that compounds monthly. Can you switch somebody into that from here?"

"Wrong building," he said, not looking up. "But it's twenty feet."

"I know where it is," Vanessa said, and picked up the dead phone, and the pen she still hadn't returned, and walked out toward the double doors with the deposit slip folded in her fist.

Antoine's grandmother had led the Seder for as long as anyone could remember, and this year, in February, she had handed him the Haggadah at the end of a long Sunday lunch and said only, "Your turn." He had carried the book home on the train like something that might bruise. It was a paperback, its spine cracked to whiteness, its pages soft with decades of thumbing, and when he opened it that night he felt the peculiar weight of a text that was not his to change but was now his to carry.

He spent two weeks preparing. He read the whole thing aloud in his room, twice, timing himself, marking where the Hebrew was transliterated for people like him who could sound out the letters but not slow down enough to mean them. He made a chart of the Seder's fifteen steps on a legal pad, and he practiced the blessings into his phone and played them back, wincing at his own flat delivery. His roommate Theo, who was not Jewish and had never denigrated anything in his life except cafeteria pasta, listened through the wall one night and came in to say it actually sounded kind of beautiful.

The gathering was at his uncle Daniel's house, twenty-three people, three tables pushed together in an L, the good chairs borrowed from the synagogue. Antoine arrived early with the brisket his father had made, and found his grandmother already seated near the head, smaller than he remembered, her hands folded on the tablecloth as though she had been waiting a long time. "You'll do fine," she said, which was not the same as saying it would be fine, and he understood the difference.

The trouble began almost immediately, and it was not the trouble he had rehearsed for. His cousin Maya, who was nine and had decided this year that she was too old to be given only the easy parts, had taken possession of the stack of extra Haggadot and was flipping through them with the concentration of a lawyer preparing a case. "I want the long one," she announced. "The one Tante reads. The part about the exodus, when they get out of Egypt."

"The whole point is that everyone gets a turn," her father said, a pugnacious note creeping in, as it did whenever Maya dug in her heels. "You can't just take the good parts."

But Maya had found something true, Antoine realized, listening to them argue over the spinach dip. The Haggadah retold the story of the Israelites leaving slavery in Egypt, but it did so in pieces, scattered through blessings and songs and questions, and whoever handed out the passages decided what the evening would feel like. Maya was not being greedy. She was asking how the story got told, and by whom, and whether a nine-year-old could hold the part where the sea split.

He made a decision that was not on his legal pad. Instead of assigning the readings the way his grandmother always had, oldest to youngest down the table, he went around the room and asked each person which passage they wanted, and then, where the requests collided, he split the long sections at the seams. Maya got the exodus narrative itself, all of it, because she asked first and asked hardest. His grandfather, who mumbled, got a short blessing. Uncle Daniel wanted nothing and was given, over his objection, the Four Questions, which he hadn't read since 1981 and delivered in a monotone that made the little kids laugh.

Somewhere in the middle of the meal, between the matzah ball soup and the main course, Antoine looked up from leading the Four Sons and saw his grandmother watching him with an expression he could not parse. Later, when everyone had moved to the living room and the Afikoman had been ransomed back from the cousins who had hidden it, she beckoned him into the kitchen. "You changed the order," she said.

"I did." He waited, ready to defend it, ready also to apologize.

"I want you to know I noticed," she said, and then, after a pause that lasted through the clatter of someone stacking dishes, "and that I didn't stop you." She took his wrist, briefly, the way she did, and went back toward the noise of the family, and Antoine stayed by the sink understanding that she had handed him the Seder the way you hand over anything that matters, which is to say without instructions, and that next year he would do some of it differently and not know until afterward which parts those were.

He was still standing there when Maya appeared in the doorway with her coat half on. "Next year," she said, "can we do the plagues outside? With the water?"

The screen door announced Hailey with its usual shriek, and her grandfather looked up from his crossword long enough to say, "Lemonade's in the fridge, glasses are where glasses have always been." He was a taciturn man, but the lemonade was always cold and there was always a glass with her name scratched into it, so she had learned years ago to translate. She set her laptop on the kitchen table between his newspaper and a bowl of peaches going soft, and opened the video her teammate Priya had sent at midnight: their robotics club's first build walkthrough, four minutes of Priya explaining the arm mechanism to the camera.

Hailey watched it twice. The mechanism was clever, genuinely clever, but the explanation eviscerated it. Priya jumped to the third step before the first, mumbled through the pivot joint, and ended with "so yeah, it basically works," which told the judges nothing. At their last practice, when Hailey had tried to say this, it had come out as "it's kind of confusing," which was the feedback equivalent of patting someone on the head. Priya had smiled, said thanks, and changed nothing. Regionals were in eleven days. Hailey wanted to say something that would actually help, and she was beginning to suspect that wanting it kindly and wanting it usefully were two different hungers.

Her grandmother drifted in from the garden with tomato leaves stuck to her sleeve and read the situation off Hailey's face in about two seconds. "Who are you figuring out how to be honest with?" she asked, which was unfair, like being x-rayed by someone in an apron. Before Hailey could answer, the back door banged again and her cousin Marcus came in, still smelling of the deli where he worked, waving his phone.

"Big news. Diego quit, so Rick offered me his Sunday shift. Time and a half, running the slicer." He did a little dance with a peach in each hand. "Seventeen-year-olds can work unlimited hours, you know. I could basically live there."

"Can you run the slicer, though?" Hailey asked, and then, because the question had a shape she recognized, she pulled out her phone. She typed "16 and 17 year olds work rules slicer" and watched the results assemble themselves. "Wait. Hold on. Marcus. It says there's no limit on hours for sixteen and seventeen-year-olds, that part's true, but the Department of Labor has a list of jobs it's declared hazardous, and minors can't do those. Meat slicers are on it."

Marcus set down the peaches. "That can't be right. Rick says everybody starts on the slicer."

"Rick wants everybody on the slicer," Grandma said mildly, rinsing a tomato.

Hailey scrolled, chasing the thought down the page the way she used to chase frogs in the creek behind this house. Last summer, when she was fifteen, Marcus had dared her to hold a frog and she had lectured him for ten minutes about amphibian skin, and he had listened, actually listened, because she had laid out the facts like stepping stones instead of dropping them on his head like bricks. She remembered that now with a small internal click. "Look," she said, turning the phone toward him, "you can work every hour Rick will give you. What you can't do is the hazardous stuff. The slicer's hazardous. So the shift as offered isn't legal, but that doesn't mean the shift is dead."

"Meaning?"

"Meaning ask Rick what else the shift includes. Prep, register, dishes. Maybe he just means Sunday busy work and you're picturing the slicer because Diego always had it."

Marcus frowned at the phone as if it had personally insulted his paycheck. Grandpa, without looking up from the crossword, said, "Boy who worked the counter before you lost a thumb tip. Ask your Rick about that too." Marcus left to call from the porch, and Hailey sat back down at her laptop feeling, for the first time all week, like a thought had actually finished itself.

She watched Priya's video a third time, and this time she wrote while she watched. Not "it's confusing." Instead: the pivot joint explanation starts at 0:47 and it's the best part, do that first. Instead: you say "it basically works" at the end; tell them the one thing you'd fix if you had another week. She drafted the message twice, deleted the opening apology, deleted the exclamation points, and kept the part where she said the mechanism itself was better than anything at last year's regionals, because that was specific too, and it was true.

Grandma set a glass of lemonade beside her and peered at the screen. "That's kinder than what you said before?"

"It's the same thing," Hailey said, then stopped. "No. It's more specific. The kindness is that she can actually use it." She hovered over send, aware that she was still not sure where the line was, whether the line was even one line, whether Priya would hear it as help or as Hailey deciding she was in charge. There was only one way to find out which version of the truth this was. She pressed send, and out on the porch, Marcus was saying, "No, Rick, all the other stuff, just not the slicer part."

Levi claimed the table beside the folding counter the way other people claimed barstools, spreading both leases across it while the washers filled, because the laundromat on Fern Street was the only place left where nobody asked him questions. He was fine. He had said so at dinner, said it again in the car, and he meant it, mostly, the way you mean anything you repeat. Apartment A sat on Halden Road, five hundred dollars a month plus utilities. Apartment B sat above the vacuum repair shop, four sixty plus utilities, and its landlord had written "utilities reasonable" in handwriting that Levi distrusted on principle. His mother had offered to look at both leases and he had said no too quickly, and now here he was doing the thing alone, which was obviously a victory and not a retreat.

He had one utility bill, a photocopy the Halden landlord had given him, marked August. Gas and electric, forty-one dollars. He wrote that number on a napkin and felt the small pleasure of arithmetic behaving itself. Four sixty plus forty-one was five hundred and one. B was cheaper by nothing. He sat back and waited for the dryer's warmth to make the conclusion feel final.

A woman at the next table was folding towels with the efficiency of someone who had done this a thousand times and resented all of them. "You commandeered the whole table," she said, not unkindly. "College?"

"Moving out," Levi said. "Comparing places." He did not say that his mother had cried in the kitchen on Tuesday, because she hadn't, exactly; her eyes had been wet but that could have been the onion, and anyway he was the one leaving, which was a decision and not an abandonment.

The woman introduced herself as Dee, said her son had done the same thing two years ago, said the boy above the vacuum shop was probably an aesthete who'd painted the walls some fashionable gray and called it character. Levi laughed and then caught himself laughing, because it was true, the listing had said "designer tones," and he had liked the look of it in the photos more than he liked any number he'd written down. He turned the napkin over so she couldn't see how little was on it.

"You've got an August bill," Dee said, nodding at the photocopy when he didn't move fast enough to hide that either. "My mother-in-law warned my son about that. August bill looks friendly, she told him, but heating in the cold months will eat you, and cooling in summer too if the place has air conditioning. She said average a whole year of bills, summer and winter both, and that'll give you the true monthly cost. One month lies to you. That's what she said." Levi said nothing, because he had been about to defend his napkin, and there was nothing on his napkin worth defending.

He found the landlord's phone number on the B lease and called right there, coins of dryer noise around him. The landlord, sounding as if Levi had woken him at noon, admitted he had twelve months of bills for the vacuum shop unit, from the last tenant, and read them out while Levi wrote on the back of the Halden lease. High numbers for the winter months, higher than Levi expected, higher than the rent difference, then dropping through spring and climbing again in summer with the cooling. He added all twelve and divided, and the answer sat on the page looking nothing like forty-one. The unit's true monthly cost was far past five hundred, past the Halden apartment even before he knew Halden's own winter numbers. He asked the Halden landlord for a year of bills too, and the man promised to text them by Friday, and Levi understood that the comparison wasn't finished, that a single August bill had nearly decided his whole year.

Dee had been listening while she folded. "So the cheap one's the expensive one," she said.

"Probably," Levi said. "I don't know yet what the other one costs in January." Saying it out loud felt strange, like admitting the napkin had been a costume. He thought about calling his mother from the car, walking her through the twelve numbers, and then thought about how he'd told her he didn't need help, and how both of those things could be true at once. He texted her anyway, just the question: do you still have our utility bills from last year. The reply came before the dryers finished: a whole folder, come by whenever. He looked at it for a long moment, then at the two leases, the true one and the one he'd wanted to be true.

He folded his clothes badly, the way he always did, shirts becoming shapes no aesthete would claim. Dee left with a wave, taking her opinions with her, and the laundromat went back to its hum. Levi gathered the leases, both of them, the folder text still unread on his screen, and carried everything out into the cold.

Evan had come to his grandfather's house for the weekend with a laptop and no plans, which was how his grandfather liked him: available. On Saturday morning the old man set a black stone paperweight on the kitchen table, igneous and glassy, as if it were the subject of the meeting, and slid a printed spreadsheet beside it.

"I have customers," his grandfather said. "Two hundred and six of them, if the list is honest, which I begin to doubt. And I have orders, a stack of them, three years deep. I want to know who has never ordered anything. Not the ones who stopped. The ones who wrote their name down at the nursery open day and then vanished into silence like ghosts."

"You want me to find the ghosts," Evan said.

"I beseech you to find the ghosts. Then I will write to them, or shame them, I haven't decided which."

The problem was simple to describe and, for the first hour, impossible to do. Evan had one table of customers and one table of orders, and every way he joined them, he got only the people who had ordered, because that was what a join did, and because he had learned SQL from a course that assumed everyone eventually bought something. His grandfather sat across from him eating a tangerine with the concentration of an epicure at a tasting menu, peeling it in one unbroken spiral, and offering commentary that was no commentary at all.

"Also," his grandfather said, midway through the spiral, "look at this. Dora sent it to me. She thinks it is me."

He turned his phone around. A clip, grainy, a man in a greenhouse yanking a seedling out of its pot and throwing it into a bin while someone off camera laughed. The caption said a local nursery owner had been caught destroying stock rather than sell it at a discount. Evan watched it twice. The man had his grandfather's slouch and his grandfather's hat, which was the trouble, because his grandfather owned one hat and so did half the men in the county.

"Is it you?" Evan asked.

"It is not me. My greenhouse has a wooden bench. This one is metal. But Dora has four hundred friends and they believe captions." His grandfather set the phone down. "Can you prove a thing like that? You are the technical one."

Evan took the phone and tried the clip in an image search first, pasting the link, and got nothing useful, and then, in a quiet hour of trying things, discovered the method himself. A video could not be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so the way in was to take screenshots of the key frames and search those images instead. He scrubbed to the clearest moment, the turn of the man's face, caught the frame, and searched it. Nothing. He caught the moment the hat came off. A result surfaced, older, from a garden supplier two counties over, same man, different caption, filmed years back as a joke about culling weak stock. He captured two more frames to be sure, and the frames kept pointing at the same original upload, and the local caption turned out to be stitched on afterward by an account that posted a great many captions.

"So you can show that Dora's version is a cut and paste," his grandfather said, reading over his shoulder. "You prove it with the picture, not the video."

"That's the trick. The video itself won't search. You have to pull stills from it, the important moments, and search those." Evan screenshotted the greenhouse bench in the background too, metal where his grandfather's was wood, and sent the whole set to Dora, who replied with a sheepish thumbs-up and no apology, which Evan decided was probably the standard currency.

Then he went back to the ghosts, because the two problems sat side by side in his head and one kept shedding light on the other. The clip had failed because he was searching the wrong shape of thing, expecting the search to see a whole video when it could only see a picture. The join kept failing the same way. He had been asking it to match customers to orders, and it answered with matches, and the ghosts were precisely the ones with nothing to match. What he needed was a join that kept every customer whether or not an order existed, left every customer in, and then he could keep only the rows where the order came back empty. He typed it, ran it, and thirty-one names appeared, ghosts at last, ranked by how long ago they had signed the open day sheet.

His grandfather put on his glasses and read the list slowly, twice. "The Hendersons," he said. "They came for the free cider, I always suspected it." He carried the page to the desk by the window and began copying names onto notecards in his upright, formal hand.

Evan left the query on screen, the empty order column showing its nulls like breath on cold glass, and wondered whether finding the ghosts and clearing his grandfather's name were the same kind of truth or only felt like it, and whether Dora's four hundred friends would even look at stills. He took a screenshot of the results, just in case, and pasted it into the message thread.

"There," his grandfather said, sealing the first notecard. "Now we write to the Hendersons."

Aaron had read the message eleven times before he answered it. Maya said she liked old diners and bad coffee, so he suggested the Starlight on Route 9, which had both, and she sent back a single thumbs-up that he spent forty minutes interpreting.

He got to the diner nine minutes early, which he knew was a mistake as soon as he sat down. Nine minutes gave him time to think. He rearranged the sugar packets, put them back, and took out his phone, not to text anyone but to hold something. His father passed through the kitchen doorway behind the counter, saw him, and raised an eyebrow. Aaron's family had owned the Starlight for two generations, a lineage his father mentioned whenever anyone asked where Aaron worked, and tonight Aaron had not told Maya any of it. He had said he knew the place. That was technically true and also a kind of lie, and he sat with that while the booth vinyl squeaked under him.

She came in at six exactly, jeans and a college sweatshirt even though she was a senior like him, and she said, "You beat me here," and he said, "Only just," which was a lie too, and smaller.

They ordered. She asked about his summer and he told her about the community college physics course he'd taken, the one real ambitious thing he'd done, and he could hear himself making it sound bigger than it was. He talked about the professor's demonstrations, a thing with a pendulum, and she listened with her chin on her hand. When he ran out of demonstrations he asked about her, and she said she'd been rejected from her first-choice school in March and had decided not to be bitter about it, and the way she said it made him think she was still deciding.

The coffee arrived. Aaron reached for his cup at the same moment Maya shifted her elbow, and the cup went over, a brown sheet across the table, coffee running into the saucer and the napkin dispenser and the edge of her sweatshirt's sleeve.

"I'm so sorry," he said. He was up with paper napkins before she'd moved. "That's, wow, that's exactly how I wanted this to go."

"It's fine," she said, dabging at her sleeve. "It's old."

"I've ruined your shirt. I've ruined the table. My dad owns this place and now I've ruined the table."

She laughed then, a short surprised sound, and he realized he'd told her the thing he'd decided not to tell her, and that it had landed better than anything he'd rehearsed. He kept wiping. His father drifted over with a rag, said nothing, gave Maya a nod, and drifted away. Aaron sat back down with a wet handful of napkins and no cup.

"Here's a thing," Maya said. "In 1966, this psychologist, Elliot Aronson, ran an experiment. There's a quiz contestant who comes off as really competent, and then the contestant spills a cup of coffee. Afterward people rated the contestant more likable. It's called the pratfall effect." She shrugged. "Screwing up in front of someone can actually help. My sister studies psych."

"So you're saying I did that on purpose."

"I'm saying you have terrible aim."

He wanted to say that he didn't believe her, that people malign psychology findings to make themselves feel better about small disasters, that a study from 1966 with one contestant couldn't stand for every spilled cup in every diner. But he also wanted to believe her, because the evening had changed when the coffee went over. Before it he had been performing a version of himself, competent Aaron, physics-course Aaron, and the performance was rigid and he could feel it straining. After it he was just a guy with wet napkins, and that guy was easier to be, more ductile, bending where the other one would have snapped.

"Maybe," he said. "Or maybe it only works for the competent person. Maybe if I hadn't spent ten minutes talking about that physics course, you'd just think I'm clumsy and boring."

"You did spend ten minutes on the physics course."

"I know."

"It was kind of sweet," she said. "The pendulum thing."

His father brought two fresh cups without being asked and set them down far from Aaron's elbow, on Maya's side. He gave Aaron a look that Aaron could not read at all, or could read in two opposite ways. Aaron put his hands in his lap and let Maya take hers first.

They stayed until the pie case went dark at eight. Outside, under the buzzing sign, she said, "This was better than the coffee deserved," and he couldn't tell if that meant there would be another one, and he decided, while unlocking his bike, that not knowing was tolerable. She was still standing there when he looked back.

"Text me when you're home," she said.

The house smelled like paint and nothing else, and Emile stood in the middle of the living room holding a phone with no signal bars, listening to it ring anyway. His mother had driven to the old town that morning to collect the last box from the old house, which meant he had six hours alone in a building where his footsteps sounded like someone else's. On the third ring, Danny picked up.

"You're calling from the future," Danny said. "How's the future?"

"Empty. There's a fridge with one water bottle in it and a floor I could sleep on." Emile sat down on the floor to prove it, cross-legged, the phone on speaker between his knees. Danny was telling him about Priya's party, the one Emile had known he would miss the moment the moving truck door rolled down, and Emile found he was listening less to the words than to the background noise of a kitchen he had eaten in maybe two hundred times. When the call dropped he sat there a while, and when he tried to introspect, to look squarely at what he was feeling, the honest answer was smaller than he expected. Not grief. Something more like vertigo, the feeling of a step that isn't there.

He went out through the garage because the front door still had no screen, and that was how he met the neighbor. She was crouched at the end of her driveway, pulling tape off a cardboard box marked BOOKS, and she looked up and said, "You're the new ones. Nobody's lived in that house since the Hendersons, and that was two years." Her name was Ruth Okafor, and this was, technically, the second time they had met; she had waved once from her porch on moving day, and Emile had waved back, and neither of them had crossed the street.

She asked what he was doing with himself all summer before college, and he said nothing much, and she said, "That's a waste of a waste," which made no sense until she explained she owned the garden shop on Delancey and needed someone for the register and the watering, mornings, and could he start Thursday. He said yes before he had decided to. Walking back across the street he kept turning it over. In the old town it had taken him a year to get a job at the pool, and that was only because Danny's sister worked there. He had known Ruth Okafor for four days, one of them only as a wave.

That night he texted Priya: I got a job from the neighbor I've met twice. She replied with a screenshot, some article his old history teacher had apparently posted, with the line highlighted: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper "The Strength of Weak Ties" found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. "Mr. Halloran says this is you," she wrote. Emile read it twice, then looked it up himself, squinting at his phone in the bare room, sitting on an air mattress with his back against the wall.

It rearranged something. All through senior year he had believed that the friends you had were the whole architecture of your life, that leaving them was leaving everything, and here was evidence that the people at the edges, the waved-at neighbors, the classmates he never quite talked to, did things his closest friends could not. He thought about how Priya had gotten her bookstore job, through a woman her mother played tennis with, someone Priya had met maybe twice, and how nobody had remarked on it, because nobody remarked on the obvious. He wanted to call Danny and lay it all out, and he picked up the phone and then set it down, because it wasn't the kind of thing Danny would want a lecture about, and because Emile wasn't sure yet what he actually thought.

Thursday morning he watered forty flats of impatiens wrong, flooding three of them, and Ruth showed him again without raising her voice. At ten a woman came in looking for something virulent, her word, to kill the moss on her bricks, and Ruth steered her to a product and then, after the woman left, said, "People always want the harshest thing for the smallest problem." Emile wrote that down mentally, or thought he did. His discernment about plants was nonexistent; he couldn't tell a weed from a seedling, and twice he pulled things Ruth had to rescue. But by the second week he could run the register, and he knew the names of four regulars, and one of them, a man named Ted who repaired bicycles out of his garage, mentioned that his nephew's roommate at the college Emile was attending in the fall was in the physics program, the exact program Emile had chosen, and gave Emile the nephew's number without anyone asking.

He didn't call the number. He carried it around in his pocket for three days, on a receipt folded twice, and he wasn't sure why. Maybe because using it felt like admitting that Danny and Priya were replaceable, which they weren't, or maybe because the whole idea, that the edges of your life mattered as much as the center, still felt like a betrayal of the year he had just had, the best year, the year of Priya's basement and Danny's terrible car and the night they walked to the reservoir. It was possible, he thought, that both things were true at once and that no principle reconciled them. The strong ties carried you; the weak ones opened doors you didn't know were doors. He could hold both. He could also be wrong.

The morning his mother came back with the last box, she found him on the porch reading Granovetter's actual paper, which he had ordered used, and she asked what it was. "A guy in 1973," Emile said, "figured out people get jobs through people they barely know." She nodded slowly, the way she nodded at things she suspected were more than they sounded.

On Saturday Danny called again, the reception better this time, and told a long story about the party, and Emile laughed in the right places, sitting on the floor of a house that was starting to smell like food and cardboard and, faintly, like them. Afterward he took the receipt out of his pocket and unfolded it on his knee, the nephew's number creased into four pale squares, and dialed.

Aaron had the moving box on his knees, the one with the ripped corner, and he was holding his phone under it so his father couldn't see the screen. The last message from Dex sat there, unsent: nothing typed yet, just the cursor blinking in the reply field.

"Forty more miles," his father said. "You could look up at the road once."

Aaron looked at the road. Corn, then a water tower, then corn. Somewhere behind the corn was Marcus Hale, who had promised to return Aaron's amplifier before they left, and had not, and now the amplifier was expropriated, legally speaking, by distance. He typed: you still have my amp. He deleted it. He typed: good luck at state. He deleted that too.

"You're doing the thing," his father said. "The thumb thing."

"There's no thing."

"There's a thing."

Aaron put the phone face down on the box. His father's hands were at ten and two, insouciant about nothing, that was the problem; the man drove like the move was a Sunday errand. Two days ago they had loaded the truck in six hours and Aaron had carried his dresser down alone because Dex had a tournament, which was fine, which was understood, which Aaron had said was fine and then thought about for two nights.

He picked the phone back up. He opened a browser instead of the messages, because that felt like work rather than weakness, and he typed: why am i so tired after moving. He expected forums. He got, near the top, a scanned table from something called the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, 1967. He scrolled it the way you scroll anything, half-attending, and then stopped.

"Huh," he said.

"What."

"Nothing." He read it again. Change in residence, twenty points. He checked the next line, sure he had it wrong. Change in schools, twenty. The same. A pair of twenties, listed side by side like the scale couldn't tell them apart. So the tiredness wasn't some private defect; the psychologists had counted it, literally, decades before he was born. Somehow that was the offensive part and the comforting part at once, and he sat with both.

"What's nothing," his father said.

"It's a scale. This psychology thing. From 1967." He angled the screen away without meaning to, then turned it back. "Moving's on it. Changing schools is too. Same points, even. Twenty each."

His father glanced over, one second, then back to the road. "Twenty points," he said. "Out of how many?"

"That part I didn't get to." Aaron scrolled. Death of a spouse was up near a hundred; the whole list ran down through vacations, which had points too, which had to be a typo. He didn't say that part. He said, "It's not the top of the list, is what I'm saying."

"No," his father said. "It's not the top of the list." A mile of corn went by. His father's thumb tapped the wheel twice, then stopped itself. "Your mother wanted to be the one driving you. In case you hadn't figured that out."

"She took the truck with Marcus's mom."

"She took the truck with Marcus's mom so she wouldn't have to watch you not say anything for two hundred miles." His father's voice stayed even, which was how Aaron knew it cost him something. "I drew the short straw. I'm saying it out loud so you know it's a straw and not a preference."

Aaron looked at the box, the ripped corner, his own name in marker on the flap. He understood, abruptly, that his father had been waiting for a conversation the way Aaron had been avoiding one, and that both of them had been counting the miles to something other than a town.

He opened the messages. The cursor blinked. He typed: you'd tell me if the move was harder on you than you act like, right. He read it, deleted "right," put "right" back, and sent it before the second-guessing could arrive. Then he held the phone where his father could see it was a phone and not a wound.

"What's Dex going to say?" his father asked.

"No idea. He's insouciant about basically everything except the triple jump." That got a small exhale from his father, almost a laugh, the first one in three states. Aaron looked up the word phylogeny while he waited, because Dex had used it as an insult last week, something about Aaron's taste in music being an evolutionary dead end, and Aaron had nodded along without knowing. It meant the evolutionary history of a group of organisms. Dex had used it wrong. Aaron screenshotted the definition and sent that too, no caption.

The phone buzzed against the box. Then buzzed again.

"Read it or don't," his father said, "but it's your exit coming up either way."

Aaron read it. The first message said: the amp's in your mom's truck, your dad asked me to leave it with her. The second one said: also it's harder than I act like. obviously. you're the one who never said anything.

Aaron put the phone down on the box, screen up this time, and watched the green sign for the exit rise out of the corn and swing overhead.

"Twenty points," he said.

"Twenty," his father said, and took the ramp.

Chase found the book on the shelf between his grandfather's old law texts and a cracked ceramic rooster, and he took it to the kitchen table without asking, which was the kind of thing you could do at Opa's house. The book was about the German government, printed in 1989, and it had a photograph of Helmut Kohl in the middle chapters. Chase was supposed to be writing a paper comparing how a parliamentary system and a presidential system replace a leader. He had four hundred words due in thirty-one hours, and none of them were written.

"Why that face?" his grandfather said, setting down two cups of coffee, one of them predictably for himself.

"I found something and I don't think it's right." Chase turned the book around. "It says Kohl became chancellor in 1982, but there was no election that year. That can't be how it works."

Opa pulled his glasses up from his collar and looked at the page for a long moment, then pushed the book back. "You have the internet in your pocket. Look."

Chase looked. His phone showed him the same thing the book did, from six different sources, and he sat back in the chair with his arms crossed. Helmut Kohl had replaced Helmut Schmidt as chancellor in 1982 through a constructive vote of no confidence. It was the only time the procedure had ever succeeded at the federal level. He read the sentence three times, because it seemed to be telling him that a country had swapped its head of government without anyone voting in a general election, and that bothered him somewhere he couldn't locate.

"So they just took him out," Chase said. "The voters picked Schmidt, and the parliament picked Kohl, and nobody asked the voters."

"That is one way to say it," Opa said, and drank his coffee.

"It's the accurate way to say it." Chase was already typing, already composing the argument in his head: presidential systems made you wait, a fixed term, a removal so difficult it almost never happened, but at least the removal meant something enormous. Parliamentary systems could turn a leader over in an afternoon. He got two paragraphs down fast, the way he got things down when he was angry, and they were good paragraphs, sharp ones, and he knew it.

Then he stopped, because he had made a list on the back of his hand, the way he did when a paper had two sides and he could only see one. On the left he had written voters lose voice. On the right, nothing yet. He looked out at the garden, where his grandmother's tomatoes were coming in late and the neighbor's radio was on. He thought about impeachment, about the presidential system he'd grown up admiring in the abstract, the one his civics teacher had practically dared anyone to criticize, and he thought about how long a doomed leader could cling to a fixed term, months of a country running without a functioning head. He thought about Schmidt, voted in, and then voted out by the people's own representatives, the same parliament the people had elected. He wrote on the right side of his hand: voters' reps can act fast. Then, underneath it, in smaller letters, he wrote both have a point, and hated writing it, and kept it anyway.

"I changed my mind about the paper," he said. "Halfway through."

"Which half?"

"The half where I was right." Chase deleted one of his good paragraphs, the sharp one, and it hurt a little, like tearing a page out of a notebook that was still usable. He started rebuilding the argument around the 1982 fact instead of against it. The paper could hold both systems up to the light and let the reader see what each one traded away, and it could end without a verdict, because he no longer believed a verdict was available to him. He was eighteen and had learned the word zeitgeist that semester, and he suspected that anyone who claimed to prognosticate which system was better was really just describing the mood they'd been handed. His own judgment felt nascent, half-formed, and he decided that honesty about that was worth more than the sharp paragraph had been.

"You will not finish tonight," Opa said, gathering the cups. "You will finish it tomorrow, and then you will tell me what you decided."

"I decided I'm not deciding."

"Then tomorrow you will tell me what you didn't decide, and why." Opa rinsed the cups and set them upside down on the towel, and the two spots where they had sat on the table were still warm when Chase put his hand flat on them and went back to typing.

The debate packet landed on Violet's desk with a slap that carried through the last rows of Room 214. Mr. Okafor had typed the resolution across the top in bold: the student council should be reorganized as a parliamentary system, its president chosen by and removable by the council's majority vote. Violet's partner, Devon, slid his packet across the aisle and tapped the margin. "We're affirmative," he said. "Easy win. Popularity contest out, accountability in." Violet had learned not to trust Devon's assessments of ease.

The real problem surfaced at lunch. Nia, the student council president, had spent the fall pushing a policy that let students distribute an independent newspaper in the front hall, and Principal Ames had suspended the paper after one issue lambasted the new dress code in language he called inflammatory. Nia had defended the paper publicly, twice, at assemblies. Now three council members were circulating a petition to remove her, claiming she had "lost the confidence of the council." Violet watched Nia across the cafeteria, eating slowly, keeping her face still. "That's a no-confidence vote," Violet said. "That's literally our debate topic." Devon shrugged. "Coincidence. We're affirmative. Use it."

They met Thursday after school in the library's back corner, where the radiators clanked and the windows fogged from the rain. Devon spread his notes: in a parliamentary system, he said, the head of government emerges from and serves at the pleasure of the legislature; a majority can withdraw support and the leader falls. In a presidential system, the chief executive is elected separately, for a fixed term, and can only be removed through impeachment, which is deliberate and rare. He wanted to argue that the first model kept leaders responsive. "So Nia should fall the moment the votes tip," he said. "That's responsiveness." Violet turned her pen over and over. "Or that's a popularity meter. The principal is the one who should be answerable, and he's not even in the equation."

The mock court was the other half of Friday's government grade. Each pair had to argue whether the school could suspend the paper, and Mr. Okafor required them to read the governing text aloud before choosing sides. Devon picked up the handout and read flatly, "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." He looked up. "That's the First Amendment. Ratified in 1791." He said it like a box being ticked, then went back to his notes on Tinker and school publications, building a case that schools could regulate student speech when it disrupted learning.

Violet stopped writing. She read the sentence again to herself, then aloud, slowly, as if the order of the words mattered: "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." "You already read it," Devon said. "Yeah, but you argued from it without hearing it. It says Congress. It doesn't say Principal Ames, and it doesn't say anybody may not abridge speech through pressure, or through a dress code, or through a student council petition." Devon leaned back. "So what, we concede?" "No. We argue the principle and admit the gap. The amendment restrains Congress, ratified in 1791, and everything since has been people fighting over how far it reaches past that one sentence. We can be honest about that and still make our case."

The honesty made Devon uneasy, but Violet pressed him through it. On the walk to the council meeting that evening, the rain gone and the pavement steaming, they drafted the debate position together: parliamentary removal by majority vote makes a leader accountable continuously but vulnerable to faction; presidential impeachment makes removal difficult, which protects independence but can shield a leader from genuine accountability. Violet said the words "I'm not sure which one is better" out loud, and Devon winced, but she kept it in the case. She had stopped being sanguine about easy resolutions; the assignment deserved her actual uncertainty, stated plainly.

The council meeting ran long under the gym's fluorescent glare, folding chairs scraping the varnish. The petitioners moved for a vote on removing Nia. Before the vote, Nia stood and read aloud, from the suspended newspaper's next issue, proofed and printed, the sentence she intended to distribute in the hall regardless of consequence: "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." The room went quiet enough that the radiators could be heard ticking. She said the amendment had been ratified in 1791 and that she was not Congress, and neither was anyone sitting there, and that was exactly why the sentence had to be spoken aloud, over and over, by whoever would speak it.

The vote was eight to seven to keep her. Violet found Devon by the doors afterward. "You still think we should argue she's removable at will?" Devon zipped his bag slowly. "I think we argue both and let the judges squirm." Violet laughed once, short, and folded the handout with the amendment on it into her back pocket. Nia was taping the newspaper to the front hall doors, one strip of tape at a time.

The playoff game was at nine the next morning, and the driveway was already losing its light by the time Dez arrived with the ball under his arm and a bag of jersey-wash slung over his shoulder. Luke's backyard hoop had a bent rim from the winter his cousin had hung on it, and the free throw line was a chalk mark that rain had softened into a ghost. It was the only court they had since the rec gym got double-booked for a craft fair, and it would have to be enough.

"Ten minutes of warm-ups," Luke said, "then we run the offense."

Dez dribbled twice, stopped, and looked at him with the particular seriousness he saved for strategy. "New rule tonight. Whoever hits three in a row, we feed him. Ride the hot hand. Coach would've said the same thing."

Coach Okafor had been reassigned by his company to a branch in Dallas on Thursday, which was how Luke, a sixteen-year-old with a bent rim, had become the person responsible for their half-court sets. He hadn't asked for it. He wasn't sure he wanted it. But the game would happen whether he was ready or not, and there was something clarifying in that, the way a deadline strips a problem down to what you can actually solve before dark.

They ran the offense. Dez was good at it, honestly, a connoisseur of passing angles, the kind of player who noticed where the help defense was drifting before it started drifting. But every few possessions he would stop the movement and force the ball toward whoever had just made shots, even when that person was Marcus, whose idea of footwork was a small hopeful hop. Twice Marcus traveled. Once he threw the ball over the fence into the Hyatts' tomato cages.

"Did you see that?" Dez said, retrieving it. "He was feeling it. Three straight. You don't take the ball out of a shooter's hands when he's feeling it."

Luke had his doubts, and he didn't yet have anything to back them with except a general unease, a sense that Marcus's made baskets and Marcus's next shot might not be connected the way Dez believed. He remembered his father's study, the shelf of old paperbacks with cracked spines, one of them a collection of writing about thinking, about how people see patterns. He'd flipped through it once and put it back. Now, while the others did layups, he went inside and found it and thumbed through the index, and there it was, a chapter on randomness and sports.

He read it standing by the kitchen window, one eye on the backyard. In 1985, three researchers, Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky, had studied the shots of basketball players and concluded that a shooter's streaks were no more common than you would expect from chance alone. The paper called the hot hand a fallacy. Luke read the sentence twice, then a third time, and felt something shift in him, the way a room looks different after you learn what a wall used to be. All those years of announcers shouting about a player being on fire, and the numbers said the fire was, at least in that study, an illusion.

He carried the book outside. "Listen," he said. "One experiment, then we go back to drills."

Dez crossed his arms. "We got a game at nine."

"Exactly. Twenty minutes." Luke found a golf pencil in the garage and an old spiral notebook with a water stain shaped like Ohio. "Everybody shoots twenty free throws. We write down makes and misses in order. Then we look at what happened right after three makes in a row. If the hot hand is real, they should hit more often after three makes. If it's the fallacy, they'll hit about their normal rate."

"It's called the hot hand fallacy?" Marcus asked, squinting at the page.

"That's what the study called it," Luke said. "I'm not saying it's the whole truth. I'm saying let's look."

The light went amber and then gray while they shot. The chalk line turned soft under their sneakers, and the ball's thump against the bent rim kept a stubborn rhythm, and mosquitoes came up from the ivy along the fence. Dez was the best shooter, which everyone knew, and he made fourteen of twenty, but after his runs of three makes he clanked the next one more often than not, and when they counted, his percentage after streaks came out almost exactly his overall percentage. Marcus, who made six of twenty, hit two in a row once and missed his next three. JJ's numbers wobbled small and meaningless, like weather.

"So it's fake," Dez said, but he said it slowly, and he was looking at the notebook, not at Luke.

"I don't know that I'd go that far. One driveway, one evening, forty free throws total." Luke tapped the page. "The study was real, and it was bigger than us. But it doesn't mean you never pass to a guy who's made three. Maybe confidence changes something the study couldn't see. Maybe what it changes is how hard he tries on defense, or how the other team guards him." He paused, hearing himself stack maybe on maybe, and decided he was okay with the stack. "What I think is this. You pass to the open man. If the open man happens to be hot, great. But we don't force it to Marcus just because he made three and everybody's yelling."

Dez was quiet for a moment, and it didn't seem like sulkiness; it seemed like a person watching an old idea get taken apart to see if it still worked. He'd always hated when other teams denigrated their rec league, called it pretend basketball, and Luke knew that underneath the trash talk Dez actually wanted the game to make sense, to have laws, to reward the people who understood it best. "All right," Dez said finally. "Open man gets the ball. But if I hit three straight tomorrow, I'm calling for it anyway."

"Call for it," Luke said. "I'll still throw it to whoever's open."

They ran the offense until they couldn't see the rim, just the pale square of the backboard and the darker blur of the ball moving through it, and Dez threw a no-look pass to JJ in the corner that JJ buried, and nobody on the whole dark court had made three in a row. "Again," Luke said, backing out to the chalk ghost with the notebook still under his arm.

The arena smelled like burnt pretzels and cold rubber, and Audrey had claimed the end of the row so she could see the whole ice instead of just the corner where her little brother kept pointing. The championship game had forty seconds left in the third period and her uncle's college team was up by one, and everyone around her, her mother, her uncle Dale, her cousin Priya, and Priya's friend Marcus, was leaning forward as though proximity could help.

Marcus was the loudest. He had never set foot on ice in his life; he'd come because Priya came, and he'd spent the first period asking what icing meant and the second period shouting coaching advice he clearly invented. Now he gripped the rail in front of them, knuckles pale, and when the goalie smothered a rebound with eleven seconds left, Marcus screamed, "Come on, we got this, we got this."

Audrey heard it and felt something snag in her mind, the way a sleeve catches on a nail. We. He said we. She had read something about that, late one night in October, in her psychology textbook's chapter on social identity, and she hadn't thought about it since. The clock hit zero, the crowd surged, and Marcus threw his arms around Priya and shouted, "We won! We won!" while her uncle wept openly into his scarf.

Outside, in the slush of the parking lot, everyone rehashed the game. Marcus narrated the final penalty kill as though he'd been on the bench for it, and Audrey watched him, feeling uncharitable and curious at once. "You said 'we' the whole third period," she said, not quite a question. "You've never even skated."

"It's the team," Marcus said. "It's, like, our school kind of. My cousin went there." He said it cheerfully, unembarrassed, and Priya laughed, and Audrey's mother told her not to interrogate guests. But it wasn't interrogation. She genuinely wanted to know why the word had bothered her when it clearly bothered her, when the truth was she'd said "we" too, once, in the second period, and then caught herself and switched to "they scored," and she couldn't say why the switch had felt like honesty rather than distance.

That night she found her textbook in the stack by her bed, its spine cracked from the fall semester, and turned back to the pages she'd half-read at midnight. There it was, in a paragraph about group identity: a 1976 study by a researcher named Robert Cialdini. After the university football team won, students wore more of the school's clothing. And when students described the games, they said "we" more when talking about wins than about losses. She read it twice. The words on the page had a provenance she could trace, a citation, a year, a method, and they described exactly what she'd watched happen in section twelve, row F, with the pretzel smell and the screaming.

She sat with it for a while, her desk lamp making a small bright territory in the dark room. Part of her wanted to text Marcus immediately, to hold the finding up like evidence at a trial, because there was a pleasure in catching someone in something. But that pleasure felt thin, almost evanescent, there and gone as soon as she noticed it. The study wasn't about Marcus being a fraud. Marcus knew he hadn't played. Everyone knew. He said "we" anyway, openly, joyfully, and nobody was deceived, least of all himself. The study was about something larger and stranger, about how a win could seep into people and make them claim a connection that a loss would leave them quietly dropping, like a hand letting go of a rail.

The next morning her uncle was still floating. He wore the team hoodie to breakfast, which he had not worn to the game, which Audrey noticed and did not say was significant, because she was watching herself now too. Over pancakes he asked what she'd thought of the ending, and she said, carefully, "Did you notice people say 'we won' but they say 'they lost'?" Her uncle frowned, half annoyed, half amused. "We had a bad period in the second," he said. "Anybody could see that." Then he went back to his coffee, and Audrey held her fork very still, because he had just done it, right there, the switch, without hearing it at all. She had done it too, last night, and the knowing didn't make her immune; that was the part she couldn't resolve.

She had two ideas in her that didn't fit together neatly, and she was honest enough with herself to admit it. One idea said the "we" was a kind of theft, secondhand glory, borrowing an achievement whose provenance was other people's years of 5 a.m. practices and stitched eyebrows and taped wrists. The other idea said that belonging was the whole point of sitting in a cold arena with your family, that the "we" was less a claim than an offering, a way of saying I'm attached to this, I'm part of the joy. The study suggested people did it without deciding to, more after wins than losses, which made it less a lie than a tide. But a tide was still not the same as a choice, and Audrey couldn't decide whether she wanted it to be.

By Monday the arena was empty again, the rink back to its public skating schedule, and Audrey went after school because Priya wanted to practice and Audrey owned skates and a vague competence. The ice was scarred and resurfaced, scarred again, its perfection from Saturday already gone, as evasive as Saturday itself. Marcus came too, wobbled along the boards, and fell twice, laughing, his palms red from the cold. When he got up the second time he said, "Okay, when I do this in college, we're going all the way." Audrey glided backward a few feet, considering him, considering her own mouth, which had almost said we.

"You could say 'I'll go all the way,'" she said. "It's your skating."

Marcus considered this with more seriousness than she expected, breath steaming, hair stuck to his forehead. "But it's better with a we," he said. Then he pushed off from the boards, arms out like a scarecrow, and Priya caught his sleeve and pulled him along, and Audrey followed, all three of them slow and unsteady and picking up speed toward the far circle.

The art shack at Camp Wenonah smelled of turpentine and bug spray, and by four o'clock on the last full day, Elijah had spread his portfolio across two picnic tables pushed together, sixteen pieces he'd made over three summers, drying in the heat like evidence at a trial he was losing. He had until the evening showcase to submit his AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio, or rather to submit what he could of it, because the deadline the College Board would not extend was the same deadline the camp bus would not delay, and the cabin wifi reached only as far as the picnic tables, barely.

"You're doing the Selected Works section?" said Priya, dropping onto the bench across from him with her own stack of charcoal drawings. "How many do you need?"

"Five," Elijah said. "And the whole section's only worth forty percent of the score." He said it flatly, the way you report a sentence you've already served.

Priya whistled. "So which five?"

That was the problem. He had a still life with a broken mirror, two self-portraits, a color study of his mother's kitchen, a copy exercise of Hopper's light, and half a dozen others, and no principle for choosing among them beyond liking them, which he distrusted, because liking was how he'd chosen everything so far, including this camp.

The art instructor, a taciturn man named Mr. Okonkwo who mostly painted watercolors of the lake and spoke maybe forty words a day, had left a single book on the table that morning: a monograph of Frida Kahlo, with a sticky note on the self-portrait with thorn necklace and hummingbird. "For the written part," was all he'd said.

Elijah opened it now, mostly to avoid his own work. The hummingbird, black and dead, hung at the throat. The thorns drew a line of blood down the neck and chest. Background leaves pressed forward, flat and crowded, closing in, while the face stayed perfectly still, composed, almost serene. He'd seen the painting before, in a textbook, and had done the thing he suspected everyone did: felt something large and vague and moved on. But the written portion of his portfolio asked for analysis, not feeling, and he didn't know the difference yet, or whether there was one.

"She looks calm and it's a lie," Priya said, leaning over.

"Or she looks calm and it's the truest thing in it," Elijah said. He turned the page and back. The leaves were the same green as the parrot in the background foliage, almost the same green as her shawl wasn't. The blood was red, precise, small. Nothing in the painting was accidental; every color had been placed, which meant every color could be discussed. "Look at the composition. Everything pushes in on her. The animals, the plants. But she's the vertical. She holds."

"Is that analysis or is that you liking it?"

He didn't answer, because the question was a good one. He took out the notebook where he'd been drafting his portfolio statement and started writing instead: the saturated greens compress the space; the hummingbird, a symbol of fallen warriors in Aztec tradition, hangs dead at the throat like a pendant; the symmetry of the face against the asymmetry of the blood. He wrote fast, and the sentences came out more certain than he felt, which bothered him, and then didn't, because he was running out of afternoon.

"Five pieces," Priya said again, tapping his still life with the broken mirror. "This one, obviously."

"Why obviously?"

"The mirror. It's doing what the thorn necklace does. Showing the wound as an object."

He looked at the still life, at the fracture running through his own painted reflection, and realized he'd been trying to litigate the choice piece by piece, each artwork pleading its case, when the actual question was what the five said together. A portfolio wasn't five best pieces; it was one argument in five parts. He pulled the two self-portraits forward, the color study of his mother's kitchen where the yellows did something he'd never been able to name and could now almost name, and, after a long moment, the Hopper copy, because light was a subject too and he could defend it.

"That's five," Priya said. "You're sure?"

"No," he said. "But I can say why I picked them, and yesterday I couldn't." It came out sounding smaller than it felt. The gain had a cost he was aware of: in learning to see the paintings as formal objects, color and composition and symbol, something had loosened between him and them, some unmediated pleasure he wasn't sure would come back. He could analyze the thorn necklace now, and quote the hummingbird's meaning, and he would never again stand in front of it the way he had at sixteen, before he knew anything, when it had simply gone through him like weather.

He photographed the five pieces in the slanting light, checking each image against the actual painting for veracity, because a smudge in the photo would count as a smudge in the score. Priya held the reflector, an overturned cafeteria tray wrapped in a white T-shirt. Somewhere across the field the dinner bell rang, then the bus horn, early, the way it was early every year when the counselors wanted to swim before dark.

Mr. Okonkwo came up the path as Elijah hit submit on the last upload. He looked at the open Kahlo book, at the notebook, at the five paintings now stacked and tied with the ribbon from Priya's hair. He picked up the notebook and read the line about the hummingbird, the pendant, the symmetry, and his face did something Elijah had never seen it do.

"Hopper copy," Mr. Okonkwo said finally. "Brave or stupid. We'll find out in July."

"Which do you think?"

Mr. Okonkwo handed back the notebook and picked up his watercolors, already half packed, and started down toward the lake where the light was going gold and wrong in the way painters wait all summer for.

Elijah closed the Kahlo book and put his thumb on the dead hummingbird for a second, then slid it into his duffel with everything else.

Brianna had commandeer the best table in the public library, the one by the window with two outlets, and she spread her things across all four chairs so no one would take them while she went back for the photocopies. The copies were of a chapter from Jane Eyre, and on the margin of page one her professor had written, in pencil, "Try reading this through a feminist lens. What does the text notice? What does it refuse to notice?" That was the whole assignment, and it was due in nineteen hours.

Derek found her an hour later, holding a coffee he'd obviously bought for himself and then felt bad about, because he set half of it beside her elbow without a word. He dropped into the chair across from her and pulled the photocopies toward him. "Is this still the reading list thing?" he asked. "Because I counted. Twenty-two books, and like three of them are by women. What is that about?"

"That's the question, actually." She tapped the margin note. "Not the exact question, but close." She read him the line she'd underlined three times, where Rochester tells Jane she is small and plain, and he means it as a kind of praise, an exception. "He's deciding what counts as valuable about her," she said, "and she keeps agreeing with him, sort of. She says she's no bird, but she says it in his language."

"Lovely," Derek said. "I have no idea what that means."

"Neither do I, entirely." She turned the page. "The litotes in it is the part I keep circling. She never says she's his equal outright. She says she's no less equal, or that he's no better, the not-this and not-that. She argues by denying the opposite instead of claiming the thing. Which is either submission with a knife in it, or just what a person does when she isn't allowed to say the thing directly."

Derek frowned at the window. In seventh grade, before either of them knew the word feminist, he had asked their English teacher why all their books were by dead men, and the teacher had said, "Those are the classics," as if that ended it. Brianna remembered watching Derek's face go sullen then, remembered how he'd shut his notebook and not raised his hand for the rest of the year. She had never connected that afternoon to this one until just now, sitting here with the same question in a better form. "You've been asking this since we were twelve," she said.

"I thought everybody just accepted it."

"I did accept it. That's the embarrassing part." She pulled her laptop over and typed the question in, expecting a syllabus or a statistic, and instead the first result was a book she'd never read: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929. She skimmed the summary and then read it aloud, slowly, because it seemed like the kind of sentence you shouldn't rush. "A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction." She sat back. "Money and a room. That's it. That's the whole theory."

"So it's not that women couldn't write."

"It's that most of them had nothing to write on, and no door to close." She looked at the photocopies, at Rochester deciding Jane's worth, at Jane denying instead of declaring, and the two texts slid together like she'd been holding them apart by force. "Okay, so a feminist reading of this passage isn't only what he says to her. It's where she's standing while he says it. She's a governess. No money of her own, no room of her own, and the novel knows it, keeps pointing at it, keeps almost saying it." She was writing fast now in the margin, in pencil, so it could be wrong and be erased. "But I can't tell if the book is criticizing that or just describing it. That part I don't know yet. That part might stay open."

Derek drank his half of the coffee and pushed the other half closer to her when he saw she hadn't touched it. "So write that. The part you don't know."

She looked at the table she'd defended all morning with books and a hoodie and a stack of someone else's novels, all of them written by men with rooms, and then at the sentence cooling on her screen. An elderly man had been standing near the window for several minutes, holding a newspaper, waiting with visible patience for one of her four chairs. Brianna swept her things off two of them and gestured him over. "Sorry," she said. "We didn't need all of these."

Thomas had three interviews scheduled before the semester ended, and the first one was on Thursday at the movie theater on Delancey, where a manager named Rhonda would decide whether he got to wear the red vest and tear tickets. The problem was his eyes. Whenever Mr. Pavano, the career-center teacher, had watched Thomas answer a practice question, he wrote the same thing on the evaluation sheet: "Eye contact: intermittent." Thomas could look at a person or he could think about what he was saying, but doing both at once felt like patting his head and rubbing his stomach.

On Tuesday he found his friend Deshawn in the library, copying a psychology article onto his palm because the printer cost ten cents a page and Deshawn had principles about that. Deshawn wanted to write the best paper in the class, not just a good one, the kind Mr. Pavano read out loud, and he was mining the database for anything that would make his argument sound like it had been written by someone with a laboratory.

"You're doing interviews," Deshawn said, squinting at his palm. "This is germane, then. There was this study, 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh. They found people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements."

"Like copying them."

"Subtly. If they cross their legs, you cross yours a minute later. If they lean forward, you lean forward. Don't make it a mirror show." Deshawn wrote the names on his wrist with the pen still in his other hand. "My whole paper hinges on whether charisma is a real trait or just a bag of tricks. I'm arguing tricks."

"Arguing you're a bag of tricks."

"Everyone's a bag of tricks, Thomas. Some bags are better organized."

Thursday, Rhonda turned out to be a large woman in a cardigan who leaned back in her chair like the chair was doing her a favor. Thomas sat across from her, and after the second question, a question about handling an angry customer, he noticed she had crossed her ankles under the desk. He waited, keeping his eyes on her face because that was the other thing he was practicing, and then crossed his own. He could not manage both at once and verbalize the answer he'd prepared, so what came out was a story about his aunt returning a humidifier to a store where the clerk had shrugged at her until she left.
