Her grandmother had the television on with the sound low and a newspaper open on the table, folded to a story about a law in another country. "Listen to this," her grandmother said, tapping the page. "Over there, the age of consent is different than here. And it's not just countries. It changes between our own states, even. Apparently in a lot of places it's somewhere between sixteen and eighteen." Sophie stopped with the spoon halfway to her mouth. Sixteen. She was sixteen. She had assumed the law was one law, the way she had assumed the blood pressure numbers were one meaning, and the newspaper was telling her otherwise, that the same fact could sit differently depending on where you stood on a map.

She wanted to say something intelligent about it, and what came out was, "So it's not the same anywhere," which was the whole of it, and her grandmother said, "Nothing is, sweetheart," and went back to the stove, leaving Sophie to turn that over with her rice. She thought about how her health textbook presented sodium as simply bad, when really it was a matter of amounts and vessel walls and months; she thought about how the news story stigmatized an entire country in two careless sentences without saying where the line actually fell there. Systems were modular, she was beginning to see, built of parts you could swap, and she had been going around treating them as single blocks.

On Thursday they presented. Dana handled the slides, crisp and rubric-perfect, and Sophie stood at the front with the cuff and explained the numbers as two pressures, one contraction, one rest, and then traced the fictional patient's year: less canned soup, more walking, the top number drifting down over months because the vessels had more give and the heart pushed against less. A boy in the second row asked whether exercise lowered the bottom number too, and Sophie said sometimes, and that the research they'd found was less clean on that point, and she did not pretend otherwise. Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard. Dana, beside her, exhaled a breath she'd apparently been holding since the question was asked.

Afterward, in the hallway, Dana said, "You told him we didn't know. That's going to cost us." "It's true," Sophie said. "The bottom number part, we don't fully know." Dana zipped her binder closed with a sound like a small verdict. "I wanted the hundred." "I know," Sophie said. "You might still get it." She genuinely didn't know if that was honest or hopeful, and she noticed she'd stopped being able to tell the difference in herself, which was maybe the unreliable part, if she was going to be accurate about anything.

She walked out past the trophy case toward the bus loop, thinking she would tell her grandmother about the presentation, and about the boy's question, and that she would say, when her grandmother asked if she'd won, that winning had not exactly been the shape of it. Her phone buzzed in her pocket, Dana's name, four words: "Check the grade portal." Sophie stood under the bus shelter with her thumb over the app, rain starting to stipple the plexiglass above her, and did not open it yet.

The debate topic was printed on the whiteboard in Señora Vega's tidy, vestigial cursive, a style nobody under forty used anymore: "Should the school day begin at ten instead of eight?" Under it, the rule that had Sara's stomach folding in on itself like a paper crane: five minutes, entirely in Spanish, no English, or the team lost a full letter grade.

"Entirely," her partner, Danny, whispered as they huddled over a single shared desk in the back corner of room 214. The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the oranges Señora Vega kept in a bowl like some ascetic offering, never eaten, just displayed. "Even the part where I panic? What do I do, panic in Spanish?"

"You say 'no sé' with conviction," Sara said. "People respect conviction."

Danny was fluent by accident; his grandmother lived with his family and Spanish came out of him the way breathing did. Sara had gotten to this class by working, flashcard by flashcard, Saturday mornings sacrificed to verb conjugations the way other people sacrificed them to sleep. She wanted the five minutes because the university admissions packet had a line about demonstrated proficiency, but also, though she would not have said this out loud, because she wanted to hold the language in her hands without feeling it slip.

At lunch they practiced in the cafeteria, which smelled of industrial pizza and floor wax. Sara got through ninety seconds on adolescent sleep research before disaster: "Los estudiantes need, uh, los estudiantes necesitan more sleep, because their brains are still, uh, developing, which is why the schedule should change." She heard the English words land like dropped trays. Danny winced. Sara put her forehead on the table next to her milk carton.

"I did it again," she said into the laminate.

"You do it every time you get nervous," Danny said. He peeled his orange, though it was Señora Vega's kind of orange, small and sour. "You know it's not a failure thing, right? There's a word for it. Code-switching. Moving between two languages in one conversation. My abuela does it constantly and nobody would call her weak in either language. It's common among people who are actually fluent."

Sara lifted her head. "I'm not fluent."

"You're close enough that your brain treats English like a door it can walk through," Danny said. "That's the thing. It's common among fluent bilinguals. It doesn't mean what you think it means."

She turned this over through sixth period chemistry, writing LA CLAVE at the top of her notes and then, feeling dramatic, crossing it out. What Danny was describing was not the opposite of skill. It was almost a symptom of it. Which meant the rule, entirely in Spanish, was asking her not to erase a weakness but to close a door on purpose, for five minutes, that fluent people left swinging. She could not decide whether that made the rule stupid or whether it was exactly the discipline she needed, and she liked even less that both could be true at once. She decided to hold the question instead of answering it, the way you hold a hot cup, testing.

Fourth period the next day, the desks were pushed into two facing rows. Señora Vega sat by the window with a stopwatch and a clipboard, sunlight moving across her bracelets. Danny went first, sailed, floated, occasionally seemed to forget he was being graded. Then it was Sara's turn, and Marcus from the opposing side folded his arms like a lawyer in a show about lawyers.

She started. The Spanish came, a little slow, then faster. "Los estudiantes adolescentes necesitan dormir más porque sus cerebros siguen desarrollándose. Si la escuela comenzara a las diez..." Marcus interrupted with a question about parents' work schedules and her mind went white, and the English came up her throat like water.

"Because, because the parents would, los padres tendrían que..." She stopped. Somewhere a pencil tapped. Marcus smirked, the specific smirk of someone winning on a technicality rather than an argument. Sara put her hand flat on the desk, felt the cool press of laminate, and thought: this is a door, and I am allowed to close it.

"Repito," she said, slowly, and each word after that was chosen like a coin from the bottom of a purse. "Los padres tendrían dificultades, sí, pero las dificultades existen en ambos casos. La pregunta no es si hay dificultades. La pregunta es cuáles podemos soportar." She heard the room go quiet in a different way, not bored-quiet but listening-quiet. When the stopwatch beeped she had thirty seconds left and a full argument on the board of her mind, unspent.

Afterward, in the hall, Danny found her at the water fountain. "You switched twice," he said. "Once to English, once from it. Second one was the impressive one."

"Which one counts?" Sara said.

He shrugged and tossed her the sour orange he had smuggled out of 214. "Depends who's keeping score."

Victoria had read the assignment twice before she understood that the trouble wasn't Holden Caulfield's life but his telling of it. The essay prompt sat open on the kitchen table, one sentence long: identify the narrator's most important claim about himself and explain how it shapes the reader's trust. Outside, the neighbor's sprinkler ticked across the lawn in its slow arc, and her mother was peeling carrots at the counter, the peeler rasping in a rhythm Victoria had known since childhood.

Her younger brother Ben dropped into the chair across from her with his own book, which he then did not open. "What's yours about?" he asked, tipping his head at her paperback, its corners soft from being crammed into a backpack. She told him it was about a boy wandering New York for a few days after getting kicked out of school, and that the boy, Holden, was telling you the whole thing himself.

"So it's true, then," Ben said. "Whatever he says happened, happened." Victoria said it wasn't that simple, and he rolled his eyes and said that was what people said when they hadn't finished reading. She let it go, but the question stayed with her after he wandered off, because it was really her question too, wearing his voice.

She found it on page fourteen, or near it, in the passage she'd underlined without knowing yet why. Holden tells the reader, plainly, "I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life." She read the line aloud to the empty kitchen, quietly, so her mother wouldn't think she'd started talking to herself. He doesn't say he used to lie, or that he tries not to. He says it in the present tense, to her, the reader, as though she were someone he could confide in.

The problem arrived in her mind fully formed, the way problems do when you've been circling them. If a narrator announces that he lies, then every account after that is suspect, including the announcement itself. He could be lying about lying, or lying only sometimes, or lying exactly when he wants to be caught at it. She wrote "trust?" in the margin and felt a small exhilaration, the kind that comes when a book stops being homework and starts being an argument you're inside of.

Ben came back for a snack and saw her still on the same chapter. "How much of it am I supposed to believe," he asked, "if he says he's a liar?" It was almost her exact thought, handed back to her, and she found she had two answers and couldn't choose between them. The first was that the confession makes him more trustworthy, because a liar who admits it is at least honest about his dishonesty. The second was that the confession is a trick, a way of buying permission to keep lying while you keep listening.

"Maybe both," she said. "Maybe he tells the truth about the things that matter to him and lies about the parts that embarrass him." She flipped back to the scene where Holden says he waved at a boy he didn't know, just because the boy was crossing the street, and then admits he only did it because he felt like it. "Look. He tells us the embarrassing thing and the excuse at the same time. He does the judging himself before we can."

Ben chewed his apple and said, "So you can't trust the story but you can trust the person telling it?" Victoria said that was close, except she wasn't sure you could trust the person either, only the pattern of him, the way he reached for certain words when he was hiding something. She noticed she had gone peevish, sharpening her sentences at him, and softened, because the peevishness was really excitement pointed the wrong way. Her mother set a plate of carrot sticks between them without comment.

She started the essay that night at her desk, her lamp the only light on the street-facing side of the house. She wrote that Holden's admission doesn't collapse the story; it builds a second story underneath, one where you watch him construct the first and wonder what he leaves out. She wrote that the reader's trust doesn't calcify into either belief or disbelief but keeps moving, adjusting with each chapter, and that this movement might be the point. Then she stopped, because there was a thing she couldn't yet put into words: whether Holden knew he was doing it. She left a blank line in the middle of the page and went to find her book.

At the window she read the liar line once more, then kept reading past it, following him out into that New York night, pencil hovering above the margin.

Alexandre's first shift at Ferreira's Market began with a tour that lasted four minutes, most of it spent on the time clock. Manny, the floor manager, showed him the dairy cooler, the loading dock, and the pallet jack he was not yet licensed to drive, then handed him a box cutter and walked away. The rest Alexandre learned by inference: the schedule taped behind the register, the laminated card in his onboarding folder that said he would earn minimum wage for ninety days, and the small blue placard by the break room sink that read, in calm letters, that this store was represented by Local 304 and that his rights under the collective agreement were posted on the board beside the schedule.

He spent the afternoon stocking canned tomatoes. A woman named Dot, who had worked the aisles for eleven years, stopped her cart beside him and watched him arrange the tins label-forward. "You're putting the store brand at eye level," she said. "Contract says house brands go on the bottom shelf. Management complains every year and every year we keep the clause. Small thing, but it was traded for something once, so we keep it." She said this the way people describe weather, and rolled on toward aisle six.

On his break he wandered to the back of the store, past the walk-in freezer, looking for the bathroom he had not yet found. Instead he found a door marked FIRE EXIT, and in front of it, a wall of cardboard boxes stacked almost to the ceiling, some of them split and leaking a smell of detergent. He stood there a moment. In eleventh grade, Mr. Okoye had spent a whole period on the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York, March 25, 1911, and Alexandre had written it on a test and forgotten it. Now it came back with the smell of that classroom, the radiator, the photocopy of a photograph. One hundred forty-six garment workers had died, many of them trapped because the exit doors had been locked. He remembered being sixteen and thinking the number was ancient history, the kind of thing that happened before people knew better.

He moved two boxes. The wall did not visibly shrink. He looked at the door handle, at the boxes, at the ceiling sprinkler that had a cobweb on it like a small flag of surrender.

At the next break he found Dot by the time clock and said, as casually as he could manage, "The fire exit in the back is blocked with boxes. Like, completely." Manny was within earshot, restocking gum, and his face went noncommittal, a diplomatic mask that clearly wanted to be somewhere else. "Truck day," he said. "It gets cleaned up." Alexandre said that in the Triangle Shirtwaist fire, in 1911, one hundred forty-six people died because the exit doors were locked, and it seemed like a bad idea to rediscover that number. Manny looked at him with something that was almost respect and almost annoyance. "You got that from a class?" "History," Alexandre said. "It stuck."

Dot set down her coffee. She walked with him to the back, looked at the boxes for a long second, then took out her phone and photographed them from three angles, which Alexandre found both alarming and funny, like she was documenting a crime scene where the crime was cardboard. She said Manny wasn't the problem; Manny was the guy caught between the owner and everyone else, and Mr. Ferreira ran the store like an autocrat with a loyalty card. "But the agreement has a health and safety clause," she said. "Section twelve. The steward can file on it and it has to be fixed on a timeline. Watch." She texted the photos to someone named Ruth, and twenty minutes later a small woman in a Ferreira's apron appeared, introduced herself as the shop steward, and asked Alexandre to show her the door, since he was the one who'd reported it.

Ruth made him sign the incident form, which he did with the solemnity of a man signing a treaty. "You know this counts," she said. "Three people have mentioned that door over the years, but nobody put it in writing. Written things have weight." Then, deadpan: "Also, if you ever want to come to a union meeting, we have cookies, and there's a guy named Paulo who thinks he's funny. He is not. But the cookies are real." Alexandre laughed, and it assuaged some of the nervousness he'd carried since the tour, the feeling of being new and therefore silent.

By closing time, the boxes were gone, moved by two stockers under Manny's supervision, and the exit door swung open onto the cold parking lot like it had been waiting years for permission. Manny stood in the doorway, looked at Alexandre, and said, "History class. Huh." He didn't say thank you and he didn't say sorry, and Alexandre understood that this was its own kind of language, spoken fluently by people who report to autocrats.

Ruth caught him at the time clock on his way out. "Meeting's Thursday," she said. "Cookies at seven." Alexandre said maybe, and found that he actually meant probably. Outside, the parking lot lamps buzzed on one by one, and through the glass he could see the clean, unblocked exit door at the end of aisle nine, and Dot pushing her cart past it, upright, unhurried, on her way to the bottom shelf.

Arianna had promised dessert for her brother's homecoming dinner, and by four o'clock the first batch of caramel was ruined. She scraped the blackened sugar into the compost bin and set the pan back on the stove, running water in it to dissolve what clung to the bottom. Behind her, through the screen door, her younger cousins were arguing about the badminton net, and her grandmother sat at the picnic table transcribing recipes from a stained notebook onto her phone, one finger at a time.

The problem was simple and stubborn. Her mother's recipe said only "cook until amber," which meant nothing to a person who had never watched sugar turn. Arianna had looked it up between batches and found a number: table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius. She had no candy thermometer. What she had was a bag of white sugar, a heavy pan, and the memory of the smell three minutes ago, when she had turned away to answer a text and come back to smoke.

"Are you doing science now?" her cousin Marcus asked, drifting in from the yard with a sullen look because the net dispute had gone against him.

"Caramelization," she said. "It's the sugar browning on its own. No butter, no cream until the end."

"So it's just sugar."

"Just sugar and heat."

He took a soda from the fridge and went back out, and she turned to the stove again.

She measured two cups of sugar and a quarter cup of water and set the flame to medium, telling herself that this time she would not leave. The mixture went clear, then thick, and then, so slowly she doubted her eyes, the edges began to color. It was like watching an asymptote in math class, the curve nearing a line it never quite touched, except that this one did touch, and past the touch everything went wrong fast. She thought about that as she swirled the pan. The line she was approaching was amber. Past it was the smell of the first batch. Somewhere in the neighborhood of 170 degrees, the sugar began to become something else, and after that it kept becoming, whether or not she was watching.

Her grandmother came to the doorway, phone in hand, and watched without comment. Arianna kept her eyes on the pan. At pale gold she lifted it off the heat, carried it to the counter, and poured in the cream, which hissed and boiled up and then settled into a sauce the color of wet sand, not yet the deep amber her mother's had been. Too early, probably. But the first batch had been too late, and between the two was a margin she couldn't see, only judge.

"It's lighter than your mother's," her grandmother said.

"I know. I pulled it early because I burned the last one."

"Early is safer. You can always cook it more. You can't cook it less."

That was the part Arianna turned over while she stirred. Her whole senior year had felt like this pan: decisions with no thermometer, choices where the only proof you had passed the threshold was the color changing under you, and by the time you were certain, you were already past it. She had picked a college in April, second-guessing ever since, and everyone kept telling her it was reversible, which it partly was and partly wasn't. The caramel could be cooked more. The burnt sugar couldn't be unburned. She didn't know which kind of decision the college was, and she was tired of pretending she did.

She put the pan back on low heat and watched the sauce darken one shade. Then she took it off, poured it into a jar, and carried it out to the picnic table where her grandmother was still transcribing, and set it down between them with a spoon.

"Taste it," Arianna said. "Tell me if it needs more."

Jasmine spread the printout of Frida Kahlo's "The Two Fridas" on the picnic table and weighed its corners with river stones from the flowerbed, because the August wind kept lifting the paper like something trying to escape. Her laptop sat open beside it, cursor blinking in a document titled Final Draft (2), which was a lie, since it was her fifth draft and the essay was due at eight the next morning.

The assignment had seemed simple a week ago: critique the painting using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism. She had chosen Kahlo herself, feeling clever about it, and now every sentence she wrote sounded like a museum pamphlet. The blue dress suggests sadness. The heart suggests pain. She read her last paragraph back and heard her own voice flatline.

Her little brother Danny came out through the screen door with a popsicle and no shirt, as usual, and draped himself across the hammock. "You're still doing that?"

"I'm stuck."

"You wrote stuff. I saw you writing stuff at dinner."

"I wrote stuff that's wrong." She turned the laptop so he could see the comment her professor had left in the margin, three sentences of red: You keep calling Kahlo "the artist" at arm's length, as though you're describing a stranger's work from across a room. Who is speaking in this essay? Jasmine hadn't answered, because she didn't know. She had been taught never to say I in a school paper, and the habit felt sedimentary, layer upon layer of teachers circling it in red the way this one was circling its absence.

Danny licked his popsicle and studied the painting over her shoulder. "Why are there two of her?"

"That's part of what I have to figure out." And that was the actual problem, she admitted to herself as Danny swung his feet. The left Frida wore European dress, the right Frida traditional Tehuana dress; the two hearts were joined by a single vein, and the European Frida's heart had been cut, the vein dripping onto her white skirt. Two selves, one bleeding out. She could see all of that. She just couldn't seem to say it as though she were the one seeing it.

She typed a sentence, deleted it, and then, out of desperation more than inspiration, opened her search history to the museum page she'd skimmed for facts. Scrolling past it this time, she stopped at a section she'd skipped before, small print under a heading she now read twice: Artist's Statement. Below the heading was Kahlo's own voice, first person, explaining why she painted, what she intended, the context she worked in. Jasmine read the little explanatory line beneath the heading, the kind of gloss museums put for visitors like her: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.

First person. Ideas, methods, context. She sat with that for a moment, the wind moving the stones slightly on the paper. The statement wasn't a confession or a press release; it was the artist saying I about her own choices, and maybe a critique could stand on the same ground. Not I feel sad looking at this, which was what she'd been afraid of, but I see Kahlo dividing her own body across the canvas and connecting the halves with a vein, and I think the composition argues that the two selves survive only in symbiosis, each keeping the other's heart beating. She was reaching with that last word, she knew. She underlined it in her notebook anyway.

"Was Kahlo saying one of them is fake?" Danny asked, squinting at the torn heart.

"Maybe. Or maybe the fake one is the one that's dying, and she's showing us that." Jasmine pulled the laptop closer and cut her first paragraph apart. She wrote: Kahlo splits the canvas between warm tones on the right and colder ones on the left, and the composition makes the viewer's eye travel the vein like a road between two countries. She stopped, read it aloud quietly, and heard, for the first time in five drafts, a person talking. It didn't exhilarate her the way finishing usually did; it was quieter than that, more like setting down something heavy she hadn't noticed carrying.

She kept writing until the light went amber and Danny went inside and the stones looked like dark heads bowed over the table. Some things stayed unresolved, and she let them. She couldn't prove what the hummingbird meant, whether it stood for freedom or for the weight of hovering, and she wrote that uncertainty straight into the essay: The symbol resists a single reading, and that resistance may be the point. Her professor might hate it. She left it in.

At full dark she read the whole draft once through by the light of the laptop screen, the painting beside her flattened into greys, all its colour stripped away, just composition remaining: the two figures, the joined hands, the small cancelled heart. She wrote one more sentence, saved the file, and closed the lid. Then she picked up the river stones one at a time and carried them back to the flowerbed, setting each one down where it had been.

Nevaeh stood at the grill in the backyard with tongs in one hand and her phone in the other, trying to collate three recipes into something her whole family would eat, which was like assembling a single photograph out of three pictures of different people. Her brother Dev wanted barbecue sauce. Her father wanted, as he put it, "no one camping in the bathroom tonight." Nevaeh wanted to walk into her dorm in September knowing she could feed herself without calling anybody.

She laid the chicken breasts on the grate and watched them whiten at the edges. In her grandmother's kitchen there had been no thermometer anywhere, not one, and yet nobody had ever gotten sick, because her grandmother could read a bird the way other people read faces. Nevaeh remembered standing on a step stool at eleven, flour to her elbows, while her grandmother turned a biscuit dough out onto the counter without measuring a single thing. "The dough tells you," her grandmother had said, pressing her thumb into it. "You just have to be listening." Nevaeh had asked how you learned to listen, and her grandmother had laughed and said, "By ruining about ten years of biscuits, baby."

Her father came out the screen door carrying two beers and a long plastic wand with a metal spike, which he set on the little table beside the ketchup like it was a piece of jewelry. "When you think they're done," he said, "don't cut into them. Use this."

"That's a thermometer," Nevaeh said. "Dad, I can tell when chicken's done. It's white all the way through, the juices run clear, I've watched you do it a hundred times."

"And I've been lucky a hundred times." He cracked a beer and lowered himself into the canvas chair that had survived four summers and one raccoon. "Your phone knows the number. Ask it."

She asked it, mostly to prove she didn't need to, and the phone answered in its bright assistant voice: "US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer." Dev, stretched on the grass with his headphones around his neck, said, "It's snitching on you," and Nevaeh told him he was a whole child and she would remember this.

The first breast looked perfect. Gilded outside, plump, juices pooling glossy and clear when she pressed it. The second looked pale and suspicious, and she would have thrown the first one back on the grill out of pure aesthetics and incinerated it. Instead she slid the probe into the thick part of the perfect one. The display climbed and settled: 160. Five degrees short, though she'd never have guessed it in a hundred years. The pale one, which she'd have grilled into shoe leather, read 168 without a single mark of beauty on it.

"Ha," she said quietly.

"Ha what?" her father said.

"Nothing. The pretty one's the liar."

She moved the first breast back over the heat and stood there holding a thermometer that had just told her that her eyes were a couple of degrees of dishonest. Dev wandered over to see the numbers change, which in Dev's world was roughly the appeal of a slot machine, and they watched the display tick upward together like it was a horse race neither had money on. When it hit 165, Dev announced, "She's safe, she's safe," in a racetrack voice, and their father said, "165, that's the number," and raised his beer to the chicken.

At the picnic table, with sauce on Dev's chin and the good plates because Nevaeh had insisted, her father cleared his throat in the way that meant a pronouncement. "I should tell you," he said. "I got that thermometer last spring. I've never once used it. I've been doing the clear-juices thing since before you were born, guessing, basically, with confidence."

Nevaeh put down her fork. "So tonight I used a thing you bought and didn't trust?"

"I trusted it," he said. "I just didn't trust myself to change. There's a difference." He looked at his plate, then at her. "Your grandmother would have called it cheating, that wand. And I'd have agreed with her for a long time. Now I think she'd have used it too, she just would have pretended it was her own idea."

Nevaeh thought about that while she chewed. She had spent the whole summer feeling like she had to pick a team, the kitchen she'd learned in or the labs she was heading toward, the dough that told you things or the numbers that told you things, and here was dinner, moist and safe, made by both methods holding hands. Maybe listening and measuring weren't rivals. Maybe the thermometer was just a slower way of learning what her grandmother's thumb already knew, and maybe she'd ruin about ten years of chickens finding out.

"So next time," Dev said, mouth full, "when you ask your phone stuff, can it also explain immunology? Because that's the only thing standing between me and summer school."

"Immunology is what you'll be studying if you keep double-dipping," their father said, and Nevaeh got up to get the biscuits, the ones she'd made from her grandmother's recipe, no measurements written down anywhere but inside her, listening the whole way.

The tutoring centre smelled of dry-erase markers and the sad coffee Mr. Petrov kept warm on the back shelf, and Sienna had claimed the table by the window because its wobble was familiar now, like an old horse that favored one leg. She spread out her problem set. Problem twelve wanted her to build a rectangle of perimeter forty and maximize its area, and she had written A equals x times twenty minus two x, and then nothing, because the nothing was the whole trouble.

"You're glaring at it," said Theo, sliding into the chair across from her. Theo was a second-year at the college, wore a lanyard with a plastic dinosaur on it, and had a policy of never giving answers, only raising one eyebrow until the student broke.

"I'm not glaring. I'm maligning it. There's a difference. Glaring is emotional. Maligning is slander, and it's deserved, because this problem is a liar. It says maximize and then gives me nothing to maximize with."

"So give it something."

She wrote x times twenty minus two x again, expanded it, and stopped. Last week Mr. Petrov had said the word derivative the way you'd say the name of a spell, and then ruined it with the chain rule, and now the whole business sat in her head like an obstreperous toddler who refused to be organized. She had a physics test riding on this. If she didn't test into the calculus section, she couldn't take the astronomy elective in spring, and astronomy was the only thing she had ever wanted unambiguously, stars being the one subject that had never lied to her.

"Expand it," Theo said. "Then tell me what you have."

"A polynomial. Twenty x minus two x squared." She looked at it. Somewhere under the toddler noise, a thought surfaced: the derivative of a polynomial is easy, it's just bringing the power down. She brought the power down. Twenty minus four x. She set it equal to zero, and it fell apart in her hands, x equals five, area one hundred, and she sat back as if the table had stopped wobbling.

"A square," Theo said, tapping her answer. "The best rectangle is always a square. The universe is lazy and fair at the same time."

"That's not fair, that's just pretty."

The sweetness of it reminded her of something, and she was gone from the room for a second. Her grandmother's kitchen, two summers ago, graph paper taped to the table, a pot of tea going cold. Gran had drawn a curve, smooth and steepening, and told her to count the squares under it from zero to one. Sienna had counted and counted, shading little strata of half-squares and quarter-squares like layers of a cake, and got something close to a third but never exactly, and Gran had laughed and said the answer was exactly a third, that a whole branch of mathematics existed to prove what a girl with a pencil could only approach. Sienna had thought that was the saddest thing she'd ever heard, all that machinery for a number she could almost see.

"Hello," Theo said, waving a hand. "You left."

"Sorry. My grandmother used to make me count squares." She pulled a fresh sheet toward herself and drew the curve, y equals x squared, from zero to one, quick and sure. "We counted the area under this with graph paper. It comes out to one third exactly, she said, but you can't get there by counting. You can only get close."

"Sounds like a wise woman."

"She cheats at cards, but yes." Sienna shaded under her curve in light strokes, the shaded region narrowing to a point at the top of the parabola. There was something here she couldn't quite say, and she tried anyway. "It's like, today I found a maximum by climbing down a slope that the function itself couldn't see. And Gran's one third is the same thing from the other direction. The curve knows things. It's just not telling."

"The curve is keeping secrets from you personally," Theo said, capping and uncapping his marker, which was as close as he got to enthusiasm.

"Don't mock me before I finish mocking myself." But she was still looking at the shaded region, because there was a question underneath the question, and it was this: if the exact answer was always inside the picture, patient, waiting for the right tool, did that mean the counting had been pointless, or did it mean the counting was the reason she believed the answer at all? She could do the procedure now. She was less sure she understood what the procedure knew.

The dinosaur on Theo's lanyard spun once on its clip. "Do problem thirteen," he said. "It's about a rain gutter, and it's even more of a liar than problem twelve."

"A gutter." She squared the paper. "Fine. Slander it with me."

The sign taped to the double doors of city hall read Civic Scholars Program, Day Two, and beneath it, in smaller print, Supreme Court Arguments Begin at Two. Keira had read it three times already, once from the stairwell, once from the water fountain, once now, because reading it was easier than opening her brief and confronting the part she had written at midnight: the paragraph arguing that the school was right to suspend the student who wore the armband. She was supposed to argue that side at two o'clock, and the side she believed at nine.

"You're wearing a path in the tile," said Dominic from the mock parliament table, where he was stacking his papers with unnecessary force. "Sit down. Help me draft a motion to remove the Speaker."

The Speaker of their mock parliament was a senior named Priya who had, in Dominic's view, ruled unfairly against his committee all morning. Keira sat, but she kept her brief on her knees. "Remove her and put who in?"

"Whoever. That's a separate vote."

Keira turned to the binder of comparative rules the program had issued, a thick document nobody had actually read, because the table of contents alone ran four pages. She found the section on parliamentary systems more out of avoidance than diligence; anything was better than the armband paragraph. Then she stopped avoiding. "It wouldn't work in Germany," she said, and felt the strange satisfaction of reading a sentence twice because it resisted her the first time. "The Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote. One vote, both things. You can't just kick the chancellor out and figure out the rest later."

Dominic took the binder from her. "A constructive vote of no confidence," he read. "Fine. Then we nominate Marcus and we do it their way." He was already writing, and Keira understood that he had heard only the procedure, not the principle underneath it: that a body should never tear something down without naming what it would put in its place. She held on to that herself, privately, the way you hold a coin you intend to spend later.

At a quarter to two the courtroom on the third floor filled with folding chairs and the smell of floor polish. The case was a free speech case, the school arguing that the armband disrupted learning, the student arguing that discomfort was not disruption. Keira was assigned the school's side, and a boy named Anselm had the student's, and he came to her beforehand in the hallway with his outline folded into eighths. "Tell me my weakest point," he said. "You'll be attacking it in ten minutes anyway."

That was the arrangement their instructor had made, and Keira had thought it a contrivance until this moment, standing in the dim hallway with Anselm's outline in her hands, his handwriting small and earnest in the margins. The weakest point was not hard to find. He had claimed that no opinion, however offensive, could ever justify a school's response, a position so absolute that it would problematize every dress code and every anti-harassment rule in the district. She told him so, and watched his face work through it. "So I concede the edge cases," he said slowly, "and keep the center."

When her turn came, she stood at the lectern facing three volunteer judges, a retired lawyer, a city councilwoman, and a college sophomore who looked as nervous as Keira felt. She had planned to open with the disruption standard, polished and airtight, but instead she heard herself say, "The school's rule is defensible only if disruption means something more than offense, and I want to be honest that on our own evidence, it didn't." A pause opened in the room. She pushed into it. "If we punish the armband because it unsettles people, then the next principal can punish a Black Lives Matter shirt, or a cross, or an empty sleeve, anything that unsettles whoever holds power. My side wins on the rule only if the rule is narrow, and the record doesn't show narrow."

The councilwoman leaned forward. "Counsel, are you conceding your case?"

"No. I'm conceding the version of it that's easy." Keira's hands had stopped shaking somewhere in the second sentence. "I ask the court to uphold a limited authority and strike the suspension, which the school defended with a specious equation of discomfort with danger. I couldn't defend that equation once I tried, and I did try."

Afterward, in the corridor, Anselm found her. "You tanked your own side."

"I limited it," she said. "There's a difference between losing and refusing to win on a bad ground." She was thinking of the Bundestag, of Dominic's motion, of a rule that said you cannot vote a chancellor out unless you have already chosen the next one, and she was thinking that she had done something like that at the lectern, torn down her own easy argument only after she had the narrower one standing in its place. What she still did not know, and said so, was whether the court would see principle in it or only a girl who could not hold a line. Anselm shrugged and said the sophomore judge had underlined something on his pad while she spoke.

They stood outside city hall in the four o'clock light waiting for the decision to be posted on the doors, Dominic beside them still rehearsing his motion, Marcus's name now written at the top of it in block letters. The doors opened inward, and a page came out with a single sheet of paper.

The community garden had a bulletin board held together by binder clips and optimism, and in June it announced the first annual Interfaith Garden Science Fair, entries due by August. Noemie had signed her name mostly because thesignup sheet had a blank line and she disliked blank lines. Her grandmother, who had pushed for the plot of tomatoes in the first place, asked her what she would enter. "Something about mitochondria," Noemie said, and her grandmother nodded as though this were a reasonable crop.

The trouble was that Noemie's relationship with biology was a truce, not an alliance. She had passed the exam on cellular respiration by memorizing a route she could recite but not inhabit: glucose in, a little ATP up front, then the long haul through the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, the mitochondria churning out the rest. It had felt like directions to a city she had never visited. The garden, she thought, might be a way to visit it. She wanted, though she would not have said this aloud even to the tomatoes, to actually understand it before she had to stand at a folding table in August and pretend she did.

Her grandmother's plot sat between a bed of collards tended by Mr. Okafor, who had opinions about soil pH, and a patch of artichokes belonging to a woman everyone called Professor Danzig, though nobody could confirm the title. The garden itself was a cosmopolitan place by any standard, which Noemie appreciated in the abstract and occasionally resented in the particular, since everyone felt entitled to comment on her tomatoes. She had learned to titrate attention the way Mr. Okafor titrated lime into his beds: a little at a time, checking for a change.

For the fair she built a walking tour. Stakes in the ground marked glucose at the gate, glycolysis along the gravel path, the Krebs cycle curling around the compost bin, and the mitochondria, represented by an old washtub, at the center of the plot. Visitors would walk the path and end at the tub holding thirty-odd pennies, each penny an ATP, which was the point she kept losing: not the pennies themselves but how the cell squeezed them out of sugar and air. She walked the route every evening after watering, saying it under her breath, and the neighbors got used to a girl muttering about electron carriers while she weeded.

Professor Danzig's contribution to the fair was a decoding puzzle, laid out on a card table under the artichokes: a strip of paper printed with the letters A, U, G, C, and a chart of codons. "Figure out what it says," she told anyone who paused. "It's a message in the cell's own language." Noemie, taking a break from muttering, picked it up. She found the beginning of the strip where it looked tidy, lined up the codons, and got methionine, then isoleucine, then a nonsense tangle that produced amino acids in an order that spelled nothing, no protein a cell would recognize. She assumed the puzzle was broken and told Professor Danzig so, with some satisfaction.

Professor Danzig looked at her over her glasses and said, "You started in the wrong place. Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine." Noemie went back, ran her finger along the strip until she found an A followed by a U followed by a G, started there, and the message resolved into a short, sensible chain. She felt the specific humiliation of having blamed the puzzle, and then the more interesting feeling underneath it, which was that she had just watched a cell's grammar work. A sequence was meaningless until you began where the cell began.

She sat on the edge of the washtub with the strip in her hand and thought about how much of her truce with biology had been a problem of entrances. She had started respiration at glucose because glucose came first on the page, and the whole thing had stayed a list. Walking it, starting where it started, had made it a place. Both were true, she supposed; the diagram was true and the path was true, and she had spent a year mistaking one for the whole. She could not decide whether that counted as learning something or as having been obtuse for twelve months, and she filed the question under things to think about on the bus to campus in September.

The fair itself, in August, was a modest triumph of folding tables and zucchini. Mr. Okafor demonstrated pH strips. A boy from the mosque down the street explained nitrogen fixation with beans in jars. Noemie walked her route fourteen times, for children, for a skeptical retired chemist, for her grandmother, who took the pennies out of the washtub at the end and counted them as though auditing her. A few people asked questions she could not answer, and she said so, plainly, and found that saying "I don't know, but I know where it starts" sounded better than a bluff.

Professor Danzig came by late, when the tables were folding. She asked Noemie what she had concluded. Noemie considered inventing something quotable about science and gardens and roots, then decided against it. "That you can know the whole sequence and still start reading at the wrong end," she said. "And that it's not the same as not knowing anything. It just feels the same until you find the start codon."

Professor Danzig nodded slowly, the way her grandmother nodded, as though the answer were a crop that had come in late but usable. She pocketed her codon chart, patted the rim of the washtub like the flank of a horse, and said, "Methionine's a funny thing to begin with. Every protein, the same first word." Then she gathered her artichokes and went home through the gate, past the stake marked glucose, into the ordinary evening.

Joseph had written the bill on the bus, three clauses and a preamble about reopening the flooded storm-water channel behind the depot as a skate bowl, and by the time the city council chamber doors opened for the youth session, the pages had gone soft at the corners from his grip. He had never stood at the microphone before. The chamber smelled of carpet cleaner and old coffee, and the councillors' long desks curved toward the mayor's chair like a shell.

"You can't just ask for it," his sister Priya had told him last week, when he'd said he was going to request the bowl at the meeting. "There's a process. You draft it like a bill, it goes to a committee, they pick it apart, then the whole council debates and votes." She was in her first year of law and had become insufferable about procedure, but she was also the only person he knew who had read the council's standing orders for fun. Joseph had rolled his eyes at her and then, at midnight, asked her to send them to him.

Tonight the youth council was running a model session in the real chamber, with the deputy clerk, Ms. Anaya, keeping time, and the mayor, Tessa Whitlock, sitting in the big chair with a gavel she was clearly trying not to be blasé about. Two dozen teenagers sat in the curved seats. Joseph's bill was on the agenda as item six, "Skate and BMX Facility, East Channel: First Reading."

Before it could be read, Wren from the environment committee stood up holding her own stack of paper. She had spent a month on flooding maps and had objections, real ones, about the channel's capacity in a hundred-year storm, and she wanted the bill referred to her committee before anything else happened. Joseph felt the floor tilt. He had wanted a vote tonight. He wanted to walk out with something decided.

"Referral is not a delay," Wren said, not unkindly. "It's how a bill gets tested. If it survives my committee, it survives."

Joseph thought of Priya saying the same thing in different words, and thought of the petition in his backpack, two hundred and forty signatures that would get older and colder while committees met. He stood. "I move that the bill be read a first time and referred to the environment committee, with a report back in two weeks, not four." It was a compromise he had not planned until the second before he said it. The chamber voted, hands rising in a loose, undulating line along the curved desks, and it carried.

The committee took him at the small side table during the supper break. Wren made him change the drainage clause; a boy called Dmitri, who wanted the bowl made of brick because he liked the sound of brick, was outvoted on the grounds that brick was insane. By the time they returned, the bill had survived amendment, which felt, Joseph thought, like being sanded down and still standing.

Then the debate, and then the vote, and Joseph watched his own hands not shake as twelve of twenty-two raised for the bill. He had expected triumph and found instead a strange, unfinished quiet. Because the mayor had not yet spoken.

Tessa Whitlock stood, holding the bill, and something mischievous crossed her face. "As presiding officer," she said, "playing the role of the crown in this little parliament of ours, I could simply refuse to sign it. Assent is not automatic, you know. I could withhold it."

Somebody laughed. Joseph didn't. He had read about exactly this, two nights ago, down a rabbit hole that had started with Priya's standing orders and ended, at one in the morning, with a page about royal assent. He stood up.

"The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708," he said, "when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill." The chamber had gone quiet enough that his voice carried without the microphone. "So if you're playing the crown, you can threaten it, but nobody's done it for over three hundred years. Assent is basically a formality now."

Ms. Anaya, at her table, raised one eyebrow, which Joseph chose to read as approval. The mayor looked at him for a moment, then brought the gavel down with a crack that made the front row jump.

"Royal assent granted," she said, and signed the printed bill with the council's ceremonial fountain pen, which was out of ink, so it left only a groove.

Afterward, people crowded around him near the water cooler, and Dmitri said the groove signature was invalid, and Wren said the whole thing was symbolic anyway since the real council still had to approve the funding in the autumn budget, and Priya texted him a single thumbs-up, which from her was practically a standing ovation. Joseph folded the signed bill along its old soft creases and put it inside his jacket, against his chest, where it wouldn't get bent.

He walked home the long way, along the fence beside the channel, where floodwater still stood in the low places, dark and unmoving, reflecting the streetlights. In two weeks the committee would report, and after that the real councillors would argue, and the money might not be there, and he could not honestly say whether the bowl would exist by next summer or ever. He only knew that he had wanted speed and gotten procedure, and that procedure, sanded and amended and almost vetoed as a joke, had ended tonight with a groove of ink on paper and his name on the first line.

At the corner of Millward Street he stopped and took the bill out again to make sure the wind hadn't taken anything from his pocket, and finding it still there, folded and dry, he put it back and kept walking.

The gym smelled like rubber and cold sweat by the time Emile's team filed in for their Wednesday practice, and he could already hear Mr. Kessler's whistle going before anyone had tied their shoes. It was mid-January, eleven games into a season that had started with a pizza dinner where everyone liked everyone, and now Marcus and Dev wouldn't stand within ten feet of each other in the layup line. Emile had watched the thing come apart in slow pieces, the way a shoelace frays before it snaps.

At the pizza dinner in November, Dev had made everyone laugh by doing impressions of the opposing coach, and Marcus had slid an entire pizza box across the table to Emile because he'd noticed Emile hadn't taken a slice yet. That was the team Emile had signed up for. He thought about it now while Dev lambasted Marcus for hogging the ball in the fourth quarter of the Lakeview game, Dev's voice echoing off the far wall of the gym, harsh enough that the JV players on the far hoop stopped to watch. Marcus stood with the ball under his arm and said nothing, which somehow made it worse.

"Enough," Mr. Keller said, and he didn't blow the whistle, which meant it was serious. He sat them all on the bleachers, the sixteen of them crowded onto two rows, breathing hard. Emile expected the usual speech about attitude and commitment. Instead Keller rubbed the back of his neck and said, almost to himself, "Tuckman, 1965. Forming, storming, norming, performing." Then, louder: "We're in the second one. It's normal. Water break, back in five."

Nobody moved at first. Marcus finally said, "Storming?" and Keller just pointed at the water fountain and walked toward his office, and that was the entire lecture. Emile sat with the words turning over in his head. Forming he understood; that was the pizza. Storming was obvious and a little too accurate for comfort. But norming and performing were farther off, like towns past the one you lived in, and he wasn't sure the bus went there.

Practice after the water break was ragged. Dev was pugnacious about every call, arguing even the ones that went his way, and Emile threw a bounce pass into empty space where Marcus should have cut but didn't. In the car afterward, his mom asked how it went, and he told her about Keller's four words, and she said it sounded like something from her management training at the hospital, which made Emile feel like the words had existed forever, in every group that had ever tried to be more than a pile of people. He didn't say any of that out loud. He said, "Fine," and looked out the window at the snow banks.

The problem, Emile decided on Thursday during Spanish class while he was supposed to be conjugating, was that knowing the stage had a name didn't get them out of it. He tried anyway. At Friday's practice he stood between Marcus and Dev in the shooting drill and made them pass to each other, banking on the theory that the storming would burn itself out faster if you fed it structure instead of letting it feed on itself. Marcus hit four threes in a row off Dev's passes, and Dev, grudgingly, called for the ball back. It was not peace. It was closer to a truce with hostages.

But on Saturday they lost by two to Cedar Ridge because Marcus, in the final possession, passed up an open shot to give the ball back to Dev, who wasn't open at all. In the locker room afterward, Marcus pulled his jersey over his head and said, muffled, "I was trying to be a team," and Emile understood that he had seen this exact problem somewhere else, in his parents' divorce, when both of them had tried so hard to be reasonable that they stopped saying anything true. Making restitution could mean fixing a thing, or it could mean paying it off so you didn't have to feel it anymore, and Emile wasn't sure which version he had been coaching them toward.

He walked out to the empty court after everyone else had gone, the janitor already running the floor buffer at the far end, its noise a low drone. The words had order in them, four neat stages like four quarters, but Emile suspected the order was the kind you drew on a whiteboard afterward, not the kind you lived inside. Maybe the storming and the norming happened at the same time. Maybe performing was just storming with better aim. He picked up a ball from the rack, spun it once in his hands, and shot from the top of the key, and it rattled around the rim twice before it fell.

The tip jar at Grindhouse Coffee had a crack down its side, and Zachary had taken to dropping his extra change into the cracked end, as though the flaw made the money more likely to stay. He had been saving since September for a used drum kit he'd found online, four hundred and eighty dollars, and by the second week of June he was sixty dollars away. The trouble was that the kit's seller would only hold it until Saturday, and his next shift was Sunday, which meant he needed someone to cover for him, or he needed the kit to still be there, or he needed something he hadn't thought of yet.

He was wiping down the espresso machine when the girl at the corner table caught his attention for the third time in an hour. She had spread out a university pamphlet beside a laptop plastered with stickers, and she kept circling the same paragraph and then staring past it, her expression cycling from doubtful to dour and back. Around her sat the usual Saturday vernacular of the shop: half-finished lattes, a bicycle helmet, a dog-eared paperback of poems nobody read.

"You keep reading that like it insulted you," Zachary said, when he came to clear her cup.

"It kind of did." She turned the pamphlet so he could see it. University open house, next Saturday, campus tours, financial aid sessions. "I'm trying to figure out if I can even afford this school, and I keep landing on the same thing. Tuition's the number everybody quotes. But my cousin says the economists count the wages a student gives up while studying full time as part of the cost of college too, right along with the tuition. Not as a sad side effect. As part of the actual cost."

Zachary set down his rag. "Wait, so if you weren't in class, you'd be working?"

"Full time. I make decent money at my uncle's shop." She tapped the pamphlet. "So every year I'm studying, that paycheck is gone, and it counts. It's like I'm paying tuition and paying my own wages to nobody."

He laughed before he could stop himself, and she raised an eyebrow, so he explained: he'd just spent nine months agonizing over a sixty-dollar gap without ever once counting the Saturday mornings he'd given up to be here, or the band practices he'd skipped because the shift schedule came first. He'd been doing his own version of her math all along and calling it something else. "My dad calls it life. Nobody ever gave it a name in front of me."

"It has a name," she said. "Opportunity cost."

The word settled over the counter like a coin into a cracked jar. He told her about the drum kit, the sixty dollars, the Sunday shift, the Saturday deadline, and she told him about the open house, which was, of course, also on Saturday, and which she had almost decided to skip because the tour was free and she'd reasoned that free meant no cost, and now she suspected that reasoning wouldn't survive contact with a single economist. They stood there a minute, two people who had walked into the same idea from opposite doors.

Then she said, "Who closes on Sundays?" and he said, "Marisol, but she traded with me last month and I owe her," and the solution assembled itself so plainly he almost distrusted it. He would call Marisol, offer to cover her next three Sunday closings, and take the Saturday shift from her today; the extra hours would close his sixty-dollar gap by closing time. The girl would take the campus tour, and she would count the tour as costing her a day's wages at her uncle's shop, and she would still probably go, because some things were worth their full price once you knew what the price was. She packed her laptop and, at the door, turned back.

"Hey," she said. "If you're counting what you gave up for those drums, don't forget the sleep."

Marisol arrived within the hour, relieved and suspicious in equal measure, and Zachary tied his apron tighter and worked the Saturday rush until his arms smelled like coffee grounds and his feet ached. At closing he counted the till, counted his tips, counted again. The total sat on the register screen, and beyond it, through the dark window, he could see the corner table where the pamphlet had been, already wiped clean for tomorrow.

Blake had promised his grandmother he would look at the kinesiology department, mostly so she would stop asking, and he was beginning to regret the promise because the kinesiology building was on the far side of campus and it had started to rain. He walked with his hands jammed in his jacket pockets, past booths for robotics and creative writing, past a student in a bee costume handing out flyers for the entomology club, and he thought, not for the first time, that a university open house was a strange way to spend a Saturday. Everything here was a decision pointed at a future self he couldn't picture. Did people actually know, at sixteen, what they'd want at twenty-six? His grandmother had broken her hip in March, and she had been morose about it all summer, lying in her recliner saying things like "I should have done more when I could," which Blake had assumed was just something old people said, a truism that meant nothing in particular.

The rain drove him under a tent near the science quad, where a banner read BONE AND MOVEMENT LAB: STOP BY IF YOU DARE. A undergrad in a lab coat was showing a girl a plastic model of a femur, and the girl kept glancing at her phone, and Blake, loitering by the table of free pens, couldn't help overhearing because the girl was nearly shouting.

"My grandma says her doctor told her the bone she has now is all the bone she's ever going to have," the girl said. "Like she wasted her one chance. Is that even true?"

"It's mostly true," the lab coat said. "Peak bone mass is reached in the early twenties in women and the late twenties in men. So the bone you build as a teenager is basically what you carry for the rest of your life. After that you're working to keep it, not add to it." He spun the femur model. "Cool and terrifying, right? You're literally deciding right now what your skeleton will be at eighty."

Blake picked up a pen and then set it down. Sixteen years old, and the window was still open. His grandmother, in her recliner, had been trying to tell him this in her vague, aggrieved way, and he had nodded at her while thinking about lunch. A hip fracture at her age had debilitated her within weeks; she'd gone from walking to the mailbox to needing a walker to cross the kitchen. He had assumed that was just age arriving on schedule, the way weather arrives, and not something with a deadline that had once been decades away.

"Can I ask something?" Blake said, stepping in. "If the peak is in the twenties, like late twenties for guys, how much does it matter what I do now versus, say, at twenty-four? Is it the same?"

"Honestly? Now is better," the student said. "Teenage years are the big building years. Twenty-four is still good, but you're closer to the top of the hill." He grinned. "You're asking very responsible questions for someone at an open house. Most people just want the pens."

"I'm not responsible," Blake said. "I'm asking for someone else."

The girl with the phone looked up. "Is your grandma broken too? Mine fell in a parking lot in March. It's like she aged ten years in two months."

"Mine fell in her kitchen in March," Blake said, and the coincidence was so exact that they both laughed, that startled laugh people make when grief shakes hands with a stranger. They compared notes. Her grandmother refused to use a cane because it made her look old. His grandmother called her physical therapist "the warden." The student in the lab coat said, "Grandmothers are the toughest research subjects we have," and gave them each a foam stress ball shaped like a bone, which Blake suspected was a joke, though he took one anyway.

He walked out from under the tent into thinner rain, holding the little foam femur, and turned the whole thing over in his mind the way you turn over a puzzle someone has handed you without the picture on the box. His grandmother's regret was not vague after all; it was specific, and it had a number attached to it, or two numbers, and one of them applied to him right now. He had always thought of decisions as either-or, the way his school counselor talked about college: pick a door, walk through it, become the person behind it. But maybe most decisions weren't doors. Maybe they were deposits, small ones, made into an account you wouldn't check for fifty years. He couldn't prove that was true. He didn't know whether calcium and push-ups would actually matter in 2070, whether he'd even like the version of himself he was building for. He only knew that his grandmother, who was rarely wrong about practical things, wished she had done more when her own window was open, and that the window she'd missed was the one he was standing in.

He found a bench under a dripping oak and called her. She answered on the second ring, suspicious, because he never called on Saturdays.

"Did you look at the kinesiology thing?" she said.

"I did. They had a plastic leg." He turned the foam bone over in his hand. "Grandma, that thing you keep saying, about wishing you'd done more? I get it now. I asked a guy about it. There's like a cutoff, and I'm before it."

There was a pause, and then the sound of her shifting in the recliner. "You're before it," she repeated, almost to herself. Then, briskly, as if to cover the softness in her voice, "So how many push-ups can you do?"

"I don't know. Ten?"

"Make it twenty by Thanksgiving," she said. "I'll count them myself when you come visit, and don't think I won't."

Mathis set the pan on the front burner and turned the dial to medium, because medium seemed like the cautious choice, and caution seemed like what a person cooking dinner for five people ought to practice. The chicken pieces sat in a bowl beside the stove, patted dry, salted an hour ago when his mother was still at work. His grandfather had been the one who cooked in this house for as long as Mathis could remember, and now his grandfather was in the hospital across town with something the doctors described in sentences that trailed off, and nobody had said out loud who was supposed to stand at this stove.

He laid the pieces skin-down and they hissed, briefly, then settled into a quiet simmer in their own juices. Steam climbed. His little sister wandered in, opened the fridge, stared into it with the blank patience of someone who expects dinner to appear.

"Is that it?" she said.

"It's cooking."

"It looks boiled."

"It doesn't look boiled. Go set the table."

She went, dragging her feet on purpose. Mathis watched the pan. The skin had turned an opaque, watery white, and a shallow pool of liquid had formed around the pieces, bubbling in a listless way, more bath than sear. He turned the heat up a notch. Nothing changed fast enough to satisfy him.

Their mother came home at six-fifteen, keys hitting the bowl by the door, and stood in the kitchen doorway with her coat still on. She looked at the pan and then at Mathis, and something in her face was careful, the way it had been careful all week, arranging itself before speaking.

"How long has it been going?"

"Twenty minutes. Maybe twenty-five."

"Chicken's done, then." She said it gently, but she said it while looking at the pale, steaming skin, and Mathis felt the judgment land before any kindness could cushion it. They ate it anyway, all five of them around the table with his grandfather's empty chair pulled only slightly away, and his sister chewed with visible effort and his uncle said it was fine, it was fine, and nobody asked for seconds. His mother washed the dishes herself, which was the loudest thing she did all night.

The next morning Mathis sat at the same table with his phone and a page of notes he'd made at one in the morning, and his grandmother found him there, still in her housecoat, reading the same paragraph for the third time. She poured coffee she wasn't supposed to have. He tilted the screen toward her without being asked.

"The Maillard reaction," he read aloud. "It's what browns the food. Between amino acids and sugars. It goes fast at around 140 to 165 degrees Celsius."

She nodded slowly, hands around her cup. "Your grandfather ruined a steak like that once, our first year married. Grey all the way through. He wouldn't eat it, and we had nothing else, so we argued about it until two in the morning." She took a sip. "After that he never turned the dial below medium-high again."

So the pan had been too cool. Not careless, not lazy, just cool, and everything pooled and steamed and stayed the color of the chicken itself. He had been cautious, and caution had produced the one thing caution was supposed to prevent. His uncle's easy "it's fine" replayed in his head, and he recognized it now as specious, a kindness shaped like an assessment, worth nothing at the table where the food actually had to be eaten.

In the kitchen that evening, his grandmother watched from the doorway while Mathis stood at the stove again. He had walked to the market with the folded bills from the jar by the fridge, the one his grandfather used for the church honorarium when he was asked to cook for funerals, a word Mathis refused to let himself finish thinking about. The new pieces went into a pan that had sat empty on high heat until it shimmered, and when the chicken hit the surface the sound was altogether different, a sharp continuous crackle, and the smell that rose off it was dark and almost sweet, a smell he recognized from a hundred dinners he had never once thought to question the source of.

He let himself absorb that, to internalize it the way his grandfather clearly had, dial first, then oil, then food, an order of operations that was also a kind of faith. He stood there uncertain only about the small things, how long, when to turn, whether the edges counted, and he decided he could be uncertain about small things and still stand at this stove.

His grandmother came closer and nudged the dial down one notch without a word.

"How do you know when to flip it?" he asked.

She tapped the pan's handle twice. "When it stops arguing with you."

The deadline was Friday, and Luca had eleven days of nothing to show for it. The gallery on Cass Street was showing a survey of self-portraiture that term because his teacher, Ms. Adeyemi, believed you could not build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme until you had stood in front of art long enough to be bored by it, and then interested again. He had requisitioned the corner bench by the south wall, spreading his sketchbook and two pencils across it like a man claiming territory, and had so far produced forty minutes of small cars and an outline of his own left hand.

His friend Priya arrived at noon with a sandwich she split without being asked, which was the kind of thing that made her easy to be around and hard to say no to. "What's your theme," she said, not as a question but as a diagnosis.

"That's the problem. Ms. Adeyemi rejected my first three. She said hands are a subject, not a theme. Then I said isolation, and she said every eighteen-year-old says isolation, and then I said, fine, doors, and she looked at me like I'd brought her a dead bird."

"Maybe you should bring her a dead bird," Priya said, and stood up. "Come on. She said bored first, interested after. You're only at bored."

The Kahlo self-portrait hung in the third room, and Priya planted herself in front of it with the air of someone conducting an inventory. "Okay. Monkey on her shoulder. Hummingbird on a thorn necklace. A butterfly, I think, near her hair. And a black cat peeking over her other shoulder like it wants to know what she's writing." She pointed at each one in turn. "What are they all doing there? Is there a key?"

There was a laminated card on the rail beside the painting, and Luca read it while she talked over him, which was their usual arrangement. The cat, the card said, is usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death. He read the line twice, because something about it snagged. "The cat's the bad omen," he said. "It peers over her shoulder. Everything else in the painting is alive and busy and hers, and the cat is just watching, like it's waiting."

"That's morbid."

"It's honest. She put the death in the corner of her own portrait and kept painting herself anyway." He looked at his sketchbook, at the forty minutes of cars and the outlined hand, and felt the idea arrive not as lightning but as permission. "Ten self-portraits. Not faces. Self-portraits with the thing watching from the corner. The cat stays the same in every one and everything around it changes."

"Your theme is a cat?"

"My theme is, I don't know, keeping going while something watches." He said it and immediately heard how it sounded, like a slogan on a mug. Priya was kind enough not to laugh and honest enough not to nod.

They spent the afternoon in the room. Priya, who wanted to study biology and had once described herself, bitterly, as "a failed polymath, decent at everything, spectacular at nothing," argued that the animals had to mean something biological too, that the monkey was her fertility and the hummingbird, suspended on thorns, was freedom caught. Luca argued back that you couldn't diagram a painting like a frog. "It's not germane what the monkey meant to her biographically if what it does in the painting is hold her," he said, and Priya said that was the most useful thing he'd said all day, which he suspected was an insult, and accepted it anyway.

By five o'clock he had filled six pages: himself at his desk with the cat on the bookshelf, himself on the bus with the cat in the window reflection, himself at his grandmother's kitchen table with the cat under the chair where the dog should have been. Some of it was terrible. The bus one looked like an ad for public transit. But two of them, the desk and the kitchen, had something in them that made him keep turning back to the pages, and he knew enough now to trust that turning back.

Ms. Adeyemi's email required the artist's statement by Friday along with sketches of all ten, and Luca sat on the bench after the gallery announced closing, drafting it in the back of the sketchbook. He wrote that the series was about what it was like to make anything while a part of you watched and predicted failure. He wrote that he did not know yet whether the watching thing was fear or grief or just attention, and that he thought the not knowing was part of the subject. He read it over and didn't cross any of it out.

Priya gathered the sandwich wrappers while the guard unlocked the front doors. "Statement done?"

"Done enough. Nine more drawings by Friday."

"That's impossible."

"It's extremely possible," Luca said, zipping his pencil case, and then, more quietly, because the room was almost empty and the cat in the painting was still peering over Kahlo's shoulder the way it had been all afternoon, "It's just going to be a long week." He stood, tucked the sketchbook under his arm, and walked out backwards, looking at the painting until the door swung shut between them.

I am, by my own account, the most honest person on the robotics team, which is why it stung so much when Dev told me I had let everyone down. I've been turning that over all summer, through the last weeks of senior year and into this party at Marisol's house, where her cousin's playlist is too loud and somebody's little brother keeps opening the screen door to let mosquitoes in. The party is for Marisol's eighteenth, and half the team is here, and of course Sami is here too, which is the whole problem, or the whole solution, depending on which version of me you believe.

Here is what I tell people happened: at regionals in March, Sami's wiring harness failed twice during inspection, and I said something, because I always say something. Here is what actually happened: I said nothing either time. I stood by the pit table with my arms crossed and watched her re-solder the same bad joint, and when she looked up at me for confirmation I gave her a thumbs up, because she'd been having a hard month and I didn't want to be the one who made it harder. We missed the alliance picks by one match. Dev, our driver, didn't speak to me on the bus home.

At the party I find him by the cooler, fishing out a cream soda that is definitely not for him since it's Marisol's dad's. "You're still mad," I say, which is a generous framing, as though his anger were an overreaction I've patiently tolerated.

"I'm not mad," Dev says. "I'm done being surprised by you." He cracks the can. "Priya told me you told her the intake arm design was 'fine.' She spent two weeks on it. It wasn't fine, and she told me she would have fixed it in a day if you'd said one specific thing."

One specific thing. That phrase has been following me around like a stray. My sister, who reads management books for fun, an amalgam of ambition and self-help she consumes the way I consume chips, threw one at me in June. She said, "In her 2017 book Radical Candor, Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly." I'd rolled my eyes at the time, some atavistic male reflex against anything with the word "radical" on the cover, but the sentence stayed. It stayed because I recognized myself in its failure, in the gap between its two halves. I had cared personally, fine. I had cared so much it made me useless.

Across the room Sami is teaching Marisol's little brother to juggle with limes, dropping them, laughing, picking them up again. She's not fragile. She never was. I'd decided she was, and then dressed my cowardice up as gentleness, told myself I was being kind when I was really being absent. There's a way of pathologizing other people's hard months, treating sadness like a diagnosis that means they can't hear the truth, and I'd done that to her without ever asking what she actually wanted.

"You should tell her," Dev says, following my eyes. "Not for me. Not for the team, we're all graduating. For you, man, because you're going to be somebody's roommate in August, somebody's lab partner, and they're going to need you to say real things."

I take my drink and cross the room, and it takes approximately forever, maybe eight seconds. Sami catches me mid-approach and grins. "Cole! Marisol said you're going to that engineering program, the big one. You deserve it."

"Thanks. Sami, hey." I put my cup down on the counter so my hands have nothing to hide behind. "At regionals, the wiring harness. I saw the cold joint before inspection, both times, and I didn't tell you because I thought you couldn't handle it that week. That was wrong of me, and it cost us a match, and I'm sorry." My voice comes out steadier than I feel. "If it happens again, tell me to shut up and check the joint."

She's quiet long enough for the playlist to change songs. Then she says, "You watched me solder that thing twice and said nothing?"

"I gave you a thumbs up."
