She was already drafting the message in her head for him, knowing he would never send her version, knowing he would send a shorter, apologetic one that said sorry to bother you somewhere in the first line. That was Marcus. The epidemiology of his problems was consistent: they spread quietly and were caught late, usually by someone else.

Her mother set her own mug down across the table and sat, which meant the flat-hunting portion of the evening had officially merged into the life-lecture portion, and Jordyn closed the laptop lid to half, muting Marcus mid-sentence about chip shop opening hours. The kitchen went quiet except for the fridge.

"So which flat is it going to be?" her mother asked.

Eric would tell anyone who asked that he wasn't nervous, and he had a whole list of reasons ready: he'd been speaking Arabic since he was four, his grandfather had drilled him every summer in Irbid, and the festival's reading table was just folding chairs under a canopy. None of that was quite a lie. But he had signed up for the newspaper segment the moment he saw it, before thinking, and now that the volunteer was handing him a photocopied article from Al-Rai, he understood he'd volunteered for the one thing he couldn't do.

"Take five minutes," the volunteer said. "Then you read it, and you tell us what it says. In Arabic, out loud."

The article was short. Three paragraphs about water restrictions in Jordan, which was lucky, because he knew the words for water and Jordan and not much else on the page. He recognized letters he'd never had to read as a unit; his grandfather had taught him to sound out street signs and cereal boxes and then given up, calling the rest school business. Eric had let him. That had always felt like an agreement between them. Sitting here, it felt more like a peccadillo he'd gotten away with for years, and the canopy's shade did nothing for the heat climbing his neck.

At the next table, a girl his age was rolling grape leaves with her mother, and she kept glancing over at him. He decided she was being blase about him, bored, already writing him off, though in truth she was only waiting for her turn at the reading table, since her mother had signed them both up.

"Ready?" the volunteer asked.

Eric read. The first sentence came out in pieces, and somewhere in the second sentence he did something he hadn't planned: he stopped decoding and started improvising. He knew what a Jordanian newspaper article about water probably said, more or less, the way he knew what his grandfather would say about the government, so he summarized aloud in the Arabic he actually had. "The water," he said, "there isn't enough, and people should not waste it." He spread his hands, made it sound like translation rather than guesswork.

The grape-leaf girl had stopped rolling. "That's not what it says," she said. Not cruelly. Just flat.

"It's the gist."

"It says restrictions on specific days." She came over, stood beside the photocopy, and pointed at a word. "You didn't read it. You performed it."

He wanted to say that performing a summary was still a summary, that his grandfather's Arabic had carried him through real conversations in real kitchens while she'd learned hers from weekend school worksheets. He didn't say it. Because she was already frowning at the page herself, mouthing the sentences, and what she said next rearranged everything.

"It sounds weird out loud," she said. "Like it's from a movie announcer. We don't talk like this at home." She read a line aloud, stiff and formal, then translated it for the volunteer, who was from Morocco and nodded along. Eric watched her, then looked at the masthead of the paper, then remembered a stack of old Egyptian newspapers in his uncle's garage that looked, now that he thought about it, exactly like this one. Different country. Same writing.

"The newspapers are in Modern Standard Arabic," the girl said, tapping the page. "Not our dialect. All of them, all over. So one written form serves everyone."

"That's why it sounds like nobody's grandfather," Eric said.

"That's why it sounds like everybody's school."

The volunteer asked if he wanted to try again. Eric looked at the three paragraphs, the words he could now pick out one by one, slow as pulling weeds. He thought about calling his grandfather tonight and reading him the water article, badly, over the phone, and being corrected, and not minding. He thought about the girl's dialect folding into the written form and the written form opening back out onto hers, two ways of holding the same language, and he still couldn't have said which one was his. He pulled his chair closer to the table.

"Line by line," he said. "Tell me when I cheat."

The county GIS server took four minutes to load, and Jackson spent all four of them watching the cursor blink like it was deciding whether he deserved answers. He was in the back corner of the public library, two days before the city council meeting where he was supposed to present a map, and so far his map consisted of a gray rectangle that was technically the city of Cedar Falls.

The assignment had started as extra credit and escalated. His geography teacher wanted a flood risk overlay, and his grandfather, over Sunday dinner, had mentioned that the apartment building on Route 9 had flooded twice in the last decade, which made Jackson wonder who actually lived in the floodplain. Not who in the abstract. Who, with names.

He clicked through the tutorial again. Layer one was the FEMA flood zone, a blue wash that swallowed the river's curves and licked up into the eastern neighborhoods. Layer two was housing stock, parcels shaded by age and value. When he overlaid them, the screen showed what he'd half expected and still wasn't ready for: the oldest, cheapest buildings sat square in the bluest water. The Route 9 apartments bloomed dark blue on the parcel map like a bruise.

"Is that what I think it is?" said Priya, sliding into the chair beside him. She'd agreed to help because her brother had been evacuated from those apartments in 2016, in a boat, an image the family apparently brought up at every holiday.

"It's a correlation," Jackson said. "I can't call it anything else yet."

"Call it unfair."

"I have to call it something the council will sit still for." He was learning, quickly, that a map is an argument, and arguments have pragmatics, a whole machinery of who says what to whom and how it lands. A color ramp was not neutral. He'd already discovered that switching the palette from red-blue to yellow-green made the same data look advisory rather than catastrophic.

What he didn't have was a count. He needed to know how many people, roughly, lived in that blue, and his parcels told him buildings, not residents. Priya dug through the county assessor's page on her phone while he layered census blocks, and somewhere in that scrolling she said, "Wait, there's a population pyramid for the whole county. Look at this."

The pyramid was a chart shaped like two mirrored Christmas trees, males on one side, females on the other, and one band in the middle bulged out wide as a shoulder. The county's age structure had a lump in it, like a snake that had swallowed something and was patiently digesting.

"That's the baby boom," Priya said. "Born 1946 to 1964. My mom calls herself a boomer like it's a diagnosis." She dragged her finger up the chart. "And the bulge has moved. It's up here now. Retirement ages."

Jackson sat back. His grandfather was seventy-six, which Jackson did the arithmetic on twice, and yes, 1947, inside the bulge, inside the snake. Last month his grandfather had showed him the apartment on Route 9, actually, where his friend Walt had moved after the house got to be too much. "Second floor now," Walt had said from the balcony. "In case the river has opinions." The building was forty years old, impecunious renters in the census tables, and painted the exact blue of a hundred-year flood. He had been standing inside his own data layer and hadn't known it.

He spent the next hour pulling the over-sixty-five population by block group and adding a third layer. Where the blue floodplain and the cheap parcels overlapped, the senior population was densest, small circles sized to the counts, clustered along the river like beads. Priya leaned in close enough that he could smell the hand sanitizer on her wrists.

"There," she said. "That's your map."

"It's one map. I made three others." He showed her: one that shaded the city by elevation, one by tenure, one that made the floodplain look almost empty by using block groups instead of blocks, which was technically legal and quietly dishonest. He was beginning to think the real skill wasn't making the map. It was choosing which map to make and admitting what you'd chosen.

The librarian, Ms. Okafor, came by at closing to burnish her reputation for leniency by giving them fifteen extra minutes, which she announced while stacking chairs with the volume of someone who meant business. Jackson exported the map, printed it in color for seventy cents, and folded it into his backpack along with the other three, the honest ones and the flattering one, because he hadn't decided yet which he'd hold up at the podium Thursday, or whether he'd hold up all of them and let the council see the choosing itself.

Outside, the streetlights had come on along the river, and Priya pointed at the water, low and brown and ordinary. "Doesn't look like much," she said.

"Neither did the pyramid," said Jackson, and held the door.

The chart came out of a cardboard tube in the back of Grandfather's study, and it smelled of dust and old varnish. Victor unrolled it across the desk, weighting the corners with a brass sextant and a tin of pipe tobacco that had not been opened in years. The North Atlantic spread out under his hands, veined with arrows: pale blue arrows running south, deep red arrows curling northeast off the American coast and across toward Ireland. Grandfather had crossed that ocean twice on a freighter before Victor was born, and the map was the only proof he ever offered.

"Tell me what you see," Grandfather said from the doorway, teacup in hand. He had promised Victor a tenner if he could explain, by Sunday dinner, why London winters were milder than Boston's even though London sat farther north. Grandfather was not a man who gave money for guesses.

Victor traced the red ribbon with one finger. It broke away from Florida, gathered strength, then bent east and widened, as though it had grown tired of America. The label read Gulf Stream. He understood currents the way he understood rivers, water going somewhere, but the ocean was not going anywhere in particular. It circled. He copied the arrows into his notebook and spent an interminable afternoon staring at them, the desk lamp humming, gulls working the cold sky outside the window.

That evening Nadia called about the physics trip they had both signed up for in the spring term. She had been to the planetarium the weekend before, with Daniel, and the two of them had argued the whole way home. "Daniel says greenhouse gases are just pollution, full stop," she said. "I said it can't be that simple, nothing that big is just one thing. He called me a sycophant for agreeing with the presenter. He was in a mood."

Victor, who had missed the show, asked what the presenter had said. "Something I keep turning over. Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14." He wrote it down as she said it, twice, because it sounded like the kind of number that changed its shape if you looked away. Minus eighteen. He stood at the bedroom window looking at the frozen birdbath in the garden, trying to hold both figures in his head at once, the earth as it was and the earth as it might have been.

On Saturday he laid the two ideas side by side on the desk: the current map, open at the North Atlantic, and his notebook, with the temperatures written in the margin. It struck him that he had been treating the Gulf Stream like a radiator, a machine that made heat. It made nothing. It only carried heat, the way the atmosphere, according to Nadia's presenter, only held it. Two systems doing the same quiet work of keeping a planet, or a continent, warmer than its latitude deserved. Warmth, he thought, was less a matter of making than of keeping. He was honest enough with himself to note the gap in his reasoning too: he could not say how much of London's mildness was the current and how much was the wind and the rest of it. He wrote that uncertainty down as well, in smaller letters, because it belonged there.

At Sunday dinner he explained it to Grandfather in three sentences, red arrows, heat carried north and east, Europe warmed by water that started in the tropics, and then added, because he wanted the tenner to mean something, "And the same is true of the air itself. Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14. So the same principle twice. The world is warm because things hold on to heat, not because they make it."

Grandfather set down his fork and looked at him for a long moment, and Victor braced himself for a correction. "Where did you get the second part?" Grandfather asked. Victor told him about Nadia and the planetarium, and braced again. But Grandfather only pushed his plate aside, reached into his cardigan pocket, and brought out a folded five-pound note, not ten. "The current part is worth five," he said. "The rest is showing off, and showing off is worth nothing at my table." Then, almost smiling, he nodded at the frost on the window. "Though I'll grant you this, lad. The planetarium never crossed the Atlantic in February." He tapped the pane with one knuckle, twice, where the ice had gathered thickest.

Chloe spread her notes across the kitchen table the way her mother laid out legal briefs, each page squared to the table's edge, and she had been at it for forty minutes before her brother came in and put his elbows directly on the translation diagram. She was trying to learn, before Monday's entrance exam, how DNA becomes protein, and she could recite it now, transcription then translation, the copying of the gene into RNA, the reading of that RNA into amino acids, but reciting and understanding were turning out to be different animals. Marcus, who was eleven and mercurial, forever swinging between sulking and showing off, dropped a plastic dinosaur onto her paper and said, "Teach me."

"You'll be bored in a minute."

"Teach me anyway. I'll pay you a dollar."

She could use a dollar, and more than that she had read somewhere that the surest way to find the holes in your own understanding was to explain something to someone who kept asking why. So she pulled the diagram out from under his elbows and smoothed it. "Okay. It's like a recipe book," she said. "The DNA stays in the kitchen, in the nucleus. You don't want to get the book dirty, so you copy out one page. That's the RNA. The copy goes out to where the cooking happens, and the cooks read it three letters at a time and build a protein." Marcus picked up the dinosaur and made it walk across the double helix. "Who's the cook?"

"The ribosome. Now pay attention, because this is the part I keep getting wrong." She flipped to her second sheet, the one with the arrow diagram of glucose being broken down, and there the trouble was waiting for her again, the same wrong number she had gotten in practice tests twice tonight. "After the copying," she said, more to herself now, "the cell burns the sugar for energy, and you count up the energy made, the ATP, and my count keeps coming out short. Every time."

Marcus, from Chloe's point of view, was a pest who had learned, or perhaps habituated himself, to interrupt her the moment she got close to anything fragile in her own head. What she did not see, from across the table, was that he was actually reading the diagram. He followed the arrows with his finger, the way he followed dungeon maps in his games, and he noticed something she had been staring straight through. "Why does it split here?" he asked. "One line comes in and then there's two of this triangle thing after it."

She looked where he was pointing. One glucose, and after the first stage there were two of the little two-carbon units, and every arrow after that point belonged to each of them, not just one. The citric acid cycle turned twice for every glucose that entered, because each glucose yielded two acetyl-CoA molecules and each one went into the cycle separately. Everything after glycolysis happened twice, and she had been counting it once. "That's it," she said. "That's why my count is wrong. It's all happening two times."

"So you owe me a dollar."

"That's not how tutoring works."

"It's exactly how it works. I found the split."

Their mother came through with a stack of folders and set a subpoena on the counter, some document that had to go out in the morning mail, and Chloe caught her eye and said, "Mom, tell him finding a bug in my notes isn't the same as understanding them." Their mother, who had learned not to referee before coffee, said, "Tell me what a protein is first, and then I'll rule on the dollar."

From where Marcus sat, watching his sister gather the pages back toward herself, it seemed to him that she had gone somewhere else for a moment, the way she did, and that he had put her there. "A protein is what the whole thing is for," she said slowly. "The DNA is the archive. The RNA is the message. The protein is the thing that actually does the work in the cell. And the sugar is the fuel that pays for all of it, and you have to count the fuel right or you think the cell is poorer than it is." She looked at the diagram again, at the single line splitting into two, and she could not quite say which was truer, that the cell was one story or that it was two stories told at once, and she decided she was allowed not to know that yet.

"The dollar," Marcus said.

She dug in the pocket of her hoodie and found a crumpled bill and put it on the table between them, holding two fingers on one corner of it. "You get this when you can tell me why the count was wrong."

He looked at the diagram, at the two triangles, and she watched him actually think, his mouth a little open, the dinosaur forgotten on its side. "Because after it splits," he said, "the circle part, the citric acid cycle, it has to go around for both of them. Two times for one sugar." She let go of the dollar, and he snatched it and was out of the kitchen, and she sat back down and picked up her pen and drew, in the margin, a small circle with an arrow going around it twice.

Gabrielle had been carrying the same manila folder to the community art studio every Tuesday for six weeks, and it still held only four finished pieces. She arranged them on the long table by the window: two watercolors of her grandmother's hands, a charcoal study of the kitchen faucet that dripped all summer, and a print she had made of the sink itself, its basin crowded with drowned moths. The theme was supposed to be hands and water, or maybe just things that repeat, and she had promised herself, and Ms. Okafor at the studio, that by spring she would have ten pieces ready. Ten felt like a real number, solid and countable, the kind of thing you could hold up to a magistrate and say, here, this is a body of work.

The studio smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee. On Tuesdays it filled with retirees painting orchards and a few teenagers who came because school art was only forty minutes and a shared sink. Marcus was there already, a senior from the public school across town, truculent as always about the drying racks, which someone had reorganized overnight into an order he did not respect.

"That's mine," he said, pulling a canvas off the rack before Gabrielle had even unpacked her brushes. "Somebody moved it into the wrong slot."

"Everything got moved. They cleaned." She watched him set the canvas down with exaggerated care, and then, because she wanted to talk to someone other than her own folder, she said, "Can I ask you something about AP Art? You took it last year, right?"

"2-D Art and Design." He said it the way people name a rival they respect. "Why."

"I'm building a portfolio. Ten pieces on one theme, plus a statement. Ms. Okafor's making me write the statement first, before I even finish." Gabrielle turned one of the watercolors toward him, the close-up of her grandmother's knuckles wrapped around a wet dish towel. "But I don't actually know what schools want."

Marcus looked at the watercolor for longer than she expected. "Ten pieces is a gallery thing," he said. "The AP portfolio isn't ten." He wiped his hands on his jeans. "The Sustained Investigation section asks for fifteen digital images. And it counts for sixty percent of your score."

"Sixty percent of the whole score?"

"That section, yeah. Fifteen images." He shrugged, as if he had delivered bad news often enough that the delivery no longer interested him. "People fail it because they make nine good pieces and then sprint in April."

Gabrielle sat down on the paint-spattered stool and did the arithmetic in her notebook, twice, because the first time the numbers seemed truculent themselves. Ten pieces became fifteen images only if every piece photographed into one image, which they wouldn't, since process shots counted, since sketchbook pages counted, since the investigation itself, the questions she was asking, had to show its own thinking. Her theme, things that repeat, was suddenly not a folder but a corridor, and it was longer than she had measured.

She worked that Tuesday without talking much. She photographed the four finished pieces from three angles each, and then, on impulse, photographed her own hands photographing them, which made her laugh out loud at the copying table and embarrassed her into silence. At home she opened a blank document and titled it Artist's Statement, which Ms. Okafor had wanted all along, and Gabrielle had resisted because writing about the work felt like explaining a joke. Now she understood it differently, not as explanation but as a map for where she still had to go. She typed: My grandmother's hands repeat the same motions her mother's did, over the same sink, in a house that no longer exists. What is inherited, and what is just worn in?

The next Tuesday she brought the statement to the studio and read it aloud to Ms. Okafor, who listened with her arms folded and then said, "Good. Now make me five more pieces that argue with it." Gabrielle spent the evening sketching the well outside her grandmother's old house in Opelousas, which she had visited exactly once, and a series of faucets from the studio bathroom, and her own hands doing nothing at all, resting, which was the hardest thing she had ever tried to draw honestly.

She did not tell her mother that the plan had grown from ten pieces to fifteen images, because her mother would have heard it as more time, more Saturdays in Opelousas, more of the money set aside for the studio's sliding-scale fees. Some of that was true. Gabrielle kept the older number in her head anyway, ten, like a first draft she could not quite delete, and let the two figures sit side by side without reconciling them. What she knew for certain was narrower than what she had believed she knew in September: that the portfolio had a shape, that the shape was partly hers and partly not, and that the part that was not hers was not therefore an enemy. The requirement had not crushed her investigation; it had invigorated it, stretched it like a spine, though she could not yet say whether the stretch would strengthen it or simply make it thinner.

In April there were fourteen images in her folder and a fifteenth half-drawn, the resting hands, still not right. Marcus had graduated and stopped coming. Ms. Okafor stood over the drying rack at closing time while Gabrielle pinned up the newest piece, a watercolor of the studio sink with her brushes soaking in it, and said nothing for a long moment.

"That one's the truest," Ms. Okafor said finally. "The hands are wrong, though."

"I know," Gabrielle said, and unclipped it, and carried it back to the table while the lights were still on.

Cameron sat on the screened porch of his grandmother's house with a block of basswood in his lap and a gouge in his right hand, shaving curls toward the floor. The printout of a wren lay pinned beside him on the table, its feathers translated into a grid of cuts. He had promised her a carving before he left for college, nine days from now, and he had promised himself it would be good, which was a different and heavier promise.

His cousin Dez, ten years old, had been watching from the doorway for most of an hour, chewing the eraser end of a yellow pencil. Now she had worked her way down to the other end. She bit the wood, made a face, and kept chewing.

"Stop that," Cameron said. "You're eating varnish."

"I always chew them." She came and sat on the step below him, holding the pencil out like evidence. Something had flaked off the yellow paint onto her tongue. "Wait. Is this the lead kind? Mr. Rowley said lead makes you sick. Like your brain. Tyler's brother said a kid died from eating a pencil."

Cameron looked at the mangled pencil, and then at the ceiling of the porch, where his thoughts tended to go when they were assembling themselves. He had spent a whole unit on toxicology in chemistry, and it occurred to him that he had never actually checked what was inside a pencil, only repeated what everyone said. He turned it over. "Okay. It's called lead, but that's the wrong word for it."

"So I ate lead."

"You didn't." He held up his own pencil, unsharpened, and tapped the gray tip. "The name goes back to the 1500s. When they found graphite, they thought it was a kind of lead ore. So they called it lead, and everybody kept calling it that. It was never the metal."

Dez squinted at him, deciding whether he was messing with her. "Then what is it?"

"Graphite. Carbon." He thought of the periodic table poster in his room at home, the same column as diamond, which he found beautiful in a way he had never said out loud to anyone. "It's just carbon. Like charcoal. Like basically pencil shavings."

She ran her tongue over her teeth anyway, suspicious. "Then why do they still say lead if it's wrong?"

"Because names stick even after they're wrong." As soon as he said it he understood that he meant more than pencils, though he couldn't have said exactly what. He set down the gouge and picked up the pencil again, turning it in the light, the cheap paint catching sun. A thing could be carrying a lie and still be ordinary, harmless, sitting in every desk in the country.

His grandmother came out with two glasses of lemonade and a dish towel over her shoulder, and she was effusive about the wren's half-emerged wing, the way she was effusive about everything he made, which he both wanted and did not trust. "That's better than the duck," she said. "The duck looked like it had been through something."

"The duck had been through something."

"Well, then it was honest." She set the glasses down and stayed standing, which meant she was working up to a request. "Dez, sweetheart, tell him what you told me this morning."

Dez went still in the way she did before big asks. "I want you to teach me. Carving. Before you go." She said it flat, without the pleading that would have made it easy to refuse. "I saved forty dollars from mowing. I'll pay for wood."

Cameron looked at his remaining nine days, which he had already budgeted in his head: two for packing, one for Marcus's goodbye party, and the rest, secretly, for this porch and this block of wood. "You don't have to pay me."

"I want to pay for the wood. I'm not a charity." Her chin was set the way their grandfather's used to set, in family photographs from before either of them was born.

He thought about his father, who called him an ideologue last spring when he'd argued too hard at dinner about art schools versus real degrees, and how the word had stung mostly because it was half true. He had principles about teaching, about not doing it for money, about what an apprenticeship was supposed to be. He also had a cousin with forty dollars in an envelope, and forty dollars meant something to her that it didn't mean to him. Maybe both things could be true at once and he could stand in the middle of them, holding neither perfectly.

"Fine. You buy the wood," he said. "I keep the money thing out of it, that's my one rule. And we start with graphite, not knives. Drawing before cutting."

Dez stood up so fast the lemonade sloshed. "Can we go to the hardware store now? Grandmother, can he drive your car?"

His grandmother held out the keys without comment, but her eyebrows did something complicated, and Cameron understood that she had been on Dez's side the whole time, that the lemonade had been strategy. He took the keys. On his way to the door he noticed he was still carrying his own pencil, and he turned back for the gouge, out of habit, out of some new instinct about which tools mattered.

In the car Dez rolled the mangled yellow pencil between her fingers, then held it out to him. "Keep this," she said. "So you remember to tell the next kid."

He put it behind his ear and backed down the gravel drive, the wren unfinished on the porch behind them, its wing half raised, waiting exactly where he had left it.

Natalie was the last one through the gym doors, carrying the cooler of sodas her mother had iced at noon. The end-of-season party was Coach Okafor's idea, held on the court itself because nobody wanted to rent a room, and the seniors had claimed the bleachers near the far basket, where the afternoon light came through the high windows in dusty columns. Natalie set the cooler under the scorer's table and looked at the five of them up there, the seniors, in their warm-up jackets with the sleeves pushed to the elbows, and understood with a small physical jolt that the roster would never assemble in this building again.

She had spent the season trying not to think about that. The team had gone 14 and 8, better than anyone predicted, and Natalie had started the last eleven games at point guard after Dana blew out her knee in January. Her own problems had been ordinary and pressing: her crossover was slow, her left hand weak, her father asking at dinner whether all this practice was worth the scholarship odds. She had answered him with numbers, because numbers were the only remuneration anyone recognized in this house. Fourteen and eight, she'd said. We're good.

"Hey, freshman," Dana called down, though Natalie was a junior. "Bring the sodas up. We're having a funeral."

Natalie climbed the bleachers with two cans held against her ribs. Dana had her knee braced and propped on the row below, and beside her Priya sat cross-legged with a battered spiral notebook open on her thigh. Priya was the team's only senior who cared about school more than basketball, and she was the one who had taped the practice schedule inside her AP Psych binder all season, as though the two calendars could reinforce each other.

"Read it again," Dana said.

Priya turned the notebook so Natalie could see. There were stages diagrammed in Priya's narrow handwriting, arrows connecting boxes labeled forming, storming, norming, performing. Then a fifth box, added later in different ink. "So in 1977," Priya said, "Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage." She tapped the last box. "Adjourning. That's the word."

"For what?" Natalie asked, though the hollow feeling in her chest had already guessed.

"For when a group's work ends and members separate." Priya closed the notebook. "I found it in October, and I've been waiting all season for it to be relevant. Which is a terrible way to say I knew this night would come."

Dana popped her soda and held it up. "To adjourning." The five seniors drank to it, and Priya laughed in a way that sounded like it could turn into crying, and somewhere across the gym a sophomore was shooting free throws alone, the ball's echo arriving a half second after each release.

From Priya's seat on the third row, the gym looked different than it had all season. She could see the whole court framed between Dana's braced knee and Natalie's shoulder, could see the shooting sophomore's arc repeat and repeat, and she noticed that Natalie had not drunk. Natalie was turning her can slowly in her hands, studying the label as though it might portend something about next year.

"You're quiet," Priya said to her.

"I keep thinking it doesn't have to be the fifth stage," Natalie said. "For us. Dana's coming back, right? And I'm back, and half the team's back. It's only adjourning for you two."

"Three," said Beckett, the other senior, from the end of the row. "Me too."

"Fine, three." Natalie set the can down on the bleacher, unopened. "But here's what I actually think. The thing that ends isn't the team. It's this team, this exact set of people, and that was ending from the first day of tryouts whether anybody named it or not. So maybe the model is right and I just don't like it. Or maybe a team isn't a group with a defined end, it's more like a relay, and the group is whoever's holding the baton right now." She stopped, hearing herself pile abstraction on abstraction. "I don't know which one I believe. Ask me in November."

Priya considered her for a moment, then reached over and took Natalie's unopened soda, cracked it, and drank half of it. "That's your remuneration for the philosophy," she said, handing the can back. "You'll get paid in September when the new kids look at you like you know something."

Dana pulled herself up on her crutches and stood facing the court. The light through the high windows had gone amber, and the dust in it hung like something diaphanous between the rafters and the floor, the same dust they had run through all winter. "One last thing," Dana said. "Everyone on the court. Yes, you too, Priya. Bring the ball."

They played, in the loosest sense: seniors and juniors and the startled sophomore, no score, Dana stationed at the free-throw line calling out plays she had no intention of running. Priya stood at the top of the arc with the ball and did nothing with it for a long moment, just watched all of them scattered across the floor in positions they had occupied for months. Then she bounced it once, hard, and let the sound fill the gym.

"Adjourning," she said, and passed to Natalie, who was already moving.

The morning of Chuseok, William arrived at his aunt's house in Fort Lee with a three-ring binder under his arm and a speech half memorized in his head. His grandfather had led the family's harvest ceremony for as long as anyone could remember, and after the funeral in June, the job had drifted, unclaimed, toward William, who was eighteen now and, according to his aunt, "the eldest grandson of the eldest son, so stop making that face." He had spent two weeks preparing, mostly to allay his own dread of standing in front of thirty relatives with no idea what to do.

Inside, the kitchen was already loud. His aunt was steaming songpyeon, his mother was slicing Korean pear with unnecessary violence, and his little cousin Jina was under the table pretending to be a cat. His halmoni sat in the corner in her good grey hanbok, watching everything with the stillness of a woman who had outlived the person usually giving the orders.

"Halmoni," William said, crouching beside her chair, "I found Harabeoji's notebook. He wrote everything down. The order of the dishes, which side the fruit goes on, all of it. I'm going to follow it exactly."

His grandmother turned the binder over in her hands without opening it. "He would have liked that you have it," she said. "Read it to me later. My eyes are tired today." Then she patted his wrist, which he understood to mean both go away and stay close.

The ceremony was set for the evening, because Chuseok falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, and the family had always held the rite at night, after the food was cooked and the children were fed. William spent the afternoon arranging the low table in the front room, consulting the binder like a law student the night before the bar. Jina abandoned her cat persona to supervise. "That's the wrong side for the rice," she announced at one point, and William, who was holding the rice exactly where the notebook said, felt a hot flash of the bellicose certainty he usually managed to keep out of family settings.

"The book says west," William said.

"Harabeoji always put it east," Jina said. "I remember because I asked him once and he said the ancestors face east so the rice faces them, and then he said don't tell anyone I explained it that way, which was weird."

William looked at the binder. Then he looked at the binder again, more carefully, and found what he had skimmed past: his grandfather's handwriting changed halfway through. The early pages were confident, decades of practice compressed into terse instructions. The later pages were shakier, and in the margins, in pencil, small corrections. Rice east. Not west. Corrected, with the date, three autumns ago.

He carried the notebook to the kitchen and set it open beside the pears. His mother leaned in, read a few lines, and laughed once, quietly. "He never told anyone he was forgetting."

"He wrote it down so he wouldn't," William said. He stood there holding the rice bowl, thinking about how he had wanted this evening to run on precision, on instructions that could not fail, and how what he was actually holding was a record of a man making mistakes and quietly fixing them. Two ideas he had been keeping in separate rooms all week, the ceremony as something performed exactly and the ceremony as something carried by people, walked toward each other and sat down together. He could not have said which was truer. He put the rice on the east side.

His aunt came out of the kitchen, saw the table, and put both hands on her hips. "Who taught you the layout?"

William weighed several answers, including a lecture on primary sources. "It's called charye," he said, which answered nothing, and which made Jina snort from under the table. "I mean. Harabeoji's notes. The corrected ones."

"Hm," his aunt said, in the tone she used for approving of things without admitting it.

At the rite that evening, William led the family through the bows, and the food stood before the ancestors' names, and his grandmother's eyes were closed and her lips were moving, and nobody mentioned that his hands shook a little during the pouring. When it ended, she beckoned him over and he knelt by her chair, expecting to be told what he had gotten wrong.

Instead she said, "Next year you will do the second pour slower. Your grandfather always rushed it." She smoothed her skirt. "He also put the chestnuts on the wrong side for eleven years. Nobody ever told him. We just moved them when he wasn't looking."

From under the table, Jina's voice said, "I can be in charge of that now. The moving things part. It's basically a job."

William looked at the table, at the chestnuts sitting precisely where the notebook had corrected them, and reached over and nudged the bowl two inches to the left. "Like that?"

The garage had been a music room since the flood, when the river left its alluvial smear across the ground floor and the piano came out here to live on the concrete, close to the lawnmower. Laurie's exam was in eleven days, and the exam wanted the first movement of Mozart's K. 545 divided into exposition, development, and recapitulation, with the bars marked in pencil where each part began. She had a photocopy, a pencil, and a mother who believed silence in the garage meant studying.

The problem was bar twenty-two. She had put the double bar there because something clearly ended, but the something that began afterward refused to sound like a development. It was too polite. Developments were supposed to wander, and this section sat at home like a cat that had never been outdoors. She played it three times, badly, because the piano's middle D stuck and had to be struck twice, which lent Mozart a stammer he had not asked for.

Theo came through the side door at four, as arranged. He was fourteen and paid her five dollars a week, which he called an honorarium, having recently discovered the word, so that the lesson would feel official. He was learning guitar chords for a girl named Priya, and Laurie's role was mostly to say "again" and occasionally "your fingers." He settled on the upturned milk crate that served as a second chair.

"Play me your G chord," she said, because it was that part of the lesson, and because part of her mind was still on bar twenty-two.

He played it. G, B, D, all three strings ringing in their amiable way. It was fine. It sat there being a G chord and asking nothing of anyone.

"Is that it?" Theo said. "Is that the whole thing?"

"Add your pinky," she said, mostly to get his hand out of the lazy position, and she pointed at the string, the fret. "That's an F."

He frowned at his own hand as if it had been stigmatized by the stretch, then got the note down. He strummed.

The chord changed character entirely. It leaned. It sounded as though it were already on its way somewhere and had only paused to take Laurie along. She stopped him with a hand. "Again."

"I didn't do it wrong that time," Theo said, wounded.

"No. Do it again anyway."

He did it again. The F on top of the G chord made the whole thing reach toward a C the way the river had reached toward the house, patient and certain. She played a C on the piano with her left hand while he strummed, and the two chords closed together like a door.

"What is that?" she said, and then, because he was looking at her as though she had asked him to define weather, "The G with the F in it."

Theo consulted his hand. "G with an F in it," he offered.

She got her phone and typed until she found it. The chord was called G7, the dominant seventh in the key of C, and it was made of exactly those notes, G, B, D, and F, and it pulled hard toward the C major chord, which was why Theo's version had sounded like a sentence waiting for its final word. She read this twice. It was strange to learn a name for something her ear had already agreed to.

She went back to Mozart with the pencil. At the end of the movement there was a G7 sitting in the second-to-last bar, and after it the final C, and she could hear now how the whole ending was a controlled fall, the G7 leaning and the C catching. That part she could mark with confidence. Bar twenty-two she left circled but unanswered, because she could hear that something changed there and could not yet say what the change was called, and writing a guess in pencil felt more honest than writing one in ink. The exposition, she decided, ended where the home key stopped being taken for granted. Or possibly at the double bar. She wrote both page numbers in the margin and drew a small question mark shaped, unintentionally, like a seagull.

"Is the lesson over?" Theo said. He had been holding the G7 for several minutes, apparently in case it expired.

"One minute." She set the photocopy on the piano rack and played the first eight bars, then jumped to the last four, skipping everything between, just exposition and ending. It sounded like a joke with the middle missing. She played them again with the middle restored, all the way through, sticky D and everything, and the movement arrived where it had always been going.

"That's the one," Theo said. "For Priya. The G with the F in it."

"That's the one," Laurie said, and marked the recapitulation with a line so firm the pencil squeaked.

Leo arrived at the field at seven with a whiteboard under one arm and his chemistry notes folded into his back pocket, the enthalpy diagrams half finished, because the exam was Monday and the tournament was Saturday and both refused to move. He set the whiteboard against the goalpost. Twelve eleven-year-olds, and their problem was simple to see and hard to fix: they passed to wherever a teammate had been standing two seconds ago, not where he was running. Three weeks Leo had been watching them, and now Coach Ruiz had a wedding to attend, and the team was Leo's until Saturday.

"We're doing passing drills," he told them when they gathered. "Not scrimmaging. Passing."

Groans. A kid named Marcus, the smallest one, didn't groan, just looked at the ground.

"Watch." Leo drew three cones on the whiteboard, spaced in a triangle, then an arrow between the second and third. "The ball goes where he's going to be. Not where he is."

Dani arrived halfway through the first drill, jogging the perimeter of the field the way he did every morning, tracking his weekly mileage like other people tracked money. During water break he dropped onto the bench beside Leo, phone out, scrolling his training app.

"How's the science project going," Leo said.

"You mean the team? It's fine."

"Your mileage. Your plan."

Dani turned the phone toward him. A graph, rising in neat steps. "The 10 percent rule," he said, like it was a law of physics. "Never raise weekly running distance more than 10 percent. That's how you build a season without breaking yourself."

Leo looked at the graph. Neat, ordered, undeniable, the way enthalpy diagrams were undeniable, and he thought of his own plan for the kids, adding one new layer to the drills each practice, small increments, because increments felt like safety. That was the whole logic of his whiteboard. He took out his phone and typed, partly to allay the worry that he was building Saturday's plan on a guess.

The search results were not what he expected. He read one, then another, then a third, holding the screen at an angle so Dani could see it.

"What," Dani said.

"It says it's a popular guideline," Leo said slowly. "But the studies haven't shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans."

Dani took the phone. Read it again himself, thumb hovering, not scrolling. "That can't be right. Everyone says it."

"Everyone says pass to the feet, too. Look where that's gotten them." Leo tipped his chin toward the field, where a ball had just rolled out of bounds because the receiver had stopped moving and the passer had led him anyway. "Maybe gradual is gradual. Maybe the 10 percent thing isn't magic, it's just, you know. One version of careful."

Dani gave the phone back and didn't answer, which for Dani was an answer. He stood, stretched, and started his second lap.

Marcus had watched the whole exchange from the end of the water line, close enough to hear the phone part, though he didn't understand most of it. What he understood was this: Leo had looked something up, and the looking-up had changed his face, and now Leo was staring at the whiteboard like it had lied to him. Marcus didn't like the drills. They made him feel slow, because he was slow, and because the cones made it obvious. But he'd also noticed, during the triangle drill, that when he ran to the empty cone before the ball came, it arrived right at his feet, and for one second he'd looked like the best player on the field.

"Leo," he called, because it seemed like the moment.

Leo looked over.

"When we do it slow, it works. When we do it fast, it stops working."

"Then we go slower first," Leo said. He walked to the whiteboard, erased the arrow he'd drawn for Thursday, and drew a shorter one. He'd been treating his progression like Dani treated mileage, some fixed increment that would guarantee improvement by Saturday, and now he understood that the increment itself wasn't the guarantee, only the caution behind it was. What he still didn't know, and said so to nobody, was how much caution eleven-year-olds actually needed, and whether Saturday would punish him for going too slow as surely as for going too fast.

"Line up," he called. "Triangle. Half speed. I want the passer calling the name before the ball moves."

They ran it half speed and it was ugly, balls wobbling, two kids colliding at the far cone. Leo made them run it again. And again. On the fourth attempt, a boy named Tomas played the ball into open space ahead of Marcus, and Marcus was already there, already running, and trapped it clean with the inside of his foot.

"There," Leo said. "That. Do that again."

Dani finished his lap and stopped at the sideline, breathing hard, phone still in his hand, screen dark.

"We're going full speed on Saturday," Leo told him, not looking away from the triangle.

"Even with the slow week?"

Leo watched the ball move, watched Marcus start his run before anyone passed to him. "Full speed. We'll find out together."

Dani sat down on the bench and opened his training app.

The argument started over a jar of jam, of all things. Jessica's grandfather insisted that his homemade chokecherry jam reached its best flavor after exactly twenty minutes of boiling, while her cousin Dara, home from her first semester of engineering, claimed that was nonsense. "There's no such thing as a perfect minute," Dara said, spooning some onto toast. "It's all in your head." Jessica, who had a calculus problem set open on the table beside her untouched plate, found herself drifting into the middle of it without quite deciding to.

"Actually," she said slowly, "there could be. If quality is a function of time, and it goes up for a while and then goes down, there'd be a peak somewhere. One exact minute where it's best." Her grandfather pointed his butter knife at her like a judge's gavel. Dara rolled her eyes, but she was already reaching for a napkin, because that was the kind of person Dara was.

"You're doing derivatives right now, aren't you," Dara said. It wasn't a question. She flattened the napkin on the kitchen table between the butter dish and the salt shaker and drew a wobbly curve rising and falling like a hill. "So say flavor is some function of minutes. You take the derivative and set it equal to zero, and you get the top of the hill." Jessica looked at the napkin, then at her notebook, where problem six asked her to locate the maximum of a polynomial she'd been circling all morning without success. Something clicked sideways in her brain, the way a stuck jar lid sometimes does when you grip it differently.

"Wait," she said. "But how do you know it's the top of the hill? The derivative being zero just means flat, right? Couldn't it be flat at the bottom of a valley too?" Dara opened her mouth, then closed it, and Jessica realized with a small shock that Dara didn't know. They sat there in the quiet while the refrigerator hummed and their grandfather, delighted to have two granddaughters doing math at his table over jam, went to put the kettle on.

Jessica pulled the napkin toward herself and drew a line straight up through the crest of the hill. To the left of the line, the slope climbed; to the right, it fell. She wrote a plus sign on the left side and a minus sign on the right, and then sat back. "If the derivative is positive before the point and negative after, then the function rises and then falls. So that point is a local maximum." Saying it aloud felt like setting a stone into a wall and finding it held. She glanced at Dara. "Positive to negative means a peak. I think that's the whole test. They probably have a name for it."

"Sign chart," Dara said, tapping the napkin. "My professor calls it the first derivative test." She was quiet for a moment, turning her toast on its plate. "Okay, I take it back. If Grandpa's flavor actually rises and then falls, there is a best minute. I was wrong." Jessica stared at her cousin, because Dara admitting error was rarer than snow in October, and because Jessica was noticing something odd about her own position, which was that she had started the afternoon on Dara's side, sort of, and had argued her way toward her grandfather's without meaning to.

The kettle began its obstreperous whistle and their grandfather remonstrated with it gently, as though it were a rude guest, before lifting it off the burner. He set three cups of tea on the table and settled into his chair with the satisfied air of a man whose jam had been mathematically vindicated. "In pharmacy school," he said, "we learned the physiology of taste buds, all those little receptors on the tongue. Nobody ever told us they could be reasoned about with, what did you call it, a derivative. I like that. The tongue and the napkin, agreeing."

Jessica copied the curve into her notebook, minus signs and all, and then turned to problem six and did it in four lines, the polynomial cresting exactly where her plus sign crossed to minus. The maximum sat there in her handwriting, plain as anything. She still didn't know whether her grandfather's jam actually rose and fell, whether twenty minutes was truly the peak or just a number he'd loved long enough to believe, and she found she could hold both thoughts at once: the method was certain, the jam was not. "We'd have to test batches," she said. "Ten minutes, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five. Blind tasting." Dara grinned and reached for another piece of toast. "Tomorrow," their grandfather said, "we boil."

Jayden set his phone face down next to his plate before his mother could say anything about it. The poll results were still open in his head anyway: fifty-two percent of students wanted the college to keep the late-night shuttle, forty-eight percent wanted it cut and the money moved to mental health services. He had fifteen hundred respondents, or rather one thousand and forty, and at eleven that night the paper's website would go live with whatever headline he chose.

"Your grandmother called twice," his mother said, spooning rice onto his brother's plate. "Twice."

His brother, Ellis, who was twelve and choleric about nearly everything lately, stabbed at a chicken nugget. "Because Dad told her I quit soccer."

"You did quit soccer."

"I paused soccer."

Jayden pushed a pea to the edge of his plate. His father asked how the paper was going, the way he asked about most things, which was kindly and without any intention of following the answer past the first sentence. But Jayden answered anyway, because it was the one thing he wanted to say out loud before eleven o'clock. He told them about the survey the student government had run, that he'd gotten the raw numbers that afternoon, that his co-editor, Priya, wanted to run the headline as "Majority of Students Support Keeping Shuttle."

"Sounds right," his father said. "Fifty-two is more than fifty."

"It's four points," Jayden said.

Ellis said that four points was nothing, that his soccer team had lost by four points and it had counted as a loss. Their mother said that was football and this was not. Jayden let it go and kept going himself, slowly, because the shape of the thing was still forming while he talked. He'd spent the bus ride home with the numbers, and then an hour at the library's statistics guide before he understood what he was even looking for. One thousand and forty students had answered. It wasn't every student. It was a sample, drawn at random, and there was a rule about samples that size, a figure he'd found and written on his wrist to remember.

"Margin of error," he said. "With a simple random sample of about a thousand people, it's roughly plus or minus three percentage points."

His father's fork paused. "Three points each way."

"Each way. So fifty-two could really be forty-nine." He moved his peas again, two of them this time. "Or it could be fifty-five. And forty-eight could be fifty-one. They overlap. You can't actually tell who's ahead."

The table was quiet long enough for his mother to say, "So the poll says nothing?"

"No. It says something." This was the part he hadn't worked out until the walk home, and saying it now, in front of the chicken and the rice, made it firmer. "It says the campus is close to split. It rules out a landslide. It just doesn't rule out either side being ahead. Priya wants to say the majority supports the shuttle, and technically more of our respondents did. But if the real number for all students could be under fifty, we'd be printing a majority that might not exist."

Priya had been inured to student government's habits by two years on the beat; she assumed every release was spun until proven otherwise, and she'd been right often enough that her instinct was worth something. Jayden usually deferred to it. But instinct and a number weren't the same kind of thing, and tonight the number was his.

"Then don't say majority," his mother said. "Say students are divided."

"That's weaker," Jayden said. "Nobody clicks on 'Students Are Divided.' And the student government wants the shuttle kept, so if we run the weak headline, they'll say we buried them."

Ellis looked up. "So the truth is boring and the lie gets clicks."

"It's not a lie. It's just not proven."

His father asked whether Priya had seen the margin of error thing, and Jayden said he'd texted her a picture of the page an hour ago and she'd replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else, which meant she was either convinced or annoyed, and with Priya those looked identical from a distance. He had also texted his journalism professor, who had not replied, because the professor never replied after eight.

Ellis announced that nothing mattered anyway, that he'd learned the word existentialism in school that day and that according to the French the shuttle question was pointless because everything was. Their mother said the French could clear the table. Ellis cleared the table.

Jayden helped dry the dishes while his mother washed, and he told her the smaller version of the problem, the one he could hold in one hand: he could write that the poll found fifty-two percent in favor, and print the sample size and the margin in the sixth paragraph where nobody read, and the student government would be happy and the paper would look decisive. Or he could put the margin in the first sentence, where it made the whole poll smaller, and take the heat. He'd spent a year inuring himself to the idea that the editor's job was judgment, not arithmetic, but tonight the judgment was the arithmetic.

"Which one lets you sleep," his mother said, handing him the pot.

He thought about it honestly, which meant admitting he didn't know whether a bigger headline would matter, whether the administration would even read past the first line, whether a future editor would have to retract something he'd implied. All of that stayed uncertain. What he had was one thousand and forty random students, three points in either direction, and a decision at eleven.

In his room he opened the draft and deleted "Majority." He typed: "Students Split on Shuttle, Poll Shows, With Results Within Margin of Error." Then he texted Priya: running this unless you object by 10:30. He set the phone on the desk, screen up, and watched the three dots appear.

Riley sat at the kitchen table with a textbook open to a chapter titled Monetary Policy and a stack of index cards he had not yet written on. His grandmother, who had come to stay for the week while his parents visited his aunt, sliced a lemon cake so friable it came apart into rubble on the plate. She set a piece in front of him and asked what all the sighing was about.

"I have to be able to explain, out loud, why a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation," he said. "Not just recite it. Explain it, like to a person."

"You could practice on me," she said, and lowered herself into the chair opposite with the air of someone granting him an enormous favor. "I raised four children on a fixed income. I know what interest rates are. I just don't know why anyone would raise one on purpose."

He began, and heard his own voice slide into what Izzy, his sister, called his lecture elocution, the roundness that crept in when he was unsure of the content, and he stopped mid-sentence. "Sorry. Let me try again like a human."

On Saturday he had gone to the farmers' market for peaches and found a girl at the honey stall with a review sheet folded into eighths, mouthing terms to herself. When a jar tipped and he caught it, she looked up as though he had been sent. "You look like you take economics," she said, which he decided to take as a compliment. "Comparative advantage. The original example. Which countries, which goods?" He said England and France, wool and wine, with more confidence than he owned. She demurred, tilting her head, and said, "I think there's Portugal in it somewhere." He had laughed it off, bought the peaches, and gone home, where the itch of it followed him to the bookshelf. The book was in the house, an old fat paperback of Ricardo's, and he found the example printed there in 1817, in a book whose full title took three lines to say, England and Portugal trading cloth and wine. He had been wrong on every count but England. He'd copied the whole thing onto an index card and then, out of some private shame, carried the card in his back pocket for two days.

"I still don't see the connection to inflation," his grandmother said now, brushing crumbs toward the edge of the table.

"Right. The connection," he said, and turned the card over in his pocket. He laid his hands flat on the table. "When the bank raises rates, borrowing costs more, so people and businesses take out fewer loans and spend a bit less, and saving pays a bit more, so money moves slower, and prices stop climbing so fast. It's like the whole economy is a party and the central bank is turning the music down. Nobody leaves. Everybody just stops shouting." He paused. "That might be a terrible analogy."

"It's the first thing you've said that I understood," she said. "Although who decides when the music is too loud?"

"That," Riley admitted, "is the part I actually can't answer. Whether they turn it down too hard and stop the party entirely, or too softly and nobody even notices. My textbook has four different economists disagreeing about it, and the chapter doesn't pick a winner. I have to present on Monday and my honest position is that the mechanism is clear and the timing is a guess."

His grandmother considered this while eating what remained of her cake in small, deliberate bites. "So you'll say that."

"I'll say I'm sure about the direction and unsure about the measure," he said. "Apparently that's allowed."

Izzy came thumping down the stairs with her earbuds around her neck, drawn, as always, by the sound of food. "Are you rehearsing again? Use the Ricardo one, that one's good." She took a corner of his cake without asking. "England and Portugal, cloth and wine, 1817. That book with the title that's longer than the chapter."

Riley stared at her. "How do you know that?"

"I was behind you at the honey stall. The whole conversation." She pointed a fork at him. "You were so confident about France, I almost felt bad for you."

He looked at his grandmother, who was smiling at the ceiling. On Monday, he decided, he would lead with the part he'd gotten wrong, and the card went into the drawer with the pencils. Izzy took the last of the cake and went back upstairs, calling down, "You owe me a peach."

Morgan laid out twelve cones in the grass, six and six, spaced exactly as far apart as the gap between her team's midfielders when they lost the ball. Again. Three times in the last match, a pass had trickled out of bounds because the girls sent it blind, without looking, without checking their shoulders first. She was seventeen and had been made assistant coach of the under-fourteens mostly because she was the only one who volunteered, but she had decided that if she was going to do it, she would do it like it mattered.

Her little brother Eli sat on the porch steps with his economics homework, radiating gloom. "I have to write a paragraph on stagflation," he announced, "and I don't care about the economy, and the economy doesn't care about me."

"Tragic," Morgan said. "Hold this clipboard."

"Who am I, your intern?"

"Yes. Unpaid. Like a real job." She handed him the clipboard anyway, and he held it with the sullen dignity of a boy who had nowhere better to be, which he did not, and knew it.

The first drill she tried was the obvious one: pass, move, receive, pass again, down the line of cones. Eli rolled balls to her and she rolled them back, feet turning, weighting each pass soft enough that a thirteen-year-old could control it. But when she imagined her girls running it, she could see the flaw. They would get good at passing when nobody pressured them, and then Saturday would come and some opposing midfielder would stand exactly where the drill had pretended no one ever stands. She sat down on the grass and thought about her own coach, Mr. Ruiz, who believed in repetition above all things, and about her club coach, Dana, who believed that nothing counted until it was chaotic. For years Morgan had assumed she had to pick one of them, the way you pick a side in a family argument.

Eli's phone buzzed. "Podcast," he said. "It's for my paragraph."

"Speaker," she said, mostly to be annoying, and he turned it up out of laziness. The voice talked about prices and wages for a while, and then, in a segment that had nothing to do with Eli's homework, mentioned a trial done in Norway in 2008, young female soccer players aged thirteen to seventeen, and something called the FIFA 11+ warm-up. Players who did it had about a third fewer injuries overall. Morgan made Eli replay it twice. "A third," she said. "That's like taking three injuries and getting rid of one."

"That's literally what a third means," Eli said. "That's why the word exists."

"Shut up, that's why you exist." But she was writing on the clipboard now, fast. Her girls spent about ninety seconds warming up, jogging in a loose circle, stretching whatever hurt, and then moaning when she asked them to do more. If she had numbers, an actual Norwegian trial with actual thirteen-to-seventeen-year-old girls, that was different from Coach Says So. Teenagers ignored authority but they respected evidence, mostly, when it suited them, which was often enough to be useful.

Here was where the two coaches met in her head, and she felt a small, unreasonably pleasant click: keep the warm-up structured, like Ruiz would, but keep it short and honest, like Dana would, ten minutes, the whole 11+, every session, and let the drills themselves carry the chaos. She redrew the cone drill with a defender added, a chaser who started three steps behind the passer, so the girls had to look up or lose the ball. Pressure built in. Repeats stayed. Both coaches, one practice plan.

Saturday morning, the girls stood in their loose circle, yawning. Priya, the captain, had already objected twice on the group chat.

"We're going to lose ten minutes of actual soccer," Priya said.

"There was a trial in Norway in 2008," Morgan said. "Girls our age, thirteen to seventeen, who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall. A third."

"In Norway," said Nia, "everything works. They have fjords."

"They have fewer injuries," Morgan said. "We have cone drills. Ten minutes."

Priya looked at the cones, then at the sky, weighing ten minutes against a season, and Morgan could see her doing the arithmetic, and could also see that she wasn't finished doing it, that some part of her was holding the number up against her own aching hip from last spring. She didn't say yes. She said, "If it's boring, I'm walking to the fence," and jogged to the front of the line.

"Then you'll be doing burpees by the fence," Morgan called, and Priya flipped her a peace sign without turning around, and the first ball rolled, and Nia's pass skipped straight past the second cone, out of bounds, into the hedge, exactly on schedule.

Ryan's grandfather kept his old law books in the sunroom, shelf after shelf of them, and that was where Ryan went first when the assignment landed in his inbox: argue both sides of a free speech case before a mock Supreme Court, alone, in front of his whole constitutional law elective. The rules said each side got eight minutes. Eight minutes to convince his classmates, and then eight minutes to convince them of the opposite.

The case his teacher had built was about a student, not much older than Ryan, who had posted a video telling people to "shut the school down, whatever it takes." Nobody had gotten hurt, but a fight had broken out in the parking lot, and the school had expelled him. Ryan's job was not to decide whether the expulsion was fair. His job was to make the best argument for the student, then turn around and make the best argument for the school, as though he believed each one down to his shoes.

He tried drafting in the kitchen and got nowhere. His grandfather drifted through for coffee, saw the sprawl of printouts, and said only, "Sunroom's quieter." That was the whole invitation. Ryan carried his papers to the long table under the window where the light was best, and for two days he let the arguments ruminate, circling each other in his head while he half-watched his grandfather putter in the garden below, a small, deliberate figure in a straw hat.

The student's side came easily. Words are not acts, Ryan wrote. A video is not a bomb. If we punish every angry thing anyone posts, we punish the impecunious kid with a phone the same as a senator with a network, and we chill the speech of everyone who might have something true and unwelcome to say. He liked that paragraph. It sounded like the editorials he admired.

The school's side was worse. Every argument he drafted felt like a police siren. He was rummaging through the shelf behind him, more out of frustration than scholarship, when he found a fat green casebook with a cracked spine, and inside it, a page his grandfather had underlined in pencil decades ago. The margin note just said, "This is the one that got away from all of us." The case was Schenck v. United States. Ryan read it twice, then a third time, and the pieces began to shift against each other like tiles in a puzzle he hadn't known he was holding.

The case had introduced a test. His grandfather's pencil led him down the margin: clear and present danger. Under it, speech could be punished if it created a clear and present danger of a harm that Congress could prevent. That was the bridge. The government side didn't have to claim that words were fists. It only had to show danger, clear and present, aimed at a harm the law was allowed to stop. Ryan sat back. His two drafts weren't opposites after all. They were two hands gripping the same scale, and the test was where the scale balanced, or failed to.

He tried it out loud that evening, standing at the sunroom table as if it were the bench. "For the school, the question isn't whether the video was offensive. It's whether it created a clear and present danger of a harm Congress could prevent." His grandfather appeared in the doorway with two mugs, set one down, and said, "Careful, though." Ryan waited. "When you argue it for the student, you're going to say that test is a hundred years old and that the Court tightened its own leash later. You'll have to hold both ideas in one head. Most people never manage it. They pick a side at seventeen and defend it at seventy." He tapped the casebook. "Underlined that before your father was born."

Ryan had planned to do exactly that, wave the test away as ancient history when it hurt his side. He sat with his coffee going cold and made himself write the harder thing instead: that the test survived in some form because every society has to answer the same question underneath it, and that utilitarianism, the trade of one speaker's freedom for many students' safety, could justify almost anything if you let it, and could justify nothing if you refused it entirely. Where the line actually fell, on a video like that one, in a parking lot like that one, he could not say. He wrote that he could not say, and left it on the page.

On the morning of the mock court, his classmates filed in with their note cards, and Ryan stood up with nothing but two pages and his grandfather's cracked green book. He argued for the student first, then took a breath, squared his shoulders, and began, "For the school, I'd ask the court to apply the clear and present danger test, and I'd ask you to notice that I used to be afraid of it."

The community hall smelled of sesame oil and steam from the rice cookers lined up along the back wall, and Layla stood near the folding tables with a paper plate of dumplings she wasn't eating. Her mother had already drifted toward the mahjong corner, leaving Layla with her nine-year-old cousin Mei, who was counting something in her pocket with the concentration of an ascetic who had just discovered temptation.

"Nine dollars," Mei announced. "Auntie Po gave me three dollars in this one and Grandma gave me six, but Grandma's envelope is redder, see?"

Layla looked. Both envelopes were red, but Grandma's was the deep, lacquered red of the shrine cabinets at the front of the hall, the red that Mei said, matter-of-factly, meant good luck and kept evil away. Layla had known that much since she was small, though she hadn't known, until tonight, that the envelopes were for children and unmarried younger relatives, which she'd overheard Auntie Po explaining to Mr. Delgado from the insurance office, who had come for the food and stayed for the generosity. Layla turned the phrase over while Mei bounded off toward the lion dance practice. Unmarried younger relatives. She was sixteen. She was, technically, all three of those things, and yet she felt like a person collecting a toll for a bridge she'd already crossed.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Daniel, who was across the hall by the door, visibly weighing whether to come in.

"Is it weird if I'm here? I don't know anyone except you."

"Not weird. Bring a plate. Say happy new year to anyone over fifty and they'll adopt you."

"Should I bow? What do I do with my hands?"

"Daniel. It's a community hall, not a ceremony. Come eat a dumpling."

She watched him read this, watched him square his shoulders the way he did before a piano recital, and felt, briefly, fond of him in a way she didn't plan to say out loud.

The trouble arrived with Auntie Po, who moved down the table dispensing envelopes like a dealer at a generous card game. When she reached Layla she paused, envelope hovering, and said, "Still in school? No ring on that finger?" Then she pressed the red paper into Layla's hand before Layla could answer, and moved on to a boy of eleven, and Layla stood there holding it. She had spent the past hour composing, in her head, a graceful refusal, something about being too old, about saving it for Mei, about how a person who paid her own bus fare probably shouldn't be collecting lucky money. The speech had been elegant, almost tangential in its indirection, and now it was useless, because the envelope was already in her hand, warm from Auntie Po's pocket, and refusing it now would require her to expostulate in the middle of the hall, which was the one thing worse than accepting.

Daniel appeared beside her with a plate piled absurdly high. "Okay, this is the best thing that has ever happened to me," he said, through a dumpling.

"There's more at the back table."

"There could not be more. There is a finite amount of more."

Layla slid the envelope into her pocket unresolved. She kept circling the question the way Mei circled the lion dancers, approaching and retreating: on one side was the plain fact that she qualified, that the custom said what it said, that Auntie Po had judged her eligible without hesitation; on the other was her own sense that acceptance was a kind of claiming, a childishness she was supposed to be outgrowing. She could not make the two fit together, and she was honest enough with herself to admit it. Maybe, she thought, she could hold both at once: take the envelope as what it was, a gift from an aunt who loved her, and leave the question of what taking it meant for another year, when the answer might be different.

Then Mei came back, breathless, holding out a small envelope of her own, folded badly from red construction paper, sealed with a sticker of a cartoon rabbit. "For you," Mei said. "Because you gave me your dumplings last time when I dropped mine, and it's new year, and I have three dollars."

Layla opened it. Inside was three dollars and a note in Mei's careful handwriting: "You are not too old. Grandma checked."

Daniel leaned over to read it. "Checked with who?"

"Grandma," Layla said, and folded the note closed. She put it in the envelope with the three dollars, and the envelope in her pocket next to Auntie Po's, and only then noticed Auntie Po watching from the far table with an expression of unmistakable satisfaction, as though the whole evening, the envelopes, the red, the luck itself, had been arranged for exactly this moment.

"There," Auntie Po called across the hall. "Now the rabbit gives back."

Layla looked down at the badly folded paper in her hand. "The rabbit," she said, "is keeping this one."

Lea arrived at the Saturday market before the sun had cleared the rooftops, dragging two crates of strawberry preserves and a folded canopy that refused to cooperate with anyone. She had until noon. At noon, in the air-conditioned office of a community foundation two blocks away, a panel would ask her one question about economics, the discipline she had declared on her scholarship application with more confidence than she actually possessed, and she intended to have an answer that did not sound like the first paragraph of a textbook she had skimmed at two in the morning.

The question, according to a friend who had interviewed last year, was almost always the same. Why does raising interest rates slow inflation? Lea could repeat the words. Prices rise too fast, so the central bank makes borrowing more expensive, so people spend less. But when she said it aloud in her car it had the hollow ring of artifice, a structure she could inhabit without believing in, and she suspected the panel could hear that hollowness the way customers could taste sugar that was hiding something.

She set up her table between a beekeeper and a woman selling alluvial soil, rich black loam bagged from the river bottom, or so the sign claimed. Lea had inherited the preserve stand from her grandmother and run it herself since junior year, which was the entire basis of her application essay: small business, real customers, actual arithmetic. Her brother Marcus, fourteen, arrived twenty minutes later with a clipboard and his headphones around his neck, and slid onto the folding stool behind the cash box without being asked.

Marcus handled the schedule now. He had handled it since April, taking the custom orders by text, telling Lea when the restaurant wanted forty jars of apricot and when the church fair needed her Saturday. He was slower at it than she was. He misread one order in May and they had made thirty jars of the wrong thing, and Lea had spent an evening furious, scrubbing the kitchen, until she did the month's accounts and found they had still earned more than before he started. Every hour she spent answering texts about delivery times was an hour she wasn't cooking, and her cooking, not her scheduling, was what the restaurants paid for. She could type faster and organize better and it still paid to hand it over, because the hour she gave up was worth more than the hour he gave up.
