She pulled the feminist book closer anyway and skimmed the index for anything about class, then put it back, because the argument in her notebook had already outrun it. She could hold both ideas, she decided, the way you hold two full cups: carefully, and with a certain acceptance about the carpet. Some of it would stay unresolved, and she wrote that down too, because it felt more honest than pretending she'd solved it, and because, if she was very lucky, the unresolved bit was where the good marks lived.

She packed up at closing, accepted the tea she had never been offered, and left the notebook on the counter by accident, which Theo discovered after she'd gone, and which meant he had to run half a street in the rain to catch her, waving it over his head like a small square flag.

"You forgot your whole brain," he said, dripping.

"Give it here," said Charlotte. "Monday needs me."

The resolution said "This house would lower the voting age to sixteen," and Julia was arguing for it, which meant that Marcus Okafor was about to argue against her, which meant she would lose, probably, the way she always lost to Marcus, who had read every book in the school library with the word "logic" in the title and wore this fact like a badge.

She stood at the podium waiting for his rebuttal, and the flaw in her own case rose up to meet her. She had said that sixteen-year-olds work, pay taxes on their paychecks, drive cars, and manage course loads that would stagger a Rhodes scholar, none of which, she now saw, proved anything about voting. Marcus would point that out. Marcus would take her weakest sentence, hold it up like a dropped glove, and hammer it while the real question sat untouched behind him.

He began, as he always did, with a definition. "Democracy," he said, "presumes a capacity for long-horizon judgment that neuroscience tells us is not fully developed until the mid-twenties." There was more, about insurance premiums and rental cars and why no one let sophomores sign mortgages, and the judges wrote things down, and Julia wrote things down too, because something odd was happening. She was writing his argument, not her response to it. She had filled half a page before she noticed.

The night before, her father had refused to extend her curfew past eleven. "Because I said so," he had finished, which was, as adages go, less an adage than a surrender. Julia had wanted to scream that he was treating her like a child, and instead she heard herself say, slowly, like walking on ice: "If I understand you, you'd say that the road home is badly lit after eleven, and that the stretch past the canal has no sidewalk, and that you'd be asleep and unable to come get me if something went wrong. Is that your reason? Because it's a better reason than the one you gave." Her father had put down his fork. He had looked at her for a long moment and said, "That's what I meant." They had settled on eleven-thirty and a text at the corner of Marsh Street, and Julia had gone upstairs feeling as though she'd performed a magic trick whose mechanism she didn't understand.

Marcus sat down. It was her turn, and she had a page of his reasoning in front of her, and she made a decision that felt like stepping off a ledge. "My opponent's argument," she said, "is actually stronger than he made it. He said neuroscience. He didn't need to. Here is his case at its best." She laid it out: judgment matures late; we already restrict rights on that basis; voting requires weighing distant consequences against present impulses; therefore the franchise should track maturity, not enthusiasm. She added the part Marcus had only implied, that working and paying tax doesn't confer a right to control the money's use, any more than paying rent makes you the landlord. "That," she said, "is the steel-man. It's the practice of restating the opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than they put it, before you answer it." Marcus's eyebrows moved a quarter inch, which for Marcus was applause.

Then, and only then, she responded. If maturity is the standard, she said, the test should be maturity, not birthday, and plenty of adults would fail a long-horizon judgment test while plenty of sophomores would pass it, so either we screen everyone or we screen no one, and screening everyone is a project no one in this room, including her opponent, actually wants. She heard herself use the word "if" four times, building little conditional houses and walking through their rooms. If the brain matures at twenty-five, then why eighteen for everything else. If eighteen is arbitrary, then the argument isn't about sixteen at all. Marcus was leaning forward now.

In cross-examination he didn't attack. "Your landlord analogy," he said. "Did you invent that just now, or are you stealing from Mill?" "I demur," Julia said. "I'd call it borrowing." The third judge, the one who never smiled, smiled.

She lost anyway, on a two-to-one decision, the dissenting judge citing "the only genuinely responsive rebuttal of the round." Marcus found her afterward by the water fountain. "The steel-man thing," he said. "That has a name. People do it on purpose?" "Apparently I do it on purpose now," Julia said. He turned the pages of his notes back and forth, the way he did when a book had misled him. "I still think I'm right," he said. "I know," she said. "That's the part I can't fix."

Walking out, she tried to decide whether she'd won something or merely lost more interestingly than usual. The two ways of thinking sat side by side in her, refusing to merge: Marcus's discipline of definitions and her father's mute, buried reasons, both real, both incomplete. She texted her father that she'd be home by eleven, and then, after a pause, by eleven-thirty, and put the phone in her pocket before he could answer.

Robert found the tube on Monday morning, propped between two books on the shelf his grandfather still called the chemistry shelf, though nothing else in the house suggested a laboratory. His grandfather had taught chemistry for thirty-one years, and then the stroke had come in March, and now the words arrived late or not at all, like buses in a town Robert had never been to. Robert had a test on Thursday. He was staying the week because his mother thought the company would be good for both of them, and because the apartment was empty otherwise.

The tube was sealed glass, the length of his forearm, and inside it the gas was the brown of old tea. A label in his grandfather's cramped hand read NO2. Robert knew the notation from class. He knew, in the flat way of things memorized the night before, that nitrogen dioxide could run both directions, pairing off into a colorless compound and unpairing again, an equilibrium. Knowing the sentence and having any sense of what it meant were, he was beginning to understand, different projects.

He carried the tube downstairs. His grandfather sat at the kitchen table with the crossword he no longer finished, pencil moving in slow, stubborn circles around one square.

"What's this for?" Robert held the tube up to the window. The brown looked denser at the bottom, though his grandfather had told him once, back when telling was easy, that gases don't settle like that. It was probably the light.

His grandfather looked at it for a long moment. Then he pointed at the kettle.

"Hot?" Robert said.

His grandfather nodded once, a small precise motion, and Robert, who had planned to spend the morning on his phone, felt something shift toward an actual morning. He filled a bowl from the kettle and lowered the sealed tube into the warm water the way he'd lower anything he suspected of being fragile and important at once. The brown deepened, slowly, then unmistakably, like weather coming in over a field. He moved the tube into a bowl of water and ice from the freezer, and the color thinned, faded toward pale, though it never vanished.

He sat with it. Heat made it darker, which meant heat made more of the brown gas, which meant the reaction ran toward the brown side when he added heat, and away from it when he took heat away. The system leaned against whatever he did to it. He checked the impulse to write this down as a rule, because rules were how you equivocated with yourself, deciding a thing was understood when it was only filed. He didn't want to file it. He wanted it in his hands.

His grandfather was watching him. Then he rapped the table twice, pointed at Robert, pointed at the pantry, and made a shape in the air with both hands: a box.

"You want a box?"

His grandfather nodded and mimed pumping something up.

Robert went to the pantry and found a cardboard box from the garage, and a ruler, and he measured it, multiplying out the sides with the pencil from the crossword. It came to about twenty-two litres, close enough, and he stood there doing the arithmetic he half remembered from a Tuesday in September until the shape of it assembled itself. One mole of an ideal gas, at zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere, would take up about twenty-two point four litres. A mole of gas would fill this box, roughly, if the box were full to the brim and freezing. The whole idea he'd been copying off the board for weeks, that abstract and unphotographable quantity, had a size you could stand next to. He picked the box up and turned it over, looked inside its plain brown emptiness, and felt the fact settle in with the warmth of something discovered rather than delivered.

"Twenty-two point four," he said. "Per mole. At zero Celsius. One atmosphere."

His grandfather's mouth worked. Then, clearly, with effort, like a man lifting something with a bad arm: "Fill it."

They couldn't, of course, not exactly, not with a mole of anything in the kitchen, and not at zero degrees. That was the part Robert refused to paper over. The box was a picture of the fact, an approximation standing in for a truth he couldn't hold. He thought about telling his grandfather this, about the difference between a demonstration and the thing itself, and then decided his grandfather had spent three decades being the kind of man who knew that difference better than anyone alive.

He carried the tube back to the bowl of ice water. The brown had gone faint again, the reaction pressed toward its colorless side, waiting, patient, ready to lean back the other way the moment he warmed it. He kept his hand in the water a moment longer than he needed to.

"When it warms up," he said, "it goes brown again. That's the whole test, isn't it. That's every question they can ask."

His grandfather smiled, picked up the pencil, and drew one slow line through the empty square.

The trail switchbacked up through pines that still smelled of last night's rain, and Luke kept one hand on his phone, scrolling through a search page he had already read three times. His presentation was at nine the next morning. Eighteen minutes long, graded, the first real grade of his first semester, and he had the science down cold except for the part he didn't, which was the part everyone would actually remember.

"I still don't have the station," he said. "I have the scientist. Keeling. I have the institution, sort of, Scripps something, in California. I have the year. But my slides say 'a remote station' and Mr. Farrell wrote 'where?' in the margin of my outline like it was a personal insult."

Beside him, Marisol stepped over a root without looking up from her granola bar. "So look it up."

"I've been looking it up. The internet has decided I need a summary of the entire Industrial Revolution instead." He pocketed the phone, then took it out again. The deadline had a way of reaching him even through granite and pine litter, a subterranean hum under the nicer sounds of the afternoon.

They had planned this hike weeks ago, before the assignment existed, and Luke had refused to cancel it on the grounds that a person could think while walking. Marisol had agreed on the grounds that she wanted to see whether that was true. Now she said, "Explain it to me. The greenhouse thing. You're always saying if you can explain it to me, you can explain it to anyone."

"I said that about my Spanish oral."

"Transferable skill. Go."

He waited until the trail leveled and he could gesture without falling. "Okay. Sunlight comes in, that's visible light, it warms the ground, the ground sends heat back up as infrared. Certain gases let the sunlight through but catch some of the outgoing heat. More of those gases, more heat caught. That's the whole engine of it. The trick in the presentation is the graph, because the graph is the receipt. It shows carbon dioxide climbing, decade after decade, this sawtooth line going up and up, and you can't argue with a line."

"You can argue with anything," Marisol said. "People argue with the moon landing."

The trail bent around an outcrop, and below them the valley opened, hazy, the town a smear of roofs. Luke stopped and pulled up the graph itself, the one he'd printed and taped inside his notebook, the one whose station he could not name. The sawtooth was there, the little annual rise and fall, and over it all the long climb. He had learned to read it the way you learn to read anything: first the shape, then the axes, then what the shape was doing to you.

"You know what the sawtooth is?" Marisol asked, leaning in.

"Seasons. Plants breathing." He turned the notebook sideways as if that would help. "That's not my problem. My problem is I'm going to stand up there and say this line comes from some mountain somewhere and someone's going to ask which one, and I'll say I don't know, and that'll be the moment the whole thing collapses. It'll look like a veneer. Like I found the picture on some blog and never asked where it came from."

Marisol took the notebook from him and looked at it longer than she'd looked at anything all day. "There's a name in the corner. Tiny. Is that a K?"

He took it back and held it at the angle where the light caught the gloss of the tape. It was a name, partly smeared, and the full phrase was almost certainly there in the original file if he could find the original file. He sat down on the outcrop, opened the search again, and this time typed the half-legible word first, before anything else. The results came back in a rush. Charles David Keeling, of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, who had begun regular carbon dioxide measurements in March 1958, on Mauna Loa, Hawaii. A volcano, of all things, chosen for its clean air. And the graph, which Luke had been staring at for a week without knowing it had a name people actually used.

"It's called the Keeling Curve," he said.

"Named after him?"

"Named after him. Keeling Curve. It sounds like a road in Scotland." He copied the words into his notes, all of it, station and date and the full institution, then read the sentence back twice to make sure he had it exactly. The hum under the afternoon went quiet. He could already see slide eleven, the sawtooth line with Mauna Loa printed underneath in the small confident font of things verified.

Marisol offered him the last piece of the granola bar, which was mostly oats and pretense. He took it anyway. They stood at the overlook a while longer, the town going gold at its edges, and she said, "So tomorrow you're going to explain to thirty tired people how the air holds heat."

"Eighteen minutes."

"You're going to point at a line on a screen and tell them it started on a volcano in 1958 and never stopped." She shouldered her pack. "Better you than me. Race you to the creek."

The laundromat on Delancey had a parking lot with exactly four spaces, two of them always taken by the shop van, and Sara had claimed the remaining corner as her personal driving school. Her mother sat inside behind the window with a paperback, one eye on the dryer and one on the lot, while Sara practiced parallel parking between a traffic cone and a folding chair she had wedged where the curb would be. She was failing at it with a regularity that had begun to feel almost scientific.

"You're crooked again," her mother called through the propped door, not unkindly. "Like a car parking itself sideways out of spite."

Sara got out and looked. The nose of the Honda pointed toward the folding chair at an angle that would have earned her an automatic fail, the kind of angle that made other drivers pity you. She had been turning the wheel the wrong way, she realized, or at the wrong moment, though she could not yet say which. That was the infuriating part: the error was somewhere in the sequence, invisible until it bloomed into crookedness.

She had her reasons for wanting the license by August, and they were not the ones her friends assumed. Not concerts, not freedom in the abstract. Her grandmother's dialysis was Tuesdays and Fridays, and her uncle, who normally drove her, had taken a job in Hartford. Nobody had said the words "you should learn," because nobody in her family said things like that directly; they reified obligation into silences and calendar gaps and the sudden appearance, on the kitchen table, of a practice test booklet. Her mother's maxim, delivered once while folding towels, had been: "We don't ask people to be grateful in this house, we just show up." Sara had found, over the years, that this sounded simpler than it was.

A boy from her school, Marcus, came into the laundromat that afternoon with a garbage bag of laundry and no detergent, having forgotten his, a fact he announced to the room with the cheerfulness of the truly disaffected. He watched Sara from the window while his socks tumbled.

"You're doing it backwards," he said through the screen.

"Thank you, Marcus. Extremely helpful."

"No, I mean the wheel. My sister taught me last summer. You pull up next to the car in front, right, alongside it, and then you back in. You turn the wheel toward the curb first." He mimed it, hands rotating an invisible wheel left. "Then when the car swings into the space, you turn back the other way to straighten out. That's the part you're skipping. You're turning away the whole time, so you just end up diagonal."

Sara sat with that for a second. Toward the curb first, then away. It felt counterintuitive, like being told to lean into a fall, but she had spent forty minutes doing the intuitive thing and it had produced nothing but geometry of shame.

She got back in, pulled forward until she was alongside the folding chair, checked her mirrors, and reversed, turning the wheel toward the curb. When the car had swung partway into the space, she turned the wheel away, and the Honda, obedient for the first time all afternoon, straightened itself against the curb like a sentence ending in a period. She sat there with the engine idling, surprised by how small the correction had been.

"See," Marcus said, mildly.

The highway was the other half of the test, and the harder half for her, though not for the reasons on the checklist. Merging required her to commit: to accelerate down a ramp toward a gap in moving traffic and trust that the gap would hold. Parking, at least, was a negotiation with stationary objects. She thought of her uncle, who had once admitted over Christmas dinner that he had taken the Hartford job partly because he was tired, and she had not known whether to be angry at him for the honesty or grateful for it, and had settled, as usual, on neither. Perhaps commitment was like the wheel: you could not tell, until you were inside the maneuver, whether you had turned too early or too late.

She practiced the merge that evening on Route 9 with her mother in the passenger seat, hands rigid on the armrest. The ramp, the acceleration, the glance over her shoulder, the slide into the lane between a pickup and a bakery van. Her mother exhaled.

"That was fine," her mother said. "That was actually fine."

"Say it like you mean it."

"I mean it like I mean it. Tuesday, you drive your grandmother."

Tuesday was four days away, and the test itself was not until September, which meant one of them would have to sit in the dialysis parking lot for three hours, and Sara understood that this was the family's way of asking her to choose. She signaled, checked her mirror, and eased into the right lane.

The laptop refused to cooperate, and the clock on Grandpa's mantel struck seven with the solid certainty of a clock that had never once cared about anyone's deadlines. Victoria had until midnight to submit the database assignment, and she was spending her evening in a riparian cottage two buses from campus, watching her grandfather's phone screen instead of her own.

"Look at this," Grandpa said, lowering himself into the chair beside her. "From the neighbours. They say the mill race burst this morning and the lower fields are underwater. Karim wants me to post it to the village group before bed, so people move their animals." The video showed brown water sliding over a fence, a shed door flapping, a street she almost recognized. "I don't like it. Something about it doesn't sit right. But I can't say what, and I can't very well accuse a neighbour of machinations without proof."

Victoria had seen something at her mother's office last spring that she hadn't thought about since. A colleague had been checking a clip on his screen and she'd asked what he was doing. "InVID-WeVerify," he'd said, not looking up. She remembered because the name sounded like a plumbing fixture. She had watched him work for a minute before her mother called her away, and what she remembered was a row of images, like film stills, each with search buttons beneath it.

"I might be able to check it," she said. "Wait." She installed the plugin on Grandpa's old browser, chewing the inside of her cheek while it loaded, and when the tab opened she read the small print aloud so they could both hear it. "InVID-WeVerify, a project funded by the European Union." The extension let her drop the video in, and then it did what she remembered: it split the video into key frames, a strip of stills, each one ready to be reverse-searched.

"Those are like fingerprints," she murmured, dragging the first frame, the fence and the flapping door, into the search bar. While it worked, her assignment sat open behind the tab, half a query abandoned on the screen. She'd been at it since four, trying to join a customer table to an orders table and surface the customers who never ordered anything, and every version she wrote either returned everyone or no one. The trick, she was almost sure, was in the join itself, in asking the question from the empty side of it.

The search results came back, and there was the fence. There was the flapping door. The matching page was three years old, from a flood in a river town two valleys over, and the street she'd almost recognized was one she'd seen in a photograph on Grandpa's hallway wall, from a trip before she was born. "It's not our river," she said. "It's an old video wearing our river's clothes."

Grandpa put the phone face down on the table, exhaling through his nose. "So I post nothing. Karim will grumble, but half the village would have been awake all night for nothing." He watched her switch back to the assignment window. "Go on, then. Don't let an old man's flood eat your future."

She went at it differently now. Instead of starting from the customers and asking who had orders, she started from the join itself and let it keep every customer whether or not anything matched, then kept only the rows where the order side came back empty. When she ran it, the result table filled with names, customers with no orders at all, each one surfaced precisely because the other table had nothing to say about them. 11:54 glowed in the corner of the screen. She checked the output twice, attached the file, and pressed submit at 11:58, then sat back with her hands still hovering over the keys, not quite believing the names would still be there when she looked again.

"You look like a woman who won something," Grandpa said.

"Maybe," she said. "Ask me tomorrow." She was already less certain than she sounded; the query was right for tonight's tables, and she had a feeling that the empty side of a join could hide things too, that absence was easier to find than to interpret. She was reaching to close the laptop when his phone buzzed on the table. He squinted at the message and turned it toward her, half laughing. It was the seed catalogue, confirming the twelve packets of sweet peas he had sworn, for weeks, he would never order.

The video arrived at 9:40 on a Tuesday morning, while Liam was still sweeping the glass crumbs out of the back workroom of Ferreira's Phone Repair. His cousin Dree had sent it to the family thread and then to him directly, twice, which meant she wanted something. He watched it standing between the shelving of cracked-screen donors and the heat gun: a grainy clip of a man in a parking lot yanking a phone out of a woman's hand, then running. Text over the top said it had happened at the Milford Plaza lot, two streets from the shop. Dree's message read, This is literally by us, share it, everyone needs to know.

Liam had worked at the shop for six weeks, long enough to have replaced eleven screens, two batteries, and one charging port that a toddler had filled with raisins. Mr. Ferreira trusted him with the register now, which underpinned a small pride in him, though he hadn't yet earned trust with anything that required judgment. This felt like it might require judgment. The video had forty thousand views already, and Dree was not a careless person, exactly, but she was fast, and speed was contagious. His thumb hovered over the share arrow.

Before he could decide, the bell over the door rang and Mr. Ferreira came in carrying coffee and his ancient laptop, the one he used for the customer database and refused to replace despite its many idiosyncrasies, including a power cord that had to be held at a specific angle. "Liam, I need the list of customers who haven't ordered anything this year," he said, setting the laptop on the counter. "For the mailing. We want them back."

Liam had watched Mr. Ferreira run queries before but never written one himself, and Mr. Ferreira, it turned out, had a dentist appointment in twenty minutes. "You know the file," he said. "Customers in one table, orders in another. Join them. My nephew showed me once." Then he was gone, and Liam was alone with the laptop, the video still open on his phone, and a task he only half understood.

He found the query software and, with the wary concentration of someone defusing something, built a join between the customers table and the orders table. He ran it. A tidy list appeared: every customer, each with their order history attached. He scrolled, feeling competent, and then he scrolled again, slower. Mrs. Okonkwo, who had bought one screen protector in 2021 and nothing since, was not on the list. Neither was the man with the raisin toddler, who had paid cash and never come back. He tried a search inside the results to be sure. Gone, all of them, every customer with no orders at all.

He called Mr. Ferreira's nephew, Deshawn, who answered on the fourth ring with the truculent patience of a college sophomore interrupted during something. "It's an INNER JOIN," Deshawn said, around chewing. "That's the default. An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so customers with no orders disappear from its results entirely." Liam wrote this down on a receipt slip. "So the people I most want," he said slowly, "the ones with nothing in the orders table, are the exact ones it's erasing." Deshawn said, "Yep," and asked if that was all, because he was eating.

Liam changed the join to the other kind, the one that said LEFT, and ran it again, and there they all were, Mrs. Okonkwo and the raisin man and dozens more, with empty spaces where their orders would have been. He stared at the blank cells for a moment. It bothered him, in a way he couldn't immediately name, that the default setting had quietly decided the missing people didn't count, and that he'd almost mailed a list built on that decision without ever noticing a deletion had occurred.

Then he looked at his phone, still open to the parking lot video, and the two problems touched each other somewhere behind his sternum. He didn't know how to reverse image search, but Mrs. Okonkwo's daughter came in most Thursdays and was, according to Dree, " terminally online." She was due for a charger pickup at eleven. When she arrived, Liam asked, feeling his ears go warm, whether there was a way to find out where a video actually came from. "Reverse image search," she said, like it was obvious. "Screenshot a frame, drop it in. Takes ten seconds." She did it for him, right there on her own phone, tapping through the frames until she found one clear enough.

The oldest result was from three years ago, from a city four hundred miles away, attached to a local news story about a phone theft outside a different plaza entirely. Somebody had re-uploaded the clip, written new text over it, and given it a new parking lot. Liam sat with that for a second, the way he'd sat with the empty cells in the spreadsheet. In both cases the missing thing had been invisible until he'd gone looking, and in both cases the default, the easy path, the INNER JOIN of ordinary scrolling, would have hidden it forever. Though he also knew, honestly, that this wasn't a perfect parallel; a missing customer was a fact of a database, and a viral video was something murkier, a thing with motives behind it, and he couldn't fully see those motives from here. Maybe whoever re-uploaded it wanted clicks. Maybe they wanted Milford Plaza to look dangerous. He couldn't prove which, and he didn't try.

He texted Dree the news link with the three-year-old date and wrote, Not our parking lot, and please don't share it. Then he printed the corrected customer list for Mr. Ferreira, with every zero-order customer restored, and clipped it to the register. When Mr. Ferreira came back from the dentist and read the video story off Liam's phone, holding the cord at its necessary angle, he scrolled the old news article twice and said, "Good," and then, pointing at the printed list with his chin, "Both of those, today. Not bad for a Tuesday." He tapped the screen of the laptop, and the cursor blinked in the query box, waiting for whatever Liam wanted to ask it next.

The festival had taken over the whole park by noon, but Amelia had not come for the food trucks or the dancers. She had come for the blue tent at the far end, where the Spanish debate table was folded, with a sign-up sheet and a kitchen timer, five minutes per speaker, entirely in Spanish. Her mother had signed the permission slip without reading it carefully, assuming it was the folk-dance workshop. Amelia had not corrected her.

Her topic was whether phones should be allowed in schools, which she had argued twice already in English, once for and once against. Her coach believed in picking a side and holding it until the timer ran out. Her grandmother, who had raised three children without a single device in the house, believed phones were rotting attention spans outright, that the mind would atrophy if you fed it nothing but screens. Amelia had spent two weeks trying to get underneath both positions, writing phrases on index cards at the kitchen table while her grandmother stirred soup and muttered.

She was third on the list. The first speaker, a college boy with a lanyard, spoke fluidly about digital literacy, and the second, a girl from Amelia's own school named Rosa, argued the grandmother's side with real fire. Then came the fourth slot, a boy everyone called Teo, who was visibly nervous and spoke faster as the timer went on. He was describing a school policy, and Amelia caught most of it, until he said, leaning forward, "Los estudiantes se sienten muy embarazados," and the small audience broke into laughter, a ripple of it, and a woman near the front hid her mouth with her hand.

Teo stopped dead. His face went red and he sat down without using his last minute, folding his arms like a child told to wait outside. Amelia leaned toward Rosa, who was still smirking. "What did he say?"

"Embarazado. He meant embarrassed. But embarazada means pregnant. He told everyone the students feel very pregnant."

"That's cruel, kind of," Amelia said, but she wrote it down on the back of an index card, because her own notes had the word in them too, circled twice, and her stomach turned at how close she had come.

The moderator called her name. The woman who had laughed caught Amelia's sleeve as she stood. "False friends," the woman said, tapping Amelia's card without reading it, as if she'd guessed. "Words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning. They get everyone eventually." She let go and turned back to the table.

Amelia stood at the podium and the timer clicked, and she began in Spanish, slower than she had practiced, each sentence placed rather than thrown. She argued that phones in schools were neither poison nor freedom, that her grandmother was right that attention could be lost and her coach was right that banning things taught nothing, that the real question was who taught students to use the tool, and that she did not yet know how schools could do this at scale. She said the last part plainly, "no sé todavía," and noticed that saying it in Spanish made the uncertainty feel less like defeat than like a door left open. She used her final thirty seconds to concede a counterargument she could not answer, because it seemed more honest than pretending.

When the timer buzzed, there was scattered applause and no laughter. Teo was watching her from across the tent, arms still folded, though less tightly now. Rosa came over afterward. "You said you didn't know. In a debate."

"I didn't," Amelia said. "I still don't."

They gave out ribbons at four o'clock, blue ones, and Amelia did not win one; a graduate student with the manner of an aesthete, praising the music of Teo's broken sentence before Teo's own turn, took first place. Amelia found Teo at the empanada stand instead, holding a plate he hadn't touched. She showed him her index card, embarazado crossed out, embarazada written above it, and said, in her careful, slow Spanish, "I almost said it too."

He looked at the card, then at her, and something in his shoulders let go. "Next year," he said, "I'm saying it on purpose. First sentence."

"First sentence," Amelia agreed, and tore the card in half and dropped it in the bin between them.

By the time Mr. Okonkwo called on her, Noemie had already decided she would win the debate, which was the first mistake, though she did not know it yet.

"Minimum wage," he said, writing it on the board. "Resolved: the government should raise it. Noemie and Priya, you're for. Marcus and Daniil, against. Twenty minutes of prep."

She liked this classroom better than any other, third floor, west light, the radiators that ticked like a slow clock. She and Priya dragged their desks together and Priya opened her laptop. Priya always opened her laptop. Noemie preferred the library, the weight of a book in her hands, but there was no time, so she leaned in and began listing arguments on a folded page of her notebook.

"Fifteen dollars isn't enough to live on," she said. "That's the whole case. Wages have to be a floor. That's what the law is for."

"Marcus will say small businesses close," Priya said, typing. "He read something about it last night, he told Daniil in the hallway. I heard them."

"You heard them." Noemie underlined her first point twice. She was certain she had heard nothing of the kind, but Priya's certainty had a way of becoming hers, and anyway it didn't matter, because the case was simple. Every civilized country had a legal minimum wage. That was the spine of her argument. She had learned it from her father, who had worked nights at a bakery for eleven years and who said, every time the subject came up, that without the law the owners would pay people in crumbs.

Marcus opened with the small business line, exactly as predicted, and Noemie knocked it down with a statistic about productivity she had copied from a poster in the corridor outside, a poster she was fairly sure was about productivity. The exchange was quick and clean. Daniil mumbled something about inflation. Then Marcus, shuffling his notes, said, "Here's the thing, though. You keep saying every country has one. That's actually not true."

"It is true," Noemie said.

"Denmark," Marcus said. "Norway. Sweden."

"What about them?"

"No statutory national minimum wage."

"They have one," Noemie said. "Everyone has one. It's like saying some countries don't have a minimum age for school."

Mr. Okonkwo, from the back of the room, said only, "Sources, please. Both of you."

At lunch she went to the library, because she did not lose, and because something in Marcus's voice had been flat and certain in a way that unsettled the physiology of her confidence, her hands cold on the table, her pulse sitting high in her throat. The librarian showed her the comparative labour tables in the reference section, and there it was, in a grid of countries: Denmark, no statutory national minimum wage. Norway, none. Sweden, none. The entry explained that pay floors there came through collective agreements between unions and employers. She read it three times. The countries she would have named as the best places in the world to work had built their floors out of bargaining, not out of a line in a statute.

She found Priya in the corridor. "They really don't have one. Denmark, Norway, Sweden. The floors come from collective agreements. Unions and employers."

"So we're wrong?"

"We're not wrong that there's a floor. We're wrong about where it comes from." Noemie was aware that this distinction felt enormous to her and might look like nothing to Priya, who was already scrolling her phone.

The afternoon session of the debate was where it fell apart, or came together, depending on which version Noemie later told. Marcus repeated his claim and cited the same tables, and Noemie, instead of denying it, said, "He's right about that." The room went quiet. "Denmark, Norway, Sweden, no statutory national minimum wage, that's true. But the pay floors still exist. They're set through collective agreements between unions and employers." She heard her own voice and it sounded steadier than she felt. "So it isn't law versus nothing. It's law versus organized workers."

"That helps you," Daniil said, confused. "That's still a floor."

"It complicates us," Noemie said. "Because it means the law isn't the only thing standing between workers and crumbs. My dad thinks it is. He worked nights for eleven years and he thinks without that statute the owners would grind everyone down, and maybe he's right about his bakery, and maybe a country full of strong unions would protect him a different way, and I don't know which one you can actually count on."

"That's not an argument," Priya whispered.

"It's two arguments," Noemie whispered back. "I'm holding both."

Mr. Okonkwo let the silence run a moment too long before he called time. Afterward, in the emptying room, he said, "You should be careful of the tautological version of your own case. 'Every civilized country has a minimum wage, therefore a country with one is civilized.' That proves nothing." Noemie nodded as though she had known this all along, though she had never once put it that way, even to herself.

She walked home the long way, past the bakery, closed now, its ovens cold, and tried to metabolize the afternoon. She would tell her father that the Nordic countries had no statutory national minimum wage, and she already knew how he would laugh and say, so the government just lets them fight it out, and she would say no, the unions and the employers set the floors together in agreements, and he would say, and who do you trust, a paper you sign or a law you can take to court. She did not have an answer. She stopped in front of the dark window and looked at the reflection of a girl who had won every argument she could remember, holding her notebook against her chest, and started writing, at the top of a fresh page, the words my dad says.

Elijah had the microfiche room to himself on a Tuesday in June, which was the only reason he had chosen it: the air conditioning worked there, and nobody asked what a seventeen-year-old was doing alone in a library at two in the afternoon. His father had lost his job at the cannery in March, and the house had become a place of careful voices, so Elijah had started taking his college application essay anywhere else. The prompt asked him to describe an issue he had changed his mind about, and he had chosen the local paper's coverage of the cannery closing, mostly because it was the only thing he could not stop thinking about.

The essay was not going well. He had written half a page about how the paper had run four stories about the closing, all of them about stock prices and company statements, and none of them about the three hundred people his father worked beside for twenty-two years. Then he had deleted it, because it sounded like a complaint, and complaints were not essays. What he wanted was a reason the paper had written it that way, and he did not have one.

He was staring at his notebook when he heard the tapping. An old man at the next table was trying to feed a quarter into the microfilm printer and missing the slot, his hand shaking in a way that suggested the shaking was not new. Elijah watched for a moment, then walked over. "Here, let me get that." He fed the coin in, and the machine groaned and printed a grainy page from 1987. The headline was about a broadcaster.

"Thank you, son." The man turned the page toward the light. "I was looking for this. My granddaughter's doing a project, and I told her I remembered when it happened, and she said, prove it." He laughed, a dry, pleased sound. "I was a raconteur at that plant over on Fell Street, thirty years, everybody's stories, and now the only audience I can hold is her."

Elijah glanced at the page. "What happened in 1987?"

"The Fairness Doctrine. That was the rule. The FCC made broadcasters put contrasting views on the air about controversial public issues, starting in 1949." He tapped the date with one crooked finger. "And then in 1987, the FCC abolished it. Gone. I remember Dan Rather having to say goodnight to it, almost." He looked at Elijah with sudden attention. "You writing something?"

"College essay. About the paper here, how it covered the cannery closing." Elijah heard himself say it and felt the familiar embarrassment, but the old man did not laugh.

"Who owns your paper?"

"I don't know."

"Find out. That's a story too." The man gathered his printout and his granddaughter's project folder, and he said, "I'd stay and talk your ear off, but she's waiting in the car, and she honks," and he was gone before Elijah could ask his name.

The library's periodical room had a shelf of bound volumes of the local paper and, more usefully, a computer with a database of business filings. Elijah typed in the paper's name and followed it the way the reference librarian, a tired woman named Ms. Okafor who had nevertheless shown him the database without being asked twice, had taught him: parent company, then parent of the parent. The paper was owned by a group headquartered two states away, and that group was owned in part by an investment firm, and the investment firm held a stake in the company that had bought the cannery. He sat back. The words on the screen did not say the coverage was shaped by that. They only said the connection existed, quiet as plumbing behind a wall.

He went back to the microfilm. In 1975, the same paper had run a labor dispute across six issues, with union quotes on the front page. In 1994, a similar dispute got two paragraphs inside, both from management. It was not proof of anything; he knew that, the way he knew a lot of things he could not yet argue. But the pattern had a shape now, and the shape had a history, and the history had a date.

He found Ms. Okafor reshelving near the window and asked whether a newspaper was bound by the Fairness Doctrine, since it was about broadcasters. She said she thought it applied to radio and television licenses, not print, and that he should verify that himself rather than trust her memory. He did, in an old media law textbook with a cracked spine, and she was right, which made the essay harder and truer. The doctrine was gone, and even when it had lived, it had never circumscribed what his paper could print. Its absence explained the air; it did not explain the weather.

He wrote until five, then read it over. The essay said what he had found, and then it said what he had not: that ownership could shape coverage, that he had watched it lean, and that he could not prove the lean was directed by anyone at all. He thought about his father reading it, if his father ever did, and he left in the part about the three hundred workers, because they were the reason, and he cut the part where he had called the paper's editors cowards, because it was trenchant and it was also cheap, and the old man's voice was in his head saying that a story was not the same as a swing.

He saved the file twice, the way his father had taught him, and copied it to a drive for the drive's own sake. On his way out he saw the old man's granddaughter's project folder still on the microfiche table, left behind, a pencil tucked in the fold. He picked it up and carried it to the front desk. "Somebody was using the machine in the back," he said. "An older man, with a laugh you could hear across the room. He'll come back for this."

Ms. Okafor took the folder and set it where lost things went, next to a pair of reading glasses and somebody's house keys. "He will," she said. "They always come back. It's the ones with unfinished business."

"Then he's safe," Elijah said, and pushed through the doors into the heat.

Victoria stopped at the third trail marker because the ink on her flashcards had begun to blur, and because the sugar maples were doing that thing in October where the light comes through them like stained glass, and she wanted to memorize something that wasn't glycolysis. Her backpack held a peanut butter sandwich, a half-charged phone, and a biology worksheet due Monday: trace glucose through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, down to ATP in the mitochondria. She had drawn the whole pathway twice at the kitchen table and both times it had come out looking like a subway map drawn by someone who had never ridden a train.

The real problem was Thursday's quiz. She had gotten a 62 on transcription, the lowest grade she had ever received in a science class, and the teacher had circled the same error four times before writing "see me" in red. Victoria had not gone to see her. Instead she had walked out the school doors, past the bus loop, past the impecunious little produce stand where the farmer sold dented apples by the bag, and all the way to the trailhead, because she thought better while moving, and because a person who fails at sitting still has to turn walking into a method.

She recited the pathway aloud as she climbed. Glucose splits in the cytoplasm, two molecules of pyruvate, a shuttle into the mitochondria, the cycle that strips carbons and loads electron carriers, the chain that uses those electrons to pump protons, the protons flooding back through a spinning enzyme to make ATP. She could say it. She could not yet feel it, and she suspected the gap between saying and feeling was exactly the gap between a 62 and an A.

At the overlook she sat on a flat rock and unfolded the worksheet again, and it was there, in the margin, that she found her old quiz, folded into quarters and forgotten. She smoothed it out against her knee. The question had given a stretch of DNA, adenine and guanine and thymine and cytosine in their pairs, and asked her to transcribe it into RNA. She had copied the sequence faithfully, letter for letter, and that was the disaster. Somewhere in her copying, a thymine had kept sneaking in where it did not belong.

The memory of Thursday came back whole. She remembered the classroom smelling like pencil shavings, remembered her friend Dara leaning over from the next desk. "You're writing T again," Dara had whispered. "In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine." Victoria had nodded and then written a T in the very next line, because her hand had its own habits. Adenine pairs with thymine in the DNA, she now understood, and guanine with cytosine; but when the message got copied into RNA, the T became a U, pairing with adenine. It was as if the language changed one letter in translation, and she had spent the whole quiz writing in the wrong alphabet.

She took out her phone and opened the photo of the worksheet. She would contextualize the pathway, she decided, by walking it: glucose at the trailhead, glycolysis at the first bridge, the Krebs cycle at the overlook where she sat, the electron transport chain at the far end where the trail looped back. She walked the loop twice, pointing at ferns and saying the steps to them, and the second time through the sequence stopped feeling like words and started feeling like a route, something her feet could keep.

A man came down the trail with a golden retriever on a green rope leash, and he watched the girl point at a fern and say "and that's where the protons go back through," to nobody, with total seriousness. He had walked this trail every morning for nine years and had seen weepers and joggers and one man who believed the trees were recording him. The girl looked up as he passed. "Sorry," she said. "I'm studying out loud. It works better if the trail has some verisimilitude, like the pathway is actually going somewhere."

"It goes to the parking lot," the man said, and the dog pulled him on.

Victoria laughed, alone again, and took the loop a third time, faster now, reciting the whole sweep from glucose to ATP without stopping, no thymine where a uracil belonged, no gaps. At the far end the trail did curve back toward the lot, toward Monday, toward the desk with the teacher's red pen and the door she had not yet walked through. She stopped where the path forked, one way down to the creek and one way up, and stood there breathing hard with the worksheet crushed warm in her hand. She could go see her teacher Tuesday, or she could keep walking. The creek was loud below her. She turned toward the water.

Vanessa had claimed the economics room for last period, and she stood at the whiteboard with the marker capped in her fist, rehearsing the argument she would have to deliver tomorrow morning. Raise the policy rate, she said to the empty desks, and borrowing costs more, so households and firms spend less, and spending that slows drags on price increases, which is how the central bank gets inflation to ease. She said it three times, and each time it sounded more like something copied from the back of the chapter. What she wanted was to make the class feel the mechanism, to watch it click behind their eyes the way it had finally clicked behind hers at midnight, but the sentence kept coming out flat, a bromide recited at a podium.

Marcus found her there because he had signed up for the same presentation slot and needed somewhere to panic. He dropped into a front-row seat and pulled out a stack of index cards, and when she tested him, asking why higher rates cool prices at all, he gave the textbook line and then ruined it with a joke about his overdraft. He expostulated with the whiteboard itself, as though the supply curve had personally wronged him, and Vanessa laughed, and for a while they traded the argument back and forth, sharpening each other's phrasing until hers was leaner, almost incisive, and she thought the presentation might survive after all.

Mr. Ferrante's rule, announced that morning and still hanging over all of them, was that the question period after each presentation would be unscripted, graded, and random. A name drawn from the attendance tin. Whoever's name came up had to answer a question from the audience about anything in the unit, trade as well as money, and Vanessa had not yet opened the trade chapters. She told herself she would study them that night. She told Marcus the same thing, twice, in a voice that made her sound more certain than she was, and he seemed to accept it, which made the lie easier to keep sitting inside her.

Marcus, on his side, noticed more than he said. He had watched Vanessa skip lunch, had seen the trade chapters still sealed in shrink-wrap when she dug for a calculator, and he assumed she was simply overloaded, the way she got before auditions. What he did not know, what nobody at school knew, was that her mother had spent the evening at the kitchen table with a refinancing letter, running her finger down a column of numbers that had moved against them, and that Vanessa had sat opposite her, mute, recognizing the very mechanism she was supposed to teach. He only knew that when he asked, half-teasing, whether the rate hikes her presentation praised might also be squeezing somebody, she snapped a no that sounded like a yes.

She studied anyway, in the library after dinner, because the tin did not care about refinancing letters. Somewhere past midnight she hit a passage about a country with vast farmland, a place that shipped out grain by the megaton and yet imported every phone and circuit board it used, and the puzzle stopped her. It seemed backwards. Rich land, and it bought its electronics from somewhere else. She read the next paragraph twice, then once more aloud under her breath, and copied the shape of it onto a card.

The next morning Ferrante drew a folded slip from the tin before her presentation had even cooled, and the name he read out was Vanessa's own. A boy in the second row, the one who asked questions to show off, leaned back and delivered his: if a country has all that farmland, why does it export grain and import electronics instead of making the electronics itself?

The room waited. Marcus watched her turn the marker over in her hands once, twice, and he could see the card in her mind, the one copied at midnight, and he could also see something else in her face that he couldn't name. Time stretched. Someone coughed. Ferrante's pen hovered.

"It's about what a country has a lot of," Vanessa said slowly. "Land, labor, capital. That's the Heckscher-Ohlin model, named after two Swedish economists, Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin. It explains comparative advantage by differences in countries' supplies of those things. A country with vast farmland is rich in land, so that's where its advantage sits. Grain uses what it has the most of. Electronics need other things it has less of."

The boy nodded as though he had known that all along. Ferrante made a note, and Vanessa sat down, her hands steady now, and found that the two halves of the night had joined somewhere without her permission: the model on the card and the letter on the kitchen table, both true at once, neither canceling the other. She could defend the mechanism. She could not say, yet, whether slowing inflation was worth what it was costing, and tomorrow she would try to say that out loud too, without a card.

After class Marcus caught her at the door. "You went quiet up there. Longer than you had to."

"I was deciding how much of the truth fits in a graded answer."

He hoisted his bag. "And?"

She pushed the door open into the corridor's noise. "I'll tell you at lunch."

The repair shop smelled of solder and lemon wipes, and Mackenzie was behind the counter because Deshawn had called in sick, which meant she handled customers alone until noon. She was eighteen and saving for a laptop before September, and so far the morning had produced one cracked screen, one waterlogged tablet, and a boy named Percy from her old statistics class who came in every Tuesday with his Chromebook and sat by the register doing homework while his mother worked two doors down at the dental office.

Today Percy had his database assignment open, and his report said something wrong. The shop's owner, Mr. Okonkwo, kept a whiteboard behind the counter for tracking repairs, and Percy kept glancing at it like it might help. "It says every customer ordered at least once," he said. "The teacher gave us a sample database. Thirty customers. I got thirty."

Mackenzie looked up from the tray of screws she was sorting. "Every one?"

"Every one." He turned the Chromebook toward her. She saw two tables, Customers and Orders, and a query with LEFT JOIN in it, which she recognized because she'd spent the whole previous week teaching herself SQL from a library book, in preparation for a class she was taking in the fall. "You're counting wrong," she said.

"I'm counting with COUNT," Percy said. "That's the whole point of the function."

She wiped her hands on her jeans and came around the counter. The screen had his query in a plain text editor, and beneath it the result grid with its single number, thirty. She read it twice. He had selected the customer names and counted them, and he had used COUNT with the star, which she remembered from the library book had a specific behavior she had never fully believed until she tested it herself one night at the public library terminal.

"Run it again," she said. "But instead of the star, count the order ID column. The one from the Orders table."

Percy typed it. The number came back twenty-six. He stared at it. He counted the rows by hand on the screen, tapping each name with his finger, and got to four customers whose order column was empty, blank in every row the join had produced.

"They're the same join," Percy said. "I didn't change the join. I only changed what I counted."

"I know," Mackenzie said.

"Then which number is real?"

She pulled a stool over next to his. Behind them the door chimed and a woman came in holding a phone with a spiderweb crack across its face, diaphanous as frost on a window, and Mackenzie took it, wrote a ticket, told her ninety minutes, and came back. She did not sit down yet. She picked up the shop's demo tablet and a screen protector and began to suture the two together with the smoothing card, working the bubbles out from the center, because the morning's repairs did not pause for Percy's grade.

"Here's what I think happens," she said, working the card. "When you LEFT JOIN, a customer with no orders still gets a row. The row just gets filled in with NULLs where the order data would go. The row exists. It's one row."

"So counting rows counts them."

"COUNT with the star counts rows," she said. "So a customer with no orders gets counted once, because of that NULL-filled row. But if you count the order column itself, the column is empty, and you get zero for that customer." She set the tablet down. "That's why your thirty said everyone ordered. And why the twenty-six is the customers who actually did."

Percy looked at the screen for a long time. "So which one did the assignment want?"

"Both, probably. It depends what question you're asking. Do you want to know how many customers exist, or how many ordered?"

"That's not fair. Both questions sound the same out loud."

"They only sound the same until you decide what a customer with nothing counts as." She said it and then heard how it sounded, and Percy laughed, and she let it go. She went back to the counter, rang up a man buying a charging cable, and answered a call about a battery replacement. When she hung up, Percy had written both queries side by side and was running them over and over, thirty, twenty-six, thirty, twenty-six, like checking a door he knew was locked.

"My mom says computers are either right or wrong," he said. "She works at a dentist's office and thinks everything is like that, one answer, like a theocracy where there's a single truth and you just obey it. But this is two true answers that don't match."

Mackenzie finished with the screen protector and held the tablet up to the light to check her work. "Then the assignment is probably asking which truth you meant," she said. "Write down why you picked the one you picked."

Percy closed the Chromebook and stood, and at the door he turned around. "The four who never ordered. Should I feel bad for them?"

She hadn't thought about it. She looked at the ticket rack, at the cracked phone waiting in its sleeve with its promised ninety minutes, and said she didn't know, and Percy pushed through the door into the heat.

The math club met on Tuesdays in Room 214, where the radiator clanked like a metronome nobody had asked for, and where Alexis had claimed the seat by the window since September. Today Mr. Ferreira had put a problem on the board that looked, at first glance, like a joke: find the area under the curve of some cubic between zero and four. She had assumed calculus was a semester away, something for college, and now here it was demanding to be understood by Thursday.

"You're integrating," said Priya, sliding into the next seat and immediately stealing Alexis's pretzels, which was their arrangement. "Sort of. Ferreira wants us to see it before he ruins it with notation." Priya's actual want, never quite hidden, was to be the first one in the room to solve anything, and she had already uncapped her green pen like a fencer saluting.

Ferreira had drawn the curve freehand, a lopsided hill rising out of the origin and dropping again somewhere past the middle of the graph. "A company's profit," he said, tapping the hilltop. "Sketch me where it peaks, and I'll show you why the area tells you total earnings." He refused to say more, which was his method, and which Priya had once excoriated in a letter to the school paper as "pedagogical withholding," a phrase Alexis still found funnier than the letter itself.

Alexis drew her own copy. She had spent the weekend on her grandmother's couch helping sort receipts for the little bakery, the one surviving on Fridays and holidays, and a profit curve was not an abstraction to her; it was her grandmother's face in March, doing arithmetic on the back of an envelope and going quiet. She shaded the region under the hill with the side of her pencil, light strokes, and thought: that shaded space is everything the bakery earns over time. The height is how fast. The area is how much.

"Your peak is wrong," Priya said, leaning over, sardonic and cheerful at once. "You put the top where it looks tallest, but look, it's still climbing there." She tapped the point Alexis had marked, where the curve was unmistakably still going up. Down the table, Marcus was arguing with his calculator, and Theo, who wanted only to finish early so he could get to orchestra rehearsal, kept checking the clock with the resignation of a man watching a bus leave without him. Theo passed Alexis a fresh pencil without being asked, because her point had gone flat, and he had noticed, and that was Theo.

She erased the dot and slid it right, toward where the hill leveled. Then she slid it too far, past the moment when the curve had already begun to fall, and Priya laughed at her. Alexis sat back and looked at the shape itself. At the very top of the peak the curve wasn't climbing and wasn't falling. It was, for one instant, flat. The tangent line up there, she said slowly, touching the summit with her pencil tip, would be horizontal. Slope of zero. She wrote "slope = 0" beside the dot and heard Priya stop laughing.

"At a local maximum the derivative equals zero," Priya said, mostly to the room, mostly to claim it, and Ferreira, from his desk, made the small gratified noise he made when someone said a true thing unprompted. Alexis didn't mind that Priya said it first out loud. What mattered was that Alexis had put her finger on the actual point, the exact spot where the tangent line went flat, and it was hers; she had found it by drawing and erasing, not by remembering.

"Now the area," Ferreira said, and the room groaned, and Theo's chin lifted off his hand. Ferreira showed them rectangles, thin ones under the curve, more of them, thinner, until the shaded region Alexis had drawn in pencil seemed to be built from countless slices. The area was the sum of the slices; the integral was what you got when the slices became infinitely thin. Alexis copied the rectangle sketch twice, once for her notebook and once, without deciding to, on a separate sheet she folded and put in her pocket. Her grandmother did not know calculus. Her grandmother knew envelopes.

What Alexis could not yet reconcile, and did not pretend to, was the tension she felt sitting there: the peak said where profit was greatest in a single moment, and the area said what accumulated over all the moments, and the bakery's March had been a month with a low peak but a long, decent area, while some Saturdays spiked beautifully and then gave back everything by Sunday. Which mattered more depended on a question mathematics could state but not answer, which was what the bakery was for.

Ferreira assigned the actual computation, the antiderivative, the constants, for Thursday. Priya had already finished and was reading a lemma in the textbook with the green pen parked behind her ear, but she moved her bag so Alexis could spread out her graph, and slid the pretzels back across the table, half of them, which for Priya was practically a sacrament. Alexis ruled a clean tangent line through the peak, made it as horizontal as her unsteady hand allowed, and began slicing the hill into rectangles thin as pages.

The acceptance email arrived at 4:47 on a Tuesday afternoon, while Alexa was supposed to be taking notes on the Missouri Compromise. Her phone sat face-down on her desk, as required, but it buzzed twice against the laminate, and she knew before she looked. She asked for the bathroom pass with a steadiness that surprised her, walked down the empty hallway with its smell of floor wax and boiled pasta, and stood in the last stall of the second-floor bathroom reading the words on a screen the size of her palm. Congratulations. We are pleased. She read it four times, and each time the sentence seemed to belong to a different person.

By Wednesday morning, half the senior class knew. Priya cornered her at the lockers before first period, breathless, insisting Alexa was done, finished, set. "You got in," Priya said. "Why would you keep writing essays for other schools? It's over."

"It's Early Action," Alexa said. "It gives you an early decision, but it's non-binding. I could still choose not to go."

Priya waved this away like smoke. "You're going to go."

That was the sentence that followed Alexa through the day, into sixth period, into Mr. Delgado's classroom with its radiator that clanked like a coin in a tin cup and its windows fogged from the December cold. The regular deadline for most of her other applications was January first, which meant she had twelve days to decide whether to finish five more essays or let them die quietly in her college portal. Mr. Delgado had given the class a work period for their term papers, and Alexa sat in the back row with her laptop open to a document titled "Why Northwestern," a document that was 212 words long and had been 212 words long for two weeks.

Derek sat diagonal from her, morose as always in December, hood up, thumbing through a printout of a rejection letter he'd received the same afternoon. He had applied Early Decision somewhere and been denied, and he wore it now the way other people wore a cast. "At least you got good news," he said, not looking up. "You can coast until June. I have to start over."

"It's not binding," Alexa said again, quieter this time, and heard how the words sounded less like freedom and more like an obligation she hadn't finished paying. Derek looked at her then, and something in his face, envy maybe, or simple exhaustion, made her feel the weight of what she was holding. She had an answer. She had wanted an answer for two years, had postulated since freshman year that an acceptance would settle everything, that the moment the email came, the anxious machinery in her chest would finally stop.

The machinery had not stopped. It had, if anything, found new work.

She typed a sentence about Northwestern's journalism program and deleted it. The radiator clanked. Someone near the front was eating an orange, and the citrus smell cut through the stuffy heat, sharp and specific, and she thought suddenly of her mother peeling oranges on the porch last summer, saying, you'll go where you go, it doesn't matter to me, which Alexa had understood even then to be a kind of lie, a generous one. Her mother wanted the big school, the famous one, the one whose name made people at church nod. The school that had accepted her was good but not famous. The school she had 212 words about was both.

Priya slid into the seat beside her, having abandoned her own term paper. "You're still writing it," she said, almost accusing. "I can't believe you're still writing it."

"I don't know what I'm doing," Alexa said. "That's the honest answer. I have one yes in my hand and I don't know if it's the right yes, and if I stop now, I'll never find out what the other answers would have been."

"So apply everywhere. Keep all the doors open. What's the problem?"

"The problem is I've been beguiling myself for two years that one letter would make the decision for me. It doesn't. It just moves the decision to December instead of April."

Priya was quiet for a moment, chewing on this. "That's still a better problem than Derek's."

Alexa glanced at Derek, at the rejection letter now folded into a small square on his desk, at his hood, at the window behind him where the fog was thick enough to draw in. She picked up her finger and drew a letter A, then wiped it away with her sleeve, because it felt like claiming something she hadn't claimed yet.

"What's the essay about?" Priya asked.

"Supposedly, why I want to go there."

"And why do you?"

Alexa looked at the 212 words on her screen. They were true words, careful words, and they had nothing in them she could point to and call a reason. She set her hands on the keyboard. "Give me until the deadline," she said. "Twelve days. Then I'll tell you both of us."

Mr. Delgado rapped his knuckles on his desk and announced twenty minutes left in the period, and the orange smell reached the back row, and Alexa began to type.

The argument began over a worksheet, of all things. Mr. Okafor had set out photocopies of Roman sources on the long tables, inscriptions and coin rubbings and a page of excerpted letters, and asked each pair to decide what the sources could tell them about ordinary lives. Dev, who sat beside Faith only because the seating chart said so, pushed the page away after a minute. "This is all men," he said. "Soldiers, governors, emperors. Ancient women left no voice. There's nothing to analyze."

Faith said nothing, but she copied the sentence into her notebook with a line under it. She had spent the summer reading about Roman Britain for a project she had since abandoned, and she had a feeling, half memory and half stubbornness, that Dev was wrong. The problem was that she could not yet say how. At lunch she went to the library and asked for the shelf on Roman Britain, and the librarian, without a word, pointed her toward the dusty end where nobody went.

She found the Vindolanda tablets in a thick illustrated book, thin leaves of wood photographed against black velvet, the writing faded to the color of weak tea. One tablet was a birthday party invitation, written around 100 CE, from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, the wife of a commander at the fort. Claudia wished her sister a happy birthday, promised a cheerful day, and asked her to come. It was domestic, ordinary, almost boring. Faith read the catalog entry twice, and then a third time, because of the last sentence. The closing lines were believed to be among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman. She photocopied the page with hands that were not quite steady.

The next morning the classroom was cold, its north windows giving off a thin, boreal light that lay in pale bars across the tables. When Mr. Okafor opened the floor for findings, Faith put up her hand before Dev could speak. "Yesterday someone said ancient women left no voice," she said, and held up the photocopy. "This is a birthday invitation. Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, around 100 CE, from the fort at Vindolanda. And the closing lines are some of the earliest known Latin we have written by a woman."

"Written by a woman," Dev said. "Or written for one."

"That's not what it says."

"That's what it means." He had turned in his seat, arms folded. "Roman elites had scribes. Her husband commanded a fort. Somebody else held the pen."

Faith had expected him to fold, and he had not, and she felt the ground shift under her nice neat discovery. Mr. Okafor, who had a habit of stepping back when students fought, wrote two dates on the board and said only, "Two textbooks disagree about that tablet. See which ones." So the class split the sources between them, and for twenty minutes the room was all shuffling and low argument.

The disagreement was real and it was not polite. One book, published in the 1990s, treated the invitation as a treasure and moved on. A second, more recent, discussed the closing lines in detail, noting that most of the tablet appeared to be in a professional hand. A third article, dense and hedged, argued about what counted as evidence at all. Faith read with her chin on her fist, drifting once into a reverie of Claudia at some northern birthday table, candles or lamplight, snow maybe, and then jerked back because Priya across the table was holding out the second book, tapping a paragraph.

"Here," Priya said. "The bulk of the letter looks like a scribe's work. But the closing lines are different."

"Different how?"

"Read it."

Faith read. The editors themselves did not agree, and she understood, slowly, that they could not, because the sources were partial and the questions kept changing. The tablet was one small wooden leaf. The historians were not looking at different tablets; they were looking at the same faded scratches and asking different things of them. One asked whether a woman could write. Another asked whether a woman's words could survive a scribe's hand. Neither question absolved the other of being a real question.

When the class reassembled, Mr. Okafor asked for conclusions. Dev went first and said the invitation was probably dictated, that the evidence was ambiguous. Faith stood with the photocopy and did not say he was wrong. "I brought this to prove you wrong," she said. "It doesn't, not completely. The closing lines are what we have, and they're some of the earliest known Latin writing by a woman, and nobody can prove whose hand made them. That's the whole thing. That's all we get."

"That's not much," Dev said.

"It's a birthday party," Faith said. "She wanted her friend to come. That's more than nothing." She set the photocopy down on the table between them, the two faded columns of ink faceup, and slid it across to his side.

Emile found the tube in the bottom drawer of his grandfather's desk, wrapped in a dishcloth and lodged between a slide rule and a tin of drawing pins. It was sealed at both ends with black wax, and inside it the gas sat brown as strong tea. He held it up to the window of the study, where the late light came through the fig tree and printed shifting leaves on the wall, and he remembered the museum in Lyon, the summer he turned sixteen, when a demonstrator had plunged a tube just like this one into a beaker of ice water and the brown had drained out of it like a stain being rinsed. Warm the tube again and the colour came back, deepened, darkened. He had stood at that display for twenty minutes while his classmates moved on to the Tesla coil.

That was two years ago. Now he was supposed to be revising for the entrance exam, and the principle behind the tube was on the syllabus, listed in the revision guide his grandfather had lent him with a dry remark about how the binding had outlasted three governments. Emile had read the chapter twice on the train down and understood it the way he understood a colloquialism he had never actually heard anyone use: he could define it, but he did not own it. His own notes said that a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change imposed on it, and the words lay on the page like borrowed clothes.

He carried the tube to the kitchen, where his grandfather was extruding dough through the old brass machine bolted to the counter, the handle turning with a sound like a slow clock. "There's ice in the freezer," his grandfather said without looking up. "And the kettle is still warm from my coffee. If you are going to do what I think you are going to do, do it over the sink."

"You knew I'd find it."

"I left the drawer open. That is not the same thing."

Emile filled a bowl from the ice tray, added water from the tap, and lowered the tube in. He crouched with his phone ready to film it, feeling faintly ridiculous, a grown boy filming a tube of gas in his grandfather's kitchen while tagliatelle piled up on a tea towel behind him. But the brown began to fade almost at once, from the bottom of the tube upward, until the gas above the waterline was pale, nearly colourless, and the part still in his fingers stayed stubbornly brown. He turned the tube, and the warmth of his hand left a smudge of darker colour on the glass where his fingers had been.

Henri watched the boy from the counter, and the sight worked on him slowly, the way the ice worked on the gas. Forty-one years since he had sealed that tube himself, over a burner in a school laboratory in Roubaix, wax dripping on his knuckles, and he had chosen that year not to take the research post in Strasbourg. He had told himself it was for the children, for the stability, and he had told himself so often that the sentence had worn smooth and stopped meaning anything in particular. He had never regretted it in a way he could point to. But watching the brown bloom back into the tube as Emile held it under the running hot tap, watching the colour return exactly as it had gone, he understood that his own life had never been sealed like that. Nothing ran backward in a man. You could not cool him down and get the earlier colour out of him again.

"Darker when it's warm," Emile said, mostly to himself. "Paler when it's cold." He said the reaction running forward, the brown gas folding into the colourless one, must give off heat, because the cold was pushing it that way, toward the pale side, and the heat was pushing it back. He did not say it confidently. He said it the way you offer a coin to a machine, waiting to see whether it will be taken.

"That is the direction I would argue," Henri said, and left it there. He was not going to hand the boy a lecture; the boy had the tube, and the tube was better than any sentence Henri could construct. The boy's father, Emile's father, had wanted every answer finished and signed, and look what that had made of him. Henri lifted the pasta sheet and draped it over the back of a chair.

Emile wrote the observation in his notebook without the mechanism, just what he had seen: brown, colourless, brown again, heat one way, cold the other. He sat back on his heels and looked at the tube, at his grandfather, at the bowl of melting ice, and knew that he half understood it and could not have said which half.
