The exam would want more than that. The exam would want it closed.

"You'll stay for dinner," Henri said. It was not a question. He fed a sheet of dough into the machine and turned the handle, and the brass extruded a pale, even ribbon through its gap, and the kitchen filled with the smell of flour and the small persistence of the crank going round.

The phone store smelled like new plastic and floor cleaner, and Emile stood at the counter holding his mother's old phone, the one with the crack running diagonally across the screen like a fault line on a map. His own phone had died three weeks ago, and he had a summer job starting Monday at the landscaping company, which meant he needed something that worked, today, before he had the money to pay for it outright.

The sales rep, a woman named Dana with a lanyard and the patient gravitas of someone who had explained the same forms a thousand times, turned a tablet toward him. "You can put it on a payment plan," she said. "Twenty-two a month for twenty-four months." Emile did the arithmetic in his head and felt something tighten. Twenty-two times twenty-four was five hundred twenty-eight. The phone's price tag said four hundred ninety-nine.

"So it costs more this way," he said. "Twenty-nine dollars more." Dana nodded without apology. "That's the interest," she said. "That's what borrowing costs. You're paying for the use of money you don't have yet." He looked at the tablet, at his own signature half-formed in the signature box, and thought about how the number was small enough to seem like nothing and large enough to be real.

Then Dana ran his information and paused. "There's a late payment here from March," she said. "Looks like a phone bill. It's showing on your credit." Emile's stomach dropped. He remembered it exactly: the app, the notification he'd swiped away during a chemistry study session, the bill that had slipped his mind for six weeks during track season. "How bad is that?" he asked. "Like, does one missed bill ruin everything?"

Dana turned the screen so he could see the breakdown. "Payment history is the largest factor in your FICO score," she said. "About thirty-five percent of it, for the general population." He read the numbers on the screen and understood, slowly, that the forgotten bill he had treated as nothing had touched the single biggest thing a lender would look at. Not all of it, not close, but the largest piece. "It fades," Dana added. "It's not forever. But it's there."

He signed, because Monday was coming and the job was real, and then he sat on the bench near the accessories wall while the transfer ran. Two college guys stood at the next counter, arguing in the easy, half-joking way of people who had read one article and become doctrinaire about it. "Credit's a trap," one said. "They design it to vilify the poor and forgive the rich." The other shook his head. "It's a tool. If you pay on time it works for you. My sister's score got her an apartment." They went back and forth, and Emile found himself unable to agree with either of them completely.

He thought about the twenty-nine dollars, about how the same force that took money from him when he borrowed could give money to him if he saved, because Dana had mentioned it offhand while ringing him up: his bank paid interest on savings, small but real, money earning money while he slept. Two directions of the same principle. He had missed a payment and that mistake would follow him, but it was thirty-five percent, not one hundred percent; the rest was still his to shape, starting with the twenty-two dollars due each month, which he now intended to automate so that neither track season nor chemistry nor anything else could swallow it again.

At home he set up the autopay and then, after a minute, moved forty dollars from checking into the savings account his mother had opened for him years ago and he had never touched. The interest rate was pitiful, something like one and a half percent, and he laughed a little at how little it would earn. Still, he watched the balance on the screen, four hundred and six dollars, and imagined it drifting upward while the phone debt drifted downward, two lines crossing somewhere in a future he couldn't quite see. His mother called from the kitchen asking if he wanted dinner. He closed the laptop and said, "Yeah, I'm coming."

Sienna had claimed the corner computer by the window because it was the only one where the screen did not glare, and because from there she could see the whole second floor of the library, including the table where her grandfather sat waiting for the printer. She was working through a tutorial on a folded sheet of paper Mr. Alvarez had given her after third period: two tables, one called customers and one called orders, and a question in his cramped handwriting, "Which customers have never ordered anything?" She had written her first attempt an hour ago and it had returned the entire customer list, which she knew was wrong, because she could see order rows sitting right there in the second table, eight of them belonging to people whose names were now on her screen as if they had done nothing at all.

Her grandfather had come along because the printer at his apartment still refused to cooperate, and because he liked to be where she was, though he would not have said it that way. He had printed a photograph, a dramatic one, a soldier carrying a child through floodwater, and he had it in a plastic sleeve, and he had already told two people at the next table that it was from the news and that nobody was reporting it. He leaned over her shoulder now, smelling of coffee and the cold outside. "Look at this," he said. "They're hiding it."

She had seen the photo before. Not this exact one, but photos shaped like it, forwarded to her by a friend's cousin in a group chat with the caption "why isn't the media covering this," and she had scrolled past. She took the printout from him and turned it over. The paper was thin, the kind her grandfather bought because he was impecunious and refused to admit it, twenty sheets for a dollar at the surplus store, and the ink had bled at the soldier's boots.

"Grandpa, let me check it," she said.

He sat down in the chair beside her, which was not his chair, which belonged to whoever was waiting for a computer, and a man in a gray coat gave him a look and then did not do anything about it. Sienna lifted the photo out of the sleeve, laid it flat on the desk, and, because the library scanner was broken, took a picture of the picture with her phone. She had learned the method from a girl in her civics class who proselytized about it constantly, before every current events discussion, checking sources the way other people checked their hair. Google had added search by image back in 2011, the girl had said, so you could upload a picture, or paste its link, and find where else it appeared on the web. Sienna had nodded at the time without really listening. Now she uploaded the image and waited for the little spinning circle.

The results came back as a list of pages, and the photograph was on all of them. The oldest entry she could find dated it years before the flood her grandfather had described. One page called it a reenactment. Another said it was from a movie. She scrolled slowly, not to hide anything from him, but because she wanted to get it right before she said anything, and that was the habit she could not trace the lineage of, whether it came from her mother, who read every contract twice, or from Mr. Alvarez, who made them show their work. She turned the screen toward her grandfather.

"So it's fake," he said.

"It's from before. It's not from last week." She showed him the page with the date. He pulled the screen closer with two fingers, the way he handled his own phone, and read for a while.

"That's a different picture," he said finally. "They look alike."

"It's the same one, Grandpa. See the shadow on the stairs."

He was quiet. Across the room the printer finished and nobody went to it. He was quiet in the way he got when he was deciding whether to argue, and she watched him decide, watched his hand move toward the plastic sleeve and stop.

Here is what her grandfather would tell her mother that evening: that Sienna had found the picture was real, only misdated, that the whole web was unreliable and had corrected itself wrongly, that a thing could be true and a machine could still call it false. He believed some version of this while he sat beside her. He was not lying when he retold it; he was remembering in the direction he preferred, the way he remembered his own father's store as thriving until the city took it, though her mother had once shown Sienna the tax records in a shoebox, and the store had been failing for years. He remembered forward, toward the version where he was not fooled.

Sienna did not know any of that yet. What she knew was the screen, and the tutorial still open behind the browser tab, her broken query with its join returning everyone, the question of which customers ordered nothing still unanswered. She looked at her code again. The join matched customers to orders, so every customer with an order got a row, and the ones with nothing got nothing, and then she had asked for the customers, and gotten them all. She needed the ones the join could not find. She needed to ask for absence, which was a strange thing to type, a request for the shape of what was not there.

She wrote it a second way, joining and filtering for the empty side, and ran it, and got two names out of the whole list. Two customers, silent in the orders table, invisible unless you asked the question exactly right. She thought of the photo then, the way it had sat in the database of the web with its true date attached, waiting for someone to join it to the question. It could be found. That was the part she was sure of. Whether her grandfather would keep the answer was the part she was not.

"They printed my thing," her grandfather said, standing, pulling the plastic sleeve toward him across the desk. "Which one's yours?"

"That one," she said. "Third from the top."

He picked up both pages, his photograph and her query, folded together, and held them up to the window light as if comparing watermarks.

The cultural center smelled of cardamom and floor wax, and the folding tables along the back wall had been pushed together into one long surface covered with newspaper. Logan's father set a bag of rice beside the stack of dates and began counting small envelopes into piles, one for each member of the family. Tomorrow morning, before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, every one of those envelopes had to reach the collection box by the stage.

"Seven," his father said, laying the last envelope down. "You, your mother, me, your grandmother, the twins, and Amma." He tapped the seventh envelope twice, as if sealing an agreement with it. "Zakat al-fitr," he said, "for each of us."

Logan knew the phrase the way he knew the exits of his high school, without ever having to use the knowledge. What he hadn't known, until tonight, was that the amount was fixed, the same for every family that could afford it, and that the whole point of fixing it was so the envelopes in the box would add up to enough for poorer families to celebrate Eid too. His father had explained none of this. Logan had simply watched him count, and then asked a question, and the arithmetic had answered itself: the man who swept this building, whose kids went to school two blocks from Logan's, would have dates and rice tomorrow because of envelopes like these.

His father wanted the counting done correctly, that much was clear. He had been a banker in Karachi before they moved here, and he treated the night before Eid like a closing, sleeves rolled, receipts clipped. But Logan could see the second want underneath it. His father kept glancing at the door, and at his phone, waiting for Amma's son, Logan's uncle Farhan, who had not come to a family gathering in three years and had, an hour ago, texted a single word: coming.

Logan had his own preoccupations. In September he would start at a college two states away, and his mother had spent the evening amortizing the tuition over ten years of projected income, laying it out like a loan officer, steady payments, interest hidden in the decimals. She was not parsimonious by nature, but she had become so out of necessity, and lately Logan had begun to suspect that thrift was contagious, that he was catching it, that he would arrive on campus already middle-aged in his spending. His government teacher would have said the financial aid office was an oligarchy of five people who decided everything behind a closed door. Logan had laughed at that in class. Tonight, counting other people's money into envelopes, he wasn't laughing.

Here was the thing he could not settle. At school, charity was presented as a private virtue, a matter of personal conscience, and Logan had absorbed that version thoroughly: you gave because you chose to, and the choosing was what made it good. But what his father was doing tonight was not exactly choosing. The amount was set, the obligation fell on everyone who could afford it, and no one was praised for it because no one was supposed to be praised for it. It worked more like a tax that nobody collected and nobody evaded, or at least nobody in this room. Logan held both systems in his head, the voluntary one and the set one, and tried to see which he actually believed in. The voluntary one felt freer. The set one, he had to admit, fed more people.

The doors opened at half past nine. Uncle Farhan came in with a paper bag from the grocery store and the uncertain posture of a man testing ice. He set dates on the newspaper without a word, and Logan's father looked at the bag, then at his brother, then pulled an eighth envelope from the box.

"You're family," his father said. "That counts."

"I brought dates," Farhan said. "I thought it was a potluck."

"It's not a potluck. Sit down and help me count."

Logan watched them work side by side, his father narrating the arithmetic, Farhan nodding, neither of them mentioning the three years. Logan slipped the seventh envelope, the one with his name penciled on it in his father's handwriting, into the box by the stage. He was still not sure whether giving because you had to was worth less than giving because you wanted to. But the envelope was in the box, and tomorrow somebody's children would eat because of it, and Logan found that the uncertainty sat easier in him than it had an hour before, like a stone that had found the bottom of a full glass.

His mother called from the kitchen that the samosas were ready. Farhan stood first, and his father stood after him, and both of them went toward the smell of frying without deciding anything out loud.

The hardware store smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and Ava stood at the register of Korner Supply on a Tuesday morning in June, filling out the last form between her and an apron. She had already written her name twice, once in her careful hand and once in her rushing hand, and both looked like they belonged to someone younger. The form was called a W-4, the manager had said, sliding it across the counter with a pen that had a chewed cap, and now she was staring at a box that wanted to know something she did not understand at all.

"It tells me how much to withhold," she said slowly, reading the top line to herself. The words were English, each one individually familiar, but the sentence had the texture of a riddle. She gathered that the federal income tax was involved, and that each paycheck was involved, and that her answers would somehow connect the two, but the connecting logic was not on the page. Her mother would know. Her mother did the family taxes every April with a shoebox of receipts and a specific facial expression that Ava had learned not to interrupt.

She took out her phone and typed, "At the job. They gave me a form. W-4? Do you know what this is." Then she reconsidered the question mark, kept it anyway, and sent it. The manager, a broad man named Dale who wore his reading glasses on a cord around his neck, was unpacking a box of tape measures two aisles over, and she could hear him counting under his breath, forty-one, forty-two, as though the tape measures might disobey him.

Her phone buzzed. "Withholding. You fill out the W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck." Ava read the text twice. So the form was not a tax itself; it was a piece of information she handed over, and the store used it to do the taking-out. That felt manageable, almost polite, like telling someone in advance how you took your coffee. She filled in the lines her mother walked her through by text, one slow reply at a time, while a customer waited behind her to buy a single bolt.

"First job?" the customer asked. He was holding the bolt in his fist like evidence.

"Is it obvious?"

"You're apologizing to the pen," he said, and paid for his bolt and left.

Dale put her on paint for the first week, which suited her, because the paint aisle had a fan and because the names of the colors were their own small literature. There was a chip called Littoral Gray, a soft blue-green, and when a woman came in asking for something to remind her of the shore, Ava turned the fan deck to that one without having to look it up. "It's a coastal kind of color," she said, and the woman held it up to the light and said it was exactly the water at her grandmother's house in Maine, and bought two gallons.

The work had a substrate of repetition under everything else, she decided by Thursday: unlocking, sweeping, restocking, the register's little songs. But things kept surfacing through it. A man came in wanting to repaint his front door in a way that would, he admitted, "aggrandize the whole entryway," and Ava had not known that a door could be aggrandized, though she recognized the impulse, having spent a fair portion of her own energy on being perceived favorably. He chose a deep red. She mixed it on the shaker machine, which sounded like a small rebellion, and thought about how much of wanting to be seen was like paint, a coat you applied over whatever the door actually was.

The paycheck arrived on the fifteenth, in an envelope with her name typed on it, and it was smaller than the number she had computed in her head on the bus. She stood at the time clock doing the subtraction again, then looked at the stub, where a line item said FED INCOME TAX, and the riddle from her first morning assembled itself into sense. She had marked that box, and the store had done exactly what she told it to. It occurred to her that she had made a real decision, with consequences, at a moment when she felt entirely ignorant, and that the decision had worked anyway, more or less, the way most of her decisions seemed to. She could not decide whether that was reassuring or slightly frightening, and she suspected it was both, and that the two feelings were going to coexist for a while.

She texted her mother a photo of the stub. Her mother replied with a single thumbs-up, which Ava interpreted as pride filtered through whatever the parental equivalent of a W-4 was, some withholding of its own.

At closing, Dale asked how the first paycheck felt. Ava considered saying smaller than expected, or educational, or fine, and chose the truest available option.

"Like I told a form something and it listened," she said. Dale laughed once, a short bark, and handed her the keys to lock the paint aisle gate.

"You'll get faster at that bolt drawer," he said, and turned off the lights over the registers, one switch at a time, while the tape measures hung in their rows, waiting for morning.

Isabelle locked the bathroom door and spread her note cards along the edge of the tub, because it was the only room in the apartment with a lock and the only place her mother's friends wouldn't drift in with questions. She was seventeen and had volunteered, somewhat against her own better judgment, to co-lead the peer health session on Friday: consent, contraception, how to actually walk into a clinic and ask to be tested. She had the facts. What she didn't have was a way of saying them out loud to thirty classmates without her voice going thin.

She practiced at the mirror. "Consent is a yes you can take back," she said, and winced, because it sounded like a poster. She tried again, softer, the way the nurse at the Riverside clinic had said it last month, when Isabelle had gone for her own appointment and stayed to ask how a person her age could get tested without a parent in the room. The nurse hadn't blinked. You book it yourself, she'd said. At your age, in this state, you don't need permission for that. Isabelle had written it on her wrist in pen before it washed off.

She was midway through the contraception cards, jogging her memory between IUDs and implants, when someone knocked. "Belle. It's me." Marcus, her cousin, sixteen and a senior of nothing much. He'd been in the living room all afternoon being quiet, which for Marcus was like a kettle deciding not to whistle.

"One second." She slid the cards under a towel and opened the door. Marcus came in anyway, sat on the tub's edge, and looked at the faucet rather than at her.

He got there eventually. There was a girl, Dara, and Dara had said maybe, and then later she had said nothing at all, and Marcus didn't know if maybe was a yes or if nothing was a no or if he was supposed to ask again or if asking again was the bad thing. It came out of him in one long breath, like a confession of theft.

Isabelle pulled the towel off the cards, not to show him, just to have her hands busy. Her mother would have said this was not a conversation for a bathroom, or really for anyone under thirty, and that girls especially should keep their knowledge quiet so as not to seem, in her mother's word, effusive. The nurse at Riverside had held the opposite view, handing Isabelle pamphlets like a woman giving out water in a drought. Between those two positions Isabelle had been circling all week, and now, with Marcus watching the faucet, she settled where she actually stood: you say the true thing plainly, and you let the other person be as knowledgeable as they want to be.

"Maybe isn't yes," she said. "And nothing isn't yes either. You ask once, and you listen to the whole answer, and if it's not a yes, that's the answer." Marcus nodded slowly, then asked what you did about the rest of it, the pregnancy worry, the other worry, the one boys at his school joked about and clearly didn't understand. She told him what the nurse had told her: that condoms were at the drugstore with no questions asked, that the clinic tested you for infections for free, that you could walk in alone. He asked what it was like there, and she described the waiting room, the fish tank, the folded magazines, an older man across from her reading a review of restaurants with the devotion of a true epicure, mouthing the word "uni" to himself while everyone around him worried.

"Also," Marcus said, as she was gathering her cards, "when Grandma took me for my physical, the nurse said her blood pressure was stage 2, and Grandma got mad about it. She said the top number was only 142 and the bottom was 88, so how could it be stage 2 if the bottom one was fine." He looked at Isabelle like she was the family's designated decoder of medical things, which, since the Riverside visit, she more or less was.

Isabelle turned that over. Her cards had a page on blood pressure, and she found it, and read it twice. "It's either number," she said. "Stage 2 hypertension means the top number is 140 or higher, or the bottom one is 90 or higher. Grandma's 142 was over the line all by itself. The bottom number doesn't have to be high too. Either one does it." Marcus said, quietly, "So she's actually stage 2," and Isabelle said yes, and thought about calling her grandmother tonight, not to lecture, just to say she'd looked it up, and would come along next appointment if Grandma wanted company.

Marcus stood, hand on the doorknob, then paused. "Friday. Your talk. Is it okay if I sit in back?" He was already turning the knob before she could answer, so she said it to the closing door: "Sit wherever you want." She picked up the cards, squared them, and started over at the mirror, saying the first line the plain way this time.

The gym had been divided in half with folding screens, and the stage was a rectangle of tape on the parquet floor where the free-throw line used to matter. Ashton stood at the edge of it with a binder under his arm, watching Priya and Marcus run the second scene for the fourth time. They kept crossing too early, both of them drawn to the tape marks like iron filings, and their lines arrived in the right order but with nothing behind them, letters read off a page.

He had taken the directing slot because no one else wanted it, and for the first two weeks he had treated it like an assignment, moving people the way Mrs. Okonkwo's handouts suggested, keeping his notes in the margin of the script. Then he had watched a senior's production the year before and understood that blocking was not traffic control. Where a person stood decided what the audience believed about what they said. He had started over with index cards, one per beat, and now the floor of his bedroom was covered with them like a vestigial model of the play, a paper stage he could rehearse in his head.

"Off-book on Thursday," he had told the cast at the start of the week, and Priya had nodded while Marcus looked at his shoes. "Off-book means no scripts in your hands. You perform from memory, the whole act, no calling for lines." Marcus had said fine. Priya had said fine twice.

Thursday came, and Priya came off book. Marcus did not. He walked onto the taped stage holding his script closed against his chest, like a hymnal, and when the scene began he opened it and read his first line off the page. The line was about leaving. He delivered it to the floor.

"Stop," Ashton said. He said it quietly, which was worse than shouting, and both actors stopped. "We said off-book today."

"I've been busy," Marcus said. "I had two tests. I know most of it."

"Do the scene without the book."

"I said most." Marcus held the script tighter. "I'm not going to stand up here and dry every thirty seconds in front of everyone."

There it was. Ashton had a rule and a Thursday and a performance in eleven days, and he had an actor who would rather defend the script than be seen failing with it. Priya sat on the bleacher step they were using as a bench and waited, arms crossed, in character even now, which Ashton noticed and filed away.

He had been reading a borrowed book on directing, the kind that liked big words, and one chapter argued that a director's real job was to historicize the moment, to set each scene at a specific time and place so the actors stopped playing ideas and started playing people in a room. Another chapter went on about phenomenology, about how the audience experiences the body in space before it understands a single word. He had underlined both passages and suspected both writers of overdoing it. But standing there, he could see the shape of what they meant. Marcus was not afraid of forgetting. He was afraid of being a person without the object, alone in the space, and every argument Ashton might make about fairness or deadlines would only make the script more precious to him.

"Give me the script," Ashton said.

"Why?"

"Because it's not a script anymore. It's a shield. Hand it to Priya."

Priya held out her hand without a word, still half in character, and Marcus looked at her, and after a moment he gave it to her. She set it behind her on the bleacher step, face down.

"Run it," Ashton said. "If you blank, stand there. Stay in the scene. The other person keeps talking, and you find your way back in. Nobody laughs."

Marcus ran it. He blanked twice, once for a long time, long enough that Priya shifted her weight and looked at the door as her character would, and that small movement gave Marcus something to answer, and he came back in with a line Ashton had never heard him say like that, quiet and late, as if it had just occurred to him. The rest of the scene was rough, was full of gaps, and it was the first time the play had looked like people instead of a reading.

Ashton called places again, and Marcus stepped to his tape mark, empty-handed, flexing his fingers once at his sides.

"Same scene," Ashton said. "And this time, when she crosses, don't follow her. Let her go."

Victor had spent three weeks drafting his bill on later school start times, and when the model parliament convened in the drafty assembly hall of the provincial legislature, he carried the typed pages like something living. The clerk, a university student named Priya in a borrowed black robe, called the house to order. Victor stood, his throat dry, ready to argue. "Bill 12, An Act to Amend the Education Act with Respect to School Start Times," Priya read, and before he could open his mouth she had moved on to the next item. Twelve seconds, maybe less. No questions, no debate, not even a vote. Around him the other students exchanged looks of pure bewilderment, and a girl named Marta whispered, "That was it? That was nothing."

At the lunch break Victor found Priya stacking the order paper and asked her whether his bill had been disqualified somehow, whether he had filled out a form wrong. She laughed, not unkindly. "That's first reading," she said. "In the real UK Parliament, a government bill's first reading is a formality. It just gets introduced, no debate, no vote." Victor stared at her, feeling oddly cheated. He had imagined the moment his idea entered the world as a public battle, not a name read into a record. "So it doesn't mean anything?" he asked. "It means it exists now," Priya said, and went back to her papers.

The committee stage came after lunch, and that was where the bleeding began. Victor had written a clause mandating a nine o'clock start for all high schools in the fictional province. A delegate from the rural party, a broad-shouldered boy named Ellis, moved an amendment allowing boards to opt out for bus scheduling reasons. Victor argued that an opt-out clause was a hole you could drive a bus through, and the room laughed, but the amendment carried anyway, eleven votes to nine. In the hallway afterward Ellis found him at the water fountain and offered something like an armistice: rural boards would accept the bill if they could breathe, and without rural boards, there would be no bill at all. Victor said he would think about it, which was true, and that it was a betrayal, which he also believed.

He thought about it through the debate that evening, sitting in the back benches while other bills rose and fell. A delegate proposing free menstrual products in schools watched her bill die at second reading on a voice vote, the "noes" rolling through the chamber like weather. Victor noticed that she did not cry, though her jaw worked. He noticed, too, that she was back at her desk within the hour, annotating a new draft in green ink. His friend Dev, slouched beside him, called this congenital optimism, the kind you were born with, and Victor envied it even as he distrusted it. Dev himself had come to the weekend to lose bills, he said, the way other people went to the gym.

What Victor worked out, slowly, in the yellow light of the chamber, was that two things he had been treating as one were actually two. He had wanted the law, and he had wanted to be right, and the committee had forced him to see that the second could cost him the first. He didn't think the trade was fair. He didn't think it was clean. But when debate on his own bill opened after dinner, he rose on a point of order and announced, to his own surprise, that he would accept the amendment as drafted. Marta, who had voted for the opt-out, looked at him strangely, almost disappointed, as though he had surrendered something she had wanted to watch him defend.

The third reading was almost quiet after that. Members who had fought him in committee now spoke of the bill as sensible, balanced, the kind of word that used to mean something before it meant nothing. The vote was called, and Victor watched the clerk tally the standing bodies in the aisles. Twenty-two for, seven against. A majority, an ordinary miracle, accomplished without anyone changing their mind about anything except him. Priya declared the bill passed, and the house moved on to the next order of business before his pulse had slowed.

The closing ceremony simulated royal assent. The Speaker, an actual retired MLA who had agreed to attend, sat beneath the carved provincial crest and read the titles of the bills that had survived the weekend, Victor's among them, in a flat ceremonial voice. "The bill receives assent and is now law," she said, and there was a small smattering of applause, mostly from parents who had drifted in for the last hour. Victor stood with the others while the Sergeant-at-Arms carried the mace out of the chamber, the old brass catching the light, the whole thing over.

Outside, in the parking lot, the evening had gone cold and the real buses were already idling. Ellis was loading a duffel bag into a minivan. "Your law's got a hole in it," he called across the asphalt. Victor shrugged into his jacket. "So does every law," he said. "I read the rest of the order paper." Ellis grinned and shut the van door, and Victor stood a moment longer listening to the engines.

The summer research slot came down to one afternoon in the optics lab, and Makayla had planned for it the way she planned for exams, which was to say too much and then sleep badly. Forty seniors from her school were rotating through the university's physics building in groups of six. Her group had drawn the spectroscopy bench on the third floor, where a graduate student named Corinne handed each of them a printed card and told them to record what they saw through the eyepiece.

Priya went first. She looked for a long time and wrote "faint dark lines, maybe three, hard to say." Then Corinne tapped the card and said, "For this demo, you're looking for bright emission lines in the green region. Four of them." Priya leaned back in, and within thirty seconds her pencil was moving. "Oh, yeah," she said. "Four. They're right there. I don't know how I missed it."

Makayla kept her eyes on the bench while the other four took their turns. Every one of them saw four lines after being told to expect four. When her turn came, she looked before Corinne said anything to her, and she saw what Priya had seen at first: dark lines, indistinct, count uncertain. She wrote that down. Corinne read it, then read it again.

"Interesting," Corinne said. "You're the only one who recorded dark lines."

"I wrote it before you told me what to look for," Makayla said. "Does that matter?"

Corinne didn't answer directly. She pulled a stool over and sat, which the other grad students in the room did not do. "Have you heard of René Blondlot?" she asked the group. Nobody had. "A French physicist, claimed to discover a new kind of radiation. He called them N-rays."

"Like X-rays," said Dario, the boy next to Makayla.

"Right. In 1904 another physicist, Robert W. Wood, went to Blondlot's lab and secretly removed a key prism from the apparatus. The observers still reported seeing the N-rays." Corinne stood up and straightened the eyepiece. "Wood didn't announce what he'd done until after. That's the part people remember."

Makayla turned her card over. On the back, in the margin, she had written her prep notes that morning, half of them definitions she'd exhumed from an old textbook in the school library, because the research program's application asked for a short essay on "how we know what we know." One of the notes said logos, from her English class, argument that persuades by reason. She had underlined it twice. Now the word looked thin to her, like it assumed reason was a thing one person could hold whole in one hand.

"Is this demo rigged, then?" Priya asked. There was an edge in her voice, and Makayla understood it. Priya had already emailed the program coordinator saying the lab visit confirmed her interest in optics.

"It's not rigged," Corinne said. "The lamp is exactly what I said it is. The question is what a single observer is worth."

Makayla thought about that on the walk to the next station, and she thought about it through the boring part of the tour, the clean room with its yellow light, and the part where Dario asked whether the university had ever retracted a paper. One result wasn't anything, she'd known that in an abstract way, but she hadn't felt it until Priya's pencil started moving. Still, she wasn't sure the feeling was fair. Priya wasn't lying. Corinne's tip about the green lines was presumably true, and Priya's second look was presumably better than her first. Expectation could point you at something real. The problem was that the pointing and the seeing felt identical from the inside, and only one of them counted as evidence.

At the bus turnaround she caught up with Corinne, who was carrying a crate of extension cords to a van. Makayla said she wanted to apply for the slot and asked, since it would come up in the essay, whether Corinne thought a study should be thrown out when the observers knew what they expected.

"One observer, one afternoon? That was never a study," Corinne said. She shifted the crate to her hip. "You'd repeat it, other people would repeat it with different instruments, people who wanted you to be wrong would repeat it. Then you'd know something."

"Unless they were all expecting the same thing," Makayla said.

"Then it takes longer," Corinne said. She loaded the crate and shut the van door.

On the bus Makayla wrote two sentences in her notebook and crossed out the second one, which had claimed too much. The first said that she had seen dark lines and had no way, from inside her own head, to certify them, and that the certification would have to come from outside her, repeatedly, from people with no stake in what she'd written. She looked at Priya two rows up, headphones in, filling out the program's online form on her phone. Priya typed fast, and stopped once, and looked out the window at the loading dock, and then typed again.

The rehearsal room at the far end of the arts building had been locked all summer, and on Tuesday somebody finally opened it. Victor walked in carrying his binder for the one-act and stopped in the doorway. The chairs were not in rows facing the front wall. They were arranged in a ring, four deep on every side, with a square of bare floor in the middle.

"Moved you," said Priya from the snack table. "The black box got double-booked. Choreography."

Victor set the binder on a chair and stood in the center of the square. He had spent a week blocking the play against an imaginary front wall. The mother sat downstage left; the son crossed to the window; the confrontation happened center, both actors facing the same direction, the way faces face in every film he had ever studied. He walked through the old blocking alone, saying the lines under his breath, and from where he stood he could see only his own imagined back.

"Your play," Priya said. He turned. She was eating pretzels and watching him with the flat patience she used on people she found interesting for reasons they hadn't earned. "You going to just stand there or rehearse?"

He got the cast together after lunch. Marcus played the son; Dana played the mother; a quiet sophomore named Elias had one scene as the neighbor. They ran the first half in the new room exactly as Victor had staged it in the old one, and it took him thirty seconds to see the problem. During the long argument, Marcus and Dana planted themselves upstage, facing away from the chairs behind them, and stayed there. An entire quarter of the audience, if the chairs had been full, would have watched two backs for four minutes.

"Rotate it," Victor said, stopping the scene. "Keep moving. If you stand still too long, someone's staring at your shoulder blades."

"Every line?" Marcus said. "That'll look random."

"Then we find where the turns go. In the arguments, probably. You shift when you shift tactics." Victor said it before he had fully thought it through, and he could feel it was half right. On a stage in the round the audience sat on all sides, so the people watching were divided, and fairness to them was a physical problem, a geometry, not a matter of one lucky front row. The whole space had to be used, and used continuously, or some section of chairs only ever saw the backs of the actors.

They worked the argument for an hour. Dana kept offering solutions that sounded reasonable and weren't: what if she faced one way for the whole scene and Marcus faced the other, splitting the difference. "Each side gets half a play," Victor said. "That's not the same as a play." She called that sophistry, which it wasn't, but he let it go because the clock was running and because she was partly right that his counterexample about windows was irrelevant. In the old room the window had been an imaginary rectangle of air on the front wall. Here it couldn't live on any wall, so it had to live on nothing, and he had to find a way to make an audience believe in an object that pointed in no direction.

He taped an X in the center of the floor with a broken corner of chalk instead, and told Elias to treat the X as the window. Elias stood at the X in his one scene, delivering the neighbor's awkward speech about borrowed tools, and turned slowly the whole time, like a man reluctant to be anywhere. It looked accidental. It looked, Victor thought, better than anything he had staged on purpose all week.

At five o'clock Priya came back through with her water bottle and watched the last run from behind the chairs on the north side. Afterward she was effusive, more than the run deserved, and Victor suspected she was being kind because she had watched him fail in that room at two o'clock. He didn't mind. He sat on the arm of a chair with his binder open and crossed out three pages of blocking diagrams, the ones that assumed a front.

"There's still the ending," Marcus said, toweling his neck. "They reconcile standing still. That's the whole point, they finally stop moving."

Victor looked at the ring of empty chairs. He hadn't solved it, and he was tired enough to admit that out loud. "I don't know yet," he said. He capped his pen. "Tomorrow. Everyone in the center, we'll turn the stillness itself." He snapped the binder shut and started stacking chairs against the wall.

The pay stub was thin paper, the kind that turned soft with sweat in a back pocket, and Lea read it twice under the fluorescent glare of the warehouse break room. Wages, overtime, and then a line she had never noticed before her eighteenth week of summer work: union dues, eleven dollars and change, taken off like tax. She had never joined anything. She had signed one form, the day she was hired, and a woman named Carol had checked her forklift certification and pointed her at aisle nine.

"You look like someone stole your lunch," said Marcus, dropping onto the bench across from her with his own stub held up to the light. He was twenty, quiet most of the time, with a scar on his forearm he never explained.

"Someone's taking money off my pay and I didn't sign up for it."

"It's called the Rand formula." He said it the way he said aisle numbers, flat, obvious. "Justice Ivan Rand, 1946. Came out of the Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario. Everyone covered by a union contract pays dues, whether they joined or not."

Lea turned the stub over as if the back might hold more. Outside the loading bay doors, trucks reversed in long beeps, and the dock plates clanged down one after another. "That doesn't seem fair," she said, and meant it, and also heard how young it came out.

Marcus shrugged. "Wage scale's fair. Overtime after forty-four hours is fair. You think this place gives that out of the goodness of its heart?" He tore the perforated edge off his stub and rolled it between his fingers. "My first year, before I understood anything, I resented it too. Then I watched the committee argue down the speed-up on the sort line, and it cost them three weeks of meetings after shifts, and they still showed up. I decided to internalize it differently. Dues are the price of the door staying open. Most of the time you don't see what the door is for."

The subtext sat between them, heavier than the words. Lea knew her mother had worked non-union at a laundry through her whole childhood, no pension, no wage scale, let go in a slow November with two weeks' pay and an apology that meant nothing. Her mother had put whatever she could into an annuity in those years, small deposits, disciplined ones, and she still called it the thing she was proudest of, because it was hers alone, because no committee had voted on it, because nobody could take it back. Two houses, two ways of thinking about what safety looked like. Lea had grown up inside the second one and was standing in the first.

She spent her lunch walking the long corridor to the union board, a corkboard thick with paper: minutes of meetings, a grievance about heat in the summer, the wage grid with its neat ascending rows, the shift premium, the safety clause about ventilation that someone had highlighted in yellow years ago. Carol was there tacking up a notice, and Lea asked her, half a question, whether the eleven dollars bought anything for someone who was leaving for university in September anyway.

"Your contract covers you while you're covered," Carol said. "That's all it promises. The rest is longer than you." She tapped the wage grid. "Kid before you, kid after you, same rows. You pay into the rows, you get the rows. You go, and it keeps going."

That night Lea sat on her bed with the stub flattened on her knee and thought about her mother's annuity statement, the tidy column of deposits, hers alone. The dues were the opposite kind of thing: money that went out into a common account she would never see itemized, spent partly on her, partly on strangers, partly on people not yet hired. Her mother would call that a bad bargain. Marcus would call it the only reason the bargain existed at all. Lea could not decide which was truer, and suspected the honest answer was equivocal, that the same deduction could be theft or inheritance depending on which month you looked at it.

In the morning she pinned the stub above her desk, next to the acceptance letter. At the end of her last shift, Marcus met her at the time clock with two coffees, and they drank them standing in the bay while the first truck of the night backed in, its beacon sweeping the concrete. "You never came to a meeting," he said. "I know," Lea said, and watched the dock plate fall.

The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and warm paper, and the air conditioning reached only the first three feet of the room, so Carter's collar was damp by the time he reached the teller line. He had forty dollars folded into his pocket, two twenties that had been one twenty until this morning, and a question he had been rehearsing since he left the house. Ahead of him a woman argued softly about a hold on a check, and the word liability drifted back over the velvet rope as though the bank itself were made of such words.

The teller who waved him forward was young, maybe twenty, with a name tag that said Priya and a lanyard heavy with pins. "Opening an account?" she asked. "Student checking takes ten minutes. You'll need to read the terms and conditions, and there's a signature card at the end. That's the consent part, basically. Your signature is you agreeing."

"I sold something," Carter said. "For twenty dollars. And I want to know if I can undo it."

Priya glanced at the queue behind him, three deep now, and lowered her voice. "Sold what?"

He told her about the bike, though telling it meant going back to yesterday evening, to the gravel drive beside Mr. Aldous's garage where the light had gone long and orange and the tire of the racing bike had spun slowly in his hand. Mr. Aldous had come out with his watering can, looked at the bike leaning against the fence, and said, "I'd give you twenty for that." Carter had needed twenty dollars. Not wanted, needed, by Friday, for the deposit on the cabin trip everyone had already paid, and the offer had seemed like a small synchronicity, the universe sliding the solution across the counter at the exact hour of his desperation. He had shaken on it right there, gravel gritting under his sneakers, the watering can dripping a dark coin of water onto the concrete.

"It's worth three hundred," Carter said now. "Maybe more. I checked online last night."

Priya pulled a blank deposit slip toward her and turned it over, as if the answer might be printed on the back. "Was it a fair price?" she asked, and when he shook his head she said, almost to herself, "Under common law, consideration just has to have some value. It doesn't have to be a fair price." She slid the slip back. "Courts don't sit around judging whether you made a good bargain. I'm doing law at night school, that's the only reason I know. Was it cash? Did you sign anything?"

"He wrote it on a napkin. From his porch. Both our names."

"Then it's signed."

The room seemed to tilt a little, the way it had in fourth grade when he learned that the sun would eventually swallow the earth, a fact too large to feel anything about in a carpeted building at eleven in the morning. Behind him a man cleared his throat. Priya's eyes went to a screen only she could see, some counter of accounts opened today, and Carter understood suddenly that she had a number to hit too, that everyone in the building was standing inside some bargain whose terms they had agreed to without reading, himself included. The whole morning had a turbid, stirred-up feeling, like the creek after rain, everything he thought was settled now moving in the water.

"Ten minutes for the account," Priya said. "It's a good one, no monthly fee if you keep a balance. And you should still go talk to him. He can undo a deal if he wants to, that's different from having to."

He opened the account because the twenty, folded and warm from his pocket, had nowhere else to live, and because the signature card waited with its empty line like a small door. He read the terms and conditions while Priya typed, the clauses rising off the page in a gray procession, liability limited, conditions subject to change, and he signed at the bottom and felt the pen drag slightly, leaving his name in blue ink, and thought of the napkin with both names on it in Mr. Aldous's careful draftsman's hand.

He walked home the long way, past the creek, and cut up Mr. Aldous's street without quite deciding to. The bike was there, leaning against the porch railing, polished, the chain oiled, the seat adjusted higher, which meant someone had ridden it already or meant to. Mr. Aldos came out with his watering can and saw him standing at the edge of the drive.

"I've been thinking about that price," Mr. Aldous said, and set the can down on the step.

"So have I," said Carter.

The assignment was taped to the back of the auditorium seats in case anyone forgot: one ten-minute play, drawn from your own life, staged by Friday. Mason had forgotten, in the sense that he had known about it and done nothing, and now it was Tuesday and Ms. Ruiz was walking the aisles collecting first drafts.

His draft was fourteen pages. It followed an entire summer, the one after his grandfather died, and it moved from the hospital waiting room to the funeral home to his aunt's kitchen to the lake where his cousins tried to teach him to fish, and then somehow to a bus station, and then to his own bedroom, where the last scene took place in September. Six locations in total. He had counted them twice on the bus that morning, hoping the number would shrink.

"Fourteen pages," said Devon, who sat behind him and read over shoulders as a matter of policy. "Ten minutes is about ten pages, max. And you've got a whole road show here."

"It's one summer," Mason said. "It's one thing."

"It's a genealogy of one summer," Devon said. "Every relative, every room. You're writing a family tree with scenery."

Ms. Ruiz reached their row. She read Mason's pages standing, flipping through them the way a doctor flips through a chart when the news is already obvious to her. "A ten-minute play usually has one setting," she said, "and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people." She handed the pages back. "You have a summer. I need a moment. Pick one."

"Which one?"

"That's not my summer." She moved on to the next row.

The auditorium emptied for lunch except for the stage crew kids hauling the spring musical's flats into the wings, and Mason stayed in his seat because going to the cafeteria with fourteen useless pages seemed worse than sitting alone with them. He spread the scenes across three seats like tarot cards. Hospital. Funeral home. Kitchen. Lake. Bus station. Bedroom. Six little worlds, and he had maybe two days to keep one and bury five.

He tried to prognosticate, the way his grandfather had prognosticated weather off the lake, reading a sky nobody else could read, and he understood now that the old man had mostly been guessing with confidence. Which scene would survive? He couldn't tell. He liked the lake scene because his cousins were funny in it, but the cousins were auxiliary, really, three extra people who came on, cracked jokes about the fish, and left. Few characters, Ruiz had said. He had nine.

The hospital waiting room had only two people in it, him and his mother, and it never changed location. By the play's own arithmetic, that was the scene. But it was the one he least wanted to stage, because in it he had told his mother he was fine and gone to the vending machines and stayed there for forty minutes, and a person sitting in an audience would watch him do that and know exactly what it meant.

Devon came back from lunch with chips and no shame. "Kill your darlings," he offered, having read this somewhere.

"Which darlings?"

"The funny ones. The cousins."

"That's what I was thinking."

"Then why do you look like you're at the funeral home scene?"

Mason laughed, or something adjacent to laughing. He gathered five of the scene descriptions and folded them into his pocket, which was not deleting but was close enough for a first draft. The waiting room stayed on the seat in front of him. He read it over. His mother's one line was "He's still sleeping," delivered three times to three different relatives, but the relatives were offstage now, voices in a hall, which meant he could keep the line and lose the people, and he wrote that down in the margin: voices, no bodies. Two characters. One room. He did not know yet whether the forty minutes at the vending machines was honesty or just an excuse for a second scene, and he decided, provisionally, to write it and see.

By Friday he had eleven pages, and Ruiz read them in the front row while the crew kids rigged a work light to stand in for the fluorescent glare of a hospital corridor. She read without expression, which Devon claimed was her highest rating.

"Who's the voice on the paging system?" she asked.

"Nobody. It's a voice."

"Good. Stage it."

Mason stood at the edge of the stage while Devon, drafted as his mother with a scarf over his head, sat in a folding chair and said, "He's still sleeping." The work light buzzed. Offstage, one of the crew kids read the paging voice off a cue card, and Mason walked slowly toward the imaginary vending machines, slowly enough that an audience might watch him not turn around.

The bathroom was the quietest room in the house, and that was why Grandpa did his blood pressure there, sitting on the edge of the tub with his sleeve rolled up, the cuff wheezing tight around his arm. Kaylee stood in the doorway with the notebook her mother had left on the counter, the one with "help him keep track" written across the top in her mother's urgent, slanted hand.

"Read it to me," Grandpa said. "The top number and the bottom."

The screen showed 148 over 94. Kaylee copied it down, then looked at the folded paper the doctor had given him at his appointment, the one he'd been carrying around unfolded and refolded until the creases went soft. There were numbers on it, ranges with lines drawn between them, and a word he hadn't wanted to say out loud in the car.

"What's hypertension mean?" she asked, because he'd gone quiet when the doctor said it, and quiet was not like him.

"High blood pressure," he said. "Same thing, fancier coat."

Kaylee sat down on the edge of the tub beside him, the porcelain cold through her jeans. Below the ranges on the doctor's paper was a single underlined word, DASH, and after it, "diet." She'd assumed it meant cutting something out, fast, the way her aunt had cauterized sugar from her kitchen after her own diagnosis, throwing away half a pantry in one Saturday. Grandpa was already bracing for that version. He'd been bellicose about it all week, grumbling that if the doctor wanted him eating rabbit food he should say so plainly.

"Can I look it up?" she asked. He waved a hand, which meant yes.

Her phone worked even in the bathroom, one bar flickering by the window. She found the letters spelled out. DASH stood for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. It wasn't a diet of denial at all; it was a plan that had been tested, an actual trial, funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and published in 1997, back when she wasn't even born. She read the line twice. Somebody had done this on purpose, with real people, and written it down.

"It's not what you think," she said. "It's not taking things away. There's fruit, vegetables, whole grains. You can still have chicken."

"Chicken," Grandpa repeated, as if she'd offered him a peace treaty. "And the salt?"

"Less salt. But there's still, like, food in it."

He watched her write it down, the way she always wrote things, half printing and half cursive, ink smudged along the side of her hand. She drew a line down the middle of the page and put the reading on the left, 148 over 94, and on the right she started a list of what he'd eaten that day. She was guessing at how the two connected. The website said the diet mattered and exercise mattered, and she could see that the numbers were supposed to come down, but how much, and how fast, and whether the reading on any single Tuesday meant anything at all, the website didn't say. The more she read, the more she understood that one number was a snapshot and the pattern was the story.

"So which number is the bad one?" Grandpa asked.

"They both matter," she said. "The top one is when your heart beats. The bottom is between beats." She pointed at the doctor's ranges, the lines drawn between them. "You want them under the line."

"And this food gets them under the line."

"That's the idea. That's what the trial was for. They tested it before they told people to do it." She liked that. She liked that somebody had checked. Most of what she'd been told to believe in school had arrived the same way, she realized, conclusions handed over already finished, and she had never once asked who had done the checking.

Her mother appeared in the doorway then, still in her work coat, holding grocery bags. "Is he doing the cuff?"

"He's doing the cuff," Kaylee said. "And we're doing the diet." She held up the notebook. "I made a plan. Sort of a plan."

Her mother came in and stood behind them both, reading over Kaylee's shoulder, and Kaylee felt her mother's hand rest briefly on the top of her head, the way she used to when Kaylee was small and brushing her teeth at this same sink. "You looked it up?"

"It stands for something. Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. There was a whole trial. Nineteen ninety-seven."

"Better than I did," her mother said quietly. "I just bought the chicken."

That night Kaylee taped the notebook page to the bathroom mirror, next to the reading, and under it wrote Monday, walk, 20 minutes, if he'll go. She knew the ending wasn't going to arrive all at once, the way it did in books, some clean denouement where the numbers dropped and everyone was safe. It would arrive, if it arrived, in small entries on different days, a graph she'd have to draw slowly. Grandpa came in to brush his teeth, saw the page, and read it with his mouth full of foam.

"Twenty minutes," he said.

"We'll walk to the mailbox and back. Twice."

He spat, rinsed, and looked at her in the mirror. "Get your shoes on, then. I'm not waiting till Monday."

The marble corridor outside Courtroom 4B smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Sophia's note cards kept slipping against her skirt. Fourteen students from three high schools had been assigned to litigate a mock case before a panel of real appellate judges, and Sophia had drawn the worst possible job: she would argue both sides. Petitioners in the morning, respondents after lunch, same girl, same bench, same fifteen minutes each.

The case was one her class had built from a real fight at a school two districts over. A student named in the file only as M.R. had posted a video mocking the vice principal, and the school had suspended her. That part was settled law, more or less. The twist her classmates had added was this: M.R. had also been banned from a private class-discussion website run by a company, and she claimed that ban violated her free speech rights too. Sophia had to argue that it did. Then, after lunch, she had to argue that it didn't.

In the morning she stood at the podium with her knees locked and said what she had prepared. She talked about the marketplace of ideas, about chilling expression, about a sixteen-year-old silenced in the very forum where her classmates gathered. Justice Kowalski, a heavyset man with reading glasses pushed low, leaned forward and asked whether the website was run by the government. Sophia said no, and he asked the question again, slower, the way you repeat something to someone who hasn't understood it the first time.

"Then walk me through it," he said. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech. It does not by itself stop a private company from restricting speech. So what is your claim?"

Her argument dissolved in her mouth. She had known the words, of course, had copied them into her outline weeks ago, but she had never actually believed them until a judge made her stand there and look at them. She said something about students feeling that the platform was their town square, and the judge said feelings did not create jurisdiction, and a girl from the other school, a redhead named Priya who'd spent the whole morning smirking, whispered something to her co-counsel that Sophia pretended not to notice.

At lunch she sat alone on the courthouse steps and ate half a sandwich. Her grandmother had once been fired from a print shop for union organizing, and the family still argued about it at holidays, her uncle insisting it was illegal, her mother correcting him each time with visible exhaustion. Sophia had always assumed her mother was being pedantic. Now she understood her mother had been protecting the family from a confusion that would cost them something later, the way you teach a kid not to touch a stove. The government couldn't punish you for speaking. A private company could, mostly, and you had to know which one you were standing in front of.

But the afternoon side was not as easy as the morning side had been hard. Arguing that M.R.'s ban was lawful felt like handing a weapon to whoever owned the forum, and the forum was where everyone her age actually lived. She stood up after lunch and made the legal argument cleanly, almost coldly, and then Justice Alvarez, a small woman with silver hair, asked the counterpoint Sophia had been dreading: "Counsel, is there anything you find troubling about the rule you're defending?" Sophia paused, and then said yes, that the law drew a line between public power and private power at a moment when private platforms felt more like governments than governments did, and that the doctrine struck her as accurate and antiquated at once, which was not a distinction the First Amendment itself could resolve.

Justice Alvarez wrote something down. Priya, sitting in the second row, was not smirking anymore.

When the judges retired to score the round, Priya came over. "The morning," she said. "When you folded on the private website. You knew, right? I could tell you knew." Sophia admitted she had known and hoped the judges wouldn't press it, and Priya laughed, a real laugh, not a smirk. "I got that exact question wrong at a tournament in October. I claimed a platform violated a girl's free speech rights and a judge spent ten minutes dismantling me. I only challenged you today to see if you'd do the same thing I did."

They were still on the steps when the clerk came out with the results folded in half. Priya took the paper, looked at it a long moment, and held it out without saying anything.

The essay question sat at the top of Addison's laptop screen like an accusation: Is it possible to describe the past without taking a side? She had come to her grandfather's house for the weekend because the internet at home was down, and because her mother had said, gently, that Grandpa could use the company.

The house was spartan since Grandma died, the spare furniture arranged as if for inspection, the study still crowded with boxes nobody had opened. Addison set up at the kitchen table while her grandfather washed the same pan he had washed before lunch. She had found the quote in her notes from class. In 1824, the German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past "as it actually was", rather than to judge it or instruct the present. Her job was to decide whether that was even possible.

"How's the paper?" her grandfather asked, drying his hands.

"Fine." She closed the laptop halfway. "Do you have any old letters? Like, from when you were young. Primary sources. My teacher wants primary sources."

He was quiet long enough that she thought he hadn't heard. "There's a box in the study. Your grandmother's side of the closet."

The study smelled of cedar and dust. Addison found the box under a stack of tax returns: bundled letters, a photograph album, a newspaper clipping from 1968 with a crease down the middle. She carried it to the kitchen table and began sorting, and her grandfather stood at the counter with his coffee, not quite watching, not quite not watching.

The clipping was about a student protest at his university. The article called the organizers "disruptive elements" and quoted the dean at length. There was no quote from any student. Addison turned the clipping over. On the back, in her grandmother's handwriting, was a single line: He was there. Ask him what he saw.

"Grandpa. This protest. Were you there?"

The coffee cup stopped halfway to his mouth. "That was a long time ago."

"That's not an answer."

He set the cup down. "I was there. It wasn't what the paper said."

She thought of a night three years ago, before Grandma got sick, when the two of them sat on the porch and Grandma told stories about her brother, the one nobody else mentioned, who had written pamphlets and lost his job for it and moved away. The family, Grandma said, had spent thirty years trying to exculpate themselves, as if his opinions were a crime they could prove they hadn't committed. Addison had looked up from the porch steps to see her grandfather standing inside the screen door, listening, saying nothing, going back to the dishes.

"The paper says the protest turned violent," she said now, tapping the clipping.

"The police turned it violent. Some kid threw a bottle, maybe. Then they waded in. I got pushed against a fence. A girl next to me got hit with a baton." He said it flatly, the way he said things that cost him. "The paper printed the dean's version. Nobody asked us."

Addison opened her laptop again. "So the newspaper is a primary source and you're a primary source, and they don't match."

"That happens."

"So which one do I believe? You're my grandfather. I want to believe you. Doesn't that mean I've already taken a side?"

He almost smiled. "Sounds like your paper's writing itself."

"It isn't." She pulled one of the letter bundles toward her. They were Grandma's letters to her sister, dated that same spring. Addison skimmed, stopped, read one twice. In it, Grandma described the protest, the fence, the baton, the girl, and one more thing: a list of names being circulated, students identified as organizers, and one of the names was her brother's, though the article had said nothing about any list. Addison looked up.

"There's a list in here that the newspaper never mentioned."

"Your grandmother kept everything." His voice had gone careful. "Even things that were dangerous to keep."

"That's why she wrote it down. Because the paper wasn't going to."

He sat down across from her, slowly, and for a while neither of them spoke. Outside, a mower started two houses away.

"So Ranke," Addison said, mostly to herself, and her grandfather raised an eyebrow. "This historian. He wanted to show the past as it actually was. No judging, no lessons for the present. Just what happened."

"The fence was real," her grandfather said. "The baton was real."

"But which things got written down, and which didn't, that's a choice somebody made. Even Grandma chose. She saved the clipping and the letter together, like she knew one wasn't enough."

She typed for a while, then stopped. "Here's my problem. If I only use the newspaper, I've taken the dean's side without meaning to. If I only use you and Grandma, I've taken yours. And if I use everything, somebody still decided what everything was."

"Then say that."

"Say what?"

"That you don't know for sure. That's what your grandmother would have said." He stood, took his cup to the sink, ran water over it. "She'd have made you put the clipping in the paper, though. Face up."

Addison flattened the crease with her thumb, then let it fold back along its old line. She set the clipping beside the letter, side by side on the table, and opened a fresh page.

"Can I copy the letter?" she asked. "The whole thing?"

"Take the box," he said, and turned off the tap.

The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Nicholas had been rehearsing in the hallway long enough to notice both. He held his outline flat against a binder, the way he had seen lawyers do it in videos, and read the first line of his argument under his breath. In forty minutes he would stand before a panel of three judges in a borrowed courtroom and argue the student's side of Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., the case his civics class had drawn by lottery. Then, after lunch, he would argue the school's side of the same case, which was the part nobody had warned him would be hard.

He had not chosen the case. Priya had pulled the slip from the coffee can and read the name aloud, and Marcus, who sat behind him, had laughed and said it sounded like a school board suing a letter. Nicholas had gone home that weekend and looked it up, partly for the assignment and partly because of something he had posted in March, a picture of his cross country coach with a caption he had deleted by Sunday but which three people had screenshotted. Nothing had come of it. Still, when he read the summary of the case, he felt the specific cold of recognition.

The case was about a girl who had posted something on Snapchat, off campus, on a weekend, and her school had punished her for it. Nicholas had assumed, before he read further, that the school was allowed to do that, that off campus was like a country the school's rules didn't reach but its arm did. Then he found the holding. In 2021, the Supreme Court had ruled 8 to 1 that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Eight justices against one. He read the sentence twice, then copied it onto an index card, because it seemed like the kind of thing that shouldn't be paraphrased.

The courtroom was crepuscular in the late morning, the blinds tilted so that light fell in gray bars across the jury box, which sat empty. A bailiff who was actually a retired accountant let them in and told them not to touch the microphone. Nicholas took the petitioner's table, the one closest to the bench, and arranged his cards in order while Priya sat beside him with the case brief and a bag of pretzels she did not open. At the respondent's table, two juniors Nicholas didn't know well spread out their notes like a poker hand they were proud of.

"Ms. Reyes, you may begin whenever you're ready," said the judge in the center, a law student named Alanna who wore her father's old robe. Nicholas stood. His first two minutes went fine, better than fine; he talked about the post being made off campus, on her own time, and he said the line from his index card almost exactly, that the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 1 in 2021 that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Alanna nodded and wrote something down, and the nod coagulated all his scattered preparation into something that felt like actual confidence.

Then the judge on the left leaned forward. "Counsel, what would you say to the school if the post had disrupted a class on Monday?" It was the question Nicholas had hoped wouldn't come, because he had two answers and they disagreed with each other. He gave the student's answer first, that punishment for a weekend post stretches the school's reach into students' private lives. Then he stopped, because the honest thing was also true. "And I'd have to concede that schools aren't helpless," he said. "I just don't think the First Amendment turns off when a student walks through her front door."

At lunch, in the courthouse cafeteria, Marcus slid his tray across from Nicholas and asked how it had gone. "I don't know yet," Nicholas said. "Ask me after round two." The problem was the second round. For an hour he had believed the student's side so completely that he could feel it in his chest, and now he had to stand up and be the school, the district that had suspended a girl for swearing on a weekend. He spread his cards on the table and tried to see the other argument, but his thoughts kept sliding back, the way a whole biome shifts when one species is removed; the case without the student's rights in it wasn't the same case at all.

When the afternoon session began, the light had moved and the courtroom was warmer. Nicholas stood at the respondent's table and argued that a school could still act when off-campus speech bled into school life, that the majority had left the door open, that the lone dissenter had a point about schools needing to reach students wherever they were. He did not fully believe it, but he argued it carefully, and once, when Alanna asked whether a school should follow students home, he heard himself say, "Not home. But maybe the bus stop in between." It was the first thing all day that felt like his own.

The panel conferred, then awarded the round to the other side, and Priya squeezed his shoulder on the way out. In the hallway, the light through the high windows had gone amber, and Nicholas stopped by the water fountain and took a long drink. He still didn't know where the line was, exactly, between a school's reach and a student's life, and he suspected the Court didn't either, given eight votes on one side and a single stubborn voice on the other. He put his index cards back in order, both sets, one for each side, and slid them into his back pocket. "Same time next week," Priya said, holding the door.

Eric had promised himself he would finish the hallway drawing before fifth period ended, and he had forty minutes left, a pencil sharpened to a needle, and a hallway that refused to be a hallway. It lay on the paper like something flattened by a steamroller, a row of lockers marching across the page with the depth of a filing cabinet. He had drawn the drinking fountain three times. Each time it sat on top of the lockers instead of beside them, like a very clean frog.

"You've redrawn that fountain so many times it's going to ask for a contract," said Priya from the next stool, not looking up from her print of crows. She and Eric had a running arrangement: she critiqued his drawing, he critiqued her titles, and both of them ignored the teacher's suggestion that they critique their own work for once.

"The hallway's broken," Eric said. "It's a hallway for people with no depth perception. Flatland High School."

Priya leaned over, held her pencil at arm's length against his paper, and squinted like a pirate. "Everything's parallel. Your lockers are all the same size, and the door at the end is the same size too. That's why it looks like a poster for a very boring school."

He knew she was right, and he hated how right she was, because he had spent two nights on the tile pattern alone. The tiles. He had drawn a hundred tiles, each one exactly, obediently square, and somewhere in the back of his mind a suspicion had been forming that the tiles were the traitors. When he stood in the actual hallway, the far tiles looked smaller. He had never once drawn them smaller. He had, apparently, been running a hallway according to his own private laws of geometry, laws the hallway had never agreed to follow.

He flipped to a clean page and started over, this time being sneaky about it. He drew one point in the middle of the paper and then, feeling like a con artist, made the locker edges run toward that point like they were late for a bus. The tiles shrank as they went. The door at the end came out small, and strange, and then, all at once, deep. The hallway opened like a drawer sliding out of the page. He sat back so fast his stool squeaked.

"Whoa," Priya said. "What did you just do?"

"I don't know. I made the lines go toward one spot." He tapped the point with his eraser. "It's like everything's running away from the viewer to hide back there."

"That's a thing," Priya said, already pulling out her phone with the guilty speed of someone who knew the teacher would confiscate it in a heartbeat. "My brother did a report on it. Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective. Drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point, to show depth on a flat surface."

"So I accidentally invented it in an art room in Ohio."

"You're about six hundred years late and an ocean short, but sure, Columbus it however you like." She grinned. "Brunelleschi would be furious that you tried to expropriate his idea with a number two pencil."

"It's not expropriation if I didn't know it existed. It's independent rediscovery. It's very dignified."

The teacher drifted past, looked at the new drawing for a long moment, and said only, "Better," which from her was a standing ovation, and moved on. Eric looked at the vanishing point and felt both pleased and slightly cheated. He had wanted to invent something, and instead he had reinvented something, which meant either that he was six centuries late or that the idea was so true that a seventeen-year-old with a mechanical pencil could stumble into it on a Tuesday.
