He understood that there was a middle step called transcription, and that after it came translation, but the diagram showed arrows and shapes and a word, ribosome, that floated on the page without weight. Nothing in his mind would stand still long enough to be copied.

On Thursday the extension agent came out to check the noxious weed growth along the creek fence, and she brought her daughter, Priya, who was starting college in the fall and who had, she said, survived this exact exam. She looked at the textbook open on the porch, looked at Edouard, and asked whether the garden was free. Edouard said it was, mostly, except for the bees.

Priya went to the truck and came back with a fistful of index cards. She wrote on them in marker, quick and sure: on some cards three letters, and on others the names of amino acids, leucine, valine, glycine. She handed Edouard the amino acid cards and kept the three-letter ones for herself. "You're a transfer RNA," she said. "Each card you hold is one amino acid, and written on the back of it is your anticodon. Three bases."

"Three like the ones you have."

"Those are codons. On the messenger RNA. Walk toward me and read yours aloud, and if we match, you hand it over."

He walked the row between the tomatoes, holding a card with leucine written on it, and turned it over. On the back she had written three letters. He said them out loud. Priya turned her card so he could see. The letters paired, and she took his card and clipped it to a string she had strung between two stakes, where three other cards already hung. "Amino acids in a row," she said. "That's the protein."

They did it again, and again, and on the fifth card his anticodon did not match her codon, and he stood in the row holding leucine, uncertain. Priya pointed to a card in his other hand, the one he'd been carrying as a second amino acid. "Check your other one." He flipped it, read the three bases, and this time the letters paired, and he passed over the amino acid that matched, and the string grew longer. It occurred to him, standing there between the tomato stakes with dirt on his knees, that he had been trying to memorize the diagram when the diagram was simply people walking toward each other holding things.

That evening he wrote to his mother, who was in the city working double shifts.

Dear Mom. The farm is fine. The calves bawl at five in the morning and I have stopped minding. I failed the midterm but I think I understand it now. I learned it in the vegetable garden from a girl who made me into a molecule. Every amino acid gets carried by its own small card that has three letters on the back, and those letters pair with three letters on the message, and when they match, the amino acid gets handed over and added to the line, and the line is the protein. That is all transcription and translation are, as far as I can tell. I still can't explain what makes the first card start walking, or why the string folds the way it does afterward. Priya says that's chemistry, next semester. Tell Dad the fence by the creek is nearly done. Love, Edouard.

He read the letter over and did not add anything about his doubts, because the doubts were not really doubts. They were borders. He knew what he knew, and he knew where it stopped, and the place where it stopped had a name and a course number.

On Saturday he found Priya at the fence pulling bindweed, and he told her about his uncle's habit of talking to the tractor, how the old man seemed to externalize every worry out loud into the air so it became something he could hear and answer. Priya laughed and said that was exactly what the index cards had done for the chapter, made the inside of his head visible on the garden path. They stood for a while in the noise of insects, and Edouard thought that somewhere in him a consciousness had been reading the same four pages over and over, and only now had something new to read.

In September, before the retake, he laid out the index cards on his bed in the city, three letters against three letters, amino acid after amino acid, and began at the beginning of the string.

Victor had told Theo he was an excellent skater, which was true in the sense that he had once, in seventh grade, completed a full lap without touching the wall. The rink's fluorescent glare found him out within eleven seconds, when his feet performed a decision of their own and deposited him against the boards with a sound like a filing cabinet falling downstairs.

"You said intermediate," Priya said, gliding backward in front of him, hands in her coat pockets, entirely at ease on the ice in a way that seemed almost personal, as though the rink had taken her side.

"Intermediate is a spectrum," Victor said from the floor. "I'm on it."

"Where on it?"

"The floor part of it." He got up, and she laughed, and the laugh did something to his chest that he chose not to examine in front of witnesses.

She had asked him out, actually, which he kept forgetting to be honest with himself about. In his own telling, the whole thing had been his maneuver: the note in AP Gov about her locker sticker for a band he liked, the three days of strategic hovering. The truth, which he set aside the way one sets aside a bill, was that she had turned around in class and said, "You're the one who owns the same shirt as me in a worse color, we should skate sometime," and he had said "Obviously," and then gone into the hallway and stared at a fire extinguisher for a while.

They did laps, halting and smooth respectively. She coached him through crossovers; he expostulated that the wall was closer than it looked, and the wall, his true nemesis on the ice, proved his point by catching his elbow. At the snack bar they split a pretzel the size of a steering wheel and argued about whether the Zamboni driver had a favorite, the way teachers had favorites. "He resurfaces a lane of honor," Priya said. "For people he respects. You'll never see it." Victor said that was virulent propaganda against a man who drove a machine that was basically a giant iron, and she laughed again, and he began to hope the evening was something they would both want to remember in the same direction.

He was careful all night, and proud of the carefulness. He asked before taking her hand on the ice, and when they stood in the parking lot afterward, cold coming up through their shoes, he asked before anything else too, and she said yes, and kissed him briefly, and he floated approximately four inches off the asphalt.

Then, walking toward her car, she slowed. "Okay, so," she said. "I think I'd rather just say goodnight here. I'm kind of done with being touched tonight. Not a verdict on you."

His first impulse was to debate it, and he saw himself doing so, some version of him already opening his mouth to point out that she had kissed him, that the yes had happened, that in the court of Victor's feelings the evidence was overwhelming. He shut that version up. Somewhere in the fog of his own confidence, a fact surfaced from a health assembly he'd half ignored: consent to any intimate contact could be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given. Yes was not a contract. Yes was a weather report, good until it wasn't.

"That's completely fine," he said, and meant it, mostly, and the part of him that didn't was a part he could admit existed without letting it drive.

"You paused," she said, watching him. "That was a good pause. I've seen worse pauses. Some guys treat a kiss like a lease."

"A lease can't be revoked," Victor said. "Consent can. Any time, even after it was given. Which I definitely knew before tonight and did not just assemble from first principles in your parking lot."

"Smooth," she said. "Devastatingly smooth." She unlocked her car, then turned back, keys jingling against her palm. "Same time next week? You can fall down for me again."

"I'll bring a helmet," Victor said. "For the boards. They've been asking for a rematch."

She grinned and got in, and he stood in the cold until her taillights turned out of the lot, then skated the walk home on the frozen patches of sidewalk, badly, gloriously, without falling once.

The restaurant had pushed four tables together under the big screen, and by the second quarter Sarah's uncle Theo had already lost a trivia bet to her cousin Marcus twice, which meant he owed him twenty dollars and a plate of nachos he kept trying to amortize by eating himself. Sarah sat between her grandmother and her best friend Priya, nominally watching the game, actually watching Marcus. He was the one who had told her, at the graduation party last month, that she argued like a lawyer and cared about nothing, and she had been carrying that sentence around ever since like a stone in her shoe.

"There's a trivia contest at halftime," Marcus announced, waving the paper flyer the waitress had left. "Winner gets fifty bucks off the bill. Sports and Olympics stuff, since the games start next month."

"I'll do it," Sarah said, before she could think better of it.

"You don't watch sports," her grandmother said, not unkindly.

"I watch the Olympics. I like the opening ceremony. All the flags."

"Lugubrious music, everyone crying," Priya agreed, tearing a piece of napkin into small flags of her own. "It's the best thing on television."

The first half was a grinding, low-scoring affair that Uncle Theo narrated like a funeral oration, and by halftime Sarah had two of the three trivia questions right, tied with a man in a trucker hat from the bar who turned out to know an alarming amount about boxing. Then the waitress cleared her throat and read the tiebreaker: which colors appear in the five Olympic rings, and why those colors.

Sarah closed her eyes. The rings were blue, yellow, black, green, and red, she was sure of that. But the why escaped her, and she could feel Marcus across the table, grinning, waiting for her to fail so he could add it to his collection of evidence that she was all talk. She thought about the opening ceremonies she had actually watched, the part she liked best, the parade where every country came in behind its flag. She had once spent a whole afternoon as a kid hunting for her own country's colors in the rings on a poster in her grandfather's study, tracing them with her finger, and her grandfather had told her the answer then, and she had forgotten it, and now it came back the way forgotten things do, all at once and slightly sideways.

"They picked the colors so every national flag at the time had at least one of them," she said, opening her eyes. "That includes the white background of the rings." She paused. "And it was Pierre de Coubertin who designed them. Nineteen thirteen."

The waitress looked at her card. "That's... that's it exactly. Wow. Okay."

The trucker hat man raised his glass to her from the bar, which felt almost better than the fifty dollars. Almost, because the fifty dollars was real, and when Uncle Theo launched into a peroration about how they should put it toward his nachos debt to Marcus, Sarah held the flyer above her head out of his reach and said the money was going to dessert, split eight ways, and that his debts were his own affair.

"You knew that off the top of your head," Marcus said as the second half started and everyone leaned back toward the screen. "Sports trivia."

"It's not sports trivia. It's flags. There's a difference."

"There's really not."

"You said I care about nothing," Sarah said, keeping her voice light, because they were in public and because she was not sure she wanted the answer anyway. "I care about a French guy in 1913 who wanted every country to see itself in one symbol. That's something."

Marcus considered this while the crowd on screen and the crowd in the restaurant roared at a fumble. "So you're saying you care about, what, symbolism."

"I'm saying I care about the specific argument that you can make something universal without erasing anybody. He didn't pick colors for his country. He picked colors so nobody's country would be left out." She heard herself and laughed a little. "Which might be generous or might just be good design, I honestly can't tell, and I'm not sure it matters which."

"That's the most Sarah sentence ever spoken," Priya said, and stole the last tortilla chip.

The game tightened in the fourth quarter, and the restaurant rose and fell with it, and Sarah found she was standing too, shouting at the screen with her grandmother's hand gripping her arm. She still couldn't have named more than three players. She was still watching. On the wall above the screen somebody had taped up a paper promotion for the Olympics next month, five rings printed small in the corner, and every time the crowd noise dipped she found her eyes drifting to it, white showing between the colors.

With eleven seconds left and the score tied, Marcus leaned over and said, "Double or nothing on dessert. Field goal is good."

"Done," Sarah said, and did not look away from the ball.

The notebook was open to a page that said, in Devi's handwriting, "You can't test what doesn't exist. Unless." Victoria had found it in her backpack that morning, shoved between the camp T-shirt she never washed and a stick of deodorant, and she had been turning the sentence over all day like a coin she couldn't decide to spend. Now it was almost nine, the kitchen table had been cleared of dinner, and her laptop hummed in front of an empty file called Student.java.

Devi had issued the challenge on the last night of camp, sitting cross-legged on a bunk while everyone else packed. Victoria remembered the mosquito coil smoldering by the door, the way Devi kept clicking a pen against her knee. "You write the class first," Devi had said, "because that's what everyone does. I'm telling you to write the test first. For something that doesn't exist yet." Victoria had laughed, and Devi had not, and the silence after that had felt like the beginning of an argument they never got to finish, because lights-out came and then buses came and then summer ended.

So here she was, at home, alone with the idea. The assignment from the online course was simple: build a Student class in Java with private fields, name and grade, and getter methods to read them. The ordinary path was obvious. Declare the fields, write getName, write getGrade, and only then, if you felt virtuous, write a little test to prove it all worked. She had done it that way a dozen times. The test was like a stamp at the end, a formality, and a green check mark could almost absolve her of ever having doubted the code in the first place. Almost. That was the word that had started to bother her at camp. Almost.

She opened a new file instead, StudentTest.java, and typed a test that called new Student("Victoria", 11) and then asserted that getName returned "Victoria". The class didn't exist. She had written a test for a ghost. When she ran it, the screen filled with red: compilation errors, cannot find symbol, the whole cascade of the compiler telling her, in its blunt way, that she had written a lie. She sat back. It was strange how satisfying the failure was, how it felt less like an error and more like a map. The red told her exactly what the world lacked.

Her mother wandered through for a glass of water and paused at the screen. "Your grandmother used to say the perspicacious ones ask before they know enough to be embarrassed. What's all the red?" "It's on purpose," Victoria said. "Supposedly. It's a thing called red, green, refactor. You write a failing test first, then make it pass, then clean up the code." Her mother sipped her water. "Who dreamed that up?" "Somebody named Kent Beck. He popularized it, Devi says. It's called test-driven development." Her mother nodded slowly, the way she nodded at Victoria's grandmother's opinions about soup, and carried her glass back down the hall.

Alone again, Victoria built the class the red demanded: private fields, name and grade, hidden away where nobody could reach in and change them, then two small getter methods that handed the values back. When she ran the test, everything went green. She caught herself grinning at a check mark, which was absurd, and grinned anyway. The green meant only that her code did what she had thought to ask of it. She began to see how someone could mistake that for proof, and how the mistake would be a quiet one, the kind you'd never notice until a name came back wrong six months later.

She scrolled a programming forum while she waited for nothing in particular and found a diagram someone had labeled the phylogeny of programming languages, Java branching off C++, C++ off C, the whole family tree drawn like a naturalist's sketch. She liked that. Ideas inherited traits the same way beetles did, small mutations passed down until someone gave them a name. Maybe that was all Beck had done, she thought, noticed a mutation that had been drifting through the population and pinned it to a board. Or maybe he'd built it from nothing. She didn't know, and the not-knowing felt okay, even interesting, like a door she could see but hadn't opened yet.

Then she did the last part, the refactor. The getter for grade was fine but ugly, cluttered with a comment she'd written to reassure herself. She deleted the comment, straightened the spacing, ran the test again. Green held. She leaned forward and started a second test, this one for a student with an empty name, just to see what the red would say about that. The cursor blinked at the end of the line, patient, waiting to be proved wrong.

Victoria spread the briefs across her grandmother's kitchen table, the good table, the one that smelled faintly of lemon wax and held a framed photograph of her grandfather standing in some montane landscape, boots laced, squinting into an altitude of light. Two stacks: petitioners on the left, respondents on the right. On Thursday she would argue for a student's right to wear an armband in a public school. On Friday she would argue the school's side, against herself, and the whole point, her coach kept saying, was that she had to mean both.

The trouble was that she did mean both, and it felt less like a skill than like a defect. In practice rounds she kept conceding mid-sentence. "Speech is not absolute," she would begin, robust and confident, and then hear herself add, "though of course the school suspended her for a silent, non-disruptive symbol, which is hard to defend." Her partner Zoe had started keeping a tally on her wrist.

Her grandmother set down two mugs of tea and lowered herself into the chair at the head of the table, where she sat every afternoon with the radio on, waiting for the four o'clock news even though she complained about every item in it. "Who's winning?" Gran asked.

"I don't know yet. That's the assignment. Both sides."

"Ridiculous," Gran said, but she said it fondly, and she pulled the petitioner's brief toward her and put on her reading glasses, which she wore on a chain like a medal.

Victoria had chosen this house for the quiet, but the quiet kept filling up. Her phone buzzed: Zoe, who had relatives in Manchester, had sent a voice note from the library. "Okay, random but listen. I've been telling my cousins about your case, freedom of speech, all of it, and they said, you realize in 2022 the UK had three prime ministers without a general election. Boris Johnson, then Liz Truss, then Rishi Sunak, all in one year, and nobody voted except the governing party changing its own leader. I didn't believe them. I looked it up. It's real. Three, in one year." Victoria played it twice. She thought about the school board in her case, appointed and then acting, and how much of what governed anybody arrived without a ballot. The fact sat strangely in her, useful and not useful at once, a coin from a country she wasn't visiting.

"Something funny?" Gran asked.

"Zoe's cousins. Three prime ministers in one year and nobody got to vote on it."

"Mad year," Gran said, and sipped her tea, and Victoria understood that to Gran this was not trivia but weather, something lived through.

She went back to the briefs. Arguing for the school, she had learned to build the genus first: all school-speech cases, then the subset of cases involving minors in compulsory settings, then the narrower subset where the symbol functioned as speech directed at other children who could not leave. Classify, then rule. It was elegant. Arguing for the student, she had learned to attack the classification itself: the armband was silent, the disruption was fear of disruption, and a school that could punish fear could invent it whenever it wanted. Two grammars for the same sentence.

What she could not do was pretend the school had acted in bad faith. The principal believed the armband would exculpate nobody and inflame plenty; his record showed he had suspended students for far worse with far less ceremony. So on Friday she would stand up and argue for a man she partly believed in, against a girl she entirely believed in, and the only honest way through, she decided at the table while Gran murmured corrections to the radio, was to stop trying to win and start trying to be right about what each side saw.

Thursday night she argued the student's side and won on points. Friday morning, in the borrowed courtroom of the county annex, she stood at the respondent's podium and said, "The school asks this court to believe that a fourteen-year-old's silence is not harmless," and she made herself believe it, for nine minutes, and the judges leaned in. She lost that round, narrowly, on rebuttal, and her coach wrote one word on the scoresheet and turned it so Victoria could read it: finally.

That evening she drove back to Gran's, tea and toast and the four o'clock news, Gran triumphant over her crossword, one clue left. "Nine letters," Gran read. "'Worth considering.'"

"Debatable," Victoria said.

Gran filled it in without asking her.

Cameron sat on the hood of his mother's Corolla with his gown balled behind him like a dropped parachute, watching the lot fill. The ceremony started in forty minutes. Forty minutes, then his name, then a handshake he had been told to practice with a firm grip and a dry hand. He had the grip down. The dry hand was not cooperating.

Dewain came around the corner of the gymnasium at a half-jog, wearing his work polo from the car wash even though it was his day off, holding his phone out in front of him like a compass that had stopped pointing north. "Cam. Cam. You got a minute? Like a real minute."

"I got thirty-eight of them, roughly."

"Then stop looking at the gym." Dewain leaned against the fender, close enough that Cameron could smell the soap they used on the cars, some industrial lemon that never quite washed out of anyone. "I need you to read something. I applied to nineteen places since March. Nineteen. I got two interviews and one shift at the wash, and Marcus says I'm slow there." He pushed the phone into Cameron's hands. On the screen was a job application, half finished, the cursor blinking in an empty box where the highest level of education should go.

Cameron scrolled up. The application was for a warehouse position, full time, benefits after ninety days. "You've been filling these out at the shop?"

"On breaks. On my phone, on the bus, whatever." Dewain wiped his palms on the polo, which did nothing, since the polo was the thing making them damp. "Marcus found a site with the actual numbers. He was reading them off to everybody last week like it was the lottery. Three point nine percent unemployment for people twenty-five and up with a high school diploma. Five point six for people without one." He said it flat, the way you recite something you have checked twice. "So it's like one and a half times harder, roughly, before anybody even looks at what you can do."

"You're not twenty-five yet," Cameron said, because it was true and because he wanted to say something that was not the other thing, the thing about the empty box.

"No, but that's the road, right? That's where it goes." Dewain tapped the screen. "So the box. What do I put? I'm not a liar. I'm not going to write something I'm not."

The lot was filling with parents in ironed shirts, with toddlers in strollers being positioned for photos against the gym's brick wall. Somewhere inside, Cameron's row was forming, alphabetical, the C's near the front, near where his mother would be pointing her phone. He had wanted this morning to be clean. He had imagined it, in fact, the night before: him in line, everything decided, the next four years already paid for in deposits and orientation fees, a road with the guardrails installed. Dewain's road had no guardrails. Dewain's road was nineteen applications and a blinking cursor.

His grandfather had an adage about this, something about how you don't fix a man's roof while your own is leaking, but his grandfather had also skipped his own graduation to work a shift, and Cameron had never known what to do with that information except carry it.

"Okay," Cameron said. "Here's what I actually think. The diploma is worth something real, that's not a story people tell you, the numbers say it. But you're not standing at that fork. You're standing where you're standing." He typed the word Some into the box, deleted it, typed partial, deleted that too. "What if we do this. You put the truth in, but we make the rest of the thing so good they can't stop at the box. Every job you've actually done, every car you've detailed, the register you ran when Marcus was out sick. We write it like you mean it."

"You're going to miss your line-up."

"I've got thirty-one minutes." Cameron pulled out his own phone and opened a notes file, and for a while the two of them worked in the shade of the Corolla, Cameron typing while Dewain talked, suturing the pieces of the application together: the summer at his uncle's shop, the forklift video course he'd half finished, the two interviews, what they had asked, what he'd wished he'd said. A woman in heels hurried past and called something cheerful at them, and Dewain waved without looking up.

When they finished, Cameron read the whole application back to him out loud, and Dewain listened with his eyes closed like it was a letter from someone far away. "That sounds like a person," Dewain said. "That sounds like a person who does things."

"That's because it is one." Cameron pressed submit. The confirmation screen came up, gray and bureaucratic, and Dewain exhaled the way people exhale at the end of a held breath, long and involuntary.

A horn honked near the entrance. Cameron stood, pulled the gown from the hood, shook it out. "I have to go. But listen. That's one application done the way it should be done. There are going to be more, and they should all be like that."

"So you'll help me over the summer?"

Cameron looked at the gym doors, at the line of gowns disappearing inside them, and at Dewain, who was already gathering up both phones to sort which was whose. His roommate assignment came in August. His orientation was in July. The summer was a space he had been quietly planning to fill with things that had no room for the smell of industrial lemon, and he knew it, and Dewain probably knew it too.

"Send me the links," Cameron said. "Every one."

Dewain held up his phone and took a picture of him in the gown, the parking lot behind him full, the gym doors open. "Go on, then," he said. "Walk."

The presentation was due Thursday, and Maya still had not sent the slides. Jessica checked her phone under the lab table while Mr. Okafor wrote the phases of carbon on the board, and when she looked up, the word allotrope was circled twice. Graphite and diamond, same element, different arrangement. She copied it into her notes without thinking about it, then checked her phone again.

Maya sat two rows over, laughing at something Priya had whispered. That was the thing about Maya; she was easy to like and impossible to pin down. On Monday she had promised the slides by Tuesday night. On Tuesday she had promised them Wednesday morning. It was now Wednesday, fourth period, and Jessica had forty percent of a presentation and a stomach that felt like a clenched fist.

After class she cornered Maya by the water fountain. "The slides," she said.

"They're basically done," Maya said. "I just have to polish them."

"You said that yesterday."

"God. Relax." Maya filled her bottle and walked off, and Jessica stood there holding the sentence she had not said, the one that went you ruined the whole thing, which was not even true, and which she knew would make Maya defensive for the rest of the week.

That night Jessica did what she always did when she could not solve something: she searched it. Feedback without fighting. How to tell someone they let you down. She found a page about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon who had promoted something called I-messages back in the 1960s, a way to raise a problem without blaming. Instead of you ruined it, you said what happened to you. I felt stuck when the slides came in late. She read it twice, then opened her notebook and practiced, writing versions the way she would practice a French verb. I felt. When. Not you always, not you never. She felt ridiculous doing it, and she also noticed that the sentences she wrote were harder to argue with, because they were only about her.

The next morning she found Maya at her locker before first bell. "Can I say something?" Jessica asked. "I felt stuck when the slides came in late, because I couldn't practice my part, and the presentation is worth a quarter of our grade."

Maya shut her locker. For a second Jessica thought she was going to laugh, and the second stretched long enough that Jessica's ears went hot.

"I kept redoing the graphite part," Maya said finally. "It looked ugly. I didn't want to hand you something ugly." She pulled out her phone, opened the file, and turned the screen around. The slides were done, all twelve of them, and the graphite diagram was redrawn in colors Jessica hadn't known Maya could use. "I was going to send them tonight. After fixing one more thing."

"You could have sent the ugly version."

"I know." Maya zipped her bag. "I guess I thought you'd just think I was flaky."

Jessica recognized the logic, because she had a version of it herself. She tended to valorize effort that nobody could see, hoarding work until it was perfect and then presenting it as if it had cost nothing. Maya did the same thing with slides. Two allotropes of the same fear, she thought, and almost said it out loud, and decided Maya would just look at her blankly, so she kept it.

They presented on Thursday. Mr. Okafor, famously irascible about students who read off the screen, leaned back with his arms crossed and stayed that way through the first four slides, which Maya had built around images instead of paragraphs. When Jessica explained why the same carbon made both pencil lead and diamonds, he uncrossed his arms. Afterward he wrote something on his clipboard and did not tell either of them what.

In the hallway Maya said, "So that thing you did. At my locker. Did you rehearse that?"

"Maybe," Jessica said.

Weirdo," Maya said, and grinned, and pushed through the doors to the bus loop.

Cohen signed the community kitchen's clipboard at four minutes past five, which meant his mother had already been gone an hour, and his sister Delia was already tying an apron behind her back like she owned the place. The kitchen ran on a folding table of donated groceries and a schedule taped to the fridge: families could cook supper here on Thursdays, take it home in foil, leave the pans clean. Tonight the table had a whole raw chicken, a bag of potatoes going soft at the edges, and a bulb of garlic so dried out it had turned friable, its papery skin crumbling between his fingers when he pressed it.

"Mom texted," Delia said, holding out her phone. He took it with wet hands and read the message while the faucet ran.

Working the double, won't be home till eleven. You two eat without me, save the dark meat, she likes it cold. Tell Cohen I saw his grandmother today. She says he cooks like her.

"Like her how," Cohen said, but Delia had already taken the phone back. He turned the chicken over on its plastic tray. His grandmother rinsed everything, every bird, every chop, a rushing of water and a flick of her wrist that scattered droplets across the counter, and he had stood at her elbow at eight years old memorizing it the way other kids memorized a swing. It felt like a credential. He carried the chicken to the sink and turned the tap.

"Stop." Delia's hand came down on his wrist. "You can't wash raw chicken."

"I've washed it my whole life."

"Then your whole life you've been wrong." She pulled the phone out again, thumbed through it, and turned the screen toward him: a page from the CDC. "It says they advise against washing raw chicken. The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the nearby surfaces."

He looked at the sentence, then at the chicken, then at the sink where his grandmother's whole method lived. "It's one chicken."

"It's one kitchen that everybody uses." She nodded at the folding table, at the family at the next burner, at the volunteer wiping down the counter his splash would have hit. "You want to be the guy who gave this whole kitchen food poisoning for tradition?"

He shut the tap off. Not because she'd convinced him, exactly. Because she'd said everybody, and he hadn't thought of the room as a room, only as a stage for his inheritance. He carried the chicken back to the cutting board and patted it dry with paper towels instead, which the page also mentioned, and which felt, in its small way, like a betrayal he was committing carefully.

He salted it while the oven climbed to temperature. His grandmother would have argued with Delia; she'd have rinsed the bird right in front of the phone screen if she had to, and she'd have been magnificent, a virtuoso of stubbornness, and some part of Cohen wanted to be like that, wanted to hold a practice against all evidence out of loyalty. Another part of him understood that loyalty was not the same as cleanliness, that a kitchen was not a shrine, that you could love somebody's hands and still refuse what they'd done with them. Both parts stood at the cutting board together, and neither one would leave.

The potatoes he cubed with the skins on, since the peels were where the soft spots weren't. He rubbed the chicken with the crumbled garlic and the dried thyme from the spice rack somebody had labeled in marker, and he slid the pan in and set the timer for an hour and twenty minutes, and then there was nothing to do but wait, which was the part his grandmother had been best at. She could sublimate her whole restlessness into stirring, could turn worry into a sauce, and standing there with an hour to fill he finally tried it: he stirred the butter and flour for gravy longer than it needed, watching it darken by degrees, and it did quiet something in him, though he wouldn't have admitted that out loud.

While the chicken roasted, Delia wrote their mother back. She read the reply aloud from across the kitchen, shouting over the timer's tick. "She says, 'Your grandmother washed it anyway.' Then she says, 'Don't tell her I said so.'"

"That's it?"

"That's the whole message."

So their mother had known. Had stood at that same sink for years, and eaten the chicken, and said nothing, and was saying nothing still, except sideways, in two sentences Delia had to read off a screen. Cohen spooned the drippings into the roux and whisked until the gravy thickened and went glossy, and he thought about how you could hold two truths in one family like that, the rinsing and the not-rinsing, the grandmother magnificent and the grandmother wrong, and never say the second one out loud where she could hear it.

He carved the bird on the foil, the dark meat set aside in its own packet, the breast sliced thin the way his mother liked it reheated. The skin had gone crisp and uneven, better in one quadrant than the others, the garlic caught in the creases. Delia held the container while he poured the gravy over everything, and at the door, waiting for her to tie the lid with string, he checked his phone one more time.

His mother had sent one more line. "Your grandmother wants to know if you washed it."

Cohen typed and deleted three answers, then put the phone in his pocket and picked up the pan. "Tell her tomorrow," he said, and carried the supper out to the car.

Claire had promised Marcus forty minutes of calculus for fifteen dollars, and she had promised her mother the money by Friday, and both promises were sitting on the kitchen table at nine at night beside a bag of corn chips neither of them touched. Marcus was in her grade but in the slower section, and his worksheet had one problem left, the one with a fraction whose numerator was just the number one.

"So you use the power rule," Marcus said. He was already writing. "One over x is x to the minus one, so you add one to the exponent and divide by the new exponent."

Claire watched him do it. Add one and you get zero. Divide by zero. He sat back and looked at the undefined expression like it had insulted him.

"That's not it," she said.

"You said the power rule works for everything."

"I said it works for what we've done." She pulled the worksheet toward her. Her own class was two weeks ahead, and she remembered the day her teacher had drawn a curve on the board and said there was a hole in the method, a single case where the rule collapsed, and then had moved on to homework collection before Claire finished copying it down. She had told herself she would look it up. She hadn't. Fifteen dollars and Marcus's quiz tomorrow were what it took to finally make her care.

"Try it on your calculator," she said. "Graph one over x and tell me what you see."

While he tapped at it, she texted Priya, whose notes were always complete, whose whole system of colored tabs seemed to underpin her GPA the way rebar underpins concrete. Priya answered in fragments, the way she answered everything. The power rule fails there. Special case. It's the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x.

"Okay," Claire said, and turned the phone face down before Marcus could see she'd needed it. "The power rule has a gap. One function falls through it, and it's this one. The antiderivative of one over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x."

"Logarithms." Marcus said the word like a diagnosis. "Why would a log just appear? That's random."

"It's not random, it's the one case that fills the gap." She wrote ln, then the absolute value bars, then x, and the bars bothered him more than the log did, so she said, "The absolute value just handles negative numbers, don't worry about it tonight." He copied it three times, the way he copied everything, as if handwriting could substitute for understanding, and she let him, because for tomorrow it probably would.

He did the last two problems alone and got them right. His mother's car pulled into the driveway and he shoved fifteen dollars at her, crumpled, still warm from his pocket. "You should be a tutor for real," he said at the door. "My cousin pays thirty."

After he left she sat with the worksheet. Marcus's cousin, thirty dollars an hour, and behind that, the tuition letter her father had left open on the counter for a week like a test he was waiting for someone else to pass. He wanted her to study something with a clear lane, had said "epidemiology" twice at dinner with the confidence of a man who had read one article, and she had said nothing, because what she wanted didn't have a name that satisfied him yet.

She picked up her pen and did the problem herself, slowly, from the graph up. One over x, the curve swooping along its asymptotes, and underneath it an area you could actually compute now, area that had been unmeasurable to her an hour ago and was only a logarithm away. She checked it against Priya's note, then closed the phone and did it again from memory. There was a question still sitting underneath the mathematics, the same one under the tuition letter, which was whether knowing the special case meant you understood the rule, or only that you'd memorized the patch. She didn't have that yet. She wrote the fact on an index card anyway, both sides, and left it propped against the sugar bowl where she would see it at breakfast.

The elevator in the Blakely Arms smelled like wet cardboard and broke somewhere between the third and fourth floor every other day, so Audrey took the stairs, counting them out of habit, the way she used to count the steps to Marisol's porch. The movers had left her boxes in the living room in a tower that leaned slightly, and her mother was already at the new job, so it was Audrey alone who carried her desk lamp up six flights and set it on the windowsill facing the airshaft. From that window she could see a strip of the school three blocks off, the flagpole, the flat roof of the gymnasium. At the old house the window had faced Marisol's window, and they had signaled each other with flashlight beams after their mothers declared lights-out, one flash for hello, two for come outside.

School started on a Tuesday. In homeroom the teacher, a narrow man named Mr. Kestler whom the other students called a pedagogue in a tone that was not entirely affectionate, assigned Audrey a seat beside a girl named Priya Raghunathan. Priya lent her a pen without being asked and told her which stairwell avoided the crowd, and Audrey decided by Wednesday that Priya was the kind of person she would have been friends with already in the old town, which was a thought she kept to herself because it felt like a betrayal of somebody, though she could not have said of whom.

At night the apartment made noises the old house had not made. Pipes ticked, and a neighbor's television rose through the floor in muffled syllables. Audrey lay awake and found herself conducting an inventory she was ashamed of: the burr of her father's voice through the dining room wall, the lemon smell of Mrs. Ferreira's cleaning fluid on the shared stairwell, the particular slant of afternoon light across the biology lab where she and Marisol had dissected a fetal pig and laughed until Ms. Danner separated their stations. She was sixteen and in an apartment forty minutes from everything, and she missed a cleaning fluid. She resolved not to say this to anyone.

In the second week, in the cafeteria, Priya pushed her tray across from Audrey's without asking and sat down. Audrey had been looking at her phone, at a photograph Marisol had sent of the homecoming banner going up in the gymnasium, and she shut the screen off quickly, but Priya had seen it. "That's your old school," Priya said. It was not a question.

"My friend Marisol. They're decorating for homecoming." Audrey folded her napkin into smaller and smaller squares. "It's stupid. I've been here two weeks and I keep wanting to be back there, and it's only forty minutes. People commute farther than that for fun."

"Nobody talks about it here," Priya said, "but I looked it up when we moved, my sister's first year at college. The research on homesickness says nearly everyone who's away from home misses something about it. Almost everybody. Not just the weird kids. And it said around twenty percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of some severity scale." She stabbed a piece of broccoli. "So a fifth of them have it bad, and the rest still have it some. I found that out the week we moved here, and it made me feel less like a failure."

Audrey turned this over. She had been thinking of homesickness as a private defect, something to be subsumed under the general project of Starting Over, the way her mother had put it, new town, new chapter, as though the missing could be filed into a folder and the folder closed. If nearly everyone missed something, then the missing was not a failure of adaptation. It was closer to a tax everyone paid. But the severity scale bothered her, because twenty percent meant four out of five rated theirs below the midpoint, and Audrey had no idea where she fell on such a scale, and she suspected she fell higher than she wanted to admit.

That night she called Marisol. The connection was thin, and Marisol was halfway through a story about Danny Okafor and the banner committee, and Audrey listened and laughed in the right places, and when the story ended there was a pause in which the old signal system would have been useful, one flash for hello, two for come outside. "I miss it," Audrey said finally. "I miss you." Marisol said, "Obviously, you dork, it's been two weeks," and told her about the float, and the conversation moved on, and Audrey lay awake afterward and understood something she could not yet put in words: that missing was not the same as wanting to return, and that both were real, and that the two did not cancel out. She could be glad the apartment had a doorknob lock her mother let her use, and glad Priya existed, and still lie awake inventorying lemon smells. She did not know whether that was resilience or just confusion. She was honest with herself about not knowing.

The next Saturday the building had a tag sale in the courtyard, folding tables carried down by residents of all six floors. Audrey's mother contributed a lamp, a penurious contribution to the communal effort that the woman from 4C noted aloud with a short laugh, though the lamp sold within the hour for four dollars. Priya appeared with her younger brother and forty minutes of the afternoon to spend, and they walked the tables, and Audrey bought a chipped ceramic bowl with a blue rim for fifty cents because it was the exact blue of the old kitchen.

They took the bowl up the six flights, stopping on the third-floor landing where the afternoon light came through the stairwell window at a slant, and stood there a moment, both of them looking at it. "My sister says it gets quieter in your head after a month or two," Priya said. "Not gone. Just quieter."

"That's fine," Audrey said. "I don't need it gone."

She set the bowl on the windowsill beside the lamp, where it would catch whatever light the airshaft allowed, and went back down for the last box.

Charles kept his first pay stub folded in his back pocket through the whole meal, and he waited for the pause that came when his uncle Ray set down his fork and leaned back from the roast.

"Eleven years I've been at that plant," Ray said. "Eleven years, and every week, dues."

Dean, who had married into the family in the spring and had driven up from South Carolina with a casserole dish his mother had lent him, pushed his own plate forward an inch. "I never paid dues in my life," he said. "Same kind of work. Freight, warehouse, the whole bit."

"Then somebody was carrying you," Ray said.

"Nobody was carrying anybody."

Charles's mother refilled the water glasses, which was what she did when the table got like this. Charles took the pay stub out and unfolded it against the cloth. There was a line near the bottom, four dollars and eighty cents, marked UNION DUES, that he had not known would be there when he signed the paperwork on Monday.

"I started at the distribution center," he said. "On Route Nine. They took this out of my first check and I didn't ask anybody first."

Ray turned toward him the way he turned toward anything with a union label on it. "Good. That's how it's supposed to work. The contract covers everybody, so everybody pays."

Dean shook his head slowly, still looking at his plate. "Not where I'm from. There's these laws. Right-to-work laws. A contract can't make you pay union fees if you don't want to. It's banned."

"Because your state chose to ban it," Ray said. "Taft-Hartley let them. Nineteen forty-seven, passed over Truman's veto, the whole act. Before that, nobody could opt out like that."

Charles wrote nothing down, but he said the year back to himself, and Truman's name, and the word veto, because those were the parts he thought he would lose. He had taken a government class his senior year in which the teacher had drawn a timeline on the board and then erased it before the bell, and he had never quite believed that anything on an erased timeline had consequences. Now there was a line on his pay stub with a dollar amount on it.

"Either way," Dean said, "in my state, I kept my money. And the wage was the wage."

"The wage was the wage because somebody up here fought for it," Ray said. "You think eleven-fifty an hour at that center of yours fell out of the sky, Charles? Your hours, your breaks, the two guys who have to lift anything over fifty pounds? That got bargained. That's what the contract is. It isn't gratitude I'm asking for, it's arithmetic."

"Arithmetic," Dean said. "Four eighty a week, fifty weeks, that's two hundred and forty dollars. A kid saving for college. Maybe he'd like the choice."

Charles's father, who had said nothing except to ask for the potatoes, cut another piece of roast and said, "Charles is eighteen. He can hold his own water." Which was his way of saying that the argument had stopped being about the two of them.

Charles looked at the stub again. He thought about Danny at the center, the guy who had shown him the scanner on his first day, who had trained in from the same orientation class and who had asked the supervisor, out loud, in the hallway, whether he had to sign the dues card or not. The supervisor had said it depended, and had walked faster. Charles had signed his card in the break room with half the orientation class watching, and a woman named Odette had said, "Good," and that had been the whole ceremony. He had felt, at the time, that he was joining something with the weight of antiquity to it, men in a hall somewhere deciding things decades before he was born, and it had not occurred to him until tonight that the thing he joined was different depending on which side of a state line you stood on.

"There's a guy I work with," he said. "Danny. He asked the same thing I'm asking and nobody answered him. He moved from Tennessee."

"Right-to-work state," Dean said.

"So he doesn't pay," Charles said. "And I do. Same building, same contract, same eleven-fifty."

"Now you've got it," Ray said.

"That's not right or wrong," Charles said. "That's just the shape of it." He heard his own voice go flat on the last part, and he let it. "I'm going to pay. I decided on the drive over here, before you two started. I read the contract in the rack by the time clock, the whole thing, and the overtime rules and the lift rules are in there, and I clocked out after six hours today because the rule said I had to, not because the supervisor wanted me to. But I'm not going to tell Danny what to do about his four eighty. He's got a mother in Chattanooga with hospital bills. That's his arithmetic."

Dean looked at him for a second longer than usual. Ray opened his mouth and then closed it, which for Ray was roughly a standing ovation.

"Judicious," Dean said finally. "For a kid with one paycheck."

"He's got three months of paychecks," Ray said. "Then he goes to college and becomes management." He picked up his fork again and pointed it at Charles, not unkindly. "First thing you do when you get that diploma, you come find me."

"And bring the pay stubs," Charles's mother said, standing to clear the plates. Charles folded the stub along its old creases and put it back in his pocket, and reached for the water pitcher before his father could ask.

Sadie had carried the sealed tubes in a shoebox lined with a towel for eleven blocks, and now they sat on the folding table between her trifold poster and a colorimeter she had borrowed from the chemistry storeroom, a squat obsolescent thing with a dial instead of a screen. The tubes held nitrogen dioxide, brown, in equilibrium with its colorless dimer, and her whole project was the sentence she had lettered across the top of the poster: a system at equilibrium, when disturbed, shifts to oppose the change. She had written it in September, when it was just something to put on a poster. She had not yet met Mr. Okonkwo's question.

The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and someone else's vinegar-and-baking-soda volcano. Her friend Priya had been placed two tables down, between a boy with a homemade wind turbine and a girl who had sensitized a webcam to track pollen drift for her project about allergies. Sadie envied the webcam. Her tubes just sat there, brown, doing nothing observable, the forward and reverse reactions canceling each other out at a rate no eye could catch.

The first judge was kind and hurried. She dipped one tube into the ice bath Sadie had brought in a cooler, watched the brown fade toward pale gold as the equilibrium absorbed the cold by shifting toward the dimer, nodded, signed her sheet, and moved on. The second judge was Mr. Okonkwo, who taught AP Chem at the school across town and had a habit of tilting his head like a bird before he spoke.

"Show me the hot water," he said. Sadie lowered the second tube into the beaker on the hotplate. The brown deepened within seconds, dark as strong tea, and she began her rehearsed line about how the system shifted to use up the added heat. He tilted his head. "Heat speeds up reactions," he said. "Both directions. Why doesn't it just run faster in both directions and stay where it is?"

Sadie opened her mouth and found nothing in it. She looked at the tube, darkening still, and said, honestly, "I don't know. That's a good question." He smiled at that, which she suspected was the point of the question, and told her he would come back before the end of the hour, and then he was gone toward the wind turbine.

She sat down on the folding chair and wrote it out in her notebook the way she did when a problem refused to be stared down. Heat speeds up both reactions, she wrote. Forward and reverse. And yet the color changes, so something must be unequal. She drew two arrows, one above the other, and looked at them for a long time. If both got faster and the mixture still changed, then one of them must be getting faster by more. Which one? The mixture had gone darker when she added heat. Darker meant more of the brown gas. More of the brown gas meant the shift was toward the reaction that made it, which meant that was the direction the heat favored, which meant, she wrote slowly, that making the brown gas must take in heat, must be the direction that consumes it. Raising the temperature sped up both reactions, but it sped up the endothermic direction more, and that was the whole reason the equilibrium moved. She underlined it, then felt the familiar doubt arrive on schedule: she had reasoned her way to something that felt true, and she had no way in this gymnasium to check it.

She took out her phone and, because Priya's older sister was a chemistry major at the state university and had answered Sadie's questions before, she typed a message. "Question. If you heat a reaction at equilibrium, both directions speed up, right? So why does it shift at all instead of just running faster both ways?" She sent it, then rearranged the tubes in the shoebox so the pale one and the dark one sat side by side, before and after, the whole argument in glass.

The reply came while a middle schooler was photographing her poster. "You're close to something big. Both speed up, but not equally. The endothermic direction speeds up more, so the equilibrium shifts that way. Check Le Chatelier again. Gotta run, lab." Sadie read it twice. It matched what she had written, sentence for sentence, direction for direction, and the match did not feel like luck. It felt like the way the pale tube and the ice bath matched: something real, held steady from two sides.

Mr. Okonkwo came back at quarter to noon, as promised. "Any thoughts on my question?" he asked, and she stood up so fast the table rattled.

"Heat speeds up both reactions, but not by the same amount," she said. "It speeds up the endothermic direction more. So the equilibrium shifts that way. That's why the tube goes darker when I heat it, because forming the brown gas is the endothermic direction, so it's the one that wins." She heard her own voice, too fast, and made herself slow down. "I got it wrong in my head this morning. I had it as the system just resisting me. It's more like a race where both runners speed up, but one speeds up more."

Mr. Okonkwo tilted his head the other way. Priya had drifted over from her table and was listening with her arms crossed. "Last year," Priya said, "you called my idea about redesigning the poster board reactionary."

"I said the format was obsolescent," Sadie said. "I said you were being reactionary about keeping it. Those are different complaints." Priya laughed, and Mr. Okonkwo wrote something on his clipboard that Sadie could not read, and the dark tube sat in its beaker of cooling water, its brown already beginning, imperceptibly, to fade.

The cursor blinked in the signature field, which was not really a field at all but a button that said "I Agree," and Audrey sat with her finger over the trackpad, not clicking it. The job was at Hollis Books, seasonal, twelve hours a week, and the agreement had scrolled past her in a gray column of text that she had, for the first time in her life, actually read. There were sections on liability and on non-solicitation of customers, which she gathered meant she could not open a competing bookstore out of her bedroom, and a paragraph about binding arbitration that she read three times and understood less each time.

Her mother came through the kitchen doorway with a towel over her shoulder. "You're not signing anything yet."

"It's a job, Mom. It's a good thing."

"On a screen? You click a button and that's a signature? That doesn't count. They need you to sign something. With a pen." Her mother said "pen" the way other people said "under oath."

Audrey rotated her chair. "I think it counts."

"You think."

"I'll check," Audrey said, which was, in her household, the polite form of "you're wrong," and she turned back to the screen and typed into the search bar: does clicking agree count as a signature. Her mother dried a plate with the slow deliberateness of someone waiting to be proven right.

The results came up in the usual jumble, law firm pages with stock photos of confident people shaking hands, and then a government page, plain and beige, about something called the ESIGN Act. Audrey read it twice. The US ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, said a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form. She sat back. Her mother had been assuming the opposite, that paper was the real thing and the screen was a toy, and the law had settled the question the other way before Audrey was old enough to have a question. She felt the incipient satisfaction of a person about to win an argument, and also, beneath it, something less comfortable, because if the click was real, then the gray column of text she had scrolled through was real too.

"Mom," she called. "The ESIGN Act. It says a signature can't be denied legal effect just because it's electronic. It's from 2000."

Her mother appeared in the doorway again, towel still on her shoulder. "So it counts."

"It counts."

"Huh." Her mother absorbed this with visible effort, the way she absorbed the fact that the car could parallel park itself. "So when you clicked accept on all those apps."

"I was twelve. Different problem."

Her mother went back to the dishes, and Audrey turned to the screen and did not click the button. That was the part her mother hadn't asked about and Audrey hadn't volunteered: the reading of it. Before, clicking "I Agree" had been a reflex, like blinking. Now she understood it as a signature, and a signature, her father liked to say, was an epigram you wrote with your name, a small compressed promise. His actual line was "a signature is the shortest essay you'll ever write," which Audrey had found embarrassing at eleven and accurate at seventeen. The arbitration clause bothered her. It said disputes would be resolved individually, not in court, and though she could not have explained the whole machinery of it, she understood that she was agreeing to give something up, silently, in advance.

She opened her email and wrote to the store's manager, a woman named Petra whose replies came in a bright green font. Audrey asked, in the most unhurried language she could manage, whether the arbitration provision was standard or negotiable, and whether she could be sent the terms as a document she could look at properly instead of scrolling through in a window designed, she suspected, to catalyze exactly the kind of skimming she had nearly done. She reread the email four times, deleted the word "superfluous," and sent it.

Petra answered within the hour, green font and all: totally fine, most people don't ask, here's a PDF, and also, if it helps, you can come in Saturday and sign the paper version, we keep copies in the back. Audrey printed the PDF, all nine pages, and spread them on the kitchen table, and her mother paused over them on her way with the laundry. "See," her mother said, tapping the signature line at the end. "Paper. Now it's real."

"It was already real, Mom. 2000."

Her mother frowned at the pages, then at Audrey, and seemed about to retreat, but instead she pulled out the chair across from her and sat down, which she almost never did in the middle of a chore. "What's all this then, if it was already real."

Audrey slid the arbitration section across the table. "That's the part I'm not sure about."

Her mother read it, lips moving slightly, a woman who signed things for a living, payroll forms and permission slips and the mortgage, and who had never once been asked what any of it meant. She looked up. "You're going in Saturday anyway?"

"To sign the paper one, yeah. Petra offered."

Her mother tapped the page once more, gently now, like patting something alive. "Take a pen from the drawer," she said. "The good one."

The pump at the community garden broke on the first Saturday of June, and by noon the okra leaves had gone soft at the edges, folding like hands. Jonathan had been coming since April to earn the last service hours his school required, but he kept coming after the hours ran out, and he could not have said exactly why. Maybe because Ms. Reyes, who ran the garden, had once let him take home a tomato still warm from the fence line, and the taste of it had enthralled him in a way that no grocery-store tomato ever had, a sweetness with something almost bitter underneath.

Now he stood at the pump with Ravi, a community college student who interned there on Saturdays, while the two of them listened to the motor grind and deliver nothing. "The city raised the water rate in March," Ravi said. "Half the gardens on this side of town turned their plots to gravel. Ms. Reyes is paying out of her own pocket." He wiped his hands on his jeans. "There's a meeting Thursday about a new hookup. Somebody's offering free water."

"Free water doesn't exist," Jonathan said, because his father said that about nothing being free, and his father was usually right in ways that took years to see.

The meeting was held under the tin-roofed pavilion, and it was there that Jonathan learned where the free water came from. A man in a golf shirt explained that a bottling company two blocks north was offering runoff from its filtration system, enough to fill the tanks twice a week, in exchange for a small thing: the garden would sign a letter supporting the company's permit application to take more water from the aquifer. "It's a win-win," the man said. "You get water. They get goodwill."

Ms. Reyes said nothing, which Jonathan had learned was her way of saying a great deal. An older man named Fitz, who grew collards on the corner plot, said the aquifer was already dropping; his well at home had gone sour with sulfur the summer before. The man in the golf shirt smiled and said the aquifer was a big system, complicated, and that one permit would hardly matter.

That night Jonathan typed "aquifer depletion" into his laptop and followed a thread he had not expected. It led him to the Aral Sea. He read the sentence three times: the Soviet Union had diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea had lost a fishing industry that had once employed about 40,000 people. Rivers sent elsewhere to grow one thing; a sea dying downstream; forty thousand people whose work simply evaporated. He thought about the bottling plant two blocks north, and the gardens south of it, and Fitz's sulfur well, and he understood that he was not reading history. He was reading a template.

The next Saturday, a group of tenth graders arrived for a field lesson, part of some school partnership, and Ravi put Jonathan in charge of the irrigation demo while he fixed the pump line. Jonathan showed them the drip tape, the timers, the rain barrels. Then a girl named Priya asked why the garden couldn't just take the free water, and Jonathan told them about the Aral Sea. "Somebody upstream got water for cotton," he said, "and the people downstream lost the sea." He pointed at the tanks. "The plant is upstream. We're downstream, until somebody else is downstream of us."

"Is that like a rule?" Priya asked.

"It's more like a heuristic," Jonathan said. "A shortcut for thinking. When somebody offers you water, ask who ends up with less."

Priya nodded slowly, and then she said the thing that turned the whole afternoon sideways. "My dad works at the plant," she said. "If they don't get the permit, he gets laid off in the fall. He told my mom last week." She looked at the okra, at the drip tape, at her shoes. "Forty thousand people somewhere. My dad here."

Jonathan had been building an argument all week, and now it stood in front of him in a polo shirt with a father. He thought of a day years ago, before the garden existed, when he and his own father had walked past this same corner and his father had called it a wasteland, and Jonathan, ten years old, had found a milkweed growing through the chain-link and had carried the seed pod home in his fist. Even then something in him had believed that a place could change. Now he was less sure whether belief was a heuristic too, and whether heuristics were honest or just comforting.

He thought about it the way his economics teacher had taught him to hold two ideas at once: the garden needed water to live; the plant's workers needed the permit to live; both of those things could be true, and the permit could still take water from someone further down the line whom no one at the meeting would ever meet. He could oppose the letter and feel clean, or support it and feel useful, and neither position covered the whole cost.

Thursday evening, at the second meeting, Ms. Reyes called for a vote. The pavilion was full, Fitz on one side and the man in the golf shirt on the other, and Priya's father stood quietly by the ice chest, a man with calluses Jonathan recognized because his own father had them too. Ms. Reyes looked around the circle and said, "Jonathan, you've been here every week. What do you think?"

Jonathan stood up. Outside, the drip tape he had repaired that morning was releasing its slow bright beads onto the okra, each one catching the last of the light before it disappeared into the dirt.

Jade folded her arms against the cold of the boathouse and watched Priya shake hands with a fence post. Not the post itself, technically, but the handrail of the dock stairs, which Priya had wrapped in a spare sock to make it feel, she said, more like a person. On Monday Priya had an interview for a rowing scholarship at a college upstate, and the night before, her grandfather had drilled her on it over video call, timing her grip with a stopwatch and pronouncing each attempt dead, dying, or alive.

"My grandfather says a psychologist proved this," Priya said, pumping the sock. "A 2000 study, some guy named William Chaplin. People with firm handshakes made better first impressions."

Jade had been stretching her hamstrings on the bench beside the dock, half listening, the way you half listen to a teammate's nerves before a hard piece. But the name caught her. Chaplin. She had read the study two summers ago, in a library book about first impressions she'd picked up because she was, at fourteen, terrified of being perceived. She remembered the year because she'd thought it was old then, and it was older now, and yet here it was, dressed in a sock, on the boathouse dock.

"Firmer than that," she said, before she could decide whether to say anything at all.

Priya stopped and looked at her. "That's the problem with you, you know. You never say anything during practice and then you say one thing like you've been keeping score the whole time."

That stung because it was accurate. Jade had spent two seasons as the quietest oarswoman in the boat, the one whose judgments lived entirely inside her own skull. The coach had tried to codify honest feedback into the team culture at the start of the fall, posting a rule on the corkboard: praise in public, critique in private, both in specifics. Jade had read it and understood it the way you understand a grammar rule, which is to say not at all until you have to speak the sentence.

"Priya," she said. "Do it on me."

Priya turned, wiped her palm on her spandex, and took Jade's hand. The grip arrived and then hesitated, the way a novice's catch does at the water, arriving and checking in the same instant. Jade held it for three seconds and let go.

"Here's what happens," Jade said. "You grab, and then you go soft halfway through, like you're afraid of hurting me. You won't hurt me. You've seen my hands." She held them up, the blisters gone to callus, the callus gone to something like leather. "Also your wrist is limp, so it's not really your arm doing it. And you look at the handshake instead of at my face."

Priya's mouth did something complicated. "My grandfather said I have a moribund handshake. He uses words like that. He said it's the weakest part of my whole application."

"That's the thing," Jade said, and then she stopped, because the thing she wanted to say was large and she hadn't finished assembling it. She sat down on the dock stairs, and Priya sat down next to her, and out on the river the novice eight went by, their blades splashing in the ragged way that Jade, six months ago, would have watched in silence.

"My grandfather thinks the handshake is everything," Jade said slowly. "Yours, I mean. Like it stands for your whole self, like it's a synecdoche. One part meaning all of you. And my coach thinks no single thing means anything, it's all just the sum of the work." She looked at the sock on the handrail. "I think they're both sort of right and I can't make them into one clean idea. A firm handshake makes a better first impression, that's what the study found. But I don't actually know if first impressions are what an interview is, or if it's more like a season, where you can start badly and fix it by the end."

Priya was quiet for a moment. "So which do I practice?"

"Both, obviously. The handshake and everything after it." Jade stood and offered her hand, palm dry, wrist straight. "Again. Firm the whole way through. Look at me, not at it."

Priya took the hand and gripped, and this time the grip arrived and stayed, certain all the way to the release. Her eyes came up to Jade's and held. For a second, Jade thought, she would have believed this was a person who had never been afraid of anything.

"That one," Jade said. "Do exactly that on Monday."

Priya grinned and peeled the sock off the handrail, wadding it into her pocket like a trophy. From the boathouse the coach's voice rang out across the water, calling the varsity women to the stretchers, and Jade went to get her oar.

Layla arrived early enough to claim a folding chair in the second row of the community center, with her notebook open and a petition of two hundred and twelve signatures paper-clipped to the inside cover. The petition asked the town to install a pedestrian signal at the crossing on Route 9, where her brother Aiden had been clipped by a pickup in October and had walked with a cane since. The town council had put the crossing ordinance on tonight's agenda, and the agenda's dry phrasing, "First reading; discussion; possible vote," adumbrated everything that mattered to her without promising any of it.

The meeting opened with the clerk reading the ordinance aloud, word for word, the way a draftsman had written it: "Section 1. The Department of Public Works shall install a illuminated pedestrian signal." A councilwoman named Ortiz interrupted to say that it should be "an illuminated," and the clerk penciled the correction in, and Layla wrote in her notebook that even a comma of the law had to be argued over before it could exist. The town attorney had reviewed the draft for conflicts with state statutes, and the public safety committee had met twice and signed off, and all of this had happened invisibly over three months while Layla called the clerk's office every Friday to ask whether anything had moved.

Then came the debate. A saturnine councilman named Braddock, who owned the hardware store and spoke slowly as though every word cost him inventory, said the town's budget could not absorb forty thousand dollars for a signal that would serve, in his estimate, a dozen schoolchildren a day. "There is a crosswalk painted there already," he said. "Paint is not nothing." Layla's hand went up before she had fully decided to raise it.

She stood at the microphone with her knees shaking and read from her notes. She described Aiden's route to school, the forty-mile-per-hour traffic, the two hundred and twelve names. She said that paint was not nothing, she would grant that, but that paint assumed drivers would look, and the driver who hit Aiden had been looking at his phone. She said she had counted the children herself, on four separate mornings, and the number was twenty-three, not twelve. When she sat down, an old man behind her leaned forward and said, "Good girl," and she could not decide whether to be pleased or embarrassed, so she was both.

The council debated for another twenty minutes, Ortiz arguing that the county might cover half the cost, Braddock conceding that point reluctantly, and then the mayor called the roll. Five voted yes, one voted no, Braddock, and the ordinance passed on its first reading, which the clerk noted would be followed by a second reading and then, upon final passage, the mayor's signature. Layla wrote down the sequence, drafting, review, debate, votes, signature, and beside it she wrote: it worked. Then, because she was honest with herself even in notebooks, she added: here, anyway.

During the public comment period that followed, a man she recognized as Mr. Pham, who taught civics at the high school but who was here tonight as a private citizen wearing a lawn-mowing shirt, stood up to ask a question of the state senator who had driven out to attend. The senator's bill, which would fund safety upgrades at dangerous crossings statewide through a matching grant program, was the reason Layla's forty thousand dollars might shrink to twenty. Mr. Pham asked why, when the papers said fifty-five senators supported it, it had still failed. "Fifty-five is a majority," he said. "What am I missing?"

The senator rubbed his eyes. "Ending most debate in the Senate takes cloture," he said. "Since 1975, cloture has required three-fifths of the senators. With all hundred seats filled, that's sixty votes." He let that sit for a moment. "So fifty-five supporters can want a bill very much and still not get to vote on it."

Layla sat with that. In her notebook she wrote 60, then circled it, then drew a line from it back to the roll call she had just witnessed, where five votes out of seven had been enough because seven was the whole universe of that decision. She had come tonight with a simple theory of change, the theory of her petition: gather enough voices and the right thing happens. The theory had worked two rows from where she sat. The same theory, scaled up, had died in a building she had never entered, not because the voices were too few to be a majority but because the rules asked for more than a majority, and she did not yet know whether that rule protected small towns like hers from being steamrolled or simply protected whoever was already standing still.

While the senator fielded another question, her phone buzzed. A text from Priya, who was at home studying for the AP Biology exam: "how was town hall?? also please explain speciation to me at lunch, i keep confusing it with evolution generally. isolated populations drift apart until they can't come back together even if you put them side by side." Layla read it twice. She typed, "meeting was good, tell you tomorrow," and then, before she could talk herself out of it, "is speciation ever reversible?" Priya's answer came as three thinking dots that vanished without becoming anything.

After the meeting broke up, people milled around the coffee urn, and Layla found herself beside the senator, who was folding his own agenda into quarters. She asked him whether the crossing bill was dead for good. "Bills don't die the way people think," he said. "They get folded into other bills, or they wait for a different Senate, or a different year." He looked at her notebook, still open in her hands. "You taking notes for a class?"

"For my brother," Layla said, and showed him the page with the circled 60.

He nodded slowly, the way Braddock had spoken, as if it cost him something. "Keep both numbers," he said. "Five out of seven, and sixty out of a hundred. They're both true at the same time, and someday you'll have to decide which one you're willing to live inside."

She walked home past the crossing on Route 9, where the painted stripes were faded to a ghost of themselves in her headlights-shadowed view, and stood for a moment at the edge of the road, waiting for a gap in the traffic.

Coralie had been given the auditorium for two weeks, a photocopied script, and four actors who were older than she was, which was the whole problem and also, she kept telling herself, the whole point. The one-act was called The Ferryman's Daughter, and the third act took place on the banks of a river, which was why everybody in the cast had started calling stage left the riparian side, and had somehow made the phrase sound like a joke that was also a fact.

The first rehearsal, she had planned everything. She had drawn the stage in her notebook in pencil, every entrance a clean diagonal, the sofa exactly where the argument was supposed to happen. Ten minutes in, the sofa had moved. Devin and Nasra carried it between scenes and set it down slightly differently each time, and by the third run-through the argument was happening three feet from where it was supposed to live, and the whole shape of the scene had gone soft, like a word repeated too often.

"You keep putting it back differently," she said, feeling the complaint sound smaller out loud than it had in her head at one in the morning.

"It's heavy," Devin said, not unkindly. "We're estimating."

The problem was that Coralie didn't want estimation. She had learned, over two years of running lights for other people's shows, that a stage only means something if it's deliberate; causality up there is manufactured, a chair placed so that a person has to pass it and remember.
