Mr. Voss had been a live sound engineer for twenty years before he started mentoring students through the arts program at Henry's school, and he had never once mentioned the hearing aids until today, when he took them out to clean them in the middle of their conversation about Henry's college audition tape.

"You can keep talking," Mr. Voss said, working a tiny brush along one of them. "I'll catch up."

Henry had come here with a real problem, and the problem was not the audition tape. It was that Dex had texted him last night, after their fourth concert in two months, and the text was still sitting on Henry's phone like a stone in his pocket. He hadn't answered it yet. Instead he watched Mr. Voss's hands move with the ease of a man who had done this ten thousand times, in bathrooms and vans and backstage corridors, and he thought about how a person ends up carrying a small case everywhere he goes for the rest of his life.

"Play me the second track again," Mr. Voss said, fitting the aids back behind his ears. "The one with the turgid strings. You told me it was supposed to feel heavy, but to me it just feels muddy." He turned the laptop toward Henry. Henry pressed play. The strings swelled, thick and slow, filling the small office, and Mr. Voss closed his eyes and conducted a little with two fingers, and Henry almost forgot the phone in his hand.

Almost. He unlocked the screen instead, and read the message again while the music ran. "Saw the audiologist today. She says long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss, and the damaged hair cells in your inner ear do not grow back. Mine's probably fine, mild, but she asked how loud my shows are. Man, we stand right at the front. Every time." Dex had ended it with, "Are you getting the ringing too? Beseech you, tell me you're not getting the ringing."

"What's that you're reading?" Mr. Voss asked, not accusing, just curious, the way he asked everything.

"A friend." Henry set the phone face down on the desk, then turned it over again. "We go to shows. A lot of shows. He went to get his ears checked because of the ringing, and he sent me this thing the doctor told him." He read it out loud, the decibels, the hair cells, the part about them never growing back, and watched Mr. Voss's face do something complicated and brief, like a window shade caught by a gust.

"Yeah," Mr. Voss said. He didn't launch into anything. He just tapped his ear, once, lightly, the way you'd touch a bruise to see if it still hurt. "That's how it goes."

"You never said."

"You never asked." He leaned back. "Besides, what would I have said? Don't do the thing that made you love music in the first place? That's a turgid speech if I ever heard one." He smiled at his own word, and Henry laughed, and then neither of them laughed, because the office was quiet and the audition tape had ended and the hearing aids were doing whatever hearing aids do in the silence.

Henry told him about the ringing. He told him about the show in March where they'd stood against the barrier for three hours and he'd heard a thin whine for two days afterward, how he'd noticed it in the shower, how he'd noticed it again last week in the library when the room was empty and it was still there, faint, like a wire somewhere under the floor. Mr. Voss listened with his whole body, which was his way, and then he opened a drawer and set a pair of foam earplugs on the desk, still in the wrapper, the kind you buy at a pharmacy for two dollars.

"Take them or don't," he said. "That part's yours."

Here was what Henry turned over on the bus home, window open, wrapper in his fist. Part of him wanted to believe the ringing was nothing, the way a person wants to believe a stain will wash out; Dex's audiologist had said his own damage was mild, probably, and Henry's was probably milder still, and there was a whole loud future out there, parties and basement shows and the front row, and earplugs felt like arriving at a funeral. But another part of him kept looking at the small pinkish case on the desk, and the two fingers conducting, and thinking about how Mr. Voss had never gotten to choose, back then, because nobody had told him, and now he carried the consequences in a case that clicked shut. Henry had been told. That was the difference. That was the whole difference, and it sat on his chest like a hand.

He didn't know everything, and he tried to be honest with himself about that. He didn't know whether his ears were already damaged, or how much, or whether the whine in the library was permanent or would fade the way the one after March had mostly faded. He didn't know if he would even keep the plugs in his jacket pocket or lose them in a week. But he knew what Dex's message said, and he knew what Mr. Voss's face had done, and he could hold both of those at once, the fun and the future, without pretending either one away. That was all discernment was, he decided, not wisdom exactly, just refusing to drop one of the things you were carrying.

At his stop he texted Dex back with one hand while the doors hissed open. "Getting it too. Library, quiet rooms, sometimes. Keep the plugs they gave you?" Then, after a minute, standing on the curb with the bus pulling away: "Next show, I'll be the guy in the back with orange foam in his ears. Meet me there." He put the wrapper in his pocket, where he could feel it, and walked home.

Mackenzie found her father in the kitchen, holding a red plastic cup he wasn't drinking from, and she knew before he said anything that he wanted to talk about the money.

The party had spilled from the living room onto the porch and the brown lawn beyond it, half the senior class milling around under string lights her mother had hung that afternoon. Someone had made a playlist that everyone complained about and nobody changed. Mackenzie had spent the first hour being hugged by people she would never see again, and each hug had felt like a small withdrawal from an account she hadn't realized was finite.

"So State sent the final package," her father said. He set the cup down on the counter beside the bowl of pretzels. "It's doable. With the loans, it's doable."

She had known this was coming. She had rehearsed for it in the shower that morning, which now struck her as ridiculous, rehearsing for a conversation with her own father. "And Amherst?"

"Amherst is Amherst." He rubbed the back of his neck. "They gave us more aid, actually. More than I expected. But there's still a gap, and the gap has your name on it for ten years."

"Nine years," she said. "The loans are nine-year terms. I looked it up."

Her father laughed, short and surprised, and for a second the kitchen was almost easy. Then he said, "Your grandmother would tell you to go. She'd say people like us don't turn down places like that." He paused. "People like her, I mean. She never got to finish."

That was the lever he always used, though he used it gently. Mackenzie's grandmother had left college in 1968 after two semesters, and the family had been narrating that departure ever since, turning one woman's decision into a parable that could be deployed for any purpose. Go because she couldn't. Or be careful because she taught us what debt does to a family. The story contextualized whatever you wanted it to.

"I need to think," Mackenzie said, and she took a cup of her own, filled it with punch she didn't want, and went out to the porch.

Dex was sitting on the railing with his gown still on, unzipped, the sleeves rolled to his elbows. He'd worn it all evening like a dare. "There she is," he said. "Salutatorian. Second-best in the county."

"Second in the school, not the county."

"I'm contextualizing." He slid over to make room. "So what did he say?"

She told him, mostly, leaving out the grandmother part because that part was hers. "He wants me to say it's fine either way. He says it's my choice. But he says it in the voice he uses when something costs too much at a restaurant."

"Ah, the plutocracy problem," Dex said. "Rich kids don't even fill out the forms. The rest of us get to decide which kind of hostage we'd like to be."

"That's very pithy."

"I've been workshopping it." He kicked his heels against the railing. Across the lawn, Priya Nair was attempting to teach Dev Okonkwo to salsa, and failing, and both of them were laughing so hard the lesson had become something else entirely. Mackenzie watched them and felt the grief arrive on schedule, the one everyone had warned her about, the strange mourning of an ending that hadn't technically happened yet. Tomorrow she would hand in her laptop and her parking pass, and the building would go on without her, and by August the halls would smell like a different cohort's mistakes.

"I keep thinking it's over," she said. "That's all I've thought about for weeks. That it's ending. Tonight everyone keeps saying congratulations like it's a finish line."

Dex looked at her for a moment, then drained his cup. "You know what the ceremony's actually called? Commencement. That's the word. It means beginning. They started using it for graduations because the graduates commence a new status. Like becoming a bachelor or a master. It's a beginning thing, not an ending thing. It's literally in the name."

"Where did you learn that?"

"Mr. Ferraro told our class in April and I've been saving it for exactly this moment." He spread his hands, presenting the fact like a magician producing a card. "You're welcome."

Mackenzie turned the word over. She had walked across a stage that morning in a cap that kept sliding, and she had been sad, and everyone had been sad, and apparently they had all been sad at a ceremony named for starting. There was something almost funny about it. There was also something in it she couldn't dismiss, though she tried, because Dex had a habit of finding one true thing and wielding it like it settled everything.

"That doesn't actually decide anything," she said. "About the money."

"I know. It's just a word."

"It's not just a word, though." She set her untouched punch on the railing. "If it's a beginning, then the debt is part of the beginning. It's not the price of something I'm finishing. It's the terms of something I'm starting." She heard how it sounded, like a decision, and she hadn't made one. "Or that's just a nice way to talk myself into nine years of payments. I can't tell yet."

Dex nudged her shoulder with his. "You'll figure it out. You're the salutatorian."

"Second-best," she said.

Inside, her father had come to the screen door with his empty cup, watching the lawn, and she thought about going in and telling him she'd decided, and she thought about going in and telling him she needed one more week, and she thought about how her grandmother, whoever she was becoming in the family's retelling, must once have stood in some kitchen weighing one life against another with no ceremony at all to name it.

Priya had given up on the salsa and was pulling people toward the grass for a group photo. "Mackenzie!" she shouted. "Dex! Get in, you can't miss this."

Mackenzie jumped down from the railing and took Dex's hand to pull him with her, her fingers still tacky from the punch, and stood in the back row where the tall people went, squinting into the flash.

Maelle spread the two articles across the library table like cards she'd been dealt, though she hadn't chosen either of them. The first was a dense Danish study following more than half a million children, its tables stretching across pages like frost on a window. The second was older, shorter, a 1998 paper in The Lancet. Her assignment sheet, folded twice in her pocket, said compare and evaluate. It did not say how to begin when two sources disagreed so completely that one of them had to be wrong.

She had claimed the table by the periodicals at four o'clock, when the afternoon light came through the tall windows and warmed the varnished wood. Now it was past six, and the light had gone the color of weak tea. Her pen had produced three sentences, all of which she had crossed out. A boy two tables over was sleeping with his cheek against a sociology textbook, and somewhere behind the reference desk a printer chunked and sighed, chunked and sighed.

The problem, she decided, was that she kept trying to decide which article won. She read the Danish paper's numbers again, then flipped to the older one, and this time she noticed something she had skimmed past before. The 1998 paper, the one claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, had been based on only twelve children. She sat back. Twelve. The other study had followed over half a million, and this one, twelve. She counted the word children with her finger on the page as though the number might change if she touched it.

"What are you grinning at?" said Priya, dropping into the opposite chair with a granola bar and no apology. Priya worked the circulation desk on Thursdays and had made it her policy to investigate anyone who looked either delighted or devastated near closing time.

"Twelve," Maelle said. "This whole paper, the one that scared everybody about the MMR vaccine and autism, it was twelve kids. That's smaller than my homeroom." She turned the page toward Priya, who squinted at the dense type and shrugged.

"That's it? That's your discovery?"

"It's not just small. It's that nobody told me the size until today. I read about this in middle school like it was a fact, like it was the same kind of thing as gravity." She tapped the Danish paper. "And then this one, half a million kids, saying the opposite. So my review isn't really about vaccines at all. It's about how you decide who to believe."

Priya unwrapped her granola bar and considered this with the seriousness of someone being paid ten dollars an hour to shelve returns. "So say that. Isn't that what a critical review is?"

Maelle didn't answer right away, because the honest answer was that she had been hoping a critical review was a thing with rules, a formula she could accede to the way she'd acceded to the five-paragraph essay all through high school, and what she was actually looking at was judgment. The vernacular of her English classes, thesis and evidence and clincher, suddenly felt like a dialect from a country she'd left. She tried to say some of this out loud and it came out clumsy, and Priya said, "So write it clumsy and fix it after."

By seven thirty the library had thinned to the sleeping boy, a man at a computer watching something with the sound off, and the two of them. Maelle had filled four pages in her looping handwriting. She had written that the Danish study's strength was its scale, that the Lancet paper's weakness was hers to name and she named it plainly, and then she had written a paragraph she was less sure of, about how a small study could still raise questions worth asking, even while it couldn't answer them. She wasn't certain that paragraph was right. She underlined it in pencil, which was her private mark for things that might be wrong.

"There's a thing I can't figure out," she said as Priya began stacking chairs. "Whether finding the flaws counts as being critical, or whether it's just being jaundiced. Like, when does careful stop and bitter start?"

Priya set a chair on a table, upside down, and thought about it for exactly as long as it took to pick up the next chair. "Maybe that's the part you write honestly," she said. "That you don't know."

Maelle looked down at her underlined paragraph, then at the two articles still lying open beside each other, the enormous study and the small one, both printed on the same ordinary paper under the same fluorescent hum. She picked up her pen, turned to a fresh page, and wrote the first sentence of her last paragraph: What remains uncertain to me is.

Dominic had never minded history until the essays started requiring him to have an opinion. On Tuesday Ms. Achterberg handed back his paragraph on the origins of the Cold War with a single note in the margin: "You have summarized two historians. Now weigh them." The two historians were Aldrich, who put the blame on Soviet expansion after 1945, and a revisionist named Korenblyum, who argued that Western capitalism needed an enemy and manufactured one. Dominic had assumed one of them was simply correct, the way a math answer is correct, and that Ms. Achterberg knew which and was withholding it out of some pedagogical cruelty. He wanted the key. Priya, who sat in front of him and underlined her books in three colors, seemed to have it.

On Thursday his class walked to the town square for the remembrance assembly, and while the head teacher droned at the war memorial, Dominic drifted along the low stone wall reading the plaques the twin-town association had bolted to it over the years. One small brass plate listed names of French mayors and deputies the association had honored, and at the bottom, weathered nearly smooth, stood the name Jean Jaurès. "That's a street," said Marcus, leaning over his shoulder. "There's a Rue Jaurès near my cousin's flat in Lyon. I thought it was, like, a cheese." Dominic traced the letters with his thumb and felt the small itch he got when a fact refused to fit its shelf. The plaque said nothing else about the man. It didn't even say what he'd done, only that the twin town had sent the plaque in 1962.

That night he looked Jaurès up, half for the essay and half because Marcus had made him promise to find out whether the cheese thing was real. Jaurès had been a socialist politician, and he had been assassinated in 1914, shot in a café months before the war began. But the part that stopped Dominic was further down the page: in the early 1900s, Jaurès had written a socialist history of the French Revolution, a multivolume work, and that history had shaped how people understood the Revolution for most of the twentieth century. The class-conflict interpretation, the textbook's phrase, the one that framed the Revolution as the bourgeoisie toppling a feudal order, had a single author with a political program behind it. Dominic sat with that for a while. A politician had written the past, and the past had stayed written that way for decades.

He started seeing the pattern everywhere, which was probably dangerous. Korenblyum, the revisionist, kept describing the Cold War as a struggle of economic classes wearing national costumes, the United States acting as the executive committee of capital, the Soviet Union as a besieged workers' state. Dominic couldn't prove Korenblyum had ever read Jaurès, and he wasn't going to claim it, but the lens had a lineage, and lineages were not neutral. Aldrich, though, was no cleaner. Aldrich called Stalin an autocrat in the first paragraph, ascribed every crisis from Berlin to Korea to one man's paranoia, and wrote as if institutions, evidence, and ordinary caution played no part, as if a whole country's foreign policy were the mood of a single patient. Dominic found a footnote in a library copy where Aldrich dismissed Soviet fears of invasion as "atavistic," which was a word Dominic had to look up and then distrusted immediately, because calling a fear primitive is a way of not answering it.

In Friday's seminar Ms. Achterberg put them in pairs, and of course Dominic drew Priya. "Korenblyum is obviously closer," she said, arranging her three pens. "The documents support him." "Which documents," Dominic said. "The ones he chose to read. The Soviet archives opened in the nineties and both of them kept their conclusions, which is a little strange, isn't it, if evidence is supposed to settle things." Priya looked at him with something that was not quite respect, more the recalibration you'd give a vending machine that suddenly produced the right snack. "So you're saying nobody can know anything." "I'm saying a historian is a person first," Dominic said, and heard how it sounded, like a fortune cookie, and said it anyway.

He wrote the essay that weekend, hating most of it and keeping one page. The page said that Aldrich explained the Cold War better when the question was who decided, and Korenblyum explained it better when the question was who benefited, and that a reader who wanted a single answer should probably ask which question she actually cared about, and why. He admitted that he couldn't weigh the two men against the evidence until he admitted the evidence had already been weighed once by whoever gathered it, and probably twice by whoever taught him to read. He handed it in feeling like he'd built half a bridge and charged people to cross it.

Ms. Achterberg returned the essays on Wednesday with grades but no comments until you asked. Dominic got the highest mark he'd received all year, and beneath it one line: "Finally an argument. Though you never say whose explanation you'd trust with your own country." He stared at that for the whole period, because he'd thought the honest part was the not knowing, and she seemed to be saying the honesty was a place to stand, not a place to live. After the bell he walked back to the square, ostensibly for the bus, actually for the plaque. He crouched, ran his thumb over Jaurès's name again, and noticed for the first time the smaller engraved line beneath it, which Marcus had been blocking with his elbow on Thursday. "Un hommage de la ville jumelle à tous les historiens engagés," it read. A tribute from the twin town, he translated slowly, to all committed historians. "Ha," he said out loud, alone on the war memorial steps. "You too, huh."

Florence had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before closing, and around her lay the evidence of a stalled campaign: three highlighters, a paperback of Jane Eyre swollen with torn paper strips, and a blank document titled, optimistically, "Essay Draft 1." The prompt on her phone read, "Identify an unreliable narrator in your chosen novel and analyse how point of view shapes the reader's trust." She had read the novel twice. She still did not trust herself to write about trust.

Her grandmother's copy sat beside the school's edition, and that was the problem, or at least the beginning of it. She had found it last Sunday in the house on Perry Street, in a box of books her mother wanted taken to the charity shop. The cover was cloth, gone soft at the corners, and the title page said Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, edited by Currer Bell, Esq. Florence had assumed the editor was the author until she opened her school copy and found no Currer Bell anywhere in it.

"It's not an editor," her grandmother had said from the armchair, not looking up from her crossword. "Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell. It didn't tell anyone the author was a woman."

"Why not?"

"That's a different question from what you asked me." Her grandmother had filled in a word, seven letters, and Florence had spent the drive home deciding whether the deflection was evasion or an invitation.

In the library now, Priya dropped into the opposite chair without asking, the way only Priya could. "You look like your essay murdered you."

"Sort of the reverse. I can't decide who's lying." Florence turned the old book toward her. "Rochester tells Jane his whole history, and he leaves out one fairly significant wife in the attic. Jane narrates the book, and she narrates him sympathetically, so we half forgive him before we even know. It's like the lying happens two layers down."

"An unreliable narrator through a reliable one," Priya said, chewing the cap of her own pen. "That's actually a decent thesis."

"It's a decent sentence. A thesis needs to go somewhere." Florence pulled the old copy back. "And then this. The whole book is Jane telling us her autobiography, except the real woman who wrote it signed it with a man's name and called it an autobiography anyway. I keep thinking that's part of the same problem, and then I keep thinking I'm reaching."

Priya leaned over the page. "Who's Currer Bell?"

"Charlotte Brontë. Nobody reading it in 1847 knew the author was a woman." Florence heard her grandmother's phrasing come out of her mouth almost intact, like a coat borrowed and worn the same way.

Priya sat back. "Okay, but is that unreliable narration? She didn't lie about anything in the story. She just didn't tell the truth about herself."

"That's exactly what Rochester does." Florence said it faster than she meant to, and then more slowly, testing it. "He doesn't lie to Jane, mostly. He just doesn't tell her the truth about himself, and the not-telling is shaped so she'll trust him. Brontë shapes the reader's trust the same direction. Every choice about what to withhold is a choice about who you're letting the reader be." She wrote two lines in the margin before she could lose them, then crossed one out.

The crossing-out felt familiar. Two years ago, in the debate club semifinal, she had done the same thing, cut an argument she privately believed because the judge would find it anachronistic, judging a Victorian novelist by modern expectations. She had won that round and had thought about it maybe once a month since. Whether that was principle or cowardice she had never fully settled, and the crossed-out line brought it back with the peculiar recidivism of old doubts, the way they return no matter how many times you've answered them. She uncrossed it. Then she crossed it out again and left both marks visible, which Priya noticed and mercifully did not mention.

"Here's my problem, though," Florence said. "If I say the pseudonym counts as narrative unreliability, I'm claiming Brontë deceived her readers, and I don't think that's fair to her. She was preempting something, not lying. And if I say it doesn't count, I'm pretending the name on the title page doesn't shape how the whole book gets read, and it obviously does. So I have to hold both, and I don't know if that's insight or just indecision with better vocabulary."

"That's the most honest thing anyone's said about an essay in this library," Priya said, "including the library."

Florence laughed, and under the laugh something assembled itself. She opened the blank document and typed a first sentence she almost liked: The most important liar in Jane Eyre may be the name on its cover. She would probably cut it tomorrow. She kept typing anyway.

At the circulation desk on her way out, the librarian, Mrs. Adeyemi, stopped her. "You left the cloth edition on the scanner bed," she said, holding out the old book. "Lovely. Where did you get it?" Florence explained the box, the charity shop run that hadn't happened yet. Mrs. Adeyemi turned to the title page and went still.

"Florence," she said. "Open the back cover." Inside, in faded brown ink, someone had written: To Harriet, who lent me the courage to send it out under my own name at last. Christmas, 1864. Below it, in the same hand, a different signature: C. Brontë was never here, but Harriet Bell was, and this was her shelf.

Florence read it twice. "Bell," she said. "Currer Bell. Harriet Bell."

"Your grandmother's family name," Mrs. Adeyemi said, "before the marriage. You'd have to ask her about the rest. I only shelved her donations for thirty years." She slid the book back across the desk. "Some narrators you have to interrogate in person, while you still can."

Florence looked at the inscription, then at the door, then at her phone, and dialed the Perry Street number as she pushed out into the cold.

The paper came back on a Thursday, folded once, with a red note across the top that read "This is not a bibliography." Ryan read it four times on the walk to the café, as though repetition might change the words, and by the time he ordered his medium drip he had stopped being offended and started being curious, which he suspected was a bad sign about his personality.

He spread the pages across the small table by the window, the one that wobbled unless you shimmed it with a napkin. Eight pages on the Hollywood blacklist, for Mr. Harmon's history seminar. He had written it the only way he knew how, the way Ms. Ellery had drilled into them all last year: quotes followed by parentheses with a name and a number, and then, on its own page at the end, the full sources under the heading "Works Cited." Harmon wanted something else. The note at the bottom of the last page said footnotes, and the footnotes wanted a style called Chicago, and Chicago appeared to want everything about each source, in an order Ryan had never seen, with punctuation placed like landmines.

"You look like a man prognosticating," said Dana, setting down her own coffee across from him without asking. She had a battered LSAT prep book under her arm, its spine cracked in the middle the way spines crack when a person studies only on the days she feels like it. She wanted to argue, though. That was the thing about Dana. She would rather debate the blacklist for an hour than do a logic game, and Ryan sometimes suspected the law school plan existed mostly to give her a stage.

"Harmon says I don't have a bibliography," Ryan said. "I have Works Cited. Apparently that's a different animal."

"Is it?"

He turned to his English paper from October, which he'd brought because it was the only model he trusted. There, in Ellery's world, every borrowed sentence ended with a small parenthetical, the author's last name and a page number tucked into the parentheses, and the whole apparatus ran silently through the text like wiring in a wall. At the back, one page, plainly titled "Works Cited," each source written out in full. He'd never thought about the system as a system. It had simply been the temperature of the room.

"What's the difference?" Dana asked, stealing his muffin. He let her, because her want was larger than his want for the muffin, and because she would argue better with fuel.

"In Ellery's class, the citation is inside the paper." He tapped one of the parentheses, (Navasky 118), then a second, (Ceplair and Englund 204). "Name and page, right there where you use it. Then the full information lives at the end, on its own page, under that heading." He held up the October paper so she could see the words "Works Cited" centered at the top of the last page. "In Harmon's class, the information goes at the bottom of the page, in a footnote, and the whole list at the end is called a bibliography. I kept writing Works Cited where he wants the other word."

"So you wrote two papers and only one of them counts."

"Half of one counts." Ryan pulled the Chicago guide toward him, the library's copy, heavy as a paving stone, and found the page on footnotes. The number in the text was small and raised, and the note below carried the author's full name, the title, the facts of publication, all of it arranged with a formality that struck him as almost doctrinaire. He said so, and Dana said the law was worse, and for a moment they were both quiet out of respect for institutions older than they were.

He started converting. The first footnote took him eleven minutes and one text to a girl from class, who replied only with a shrug emoji. The second took four. By the fourth he could feel the logic of it, the way the raised numbers let the page keep talking while the evidence waited politely at the bottom, and he caught himself revising a sentence as he went, tightening a claim about the studios' testimony before Congress. He had written that the witnesses lied. That wasn't quite it. Lying implied shame, or at least concealment, and there was something worse in the transcripts, a mendacity so casual the men seemed bored by it. He typed the new sentence, then stopped.

"That's an argument," Dana said, reading over his shoulder. She had abandoned the logic games entirely, which Ryan noted and filed away for later use. "Before, you were just reporting. Now you're saying something someone could fight you about."

"That's the assignment, apparently. Harmon wrote 'Where do you stand?' on my draft, and I stood nowhere. I stood in a shrub."

"The shrub is very you." She drank her coffee and looked out the window at the parking lot, where someone was trying to parallel park a truck clearly designed for other purposes. "For the record, I think the parenthetical way is better. Cleaner. You don't have to keep dropping your eyes to the bottom of the page."

"Ellery would like you."

"Everyone likes me. It's a curse." But she had already pulled the prep book back toward herself, as if remembering she had her own paper due, in a sense, and Ryan went back to his footnotes, marking each raised number in pencil first, then ink, then checking each one against the guide like a man checking a lottery ticket twice.

The argument took shape around the fourth page, when he realized his two strongest sources disagreed with each other about whether the studio heads believed their own testimony, and that his whole case depended on which one he trusted, and that he could not fully decide. He left both in. He wrote a sentence saying the evidence cut both ways, footnoted it, and felt the small vertigo of admitting uncertainty in a document that was supposed to be an argument.

At the table by the window, the sun moved off the paper and onto Dana's prep book, and she closed it, and the truck in the lot finally slid into the space on the fifth attempt.

"Works Cited or bibliography?" she asked, nodding at his last page.

"Bibliography," Ryan said, and typed the word at the top of it, slowly, as though it might still change its mind.

Mackenzie had until Friday, and it was already Tuesday evening, and the essay was supposed to be about how historians' views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, a topic she had chosen in a fit of ambition she no longer remembered fondly. She spread her books across the table by the library's tall windows, where the late light came down in dusty columns, and opened her notebook to a page that said only, in her handwriting from Sunday: figure out what historiography even is.

She had figured that much out by now. Historiography, as far as she could tell, meant arguing about the arguers. It meant reading Carlyle and finding a great man thundering across the pages, then reading a Marxist historian who saw no men at all, only classes shifting like tectonic plates. What she could not figure out was how to organize any of it, how to make the pile of quotations into a shape. Her teacher, Ms. Adeyemi, had written one comment on her proposal: "Good topic. Now take a position. You can hold two ideas and still choose." Mackenzie had underlined it twice and understood it not at all.

The boy at the next table kept glancing at her stack of books. He had a chemistry textbook open and a look of genuine despair. "You're doing the French Revolution thing," he said, not a question. "The historiography one. Half the class is doing it."

"And you're doing chemistry, apparently."

"Due Friday," he said. "Yours too?"

"Friday," she said, and the word landed between them like a shared sentence.

His name was Theo, and it turned out he worked at the library shelving returns, which was why he knew where everything was, including the things nobody asked for anymore. When she told him her problem, that she needed older sources, he led her back into the stacks, past the bright new displays, to a section that smelled faintly of dust and glue. "Nobody comes here," he said. "This whole area's kind of moribund." He pulled a slim volume off the shelf, a survey of modern European history printed decades ago, its jacket gone soft. "Old books say old things. Might help."

She took it to a carrel and read, at first only skimming for the Revolution chapter. But on the way there, a heading caught her: a few pages on the Cold War, written in a voice of settled certainty. The book laid the outbreak of the Cold War chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe, one side blamed, the other side absolved, the whole thing delivered as though it were simply what had happened. Mackenzie sat back. She had never thought of a textbook as having an opinion before. It was like discovering that a mirror could choose what to show you.

There was a flashback then, unbidden: her grandfather's apartment two winters ago, the radiator clanking, a documentary about the Cold War on his small television. She had been fifteen and half watching while scrolling her phone. Her grandfather had said, "That's not how it was," at the screen, and when she asked what he meant, he'd only said, "Depends who's telling it," and she had gone back to her phone, and he had died that spring. She hadn't introspect on it much since; there had been no reason to. Now, at the carrel, she felt the cost of that, the conversation she hadn't bothered to have, sitting right next to the strange gain of finally understanding what he meant.

She went back to the Revolution sources with new eyes. She reread Carlyle and the Marxist and a revisionist who blamed the whole upheaval on a nobility too rigid to reform, and this time she saw them not as competitors for the truth but as a sequence, each answering the anxieties of its own decade. She began to write fast, filling a page, then stopping. The trouble was that taking a position felt like betraying someone. If she argued that each generation rewrote the Revolution to suit itself, didn't she still have to say which reading was best? Ms. Adeyemi's comment surfaced again: you can hold two ideas and still choose. Maybe the choice wasn't between Carlyle and the Marxists. Maybe the choice was between pretending certainty was possible and admitting it wasn't, and choosing the second was itself a position, an honest one, though it left a hollow place where conviction was supposed to live.

At nine o'clock the overhead lights dimmed once, the library's way of saying thirty minutes remained. Theo appeared at the end of the aisle, coat already on. "Any of it useful?" he asked. "The moribund section, I mean."

"Useful," she said, and surprised herself by laughing a little. "Did you know people who wrote about the Cold War back in the fifties were called orthodox or traditionalist historians? That's what the book called them. They mostly blamed the whole thing on the Soviets." She held up the volume. "The author was one of them, I think. He didn't say so. He just wrote it like weather."

"Like weather," Theo repeated, weighing it. "So the book's wrong?"

"No," she said slowly, closing it and running her thumb along the soft edge of the cover. "That's the part I can't get to the bottom of. Wrong isn't the right word. It's just that a fact from one decade isn't the same fact in another." She slid the book into her bag next to her notes, half a draft, three days left, her grandfather's unhad conversation folded somewhere into all of it. She zipped the bag and stood. "I'm going to say that, I think. That I can't tell the difference between what they knew and what they believed. And that maybe neither can I."

Theo held the door, and the cold outside hit her face as she stepped through it, the streetlights already on, the essay unfinished and finally, somehow, begun.

Olivier sat on the closed lid of the toilet with his father's blood pressure cuff open on his knees like a stubborn book. The instruction sheet had fallen behind the radiator, so he was working from memory: arm at heart level, feet flat, still. He had told his father he would figure the thing out before Friday, when the visiting nurse came, and his father had laughed in that dry way of his and said, "You're the college man now, go on." The bathroom was the only room with a door that locked and a chair at the right height, so the bathroom it was.

He wrapped the cuff above his own elbow, pressed start, and watched his arm squeeze until his fingers tingled. The numbers came up: 122 over 78. He wrote them on the mirror in dry-erase marker, the way he kept his formulas for exams, and sat with them a while. Systolic, the top number, was the heart pushing; diastolic was the resting between. He understood the mechanics well enough from the diagrams, but what he wanted was to know what the numbers meant when they moved, which ones mattered, and how a person could actually change them instead of just worrying about them.

His phone buzzed against the sink. It was Danny from his orientation group, who had gone to the campus clinic that morning for a sports form and come back quiet. "They asked if I wanted STI testing while I was there," Danny texted. "I said no thanks. I feel completely fine, so what's the point, right?" Olivier looked at his reflection, at the numbers on the glass, and thought about how his own arm had felt nothing unusual before the cuff had proven it was doing something. Feeling fine and being fine were not the same measurement. He remembered the nurse at his own physical in June saying it plainly while she snapped off her gloves: "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one." She had said it like a weather report, no drama, and moved on to his knee reflexes.

He texted back: "Feeling fine isn't proof. Those two often have no symptoms at all. Testing is the only reliable way to know." He hesitated over whether to add more, whether to be effusive about it the way his mother would be, piling on reassurance, and decided against it. "It's a swab and a pee cup," he added. "They do it in ten minutes." Three dots appeared, disappeared, appeared again. Then: "Ok. Going back Thursday."

That settled something in him, and he turned back to the cuff with more purpose. He dug his father's last lab report out of the magazine basket, where his mother stashed everything that mattered under everything that didn't, and found the clinic's number: 146 over 94, from March. He compared it to his own reading, then to the classification chart he pulled up on his phone, holding it away from the sink because his father had once dropped a phone in the tub and never let anyone forget it. His father's top number sat well above the line for hypertension, which explained the new medication bottle on the windowsill, the one nobody had named out loud at dinner.

What Olivier wanted now was a way to say something useful without sounding like a pharmacist. He read that cutting sodium mattered, that regular aerobic exercise could lower the numbers over months, that weight and alcohol counted too, and that one reading was never a verdict because people's pressure rose just from having it taken. He thought of his father going quiet whenever the subject came up, the small detente between his parents about the salt shaker, and he decided to stop approaching it as a lecture and start approaching it as a plan. He wrote on the mirror, beneath his numbers, "walk after dinner, 30 min," and "no canned soup," and "check BP twice a week, same time."

When his father knocked, Olivier unlocked the door and had him sit on the toilet lid, jacket off, arm bare. "Feet flat," Olivier said, and wrapped the cuff the way he had practiced, checking that the marker sat over the artery the way the diagrams insisted. His father submitted to it with raised eyebrows, saying nothing, watching his son instead of the machine. The cuff hissed, tightened, released. 138 over 89. Better than March, worse than fine.

"Down eight," Olivier said. "That's the medication doing some of it. The rest, that's the walking you already started." He wiped a space on the mirror and wrote the new numbers next to the old ones, the evidence of March beside the evidence of tonight, and capped the marker. His father leaned forward, elbows on his knees, studying the glass.

"You've been rehearsing in here like it's finals," his father said.

"Thursday I'm going with Danny to the clinic," Olivier said. "He wants company." His father looked at him a moment longer, then stood and pulled his jacket back on, and paused with his hand on the light switch, leaving it on. "Walk starts after dinner," Olivier said. "You, me, thirty minutes. I already told Mom."

The U-Haul was still in the driveway when Aidan started walking, because if he stayed to unpack one more box he was going to call Dezi and say something he'd regret. Dezi had wanted him to fight for it, had gone pugnacious on the last night, saying things like "make them un-move you" as though the decision had been his to lose. Aidan walked instead, past strip malls still under construction, until the air conditioning of the public library hit him like weather.

He found a table near the periodicals, second from the window, and spread his phone and a paperback across it like a man claiming territory. He did this the next afternoon too, and the one after that, nodding at the librarian who had started saying "back again" in a tone he couldn't classify as mocking or kind.

On Thursday a girl with a lanyard full of enamel pins sat down across from him without asking. She opened a battered notebook and wrote what looked like an essay, occasionally glancing at him as though he were furniture she was still deciding about.

"You're new," she said finally. "I'm Priya. I do my reading here because my house has four younger siblings and zero quiet."

"I'm between houses," Aidan said, which was technically true and sounded less pathetic than "I don't know anyone."

Priya came back the next day, and the day after, and gradually their exchanges lengthened from weather to teachers to whether the town's only good burrito place was a myth. When she learned he'd arrived from a city three hours south, she asked what he missed, and he said "everything" and then, embarrassed by the size of it, "this coffee place where we all hung out. It sounds stupid."

"It doesn't," she said. She flipped her notebook to a page she'd apparently prepared, which he found both alarming and endearing. "There's this thing we studied in sociology. Sociologist Ray Oldenburg, in his 1989 book The Great Good Place, called them 'third places'. Cafes, libraries. Where people meet outside home and work."

Aidan turned that over for a second, his thumb marking his page. "So home is first and work is second."

"School counts," she said. "The point is the in-between."

He had been thinking of the move as a subtraction, friends and haunts lifted out and nothing put back. The idea that the space between home and school was a thing with a structure, a thing a person could walk into on purpose, rearranged something in him. He'd assumed he would acclimate by endurance, gritting through the semester until the town stopped feeling foreign. Maybe instead you could build it, deliberately, one repeated table at a time.

That weekend he tested the theory. He tried a diner where the waitress refilled his coffee without asking, and a game store where the clerk talked to him for ten minutes about a tactical RPG, and both were fine and neither was it. On Monday he was back at the library table by four, and when Priya arrived he'd pushed his paperback to one side to make room, an act so small he almost didn't register doing it.

"Verdict?" she asked.

"Pending," he said. "The diner had good pie but no Priya." She rolled her eyes, but she was smiling at her notebook, and he understood that he had given something away.

Still, he was honest enough with himself to know the theory had holes. His old coffee place hadn't worked because of architecture; it had worked because Dezi had dragged him there the first week of ninth grade and because Marcus's sister worked the counter and let them linger past close. Oldenburg, whoever he was, couldn't have scripted that. Third places might be found or built, but the people inside them arrived by accident or by the slow accumulation of afternoons, and Aidan couldn't control that part. He only knew that sitting at the same table had raised the odds, and that raising the odds was all he had.

In October, Dezi texted a photo of the coffee place, the old corner booth, Marcus's hand giving a thumbs-up. Aidan looked at it for a long time, feeling the pull of what he'd lost and the strange counterweight of what he was assembling here, unable to say which one was supposed to win. Then he screenshotted it, set his phone down on the library table, and turned it toward Priya.

"That's them," he said. "The original third place."

The ruler belonged to Mya's grandfather, a steel one with a cork backing, and it left a faint line of graphite along the curve when she laid it flat against the graph paper. She was at his kitchen table in the last week of August, three days before she moved into the dorm, and the air in the house smelled of tomato plants and old newspapers.

"Again," her grandfather said. He sat across from her with his coffee, not watching the paper but not not watching it either.

She had drawn the curve herself, y equals x squared, on axes she had ruled out carefully the night before. Under it she had shaded a region between x equals zero and x equals three, a shape like a sail. The problem was to find the area of the sail. She had computed an answer, nine, using the rule he had copied out for her from a library book, and then she had gotten something else, six, doing it a second way, and the disagreement was the whole reason for the morning.

"You trust the rule," he said, "or you trust the counting?"

She didn't answer right away. The first method was the antiderivative, the book's method, clean and abstract: raise the exponent, divide by the new exponent. The second was hers, ugly and stubborn. She had cut the shaded region into thirty thin rectangles, computed each one's area, and summed them. Thirty strips, six and something, close to six. Six was wrong. She could feel that it was wrong the way you can feel a coin is counterfeit, but she could not say why, and the feeling by itself was worth nothing. Her calculus teacher in the fall would want reasons, and so, she suspected, did the universe.

"The strips are too fat," she said finally. "The little triangles above them, I left all those out."

"So make them thinner."

"I'd be here till Christmas."

"Then sequester yourself," her grandfather said, and pushed the pencil cup toward her. "You've got till the tomatoes need watering."

She cut the sail into a hundred strips instead of thirty, working fast, her arithmetic degrading as she went, and the sum crept up toward eight, then past it, and something moved in her that she distrusted, a small triumphant warmth, because eight was closer to nine but still not nine, and warmth at an approximation was exactly the kind of sloppiness she was supposed to be above. She remembered then, without meaning to, a afternoon in June, the math club picnic behind the school, where Marcus had argued with their coach about a homework problem. Marcus had taken a ruler, an actual wooden ruler, and laid it along the curve he had graphed, tilting it until it touched the curve at exactly one point, and read off the slope by counting grid squares. He had computed the derivative by formula first, and the ruler lying along the curve was his check, his tribunal and his appeal court at once. "The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point," he had said, tapping the ruler, "so the ruler is the tangent line and the slope tells me if my answer's any good." The coach had frowned and taken the ruler away and said something about rigor, and Marcus had stood there holding nothing, looking sullen, and Mya had privately sided with the coach, because rigor was the whole religion of the club, and she had wanted to belong to it.

She sat now with her hundred strips and her two answers, and the memory sat with her, and she understood something about Marcus that she had refused to understand in June. The ruler was not a rejection of rigor. It was rigor of a different kind, the kind that tests the formula against the world instead of against itself. Her strips were fat, yes, but they were honest in a way the antiderivative was not, because she could see every one of them. The formula gave nine without showing her anything. A thousand strips would have shown her everything and taken her a week.

So she did a third thing. She took the ruler and laid it along her curve at x equals three, tilted it until it touched at just that one point, and read the slope off the grid the way Marcus had, counting squares: six across one, or near enough. The book said the derivative there was two times x, which was six, and the ruler agreed, and the agreement ran through her like cold water. The formula could be checked. It could be laid against the paper, against the physical graph, against the world. That meant the nine was probably right and the strips were probably converging toward it, fat triangles and all, and she did not have to choose between the two methods the way she had thought she did, the way Marcus and the coach had chosen and both lost.

She wrote the two answers at the top of the page, nine and eight-something, and between them she drew a bracket, and under the bracket she wrote, "with thinner strips." It was not a proof. She knew that. Somewhere between her hundred strips and the infinite strips she was not going to draw, the answer crossed from eight to nine, and she could not yet say where or how, and she was not going to pretend she could.

Her grandfather came back from the garden with two tomatoes and set one beside her paper, red against the graphite. He looked at the page for a long moment.

"Which one's right?" he said.

"I don't know yet," Mya said. "But I know how to find out."

She picked up the ruler and drew the next curve.

The departure board still said DELAYED in amber, and Camille had been at Gate 14 long enough to memorize the shops across the concourse. She opened her laptop on her knees, careful of the coffee on the seat beside her, and logged into the trial account her workshop instructor had extended for two more weeks. The map that loaded was a mid-sized city she had never visited, parcel boundaries in gray, and she had until Thursday to finish the exercise: overlay the floodplain layer on the housing layer and see what the city looked like when both were true at once.

She had learned the buttons on Tuesday, in a basement lab with bad ventilation. Now she was learning the harder part, which the instructor had called "asking the map a real question" rather than just making colors appear. Camille set the flood zone to translucent blue and watched it settle over the parcels like water finding its level. Whole blocks sat inside it. Some of those blocks held houses worth four times what the houses across the river were worth, and some held houses the county had bought out and demolished after the last big flood, leaving the map's neat rectangles standing for empty lots.

A man two seats down was arguing into his phone about an affidavit. "I signed the thing, Denise, I signed it in March," he said, peevish now, his free hand flat on his knee. "The affidavit says the elevation certificate was filed. If their office lost it, that is not my problem." He hung up, stood, sat back down. Camille kept working, but the word stayed with her. Her father had signed something similar three years ago, a sworn statement that their street had flooded twice in one decade, for a claim that was eventually denied on a technicality. She had been fourteen and had thought paperwork was paperwork. She understood now that a map like this one was the argument that came before the paperwork, the picture that made a claim believable or dismissible.

The boy across the aisle, maybe her age, backpack between his feet, leaned over. "Is that a flood map?" he asked. His name, when they got that far, was Sef, and he was flying home from a college visit. His uncle worked in emergency management, he said, which was why he knew what a floodplain was at all.

She tilted the screen so he could see. She was building a query now, the step she had gotten wrong in the lab. She wanted to select only the parcels that were both inside the floodplain and classified as rental housing, then operationalize density as a number the software could actually count: units per acre, summed per block. In the lab she had selected one layer and then the other, and the software had quietly returned everything, because she had not told it the two conditions had to overlap. Her instructor had circled the error on the printout without fixing it. Camille had spent that evening figuring out that the software did exactly what she said, never what she meant.

"That's the east side," Sef said, studying the highlighted blocks. "My uncle says that's where nobody leaves when they order evacuations, because half of them are renting and they think they'll be robbed." He paused. "It's weird, though. Cities keep growing, right? People have two kids, the two replace them, it evens out. You'd think the numbers would just stay the same."

"They don't," Camille said. "It's 2.1, not 2. I read it last night. In countries with low death rates, you need a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman to replace the population without migration."

"Point one?"

"About 2.1," she said again, because she had checked the number twice, and she did not know the reason behind it, and she said so. "I can't tell you why. I can just tell you that's the figure." She found this happened more and more: she could carry a fact carefully, whole, without being able to see under it. The honesty of that surprised her. She had expected learning to feel like mastery, and instead it felt like carrying trays through a crowded room, steady hands, eyes down.

The query finished. The east side blocks turned red, dense and low, and one parcel near the river stayed stubbornly gray. She clicked it. The attribute table said the owner was a limited liability company, the land use was listed as vacant, and the flood layer said thirty percent of it sat inside the high-risk zone. She could overlay the two layers, but she could not overlay the company's intention, or the city council's, or what an affidavit would say about that lot if someone ever swore one.

The board changed to BOARDING, and the peevish man was first in line, boarding pass in his fist. Sef stood, shouldered his backpack, and said, "Two point one. I'm going to look it up when I land."

"Tell me if you find out why," Camille said. She closed the laptop without shutting the map down, holding the image of that gray parcel in her head as she joined the line.

Grandmother's copy of the Torah had been in the sideboard for eleven years, and Luca had told himself for eleven years that he would read it before he had to read it aloud. Now the family was spilling into the dining room, aunts arguing about chairs, his little cousins underfoot, and the book was still in his hands, unfamiliar as a stone from another country.

He was seventeen, and this was the first year Grandfather had not led the ceremony. "You," Grandfather had said in September, tapping the table with one finger. "Next spring, you do it." Luca had said yes the way you say yes to a dare, and then had spent months not practicing, which he now understood was its own kind of choice.

The room quieted, mostly. Uncle Marco kept talking about parking until Aunt Rina put a hand on his arm. Luca opened the book. He had planned to begin with the blessing over the candles, the one he knew by heart, but his eye caught the page marker, a faded ribbon set at Leviticus, and he heard himself say, "First I want to read something." His own voice surprised him. He read the verses about the fields, how the corners were not to be reaped, how the fallen gleanings were to be left where they lay for the poor and the stranger.

"So what does that have to do with us?" said his cousin Emma, sixteen and delighted to find a flaw. "None of us farm. Uncle Marco sells software."

"We have a balcony with two pepper plants," Uncle Marco offered, and the table laughed, and Luca laughed too, but inside he was doing arithmetic. His grandfather had farmed, once, in another country, before Luca was born. Luca had grown up on the story of the orchard, how the whole town came through in October, but he realized, standing there, that he could not say whether the story was true or whether he had built it out of photographs and his grandfather's silences. He had begun to suspect that half of what he remembered about the man was invented, sanded smooth, a story that flattered both of them.

"Grandfather," Luca said. "When you had the orchard. Did you leave the corners?"

The old man had been watching Luca all evening with an expression Luca wanted to read as pride, though he knew he might be wrong about that, too. "You read it wrong," Grandfather said.

"I read it exactly," Luca said, and heard the sycophant in himself, the boy who wanted credit before he wanted the truth. He steadied. "I mean, I read the words right. Leviticus says don't reap the corners, and don't gather the fallen gleanings. Leave them for the poor and the stranger. I read that."

"Then you read it right," Grandfather said. "I meant why you read it. Why there, why first." He turned his water glass a quarter turn, the way he did when he was deciding something. "My father left the corners because the rabbi said to. I left them because a woman named Besa came every autumn with her boys, and if I reaped to the edges, they were destitute that winter. Same corners. Different reasons. You have to decide which one you are."

Emma, softened by the name, said, "So it does mean something for people who don't farm." Luca said, "It means you don't take everything. You leave a margin, on purpose, for people you don't know." Even as he said it he was checking it against the text in his head, corners, fallen gleanings, the poor, the stranger, and it held, and he was briefly and privately amazed that a rule about wheat could walk three thousand years into a dining room in a country with supermarkets.

They got through the candles. He said the blessing over the wine without stumbling and the one over the bread with only one glance down, and his aunts beamed at him in a way that beguiled him, he could feel it working on him, the warm current of being the boy who did it right, and he distrusted it even while he leaned into it, because Grandfather had just told him the corners were the point, and approval felt like reaping to the edges.

Between courses, Grandfather leaned over, close enough that only Luca could hear. "Besa," he said. "My mother." Luca looked at him. Not Besa the widow from the village, the one Luca had instantly imagined gathering fallen fruit at the field's edge. His great-grandmother. The stranger his own great-grandfather had left the corners for.

"She wasn't poor," Luca said slowly, testing it.

"Everyone was poor," Grandfather said. "That's not the point. The point is you told them a stranger got the corners, and I let you." He sat back and forked a piece of brisket, his face giving away nothing, the way it had given away nothing for eleven years.

Luca stood to pour the next round of wine, bottle circling the table, and when he came to his grandfather's glass he held it there a moment longer than he needed to. "Next year," he said, "you tell it your way."

His grandfather looked up at him across the candles. "Whose way do you think it was tonight?"

Kate's father had emptied the third stall of the garage so she could practice steering between two trash bins he'd spaced with a tape measure, and she had hit the left bin four times in a row. "You're overcorrecting," he said from a folding chair, and she said nothing, because answering would have required letting go of the wheel, which she was not prepared to do. The cones of light from the open garage door fell across the driveway in the late afternoon, and the bin waited for her fifth attempt with what she considered lugubrious patience, dented and grimy and clearly expecting failure. She backed up, turned the wheel, watched the mirror, and stopped an inch from the rubber. When she got out and looked, the car sat between the bins with maybe a foot on either side, and her father said, "That's a park," and she felt something in her chest unclench.

The test was in nine days, at the exam station across town, and the part she feared was not the parking. It was the highway. Her permit allowed her to drive with an adult, so on Saturday her father rode shotgun on Route 52 south, where a construction project had narrowed the road from two lanes to one. Traffic slowed to a crawl a half mile before the merge. Cars in the right lane sat bumper to bumper, and ahead the left lane ran clear and empty to the orange signs, and Kate, in the right lane, watched a pickup straddle both lanes at an angle, blocking the left lane with its body so nobody could pass.

"Jerk," her father said, but mildly, like he was identifying a species of bird. Kate's hands tightened. She had been raised, or had raised herself, on the conviction that waiting politely in the long line was the honest thing, that anyone who zoomed up the empty lane was cheating, and the pickup driver was enforcing that belief with two tons of steel. She signaled and began creeping forward with the line.

That night her friend Priya texted her a screenshot of a page from Minnesota's Department of Transportation, with a message underneath: "for the girl who is afraid of everything except her own opinions." The page said the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. Kate read it three times, then texted back, "so the pickup guy was wrong AND righteous?" and Priya sent back only a shrugging emoji, which Kate felt was accurate.

She thought about it while brushing her teeth. All her life she had trusted the logic of lines: first come, first served, cutting is wrong, the people who cut are the reason the line is slow. But here was the state itself, with its signage and its statistics, saying the early mergers made the backup longer, that using both lanes was not cheating but the intended design. Two authorities she believed in were facing each other across an orange barrel, and she couldn't make them both right. She was honest enough with herself to admit she didn't fully see how it worked, only that it had been measured, and that the measurement disagreed with her gut, and that her gut had been shaped mostly by the fear of being honked at.

The following Saturday they drove Route 52 again. This time, approaching the backup, Kate held the left lane. Her father said, "You sure?" and she said, "It's called the zipper merge," and kept her speed steady while the right lane stood still beside her, drivers watching her pass. At the merge point she signaled, and a woman in a hatchback left her a gap, one car, and Kate slid in, and the woman went next after her, and then the pickup behind, and for a moment the two lanes knitted together like the teeth of something. Nobody honked. One man shook his head at her, slow and lugubrious, mourning for the moral order, and she lifted two fingers off the wheel at him, not quite a wave, not quite an apology.

Later, in the garage, she ran the parking drill again in the cooling evening, the radio on, backing between the bins until it stopped being luck and started being sequence. Her father came out with two glasses of water and stood drinking his in the doorway. "You know," he said, "when I was your age I thought driving was pure hedonism. Just freedom, windows down." Kate laughed, her head upside down checking the mirror. "You grew up in Duluth. Freedom to drive where, the lake?" He considered this. "The other lake," he said.

She knew she might still fail. She knew the examiner might not leave her a gap, that the parallel space on test day might be tighter than the bins, that some fear, however well reasoned at, could incapacitate her at the exact moment her foot needed to move from brake to gas. The uncertainty sat in her like a stone in a shoe, small and portable. But the bins stood there under the work light, and the car was warm, and she had a half hour of daylight left.

She pulled forward, lined up her mirror with the left bin, and began again.

The grill had been his mother's territory, and for three months after the funeral nobody had touched it, so that the cover had gone stiff with rain and the propane tank sat in the corner of the yard like a mourner who refused to leave. Eli dragged the cover off on a Saturday in June because his aunt and cousins were coming at six, and because someone had to make dinner, and because his father, who could talk for an hour about deconstructing a Bowie album, went silent whenever a kitchen timer beeped.

He'd found the recipe in his mother's handwriting, a marinated chicken breast with lime and cumin, folded twice and slipped into a cookbook as if she'd meant to come back to it. He'd never grilled anything in his life. He'd watched her, though, the way you watch a parent doing something ordinary, which is to say barely at all, and so his memory was mostly of her wrist turning the tongs and the smell of smoke in her hair when she came inside.

The coals were uneven, one side blazing and the other sulking, and the chicken sizzled when he laid it down at an angle she might have chosen. He turned it after four minutes and saw the pale underside, the meat still slack and translucent at the edges. His cousin Delia, fifteen and merciless, had already asked twice whether they were going to eat before dark.

He cut into the thickest breast with a paring knife. The juices ran faintly pink, or maybe it was the marinade, and he crouched over the plate on the picnic table trying to decide, and deciding, in his experience, never actually settled anything. It was like the college essay he'd been drafting for two weeks, the one about whether honesty obligated him to tell admissions that his junior-year grades had collapsed the semester his mother was sick, or whether grief was a reason that could extenuate without excusing. He'd written four openings and deleted three.

His father came out with a beer he wasn't drinking and stood at his shoulder. "Don't guess," he said, and held out a thin metal wand with a wire, a digital thermometer from the drawer by the stove, still in its plastic sleeve. "Read the box."

Eli slit the sleeve with the paring knife. The card inside, in small print, said US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. He read it twice, then held it up so his father could see he'd read it. "A hundred and sixty-five," he said.

"Then find out what you've got."

He pushed the probe into the thickest part of the breast, avoiding what he guessed was bone, and the display climbed through the nineties, the low hundreds, and stalled at 152. He'd nearly talked himself into pulling the meat off when the number ticked up again, 158, 161, and he stood there watching digits the way his mother used to stand watching the door for his father to come home from a gig that ran late. It reached 165 and the display blinked, and he moved the probe to a second breast and found 168 already, and to a thinner one that read 151, and he learned in those few minutes that a grill was not one temperature but a dozen arguing ones.

While the smaller piece cooked he thought about a kid from his debate team, Marcus, who had organized a food drive the same spring Eli had stopped answering texts, and who had called him once in April, not to recruit him, just to ask if he was eating. Eli had said yes, which was true on technicality, cereal and the leftovers his aunt left in foil. Marcus hadn't asked again. Eli had admired him for that, and resented him slightly, too, because there was something about a person whose altruistic instincts ran so clean that it made your own flinching look like a character flaw. He suspected Marcus of being genuinely good, and he suspected that some people would call that naive, and he could not fully decide which suspicion was the slander.

Dinner, when it finally happened, was fine. Delia ate two breasts and said nothing, which from Delia was a review. His father ate slowly and said, "This is hers. The lime thing." Not a question. Eli said yes, and didn't add that he'd doubled the cumin because he couldn't remember whether she doubled it or he was inventing a version of her that never existed. Some frauds were deliberate; he was beginning to understand that others were just memory doing its best work with bad materials, a charlatan who believed his own pitch.

Afterward, alone in the blue dark with the tongs and the foil and the plate of bones, he turned the essay over in his mind again. Maybe he would write it plainly, the semester and the reason, and let the admissions reader decide what weight the reason carried, the way the thermometer had let the chicken decide whether it was done. Or maybe he'd close the grill, go inside, and open a new document, blank and cool, the cursor blinking at him from the corner of the screen.

The apartment was thirty minutes from campus by bus, third floor, with a balcony just wide enough for one chair, and Dev had sent the lease to all three of them that afternoon with a single line: "Read it tonight, we sign tomorrow." William opened the file at his desk, the fan pushing warm air across the back of his neck, and began at the beginning, because that was the kind of person he had decided to be this year. The first pages were dull in a way that felt almost physical: recitals, definitions, a section titled "Terms and Conditions" that ran to eleven paragraphs. His eyes wanted to slide. He made them stay.

It was in section fourteen that he stopped. The clause said that the tenants would be liable, jointly and severally, for all rent and damages under the lease. He read it twice, then pasted it into a search bar. The results came back fast and flat and changed the shape of the evening: under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share. He sat back. He and Dev and Priya were each planning to cover a third of the rent. The landlord, apparently, did not care about thirds.

He called Dev first, and Dev laughed before William had finished the sentence. "So if Priya bails, we cover her part. Obviously. That's what friends do."

"That's not what it says," William said. "It says if Priya bails, either of us can be made to cover all of it. Not her third. All of it. The whole rent, every month, until the lease ends."

There was a pause long enough that William could hear a television in the background of Dev's room. "That can't be right," Dev said. "That's ridiculous."

"It's right. I'm reading it right now."

Priya joined the call a minute later, breathless from somewhere outdoors, and William walked them through it again, slower this time. He had spent the last hour with the document, sequestered at his desk with his phone face down, and he had worked out the arithmetic more than once, hoping it would come out differently. It did not. If one of them lost a job, the other two were not exposed to a share; they were exposed to everything.

"So we don't sign," Dev said.

"We want the apartment," Priya said. "It's two blocks from the river. It's the only one we can afford, and affording it is exactly the problem, so."

William turned in his chair and looked at the printout he had made, six pages of it, clause fourteen circled in pencil. His father had signed things his whole life, he thought, shift contracts, a truck loan, papers he never read, and called that practicality. William had always privately considered it a lack of acumen, an older man's carelessness dressed up as toughness. Now he was less sure which of them was being naive, the man who signed without reading or the boy who imagined that reading was the same as control.

"We could do a side agreement," he said. "Between the three of us. If the landlord makes one of us pay more than a third, the others owe that person the difference. It doesn't change what we owe the landlord, but it changes what we owe each other."

"That sounds tautological," Priya said. "We'd be signing a contract to enforce the contract we already agreed to by being friends."

"It's not the same thing," William said, though he could hear the weakness in it. "One of them is legally enforceable and one of them is us trusting each other, and after tonight I'd rather have both."

They argued for another twenty minutes. Dev wanted to sign the lease as it stood and trust the friendship; Priya wanted to ask the landlord to strike the clause entirely, which William doubted would work and Priya suspected he only doubted because he liked knowing things. In the end they agreed to the side agreement, drafted in a shared document while they were still on the call, three signatures to be scanned by noon.

William drafted it himself, and it was almost midnight when he noticed the message waiting below the thread. It was from Priya, sent an hour earlier, before they had agreed on anything. She had written to the landlord asking about removing clause fourteen, and the landlord had already replied: the lease had been generated for three tenants, but joint and several liability was standard, and if they preferred, it could be rewritten for a single tenant with two occupants, which some renters found simpler. A single tenant. One name, one obligation, no shares at all.

William read the reply three times, then called her, and she picked up on the second ring.

"You already sent this," he said. "Before we decided anything."

"I sent it before I knew what we'd decide," Priya said. "I wanted to know what our options were." In the quiet that followed, he could hear her walking, her footsteps on pavement somewhere between the river and home. "My parents would co-sign for me alone," she said. "They offered. I didn't tell you because I wanted us to figure it out together, and now we have, and I still don't know if I'd be helping you both or just making sure I'm the one who's safe."

William looked at the side agreement open on his screen, his own name typed into the first signature line, and found he could not tell either.

"So what do we do?" Dev's voice came from the other line, where he had apparently been listening the whole time.

William reached for his pencil and turned back to clause fourteen, the circle he had drawn around it already smudged gray. "Tomorrow," he said, "we go in together, all three of us, and we don't sign anything until every line has been read out loud."

The library closed at nine, and by seven Charlotte had spread her laptop, a paperback on Java, and two granola bar wrappers across the study table nearest the sockets. Her screen held a file called Player.java, forty lines her teammate Dara had written the night before the deadline for their intro programming course. The autograder had returned 0 out of 20 at four that afternoon, with no message except a wall of red compiler errors, and the professor's email had said only: teams resolve their own builds. Charlotte had until midnight.

She read the file top to bottom first, the way you read a letter you already suspect is bad news. Dara had built a Player with private fields: score, name, active. So far, so good. Charlotte's own half of the assignment, the test class, sat open in the other window, and every test she had written called methods that the compiler claimed did not exist.
