Half was an honest fraction, and she found she liked it less than either extreme, because a number like that made you choose anyway. It didn't tell you whether you were in the half that survived or the half that didn't, and it didn't tell you whether the belt itself was freedom or leash, or whether those were even different things.

Afterward, in the strip mall parking lot, Mr. Okafor filled out her progress sheet. "Control is good," he said. "Confidence will come." He tore off her copy and held it out, and as she took it he added, "Same time next week," in a tone that assumed she would say yes.

Her grandmother was idling at the curb in her enormous Buick, and Samantha got in, and reached, out of habit older than memory, for the seat belt. The buckle hung up halfway down the door pillar, the old fabric gone stiff, and she had to feed it back through with two hands while her grandmother watched with an expression that was not quite disapproval and not quite its opposite.

"Your father never wore his," her grandmother said, pulling out into traffic.

Natalie had carried the fragments to school in a shoebox lined with a dish towel, and through first period the box sat in her locker like something breathing. In the art room, fourth period, she finally opened it on the counter near the window: seven pieces of her grandmother's rice bowl, the celadon glaze catching the light along edges sharp enough to matter. Mr. Ferreira wandered past, glanced in, and said nothing, which was the reason she had chosen his room and not the ceramics studio, where Ms. Okoye would have asked questions.

The bowl had broken on Tuesday. Her grandmother had been napping, the apartment warm and smelling of barley tea, and Natalie had reached over it for the good brushes her grandmother kept in a jar behind the stove, the ones she never used anymore because her hands shook. The bowl had been under a cloth. That was all. It had not even made much of a sound, just a settling, and Natalie had stood there with her grandmother's brushes and her grandmother's broken bowl, sixty years of a life in pieces on a linoleum floor.

Her first plan had been glue and paint. There was a kit in her backpack, cyanoacrylate and a tiny bottle of green acrylic she had mixed to match the glaze, because her grandmother's eyes were going but not that gone. The plan was simple and it was a lie, and both of those things had recommended it. She had even rehearsed the sentence: I found it like that. She laid the pieces out now in their rough circle, and the jagged lines between them adumbrated a shape she couldn't name, a map of the moment her hand had knocked against cloth.

Priya leaned over from the next table, brush in her teeth, hands black with ink. "Whose is it?"

"My grandmother's. Was." Natalie turned one piece over. "I'm fixing it before Sunday. She's making rice for the equinox thing and she'll want it."

"You're going to fake it." Priya said it without judgment, the way she said everything, and set her brush down. "You could fake it. Nobody would know."

"I would know." Natalie heard how it sounded, like a line from a movie, and hated it, and meant it anyway. She had spent two days weighing the truth against her grandmother's face when she saw the bowl, and the truth kept losing. Her grandmother had come to this country with two suitcases and a sister, had been impecunious for decades in a way Natalie only understood in fragments, stories about washing dishes in a restaurant that served food from home. The bowl was from home. It had crossed an ocean in a rolled sweater. It was the only object in the apartment her grandmother had ever called by a name.

Priya pulled out her phone, typed, scrolled, and turned the screen around. Natalie read it twice. A photograph of a mended bowl, black seams running through it like rivers drawn in ink, and every seam blazing with gold, so that the breaks were the most alive part of the thing, more visible than they would ever have been unbroken.

"Kintsugi," Priya read. "It's a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold." She looked up. "It treats the break as part of the object's history instead of hiding it."

Natalie took the phone and read further, past the bright photographs, into the practice of it: the lacquer, the curing, the weeks it took. Real gold, real urushi lacquer that could blister her skin, patience measured in months. She thought of her cheap kit, the acrylic paint, the rehearsed sentence, the whole small hegemony of pretending nothing had happened, and she understood that she had been weighing the wrong things. She wasn't choosing between truth and her grandmother's face. She was choosing what the bowl would be for the rest of its life: an object with a scar, or an object with a secret.

"It takes months to cure," she said. "Properly. I have five days." Mr. Ferreira, watering the paint sinks like a man tending a garden, said from across the room, "Some things you can't speed up," and nothing else. Priya was already scrolling again, muttering about mica powder and epoxy and a craft store two bus transfers away, and whether a girl on a babysitting income could afford even the fake gold. Natalie swept the fragments gently back into the towel, folding it over them the way her grandmother folded wrappers, corners first.

At the craft store she stood a long time in front of two options: gold leaf she could not afford and a small jar of mica powder the color of a struck match. She bought the mica. On Sunday she would set the bowl on the table, seams rough and glittering where they should have been lacquered and smooth, and she would not say I found it like that. She would say something else, though she did not yet know what, and she practiced nothing on the bus ride home, only held the shoebox on her lap with both hands and watched the mica gold shine through the cloth every time the doors opened and the light came in.

The laminated diagram of a condom was giving Rosalie trouble, mostly because she kept dropping it. "It's like putting a sock on an octopus," she muttered, and Dex, the other counselor-in-training, snorted so hard that orange juice came out of his nose. They were sitting on the floor of the camp infirmary, which smelled of iodine and pine, surrounded by pamphlets they were supposed to master before Thursday, when the health educators would descend on the cabins to run the peer sessions. Rosalie had volunteered for the sex-ed track partly because her aunt ran a clinic back home and partly because it terrified her, and she had a theory that terrified things made you pay attention. She smoothed the diagram flat and tried again, this time slowly, narrating in her best documentary voice: "Pinch the tip. Roll it down. Check for damage." Dex applauded with two latex gloves he'd blown up like balloon animals.

The consent lesson was harder to practice because there were no diagrams. It was all words, and words were slippery. "You say yes freely, and you can change your mind, and being talked into it isn't the same as wanting it," Rosalie recited, and then she paused. "But how do you teach someone to hear the difference between a yes and a resigned yes?" Dex shrugged and lobbed a glove animal at her head. "You don't teach it," he said. "You make them practice saying no to something small. Like no to the second helping of mystery casserole. Then no to bigger stuff." Rosalie turned this over. It was simple, maybe too simple, but there was something in it, the way there was something in her aunt's old line that consent was a conversation, not a signature.

Wednesday was the field trip to the county clinic, twenty minutes down a road so sullen the bus seemed to sink into it, rain puddling gray in the potholes. Inside, the clinic was bright and ordinary, like a dentist's office with better magazines. The teens were allowed to shadow the intake desk as long as they didn't hover over patients. Rosalie stationed herself by the rack of pamphlets and read everything, including the fine print nobody read, because fine print was where the world kept its honesty.

That was where she found the number. The combined pill, the pamphlet said, perfect use, fewer than 1 in 100 pregnancies in a year. Then, typical use, about 7 in 100. She read the line twice, then a third time, feeling the small vertigo of a fact rearranging her assumptions. Seven in a hundred. She had somehow absorbed the idea that the pill was basically a wall, and the pill was mostly a wall, but the wall had a gap, and the gap had a shape, and the pamphlet named it: often because doses are missed. Not because the pill failed. Because people were people, with bad weeks and forgotten alarms and backpacks left in canoes.

A girl in the waiting room, fifteen maybe, with wet braids and her phone in her lap, was watching the nurse demonstrate how to set a daily reminder alarm. "Why does she keep going on about the alarm?" the girl said, not rudely, just baffled. "It's one little pill." Rosalie felt her mouth open before her brain had approved anything. "With typical use," she said, "about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed." The girl stared at her. "Seven out of a hundred," Rosalie added, "not one out of a thousand." The nurse glanced over and, mercifully, said nothing at all, which Rosalie decided was the highest professional compliment available.

The girl's name was Thea, and she followed Rosalie back to the pamphlet rack like a duckling with opinions. "So the alarm is the actual birth control," Thea said. "The pill is just the chemical part, but the alarm is the, like, human part." Rosalie opened her mouth to correct this and then closed it again, because it was almost right and possibly better than right, a way of thinking about the whole thing she hadn't built herself. "Sort of the enthalpy of the situation," said Dex, drifting over. "The pill's the reaction, but the reminder is the energy you have to keep putting in or the whole thing stops." Thea looked at him. "Are you a chemistry person?" "Regrettably," said Dex. "Do you want to hear about entropy?" "Regrettably, no."

By the campfire that night, Rosalie had filled an index card with the things she would say on Thursday, and beside it another index card with the things she still didn't know how to say. On the second card: how do you make "get tested" sound like ordinary maintenance instead of a verdict. Whether a resigned yes ever looked like a real yes from the inside. Whether seven in a hundred felt like a lot or a little to someone actually taking the pill. She had decided, on the bus home, to present both cards honestly, which felt risky in a way that made her pulse go quick, the good kind of quick.

Thursday came with sun. Rosalie stood in front of nine fourteen-year-olds, held up the octopus sock, and dropped it immediately. The campers laughed; she laughed; she picked it up. "Okay," she said. "Today we're going to talk about alarms."

Aiden had until midnight, and the kitchen clock kept proving it. The portfolio submission closed at eleven fifty-nine, and the piece he wanted to send, a drawing of the river by his grandmother's old house, existed only as a photograph in his phone and forty loose squares of paper on the table. The idea had come to him in fragments all week: draw the river small, many times, on separate scraps, and then assemble them so the water broke apart and reassembled like memory does. Now the scraps were spread across the table like silt, an alluvial fan of graphite and eraser dust, and he had to decide how they fit before he could photograph the whole thing and upload it.

He picked up two squares, held them side by side, and put them down again. His grandmother had taught him one way of drawing, which was patience: build the tone slowly, one faint layer after another, until the paper held the light. His art teacher had taught him another way, which was risk: make the thing wrong on purpose, tear it, collage it, let the seams show. For months he had been pretending those were two different careers, as if he had to pick a life the way you pick a major. Tonight the deadline made pretending expensive.

Maya padded into the kitchen in her pajamas, holding a pencil with a wet, splintered end. She was seven, and she had been sent to bed an hour ago, and she was crying in the quiet, hiccupping way that meant the fear had been building in the dark by itself. "I ate some," she said. "The paint part and some of the lead. I was chewing it and I swallowed."

"You swallowed the lead?" Aiden pulled her onto the chair beside him.

"The gray part. Lead is poison. Marcus at school said lead gets in your bones and you get sick." She held the pencil out like evidence at a trial, and her hand was shaking a little.

Aiden turned the broken end toward the light. He remembered his father saying something once, offhand, over homework, and he reached for his phone to check it before he promised anything, because Maya took promises literally. He read, then read again, and put the phone down. "It's not lead," he said. "It's called graphite. Pencil lead has never actually been made of lead, not ever. They only call it lead because back in the sixteenth century people thought graphite was a kind of lead ore. It isn't. It's just graphite and clay."

Maya looked at the wet gray end. "So I'm not poisoned?"

"You're not poisoned. You're just gross." He wiped the pencil on a napkin, which made her laugh, and the laugh broke the fear open and let it drain. She leaned her chin on the table to watch him work, and after a while she began sliding squares toward him, playing advisor, and he let her, because her eye was untrained and therefore strange.

"Those two go together," she said, pushing a dark square and a pale one. "The dark part is where the water's deep."

He would not have put them together. The pale square was one of his best, the river at noon, and gluing it next to the heavy one would make both harder to read. But he tried it, holding them at the joint, and something happened that hadn't happened in three hours of arranging: the river had a bottom and a surface at once. The two ways of drawing, the patient and the torn, met in the seam and neither one lost. He thought of how his father talked about their mortgage, how they'd amortize the cost of the roof over years, spreading one impossible number into many survivable ones, and he understood that he was doing the same thing with the drawing, spreading one impossible river into forty small decisions. Some of them could fail and the whole thing would still hold.

He worked while Maya drifted asleep against his arm, which cost him his right elbow and slowed every stroke. He gained the seam and lost the hour. At eleven he had the full assembly on a sheet of cardboard, and he saw immediately that it was too big to photograph well in the kitchen light, and that the two squares he loved most, the noon square among them, caught glare no matter how he angled the lamp. He tried the porch light, the stove light, the flashlight propped in a bowl. Each version flattened some part of what the piece actually was, and there was no time to solve it, only time to choose which failure to send.

At eleven forty he set the phone on a stack of cookbooks, framed the whole piece with the noon square blazing out one blank corner of it, and pressed record. The file uploaded slowly, the progress bar crawling while the clock in the other room struck the quarter hour. He thought about how his teacher would see the glare and call it sloppy, and how his grandmother, if she were still alive to see it, would have known instantly that the glare was the water. Both of those readings were true, and he could not make them be the same one, and he submitted anyway at eleven fifty-three with Maya asleep on his shoulder and his arm gone completely numb beneath her weight.

The confirmation page loaded. He sat still, listening to Maya breathe, looking at the forty squares drying on the cardboard, the seams already beginning to curl.

"Aiden," Maya said, not waking up, "the dark part is where it's deep."

The funeral was at eleven, and Colton arrived at ten because his mother said the family should be there early, though nobody explained what they would do with the extra hour. The sanctuary smelled of lilies and furniture polish. His grandfather's photograph stood on a table beside the casket, a picture from twenty years ago: Grandpa Walt in a linen shirt, squinting into what had to be bright sun, standing somewhere in Kenya where he had taught school for two years before Colton was born. Behind him in the photo stretched the savanna, gold grass running out to a flat horizon, a lone acacia throwing a shadow like a sundial.

Colton's mother hugged people near the doorway. His father talked quietly with the pastor, a tall woman named Reverend Okafor who had only met Walt once, at a hospital, which struck Colton as a strange qualification for delivering a eulogy. Colton walked down the center aisle and stopped at the photograph. He had come here wanting something, though he had not let himself name it. He wanted to be sure he was grieving correctly. That was the want, and it embarrassed him.

Three days before, cleaning out his grandfather's apartment, he had found a book on the nightstand with a bookmark still in it. Continuing Bonds, it was called, published in 1996, by three authors whose names he had copied into his phone because they sounded like a law firm: Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman, Steven Nickman. He had read the bookmarked chapter late that night with his desk lamp on, and it had said something he kept turning over. It argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on. Colton had always assumed the opposite, that the whole point was to let go, that the healthy people were the ones who packed the apartment in two days and did not cry at the leasing office.

"You're the grandson," said a voice behind him. A woman in her seventies, small, wearing a green coat, held out her hand. "I'm Phyllis's friend. No, not that Phyllis. I'm Ruth. I played chess with your grandfather on Thursdays."

"He mentioned you," Colton said, and it was true, though it had sounded like a small thing at the time, chess on Thursdays, two old people in a library meeting room.

"He said you argued with him about everything," Ruth said. "He was proud of that. He said you enunciated your positions like a lawyer." She smiled at the photograph. "He told me you'd want to say something today and wouldn't know if you were allowed."

Colton felt his face go warm. "How did he know that?"

"Because you argued about everything and then asked whether it counted." She patted his arm once, the way you close a book you intend to reopen, and went to find a seat.

The service began. There were hymns, and Colton held the hymnal with its vestigial ribbon marker, faded red, hanging loose from a spine nobody had opened in years, and he sang where he knew the words. Reverend Okafor read a psalm and then spoke about Walt's life, the teaching in Kenya, the forty years at the public library, the wife who had died before Colton could remember her. She said the word "loss" eleven times. Colton counted without meaning to. She never said the word for what he actually had, which was not an absence but a presence with nowhere to go.

When she opened the floor for remembrances, three people stood. A cousin told a story about a fishing trip. Ruth did not stand; she only looked at Colton across two rows of folded hands. The organist began the closing music before he had decided anything.

Afterward, in the fellowship hall with its folding tables and coffee urns, Colton's mother pressed a plate of cookies into his hands and he carried it around like a task. He found Ruth by the window. "I read a book of his," he said. "Continuing Bonds. He had it marked."

"Ah," Ruth said. "He bought that after Miriam died. He said it gave him permission."

"Permission for what?"

"To keep her. He'd talk to her while he cooked. Terrible cook. He'd say, Miriam, how much salt, and she never answered, and he said that was still her doing, in a way." Ruth sipped her coffee. "I told him he was being morbid. He said the book said otherwise. He lent it to me. I never gave it back."

Colton set the cookie plate down on the sill. "So it's normal. That's what the book says. Keeping the connection. Not a failure to move on." He heard his own voice enunciate it, lawyer-like, and almost laughed.

"That's what he took from it," Ruth said. "I took something smaller. I took that grief is not one size."

The afternoon light moved across the parking lot. His mother was at the door, hugging the last guests, and his father was loading lilies into the trunk with the careful concentration of a man avoiding his own thoughts. Colton understood, standing there, that he could hold both ideas without choosing: the book's claim, which felt like a hand on his shoulder, and the honest uncertainty underneath it, the question of whether talking to someone who cannot answer is connection or only rehearsal. He did not know. He was sixteen, and he had never grieved before, and nobody had taught him the rules because there might not be rules.

At the apartment the next weekend, his mother handed him a box. "These are yours if you want them," she said. Inside were the chess set, a small carved elephant from Kenya, and the book. He took the book out and put the bookmark back where his grandfather had left it, page one hundred and twelve.

That night he set up the board in his bedroom, the way Walt always did, white toward himself because Colton was learning. He moved a pawn to e4, Grandpa's favorite opening, the one he called "honest chess."

"Your move," Colton said.

Chloe's father had volunteered to teach her, twice, and twice she had said no, and the second time she had heard him go quiet on the other end of the phone in a way that made her stomach drop. So now it was Dana, an instructor with a lanyard and a clipboard, sitting in the passenger seat of a car with dual brakes, and Chloe was adjusting a mirror that didn't need adjusting.

"Pull out when you're ready," Dana said. "Easy does it."

The driveway emptied onto a quiet street of lampposts and parked sedans. Chloe turned the wheel too early, corrected, and heard a tire kiss the curb. Her hands were sweating through the gloves she had bought for this, which now seemed like an encumbrance, a costume for a person who knew what she was doing. She pulled them off and dropped them in the cup holder.

The first ten minutes went tolerably until they reached the road with traffic. A silver hatchback sat ahead of her at the speed limit, and Chloe, without deciding to, drifted closer. And closer. Dana said nothing. Chloe watched the hatchback's bumper fill the windshield, felt the visceral pull of it, the strange certainty that being near the car in front meant being safe, meant moving, meant keeping pace with everything. Her father used to tailgate on the highway, one hand loose on the wheel, and her mother would say his name in a flat voice and he would ease off without answering. Chloe had always sat in the back and counted the seconds between her own breaths.

"You're crowding that car," Dana said finally. "Pick a fixed point. A sign, a lamppost, anything that isn't moving. When the car ahead passes it, start counting. One-thousand-one, one-thousand-two. If you reach that same point before you finish counting, you're too close. It's called the two-second rule."

Chloe glanced at her, then back at the road. "A lamppost?"

"Any fixed point works."

The next lamppost came up on the right, tall and pale. The hatchback passed it, and Chloe began counting, silently at first, then aloud, because the silence made her rush. One-thousand-one, one-thousand-two. She reached the lamppost before she finished. Her mouth went dry. She eased off the gas and watched the gap widen, silver and ordinary in the morning light.

They drove to the end of the street and back, and Chloe ran the count at every lamppost, every mailbox, once at a faded stop sign whose paint had gone the color of chalk. Some counts she passed easily, and some she barely made, and twice she caught herself drifting forward again, thinking about her phone in her bag, thinking about the form due for housing, thinking about anything except the road. She was beginning to internalize it, the way the counting reached her before the worry did, the way the lamppost arrived as a question rather than a blur. At a red light Dana asked how it was going, and Chloe said, "I keep failing it and fixing it," and Dana laughed and said that was the whole job.

At the far end of the route, Dana told her to pull into a driveway, some stranger's driveway with a basketball hoop and a sprinkler ticking across the grass, and put the car in park. "That's enough for today," she said. "You did fine." Chloe kept her hands on the wheel. She was thinking about her father, about the third time she hadn't called him, about whether a person could be sorry for a choice and still certain it was right, and she could not make those two things sit together no matter how she turned them. Maybe the counting worked like that too: you watched something pass a fixed point, and you measured yourself against it, and the answer told you only whether you were too close, never whether you were where you belonged.

She turned the key and the engine died. "Can we do one more loop?" she asked. "I want to try the lampposts without you telling me."

Dana clicked her pen and wrote something on the clipboard. "Back out when you're ready," she said.

Sierra had claimed the window seat before anyone else was awake, her copy of Pride and Prejudice wedged against the radiator and her notebook open to a page headed with two words in careful capitals: FEMINIST. MARXIST. The assignment was due Monday: choose a lens, apply it to one passage, and be prepared to defend the choice in seminar. She had underlined the scene where Mr Collins proposes to Elizabeth, and then, in the margin, written nothing, because she could not decide what she actually thought.

Her cousin Priya came over at eleven with a thermos and her own battered paperback, because Priya's first-year seminar was doing the same novel and their mothers had decided the cousins should study together whether or not the cousins agreed. Priya dropped onto the floor, poured coffee into the thermos lid, and read the two capitalized words upside down.

"You can't do both," she said. "Pick one and get on with it."

"The professor said we could combine them if we could justify it."

"Then justify it." Priya flipped her book open to a page dog-eared in three places. "My book club argued about Mrs Bennet for forty minutes on Tuesday. Marcus called her a gold-digging caricature. Vulgar, grasping, all of it."

Sierra turned her own book to the early chapters, where Mrs Bennet nags and flutters and mortifies her daughters. "She's written to be laughed at," she said. "Austen keeps letting her embarrass everyone."

"Except," Priya said, and she slid a finger down her page, "Marcus's mother started the meeting by asking whether he'd read the legal background. He hadn't. I hadn't either." She found the passage and turned the book so Sierra could see it was the same paragraph in both editions. "The Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home."

Sierra read the line twice. "None of them. Not even a share?"

"Not a share. When Mr Bennet dies, the house goes to a cousin they've never met. Mrs Bennet and all five girls are out."

Sierra set her coffee down on the windowsill and pulled the notebook onto her knees. She wrote the word entail and boxed it. "So her matchmaking," she said slowly, "isn't greed. It's the only pension plan she has. If the daughters don't marry, there's nothing."

"There's marrying Mr Collins," Priya said. "That's the offer on the table. He's going to own their house."

They sat with that for a moment. Outside, a delivery truck reversed up the street with its warning beep, and the cat pushed between them and settled on Priya's ankle.

Sierra drew two columns. Under the first she wrote property is the trap: the estate is the family's whole solvency, and the law that protects the estate is the same law that disinherits the daughters. Under the second she wrote marriage is the labor market: for women with no inheritance, a husband is an employer, and Elizabeth is refusing the only job offer that guarantees survival. She looked at the columns and thought they belonged together, that separating them would be a lie, that the money and the marriage in this novel were the same machine seen from two sides.

"Here's my problem," she said. "The feminist reading makes Elizabeth the hero for refusing Collins. The Marxist reading makes her refusal a luxury. Charlotte Lucas takes Collins and the reading says she's pragmatic, or compromised, or both, and I can't tell which."

"Maybe she's both," Priya said. "She's twenty-seven and plain and she takes the house."

"That's not an answer, though. That's a shrug."

Priya drank her coffee and considered the notebook. "Your professor really allows combined lenses?"

"If it's a considered position. Not a mush."

"Then don't mush it. Say what each lens sees, and say where they collide, and say you don't know which is truer."

Sierra wrote collision in the margin between the columns and circled it. She read back over her lines about property and labor and thought the phrasing sounded borrowed, like something a textbook would presage with the phrase as we have seen. She crossed out both column headings and started again in plainer words: the law hands the house to a man none of them chose. Charlotte takes the man because she cannot take the house. Elizabeth refuses both and Austen rewards her with Darcy, which is the part Sierra could not make fit any lens at all, because Darcy's ten thousand a year forgives everything the argument has just exposed.

She said this out loud, more or less, and Priya laughed.

"So your conclusion is that Austen cheats?"

"My conclusion is that I have a conclusion for Collins and Charlotte and Mrs Bennet, and Darcy is a separate problem." Sierra closed the notebook and looked at the window, where her own reflection sat ghosted over the street. The seminar was Monday. She had a thesis, two columns, one circle, and a hole shaped like a man with ten thousand a year.

"Start with the entail," Priya said, standing, gathering her thermos. "Lead with the fact. Let them fight about Mrs Bennet after."

Sierra opened the notebook again and, at the top of the first column, wrote: Begin with the house.

Wyatt counted the foil packets in the cooler and found he was one short of what his list required. His mother had handed him the list in the parking lot, folded twice, and told him that if he was going to spend a week at the campsite with his cousin Dez and nobody's parents, he would plan the food like an adult. Seven dinners, cooked in two batches, frozen in the meal kits she had labeled in her slanted handwriting. He had shopped for the ingredients himself, comparing prices on ground turkey for eleven minutes, and had cooked the first batch on Sunday in their kitchen at home while she watched from the doorway and said nothing.

The second batch he cooked at the campsite on Wednesday, on the propane stove, with Dez narrating his errors. The rice caught on the bottom of the pot. The beans were fine. They portioned everything into the foil packets, froze them flat in the ice chest with the last of the freezer packs, and the system worked, more or less, which surprised Wyatt more than he admitted. His whole life, meals had appeared. Now he understood that a week of dinners rested on decisions made days earlier, on thawing times planned backward from hunger, and the planning was what underpinned everything; the cooking itself was almost incidental.

On Friday they hiked the ridge trail and got back late, and Wyatt lay in the tent listening to the campground settle into its quiescent evening state, the generators off, the last kids called in. He was half asleep when he remembered. Thursday's chili was supposed to have moved from the ice chest to the cooler's upper shelf, the thawing shelf, his mother's phrase, twenty-four hours before dinner. It was still down with the freezer packs, a brick of chili at the bottom of everything.

He sat up. Dez was awake; Dez was always awake when Wyatt moved.

"Tomorrow's dinner is still frozen," Wyatt said.

"So thaw it," Dez said, already uninterested.

"Mom said you can't just leave it on the counter."

"Then what did she say?"

Wyatt worked through it in the dark. "She said three ways are safe. The refrigerator, which we don't have. Cold water. Or the microwave, which we also don't have." He heard the shape of his own sentence and realized he had learned it whole, without meaning to. "Not the counter. Frozen food can thaw in the fridge, in cold water, or in the microwave, but not sitting out on the counter."

"Is that metaphysics or is it just a rule?"

"It's a rule."

"Everything's a rule until you ask why," Dez said, which was the kind of thing Dez said, and then he rolled over.

In the morning Wyatt stood at the picnic table with the frozen packet and two buckets. He had read the label, and his mother had drilled one number into him: cold water thawing meant changes of water, which meant he could not simply drop the packet in the lake and go fishing. But he also wanted to hike the loop trail before the day heated up, and the trail would take four hours, and the packet in a bucket of cold water would need his attention partway through. Here were the two ways of thinking he carried: his mother's, where safety was the floor under everything, and Dez's, where rules were negotiable until you personally watched one fail. He set the packet in the first bucket and weighted it with a clean stone so it stayed under.

He changed the water once, dumping the old into the fire pit, refilling from the spigot by the washhouse. Then he and Dez hiked the loop, and on the way back Wyatt thought about how his mother would have solved it, and how Dez would have solved it, and decided that cold water with changes was the position he could defend to both of them. What he could not settle, even walking downhill with the sun on his neck, was whether he believed the rule because he understood it or because she had said it in a voice that ended discussion. He suspected the second and did not like suspecting it.

The chili went into the pot at six and came out steaming at six forty. Dez ate two servings and said it was better than the first batch, which was probably a lie, and Wyatt ate his and thought the burnt-rice taste from Wednesday was gone because he had stirred properly this time, a small competence he had not possessed a week ago. Tomorrow was the last packet, already upstairs on the thawing shelf, where it had been since noon. He washed the pot in the third bucket of water and hung the towel over the line, and Dez said, "Same time next summer, you cook, I carry," and Wyatt said, "Deal."

Charlie arrived at her grandmother's house with a printed assignment sheet, a dying laptop, and eleven hours until her economics presentation. The assignment read, in her teacher's terse hand, "Explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. Use a real example." She had scribbled three false starts on the bus, each one dissolving into circular sentences about supply and demand, and now the whole thing had to be rebuilt from nothing by morning.

She set up at the kitchen table, between her grandmother's jade plant and a bowl of walnuts still in their shells. Her grandfather found her there within ten minutes, as he always did, drawn to the sight of a grandchild doing homework the way his old border collie had been drawn to a moving bicycle. He was garrulous by nature and had grown more so since retiring, and he settled into the chair opposite her with his coffee and began, without preamble, to ask what she was studying.

"Inflation," Charlie said. "And interest rates. It's due tomorrow." She unwrapped a sandwich her grandmother had requisitioned from the deli in town, turkey with too much mustard, and pushed half of it across the table as a tax for his company.

Her grandfather told a story then about a trip he and Charlie's grandmother had taken to Lisbon decades ago, before Charlie's father was even born, when the exchange rate had been so punishing that they had eaten bread and oranges for two days to afford the museum tickets. Charlie half listened, typing, until a phrase snagged her. "It got better halfway through," he was saying. "The rates went up back home and suddenly our money went further over there. Your grandmother noticed it before I did. She notices everything."

Charlie stopped typing. On her laptop sat the trip she herself was planning, a school excursion to Porto in the spring, and pinned above her spreadsheet was the exchange rate she'd checked obsessively since September. It had improved in October, quietly, week by week, right around the time the news had been full of the central bank's rate announcement. She had been glad about it without ever asking why. She pulled up an old article, then another, then the bank's own press release, and found the sentence she needed buried in paragraph six: after the rate increase, foreign savings had flowed in, and the currency had strengthened.

"So if the currency is stronger," she said slowly, mostly to herself, "everything we import gets cheaper. For us. The oranges, the olive oil, the laptop parts." She wrote imports cheaper in her notes and underlined it twice. Her grandfather had drifted on to describing the pine forests outside Lisbon, an entire biome of trees he swore grew out of pure sand, but she wasn't listening anymore. She was following the chain. Stronger currency, cheaper imports, and cheaper imports meant prices stopped climbing, which was the whole thing her teacher had asked for, the entire mechanism hiding inside a spring break spreadsheet.

"It's not the whole thing, though," she said out loud, and her grandfather paused mid-sentence about sand. "Rates go up, people pay more for mortgages, they spend less, that slows prices too. But I can't pretend it's tidy. Half the class will say one thing and half will say the other and they're both kind of right, and nobody actually knows how much of it works or how fast." She hated this about economics, and she also loved it, the way it refused to behave like physics.

At the sink, drying a dish nobody had asked her to dry, her grandmother spoke for the first time in an hour. "I banked the money for that Lisbon trip," she said. "Watched the rate change on the board every morning at the branch. Six weeks it took. Then it moved in four days." She set the dish in the rack and looked at Charlie with an expression that was almost amusement. "Your grandfather tells it like it was luck. It wasn't luck. But it also wasn't anyone's plan. The savings came from everywhere at once, from people we never met."

Charlie wrote that down too, though she wasn't sure yet where it fit, whether a presentation could hold a fact and its shadow at the same time. It was nearly midnight when she rehearsed the first slide for them at the kitchen table, the walnuts still between them, one cracked open and abandoned. She said the strongest version she had, the one with the chain in it, and then she said the honest part, the part about not knowing. Her grandfather applauded with two fingers against his mug. Her grandmother turned off the overhead light, leaving only the small lamp, and said, "Do it again. Slower."

"Everything I have is in the chain," Charlie said. "Rates go up, savings come in, the currency strengthens, imports get cheaper, and that pushes prices down. That's the slide." She squared her notes against the table's edge. "The part I still can't answer is whether it was worth it, and to whom."

Her grandmother sat back down.

Emily's grandmother lived on a quiet crescent in Oshawa where the curb curved gently and the neighbours' hedges made natural parking markers, which was the only reason Emily had agreed to spend the last weekend of August there. Her road test was Tuesday morning. If she failed, she would be starting college in a new city without a licence, dependent on buses and the goodwill of strangers, and she had already promised her roommate a ride to the IKEA.

"Again," her grandmother said from the lawn chair, "but slower on the wheel this time."

Emily pulled alongside the hedge, reversed, and cut the wheel. The back tire kissed the curb with a thump she felt in her teeth. She remonstrated with the car, and with herself, out loud, saying that the car was not the problem, that the car was fine, that her hands were simply two seconds ahead of her eyes. Her grandmother laughed into her iced tea and told her that her grandfather, God rest him, had failed parallel parking twice in 1974 and had never once admitted it.

The memory surfaced without permission: Emily at eleven, perched on the bench seat of that same man's pickup, watching his hands move on the wheel with an unhurried certainty she could not yet name. He had let her steer down the cottage lane, his palm hovering over hers, and when she'd asked how he knew how much to turn, he'd said, "You don't know. You feel the car getting ready, and then you do it." She had thought that was nonsense. Now, at sixteen, with a test in forty-nine hours, she suspected it was the truest thing anyone had ever told her about driving, and she still couldn't do it.

Inside for lunch, her grandmother was on the phone with Mrs. Okafor, the loquacious woman who rented the basement apartment and who was moving to Hamilton in September. Emily caught only fragments while she made sandwiches: something about her new landlord, six hundred dollars, "before I even sign." After her grandmother hung up, Emily asked.

"He wants a damage deposit," her grandmother said. "Six hundred, on top of first and last. Priya's a nurse, she has the money, but it felt off to her. It felt off to me too, so I told her to check. Then I got to thinking about you and your parking and forgot to call her back."

Emily already had her phone out. She found the Ontario landlord and tenant rules and read the relevant line twice, because the words were precise in a way that made her sit up straighter. A landlord could collect a rent deposit, but no more than one month's rent, or one rent period if the rent was paid more often than monthly. A landlord could not charge a damage deposit. Not a smaller one, not a reasonable one. Not at all.

She called Mrs. Okafor herself, because her grandmother was already back outside moving the lawn chair to a different angle of the hedge. "He can ask for a rent deposit," Emily said, reading it back to her almost word for word, "one month's rent at most, or one rent period if you pay more often than monthly. But a damage deposit he can't charge you. It's not allowed here."

There was a silence on the line, and then a low, satisfied sound, the sound of someone whose unease had just been given a shape. Priya thanked her, said she would say the word damage deposit very calmly and watch the man's face, and hung up.

Emily sat for a moment with the strange pleasure of it. She had not argued anyone into rectitude; she had merely looked something up and said it out loud. Yet the looking up mattered, she thought, the way checking your mirrors mattered, the way her grandfather's feeling-the-car-getting-ready mattered. There was a kind of knowledge that waited quietly in you until the moment it was needed, and the job of a person, maybe, was to keep stocking it. Whether she'd actually parallel park on Tuesday, whether Priya's landlord would fold or fight, she couldn't know. Both things stayed uncertain, and she found she could hold them, uncertain, without dropping them.

That evening she made her grandmother sit in the passenger seat and drove her to the on-ramp at Harmony Road. The merge was worse than the parking: the pickup lane was short, the transport trucks were fast, and the first time she accelerated toward the flowing traffic her whole body wanted to brake instead. She merged anyway, lagging, half a lane behind where she should have been, and a driver let her in with a flash of lights.

"Again," her grandmother said, as though they were still at the hedge.

Emily took the next exit, looped back, and came at the ramp a second time, faster, her eyes flicking from mirror to mirror to the gap that was opening beside her like a door being held. She slid into it. In the back seat, invisible until now, her grandmother's purse shifted and settled, and out of it slid the little cloth fox her grandfather used to keep on the dashboard, which she had never known was still there. Emily reached back without looking and set it on the dash, facing forward.

The line at the First Meridian branch moved in stops and starts, and Xavier read the flyer again while he waited. Youth Financial Literacy Day, it said in blue letters, with a contest underneath: explain a current economics topic to a bank officer in under three minutes, and the best explanation won a five-hundred dollar savings bond. Five hundred dollars was a laptop that would last through his first year of college, or most of one, and his mother had already said the family budget could not augur well for anything beyond tuition itself. He had signed his name on the sheet by the door before he could talk himself out of it.

The contest table sat between the loan desk and the brochure rack, and behind it sat a loan officer named Ms. Okafor, who looked up from a clipboard and said, "You're the two o'clock. Xavier, right? Whenever you're ready, tell me how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation." She clicked a timer, and Xavier began the way he had begun in front of his bedroom mirror: rates go up, borrowing costs more, people buy less, prices stop climbing so fast. The words came out flat, strung together like beads without a string, and Ms. Okafor's pen did not move.

"You've listed the steps," she said when he finished, "but my nephew could memorize steps. Why does expensive borrowing actually cool prices? Make me see it." The timer said he had used forty seconds of his three minutes, and now his prepared speech was spent. He stared past her at the mortgage rates posted on the wall, and his truculent first instinct, to insist that he had already answered, gave way to something more useful: the realization that he did not actually understand the thing he had memorized.

He thought of his grandfather, in the summer before tenth grade, sitting on the porch with a newspaper folded to the business section. "You want to know what an interest rate is?" his grandfather had said, setting down his coffee. "It's the price of money itself. Everything has a price, even borrowing." Xavier had nodded then without grasping it, the way he nodded at most things adults said, but the sentence came back to him now standing in the bank, and it landed differently. If money had a price, then the central bank was a merchant who could set that price, and everyone shopping for money, for cars, for houses, for inventory, felt the change.

"Can I start over?" he asked. Ms. Okafor reset the timer and leaned back. "Think of interest as the price of money," he said. "When the central bank raises that price, a loan for a car costs more each month, so some families decide the old car will do. A store owner who wanted to borrow to expand puts it off. Meanwhile saving pays better, so people who were going to spend anyway let the money sit." He was building it as he spoke, testing each plank before putting his weight on it. "Less money chasing the same goods. Sellers can't keep raising prices if the buyers have thinned out."

Ms. Okafor's pen moved for the first time. "Better," she said. "Now, is it certain? Does raising rates always bring inflation down, exactly as intended?" Xavier hesitated. He had a flashback of a different kind then, two nights earlier, hunched over his economics essay at the kitchen table. The assignment was to criticize Ricardo's famous trade example, but the instructions insisted that he first list the simplifying assumptions behind it, and he had found them buried in the chapter: Ricardo's original model treats labor as the only cost of production, and assumes that cost stays the same however much of a good is made. No land, no capital, no factories wearing out, no workers demanding more as output grows. He had written the list out in his own hand before he was permitted to say a word against the model, and his teacher had scrawled across the top of the draft, "You cannot attack a model fairly until you can state what it leaves out."

"No," Xavier said slowly. "It's like the Ricardo essay I'm writing for class. His model makes assumptions to keep the argument clean, and the people who attack it usually attack the assumptions, not the logic. Rates are the same kind of thing. The central bank's plan assumes people and businesses respond to price signals in a predictable way, that debts don't crush anyone on the way down, that nothing else goes wrong at the same time. The logic of less borrowing, less spending, slower prices makes sense to me. What I can't promise is the timing, or who gets hurt while it works through." He felt the heat in his face, because it sounded less impressive than the memorized speech, like an admission rather than a performance.

Ms. Okafor set the pen down entirely. "Do you know how many people walk up to this table and promise me certainty?" she said. "Teenagers with YouTube voices, grown men with podcasts. You're the first one today who told me where the fog starts." She made a note on the clipboard he couldn't read, and Xavier stood there in the middle of the branch, the line of customers shuffling behind him, the teller windows chiming softly, aware that the savings bond might go to some kid with a smoother answer in the next hour.

"Results get mailed Friday," she said, sliding a business card across the table. "And finish that essay. Models are encumbrances until you understand their assumptions, then they're tools." She looked past his shoulder and called, "Next."

Kate had told her mother, twice, that calculus was going fine, and by the second telling she had almost believed it. The kitchen table was hers until six, the hour when her father came home and wanted dinner. She had the textbook open to the chapter on integrals, a page of rectangles drawn under a curve like teeth, and a worksheet that asked for the area beneath f of x equals x squared from zero to three. She could do the antiderivative. She had memorized the rule on the bus, the exponent climbing, the exponent descending, and she wrote x cubed over three with the confidence of someone copying a recipe.

The problem came on the back of the sheet, the last one, marked with a star. Find and classify the critical points of f of x equals x cubed. Kate took the derivative, set it to zero, and got x equals zero. Then, in the blank, she wrote maximum, because that was what the tutor's examples had always been. She checked her answer the way she checked most things, by wanting it to be right.

Her brother Danny was at the counter eating cereal at four in the afternoon, which he did on the days he had skipped school. He was twenty, home from a job he maligned so constantly that Kate had stopped asking about it. "You drew it yet," he said, not a question, milk on his chin. He had failed calculus twice and spoke about it with the affection people reserve for a sport they almost made varsity in.

"Drew what."

"The one with the star. Graph it first." He came around the table, leaned over her shoulder, and she could smell the cereal on him. "Mr. Ferreira used to say that. We called him a charlatan because he made us draw everything. Then I got the same question on the exam and I couldn't draw it fast enough."

Kate didn't want to draw it. Drawing felt ancillary, decoration for people who couldn't do the algebra, and the algebra had already told her maximum. But Danny pulled the pencil out of her hand and put a dot at the origin, and she said fine, fine, and plotted the points herself. Minus one gave minus one. One gave one. Minus two gave minus eight. She connected them and the curve went up through the dot like a road passing through a town without stopping. The derivative was zero at zero, she was sure of that, she had checked it twice, and still the graph kept rising, straight through the point she had labeled a maximum.

She erased the word maximum and sat there with the point unclassified.

Danny watched from the counter now, his spoon idle. He had told the story of that exam many times, and each time the version changed. In the first telling, years ago, he had failed because he hadn't drawn the graph. In the current version he had drawn it and been marked wrong anyway, which Kate suspected was the part he was inventing. He was not a liar exactly; he was someone who tried out pasts until one fit. She had caught him at it at Thanksgiving, describing a boss who had since become two different bosses. He believed each telling while it lasted.

"You going to write nothing," Danny said.

"The derivative's zero there," Kate said. "But it's not a max. It's not a min either. It just goes through."

"So write that."

"There's no box for that." There wasn't. The worksheet wanted a word, and the curve offered only passage. She thought about telling her mother that calculus was going fine, and about the tutor who had told her, once, that the examples were always extrema because extrema were the pretty cases. She had nodded as though she understood. She hadn't. She understood a little more now, sitting with a point that was flat for an instant and climbing the whole way anyway, and she noticed she couldn't say which had failed, the algebra or her reading of it.

Danny rinsed his bowl and put it in the rack, the wrong rack, and left the kitchen without saying anything else. Kate copied the graph onto a clean sheet, drew the tangent line at the origin lying flat while the curve rose past it on both sides, and wrote underneath, in small letters, "derivative zero at x = 0, but the function keeps rising through that point." Then she heard her father's key in the door.

"What's for dinner," he called.

Justine spread the binder open on the bleachers at the far end of the soccer field, where the paint had worn to a color that was no longer white. She had four days before the club's Friday deadline, the day Coach Reyes wanted every returning player to submit a written weekly training plan, warm-ups and rest days included, before preseason camp began. Justine had never planned anything larger than a homework schedule, and she suspected her first draft, six days of running and drills, was the kind of document that looked diligent and was actually a small act of self-sabotage.

The problem was that she didn't know what rest was for. She understood it the way she understood weekends, as an absence, and an absence couldn't be trained for. She was still adjudicating between two versions of the week, one with hard days stacked at the front and one spread evenly, when her younger sister Priya came limping across the grass in cleats two sizes too big.

"Careful," Justine said. "You'll turn an ankle in those."

"Can't be worse." Priya lowered herself onto the bench with the caution of someone much older. "I can barely walk."

Priya had gone to her first real pickup game on Tuesday, seventy minutes of full sprinting after a summer of nothing, and she had come home glowing, barely sore, telling everyone the whole thing. Now it was Thursday, and she was walking like her hamstrings had been replaced with rope.

"You felt fine Tuesday," Justine said slowly.

"I felt amazing Tuesday. That's the weird part. It's worse now than it was right after."

Justine turned this over. She had always assumed soreness was an immediate bill, paid on the spot, the body's receipt for what you'd just done. But Priya's bill had arrived two days late. She wrote in the margin of her draft, peaks 24 to 72 hours after, then underlined nothing, wanting the numbers bare on the page. "Delayed-onset muscle soreness," Priya read over her shoulder. "That's what the girl with the physio ball called it. She said everybody gets it after the first hard session."

So the body kept its own calendar, and it wasn't hers. Justine looked at her stacked-front draft again and saw it whole: if she trained hard Monday, the worst of the ache would land Tuesday through Thursday, exactly when she had scheduled the next two hardest sessions. Her careful plan would have her doing speed work on legs already seized two days after Monday's efforts. It was deleterious in a way she hadn't been able to see before, because the damage arrived disguised as distance, delayed far enough from its cause that she would never have connected them. Her old way of thinking, that effort was paid for immediately, had quietly been wrong, and the new way of thinking, that the bill traveled, made her want to rebuild the entire week around a lag she couldn't feel.

She restructured it. Hard Monday, easy Tuesday and Wednesday, hard Thursday, easy Friday, rest Saturday entirely, and a warm-up before everything, which she had skipped in every draft until now because it hadn't seemed like it did anything. Maybe it was the same error again, an effect separated from its cause. She didn't know. That was the part she kept circling: she couldn't yet tell which other invisible delays were hiding in the week, whether the Saturday rest would pay off the following Monday or whether rest was less like an investment and more like simple mercy. The solvency of the whole plan was unproven; she had no way to know if it could meet its obligations until she lived inside it for a season, and no spreadsheet she could build in four days would change that.

"Why are you smiling at your binder like that?" Priya asked.

"Because Tuesday you felt great, and today you can't walk, and I only just found out those two facts belong to each other." Justine closed the binder and stood. "Come on. Warm-up, then an easy lap. Easy. Nothing that shows up on Sunday."

Priya groaned, but she pulled herself up and started a wobbling high-knee skip toward the far goal, and Justine followed her out onto the grass, watching the way her sister's stride evened out by the halfway line, one small piece of evidence arriving exactly when it chose to.

The camera above the pastry case was small and matte black, and Arianna had worked at Corvo's for five weeks before she noticed it at all. She noticed it on a Tuesday because Dev, the closing manager, paused behind the register and tilted his head toward it. "Corporate installed those last month," he said. "They say it's for training. It records us making drinks, and some software scores the shots we pull." He said this without heat, the way he reported the weather, and moved on to restacking cups.

After that she could not stop noticing it. Her hands felt slower over the portafilter, though she had measured the same dose a hundred times. When she dropped a stir stick she looked up first, checking whether the little lens had registered the fault. By Thursday she was wiping the counter in long, even strokes even when no one was sitting at it, and she understood, in a sidelong way, that the camera had changed her without ever speaking.

A regular named Marcus came in at four, as he always did, with a battered paperback and an order he never varied. He was a philosophy student at the community college, reticent about most things, though he liked to argue gently with whoever worked the counter. That afternoon Arianna asked him, almost against her will, whether a camera could make you a different person just by existing. "That's an old question," Marcus said, pleased. "Look up Jeremy Bentham's panopticon. His 1791 prison design. A central tower in the middle, and the inmates can be watched at any time without ever knowing whether they actually are." He stirred his americano. "The point isn't the guard. The point is the not knowing."

She looked it up on her break, hunched over her phone at the corner table. The drawings were clean and terrible, a ring of cells around one bright circle of tower. She read that prisoners, unable to tell when eyes were on them, came to police themselves, and she thought of her own even, performative counter wipes, and felt a small cold recognition settle in her chest. Not shame exactly. Something more like being caught in an argument she hadn't known she was having.

That same week the new scheduling system arrived. Corporate had rolled out software that built the rota automatically, taking in availability, sales data, and something the memo called "team performance metrics," whose provenance no one at the store could explain. Dev's hours were cut first. He was thirty-one and had been at Corvo's six years, and the software had, as far as anyone could tell, weighted the camera scores. "I train the new hires," he told Arianna on Friday, counting out change. "A machine watched me make a cappuccino and decided I'm bad at my job. And nobody can tell me what I did wrong, because nobody knows what it was watching for."

Arianna had a physics test the next morning, but she stayed an hour past her shift, sitting with Dev while he closed. They pulled up the scheduling dashboard on the store laptop and clicked into every menu. The system offered no reasons, only rankings. She understood, dimly, that an algorithm's judgment could be as unanswerable as Bentham's tower, except that this one also signed the paychecks. She kept thinking she ought to be able to predicate an appeal on some fact, some number she could point to, and kept finding that the facts had dissolved into the software's opinion of them.

That night she wrote an email to the regional manager, drafting it twice before sending. "I've worked here since September," she wrote, "and I've never been told what the camera measures or how the schedule is made. Mr. Okafor has trained every barista in this store. If the system disagrees, I'd like to see the reasons. If there are no reasons, I'd like to know why we're pretending there are." She read it over, wondered if it was too sharp, and sent it before she could soften it. Then she went back to her physics, and the equations came slowly.

On Sunday the reply came, short and corporate, thanking her for her engagement and noting that the metrics were proprietary. But Monday's schedule posted with Dev's hours restored, unexplained, and when he saw it he stood very still in front of the sheet for a moment before saying, "Huh." He didn't thank her. He made her a drink off the menu, something with cinnamon he'd invented years ago, and set it on the counter in front of her.

Arianna took it to the corner table, under the camera she still couldn't tell was on. Marcus came in at four and asked how the panopticon research was going. "It wasn't research," she said. "It was just my job." He laughed and opened his paperback, and she sat with the cooling drink, still unsure whether she'd won anything or only been handed a quieter version of the same arrangement. The lens sat above the pastry case, small and matte black, watching or not. She picked up the cup and took a long sip.

The festival on Carroll Street smelled of honey and frying dough, and Madeline had exactly one hour before her grandmother's bus arrived from the church on Fifth Avenue. One hour, and she still hadn't found the gift. Her family had celebrated Christmas on December 25 like everyone else on their block, with the plastic tree and the socks, but her grandmother kept the old date, and this year she had asked, almost shyly, whether Madeline might come to the street festival with her afterward. Madeline had said yes before she understood what she was agreeing to.

The cold seemed to invigorate the crowd rather than thin it. Women in headscarves sold pirozhki from folding tables, a man in a fur hat argued cheerfully with a teenager over the price of painted wooden ornaments, and somewhere behind the stalls a choir was warming up, the basses humming low enough that Madeline felt it in her ribs. She moved through it all with her hands in her pockets, noticing how the whole street had decided that Christmas was still coming, that the neighbors' discarded trees lying frozen at the curb meant nothing here.

"You look lost," said a girl behind a table of jam jars, maybe nineteen, with mittens that had lost their fingers. "Lost people always walk in circles. You've passed my table three times."

"I'm trying to find a present for my grandmother before her bus gets here. Fifty-one minutes." Madeline said it and heard how ridiculous it sounded, and the girl laughed, which made it sound even more ridiculous.

"Sit," the girl said, pointing at a milk crate. "Tell me about her."

So Madeline told her: that Babushka Vera had been married in a church with towers like upturned onions, that she still crossed herself in a way that made Madeline think of water, that last week she'd said something Madeline couldn't stop turning over. She'd said, "We have Christmas on January 7, because our church keeps December 25 on the old Julian calendar, two weeks behind yours." Madeline had assumed, all her life, that the family was simply late, or disorganized, or stubborn. "I never asked why two Christmases exist in one family," she said now. "I just got used to opening my stocking while she was still fasting."

The jam girl, whose name turned out to be Anya, nodded without surprise. "My mother does the same thing. In January the stores put everything on sale, so we eat better than the December people." She leaned across the jars. "But you said your grandmother is coming from Fifth Avenue. That bus stops running early on festival days. Check."

Madeline checked. The bus, according to a schedule taped inside a festival booth, would stop at the corner at six o'clock, not seven, because the street was closing for the procession. Which meant she had eleven minutes, not fifty-one, and her grandmother would arrive at a corner with no one standing on it. She stood up so fast she knocked over the milk crate.

"Go," Anya said, but then, as Madeline turned, "wait," and pressed something into her hand. A small jar, dark, unlabeled. "Rowanberry. My grandmother's recipe. Tell yours a girl at the festival gave it to you, and she'll know exactly what that means." Madeline ran the six blocks with the jar cupped against her stomach like a small heart, past the choir now singing in full voice, past a man selling candles who called out "Almost too late!" in a tone of such theatrical grief that she laughed out loud while running, which hurt her throat in the cold air.

She reached the corner as the bus hissed open its doors, and there was Babushka Vera in her gray coat, looking small and certain, the kind of stoicism that Madeline understood now was not hardness but a way of carrying things. "You came," her grandmother said, as if Madeline had done something remarkable by standing on a cold corner. Madeline held out the jar, and her grandmother took off one glove to touch the glass, reading the jam's color like a language Madeline didn't speak yet. "Rowanberry," Vera said softly. "In January, always rowanberry." Behind them the procession was beginning, and Anya, Madeline realized, would be closing her table now, stacking her obsolescent milk crates for another year. "Tell me about this girl," her grandmother said, tucking the jar inside her coat, right against her heart, and taking Madeline's arm.

The essay was due Friday, and by Tuesday Rachel had written the word "historiography" eleven times without once believing it. The assignment sheet asked her to trace how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, which sounded, at first, like a bus route: here is stop one, here is stop two, please remain seated. Mr. Okafor had eviscerated her first attempt with a single comment in the margin, "You are narrating the Revolution, not the arguments about it," and she had sat with that sentence for two days the way you sit with a splinter.

The class trip on Wednesday was to the Livingston House, a Georgian mansion whose owner had gone bankrupt importing fake Sèvres porcelain and whose ballroom now hosted travelling exhibitions. This one was called Liberty and Its Discontents, a title someone had clearly enjoyed. Rachel's friend Priya drifted toward a case of miniature guillotine souvenirs, actual objects Victorians had kept on their mantels, and said, "People are strange," with the satisfaction of someone confirming a long-held thesis.

The argument started near the wall of timelines. Danny Okonkwo, who had read everything and retained it the way velcro retains wool, was holding forth to a cluster of classmates. "The Terror was a detour," he was saying. "1789 was about rights and constitutions. Then the war came, the invasion threat, and everything derailed. You separate the ideals from the accident."

"You're describing the Revolution you wish had happened," said Marcus, a boy from the other seminar group whom Rachel knew mostly as a source of unwanted footnotes. "The violence was there from the start. You don't get 1789 without it."

"That's a claim, not an argument," Danny said.

Rachel, who had been standing there with her notebook open and nothing in it, felt the recalcitrant shape of her essay suddenly shift. She had been treating the interpretations as beads on a string, each era handing the next its verdict. But here were two people arguing in front of her as though the question were alive, and the question was not what happened in 1793 but whether what happened in 1789 already contained it.

"Schama," Marcus said, as if the name settled things. "Citizens. It came out in 1989, for the bicentenary, and he argued that violence was an essential part of the Revolution from 1789 onward. Not a betrayal of it. Part of it."

"That's one book," Danny said.

"It's a pretty big book."

Rachel wrote the name down. In the coach back, she pressed Marcus for details and he gave them with the reluctance of someone surrendering ammunition. She spent that evening not writing but reading, and the reading was not the smooth accumulation she had planned. Schama sat in her mind next to the textbook narrative of noble ideals corrupted by circumstance, and the two refused to merge, like oil in water she kept stirring.

The confounder, she decided on Thursday, was that everyone sounded persuasive alone. The nineteenth-century writers she'd found were themselves reacting to their own revolutions and restorations, so their Revolution was partly a mirror. Schama published at the bicentenary, a moment when a country was throwing parades, which made his emphasis a kind of counterpoint to celebration, or maybe just a version of the same argument England had been making since 1790, or maybe neither, and here Rachel stalled again, because the honest version of her essay required saying which, and she did not know which.

She went to find Danny at lunch, partly to be fair and mostly because she wanted to watch him lose. "You read Schama?" she asked.

"Skimmed him." He peeled an orange with unnecessary violence. "He's good on crowds. He wants the violence to be the story, though. Everybody picks a Revolution."

"Maybe that's the essay," Priya offered, stealing a segment. "Not who's right. Why each of them needed the Revolution to be their way."

Rachel considered this. It had the appeal of an exit, and she distrusted it for exactly that reason. If she wrote only that historians were creatures of their moments, she could eviscerate all of them from a safe altitude and commit to nothing, which was its own kind of dishonesty, the smug kind. The better essay, she thought, would stake out a position and then admit where the ground was soft.

Friday morning she wrote the last paragraph at her kitchen table while her mother vacuumed around her in widening circles. She argued that the Revolution's meaning had been contested from the beginning because the Revolution itself kept changing, and that the interpretations changed as their questions did; then, in the final sentences, she took Schama's side, provisionally, on the grounds that a revolution which required the crowd in the street from its first weeks had already chosen a instrument the crowd would keep using, and then she wrote a sentence beginning "What remains uncertain," and let it stand.

Mr. Okafor returned the essays the following week. He put hers down last, held it a moment, and said only, "Come see me about the last page." She went, expecting the worst, and found him pointing at the uncertainty sentence with the cap of his pen.

"This is the strongest thing in here," he said. "Most students would have cut it."

"I nearly did."

"Well," he said, and slid it back across the desk, and on the cover page, beside the grade, he had drawn a small and unmistakable guillotine.

The interview workshop was held in the cafeteria on a Wednesday, and Thomas sat with the robotics team at the long table by the windows. Ms. Reyes had secured ten mock interviews with a recruiter from Halden Manufacturing, and everyone who wanted the summer internship had to do one. Thomas wanted it. So did Dara, who had built the arm assembly for their competition robot and who had, at the regional finals, refused to let anyone else touch it. The arm had jammed in the second match because Dara had skipped the torque check, and nobody had told him, because Dara's moods were mercurial and nobody wanted to be the one who set him off. They had lost by four points.

Ms. Reyes, who could expatiate for a full period on the history of the tournament if you let her, kept this short. She handed out a packet and a school indemnity form, the one parents signed so the district was not liable for equipment taken off campus. "Sign it, get it signed, bring it Thursday," she said. "That's all from me." Then she left them with the packets, which was unusual, and Thomas read his at the table.

The packet listed sample questions. Priya, across from him, read one aloud. "Behavioral interview questions, like 'Tell me about a time when...', are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior." She said it flat, the way you read a definition off a page, then added, "So they're going to ask about stuff we actually did." Thomas looked at the list. Tell me about a time you failed. Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate. He had a failure, the arm, but it wasn't only his, and the teammate he'd disagreed with was Dara, except he hadn't disagreed with him out loud. He'd said nothing.

That evening he drafted an answer anyway. He wrote that the arm had jammed, that the team had lost, and that he had learned to speak up early. Then he crossed out the last part, because it wasn't true yet, and a recruiter asking about past behavior would be asking about a past in which he had stayed quiet. On Thursday he signed the indemnity form, got his mother's signature, and found Dara in the lab before the interview, tightening a bolt on the rebuilt arm.

"I have to tell you something about regionals," Thomas said. Dara's shoulders went stiff, the way they did. "The arm jammed because the torque check got skipped. I saw it wasn't on the checklist and I didn't say anything. That part's on me. But the check itself, that's on you, and I'm telling you now because we have a tournament in March and I want us to still be a team when it's over."

Dara held the wrench a long time without using it. "You could have told me at regionals."

"You'd have thrown something."

"I would not have thrown something." He set the wrench down, which was its own admission. "Fine. The check is mine. Say the specific thing, not the thing about my temper."

"The torque spec is in the build log, page nine. Twenty minutes, before every match. That's the specific thing."

Dara wrote it on his hand. At the mock interview that afternoon, the recruiter, a woman named Okafor with a badge and a legal pad, asked him the question about a time he had let a teammate down. Thomas told the torque story, including his own silence, and she wrote for a while and said, "That's a usable answer." He didn't know until later what a usable answer was worth.

The twist came two weeks after Halden posted the placements. Thomas got the internship, and so did Dara, and at the first team meeting Dara stood up with the build log and read the new checklist he'd written, torque spec on page nine, his initials in the margin of every row. Then Priya, who had been at the interview day, told Thomas what she'd heard through the wall of the counseling office. When Okafor had asked Dara about a time someone gave him hard feedback, Dara had told the torque story from his side. He'd said, "A teammate told me my process failed, and his, and then he told me exactly how to fix mine, and we both got hired off the same loss."

Thomas sat with that. He didn't know if he'd earned it or if Dara had just said the one true thing available to both of them, and he suspected the answer was that there was no difference. He opened his notebook to the page where the crossed-out sentence was, the one about speaking up early, and left it crossed out, and turned to the March checklist instead.

Dara tossed him a wrench. "Page nine," he said. "You check it this time."

Justin clipped the tuner to the head of his cello the way Ms. Ferreira had shown him, but he waited before plucking the string, because his father's voice was still in his head. His father called tuners crutches, little plastic ideologues that wanted every note to be a number and nothing else, and he had made Justin tune by ear for three years, matching the open strings against the piano in the living room until the beats between the notes slowed and finally vanished. That was the true way, his father said. The machine had no opinion worth having.

Ms. Ferreira, meanwhile, was insouciant about the whole question. She kept the tuner in a drawer with the rosin and the spare bridge, pulled it out when a student sounded sour, shrugged when they didn't. "Play your A," she said now, and Justin played the open A, the tuner's needle settling dead center on the screen. He felt a small, absurd pride, as if his ear had been audited and passed.

"Good. Now the A at the top of that scale we worked on. Fourth position."

He shifted up the fingerboard, found the note, drew the bow across it, and the tuner did something he hadn't expected. The screen didn't read 440 anymore. It read 880. He played it again, watching the needle hold steady at the new number, then slid back down to the open string and watched it fall to 440. Down, 440. Up, 880. Exactly double, both times, the needle agreeing with itself like a witness who never changes a story.

"Ms. Ferreira," he said, "why does it say eight hundred eighty up there and four hundred forty down here? It's the same letter."

She looked up from the music she was marking. "That's what an octave is. Same name, double the number." She tapped the screen once. "Play it again if you want."
