He played it three more times, up and down, and she let him, going back to her pencil, because she had learned long ago that a student who found something on his own would remember it longer than anything she said. The lesson after that was the duet, and the duet was the actual problem, because Sabrina from his orchestra class had agreed to play it with him at the November recital only if he could hit the high octave passage cleanly. She had said it kindly, which somehow made it worse. "The melody goes up an octave there," she'd said. "You always slide into it flat."

He had slid into it flat at every lesson for a month. Ms. Ferreira had tried singing the arrival note, had tried having him drone the low A while she played the high one, had tried metaphors about reaching for a glass on a high shelf. Nothing held. And now, in the studio with the tuner clipped to his scroll, he began to wonder whether the machine his father distrusted might actually tell him something his ear could not yet hear.

Here is what he worked out, slowly, in the twenty minutes of practice time Ms. Ferreira gave him at the end of the lesson while she wrote out next week's assignment. The low A was 440. The high A was 880, exactly twice, a fixed and public fact. That meant the octave wasn't a feeling, wasn't a metaphor about shelves or sunlight or anything Ms. Ferreira's folksier students might have preferred. It was a specific target, and a target could be drilled at. He played the low A, looked at 440, then shifted up and tried to land the high one so the needle swung to 880 without wandering. First attempt, 843. Second, 902, sharp, which surprised him; he'd assumed he was always flat, and apparently his errors were more imaginative than that. By the eighth attempt he hit 880 twice in a row, and his hand, without his permission, seemed to memorize the distance.

But he also noticed something the tuner could not do. When he watched the needle, his tone went dead, the bow arm stiffening while his eyes did the listening. When he closed his eyes and thought 880 rather than looked for it, the note came out rounder, more alive, though sometimes he still missed. So the machine gave him the map and his ear had to drive the car, or something like that; he didn't have the sentence yet, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it might take years to finish.

His father picked him up outside the studio, saw the tuner still clipped to the scroll, and raised one eyebrow in a way that adumbrated an argument about the purity of musical tradition, a lecture Justin could already recite from memory.

"Before you start," Justin said, getting into the passenger seat, cello case thumping into the back, "let me tell you what eight hundred eighty means."

"I know what my insurance premium means, if that's what you're asking."

Justin laughed, then played the two notes in the air, plucking them on his knee, one low, one exactly double. "Sabrina's going to hear this at the recital and owe me a milkshake."

The radiator under Nadia's window made a sound like a spoon in a kettle, and Laura had stopped noticing it until Nadia's brother Samir came in from the balcony with a stack of papers and dropped them on the table between the cereal bowls.

"They want it in writing by Friday," he said. He was twenty-four, three years into a job at the hospital, and he was trying to buy a flat. "The bank's agreed in principle. It's real, more or less."

Nadia picked up a page and turned it sideways. "More or less is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

Laura had come over to work on their presentation for English, a comparison of two war poets that neither of them had started, and the folder of poems was still zipped in her bag. But the papers had a gravity to them, columns of figures and a stamp in the corner, and she found herself leaning across the table before she'd decided to.

"The whole thing's four hundred and twenty," Samir said, tapping a number. "I've got sixty saved. That sixty is the down payment, the part I pay upfront so I borrow less. The loan covers the rest, and then it's mine, in theory, in twenty-five years."

"It'll never be yours, you'll be paying the interest forever," Nadia said, in the jaundiced way she said everything about money, as though the whole economy had personally disappointed her. "You should just rent like Mum does. Renting's simpler. One deposit at the start, that's it."

The word snagged somewhere in Laura's head. "Wait," she said. "Deposit. Like the deposit we paid on this flat? The one you get back when you leave?"

Samir looked at her for a second, and then he laughed, not unkindly. "No, different thing entirely. Same word. When I was in Manchester the adviser kept saying deposit, and I thought he meant my renter's deposit from the old place, like I'd somehow use that. Took me half the meeting to work out we were talking about two different things." He pulled a pen from behind the radiator, where Nadia stored everything, and wrote on the back of an envelope. "Here. Down payment. That's what we call it. A deposit's the British word for the same thing. The part of the home's price the buyer pays upfront, so less must be borrowed."

"That's a terrible system," Laura said. "Two meanings of one word for the two biggest payments of your life."

"It's the phonetics that get you," Samir said, pleased with himself. "Same sounds, same stress, and your brain just files it under the first thing you ever learned the word for. I sat there nodding along like I understood."

Nadia went to the kitchen for tea, and Laura read the papers more slowly than she'd read anything in weeks. There was a line for the mortgage, which she'd always thought of as one thing and now saw was a loan like any other, something a bank gave you and then watched you repay with an expression of professional patience. There was a line for the survey, the legal fees, the insurance. There was the sixty thousand, marked as the buyer's own contribution, and beside it the borrowing, which was three hundred and sixty, and she did the subtraction twice because the number seemed too large to be a subtraction a person could live inside of.

Her parents rented. She had watched her mother photograph every scuff on every wall the day they moved into their house, because the deposit came back only if the walls matched the photographs, and she had understood, at thirteen, that a certain amount of money belonged to her family only in the sense that it was being held somewhere, waiting, possibly forever. She had thought that was what money did when it came to housing. It waited. Now she saw there was another whole architecture underneath it, one where money went in first and bought a share of something, and the waiting happened afterward, for decades, in monthly pieces.

Samir was on the phone now by the window, saying "yes, I can transfer it Monday" in a voice pitched lower than his normal one, and Nadia came back with two mugs and set one down in front of Laura without asking.

"Don't let him make it sound heroic," Nadia said quietly. "Mum says the bank owns it till the end. He says he owns it from the start. They've been arguing about it since Easter."

"They're both right, maybe," Laura said. "Or it's both at once, and which one you are depends on which month you ask." She turned the envelope over, where Samir had written the two words side by side, down payment, deposit, and then a small arrow between them. She took out her phone and photographed it, telling herself it was for the presentation folder, knowing it wasn't.

"Whose are you?" Nadia asked. "The renters or the buyers?"

"I don't know yet. I don't even know what I'll be earning." Laura said it plainly, because it was true, and because around Nadia she could say true things without dressing them up. "I like that he's paying toward something. I like that Mum can leave any year she wants. I can't get both."

Samir hung up and turned around, holding the envelope. "You took a photo of my handwriting?"

"It was good handwriting," Laura said, and pulled the poetry folder out of her bag at last, and unzipped it on top of the mortgage papers. "Now explain to us what a war poet and a bank have in common, because we have six hours and no thesis."

Samir sat down and stole a spoonful of Nadia's cereal. "They both know exactly how much everything costs," he said, "and neither of them ever says it out loud."

Grandpa's house smelled of cedar and old vinyl, and in the back room stood a violin that had belonged to Great-Uncle Theodore, who had, according to family legend, once played for a room of unimpressed chickens. Ryan had inherited the instrument in June, along with a beginner's book and a standing invitation to practice there on Saturdays, because his apartment had thin walls and a neighbor who referred to herself, without apparent irony, as a connoisseur of silence.

On the third Saturday, his nine-year-old cousin Priya showed up with her own violin, half-sized and sparkly at the chin rest. She had a lesson nearby and their grandfather had offered to keep her for the afternoon. While Ryan wrestled through a page of quarter notes, chin cramped, eyes pinned to the staff, Priya wandered to the piano in the hallway and picked out, plink by plink, the melody of a commercial she liked. Then she did the same thing on her violin, from memory, in tune.

"How," Ryan said, not as a question so much as an accusation.

"I just hear it," Priya said, shrugging, as if he had asked how she breathed. "Can you play the ice cream song?" She hummed it. He could not. His fingers knew where to go only when the notes were printed in front of him, marching in orderly black ranks. Take the paper away and he had nothing, which was galling in a way he couldn't quite articulate to a fourth grader.

He thought of the autumn audition, back before he owned a violin at all, when the middle school orchestra teacher had asked him to echo three notes on the piano and he had laughed nervously and said, "I'm more of a reader." He hadn't gotten the seat. Mr. Kessler hadn't even looked up from his clipboard, just said "Mm," in a tone Ryan still remembered with a small internal wince. Priya would have echoed those notes and then harmonized with them out of pure boredom.

"What does your teacher do," he asked, "in lessons? Do you get books?" Priya said yes, actually, a red one, but they mostly copied her teacher first, listening and repeating, and they didn't read the notes yet, even though she'd been playing two years. Ryan frowned at that. Two years without reading seemed, at first glance, like a scam, or at minimum a doctrinaire way of doing things, some rigid philosophy imposed on small children. He was halfway into composing a lecture about it when Priya said, "It's the Suzuki method. My mom says it's how you learn to talk first, before you read."

He opened his mouth to argue and then closed it, because the comparison landed before he could get defensive. Nobody handed a baby a phonics workbook. Babies heard, imitated, garbled, improved. Priya's fingers had a vocabulary his didn't, though he could decode anything on the page, name the key, count the rhythm. She spoke; he read aloud, slowly. Neither was worse, exactly. They were just built in a different order, and the uncomfortable, interesting truth was that he would need both, and Priya would too, eventually, when the red book gave way to actual notation.

Their grandfather appeared in the doorway holding two glasses of lemonade and his own want, which he had been carrying around all summer: he wanted to hear Theodore's violin play "Shenandoah" just once before he stopped being able to say the sentence casually. He had assumed Ryan would learn it from sheet music, properly, the way their family did things. Now he looked between the two of them, and Priya, who loved an audience more than she loved dessert, offered to learn it by ear if he would hum it. "You hum terribly," Ryan told him. "Debatable," said Grandpa, and hummed anyway, wavering on the high part.

Priya got the phrase in four tries. Grandpa acceded to her rhythm, slowing his humming to her tempo rather than the reverse, which Ryan understood was a kind of surrender for a man who conducted from his armchair. Then Priya taught the phrase to Ryan, note by note, no paper, and he got it wrong, and wrong, and then, suddenly, right, and the sound of it coming out of Theodore's old violin made all three of them go quiet. "Again," Grandpa said, and set down his lemonade.

The festival occupied the whole of Rosenstein Park, and Nathan had been assigned to the debate tent for two hours, which he suspected was his rabbi's way of keeping him from the food stalls. The topic on the chalkboard read: Does an ancient rule still bind us when the world it was written for is gone? His opponent was Dvorah Katz, a college freshman home for the holiday, who kept her notes in a leather folder and had already won the first round against a boy from the synagogue across town. Nathan's folder held one index card, a photocopy, and his phone.

"When you build a new house," Dvorah said, opening, "you shall make a parapet for your roof, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if anyone falls from it. Deuteronomy twenty-two, verse eight. A lovely verse. It is also about a flat roof in the ancient Near East, where people slept and dried figs on their rooftops. We live in houses with pitched shingled roofs nobody stands on. The verse described a world we can't visit. Reverence for a text does not require us to pretend its roof is ours."

Nathan had prepared something about timeless principles, and he delivered it, and it came out sounding exactly like the bromide it was, a comfort offered to people who didn't need comforting. Dvorah smiled without malice. From the third row, his little sister Miri mouthed, You're losing.

But then a man in the audience, farmer's arms folded, raised his hand and said the argument wasn't hypothetical for him. Last spring his nephew had nearly drowned in the cistern behind his barn, and he wanted to know whether Nathan's tradition had anything to say about that, or whether it only worried itself with roofs. The tent got quiet. Dvorah looked interested, which was worse than contempt.

Nathan looked at his photocopy. He had found the roof verse three nights earlier, in his kitchen, half doing homework, half not, and it had struck him as strange in a way he couldn't name, a law about architecture that cared about a stranger's body falling. He had gone looking and found the tradition's own extension of it: not just the parapet, but other hazards on one's property, the same obligation carried outward from the roof to whatever else could hurt somebody. He had meant to save it for his rebuttal. Now it was the whole rebuttal.

"The verse is about a roof," he said. "But the tradition never let it stay a roof. It took the parapet and extended it to other dangers on your own property. So the question isn't whether ancient people had flat roofs. It's whether you have a cistern." He paused, because the next part he was still working out himself. "You can interpolate from the rule, or you can file it away as history. The text itself doesn't tell you which. It just says: someone might fall, and you would be responsible." He looked at the farmer. "It doesn't say the person who falls is your nephew. It doesn't say they're family at all."

Dvorah took her phone out during the break, and afterward she showed Nathan what she'd found: a message from her ethics professor from last semester, who had assigned them the roof verse the first week of class. In it she had written to him asking how a rule so specific could ground a modern duty, and he had replied with a question instead of an answer: When you read a law that protects a body you'll never meet, what exactly is out of date about it? She had gotten an A on the paper and still didn't know if she believed her own conclusion, which she said was the honest way to leave it.

They were asked to summarize, and Nathan found that he couldn't, or wouldn't, close the thing the way a summary wants to be closed. He said the parapet rule looked small and turned out not to be; he said he had come in believing either that old rules ruled or that they didn't, and now he held something with more hinges on it, and he was not going to pretend that was the same as certainty. Dvorah said the seismic shift in how people live is real, and the rabbis who extended the roof rule knew that, and extended it anyway, which she called either wisdom or evasion, depending on the day. The audience voted, and it split almost exactly in half, and the moderator declared the round a draw.

Afterward the farmer shook Nathan's hand and said he was putting a grate over the cistern next week, law or no law. Miri appeared with two paper trays of kibbeh and gave one to Dvorah too, an act of diplomacy Nathan suspected was aimed at him. He walked them both toward the ferris wheel, the photocopy folded into his back pocket, still warm from his hand, and when Dvorah asked what he'd argue if they did this again next year, he said, "Ask me then. I'll have read more."

"Try the verse about the bird's nest," she said, and pointed at the line for the wheel.

Kyle got to Room 114 twenty minutes early because the projector remote had failed on the last presenter and he did not want that to be him. He was presenting with Dana Okafor on Thursday's slot for the peer health unit, and their topic, which Ms. Reyes had assigned with a flatness that suggested she found it less awkward than they did, was consent, contraception, and how to actually get tested at a clinic. Kyle had argued for the testing clinic. Dana had wanted consent. They had compromised by drawing straws for the order.

He set his laptop on the cart and opened the slides. Third slide, the numbers. He had found them Monday night, after his first search, which had been a mistake of optimism. He'd expected the box's claim, ninety-something percent effective, to hold, and instead the first result said that with typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy. He'd read it twice, then closed the tab and reopened it, as though the number might renegotiate. Mostly, the page said, because condoms are not used correctly every time. He had sat with that for a while. It wasn't the kind of thing you could unknow, and it felt dishonest not to say it out loud to the class that would, in a few years or sooner, be relying on it.

Dana arrived at 7:52 with a paper bag of clementines and no apology. "The remote's dead again," she said, peeling one. "So we go old school. Whiteboard." She pointed at his screen anyway. "Is that the condom slide? Good. Can I do that part? Priya asked me yesterday what typical use even means and I froze like an idiot. I want to get it right this time."

Kyle hesitated. He had built that slide at one in the morning, arranging the numbers so nobody could misread them, and some small possessive part of him wanted to deliver it himself. But Dana had practiced the consent section in front of her bathroom mirror, he knew, because she'd told him, and it seemed strange to guard a statistic he hadn't invented. "Sure," he said. "But you can't soften it. That's the whole point. If we say it's basically fine, we're lying."

"I wasn't going to extenuate it," Dana said, looking at him with the particular seriousness she brought to student council budget meetings. "If anything I'm going to write the number huge." She uncapped a marker and wrote 13 OUT OF 100 across the board in letters tall as the whiteboard allowed, then stood back. "It looks like a horror movie," she said, almost pleased.

The class filed in at 8:05, half of them still chewing whatever they'd bought from the vending machines. Ms. Reyes sat in the back grading quizzes, which Kyle took as a vote of confidence or of exhaustion. Dana went first, and her consent section was better than Kyle had expected: she had them practice saying "no, thanks" and hearing it back without a counteroffer, which got some laughter until she pointed out that the laughter was exactly the problem. Then she handed him the marker.

Kyle walked to the board. "Okay," he said. "Condoms. Real quick, what's on the box." Someone said ninety-eight percent, and he nodded. "That's perfect use. That's the lab. The real world is different. With typical use, about 13 out of 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy." He tapped Dana's giant number. "And it's mostly because they're not used correctly every single time. Not because the thing itself is broken."

A boy in the second row, Marcus, who Kyle knew mostly as a loud voice at basketball games, put his hand up and then didn't wait. "Thirteen? That's terrible. Why does everyone say they work?"

The question sat there. Kyle had prepared an answer, but standing in front of the room he could feel the honest one pushing up instead. "Because they do work," he said slowly. "They work against infections. They work when they're used right, every time, which is harder than it sounds, and I don't actually know how much harder because I've never had to find out. The point isn't don't use them. The point is you can't only use them and assume the box number applies to your actual life." He heard himself and winced inwardly at how teacherly it sounded, but Marcus was nodding, so Kyle let it stand.

They ran through the clinic section last, which Kyle had made into a photo tour: the front desk of the county clinic, the forms, the part where you could check a box saying you wanted results by text instead of by phone. He mentioned that appointments were free and confidential, that nobody called your parents, and that walking in was the hardest part, which several people wrote down, even Marcus, whose pen had been idle until then.

Afterward Dana caught him at the door while the next presenters dragged in a poster on sleep hygiene. "That was good," she said. "The part where you said you didn't know. Priya's going to ask you something after second period, by the way. She texted me during Spanish. Something about the clinic hours."

"I don't know the hours," Kyle said.

"Then we look them up together," Dana said, and pushed the paper bag of clementines toward him.

Hudson had always considered himself the kind of person who noticed things, which was why it bothered him so much that he'd never once looked closely at a receipt. In Mr. Okonkwo's business class, third period, the assignment on the board read: bring in one paycheque, one receipt, one tax return, and tell us what the numbers are actually doing. Hudson raised his hand before he'd fully thought it through. "I work at Pelletier's Hardware," he said. "I can get all three by Friday." Mr. Okonkwo said, "Then you're our first presenter," and Hudson sat back down feeling like a man who had volunteered for something and would now have to do it.

At the store that evening, a customer in a canvas jacket slid a box of screws across the counter and squinted at the register display. "Why's the tax so low?" the man asked. "GST used to be seven percent." Hudson glanced at the screen, where 5 percent had been added, small and certain. He was pretty sure the man was wrong. He was, in fact, nearly sure, though if you'd asked him where that sureness came from, he couldn't have told you. "That's the rate," Hudson said, which was less an answer than a way of ending the conversation. The man took his receipt, folded it without looking, and left, and Hudson was left holding a duplicate copy with the GST line printed on it, wondering whether he'd just defended something he only believed by habit.

He pocketed the duplicate, which was probably against some rule, though he told himself the store made copies precisely so that nothing would be lost. He metabolized problems better with paper in his hand. At break he spread it on the counter beside his own paycheque stub and looked at them together. The stub was the more humiliating document. Gross pay, then a claw of deductions below it: income tax withheld, CPP, EI, each abbreviation a small door he'd never opened. He'd assumed his paycheque was simply his paycheque. Apparently the government had been reading over his shoulder the whole time, taking its share before the money ever reached him, with the promise, according to Mr. Okonkwo, that some of it came back at tax-return time if you'd overpaid.

In class on Thursday, Priya had brought her mother's return, and the desks were pushed into a circle so everyone could pass documents around like evidence. Priya's mother had a home office, and there was a whole section of the return devoted to deductions, amounts subtracted before the tax was calculated. "She claims a portion of the rent," Priya said. "And her internet." A boy named Deshawn whistled. "So the government doesn't actually know what to charge you," he said. "You tell them." Mr. Okonkwo, who was eating a small container of olives with what Hudson considered an almost epicurean devotion, said only, "Keep looking," because he believed, or claimed to believe, that the numbers would teach themselves if you stared long enough.

Hudson hadn't stared long enough. He'd stared at the GST line for two shifts, and the man's seven percent kept returning to him the way a wrong note in a song returns. Finally, on his phone during his lunch break, half behind a rack of paint trays, he looked it up. He found a government page, plain and unarguable, and read it twice. The Goods and Services Tax had come in on January 1, 1991 at seven percent. It had been five percent since January 1, 2008. He sat with that for a moment. The man hadn't invented the number; he'd just stopped keeping track sometime in the last fifteen years, and Hudson had defended the right answer for the wrong reason, with nothing behind it but the register's authority. It was an odd feeling, being right and unearned at the same time.

He wasn't sure, afterward, which bothered him more: that a citizen could be so casually wrong about a tax he paid every week, or that Hudson himself had matched him, error for error, in the opposite direction. Maybe that was the whole system, he thought, spreading his pay stub and the receipt and a blank return form across his bedroom desk that night. Maybe the country ran on a kind of technocracy where most people, including him, signed and paid and believed without verifying, and the ones who did verify, like Priya's mother with her deductions, got to keep a little more. But he could also see the other side of it, the side his father took: that the five percent on the receipt was the price of the road he'd biked to work on, and that a person who understood that might pay it gladly. Hudson held both ideas at once and could not make them sit still together.

At the front of the class on Friday, he put the receipt on the document camera, the GST line blown up huge on the wall. "This is five percent," he said. "It's been five percent since January 1, 2008. Before that, from when it started on January 1, 1991, it was seven percent." Deshawn said, "So the guy was remembering the nineties." "Or the two thousands," Hudson said. "Either way, he was remembering, and I was just repeating." He showed the pay stub next, pointed at the income tax withheld, then Priya's mother's return with its deductions subtracted before the tax was figured. "The cheque takes," he said. "The return gives some of it back. The receipt takes a little more, every time."

After class, Mr. Okonkwo rinsed his olive container in the fountain and said, "You went and found the date. Most people wouldn't bother." Hudson said he hadn't bothered either, at first, and Mr. Okonkwo nodded as though that were the actual lesson, though he never said so. Walking out, Hudson passed the vending machines, bought a bag of chips, and stood in the hallway reading the receipt all the way to the bottom, where the GST sat at five percent, small and correct and, for the first time, actually known to him.

The folding chairs had been set in rows across the basketball court, and the banners from conference championships hung motionless in the heat, and John stood in the hallway outside the gymnasium with a cardboard cap sliding down his forehead and an envelope folded into his gown's inner pocket. The envelope held his father's handwriting on one side: open after. He had carried it for eleven days without opening it, a feat he managed mostly by not being home.

"You're humming," said Priya beside him, adjusting her tassel for the fourth time. "You always hum when you're nervous. It's your mannerism, like cracking knuckles." John stopped, then started again, softer. The tune was the one everyone knew, the one that walked brides of learning down gymnasium aisles across the continent, and he realized he had no idea where it had come from. It felt older than the building. It felt like it had always been here, the way the pledge of allegiance felt like it had always been in classrooms, which he knew was wrong, because everything came from somewhere.

"Do you know what this song even is?" he asked. Priya shrugged. Behind them, Mr. Okafor, who taught shop and had agreed to marshal the line, checked his watch and told them they had six minutes. John pulled out his phone, shielded it against his gown, and searched. The first result made him laugh out loud, a short bark that turned heads down the line. "It's Elgar," he said. "Pomp and Circumstance March Number One. It premiered in 1901, in Liverpool." He said it again in his head, letting the facts settle. Liverpool, not Boston, not Toronto. A march written by an Englishman a hundred and twenty some years before this gymnasium was even a twinkle in a school board's eye, and now it belonged to every graduate in North America by pure accumulation. Things traveled. Things got adopted and worn smooth and nobody asked anymore.

Priya peered at his screen. "So we're walking in to a Liverpool march." "We're walking in to a Liverpool march," John said, and pocketed the phone as the double doors swung open and the band, eleven students who had learned the piece in three weeks, struck up the first chords.

The problem was not the march. The problem was that in the envelope his father had written something, and John had a suspicion, and the suspicion had kept him from sleeping properly for a week. He was supposed to leave for State in August. He had already paid the housing deposit with money from two summers at Delgado's garage, where his father had gotten him the job, where his father had worked since before John could read. Then in April his father's shoulder had gone bad, the real kind of bad, surgical, and Delgado had said, carefully, in the tangential way men said important things, that the shop could use a steady pair of hands through the fall. Nobody had asked John anything. His father had simply stopped discussing the fall entirely, which was itself an answer.

They processed in. John found his row, sat, folded his hands, watched the principal shake hands with the school board president. The speeches began. The salutatorian talked about roads and journeys. John's mind kept circling back, and he tried to forestall the spiral by counting the ceiling tiles, but the counting turned into a rhythm and the rhythm turned back into Elgar, who had written a march for a city in England and could not have imagined this: eight hundred folding chairs, a boy in a rented gown deciding two lives in one afternoon.

When they stood to cross the stage, row by row, the line moved faster than he expected. Priya went before him, pumping her fist, and then there was a gap, and a woman with the name cards said "John," and he walked. The handshake, the scroll, the flash of his mother's camera from the bleachers, his father beside her with his arm in a sling, standing anyway, mouth open in a shout John couldn't hear. And it was on the way back down the stairs that he understood what he had been refusing to understand for eleven days: his father had not written open after so that John would make a decision. He had written it so that John would know that his father had already made one, whatever it was, and that John could stop carrying the weight of guessing. The envelope was not a demand. It was a hand letting go, or reaching out, and John would not know which until he read it.

Afterward, in the parking lot, caps and gowns already peeling off in the heat, John sat on the tailgate of his father's truck and opened the envelope. Inside was a single sheet and a photograph of the two of them outside Delgado's, John fourteen, holding a wrench too big for his hand. The sheet said: Go. We'll figure the shop out. Your mother says to tell you she's proud. P.S. Elgar, right? Looked it up. English fellow. Funny that we all march to it. John laughed, folded the letter along its creases, and put it in his wallet behind his driver's license.

His father came across the lot, sling swinging, keys jingling. "You opened it." "I opened it." "And?" John slid off the tailgate and stood. "And I'll call Delgado tonight. Tell him thanks, and that I'll be back Christmas break if he still wants hands." His father looked at him a long moment, then nodded once, the way he did when an engine turned over clean. He tossed John the keys. "You drive," he said.

Hunter got to the counter at 7:52, eight minutes before the manager locked the door and turned the sign, and ordered the largest black coffee they would sell him. The mug warmed his hands while his phone sat face down on the table like a card he was refusing to turn over. Maya and Devon were already wedged into the corner booth, arguing the way they argued about everything, which is to say loudly enough that the last barista kept glancing over.

"It's simple," Devon said. "You get the grades, you get in. Dana had a 4.0 and she's at Ridgemont. Case closed."

"That is not what happened to Dana." Maya peeled the sleeve off her cup in one long strip. "My cousin had a 4.0 and got flat rejected from three schools. Grades don't guarantee anything."

"Then what's the point of working for them?"

Hunter turned his phone over, then face down again. He had been turning it over for two days, since the email from Weldon had arrived with a subject line he still hadn't opened. The deposit deadline was midnight tonight. His mother had already filled out the forms for Hartley, the safety school, the one with the good program and the wrong everything else, and she'd said, gently, that they couldn't hold both checks past Friday.

"Guys," he said. "You're arguing past each other."

"Nobody asked, Hunter."

"I know nobody asked." He pulled a napkin toward him and borrowed Maya's pen. "Look. Devon says grades get you in. Maya says grades don't get you in. Both of you have examples. So maybe the truth is weirder than either of you is saying."

Devon leaned back with the particular boredom of a boy who had heard Hunter do this before. Maya, at least, leaned in, because Maya liked an argument the way some people liked storms, and watching her follow a line of reasoning had a way of enrupturing a whole table, even strangers two booths over.

"Think about the sun," Hunter said. "Direct sunlight. For it to hit you, the sun has to be above the horizon. No sun above the horizon, no direct sunlight, period."

"Obviously," Devon said.

"But the sun can be above the horizon and you still don't get direct sunlight, because you're standing in a shadow. Something's in the way. So the sun being up is necessary but it's not sufficient." He wrote the two words on the napkin and underlined them. "Necessary means it has to hold for the thing to happen. Sufficient means it's enough by itself. Grades are like the sun. If you don't have them, you're out. But having them doesn't mean you're in. Something else can cast a shadow."

The barista began stacking chairs somewhere behind them. Maya was quiet for a second, which for Maya was a tectonic event, a whole continent of argument shifting before it settled. "So Dana and your cousin both had the sun," she said slowly. "And your cousin was standing in a shadow."

"Something like that. Maybe the essay. Maybe nothing he could see."

"That's depressing," Devon said.

"It's not." Hunter found he actually meant this. "It just means the argument changes. Stop arguing whether grades are enough. Start arguing what the shadows are, and which ones you can move out of."

It was Maya who noticed his phone, who reached over and flipped it before he could stop her, and who read the subject line out loud with her eyebrows already climbing. Weldon Admissions Decision. Sent forty-nine hours ago. The whole booth went still, and the espresso machine hissed into the silence like it had opinions.

"You haven't opened it," she said.

"The deposit's due at midnight. If it's a no, I send Hartley's check tonight and it's done. If I open it and it's a no, it's still done, just sooner." He picked the phone up. It was heavier than a phone should be. "If it's a yes, then I have to figure out money in three hours, and my mom already signed the other forms, and I don't even know which of those is the shadow and which is the sun."

"Open it," Devon said.

"Hunter," Maya said, quieter, "the sun being up doesn't mean you get the light. But you're never going to know what's in the way from under this table."

The barista called last call from the counter with her keys already in her hand. Hunter pressed his thumb to the screen, watched the blur of the loading circle, and pulled the phone close so only he could see it, while Maya and Devon leaned in on either side of him and the first chairs went up on the far tables, one by one, like a count reaching zero.

The line outside the fire station moved in short, patient shuffles, and Sophia stood in it with her registration card going soft at the edges in her hand. Behind her, Marcus was still talking about the poll from Tuesday, the one he had screenshotted and sent to the group chat at midnight.

"Four-point lead," he said now, tapping her shoulder as if the number itself needed emphasis. "Margin of error is three. So even at the worst case, it's still a lead. It's basically over."

"It's not basically over," Sophia said. The man in front of them, older, in a coat too warm for November, glanced back and then returned to his newspaper.

"Three from four is one," Marcus said. "One is still bigger than zero. That's arithmetic, Sophia."

She had done that same arithmetic herself on Tuesday night, lying on her bed with her phone held above her face, and it had felt airtight, almost like a proof. She remembered the satisfaction of it, the way certainty had settled over her like a warm blanket. She had even typed a message to the chat saying the race was decided and it was pointless to argue about it anymore. She had never sent it. Something about the typing had slowed her down, the way copying a sentence slowly can transcribe doubt into a person, and she had deleted it instead and lain in the dark listening to the radiator tick.

The line advanced. Inside the station, the smell changed to floor wax and burnt coffee, and volunteers at folding tables called out street names in flat, unhurried voices. A woman with a lanyard checked Sophia's card, circled something, and pointed her toward a machine she didn't recognize from the diagrams she'd studied.

"First time?" the woman asked.

"First time."

The woman's smile was brief and genuine. "It goes faster than you think."

While Sophia waited for the machine, an argument caught her attention from the far table, where a younger poll worker in a hoodie was talking with a man holding a printed page. "You can't read it like that," the poll worker was saying. "The margin of error applies to each candidate's share, not to the gap. The margin of error for the lead is about twice as large."

Sophia stood very still. The words arranged themselves in her mind next to Marcus's arithmetic, and the arithmetic came apart. A four-point lead with a three-point margin of error was not a floor of one. Each share could move; the lead itself could move by more. She turned the idea over and could not make it sit still. Six, roughly, was the number for the gap, and six swallowed four whole.

"Marcus," she said quietly, when she was back beside him in the line for the stickers, "I think we had it wrong. The three points, it applies to each candidate's share. Not to the lead. The lead's margin is about twice as large."

He frowned at her, then at the gymnasium floor, the scuffed lanes of a basketball court visible under the folding tables. "Who told you that?"

"I heard it. Just now. And it makes sense of why I couldn't sleep Tuesday."

"You couldn't sleep over a poll?"

"I couldn't sleep because I was sure, and being sure felt too easy."

He didn't answer right away. A volunteer handed them stickers, the cheap kind, the adhesive already evanescent against her jacket sleeve, and Marcus pressed his onto his notebook like it was something to keep. She thought of her mother, who had once admitted, over dishes, that she hadn't voted in her first eligible election because the polls had said it was a landslide anyway, and who had refused, ever after, to tell anyone which election it was. The memory had always seemed like a small shame in the family. Now it seemed like something more complicated, a whole vote surrendered to a number that could not carry the weight assigned to it.

At the machine, Sophia made her choices. Her hand hovered longer than she had expected it to, not from indecision about the candidates but from the strangeness of the act itself, this private, unprovable moment that no poll had ever measured and no margin could contain. In her biology class they had spent October building a phylogeny of the hominids, tracing which fragments of skull descended from which, and she had learned that a tree of life is only as honest as its uncertainty, that scientists draw some branches with solid lines and some with dotted ones. The poll's dotted line had been the gap all along, and she had traced it solid.

When she came out, Marcus was waiting under the bare maple by the curb, breath fogging.

"So it could be losing," he said. It wasn't quite a question.

"It could be a lot of things. That's what the number actually says."

"It says less than I thought it did."

"Everybody says it says more than it does," Sophia said. She looked back at the fire station, at the line still stretching out the door into the gray afternoon, people waiting on the strength of numbers they mostly hadn't examined. Somewhere in that line was someone deciding not to bother, the way her mother once had. Somewhere in it was someone sure of an outcome the way she had been sure on Tuesday night.

"Then what's the point of polls?" Marcus asked.

She zipped her jacket higher. "They tell you where the fog is," she said. "They don't tell you what's inside it."

She started walking toward the bus stop, and after a moment, she heard his footsteps behind her.

The book club met in the back room of the library on the first Sunday of the month, and Ashton arrived early enough to claim the chair by the window, where the radiator ticked and the October light fell across six copies of The Remains of the Day like an accusation. He had read the whole novel in nine days, which surprised him, because he had expected it to be dry, a butler droning on about dignity. Instead he kept stopping to argue with the page.

Ms. Okafor, the librarian who ran the club, had given them a handout: two short passages, one where Stevens describes Miss Kenton's announcement of her engagement, one where he describes his father's death, which occurred on the evening of a crucial conference. The instructions said to try reading the passages through a critical lens, Marxist or feminist, and to note what the lens revealed and what it might obscure. That word, obscured, had bothered Ashton all week.

Priya, who was seventeen and wanted badly to be the one who said the smart thing first, had already spread her notes across the table. "The Marxist reading is obvious," she said, before anyone had settled. "Stevens gives his whole life to Lord Darlington's service. He's labor, and Darlington is capital, and Stevens never once names the asymmetry. He calls it dignity. It's ideology. That's my thesis." She said thesis with real satisfaction, the way someone might display a new coat.

Ashton looked at his own marked-up page. In the passage, Stevens reported, calmly, that on the night Miss Kenton told him of her engagement, he had been extremely busy, that a vital matter concerning the guests had arisen, and that he could not recall feeling anything worth recording. And then, in the very next sentences, he described the exact hour, the exact light in the corridor, the exact words she had used, with a precision that most people reserve for things they cannot stop thinking about.

"It's weird," Ashton said slowly. "He reports everything accurately. Every detail. But he misreads what the details mean." He tapped the page. "Look at the evening his father dies. He says the conference was of great importance, so his behavior was correct. But the novel is from 1989, and Ishiguro built it so that the facts stay true and the interpretation collapses. Even his own feelings. He says he felt nothing, and then he does things that only grief does. He stood on the landing, he said, and looked out over the grounds. Who remembers the view if they felt nothing?"

Priya frowned, which was not the same as disagreeing. "That's just close reading, though. That's not a lens."

"It changes the lens," Ashton said. "Because if I do the Marxist thing, like you did, I say Stevens is a servant who has been trained to abrogate his own judgment to his employer, and his employer turns out to be a capricious man backing the wrong side of history. That works. But it doesn't explain the part that actually kept me up. He isn't only deceived about Darlington. He's deceived about himself. The class analysis explains what happened to him. It doesn't explain what he keeps doing to the record."

The radiator ticked. Ms. Okafor poured tea from a scratched thermos, and the smell of bergamot drifted down the table. She did not offer an opinion, which everyone had learned was her way of offering one.

Priya was quiet for a moment, turning her pen over. Her thesis, Ashton realized, had been her ticket to saying something impressive before anyone else, and it had just been made smaller in front of her. Then she leaned forward. "So do the feminist one on Miss Kenton," she said. "If he misreads his own feelings, he misreads hers too. She announces her engagement like it's an ultimatum, and he files it under personnel. A feminist lens says she's the only person in the house who knows what she wants and says it out loud, and the whole book is narrated by a man who doesn't, about her."

"That's better than my second paragraph," Ashton admitted. He wrote it down, then crossed out half of it, then wrote it again. What he could not get onto the page was the part he was least sure of: whether the two lenses added up to one true reading or just argued with each other, the class critique saying Stevens was shaped by a system, Priya's reading saying he still chose, nightly, the filing cabinet over the person.

They read the last passage aloud together, the one where Stevens stands at the bus stop as Miss Kenton leaves. The clock in the main library struck the half hour through the wall. Priya underlined one line twice, and slid the book across the table so Ashton could see it. "He says he was upset for professional reasons," she said. "He says that. Those exact words."

The gymnasium had been arranged into rows of folding tables facing a raised platform, and by eight forty-five the Grade Eleven model parliament was already arguing about whether the Speaker's coffee counted as a recess privilege. Brandon sat in the third row for the government side with his bill clipped to a binder, the pages soft from being thumbed through all week. It was called the School Food Disclosure Act, and it required the cafeteria to post where its produce came from. He had drafted it alone at his kitchen table on a Tuesday night, folding in a clause his older sister suggested about allergen labels, because she said a bill with two ideas in it was harder to dismiss.

The clerk read the title for first reading, and Brandon rose to move that the bill be read a first time and printed. It passed without debate, which he had learned was the custom, bills being introduced like strangers at a door. Then came the part he had not prepared for. The Speaker assigned the bill to committee, six members drawn from both sides, and for two days they took it apart in a corner classroom with a whiteboard that still bore the ghost of a chemistry diagram, some igneous rock cycle half-erased behind the chair's head.

The committee was where his bill changed. A girl named Priya from the opposition moved an amendment that would exempt the cafeteria's outside vendors from the disclosure rule, on the argument that the school couldn't compel businesses it only rented space to. Brandon resisted it at first, and then, listening to the committee chair read the amendment aloud a second time, he heard the logic of it sitting there plainly, like a coin on a table. He voted with the amendment. One of his own caucus members called him a pragmatist in a tone that made it sound like a diagnosis, and another, later, in the hallway, called him an egoist who just wanted the bill to pass with his name on it. He carried both words around for an evening before deciding they were not the same accusation, and that only the second one was unfair.

Second reading was the debate on principle, and it went longer than anyone expected. Brandon spoke for four minutes on the idea that students deserved to know what they were eating, and an opposition member named Theo spent six minutes on the cost of signage and the burden on the cafeteria manager, who, he pointed out, was one woman with a laminator. The chamber divided, and the tellers counted raised hands. The bill passed second reading by a margin of three, which felt to Brandon like walking across a frozen creek and hearing one small crack beneath his left boot.

Between readings, Theo found him at the water fountain. Brandon expected a fight and got something else, a quiet question about whether the committee's amendment had actually weakened the bill's purpose, since the vendors supplied nearly half the food. Brandon said he had thought about that too. He said the amended bill covered less ground but stood on firmer ground, and he admitted he was not certain the trade was worth it. Theo said he wasn't certain either, which was, in its way, the most honest exchange of the whole conference.

On the final morning the Speaker called the bill for its last stage. "We now proceed to third reading," she said, "the final debate and vote on the bill as amended, after its details have been examined in committee." Brandon wrote the words in the margin of his copy, not because he would forget them but because he wanted the sentence to exist in his handwriting. Everything the committee had done, the amendment, the clause on allergens, the exemption Priya had argued for, all of it was now fused into the text he was standing to defend, and this was the last door it had to pass through.

Debate was brief and almost gentle. Theo rose to speak against the bill one more time, but he did not proselytize about cafeteria freedom the way he had on second reading; he simply restated the cost concern, said the amended version had addressed most of his objection, and sat down. Priya spoke in favour. Brandon closed for the government with a short speech he had rewritten at midnight, saying the bill was smaller than the one he had drafted and better than the one he had imagined, and that he had learned the difference between those two things in a corner classroom with a half-erased rock cycle on the board.

The chamber divided. The tellers counted. The Speaker announced that the bill had passed third reading and declared, "I do assent to this bill," tapping the gavel once, and the clerk recorded the assent in the minutes of the day. Under the rules of the model parliament, the Food Disclosure Act was now law, binding in theory on a cafeteria that would never hear of it. Brandon looked down at his binder, at the sentence he had written in the margin, and then across the chamber at Theo, who caught his eye and gave a small shrug, palms up. Brandon shrugged back, picked up his pen, and drew a thin line under the words on the page.

The basement smelled like laundry detergent and old carpet, and Dev's laptop was propped on a milk crate because he'd broken the hinge again. Zoe pulled her chair up beside him and opened her notebook to a page with "Java, Day 1" crossed out and "Day 4" written above it. She had a problem due Sunday night, the first real one: build a class with private fields, give it getter methods, and test that it worked. On the bus over she'd been wondering whether the private thing was just a rule someone invented, or whether it actually did something, and she hadn't decided yet.

"Okay," Dev said, cracking his knuckles like he was about to lift something. "Make a Patient class. Everything goes inside it."

She typed the fields first: name, age, and an integer for antigen count, because the assignment said to model something from her other life and she'd spent the whole term in that other life memorizing what an antigen was, the molecule that triggers an immune response. She declared them private without quite knowing why, the way you lower your voice in a library.

"Try to touch one from outside," Dev said. "Go on. Write patient.age."

The compiler underlined it in red before she'd even finished the line. "Cannot access." She stared at the red squiggle with a strange satisfaction, like the language itself had drawn a curtain. So that was it: private wasn't a suggestion, it was a wall you couldn't argue with. She wrote the getter instead, getAge, small and formal, and when it returned the number she'd loaded in, she felt the wall had a door, and she was the one holding the key.

Then Dev, who could never leave anything alone, said, "Now make it interesting. Put your patients in a list and search it." He'd been pontificating all evening about how he was going to double major in computer science and economics and corner some market or other, and she'd learned to take about forty percent of what he said seriously. She wrote the loop that checked each patient in turn, printed the timing, and then she remembered the thing her cousin had mentioned at dinner, the fast one, the one that kept cutting the pile in half. Binary search. It jumped straight to the middle item and worked from there.

She added it. She ran both searches. The numbers came back, and she sat forward, because they were the same. Almost exactly the same, run after run. The clever one wasn't beating the simple one at all. She rubbed her eyes and looked at the milk crate as if it might confess.

"Wait," she said slowly. "To get to the middle, I still have to start at the front and walk through the nodes one at a time. The list isn't like an array where you just land in the middle." She scrolled through her own code, and there it was, a while loop inside the binary search, stepping forward link by link just to find the center. Every time. Every cut. "So it doesn't matter that I'm halving the search. I'm paying for the halving by walking the whole first half anyway." Dev leaned over and looked, and for once he didn't say anything for a second.

"Do you fix it?" he asked finally. "Like, is there a fix?"

"That's what I don't know yet." She tapped the pen against her notebook. Maybe the answer was to store the data some other way, some structure she hadn't learned, or maybe binary search just wasn't for this kind of list, the way you don't use a fork for soup. The assignment hadn't said anything about search speed. It had only wanted the private fields and the getters and the tests. She wrote three test methods, watched them all go green, and felt the small clean click of that, even with the bigger question still open beside it.

Outside, someone's car alarm went off and then thought better of it. The basement clock said nine-forty. Zoe saved the file twice, which was a habit, then closed the laptop halfway and looked at the red squiggle still burned somewhere in her memory. She was starting to think that understanding a thing meant knowing both where it worked and where it turned useless, that even fast ideas had places they went moribund, and she wondered, not unhappily, how many other things she'd been taught would turn out like this.

"Same time Thursday?" Dev asked, already stacking the milk crate under the desk.

The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Brody stood in the middle of the living room where the previous family had left faint rectangles on the carpet, and the movers had set his boxes along one wall in a line that looked like a small city seen from a plane. Somewhere outside, a sprinkler ticked across a lawn that didn't know him yet.

He found his phone in his back pocket and texted Marcus first, because Marcus would be awake even at ten in the morning on a Tuesday. "Landed. House is empty." Then he took a photo of the boxes and sent that too, because Marcus liked evidence.

The reply came in pieces, the way Marcus always texted, a thought arriving and then being corrected. "looks like a prison." Then, "of boxes." Then, "you find the kitchen yet."

Brody walked through the rooms to check. Kitchen: white counters, a window over the sink facing a backyard with one tree. He opened the fridge, which hummed at him like it was clearing its throat, and found nothing inside but a roll of quarters his mother must have left for the moving truck guys. He took two quarters and put them back. Even the small kindnesses in this house belonged to someone else's plan.

Upstairs, in what would be his room, he sat on the floor between two boxes and did the thing he'd been avoiding for the whole drive, which was to look at how many days of summer were left before school started. Twenty-six. Under that calculation sat a heavier one, the thing he'd read three nights ago at two in the morning in his old room with the walls already stripped of posters. He'd gone down a rabbit hole about making friends after a move, and one page had stopped him cold: a researcher named Jeffrey Hall, in a 2018 study, had estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together. Ninety hours. He'd lain there doing the arithmetic against the ceiling. If school was seven hours a day and you counted every minute, it would take almost thirteen school days, and nobody counted every minute, because most minutes you were just sitting near people, which didn't count, or did it, he didn't know, nobody had defined near.

He'd tried it out on Marcus before he left, sitting on the tailgate of Mr. Alvarez's truck while they loaded the last of the stereo equipment.

"Guess how long it takes to make a real friend," Brody had said. "Guess the hours."

"From nothing? Or from like, knowing the guy?"

"That's the thing, there's a difference. Casual friend to actual friend. This study says about 90 hours together."

Marcus had whistled, low, the way he did when a price came back higher than expected. "How long did we take?"

Brody had done that math too, lying awake. Six years of lunch periods, but you couldn't just multiply, because the first two years they'd barely spoken, and then the camping trip, and then junior year when Marcus's parents split and Brody had come over every day for a month without being asked. Whatever the real number was, it was enormous, and it was already spent, and that was what made it valuable and what made leaving feel like theft.

In the new room, he texted: "90 hours to make a real friend. im doing the math and its brutal."

"so skip casual. go straight to loyal," Marcus wrote back. Then: "join a club. same faces every week, it compounds."

Brody almost laughed at the idea of Marcus giving him advice, since Marcus's usual strategy in any new group was to become a sycophant to whoever seemed in charge, complimenting shoes and laughing at jokes that hadn't earned it, until he'd secured a position and could relax into being himself. It had worked, more or less, for years. Brody had watched it work and had never once considered it tenable for himself, not because he was nobler but because he couldn't act that well. The two of them had built their friendship on the difference, on Brody saying the flat thing and Marcus saying the smooth one.

The trouble was that now, in a town where he knew nobody, the flat thing felt like a luxury. You needed standing before bluntness read as honesty instead of hostility.

He got up and went downstairs, where his mother was taping labels onto cabinet doors so the unpacking wouldn't incapacitate her tomorrow, she said, when the fatigue hit. She had a system for everything. She looked up when he came in, and he could see her doing her own arithmetic, counting his silence like a bill coming due.

"There's a bike shop on Marsh Road," she said. "The sign said they're hiring. I know you didn't ask."

"I didn't ask."

"I know." She went back to her labels, then stopped, tape hanging off her thumb. "There's also a flyer at the grocery store. Some astronomy club, meets at the community college Thursdays. I took a picture of it, but I didn't sign you up for anything, I just. Took the picture."

He looked at the photo when she sent it to him, standing in the empty kitchen with the fridge humming behind him. Meets weekly, all levels, beginners welcome. Thursday nights from now until the school year ended. He counted the Thursdays out of habit, then counted the hours, three per night, and found the number was big enough to be a promise even though it was only arithmetic, and only about being in the same room.

He texted Marcus the flyer photo. Under it he wrote, "same faces every week."

He pulled his shoes back on, found his bike leaning against the garage wall where the movers had left it, and rode toward Marsh Road to see what a town he'd never chosen looked like at street level, the sun hot on the back of his neck, the flyer's picture still open on his phone in his pocket.

Hayden had waited until eighteen to learn to drive, which his mother said was sensible and his uncle said was cowardly, and the truth was neither, or both. He had put it off the way he put off dentist appointments, and then the summer before college had arrived with no more excuses in it. Now he sat in the driver's seat of the family Corolla in the empty lot behind the church on Delmar, his hands at ten and two, his mother in the passenger seat with her coffee held between her knees like something fragile.

"Foot on the brake, then start it," she said. He did, and the engine came alive under him, a vibration he felt in his teeth. He had imagined this moment for years, and in the imagining it had always felt like freedom, but the actual feeling was closer to being handed something heavy and breakable in a crowded room.

He let the car creep forward in the lot, turning wide, careful circles around the light poles. His mother adjusted the mirror on her side without comment, which he understood as a comment. When he braked too hard the second time, she set her coffee in the cup holder and said, "Smoother. Like you're setting it down, not catching it." He tried again and the car settled without lurching, and something in him loosened, and then immediately tightened again, because loosening was exactly what he could not afford.

They had been at the licensing office that morning, him filling out forms at a counter too low for his height. Two rows behind him, a girl about sixteen waited with her father for her permit test, reading a poster on the wall out loud to him in a bored voice. "Drivers aged sixteen to nineteen have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven," she recited, and then added, "Cheerful." Her father didn't look up from his phone. Hayden had copied the fact onto the back of his receipt without deciding to, the way you write down a phone number you don't trust yourself to keep.

In the lot now, circling, he thought about that number. Three times, per mile. He was eighteen, so he was inside the statistic, one of the counted, and the fact sat strangely with the confidence that was supposed to come from waiting, from being careful, from being the kind of person who read posters all the way through. His uncle's voice was in his head, saying the only way to get past it was miles, that caution this late was just fear wearing a costume. And his mother's was there too, quieter, saying nothing was worth the phone call at night. He had always let those two voices argue and stood apart from both of them, which had felt like wisdom and now felt like a stall.

"Take us out to Delmar," his mother said. "Real road. You're ready."

"Am I."

"That wasn't a question I was asking." She said it lightly, but her hand had gone to the door handle, and he understood that her body had made its own assessment. He signaled, checked the lot's exit, and pulled into the street, where the world stopped being a closed course and became other people, a man on a bicycle, a kid chasing a ball into a driveway, every one of them someone's whole life moving at speed past his windshield.

He drove at the limit exactly, which felt both tenable and absurd, like walking through a museum in a raincoat. At the light on Fifth he stopped early, and his mother laughed, a short sound, almost proud. "You know I totaled a car at seventeen," she said. "Your grandmother's Buick. A telephone pole. I paid her back for two years from the video store."

"Reparation," he said.

"Sweaty envelopes of cash, but sure." She was looking out the windshield, not at him, which was how she said serious things. "I'm telling you so you know the number on that poster is people. It was almost me."

He turned that over while the light held. Three times per mile, almost three times, for kids like the girl at the counter, like him, like his mother at seventeen with envelopes of cash. He could not make it mean don't drive, and he could not make it mean drive anyway and be brave, and maybe he would spend the next ten years finding where he actually stood, somewhere between his uncle's contempt and his mother's hands on the door handle. The light turned green. A horn sounded behind them, one short insistent note that seemed to presage the whole decade ahead of him, and his mother said, "Go," and he went.

Tyson had taped the week's plan to the inside of his locker at the rec center: Monday ballhandling, Tuesday conditioning, Wednesday shooting, Thursday rest, Friday scrimmaging, Saturday shooting again, Sunday nothing at all. He had written REST and NOTHING in capital letters, as if the words might otherwise be skipped over, and beneath them, in smaller script, warm-up before everything, ten minutes, no exceptions. His teammate Dez leaned against the adjoining locker and read the schedule upside down.

"Thursday you're not touching a ball?"

"Rest day. It's part of the program."

Dez pushed off the locker and spun a ball on one finger. "Rest is for people with plans. You planning to sleep through college too?"

Tyson took the ball out of its rotation and started his warm-up, the one he'd copied from a conditioning handout: ankle circles, hip hinges, slow defensive slides from sideline to sideline. The gym smelled like rubber and floor wax, and the morning light came in high and yellow through the windows near the ceiling. He was three slides in when his wrist caught the rim of a memory from the night before, 2 a.m., phone flat on his chest, highlight reels autoplaying while his shot chart from last Saturday sat unsolved in his head. He'd missed six free throws in that game. Six. And he'd planned every drill for the week but hadn't planned a single hour of sleep.

After warm-ups he shot fifty free throws and made thirty-one. He wrote the number on the tape edge of his water bottle with a grease pencil, because his father had once told him that what gets measured gets managed, and because writing it down made the miss feel like data instead of failure. At the bleachers, his friend Priya was doing homework, a stack of note cards on her knees about ancient governments for some elective. He sat down beside her, breathing hard.

"I'm designing a training program," he said. "Whole week, drills, rest days, warm-ups, everything. But my free throws are garbage and I don't know which part is broken."

Priya flipped a card. "Theocracies," she read. "Rulers claim to speak for God." She looked at him. "Maybe your problem is that you treat your plan like a theocracy. You wrote it, so it can't be wrong. Everything's already decided."

Tyson laughed, then stopped laughing. That was, more or less, what he'd done. He'd planned the work and assumed the recovery would take care of itself, as if a body were a machine that ran on drills alone.

That night he searched for sleep and basketball on his laptop, expecting fluff, and found a study instead. Stanford, 2011. Basketball players who aimed for ten hours in bed nightly, and over the season their free-throw average went from 7.9 successful shots out of 10 to 8.8. He read the sentence three times, then once more out loud, quietly, because his little brother was asleep down the hall and it was already later than it should have been. He copied the numbers onto a fresh index card, Priya-style, and propped it against his lamp. Then he set an alarm not for waking but for going to bed, at 10:15, which felt absurd, like being tucked in by his own schedule.

The week that followed was not seismic. Nothing collapsed and nothing transformed. He still missed shots, still scrolled too long on Wednesday, still caught Dez grinning at him when he left the gym at 8 p.m. sharp with the outdoor court half full and the good games just starting. "Sleeping already?" Dez called after him, and Tyson raised the index card over his head without turning around, like a hall pass.

On Friday he warmed up the full ten minutes, even though the scrimmage was waiting, even though his pride said slide faster, get on with it. He'd been afraid the routine would desensitize him to the urgency of playing, that structure would sand the edge off his game, and he'd been wrong about that too: the ankle circles and slow slides made him feel readier, not duller. In the scrimmage he got to the line twice. First trip, both shots went down. Second trip, he made one and missed one, and the miss rattled the back rim in a way he recognized, the same tired, late flick of the wrist from Saturday, from the nights the plan didn't cover.

Afterward he sat on the bleachers with the grease pencil and added a line to the bottle: fifty more, starting tomorrow, after a real night of it. Priya gathered her note cards and sat down next to him, and he handed her the index card from his bag so she could see what he'd found. She read it and raised her eyebrows.

"Ten hours in bed," she said. "That's a lot of hours."

"Seven point nine to eight point eight," he said. "Out of ten." He took the card back and slid it into the pocket with his car keys, where he'd actually find it again.

Dez's game was still going at the far basket, sneakers squealing, somebody calling for the ball. Tyson pulled his hoodie on and watched for a minute, uncertain, the old pull still there, the pull to stay and play until the lights cut out. Then he stood, and swung his bag over one shoulder, and said, "Ask me tomorrow how the free throws went."

The packing tables ran the length of the warehouse, and by half past four the October light through the high windows had gone the color of dishwater. Mackenzie had been stacking crates of canned peaches since seven, with forty minutes off at noon, and her hands knew the rhythm so well now that her mind had gone somewhere else entirely. It had gone to the meeting on Saturday, and to her father, who had said at supper that a man should be grateful for steady work and keep his mouth shut about the rest.

Ruth, who ran the second table, had not kept her mouth shut. She was older than the rest of them, maybe forty, with a son in Michigan, and she had spent two weeks collecting signatures on a folded sheet of paper she kept in her apron pocket. Mackenzie had watched her move down the aisle between tables, quiet as inventory, pausing at each woman's elbow. The word she used was union, said low, and the word she used after it was together, and some of the women signed and some looked at the floor and Mrs. Prue, the floor supervisor, developed a habit of appearing wherever Ruth happened to be standing.

That was Mackenzie's nemesis, if she was honest about it, though the word felt too grand for a squat woman with a clipboard. Mrs. Prue had cut Mackenzie's hours the week after her father complained about a short paycheck, and Mackenzie could never prove the two things were connected, which was somehow worse than a punishment she could name. She had learned that most unfairness arrived like that, in the shape of ordinary decisions that could each be defended on their own.

"Sixteen cents," said Dot, at the next table, not looking up from her crate. Dot was seventeen and had been there a year and a half. "Sixteen cents an hour, and Saturday they want us till nine again. I asked Mr. Hallis for eighteen and he said I was lucky to have the sixteen."

"My father says the same," Mackenzie said. "Lucky."

Ruth came down the aisle with her folded paper and, folded inside it, a scrap of newspaper she had been carrying since Tuesday. She laid it flat on Mackenzie's table, between two crates. It was a clipping from the front page, and Mackenzie read it slowly, because reading was still slower for her than lifting.

"October twenty-fourth," Ruth said. "Last Monday. There's a law now. The Fair Labor Standards Act." She tapped the page. "Took effect on the twenty-fourth of October, 1938. First federal minimum wage in this country, twenty-five cents an hour."

"Twenty-five," Dot repeated. She set down the can she was holding. "I'm making sixteen."

"And a maximum workweek of forty-four hours," Ruth went on. "Forty-four. That's the law, not a favor."

Mackenzie looked at the clipping and then at the clock above the loading door, and did the arithmetic twice because she didn't trust herself the first time. Sixteen cents against twenty-five. Fifty-two hours last week against forty-four. The numbers sat there, plain as weights on a scale, and she thought of her father saying lucky, and she thought of Saturday's meeting, which she had decided, that morning, to skip.

She had skipped things before. Two winters ago, when the girls at school had organized to confront a teacher who graded the boys more generously, Mackenzie had stood in the corridor while the others went in, and she had told herself she hadn't really agreed with them anyway, which was a lie she had maintained so long it had almost become true. Afterward the teacher's habits changed, slightly, for a term, and the girls who had gone in never quite trusted her again, and she had understood that there was a cost to standing in the corridor, only nobody billed you for it at the time.

"You can't just demand it," she said to Ruth. "Mr. Hallis will say he can't pay it. He'll say the company goes under."

"He'll say it," Ruth agreed. "But there's the law, and there's the lot of us, and there's what we can do together that none of us can do alone. That's what the meeting's for. Bargaining, when you're not alone." She didn't raise her voice. She never raised her voice, which Mackenzie had noticed was different from her father, whose opinions always arrived at full volume, gratuitous, like applause for himself.

Mackenzie looked down the row of tables, at Dot still holding her can, at the older women who had been there since before Mackenzie was born, at the clock that would not stop for any of them. She picked up Ruth's pencil, which was lying beside the clipping, and it was heavier than a can of peaches or lighter, she genuinely could not tell.

"Sign it," she said, mostly to herself, and then, louder, to Dot: "Twenty-five. Write down what you're making now, so we can show the difference."

Mrs. Prue came around the corner with her clipboard, and Mackenzie signed anyway.

Kaylee stood in her grandmother's doorway with a shoebox under her arm and the smell of cempasúchil already reaching her, dense and almost sweet, like the air itself had been instructed to guide someone in. Inside, the living room had been rearranged overnight. A table stood draped in white cloth, three tiers rising like steps, and on every tier marigolds, fresh-cut that morning, their orange so loud it seemed to argue with the candles.

"Put him at the top," her grandmother said, not turning from the kitchen. "With your mother's father. They got along, even at the end."

The shoebox held what Kaylee had rescued from her dorm room in September, when her father mailed it to her without a note: two photographs of her grandfather, a folded paper with his handwriting on it, and a small tin of the mints he used to carry. She had taken the box to college intending to do something with it, and instead it had sat under her bed for two months, going nowhere, until she came home for November first with a presentiment she could not name, the sense that if she didn't carry it to this table now, she would carry it unopened for years.

Her little cousins were already arranged around the altar like a tribunal. Paloma, who was nine, had appointed herself inspector. "You have to have marigolds," Paloma announced. "The bright color and the smell guide the souls home. That's the whole point. Otherwise he can't find us."

"He'll find us," Kaylee said.

"He can't. That's the whole point," Paloma repeated, with the finality of a customs officer.

Kaylee set the shoebox down and lifted out the first photograph, her grandfather in his work shirt, squinting into a sun she could feel through the paper. On November 1 and 2, her grandmother had explained once, years ago, families built these home altars, called ofrendas, and Kaylee had nodded the way children nod at things they assume will always be explained again later. Now no one was explaining. Her grandmother was ladling something in the kitchen, and her father had not yet arrived from the airport, and the task of deciding where her grandfather belonged on this table had fallen, without ceremony, to her.

The photograph of her mother's father already occupied the top tier, framed, surrounded by marigolds and a shot glass and a tiny guitar made of clay. Beside it was an empty stretch of white cloth. Kaylee hesitated there, photograph in hand, and found herself thinking about the funeral in the spring, which she had left early. She had told everyone it was a migraine. In truth something in her had gone torpid, a heaviness in her limbs that no weeping would move, and she had sat in the parking lot while they lowered him, furious at herself, and then not furious, just empty, and then furious again on the drive back to school. She had never told anyone she wasn't in the room when it ended.
