She placed the photograph on the top tier, next to the other grandfather. Then she opened the folded paper, because keeping it folded on an altar felt like a lie. It was a grocery list, she discovered. Masa, piloncillo, batteries, and at the bottom, in his cramped hand, a note to himself: tell Kaylee about the well. She had no memory of any well. She stood holding a grocery list that had survived him and felt the loss double itself, once for the man and once for the conversation that now could not happen, and she could not decide whether putting the list on the ofrenda was reverent or strange.

"What's that?" Paloma asked, leaning in.

"A list," Kaylee said. "Things he meant to get."

"Put it down anyway. He might still want them."

Her grandmother appeared with a plate of pan de muerto and studied the arrangement over Kaylee's shoulder, saying nothing, which Kaylee had learned was her grandmother's form of approval. But her father's key sounded in the door, and Kaylee felt the old question rise before he even entered, the one she'd carried since spring: whether to tell him about the parking lot, or whether some failures are better left as private weather. He came in smelling of airplanes, hugged Paloma, looked at the altar, and stopped when he saw the photograph.

"You put him up," he said quietly.

"I did. Up top, with your father."

He set down his bag. Outside, someone's stereo started, and the candles bent in a draft from the kitchen. Kaylee smoothed the grocery list flat beside the photograph and said, before she could weigh it any further, "Dad, there's something I have to tell you about the funeral."

The debate topic was posted on Monday: should cities make public transit free? Chloe had five days to argue it entirely in French, for five minutes, in front of a class where half the students actually spoke French at home. She did not. She had taken the language since seventh grade, could read it slowly, and had never once had to produce an opinion in it under pressure. Her partner, Margot, flipped a coin in the cafeteria to decide sides, and Chloe lost, which meant she would be defending free transit, a position she wasn't sure she held.

She started with French news articles, because Madame Rossignol required two sources in the target language. The first one she opened began, in small gray type, "PARIS." Chloe skipped past it, the way you skip a serial number, and read the piece. It was about a city cutting bus fares to zero for residents, and the reporter interviewed riders who loved it and a budget analyst who called it a gift to people who already rode the bus. Chloe copied three phrases into her notebook, then two more from a second article that started the same odd way, with a city name sitting alone above the first sentence.

On Wednesday the class met in small groups to test arguments. Margot went first, summarizing a French article about transit funding, and Chloe noticed she said the story was about Lyon. The boy across from them, Elias, tilted his head. "It says Paris," he said, pointing at the top of the page. Margot leaned in, saw the small gray word she had sailed past, and went pink. "What is that thing even called?" she asked. "A dateline," Elias said. "The city where the story was reported, before the first sentence." Chloe sat very still, because she had skipped it too, twice, and had half a page of notes built on the assumption that everything she'd read came from France. One of her articles, it turned out, was filed from Brussels.

That afternoon she went back through her sources, and the exercise made her argument stranger and better. The reporters in different cities cared about different things. The French piece worried about who paid; the Belgian piece quoted a rider who said free buses were a truism of good government, so obvious that only a fool would argue against it, and Chloe felt her resistance rise at that, because an argument that can't lose isn't an argument at all. In her draft that night she wrote a line she liked and then crossed out: "Free transit is good because it is free" was tautological, a circle, and Madame Rossignol would eat her alive. She fell asleep with the crossed-out sentence still visible through the page.

Thursday, her weakest moment came in the practice room. Chloe stood to deliver her opening and discovered that the word for "fare," le tarif, had left her head entirely. She stood there with her mouth open, and Margot, playing opposition, said gently, "Prix?" Which was the wrong word, price, not fare, and Chloe knew it was wrong and used it anyway, and the whole argument wobbled off its rails for a sentence and a half before she dragged it back. Afterward Margot said the failure had actually sounded human, like someone thinking rather than reciting, and Chloe wasn't sure whether that was kindness or truth.

What she worked out, in fragments, on the walk home, was a position with two halves that didn't fully fit together. Free fares help the poorest riders immediately, that part she believed. But her Brussels source suggested something her Paris source disputed: that making transit free can starve service quality, hurting the same riders later. So her closing argument became a compromise she could say honestly in French: free fares should be funded as an addition, never as a substitute, and she would admit, out loud, in her third minute, that no one yet knew whether cities could sustain that, herself included. Uncertainty, stated plainly, in a foreign language, with a clock running.

Friday came. Madame Rossignol set the timer on her desk and said "Commencez," and Chloe began, "Je vais défendre la gratuité des transports," and her voice shook on the second word and steadied by the fourth. At the halfway point she reached her admission, the sentence she had rebuilt five times, and she heard the class go quiet in the particular way a room does when someone says something true instead of something safe. Elias, scoring for the other side, looked up from his rubric. When the timer rang, Madame Rossignol asked where Chloe had found the nuance about funding, and Chloe said, "Dans mes sources. Il fallait vérifier les datelines."

Then came the twist Madame Rossignol had saved for last. The final assessment would not be Chloe defending free transit after all. The coin flip, it turned out, had been Margot's small deception: she had already been assigned the opposition side by Madame Rossignol on Monday, and she had wanted Chloe to build the case for free transit because she needed to practice tearing it apart against a real opponent. Margot confessed it in the hallway, waiting to see if Chloe was furious. Chloe considered the betrayal, considered that her notes were now argument and counterargument both, and considered that on Monday she would have to win against everything she herself had written.

"À lundi," Chloe said.

The skate park had emptied an hour before sunset, and Anais had the shallow bowl to herself, which was the only reason she'd brought her physics notebook here at all. She sat on the coping with her back against the fence, the notebook open to a diagram of two charged plates, and above the diagram a question that had been circling her all afternoon: what is the field strength at a point between the plates? She had a battery, a distance, a voltage. What she didn't have was any feeling for what those numbers meant, whether they were large or small, whether the field between the plates was something you could stand inside of, so to speak, or just an artifice of the homework problems, a tidy rectangle drawn on graph paper that existed nowhere else.

She was still staring when two boys came through the chain-link gate carrying a plastic launcher, the kind that fired a small ball with a spring, and a tape measure they let unroll and drag behind them like a tail. The shorter one, whose expression had a saturnine set to it, as if he'd already decided the afternoon would disappoint him, set the launcher on the flat concrete near the bowl's rim and clicked the angle to thirty degrees. The other one, Dev, fired it. The ball sailed out in a low, hugging arc and struck the concrete a good distance away, and the saturnine boy walked to the mark and set a bottle cap on it.

They adjusted the angle again, this time way up, and Anais could see from across the bowl that it was steeper, a tall thin trajectory. She watched the ball climb, hang at the top, and fall. It bounced once and rolled, and Dev walked toward it, then stopped, then looked back at the bottle cap.

"No way," he said. "It's on the cap."

The saturnine boy crouched and picked the ball up off the mark. "That's broken," he said. "One goes low and far, one goes high and straight up and down. They can't land the same."

But they did it again, and again, and Anais found herself leaving her notebook on the coping and drifting over, her shoes scuffing the concrete. "What angles are those?" she asked.

"Thirty and sixty," Dev said, still holding the ball like evidence.

She stood very still, because thirty and sixty added up to ninety, and somewhere in the back of her mind a teacher's voice had said something about complementary angles, something she had filed away as a trivia item and never touched. "Do it at forty and fifty," she said. It felt like a test she was setting for herself as much as for them.

They did it at forty and fifty, same spring, same ball, level concrete, and the two landing marks sat close enough that the bottle cap covered both. Dev whooped. The saturnine boy sat down on the launcher, which was probably not good for it, and said, "Nobody threw the ball different. Same speed. It just... lands there either way." He said it the way people say things they don't yet believe.

Anais walked back to the fence, but she was walking differently now, the way she walked when a problem had stopped being flat. She sat down and looked at her two charged plates and thought about what a field between them might actually be like. If the plates were two walls and you stood in the middle, the field would push you, every point between them, the same push at every point. She'd been treating the field as something that varied, that had interesting geography, and the homework number kept coming out wrong. But if the push was the same everywhere inside, then the point in the question didn't matter at all. The whole space between the plates was one uniform thing.

She divided the voltage by the distance between the plates, wrote the answer, and then, because the boys were still firing, wrote it a second time in the margin to see if it would dare come out different. It didn't. She wondered whether that sameness was a real property of the world or a convenience of the diagram, whether real plates out here in the air, with wind and dust and crooked edges, would keep that promise the way the concrete had kept its promise about thirty and sixty degrees. The concrete had ignored the air, mostly, and been honest anyway. Or honest enough. She couldn't say where the line was, and she left a small question mark next to her answer, not because she doubted the arithmetic but because she wanted to remember that she didn't know everything the number was standing for.

"Hey," she called to the boys, holding up the notebook. "You want to see something weird that's not weird at all?" Dev jogged over, and she turned the page toward the dying light, her pencil still in her hand, the question mark visible at the edge.

The muffin broke apart in Aaron's hands before it reached his mouth, its edges friable with overbaking, and he ate it in pieces over the sink while his father read the practice schedule aloud. Tuesday, parallel parking in the church lot. Thursday, the highway. His father said it the way he said most things, as if the words themselves could keep everyone safe, and Aaron scraped the crumbs into the drain and said he understood.

He did not entirely understand. His father's whole theory of driving was slowness. Drive under the limit. Leave three cars' distance. When in doubt, stop. It had served him for thirty years and two accidents that were both, according to him, the other driver's fault. Aaron had absorbed it so completely that on his first lesson he had braked for a plastic bag drifting across the road, and the instructor, a wiry woman named Dana, had gripped the wheel and said, "Okay. We know your baseline."

Tuesday they set up cones in the church lot, two garbage cans standing in for the cars he would someday have to park between. Dana's method was mechanical and precise: line up your rear axle with the front car's bumper, turn the wheel fully, watch the corner of the cone in your mirror. It worked the way a proof works, the same answer every time. But Aaron kept drifting out to check his position, easing back, correcting, and Dana said, "You're treating it like your father's method. Small and slow and safe. Parking rewards that. Mostly." She made him run it again, tighter, until the tires whispered against the curb and stopped.

At home he described it to his father, who was sanding a chair leg at the kitchen table, the wood dust settling over the newspaper. "Tires shouldn't touch the curb," his father said. "That's how you ruin a sidewall." Aaron said touching wasn't the same as scraping, and his father looked at him for a long moment, then went back to the sandpaper. Later, washing his hands, Aaron found himself trying to subsume the afternoon under something larger, one principle that would cover both Dana's geometry and his father's caution, and he couldn't quite get it to close. Slowness was safe in the lot. He was almost sure slowness was not safe everywhere. He didn't yet know what that meant.

Thursday it meant the on-ramp. The ramp rose in a long curve toward the interstate, and Aaron signaled, checked the mirror, and then did what his body had been trained to do, which was hesitate. He held the car at forty while the traffic in the right lane came up behind him at seventy, and the pickup truck behind him on the ramp closed fast, swung onto the shoulder, and blew its horn as it passed. Ahead of him, a sedan braked hard to let him in, its rear end dipping, another car braking behind it in a slow accordion all the way up the lane.

"Pull off at the next exit," Dana said, and her voice was level, which was somehow worse.

They sat in a gas station lot and she asked him what he thought had gone wrong. "I was going too slow," Aaron said, and then, working it out in real time, the way she seemed to want: "Merging slowly makes everyone brake. So the safe thing is to get up close to traffic speed first, then merge." Dana nodded once. "That lane is the acceleration lane," she said. "Use it." That was all. She opened her thermos and let him sit with it.

On the second ramp he pressed the accelerator and felt the car gather itself, the engine climbing through its registers, and the traffic beside him was suddenly legible, cars moving at something like his own pace, gaps readable, no one diving for the brake. He merged the way you hand someone a cup of coffee they're already reaching for. Behind him nothing slowed down. His hands were shaking anyway, and Dana said, "Better," which from her was practically a speech.

That night his father was at the kitchen table with his philosophy book, the one he read slowly with a pencil, and Aaron sat down across from him with the last of the muffins, the good ones his mother had bought as a reward, dense and not at all friable. "How was the highway," his father said, not looking up. "You went fast." Aaron turned the muffin in his hands. "Fast and then merge," he said. "If you merge slow, everyone behind has to brake. So speeding up on the ramp is the safe move. It's the opposite of the lot. In the lot, slow is safe. On the ramp, slow is the danger." His father put the pencil down. "Speed is a danger," he said. "It's in the statistics." "So is hesitating," Aaron said. "Today it was."

His father looked at him the way he looked at a proof that wouldn't resolve, and Aaron could see the two truths refusing to sit inside one rule, and he could see his father seeing the same thing. Neither of them tried to fix it. His father picked the pencil back up and said, "The metaphysics of it is, you were raised by a cautious man and you're taking your test in a careless world," and Aaron laughed, and his mother came in and asked who wanted tea, and his father said he would have coffee, and Aaron, still turning the muffin, said, "Park it on the counter here."

The pan had been Grand-père's, and before that his mother's, though nobody in the kitchen could say anything about her except that she came from somewhere near Lyon and cooked with a violence Edouard had only heard described. He set it on the burner now, poured in a film of oil, and laid the chicken thighs skin-down, the way he had watched the old man do a hundred times without ever once asking why. The oil spat. The skin turned the color of parchment and stayed there, pale, sweating, steaming in its own juices while the kitchen window fogged over his father's newspaper on the table.

"You're cooking tonight," his father had said that morning, not quite a question, and Edouard had said yes, because in eleven days he would be in a dormitory three hundred miles away and this was the last dinner he could make in this kitchen. He had planned it for a week. Chicken, the potatoes from the bag on the back porch, the green beans his mother still bought at the same stall every Saturday because the vendor had known Grand-père. He wanted the meal to be good enough that his father would say something other than pass the salt. That was the whole want, and it embarrassed him, and he kept it anyway.

His mother came in at six with the beans and stopped at the stove. "It's not browning."

"I know." He pressed the thigh flat with the spatula. Water pooled and hissed and evaporated into more steam. The skin had gone gray, an obedient gray, cooked through and flavored by nothing.

"Turn it up, maybe."

He turned it up. Nothing changed that mattered. At seven he called them to the table anyway, because the potatoes were ready and his father did not like waiting, and they ate chicken that was moist and soft and completely without character, like something served to a sick person. His father ate three pieces without comment, which was its own sentence. Edouard pushed his own portion around the plate and thought about the funeral in March, where the priest had eulogized a man he had never met, some parish abstraction, while Edouard sat in the second row unable to stand up and say anything true.

He did the dishes alone. In the drawer beneath the dish towels he found Grand-père's grease-stained notebook, kept there since the apartment was cleared out, pages of lists and sums in a cramped hand. Halfway through, one page was different: temperatures. The pan must be much hotter, it said. Then, in French, then in English, as if he had been teaching someone: between 140 and 165 Celsius the browning goes fast. Amino acids and sugars. Maillard. Edouard read it twice and understood that he had been told this, probably, at eleven or twelve, standing on a chair at this same counter, and had not listened.

The next evening he took the last four thighs from the refrigerator an hour before dinner and left them on the counter, dry, unwrapped, because the page said dry. He set the cast-iron pan over the burner and let it sit, empty, while he trimmed the beans, and when a drop of water skated across the surface and vanished in a breath he laid the chicken in without moving it. The sound was different, a low sustained roar, and within two minutes the edges had gone the color of dark honey and were still going, and he thought: there it is, that was the whole distance, a hundred and forty degrees he had never bothered to want.

His mother had watched all of it from the doorway without speaking. She had come home early, hoping, she admitted to herself, to find the kitchen failed and empty so that the boy would feel free to leave on schedule, and instead he was standing over her father-in-law's pan with his sleeves rolled, and the smell in the room was the smell of every Sunday of her marriage's first ten years. She could not decide whether that was a gift or a small theft. The pan's provenance was muddled enough already: her husband claimed it, her son had inherited it in practice, and the woman from Lyon had presumably bought it for almost nothing at a market that no longer existed. It belonged to everyone and no one, an object out of its own time, anachronistic in a kitchen with an induction cooktop in the cupboard that they never used.

"Dinner," Edouard called toward the hall. "It's ready now, while it's hot."

His father came in and sat and looked at his plate for a moment before eating. The skin crackled. Underneath, the meat had kept its juice, and the flavor went deep, the way food had tasted when there were four of them at this table instead of three.

"The pan was hotter," Edouard said. "That's all it was."

His father took another piece of chicken, then a piece of bread, then, for the first time in Edouard's memory at this table, he reached across and served himself from his son's platter. "You'll want to take the notebook with you," he said. "It's yours, I think."

Edouard looked at the last thigh, golden, still ticking faintly in the cooling fat. "I'm not taking the pan."

"Then I'll hold it," his father said, "until you come back for it."

Charlotte had been trying to draw her grandmother's hallway for three days, and it still looked like a child's diagram of a hallway, all doors and rug pressed flat against the paper like pressed flowers. She sat on the bottom step with her sketchbook propped on her knees, and the actual hallway stretched away from her, long and dim, narrowing toward the window at the far end. That was the part she could not get. The hallway itself did the thing; her drawing refused to.

Her grandmother came through with a load of laundry balanced on one hip and paused long enough to look over Charlotte's shoulder. "That's the hall, all right," she said, which was not the same as saying it looked like the hall, and they both knew it. She went on toward the kitchen, and Charlotte heard the washing machine begin its low churn.

She tried again. She drew the doors upright and parallel, the rug a long rectangle, the window a small square. Everything correct, everything wrong. The doorframes at the far end ought to be smaller, she could see that plainly when she looked up, but when she drew them smaller they seemed merely distant in a vague, floating way, unattached to the floor. She wondered whether the problem was in her hand or in her eye, whether she was drawing what she knew rather than what she saw. How would a person even begin to separate those two things?

In the afternoon she went looking for distraction and found her grandfather's study, a room she was usually circumspect about entering because of the model ships. On the desk, though, lay a paperback with a cracked spine, open to a page of diagrams. The book was about Florence, about the building of a cathedral dome, and Charlotte flipped through it without much hope until she reached a picture of a painted panel showing a baptistery so convincing, so present, that she turned the book around to see if the image changed. It did not, and yet it kept insisting it had depth.

She read the facing page twice. Around 1420 in Florence, a man named Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, a technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface. He had painted a view of a building and set it up so people could compare the picture with the real thing. She sat back on the carpet. Lines that meet. She thought of the hallway's ceiling edges and floor edges, how in her own eyes they ran toward each other the farther she looked, how the whole corridor seemed to lean inward around that far window. She had noticed it a hundred times without noticing it.

She carried the book to the bottom of the stairs, took out a ruler, and drew the hallway again. This time she put a single point in the middle of the paper, out where the window would be, and let every edge run toward it. The ceiling lines slanted down toward it, the rug's edges slanted up, the doorframes shrank along paths that all converged. When she finished, the hallway was there on the page, receding, holding depth in its flatness. She held the sketchbook at arm's length and compared it to the real hall until her grandmother's slippers appeared at the edge of her vision.

"What on earth are you doing sitting on the floor like that?"

Charlotte turned the page toward her. "It's called linear perspective," she said. "You draw the lines so they meet at one point, and it makes it look deep."

Her grandmother put on her glasses and studied it, tilting her head. "Well, that's the hall," she said, and this time the words meant exactly what they said. She tapped the far window with one finger. "That's where it all goes, isn't it. Everything heads for that bit of light." She went off to see about dinner, and Charlotte stayed on the step, looking from the drawing to the hallway and back.

There was something she could not quite settle, and she let herself not settle it. The trick worked because it lied so carefully, because a flat page could imitate the world only by pretending to be something it was not, lines that never truly touched in the hallway converging cleanly on her paper. And yet the hallway itself was honest, was simply there, and her drawing was honest about it in a lying way. Perhaps every drawing was a counterpoint like that, one truth set against another. Or perhaps she was overcomplicating it, and the hallway was a hallway and the drawing was a good drawing and dinner was at six.

In the kitchen the gravy had begun to coagulate where it sat too long, and her grandmother called for her to come stir it. Charlotte closed the sketchbook, keeping her thumb between the pages, and went.

The waiting room smelled like spearmint and carpet cleaner, and Hunter had been sitting under the fluorescent light long enough to memorize the poster about gum disease. His father's blood pressure was the reason they were both here, in a way. Dad's physical last week had come back with a number the doctor called borderline, and Dad had shrugged it off, so Hunter had decided, without exactly saying so to anyone, that he would learn what the number meant and explain it in a way his father could not shrug off.

The hygienist, a woman named Carol with reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, wrapped the cuff around Hunter's arm without asking. "New machine," she said. "We take everyone's now. You'd be surprised how many people find out they have a problem in a dental chair." The cuff tightened, hugged, released. Carol tilted the screen toward him. "One twenty-four over seventy-eight. That's a good one."

"What do the numbers actually measure?" Hunter asked.

"Top one's the pressure when your heart beats. Bottom one's between beats, when it rests." Carol stripped the cuff off and folded it. "Your dad got a high one somewhere, didn't he. I can tell by the question."

"That obvious?"

"Only to people who ask it that way." She pointed her pen at the poster. "Salt makes you hold fluid, more volume in the same pipes, more pressure. Exercise widens the pipes over time, kind of, makes the whole system run lower. It's plumbing plus habits. Nobody's born with their final number."

Hunter turned that over while Carol printed his chart. Plumbing plus habits. Not a verdict, a reading. That distinction felt important, and he held onto it the way he held onto a locker combination, testing it twice.

His grandmother, in the chair beside him waiting for her own appointment, was scrolling her phone with one finger, the way she did everything, deliberately. "Listen to this," she said. "A country in Europe, they're raising the age of consent to seventeen. Seventeen. There's a whole argument about it in their parliament."

Hunter leaned over. He had never thought about it having an age at all, or rather he had assumed it was simply eighteen everywhere, the way eighteen was the age for everything he'd been told about. "It's not the same everywhere?"

"Goodness, no. It differs by country. And your cousin Denzel was telling me it's not even the same across our own states, that it falls between sixteen and eighteen depending on where you are." She set the phone face-down on her purse. "I suppose lines on a map decide things we think are just true."

He looked it up himself, quietly, while Carol called his grandmother back. Country to country, state to state, sixteen to eighteen, a patchwork he had never noticed. He thought of the blood pressure numbers, how the same body could read differently depending on what had been done to it, and how the same fact could be legal in one place and not another, and how neither system was as fixed as it looked from the outside. He did not fully know what to do with that yet. It sat beside his locker combination, unfinished.

A man across the room was flipping through a local paper with unnecessary violence, and every page he turned he seemed to shake, like the paper had personally offended him. Beside him, his son, maybe ten, read over his shoulder and asked why they kept writing about the aquifer, and the man said, "Because we drink out of it, that's why," and Hunter understood from the words alone: water under the ground, drawn up, argued over. It was a gratuitous amount of anger for a waiting room, though maybe the man was angry about other things and the newspaper was just the nearest target. Hunter's father did that too, anger misplaced onto objects, onto the lawnmower, onto the salt shaker Carol would have confiscated.

When his own name was finally called, Hunter sat back in the chair and let the dentist look at his molars, and when the chair came up he asked, before he lost his nerve, "My dad's pressure was high. If he walks every day and cuts salt, how fast does it change?"

"Weeks to months, if he actually does it," the dentist said. "The body's not instant. But it responds." He looked at Hunter more carefully then. "You want to tell him that?"

"I want to tell him why, not just that."

"Good luck," the dentist said. "I've been telling patients the why for thirty years. Some of them hear it. Some of them just hear a number."

On the drive home, his grandmother asked him to beseech the pharmacist to fill her prescription before five, using the word the way she always did, as if asking were a formal ceremony, and Hunter said he would. At the pharmacy, while the labels printed, he texted his father: Numbers move. Walking and less salt, that's the actual mechanism, not a lecture. He stared at the message for a long moment, thumb over send, thinking that he knew what the numbers meant and did not yet know whether his father would care, and then he sent it anyway and picked up the white bag with his grandmother's name on it.

His phone buzzed against the counter before they reached the car. "Fine," it said. "Walk with me tomorrow. Six a.m."

"Six," Hunter said out loud, to nobody, to the bag, to the whole plumbed and shifting world. "Okay. Six."

The textbook fit on the counter between the register and the lottery scratch-offs, which struck Makayla as the most hopeful arrangement in the store. She had six weeks until the placement exam at Middlesex County College, six weeks to learn enough calculus to skip the remedial course that would cost her a semester and nine hundred dollars she did not have. Between customers she worked the practice problems, and when the bell over the door chimed she covered the page with the flyer for Dev's cold brew special, as though the derivatives were something she'd be embarrassed to be caught wanting.

Dev wanted the cold brew special to work more than he let on. He had raised the price twice since June, and each time he watched the cooler like a man waiting for a verdict. "Nobody vilifies a dollar-fifty increase," he said, tapping the handwritten sign. "But nobody buys it either. There's a number out there, the right price, and I don't know it and the guy who delivers the cups doesn't know it."

Makayla, restocking the day-old pastries whose edges had gone friable enough to shed crumbs down the whole front of the case, said she thought the right price might be a maximum. Not a guess, a point. She had just spent an hour on a page headed Locating Maxima, and the idea had begun to feel less like math and more like a claim about the world: that somewhere between too cheap and too expensive there was exactly one best spot, and the derivative would put her finger on it.

That was the part she couldn't yet hold onto. She could run the rules, bring the exponent down, subtract one, set the whole thing equal to zero. She could do it the way she'd learned to do everything, which was to memorize the motion and trust it. But when she tried to say why setting the slope to zero found the top of a hill, the explanation went friable in her hands too, crumbling before she could hand it to anyone. She had two ways of thinking and no bridge between them.

Ana came in at four-thirty with her book bag and her tutoring money rolled in a rubber band. She was fourteen and preparing for the same placement track two years early, and she installed herself at the ice cream freezer's lid, using it as a desk. Makayla had started helping her on Tuesdays, informally, in exchange for Ana's mother sending over samosas. Today Ana pointed at Makayla's open book, at the tall thin symbol, and asked why the integral sign looked like a stretched-out letter.

Makayla opened her mouth and then closed it, because she didn't know. She flipped to the back of the chapter and found a sidebar boxed in gray, a paragraph about notation, and read it quietly first and then aloud. Gottfried Leibniz introduced the integral sign in 1675, basing it on an elongated letter s, because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum. "An infinite sum," Ana repeated, as if tasting it. She looked at the symbol again and decided it was better than the other notation, the scrawny prime marks, which to her looked like a cat had scratched the page. Makayla didn't argue. Something about the long s settled her anyway, the thought of a man in 1675 deciding that a shape should carry a meaning, that a curve's area was a sum of slices too thin to see.

She turned back to Dev's problem while Ana worked her own page. She wrote a revenue function on the back of the cold brew flyer, something she made up out of the numbers he kept mutbling about: p dollars per cup, cups sold falling as the price rose. She chose R equals 200p minus p squared, because she could differentiate it without hesitating, and then she made herself slow down. The derivative, she said to Ana more than to Dev, is the rate of change. At the top of the hill the rate is zero for one instant, neither climbing nor falling. She brought down the two, set 200 minus 2p to zero, and got p equals one hundred, which made Dev laugh so hard he had to lean on the cigarette rack, because nobody in this neighborhood would pay a hundred dollars for coffee. The function was wrong; the method, she thought, was not.

What she couldn't decide, walking Ana out past the friable donuts and the indemnity notice Dev kept taped inside the register in case the cooler ever died, was whether understanding had to come before the rules or could arrive after them, quietly, the way the meaning of the long s had arrived three hundred years after the man who drew it. She stood in the doorway with the exam book under her arm and Ana already halfway down the block, and Dev called out from behind the counter, "So what's my price, math girl?"

"Lower it," she called back, "and watch the cooler for a week." She held the door open, letting the evening air in, the flyer still in her hand with the hill and its single perfect top drawn on the back.

Jayden's sister Thea had agreed to drive him to the airport only if he explained, before they reached the departures curb, what exactly he was doing in Japan for a year. He had forty minutes of highway left to figure out an answer that didn't sound like a brochure.

"It's an exchange," he said. "I go to school there. I live with a family. That's the whole story."

"That's the itinerary," said Thea, merging past a truck whose mudflaps declared it the property of someone named Duke. "The story is why. You turned down a summer program with your actual friends for this. I want the reasoning." She tapped the wheel twice, judge's gavel style. "You have until the parking garage."

The reasoning, if he was honest, was a diagram he'd seen in March and could not stop seeing: a population pyramid of Japan, wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, the exact opposite of the classic triangle his geography teacher had sketched to show a country full of children. Jayden had sat in that classroom feeling something rearrange. He had always thought of countries as fixed quantities, populations as weather, things you experienced rather than read. The pyramid suggested populations were architecture. You could look at the shape and know things. He'd looked up the number himself, late at night, half convinced he'd misread it: about 29 percent of Japan's people were aged 65 or over in the early 2020s, one of the oldest populations in the world. He'd checked it twice on two different sites, because a number like that felt like a rumor about the future.

"Okay," he said, digging out his phone. "Look." He held up the pyramid, top-heavy like a spinning top balanced wrong. "The bars are age groups. Men left, women right. Wide up here means lots of old people. Narrow down there means fewer kids. So if you're the government and you see this, you don't build the same stuff you built fifty years ago. You're deciding between schools and nursing homes. Whole towns with empty classrooms. That's the part that enraptured me, honestly, that you could predict a country's needs from one picture."

Thea glanced at the screen, then back at the road. "So you're flying nine thousand miles because of a bar chart."

"Because of what the bar chart means," Jayden said, and immediately wished he hadn't said means, because it invited the obvious question.

"Means how?" said Thea, obligingly.

He started to answer with the statistic, the clean 29 percent, the ranking, and then something snagged. The number was solid; it was everything around it that wobbled. "Here's my problem," he admitted. "I've got two ways of thinking at war in my head. Way one: the pyramid. It's basically arithmetic with ambitions. Wide top, old country, plan accordingly. Way two: the family I'm staying with has a grandmother. To the grandmother, the pyramid isn't a forecast, it's Tuesday. She's not a bar. And I can hold both of those in my head at the same time, but I can't make them shake hands yet." He drew the shape again on a napkin, adding a stick figure at the top, elderly, holding what was probably meant to be a cane or possibly a fishing rod. "I keep thinking about this village I read about, right on the coast, littoral, the kind of place where the school closed and the kids left and the beach is mostly herons now. On the pyramid that village is half a bar. In real life it's somebody's whole mailbox."

"Epistemology at seventy miles an hour," said Thea. "I did not agree to this."

"You literally asked."

"I asked for a reason, not a crisis." She was grinning, though, and she took the airport exit without signaling, which was her signature move. "So which is it? Are you going to be the kid who trusts the chart, or the kid who throws the chart out the window for the sake of one grandmother?"

"That's a false binary and you know it," Jayden said, but the question sat in his lap like the napkin. He looked at his sketch again. He didn't actually want to throw the chart out; the chart was why he'd applied in the first place, that vertiginous moment of realizing a picture could know a country's future. But he didn't want to be someone who mistook a shape for a population, either. Maybe, he thought, the position was this: the pyramid tells you what to expect and nothing about what it's like. He could carry both. He said so, out loud, and Thea said, "That's not an answer, that's a truce," and he said, "Truces are answers," and she pulled into short-term parking with eleven minutes to spare before he absolutely had to be at the check-in counter, deadline achieved by the ancestral method of running.

At the gate, backpack half unzipped, he texted her the napkin photo: the top-heavy pyramid, the ambiguous stick figure, and beneath it, in his cramped handwriting, "29% over 65. Will report from inside the bar."

Thea replied with a single heron emoji and, a moment later, "Go learn what Tuesday is like."

Madeline arrived at the community art studio twenty minutes early, which she told herself was diligence, though she suspected it was fear dressed up in better clothes. The Thursday evening class was called Looking Harder, and the instructor, a quiet woman named Reva, had pinned a print of Frida Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace to the corkboard at the front. Madeline had chosen the class because her college application essay had been due, and she had needed, urgently, to be a person who did things like this. She had gotten in. The essay was submitted, the acceptance letter folded into her desk drawer at home, and yet here she still was, sitting on a stool with a notebook, unsure why she had come except that quitting after the payoff felt like a small fraud she didn't want to commit.

There were five other students, most of them older, and one boy about her age named Tobias who was eating sunflower seeds out of his jacket pocket and spitting the shells into a paper cup with startling accuracy. He had set up an easel in the corner, which was odd, because the class was about looking, not painting. On his easel were two small canvases of the same tree: one at dawn, the branches rinsed in pale blue, and one at dusk, everything amber and heavy. He kept standing back from them, frowning, as if distance might reveal something proximity withheld.

Reva began with the Kahlo. "Tell me what you see," she said, and Madeline's hand rose before she had decided anything. "The hummingbird is black," Madeline said, "which is wrong, hummingbirds aren't black, so the wrongness has to mean something. And the thorns come from the monkey, not from her, like someone else's cruelty that she's wearing." A woman in a green cardigan nodded slowly. Reva wrote colour, composition, symbolism on the whiteboard and said only, "Keep going. Formal analysis means you stay with what's in front of you."

Madeline kept going, but she found herself drifting toward Tobias's corner, because his frown had deepened into something that looked like despair. During the break he stood beside his two trees with his arms crossed, and when she came near he said, "It's the same tree twice. That's all it is. Two times of day. Is that enough?" He said he had thought repetition would make the paintings feel like studies, serious, the way artists' repetitions were supposed to feel, but looking at them now he thought they might just be the same idea twice, which was worse than one bad idea.

Madeline said, without planning to, "Monet painted the facade of Rouen Cathedral more than thirty times, in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year." She had read it in a library book the summer she was fifteen, the summer her grandmother was dying and Madeline spent whole afternoons in the art section because it was quiet there and nobody asked her how she was doing. Tobias looked at her. "Thirty," he said. "More than thirty views," she said. "Different light, different times of day and year." He turned back to his canvases as if she had handed him something heavy.

She had not told him the rest, which was that she had once believed she understood the Monets completely, and now suspected she had understood them not at all. At fifteen she had thought the cathedral series proved that attention itself was enough, that if you looked hard enough at one thing, truth accumulated like sediment. Now, at eighteen, standing in a studio that smelled of turpentine and someone's microwaved soup, she thought the series might presage something harder: that the object dissolves under attention, that thirty views give you thirty cathedrals and no solid one, that the tree Tobias had painted at dawn and the tree at dusk might not agree with each other about being the same tree. She had applied to college as an art history major partly on the strength of that fifteen-year-old certainty. She wondered whether the admissions office would want it back.

"Paint it at noon," she told Tobias. "And in rain. And in January, when it's bare." He was already sketching, the pencil moving fast, and she felt a small complicity with him, as though they had agreed on something neither of them could fully state. Or perhaps, she admitted to herself, she had simply needed someone to practice her half-knowledge on, someone who wouldn't know that the confidence in her voice was borrowed from a dead summer.

When the class regathered around the Kahlo, Reva asked Madeline to finish her analysis. Madeline looked at the print: the parrot, the dark leaves, the necklace of thorns drawing a thin line of red, the face that gave nothing away, impermeable to the viewer's wish for an easy reading. She said, "I think the colours are doing what the thorns are doing. The green of the leaves and the green of the background are almost the same green, so the beauty is continuous with the hurt, and I can't find a place where one stops being the other. But I don't know if that's what she intended, or what I'm imposing." The woman in the green cardigan said, "Does it matter which?" and Madeline said, "I genuinely don't know," and was surprised, saying it, by how much the not knowing felt like a position rather than a failure.

Later, gathering her notebook, she saw Tobias had taped a scrap of paper to his easel. On it he had written thirty times, and under that, noon, rain, January. He was packing up his seeds, the paper cup full of shells, and he caught her looking at the note and grinned, embarrassed. "More than thirty," he corrected himself, crossing it out and writing it again. He lifted the two tree paintings off the easel and slid them into his portfolio, one over the other, dawn hidden inside dusk. "Same tree," he said, "but I'm keeping both."

The food bank shared a back wall with the public library, and Simon had chosen it for exactly that reason: he could work his Saturday shift and then walk ten feet to return his books before the fine compounded. His mother had suggested volunteering in the first place, framing it as something colleges liked to see, and Simon had not argued, though the framing bothered him for reasons he could not yet articulate. He arrived at eight wearing his least wrinkled shirt, was handed a hairnet, and was stationed at a folding table beside a woman named Dorotea who sorted cans with the unhurried confidence of someone who had done it a thousand times.

The work was simple and then suddenly it was not. A donation bin had come in from a grocery drive, and Simon's job was to check dates, sort the good from the bad. He picked up a tin of tomatoes, read the stamped line, and put it in the discard tub. Then a jar of applesauce, same destination. By the fourth or fifth item he had a rhythm going, and the discard tub was filling faster than the keep crate, which struck him as wrong in a way he could not immediately locate.

"Wait," Dorotea said, without looking up. She reached into the discard tub, retrieved the tomatoes, and held the date toward him. "Why is this in here?"

"It's past the date," Simon said, and heard how thin it sounded.

She turned the tin over in her hands, studying the label rather than him. "That's a best before date. It marks when the quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe." She set the can down between them. "Sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat. There's a different kind of date for the unsafe stuff, and that's not what this says."

Simon looked at the tin, then at the tub, where the applesauce and a sack of rice and a box of crackers sat in the ignominy of his judgment. "So I threw out everything that's a week or two past?"

"You did." She said it without unkindness and handed him the tub. "Happens the first shift. There's a flyer in the office about it, if you want to read the actual policy."

He did want to, which surprised him. In the cramped office he found the flyer taped inside a cupboard door, and he read it twice, then went back out and began rescuing cans from his own discard pile, rechecking each date, restoring them one by one to the keep crate. The labor of undoing his error felt strangely clarifying. All morning he had been operating on a rule he had absorbed from his own kitchen, from his mother's punctilious purging of the pantry, and the rule had never once been examined.

During the lunch break, Dorotea sat with him on the loading dock, and they split a bag of the donated crackers he had almost thrown away. He asked her whether it troubled her, the ambiguity of it, the fact that "may still be safe" was not the same as "is safe," that someone would eventually open a can whose quality had declined and make a judgment call with their own stomach.

"Every day," she said. "I've decided I can't predicate the whole bin's fate on the worst case. Some pundit on the news says one thing, the health department says another, and I'm out here with a folding table and a hairnet doing my best translation." She bit a cracker, chewed. "You learn to hold two ideas at once. The food matters and the caution matters and neither one gets to win all the time."

Simon thought of his grandfather, an ascetic man who kept almost nothing in his cupboards and wasted almost nothing, who would have regarded a discarded can the way others might regard a sin. Two different inheritances, his mother's caution and his grandfather's thrift, and neither, he now suspected, was complete on its own. He did not say any of this aloud, because he could not yet say it without sounding like a college application essay, which was perhaps the thing he had been circling all morning.

Back at the table, he sorted for another two hours, slower now, reading each stamp twice. When a can came through that was months past and slightly swollen at one end, he set it aside without hesitation, and Dorotea nodded once. But a sealed tin of peaches, three weeks over its date, he wiped clean and placed in the keep crate, and he sat with the small uncertainty of that, and kept working. At five o'clock he carried the crates to the shelf, walked through the connecting door, and set his library books on the returns desk, one by one.

Nevaeh had promised herself she would finish the summer reading before August, and now August was three days away, and she was sitting on her grandmother's porch with the novel open on her knees and a legal pad full of crossed-out sentences. The assignment asked one question: is the narrator trustworthy, and how does the point of view shape what the reader is allowed to know? She had written four attempts at an answer. All four sounded like a person quoting a textbook she hadn't read.

"Still fighting that book?" her grandmother asked, coming out with two glasses of lemonade and a plate of saltines with peanut butter, which she considered a complete snack.

"It's not the book, it's the narrator. He keeps saying he's the reasonable one, but every time something happens he's the only one who saw it." Nevaeh flipped to a dog-eared page. "Like here, he says the neighbor slammed the door on him, but there's no one else to ask. It's all first person. Him, him, him."

Her grandmother settled into the other rocking chair and put her feet up on a milk crate she had owned since before Nevaeh's father was born. "When I was in school we had to memorize a speech from Julius Caesar. My elocution teacher would smack the desk with a ruler if we mumbled." She said this with obvious nostalgia, as if the ruler had been the fun part.

"You're saying my problem is diction?"

"I'm saying you've been reading with your elbows." Her grandmother sipped her lemonade. "Read me a piece. Out loud. Sometimes the thing tells on itself when it has to go through the air."

Nevaeh read the scene where the narrator described the neighbor slamming the door, doing a voice for him that made him sound faintly like a martyr. Her grandmother laughed into her glass. "That man is lying," she said immediately. "Or at least editing. Nobody slams a door that politely."

But polite or not, the book gave Nevaeh no way to check. She sat with that for a minute, rocking. The whole novel was locked inside one skull, and the skull had opinions. Then she turned to a blank page on the legal pad. "Grandma, help me try something. What do you think the neighbor was actually doing in her kitchen right before she closed the door?"

"Cooking something with onions, I'd guess. And probably deciding this man was the kind who'd stand on a porch until you agreed with him."

Nevaeh wrote it out, the scene again, but from across the street, through the neighbor's window. The neighbor could hear the narrator talking, could not hear what he said, could see him smile in a way she found rehearsed. It took ten minutes and it exhilarate her more than any page she'd written all summer, though when she read it back it was rough, inchoate in places, more of a sketch than a scene. Still. Something had shifted. In her version, the reader learned what the neighbor thought, and what the narrator looked like from outside, and how wrong his account of his own charm had been. She held up the two pages side by side like a woman comparing paint samples.

"So you fixed him," her grandmother said.

"Not fixed. Saw him. The first version, the one in the book, all we get is what he sees and what he decides to tell us. He's the only window." She tapped the second page. "And this one, I'm basically pretending to be somewhere else entirely, some narrator who can go into anyone's head, hers, his, the dog's if I wanted. That's the difference. That's the whole assignment, maybe."

"Then write that down before you lose it."

Nevaeh thought of Mr. Okafor's classroom in the spring, the day he'd assigned the book. He had drawn a stick figure on the board with a speech bubble and said, "Remember, this is a person, not a camera," and she had written it down without understanding it, the way she wrote down most things that year, hoarding sentences the way her grandmother hoarded buttons in a coffee tin, certain they'd matter later and unsure how. It had been a rough year for certainty generally. She had applied to six colleges and gotten into her safety and been deferred by her first choice and told everyone she didn't care, which was itself, she now suspected, a first-person account with editing.

She started a fifth draft on the legal pad. "The narrator reports only what he sees, knows, or chooses to say," she wrote, then paused, because that wasn't quite the whole of it either. She still couldn't prove he lied about the door. Maybe the neighbor really had slammed it, onions or no onions, and Nevaeh's rewrite was just a different bias wearing a nicer dress. She wrote that down too, in the margin, with a question mark.

Her grandmother leaned over to look. "You're putting your doubts in the actual paper?"

"He said we could. He said the smart answer to an unreliable narrator is not 'he lies,' it's 'here is exactly how much we can know and no more.'"

Her grandmother considered this, then stole a saltine off Nevaeh's plate. "In my day we just said the man was no gentleman and got on with it."

"Your day had rulers, Grandma. You had resources." Nevaeh laughed, underlined the question mark twice, and reached for the last saltine at the same moment her grandmother did.

Kevin stood at the edge of his own graduation party with a plastic cup of warm lemonade and watched his grandfather argue with a folding chair. The chair had collapsed under an earlier guest, and his grandfather, an irascible man who treated furniture as a personal adversary, was trying to force it back into shape while muttering in Portuguese. Kevin's mother had told him that morning to keep the peace, and he had spent the afternoon attempting to propitiate both sides of a family that had split along a fault line no one would name: the side that thought college was a sensible next step, and the side that thought Kevin was being stolen from them.

The diploma lay on the table beside the cake, still in its navy folder. His cousin Bruno picked it up first. "You're not even going to look at it?"

Kevin took the folder back, opened it, and frowned. The certificate sat flat inside, unfolded, corners sharp. "They didn't even fold it," he said. "That's the whole thing, apparently."

"The whole thing?"

"The word diploma. It's Greek. It means paper folded double." Bruno raised an eyebrow, and Kevin shrugged. "They used to fold official documents in half. That's where the word comes from. I found it out Tuesday, reading in the library instead of packing."

"So they gave you a folded-paper word for a flat piece of paper," Bruno said. "Congratulations."

Kevin's father appeared with the potato salad, set it down, and fixed on the folder with the expression he reserved for tuition statements. "You should frame it," he said. "Your tio Rui says Framingham State will take you in the spring, no debt, work at the shop until then. He's holding the position."

"He told me the same thing twice today," Kevin said. "Once with the position, once with the truck."

"That's not an offer you get twice."

Down the yard, his grandfather had given up on the chair and was instead telling Kevin's Aunt Lucia that the university had mailed them a bill for a dormitory Kevin had not yet seen. Kevin had heard two maxims from his father over the years, and the second one, delivered usually at the kitchen table over the bills, was that a man carries what his family gives him and nothing more. The first was that education is the one thing they cannot take back. He had never noticed until tonight that the two did not sit together comfortably, and that his father recited each with the same certainty.

He walked down to the table where his grandfather sat now, chair abandoned, and set the diploma folder in front of him. His grandfather opened it, ran a thumb along the embossed seal, and read Kevin's full name, including the middle name Kevin had tried to drop in ninth grade.

"Paper folded double," Kevin said. "That's all it is, word-wise. The Greeks folded the documents in half and the name stuck."

His grandfather looked at him for a moment. "Folded double. So it was small enough to carry in a coat."

"I never thought about that part."

"A man who carries his papers folded can run faster," his grandfather said, and closed the folder, and folded it in half himself, decisively, so the navy leather bent around the certificate. He set it back on the table like a completed transaction. "There. Now it is what it says it is."

Bruno caught Kevin's eye across the yard and mouthed, is that allowed? Kevin found he did not care whether it was. His father arrived at the table, saw the bent folder, and picked it up, and for a second Kevin braced for the argument, the two sides, the whole afternoon's careful diplomacy. His father unfolded it, looked at the crease running across the certificate, and then folded it back along the same line his grandfather had made.

"Tio Rui's holding the position until January," he said. "The dorm opens in September." He held the folder out to Kevin. "You can run fast either way, I suppose."

Kevin took the diploma and put it in the inner pocket of his jacket, which was hanging on the fence, which was where the dog was currently dragging it toward the hedge.

Brody arrived at the park eleven minutes early, which he decided he would spend looking casual, and which he in fact spent retying his shoes twice and rehearsing the phonetics of her name under his breath. Nadia. Three syllables, stress on the first, no mystery to it, but he mouthed it anyway like a spell that might fail if pronounced wrong. She had suggested the park over coffee, something about hating the acoustics of cafes, and he had said "totally" as though he had opinions about acoustics. He was standing now under an oak, one of a long arboreal line bordering the path, each tree dropping its seeds into the fountain with a faint plastic tick.

She came up the path with two paper cups, handed him one without ceremony, and said, "I didn't know what you take, so it's black and you can suffer." He laughed harder than the line deserved, then adjusted down to a normal laugh, and they started walking. The first ten minutes went fine. There was a dog wearing sunglasses. There was a man doing tai chi with a pool noodle. There was a goose that seemed to hold a grudge, though against what neither of them could say. By the time they reached the far end of the duck pond, the conversation had begun to thin, and Brody felt the silence coming the way you feel weather change.

"So," Nadia said, and then nothing followed it. He tried to propitiate the moment with a fact about geese, something he'd read about mate selection, and it landed wrong, possibly because he misremembered it, possibly because geese were not the point. She nodded politely. A seed ticked into the fountain behind them. He could feel the date sliding toward the parking lot, toward the polite text two hours later, toward nothing.

"Okay," she said, stopping on the bridge. "Can I try something? I read about this study once and I've always wanted to actually do it, and you're the closest available stranger." He said yes before she finished the sentence, which was either eager or honest, and she sat down on the wooden rail, cup balanced on her knee. "In 1997, this researcher, Arthur Aron, had pairs of strangers take turns asking each other thirty-six questions. The questions got gradually more personal as they went. And afterward those pairs ended up feeling closer than pairs who just made small talk." She looked at him to see if he thought it was stupid. He was already sitting down.

"That's the whole procedure? No eye contact ritual, no chanting?" "Just the questions. We take turns. And we answer honestly, which is the part I think people skip." She held up a hand as if she had the list memorized, though he suspected she was inventing. "Question one. Given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest?" He said his grandfather, who died when Brody was nine, and who he could no longer picture without a photograph, which he admitted was the actual answer rather than the charming one. She said a novelist she'd written a fan letter to at thirteen and never mailed.

The early questions were easy, almost silly, and they traded them like warm-up pitches while the goose patrolled below the bridge. But by the time she asked him to name the thing he was most grateful for in the last year, something had shifted; he found himself describing his mother's remarriage in more detail than he'd given anyone, including his best friend, including himself. He asked her about the perfect day and she answered with a day that had already happened, last October, alone, and then looked startled at having said it. "Interesting," she said, into her cup. "I didn't plan to say that."

They worked up through the middle of the list, where the questions stopped being clever and started being surgical. What friendship meant to each of them, said out loud, which turned out to be harder than having one. Whether there was something she'd dreamed of doing for a long time and why she hadn't done it. Brody gave his answer to that one and heard his own voice sound unfamiliar doing it. He noticed, somewhere in there, that he was both more himself and more constructed, that the closeness in the study was real and also something they were performing their way into, and he couldn't tell whether those were different things or whether it mattered. He decided it probably mattered and that he didn't care yet.

"Last one," Nadia said. The light had gone long and low across the pond, and the goose had given up on them. "Of all the people in your family, whose death would you find most disturbing." He took a slow drink of his terrible coffee. She watched him with her head tilted, waiting, and the fountain ticked behind them with its plastic seeds.

"My dad," Brody said. "Because I'd have to finish becoming someone without him watching. Your turn." She was quiet for a second, then laughed, not at the question but at herself. "I was going to lie," she said, "and say my grandmother. But it's my sister." She set her cup down on the rail. "Question thirty-six, or wherever we stopped. You get one more, and I get one more, and then I think they close the gates at dark."

The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Jaxon had claimed the same corner of it every lunch period for three weeks, tucked behind the folded choir risers where nobody would hear him fail. He had wanted the violin since Mr. Reyes announced the spring assembly would include a small student ensemble, and he had traded two months of mowing the Hendersons' lawn for a rented instrument with a cracked chin rest. His problem was simple and humiliating: he could not keep the strings straight. He would reach for a note on one string and hear it come out on another, and every morning his fingers seemed to have forgotten everything they learned the day before.

The fourth string was the worst. He knew there were four, obviously, but which one was which, and in what order, kept sliding around in his head like beads on a wet string. He tried to cogitate his way through it during algebra, drawing little ladders in his notebook margin, and Mrs. Okafor had to say his name twice before he looked up. "Sorry," he said. "I was somewhere else." He could not exactly say he was somewhere on a stage, in May, holding an instrument he had not yet mastered.

The person who changed everything was Priya, a sophomore who had been playing since she was six and had been assigned to tune the rental violins before rehearsal. He watched her do it on Tuesday, ear tilted, fingers twisting the pegs with tiny confident turns. When she handed him his violin, he put it under his chin and, out of nerves more than intention, set his bow on what he thought was the highest string and pulled a note so low it startled him. Priya laughed, not unkindly. "You're on the G," she said. "That's the lowest one."

"Lowest to highest," she said, tapping each string with the tip of her bow as she spoke. "G, then D, then A, then E. Good Dogs Always Eat." She said it flat, the way you'd recite a locker combination, and turned to the next violin. But Jaxon stayed with his hand hovering over the strings. Good Dogs Always Eat. G, D, A, E. From the fat one near his thumb up to the thin one nearest his face. He played them in order, one open bow stroke each, and for the first time the instrument felt like a landscape instead of a scrambled wire fence.

At Thursday rehearsal Mr. Reyes had them tune as a section, and Jaxon heard something he had missed before. Each string, played open next to the one above it, rang out in the same interval every time, a bright hollow sound like two doorways opening into the same room. Priya was beside him, tightening her bow. "Perfect fifths," she said, when he asked what that ringing was. "That's how they're tuned. All the way up." He tested it again after rehearsal, alone behind the risers: G to D, D to A, A to E, the same interval each time, climbing. The regularity of it steadied him. The order was not arbitrary; it was a pattern he could hear as well as recite.

He still sounded bad. That had to be admitted. The assembly was four weeks away, and while he no longer confused his strings, his fingers landed flat, his bow arm wavered, and the piece Mr. Reyes had chosen had a shift into third position that Jaxon approached each time like a man stepping off a curb he could not see. He began to wonder whether he had any business taking a seat in the ensemble at all. If he dragged the sound down in front of the whole school, the culpability would be entirely his; nobody had begged him to do this.

His younger sister, Marisol, found him practicing on the auditorium stage on a Saturday, when the building was open for set construction. She sat in the third row with her backpack still on, eating pretzels, watching him run the passage twelve times. On the thirteenth, his hand seized and he lowered the bow. "You sounded better that last one," she offered.

"Thanks," he said, and then, because she was there and he could not say it to anyone else: "I don't know if I should play or tell Reyes to find someone else." He laid the violin across his knee. "I finally get the strings, G to E, I can hear the fifths now, and it doesn't matter, because my left hand is still stupid." It came out petulant, he knew it the moment it left his mouth, a little kid's complaint dressed in a bigger vocabulary, and he was ashamed of the tone more than the admission.

Marisol crumpled the pretzel bag and came up onto the stage. "Play the strings in order," she said. "The way you told me in the car. All four." He did, slow whole bows, G, D, A, E, each one opening into the next, the same ringing stairway climbing toward the thin bright E. When the last note faded into the rafters, she was quiet for a second, and then she said, "Do it again."

The folding chairs ran out before the cousins did, so Logan ended up on the piano bench in the corner of Aunt Rachel's living room, wedged between a stack of Haggadot and a bowl of pistachios. He had been to this Seder every year of his life and had never once had to do anything but eat and find the afikoman. That was the privilege, he was beginning to understand, of no longer being the youngest.

His cousin Sophie, seven, had that honor now, and she was hiding behind the ficus with a paperback Haggadah clutched to her chest like a wounded animal. When Logan brought her a plate of parsley, she looked up at him with wet eyes. "I can't do it," she whispered. "It's too many words."

"Do what?" he asked, though he already knew. He had watched his older brother, years ago, stand on a kitchen chair in this same room and recite in a voice that shook, and he had listened to his grandfather say, "The youngest asks the questions, that's how we begin." Nobody had explained it further. It was simply what happened, the way the youngest was always the one who had to ask why this night was different from all other nights.

"I have to ask the Four Questions," Sophie said. "In front of everybody. Aunt Mira already practiced with me twice and I messed it up twice." She opened the Haggadah to the marked page and turned it toward him, and there they were, printed in Hebrew above an English translation that began with the question he had heard every spring of his life: Why is this night different from all other nights?

Logan had an idea about how to learn things, formed mostly through cramming for chemistry exams: break it into pieces, then make the pieces into a rhythm. "Forget everybody," he told her. "Just do the first line for me. Quiet, just us." She swallowed and started, and her voice was so thin the words barely cleared her teeth, so he said, "Enunciate. Like you're telling a secret you actually want someone to hear." She tried again, louder, and a small astonished smile crossed her face when she finished the line without stumbling.

They worked through it in the corner for twenty minutes while the aunts argued over whether the charoset needed more wine and Uncle David told his annual story about the year he was impecunious and unemployed and someone's Passover dinner had been the best meal of his month. Sophie's brother Noah, home from his first year at college, drifted over at one point and began coaching too, but his method was all commands, tap the table on every syllable, chin up, project, and Sophie shrank with each instruction. Logan caught Noah's eye and tilted his head toward the kitchen, and Noah took the hint and went to bother the brisket instead. It occurred to Logan that there were two ways to get a kid through a performance: you could drill her like a soldier or let her discover she was capable, and he genuinely did not know which one his grandfather, who prized discipline, would call correct. Perhaps both, he thought. Perhaps it depended on the kid, which was a kind of discernment no rulebook could supply.

When Aunt Rachel dimmed the lights and lit the candles, Sophie's hand found Logan's sleeve and gripped it. The room settled. Grandpa raised his cup, and everyone leaned toward the youngest person present, who was still behind the ficus, and Sophie stepped out. Her shoes squeaked on the hardwood. She folded her hands in front of her like a news anchor, took the breath Logan had taught her to take, four counts in through the nose, and began.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?"

Her voice did not shake. It carried across the candles, across the folded chairs, all the way to the kitchen where Noah had gone, and Logan heard the pencil he'd been tapping go still. She asked about the matzah and the bitter herbs and the dipping, each question steadier than the one before, and when she finished, the whole table said the response together, a low rolling murmur Logan had never listened to properly until now. Sophie looked at him across the room and grinned, and Grandpa, wiping his eyes and pretending it was the horseradish, said, "Sophie, sweetheart, you may sit. Somebody pour this girl some grape juice."

Logan slipped her the first cup himself.

Annabelle sat on top of the climbing dome with her physics workbook wedged against her knees, because the playground was the only place her little brother would agree to spend the afternoon and the homework was due tomorrow. The problem was a soccer ball kicked at fourteen metres per second at thirty degrees above the horizontal, and for three days she had been treating the motion as one thing, one arc, the way a ball in flight looks like one thing. The textbook kept insisting it was two. Split the velocity, the margin note said in her own handwriting from Tuesday, when she had copied the phrase without believing it.

Below her, Marcus was negotiating with a four-year-old over a dump truck, so she had maybe ten minutes. She drew the kick again: a horizontal arrow, a vertical arrow, a slanted arrow between them. The horizontal part carried the ball forward at a constant rate, untouched by gravity; the vertical part rose, slowed, stopped, fell. Two stories about one ball, running side by side. She tested it on the swing set across the sand, a girl pumping her legs, and found she could not look at the swing the old way anymore.

Her phone buzzed. It was Deshawn from her lab table, and the message was a photo of his homework with the caption: check question six, I got something different. His answer and hers matched to two decimal places, but his units said newtons per coulomb and hers said volts per metre. They had been fighting about units all semester, actually, ever since he had called her method sloppy on the electric fields quiz and she had stopped sitting near him. His note under the photo said: mine has to be right, force over charge makes sense. Yours is just voltage divided by distance.

Annabelle typed back that voltage over distance made perfect sense, then deleted it, because it didn't yet, not perfectly, and she had learned something in the last hour about claiming certainty she hadn't earned. She sat with the two answers. Same number, different words. On the dome, her brother had moved on to the slide, and she watched him climb the ladder, rung by rung, each rung a separate decision about height, while the slide did all the horizontal work at once.

It occurred to her that the fight with Deshawn depended on a taxonomy she had never questioned, the idea that different units must name different quantities, that force-over-charge and voltage-over-distance belonged to separate drawers in some cabinet of physics. The ball had broken her of that once already today. The arc looked like one motion and was two; the two unit expressions looked like different quantities and might be one. She couldn't prove it from where she was sitting. All she had was the coincidence of the matching number, and coincidence was a thing Mr. Okafor warned them about, tangential evidence, he called it, evidence that touched the conclusion without supporting it.

She texted Deshawn: same number, same question, maybe same thing. He replied with a screenshot of the inside back cover of the textbook, the unit equivalence table she had never once opened, and there it was in small print, volts per metre and newtons per coulomb listed as equals. Neither of them had been wrong. That was the part that unsettled her, sitting there in the late sun while a toddler dropped sand out of a bucket in a thin, even stream, like a very small demonstration of constant flow. She had spent a week predicating her opinion of Deshawn on the assumption that one of them had to be the sloppy one, and the assumption had turned out to be the sloppy part.

She thought about telling him she was sorry, and did not type it, and then thought about how last month she would have sent something sharp instead, something about him checking his facts before he insulted her methods, and how the table in the back of the book would have let her be right and alone at the same time. Marcus fell off the bottom of the slide and looked around to see whether anyone had witnessed it. She raised a hand so he would know that she had, and that it was fine.

She finished the soccer ball problem on the walk home, holding the workbook against her hip, working the vertical half first because gravity was the part she trusted, then using the time it gave her to carry the horizontal half across. At the corner she stopped under the streetlight and sent Deshawn one more message: the ball thing and the units thing are kind of the same thing, I think. Two ways of looking that don't fight each other. Then, after a pause: I'm still not sure I'd predicate a whole grade on that. He started typing, stopped, started again. The message, when it came, was only: want to split the reading for Friday? Marcus pulled her sleeve toward the crosswalk, and she put the phone in her pocket and followed him.

The polling station occupied the gymnasium of Roosevelt Middle School, and Charlie had claimed a folding table near the door where the line couldn't help but pass her. She was there for a civics project, an exit poll with a clipboard and a stack of questionnaires, due by email at nine o'clock that night. Her teacher had asked for one page on a question Charlie had circled twice before deciding to take it seriously: whether it should be harder or easier to remove a head of government. She had until the polls closed at eight to collect responses, and after that her page would have to stand on whatever she had gathered.
