It was his grandmother's handwriting, small and upright, a column of dates and numbers. 138 over 84. 132 over 81. 135 over 86. Beside each entry a note in the margin: felt fine, gardened, slept well. There was a folded sheet of paper clipped to the back cover, some photocopy from the doctor's office, and he read it twice by the light under the sink.

Three summers ago he had found a different notebook in a different room of this house, his grandfather's, full of bird sightings logged months after the funeral, the last pages blank. He had put it back and never said anything, and he had thought about that silence a hundred times since, the way it had felt like protection and also like a locked door. He sat down on the bathroom floor with the new notebook and did not put it back.

At dinner his grandmother talked about the neighbor's fence and a cousin who was trying to monetize her baking videos, selling the recipes as a digital download, and Grandma said the word monetize like it was a species of rodent she had identified but declined to chase. Nolan pushed his potatoes around and thought about how a person could build a whole artifice of being fine, a beautiful one, hand-stitched in a column of small upright numbers, and how impermeable it could be, and how he had stood outside it before with his grandfather's notebook and let it hold.

"Grandma," he said when the plates were cleared. He set her notebook on the table, open to the last month of entries. "I found this when my phone fell behind the sink. I'm sorry. But I read the sheet that was clipped to it."

She looked at the page for a long time, then at him, and her jaw set in the way he recognized from arguments about her driving at night.

"Those numbers," he said. "The guideline sheet says stage 1 hypertension starts at 130 over 80. Yours are in that range. That's stage 1 hypertension."

"I know what my numbers are," she said. "I write them down every morning before the coffee, like Dr. Okafor asked. That's the whole point of writing them down, so I know." She closed the notebook with one hand and kept her palm flat on the cover.

"Have you shown them to her? To Dr. Okafor?"

"They're for me to keep track. I don't need to run in every time a number wobbles. Your grandfather turned every ache into a production, appointments and waiting rooms, and I sat in those chairs for forty years. I am not doing that."

"That's not what I'm saying. You don't have to do what he did. Just show her the page. One page." He slid the clinic card out of his pocket, the one he'd grabbed for his presentation, the county clinic on Meridian, and then felt how absurd it was, a card about condoms and testing sitting on her tablecloth. He picked it back up and put it away.

She turned the notebook over, then over again, as if the answer might be printed on the back. Outside, the neighbor's dog started at something along the fence line.

"Thursday, after your little speech," she said. "You can drive me."

The wind coming off the parking lot kept lifting Charles's cap off his head, and he held it down with one hand while the other balanced a tray of glasses he'd carried out to the patio at Rossi's, where his family had taken over the long table by the fence. He had graduated three hours ago. The tassel kept swinging into his eyes, and when he finally sat down, the cap slid sideways and knocked over his water.

"Why do they even make these things this shape?" he asked, shoving it into the seat beside him.

His cousin Danny, who was seventeen and had opinions about everything, said it was probably some old tradition nobody remembered the reason for. Charles's grandmother said it looked like a priest's hat. His phone buzzed before anyone could settle it, and he read the message under the table.

It was from Mr. Alvarez, his manager at the restaurant, and it arrived like a stone dropped in a glass. "Need to talk before your shift tomorrow. Nothing you did wrong. Come at two." Charles read it four times. He had worked at Rossi's for two years, since the month his father's printing business had slid into insolvency, the bills arriving in envelopes that got thinner and more threatening, and his paycheck had been the steady thing in the house while his mother picked up extra shifts at the hospital. Nothing you did wrong. Then why did his stomach turn?

His little sister Nadia, across the table, was watching him. She was fourteen and had wanted to come to Rossi's since she was nine, when Charles had first described the back room with its wall of signed photographs and the tub of parmesan the size of a birdbath. For her, tonight was not about him. She had dressed up in a skirt she'd saved for months and kept asking their grandmother to take pictures of her under the string lights.

"Is something wrong?" she said.

"Work stuff," Charles said, and put the phone face down on his tablecloth.

His father raised a glass and gave a short toast about doors closing and opening, which everyone drank to quietly. Charles kept thinking about two o'clock tomorrow. He tried to reason it out the way he did in his ethics elective, laying positions side by side. Maybe Alvarez was cutting hours, which would be survivable; maybe he was being let go, which would not. Maybe "nothing you did wrong" was the literal truth, a matter of costs and mercurial summer crowds, and Charles's instinct to search his own conduct for the fault was just guilt looking for somewhere to land. The restaurant had been half empty for three Fridays running. He couldn't exonerate himself of a crime he hadn't been accused of, and he couldn't convict the economy on suspicion alone. Both readings fit the message. That was the part that kept him circling his breadstick like a shark.

Danny leaned over. "You look like you're doing math."

"I'm deciding whether to be worried."

"And?"

"I'll know at two."

Danny stole his breadstick, which Charles allowed.

Nadia, meanwhile, had gotten their grandmother to walk the whole patio with her, taking pictures of the kitchen door, the chalkboard menu, the spot where the hostess stand was. Charles watched her and understood, suddenly, that she wasn't decorating his night. She was claiming hers. When they were small he'd told her Rossi's stories like bedtime serials, the dishwasher who'd once been a boxer, the night the power went out and everyone ate by candlelight, and she'd absorbed the place as a kind of promised land. She'd never once eaten here. Their father had always said someday.

A card arrived with the tiramisu, signed by the whole kitchen staff, and Charles felt his throat tighten. Then Nadia appeared at his elbow with his cap, which she'd rescued from the chair.

"Put it on," she said. "For one picture. Me and the graduate at Rossi's."

The wind took it again immediately, and Charles held the board flat against his head with both hands. "You know it's called a mortarboard," he said. "It resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar."

"That's the dumbest name for a hat I ever heard."

"That's what the card from Mr. Alvarez's daughter says, anyway. She printed it out for the graduation display in the lobby." He had found it there this morning, taped between photos of other servers' graduations, and had stood reading it while the lunch prep clattered behind him.

Nadia laughed, took the picture, and checked the screen. In it, Charles is grinning under his flat square hat, the wind caught mid-theft, and behind him the kitchen door is open a crack, showing a sliver of the world he would walk into at two o'clock tomorrow.

"Send me that one," Nadia said.

"You already have it."

"Send it anyway. It's mine too."

He thumbed it to her, and the phone buzzed once against the tablecloth, right beside the other message, the one he had not opened again. He left both of them where they lay, face up now, and reached for the last piece of bread before Danny could take it.

Lea spread the printout on the picnic table and weighted its corners with two tomatoes and a jar of screws, because the backyard wind in August treated paper like a personal grievance. Her grandfather came out with his coffee, moving carefully on the bad knee, and lowered himself onto the bench across from her.

"You're studying out here now," he said. It wasn't quite a question.

"Practice for my roommate," Lea said. "First-year seminar. We have to explain something scientific to somebody who doesn't know it, and I picked you."

"Flattered, I'm sure." He squinted at the graph. "That looks like somebody's heartbeat on a monitor."

"It kind of is. Sort of." She traced the jagged line with her finger, the small sawtooth rises and falls stacked on a steady climb. "This is carbon dioxide in the air, measured at a place called Mauna Loa, in Hawaii. Every year it wiggles up and down because of the seasons, but underneath that it keeps going up. Like stairs."

He leaned in. She had rehearsed this part in her bedroom and again walking to the bus stop, and now, in the actual air, with an actual person, the words came out slower than she wanted but truer. Sunlight comes in, she said, and the Earth sends heat back out toward space, but carbon dioxide and other gases hold some of that heat in the atmosphere, the way the glass of a greenhouse lets light through and keeps warmth from leaving. It was not a perfect comparison and she said so. The gases don't form a lid; they're mixed through the whole sky, absorbing and re-emitting, and the extra warmth is spread thin everywhere rather than pooled in one place.

"Then the graph," her grandfather said, tapping the paper with one finger. "What's this line crossing here, where you drew the arrow?"

"That's the part I'm trying to pin down." She had circled the point where the scribble of the line finally lifted above a horizontal line she'd drawn and labeled 400. "The daily average passing 400 parts per million for the first time in the record. It matters because it's a number nobody alive has ever seen before, but I can't remember what year it happened, and if I tell you wrong on Tuesday, my whole presentation is suspect."

"So look it up."

"My phone's dead. The charger's inside and it takes forever." She said this with the querulous tone she'd been trying to shed all summer, and she heard it and laughed at herself. "See, that's why I need the practice."

Her grandfather drank his coffee and looked at the garden, where the zucchini had gone feral again. "You said Mauna Loa. There used to be a fellow on the news who talked about Mauna Loa, back when your mother was small. Keeling, maybe." He set the cup down. "I remember the news saying four hundred, and I remember it felt like a number you were supposed to flinch at, and I remember it was before your mother finished college. She finished in 2014."

Lea sat with that. Her mother had graduated in May of 2014, so the crossing had happened before that, which put it somewhere in 2014 or earlier. She looked at the graph again, at the arrow, and thought about how to adjudicate between her grandfather's memory and her own blank. Memory was a witness, not a record; but a graph without a date was a record with no address. She needed one more fact, and the only place to get one was inside.

She left the tomatoes on the corners and went in through the screen door, found the charger, waited by the outlet while the phone took its first sip of power, then searched with what charge it had. When she came back out, the wind had moved one tomato and the paper had shifted but held.

"May ninth," she said, sitting down. "Twenty thirteen. The daily average at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record. May 9, 2013."

"Before your mother walked," he said.

"A year before." She wrote the date beside her arrow in small print. "So your memory was right, just not exact."

He studied the graph a while longer, and she let him, because she understood that he was doing something she hadn't planned for the presentation: he was taking it personally, matching a jagged line against a daughter's graduation and a granddaughter's first semester. She would not put that in the slides. But she thought she might keep it, the way he'd once told her that a person who notices where he was standing when the world shifts has a kind of sentience about his own life, an awareness of being present for something.

"Okay," she said, squaring the paper. "From the top. You're my roommate, you're from a family that thinks climate science is a scam, and you just asked me why the graph matters."

"Then answer her this," her grandfather said, folding his hands on the table. "If the heat is spread thin everywhere, how does anybody measure it at all?"

Lea looked at the sawtooth line, and the wind lifted the paper's edge under the tomato, and she started to answer.

Aiden knelt in the bed at the far end of the garden and pulled a weed that came up with more soil than root, which meant he'd snapped it and would meet it again next week. The Saturday morning had the smell of cut basil and wet cardboard mulch, and someone's radio near the shed was playing a station that seemed to consist entirely of weather reports and gentle disappointment. He was trying to finish weeding before eleven, because at eleven the garden's little folding table was supposed to hold a petition, and the petition was his.

"Is this the thing about Fairmont Road?" asked Rosa, who had the plot beside his and grew more tomatoes than any one household could reasonably want. She was carrying a watering can in each hand like a scale weighing some invisible argument.

"It's the thing about the road eating the garden," Aiden said. The plan the council would vote on next month would widen Fairmont by two lanes and take the garden's southern strip, where the fig tree stood and where the compost sat in various stages of decay, plus the fence and about a third of the plots, his own among them. He smoothed the petition on the table and weighted its corners with four of Rosa's tomato seconds, since no one had thought to bring rocks.

"People want the road wider," Rosa said, not unkindly. "My brother sits in that traffic every day. He says it adds forty minutes to his life, taken out of him one evening at a time."

"I know." Aiden had spent two evenings reading everything the transportation office had posted online, most of it dense enough to be a form of punishment, until he'd found a study from another city where they'd widened a highway and the congestion came back within a few years. He'd read the sentence four times. Faster trips attracted more driving until the new space filled. They had a name for it, and once he had the name he kept finding it everywhere, in articles, in a footnote, in a comment by a planner who sounded tired in a textual way.

By eleven, seven people had signed, and two of those were gardeners who had already signed at the Wednesday meeting, which Rosa counted as fraud until Aiden pointed out it was mostly enthusiasm. Then a man in a polo shirt arrived, council badge clipped crookedly, and stood in the path with his hands in his pockets in the manner of someone who intended to be reasonable at you.

"Councilman Bere," he said. "Just listening today. Nice place." He looked at the fig tree the way one looks at a beloved dog that has chewed something expensive.

Aiden wiped his hands on his jeans and introduced himself, and the conversation went where he'd expected. Congestion, commute times, the will of the voters, growth. "The road is a funnel," Bere said, gesturing with an open palm down the invisible length of Fairmont. "You can't pour more through a narrow funnel. Any polity that grows has to grow its arteries."

The phrase made Aiden oddly bolder, the way a badly chosen metaphor will. "But adding lanes to a congested highway often doesn't reduce traffic for long," he said. "Faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills. It's called induced demand." He heard his own voice land the last two words more loudly than he'd planned, and a pigeon left the fig tree in what felt like editorial comment.

Bere smiled the smile of a man who had been to many meetings. "That's one theory among several, son."

"It's what happened in the study I read," Aiden said, and then, because he wanted to be honest even while arguing, "I don't know everything in it. It was another city, a highway not a street, and I might be missing something about how roads work here. But if it's even partly true, you spend the money, you take the fig tree, and in a few years everyone's still sitting in traffic, except now there's no garden." He watched Bere's face do a small calculation, not about traffic, about votes.

"The garden doesn't move the commuter," Bere said. "That's the hard arithmetic."

Rosa arrived with a bag of tomatoes and set it on the table with a thud that aggrandized the gesture beyond what six pounds of fruit could justify, though Aiden suspected the effect was intentional. "Take these home," she told Bere. "Then tell your household the arithmetic while you eat something this soil made." Bere laughed, actually laughed, and took two, and signed nothing, and said he'd want the study emailed to him, which Aiden suspected was a polite exit but wrote down anyway on the back of a seed packet.

By afternoon the petition had nineteen signatures, one coffee ring, and the faint smell of tomato where the weights had been. Aiden pulled the rest of his weeds with more care, getting the roots, and thought about how the garden itself was an argument: cheap land, cheap food, a fig tree nobody had budgeted for, set against forty minutes of a stranger's evening, which he could not honestly say mattered less. He didn't know yet how the council would vote, or whether his one incisive fact would outlast a man's commute, or whether he had just aggrandized a difference of eleven lanes' worth of nothing.

Rosa came back with her empty watering cans. "He took the tomatoes," she said. "Aiden. He took the tomatoes."

He looked over at the fig tree, its leaves still holding the afternoon light, and started gathering the stones he'd finally found to weigh the petition down.

The apartment complex had said noon, and the odometer said they'd make it with eleven minutes to spare, which Andrew's father treated as a personal triumph and Andrew treated as evidence that the universe was committed to seeing this through. He sat in the back seat with a box of records on his lap because the trunk was full, and every mile marker outside Canton felt like a notch being cut into something. His little sister Priya, thirteen and garrulous in the way of someone who has decided the trip will be unbearable unless she narrates it, had been talking since the county line.

"You could write actual letters," she said now. "People used to do that."

"Nobody did that. You're thinking of movies."

"I'm thinking of Grandma." She kicked the back of his seat, lightly, twice. "You could also just accept that you'll never talk to Danny again and it'll be fine."

"That's a cheery theory."

"It's not a theory. It's a prediction." She paused, then leaned into the gap between the front seats. "Hey, Mom, at orientation they told us about this study. In student housing. 1950. Festinger, Schachter, and Back. They found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends."

Andrew's mother said something agreeable from the front. Andrew looked out the window.

"How do you even remember that," he said.

"Because I thought it was sad. Danny's not going to be near your stairway. He's going to be near some kid named Kyle." She said the name Kyle with the flat cruelty only a thirteen-year-old could manage. "You'll be near some kid named Kyle."

He didn't answer, but the fact stayed with him the way a stone stays in a shoe. He turned it over for forty miles. It seemed to suggest that what he had with Danny, with Marcus, with the whole ragged crowd of them, was not chosen so much as arranged, that the friendship was an accident of geography, two lockers side by side, a cul-de-sac that funneled them together every afternoon until the closeness was indistinguishable from love. He had always believed, privately and without examining it, that he had picked those people, that some quality in him had recognized some quality in them. If the study was right, the picking had been done by a stairwell. He tried to decide whether that made the friendships smaller or the world larger, and couldn't, and the not-knowing sat in his chest alongside the leaving.

His phone buzzed against the box. Danny: are you there yet. Then, before Andrew could type: remember when marcus fell in the creek trying to save that shoe. Andrew laughed out loud, alone in the back seat, and typed back a whole paragraph about the shoe, the look on Marcus's face, the June light on the water. Then he deleted the paragraph, because it felt like a eulogy, and sent instead: we should visit the creek before it gets cold. I'll come back.

Danny's reply came as the exit sign appeared: deal. and you'll meet my new friend kyle probably. he's actually ok. Andrew stared at that. Kyle, apparently, was a person, a person who lived near Danny's stairway now, or near his locker, or whatever the geometry of their junior year was going to be, and Danny was already softening toward him, already being shaped by proximity the way water is shaped by a channel. And wasn't Andrew going to do the same thing? Wasn't there some kid in his own building already, unmet, near his own shared stairway, waiting to be grafted on? He had spent the whole drive thinking of himself as someone being subtracted, and it had not occurred to him until now that he was also being added to something.

"It's not either/or," Priya said, when he said some of this out loud, awkward and halting, because saying it at all cost him something. "The study doesn't say you only like who's nearby. It says you're more likely to become friends with them. Likely. It's not fate, it's odds." She said this with the terrible offhandedness of someone quoting something she'd absorbed without effort, and then ruined it by adding, "Also I already told you this, you weren't listening."

But he had been listening, or at least the fact had been listening for him, and the two ideas began to fit together in a way he could almost hold. The old friendships had been given their chance by a street and a stairwell, yes, by nothing he'd chosen; and still, given that chance, he and Danny had built something on it, had made a thousand decisions small as breath to keep showing up. Proximity was the confounder he'd been blaming, or maybe it was just the door, and doors didn't tell you what to do inside the room. He couldn't prove which it was. He might lose Danny anyway. He might find that some kinds of distance really do thin a thing out, and he would have to stand in his new stairwell, a stranger, and find out what he was without the old arrangement holding him up. He could admit all of that and still send the text he was composing, so he did: saturday after next. i'll take the bus. ask your mom if i can sleep on the couch.

His father pulled into the complex lot at 11:52, and they all sat for a moment while the engine ticked, looking at the pale buildings, the long shared stairways, the doors packed close as teeth. Priya was already unbuckling. Andrew picked up the box of records and got out into the heat, and from the second-floor walkway a boy about his age was carrying a mattress with his father, sweat-dark shirt, and as they passed each other the boy said, "Stairwell C is faster, the elevator's broken." Andrew shifted the box against his hip and said, "Thanks," and then, after a few steps, called back up the stairs, "Hey, what's your name?"

The basement of St. Brigid's smelled like burnt sugar and folding chairs, and Lucas stood at the counter with his grandmother's recipe box open in front of him, trying to remember whether the blessing came before the soup or after. For thirty-one years his grandfather had led the Christmas Eve supper, the whole extended family crammed between the radiator and the nativity mural, twelve dishes carried down the church steps in dish towels. This year Grandpa Ray was in room 412 of County General with a wire in his chest, and he had told Lucas, on the phone, in a voice like gravel being poured slowly, "You know the order. I wrote it down." The notebook was on the counter. Lucas had not opened it yet.

He opened it. Inside was a schedule in pencil: candles, blessing, soup, readings, the honeyed bread, the carol his mother always mangled, the toast at the end. Underneath, in the margin, his grandfather had written Lucas practices Sundays and boxed it twice, hard enough to tear the paper a little. Lucas set the notebook down flat and went to find the ladles.

His uncle Denny arrived early to set up tables, which he did loudly, clacking metal legs like a man aggrandizing a small task into a public works project. "So you're running it," he said. "You know what you're doing?"

"I have the notebook."

"Ray's a hard act. People expect the full performance, the Latin bit and everything."

"I'm not doing a performance."

"Good luck telling Mom that."

The family came in a slow flood, coats and casseroles and the little cousins who went straight for the mural to argue about whether the donkey was the same donkey from last year. Lucas's mother set down her dish, hugged him too hard, and asked him three questions about the soup he could not answer. Then she lowered her voice. "Your grandfather's on the phone. He wants to talk to you before you start."

Lucas took the phone into the stairwell, where the plaster was cold against his shoulder.

"You're doing the whole thing," his grandfather said. Not a question.

"Yes."

"I heard you had practice this morning. Coach called it for Christmas Eve morning, seven a.m."

Lucas looked at the linoleum. "I went. I got back by ten."

There was a long breath on the other end, the mechanical lift of the hospital bed. "Sundays," his grandfather said. "All season you've been gone on Sundays. That used to mean something in this family."

"Grandpa." Lucas had the argument ready; he'd been carrying it for a week like a stone in his pocket. "In Mark, chapter two, verse twenty-seven, Jesus says the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath. He says it to people criticizing his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath. Picking grain. On the day of rest. And he took their side."

Silence, except for a monitor somewhere beeping in its patient rhythm. Lucas waited, listening to his own heartbeat doing something similar.

"Second chapter," his grandfather finally said. "You memorized it to beat me with."

"I memorized it because it's true. The day is for us. Not the other way around. I went to practice and then I came here to do this, and I'm going to do it right, and both of those things are the point."

Another silence, and Lucas understood that what he was hearing was not surrender but something closer to a detente, two positions agreeing to stop firing across the same ground they would still argue about at Easter. His grandfather said, "The blessing goes before the soup. Readings after the bread. Don't let your mother sing the second verse alone, she'll flat on 'dispersed.'"

"I know."

"You don't know. You think you know." A wheeze that might have been a laugh. "Start with the candles. Nobody expects much from a beginner."

"Is that a compliment?"

"It's the notebook talking, not me. Go feed them."

Lucas carried the phone back in and lit the candles with the long match from the utility drawer, the kind that always smelled faintly of sulfur and of every year before this one. Twelve dishes steamed on the counter in an order that mostly matched the pencil schedule. His cousins were seated. His mother had the hymnal open to the wrong page and did not know it. Uncle Denny raised his glass early, out of turn, and Lucas touched his arm and shook his head, and Denny, for once, put it down.

He stood at the head of the table, notebook open, and said, "The Sabbath was made for man," and looked up at all of them. "So let's eat."

His mother started the carol anyway, half a beat early, and flat on 'dispersed,' and everyone came in behind her.

The draft came back on a Thursday with a red margin note that read, in Mr. Okoye's cramped hand: "This is a fact, not a thesis. What are you actually arguing?" Ashton had written nine pages on the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, and his opening sentence, underlined twice, stated that the law denied enslaved people legal rights. Mr. Okoye had circled it and written "Everyone accepts this" beside the circle, and then, at the bottom, "Revision due Monday. Footnotes this time. Chicago style."

He had been planning to spend the weekend at his grandfather's house anyway, his mother dropping him off with a duffel bag and a grocery bag of his grandmother's oatmeal cookies, and so he spread the problem across the dining room table on Saturday morning like a surveyor laying out terrain. His grandfather, a retired history professor, put down his coffee and looked at the pages for a long moment without touching them.

"So the man wants footnotes," his grandfather said. "Good. Footnotes are where you show your work. Like a carpenter leaving the joints visible."

"Can you just tell me what to argue?" Ashton asked.

"No." His grandfather picked up his mug and carried it toward the sunroom, where the light was better for the crossword. "But there's a box of my old handbooks in the closet if you want company. Don't disturb the mice."

The box held forty years of style guides, some older than Ashton's mother. He found the citation format easily enough; Chicago wanted numbered footnotes at the bottom of the page, a full citation the first time, shorter after that, and a bibliography alphabetized at the end. He practiced on the back of a utility bill, writing his own name into a fake citation, and felt a small, private satisfaction at how official it looked. But the thesis problem kept circling back. He went looking for it the way his grandfather had taught him to look for anything, by finding the shelf where an answer might live.

In a handbook from 1974, under a section about forming an argument, he read a sentence he copied onto an index card because it seemed to belong to someone more organized than he was: a research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts. He read it twice. Then he read his own circled sentence again and felt his ears go warm, the way they did when a joke landed a beat after the punchline. His whole draft had been standing on something nobody would ever bother to fight about. It wasn't wrong; it was worse than wrong, in a way, because there was nothing to do with it. A fact just sat there. You couldn't lean on it.

"I found something," he said, carrying the index card to the sunroom.

His grandfather read it over the top of his glasses. "Arguable," he said, and handed the card back. "That's the word your teacher wants."

Ashton sat on the floor beside the crossword chair and started pulling the thread. If a thesis had to be something a reasonable person could dispute, then somewhere out there was a reasonable person who would dispute his, and he had to imagine that person clearly enough to answer them. His grandfather, it turned out, had spent two decades studying dissident writers, Czech and Russian ones, people whose crime had been publishing things that everybody in power agreed were not worth disputing. "They got prison for arguing," his grandfather said, filling in a seven-letter word for patience. "So I've always had a soft spot for a good dispute." Which raised a question Ashton liked better than any he'd started with: who, in 1850, had actually argued that the Fugitive Slave Act was a good thing, and what did they say, and were they stupid or just afraid or something more complicated?

His first new thesis was too big, something about the whole North being complicit, and his grandfather disabused him of it over lunch by asking four questions he could not answer, none of them cruel. His second drifted into territory about the economics of shipping routes, which was interesting but tangential, and Ashton cut it himself before anyone could point that out, noticing as he did that cutting his own favorite paragraph felt like a kind of growing up, though he wouldn't have said so. The third attempt he wrote on the index card and turned face down while he worked on the footnotes, because he wanted to come back to it cold, the way Mr. Okoye would.

By Sunday evening he had eleven pages, twenty-three footnotes, a bibliography with both primary and secondary sources separated the way the handbook showed, and a thesis he thought a reasonable person could genuinely hate: that Northern judges who enforced the law were not simply cowards, but men who believed they were saving the Union, and that this belief did more damage than cowardice would have. He was not sure it was right. He was not even sure he believed it on Tuesdays. But it could be argued with, and that seemed, for the first time all weekend, like a real thing for a paper to be.

His grandfather read the last page standing at the counter, still holding his reading glasses in one hand. "I'd dispute this," he said finally. "I'd dispute it hard."

"Is that bad?"

"It's the point." He set the pages down and squared their edges against the counter with two sharp taps. "Monday, then."

On Monday morning Ashton got to school early and slid the revision under Mr. Okoye's door before first period, and it was only at lunch, checking his citations one more time in the library, that he discovered the entire bibliography was still in his grandfather's kitchen, sitting beside the cookie tin, exactly where he had left it.

Marcus had told everyone at school that his grandfather walked out of a factory in 1985 and never went back, which was true in the sense that he once left early on a Tuesday and true in no other sense. The assignment was an interview about work, due Monday, and Marcus had put it off until the last possible dinner, so now the recorder app on his phone sat between the salt shaker and his grandfather's plate like a small stone nobody wanted to touch.

"Ask him about the union," his mother said, ladling stew. "That's the interesting part." His grandfather made a noise that could have been agreement or the opposite. Marcus pressed record.

"Did you ever go on strike?" Marcus asked. He was imagining picket lines, the way he imagined most things, in movie lighting.

"We voted on one. Never had to walk." His grandfather tore a piece of bread and dragged it through the stew. "We had a contract. Every three years we sat down across from the company and argued about wages, hours, safety. If we couldn't agree, we could strike, and they knew it, so mostly we agreed." He chewed for a while. Marcus found himself leaning forward without deciding to.

"So the union got you your wage?"

"The union got us the table. We brought the wage to it." His grandfather looked at Marcus in that way he had, as if checking whether the boy was worth the trouble of the explanation. "Union members were common then. Ordinary. Your teacher would tell you it's not like that anymore."

That night Marcus looked it up, because the internet made looking things up a kind of reflex, like swallowing. The Bureau of Labor Statistics had a page. Union membership among wage and salary workers was 10.0 percent in 2025. He scrolled and found the older number, from 1983: 20.1 percent. He did the subtraction twice. Roughly half, and then roughly half again, like a photograph fading in stages. He sat with the two numbers longer than the assignment required, wondering what a country looks like when twice as many people bargain together, or when half as many do, and whether it looks like anything at all from the outside.

He texted his friend Dana, who worked weekends at the coffee place by the highway. "Do you get overtime after 40 hours?" he typed. "legally yes," she wrote back, "but they schedule me 39.5 so they never have to pay it. also no breaks some shifts. manager says if I don't like it there's a line of applicants." She added a thumbs up, which he understood to be bitter. He thought about his grandfather's table, the company on one side and everyone on the other, and about Dana alone in a room where the other side held all the chairs. He wrote back, "there's supposed to be a law about breaks," and she wrote, "there is. it's load-bearing the way a screen door is load-bearing," and then, "anyway how's the history paper." It wasn't a history paper, exactly, but he let that stand.

At the next dinner he brought the numbers with him the way you bring a present you're not sure will fit. "I found it," he said. "Ten percent of wage and salary workers are union members now. In 2025. It was 20.1 percent in 1983." He said it carefully, all of it, because he'd promised himself he wouldn't get it wrong in front of his grandfather.

His grandfather set down his fork. "Half," he said. "In my working life, half."

"You said you walked out of the factory," Marcus said, and felt something shift under him.

"I retired from it. Thirty-one years. Dues card in my wallet the whole time." His grandfather took the wallet out, an old leather thing gone soft as cloth, and thumbed through it without finding whatever he was looking for. "You've been telling people the other version?"

"I might have improved it," Marcus admitted. His mother laughed into her water glass. He was aware that he improved things often, that his memory was a painting rather than a photograph, and that this was a problem he hadn't solved and wasn't solving now. He thought about writing the interview up honestly, strike vote and all, and about how much duller it was than the version he'd been carrying around, and how the dull version had a kind of weight the shiny one didn't.

"Write down what I actually said," his grandfather told him. "The table part. The part where nobody walked out because we didn't have to." He pushed his plate toward the center of the table, where the stew bowl sat between them, and tapped the wood twice with two fingers, the way a man knocks on a door he half expects to be answered.

"Pass the bread," he said.

Luca had come to Camp Abernathy for the sailing, and it was therefore a personal injustice that his favorite hour of the day was now the one spent in a basement lab with eleven other teenagers and forty laptops that smelled like warm dust.

"You signed up for Competitive Programming," said Priya, without looking up from her screen. "It's on your lanyard. It's practically tattooed on you."

"I signed up because my mother said I couldn't convalesce on a couch all summer. Her word. She looked it up so she could use it in the argument."

The project that week was to build a class in Java. Not just a program, a class, with private fields the outside world couldn't touch and getter methods standing politely at the door, and then to test it until it confessed everything. Luca had named his class Catalog, a thing that held a sorted array of item codes and answered whether a given code existed. Priya had named hers DragonHorde. "Because the fields are private," she said. "Like treasure. Nobody touches the hoard without a getter."

He liked that more than he wanted to admit. He'd been raised on his grandfather's cooking, all patient layering, nothing measured, and on his father's spreadsheets, where every cell was audited and every column had a rule. He'd never decided which way of thinking was his. The Catalog felt like both: a warm middle with a fence around it, and Luca sat there at his keyboard enjoying the impossible idea that he had invented a small, orderly country.

Then Friday came, and the competition dataset. Eight million item codes, sorted, waiting to be searched. The camp leaderboard, projected on the wall, ranked every team by speed. Luca's tests had all passed in the lab, small arrays, dozens of cases, green checkmarks like a lawn. He ran the big dataset and his program crashed with an error about a number that couldn't fit where he'd put it.

"That's not a speed problem," said Marcus from two seats over, leaning back in his chair with the serene confidence of a boy who had once eaten an entire lemon on a dare. "That's an arithmetic problem. Look at your midpoint line."

Luca looked. His binary search computed its middle as low plus high, then divided by two. On the test data it was fine. On the huge array, he was told, adding those two numbers could overflow, could go past what an int could hold, and the whole search came apart. Marcus pointed at the screen with a pencil. "Try low plus, in parentheses, high minus low, then divide by two. Same middle. No overflow."

Luca changed one line. The program ran the entire eight-million-code dataset and finished so fast the leaderboard had to blink twice to believe it. He spent the rest of the hour half triumphant, half annoyed, because the fix was small and the difference between his way and Marcus's way was a thing he hadn't known existed. He had trusted his tests, and his tests had trusted small numbers. It occurred to him that being right in the lab and being right in the world were two different jobs.

"You're doing the face," Priya said. She saved her file with a dramatic click. "The face of a boy discovering that the universe has fine print."

"Everyone thinks they're the main character until an int overflows," Luca said, and Marcus snorted so hard he knocked over his water bottle, which missed every laptop, a miracle the whole lab agreed to never report to the counselors.

The next morning, Saturday, was sailing, and Luca convalesced on the dock in the sun while the wind took a day off. Priya sat beside him with her laptop, which she had carried to the dock like a pet. "The autocrat has a bug," she announced. By the autocrat she meant the head counselor, Dennis, who had decreed that the leaderboard be wiped and the competition rerun that afternoon, since he refused to believe Luca's Catalog had beaten his favorite team. Dennis's rerun, it turned out, ran on an old machine in the boathouse, and Dennis's own sample search program, which he had written himself years ago and never once changed, crashed on the huge dataset in front of everyone.

"Let me guess his midpoint," Luca said.

"Low plus high, divided by two," said Priya, grinning. "Endemic. It's everywhere. Half the code on that machine has it."

Luca thought about walking up to Dennis and telling him about the one line. He thought about the two ways he knew of being in the world: his grandfather's, where you'd say nothing and quietly fix the man's soup, and his father's, where you'd present the audit in writing. He honestly did not know which was kinder, or which would work, or whether knowing the answer to an overflow question had anything to do with knowing the answer to a people question. He suspected it didn't. He suspected it might.

He ended up doing neither, exactly. He printed the fixed line on a scrap of paper, folded it once, and left it on the boathouse bench where Dennis kept his sunglasses. Then he went back to the dock.

Priya watched him do it and said nothing for a while. Then she said, "You know he's going to think it's a note from a secret admirer."

"It's a note from a secret admirer," Luca said. "I admire people who fix one line instead of arguing about the whole program."

Down the lake, a sail finally caught some wind, and a small orange boat tipped, righted itself, and kept going.

Tyson had forty minutes before his grandfather's Buick had to be back in the driveway, because Grandpa had a card game at noon and the car was his ride. That was the whole window: one driving lesson, in the parking lot of the closed Kmart and then on the flat streets behind it, with his grandfather sitting in the passenger seat folding and unfolding the map he refused to use.

"Clutch, no. This is an automatic, boy. Just brake and gas." Grandpa tapped the dashboard with two knuckles. "Now, first thing you learn, and I mean learn it good. If you ever have to stop fast, you pump the brakes. On and off, on and off, or you'll lock up and slide straight into whatever you're heading for. Your father learned it that way. I learned it that way."

Tyson put the key in and turned it, and the engine caught, and something in his chest did too. He had waited all summer for this. In September he would be at college in a town where nobody drove him anywhere, and the difference between a person with a license and a person without had started to feel like the difference between two separate lives. He eased out of the driveway, the whole car feeling borrowed and enormous, and did not mention that the instructor from the driving school, a calm woman named Ms. Okafor, was coming at eleven.

She arrived while Grandpa was still lecturing, and she contextualized the whole arrangement in one sentence: "So you're the experienced driver, I'm the certified one, and Tyson gets both of us." Grandpa laughed at that, maybe harder than the joke deserved, and moved to the back seat with his map.

They did laps of the Kmart lot, and Tyson found the bite of the steering wheel in his hands, the way a turn was a conversation rather than a command. Then Ms. Okafor had him pull to the edge of the lot. "Before we go on the street, one thing. This car has anti-lock brakes. In a real emergency, you press the brake firmly and hold it, all the way down, and you keep holding. Don't pump. And you can still steer while you're braking." She said it once, flat and quick, and moved on to mirror positions, as if it were no more important than anything else.

Grandpa's voice came from the back seat. "That can't be right."

"That's the current training," Ms. Okafor said, not turning around.

Tyson drove them out onto Fenwick Road, and for ten minutes there was only the small work of it, signaling, checking, the reverie of imagining himself pulling into a dorm parking lot next fall broken by Ms. Okafor's hand on the dash. A dog, a big one, cream-colored, had come off a porch and was standing dead center in the road. There was no time to be polite about it.

He pressed the brake, hard, and held it. The pedal did something under his foot, a quick shuddering he had never felt before, and the car slowed with a grinding sound like the whole machine was arguing with itself, and Grandpa shouted "Pump it, pump," from behind, and Tyson held on because holding was the thing he had been told, and the wheel was still alive in his hands, so he steered. The Buick came to a stop angled toward the curb, and the dog, unbothered, trotted around the front bumper and sat down on the lawn it had come from.

Nobody said anything for a moment. Then Grandpa said, quietly, "We would have slid into that fence in my day."

"Your day's brakes were different," Ms. Okafor said, and Tyson felt the two of them settle something without his having to referee it. He had heard both versions now, the pumping and the holding, one from a man who had driven fifty years without an accident and one from a woman with a clipboard, and he could not have said which teaching tradition was wiser overall, only that today, in this car, the new way had stopped them. Maybe the old way had saved other people on ice in 1974. He would probably pump if he ever drove Grandpa's first truck, if that truck still existed anywhere but in stories. Some things stayed uncertain, and he let them.

He signaled, checked the mirror, and pulled back onto Fenwick Road. In the back seat Grandpa folded his antiquated map into a small square and tucked it into his jacket pocket, and Tyson drove home three minutes under the wire, stopping smoothly at every sign.

At the curb, Grandpa leaned forward between the seats. "You held it," he said. "Good instinct."

"It wasn't instinct," Tyson said. "She told me."

Grandpa patted the shoulder of the seat twice, almost like patting Tyson himself. "Same thing, at your age." Then he got out, straightened his jacket, and walked up the driveway whistling toward the house, calling back over his shoulder, "Card game at noon, but the evening's free. Want to drive me there instead?"

The party was in Derek's backyard, and Brooklyn had until midnight to fix the thing she'd been avoiding for nine days. His mother had strung lights between the fence posts and set out a cake that said DEREK 17 in icing already melting sideways, and somewhere behind the speakers Brooklyn's phone sat with the notification she kept half-reading: Marisol had sent the final draft of their history essay, the one Brooklyn was supposed to edit, the one due at 11:59.

"You're doing the face," Derek said, dropping onto the cooler beside her. "The essay face. You look like you're being followed."

"Marisol wrote six paragraphs on urban renewal and only one on the resistance movement, which was the actual assignment. And she keeps saying 'thus.' Thus, thus, thus. It's like being yelled at by a thesaurus."

"So tell her."

"It's not that simple."

"It's exactly that simple."

Derek was canny about most things, but he had never been the weaker half of a partnership, and Brooklyn didn't expect him to understand what it was like to be the one whose feedback could flatten somebody. Last year, when she'd told a lab partner his data tables were "a mess," he'd stopped contributing for the rest of the semester, and she had spent those months doing the work of two people while pretending that was a victory of standards. Marisol was her best friend on the team, fragile in the specific way of someone who had transferred schools twice and was still auditioning for every room she entered. Brooklyn had already typed three drafts of a comment, and every one of them was a lie of politeness, a lot of "really strong start!" that would codify, over time, into Marisol believing Brooklyn thought she was fine, when Brooklyn actually thought she was talented and off course, which was worse to leave uncorrected.

She scrolled through her saved articles while Derek blew out a rumor of candles on the half-melted cake. In the fall she'd bookmarked a write-up of a 2014 study led by David Yeager, because her older sister had mentioned it during a fight about Brooklyn's "brutal honesty." Students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. One sentence of belief attached to the hard feedback. Brooklyn had filed it away as an excuse for her sister's side of the argument and never used it, and now here it was, suddenly operational, at a birthday party, with two hours on the clock.

The flaw in her plan was that Marisol was at the party, leaning against the fence with a paper cup of sparkling cider, which meant Brooklyn couldn't hide behind a screen. She considered texting the feedback and driving home. She considered softening everything into mush. Then Derek's cousin turned the music up, someone's little brother stepped in the cake, and in the general disruption Marisol wandered over and asked the question Brooklyn had been dreading: "Did you read it? Be honest."

There it was. The invitation, which was also a trap, which was also, possibly, a door.

"Can I try something weird?" Brooklyn said. "I read this thing. A study, 2014, David Yeager. Students revised their essays way more often when the criticism came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. So here's my note." She took a breath that tasted like sugar and someone's grape vape. "I think you're the best writer on our team, and I think this essay is underneath what you can do, and I'm saying that because I believe you can fix it, not to be nice. You have six paragraphs on renewal and one on the resistance, and the resistance was the assignment. Also, please stop saying thus."

Marisol blinked. Across the yard, Derek was conducting the little brother toward the sprinkler, which was its own kind of countdown. "So you're saying my structure is broken," Marisol said slowly.

"Your structure is the problem and your sentences are the prize. Cut paragraph four entirely. It's a nice paragraph going nowhere, like a man explaining directions he doesn't know."

That got a laugh out of her, a real one, and then a quieter look, the kind that meant the sentence of belief had landed somewhere behind the joke. "Okay," Marisol said. "But I can't rewrite it by midnight alone."

They ended up sitting on the porch steps with the draft between them on Brooklyn's laptop, the party going on without them, someone launching a doomed attempt at karaoke while they cut and rebuilt and argued gently about the word thus. Marisol kept the word exactly once, on purpose, out of spite, and Brooklyn let her, which felt less like losing and more like negotiating the border between honest and cruel, a border she now suspected she would spend her life mapping rather than finishing. At 11:51 they submitted, and Marisol closed the laptop and said, "You know you're not allowed to leave the team now. You're stuck being the one who tells me the truth."

Derek appeared with two plates of salvageable cake. "The birthday boy demands you acknowledge his party."

"We acknowledge it," Marisol said, and Brooklyn, tasting icing, raised her plastic fork to him.

The popcorn machine had a smell Luke could already tell he would stop noticing by August, the way he'd stopped noticing the chlorine smell at the neighborhood pool after two summers of swim lessons. The manager, a woman named Corinna with a lanyard full of keys, walked him past the concession stand toward a cramped office in back where the walls sequestered the noise of the lobby into a muffled hum. She slid a laminated sheet across the desk, and there it was: eight dollars an hour, weekends and two weeknights, a start date circled in green pen.

"You're hired," she said, "pending the paperwork, which is mostly the part where you promise not to steal candy." She said it without smiling, which made it hard to tell whether it was a joke or a test.

The person training him on concessions was a tall, morose senior named Dev who wore his visor like it had been assigned to him as a punishment. Dev showed him how to layer the butter in thirds so it reached the bottom of the bucket, how to tear the ticket stubs with one motion, how to spot the customers who would ask for a refund no matter what you did for them. By the second week Luke had the rhythm of it, and Dev had begun, grudgingly, to talk.

"I'm gone at the end of the month," Dev said one Tuesday while they restocked napkin dispensers. "Maybe sooner. I got a better gig at the climbing gym. I'm thinking I just don't show up. Let her figure it out."

"Wouldn't you give notice? Two weeks or whatever?"

Dev laughed, a single dry note. "Why? What are they going to do, fire me?"

That night Luke sat on his bedroom floor with his phone and looked it up, because Dev's answer had felt too easy, the way things feel easy when someone has already decided. He found it on a state government page, plain as a bus schedule: most employment in the United States is at-will, which means the employer can end the job at any time, for any reason that isn't illegal, and the worker can quit the same way. No notice required on either side. He read it twice. Something about the symmetry unsettled him, though he couldn't have said why at first, and he fell asleep still holding the phone.

The next shift, a Saturday, the lobby smelled like rain because a storm had chased a whole showing's worth of people inside early, dripping and loud. Luke found Dev behind the counter wiping down the pretzel warmer with the commitment of someone performing a small funeral. Luke had spent the walk over assembling what he thought of as his case, a little structure of reasons, though he was aware that stacking reasons was not the same as being right.

"You don't have to give notice," Luke said. "I looked it up. It's at-will, both directions. Corinna could let you go tomorrow for basically any reason, and you can walk out the same way. Legally it's clean."

"So then why are you still standing there?"

"Because legal is the floor, not the ceiling." It came out before he could soften it, and Dev looked at him with something between annoyance and curiosity. Luke pushed on. "She's short-handed already. If you vanish on a Saturday, somebody else's night gets wrecked, and that somebody is probably me. But I get that she'd cut you tomorrow if the schedule got tight, and she wouldn't owe you a reason. So it's not like you owe her loyalty. I just don't think the answer is obvious in the direction you want it to be."

Dev stopped wiping. The pretzel warmer ticked as it cooled, and out in the lobby a kid was arguing with his father about whether they'd missed the previews. "You sound like my econ teacher," Dev said. "He'd call that rationalism or something."

"Maybe. But here's the thing I keep going back and forth on. Two weeks from you costs you almost nothing, and it saves a real person a real mess. That math seems simple. And then I think, no, it's not a debt, she never promised you anything, and pretending there's an obligation when there isn't is its own kind of dishonesty." Luke shrugged, palms up. "I can't fully get both of those to fit in my head at once. I'd rather admit that than fake certainty."

Dev was quiet through the next rush, or quiet for Dev, which meant he only complained twice. When the lobby thinned out, he pulled the schedule binder from under the register and turned it to the following month, and Luke watched him study it, chewing the inside of his cheek. "The climbing gym starts me on the fifteenth," Dev said. "If I gave her the tenth through the fifteenth, that's five days. Five days of wearing this visor." He closed the binder, then opened it again, like he was checking whether the days had moved.

At closing, Corinna came through the empty lobby pulling the gates down behind her, and Dev was still standing at the counter with the binder in his hands, thumbing its edge, waiting for her.

The crystals were supposed to be the grandiose part. Logan's poster board, propped against the toaster, read The Hidden Architecture of Salt in block letters he now regretted, and beside it sat the jar of copper sulfate solution from which, after two weeks of patient evaporation, he had harvested a cluster of blue crystals weighing exactly 4.1 grams. The rubric wanted quantitative analysis. Mrs. Okonkwo had written "Where are your numbers?" in red pen at the bottom of his proposal, which was either a demand or a verdict.

He spread his notebook on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a bowl of bananas going soft at the stems. His little sister Priya sat across from him eating cereal with the concentration of someone watching television, except there was no television, only him.

"You're supposed to start from the mass of reactant," she said, milk dripping off her spoon. "I looked at your poster. It has zero numbers."

"Thank you. Extremely helpful."

He had dissolved 10.0 grams of copper sulfate pentahydrate in the water, and he knew from the side of the bottle that its molar mass was 249.7 grams per mole. He wrote it down, then divided, and got 0.0400 moles of the reactant. The reaction was a one-to-one affair, he was fairly sure, hydrate to anhydrous salt, so 0.0400 moles of copper sulfate should have come out the other end. He multiplied by the anhydrous molar mass, 159.6, and arrived at 6.4 grams. He sat back. Six point four grams was what the universe owed him.

The problem was the scale, which was his mother's kitchen scale, and the crystals, which weighed 4.1 grams. He weighed them again. He weighed the empty jar lid and subtracted. He weighed a banana, out of distrust, and got a number so reasonable it offended him. Two point three grams of copper sulfate had simply failed to appear, or had appeared and then failed to stay, and he had no idea which.

"Are you crying?" Priya asked.

"I'm doing math."

She came around the table and stood over his shoulder, which she did whenever she sensed weakness. "So how much did you get and how much were you supposed to get?"

"Four point one. Should have been six point four."

She tapped his notebook. "There's a thing for that. We did it in class. Percent yield. Actual divided by theoretical, times one hundred." She said it the way she said multiplication tables, bored and certain.

He wrote it down. Actual mass, 4.1. Theoretical, 6.4. He divided and got 0.64, carried the division out one more place to be sure, and multiplied by 100. Sixty-four percent. Sixty-four percent of the copper had cooperated; the other thirty-six percent was somewhere in the solution, still dissolved, or stuck to the string, or lost when he'd decanted the liquid into the sink because it had started to smell like the inside of a penny left in rain.

The question was what to do with the number. He could hide it, report only the moles, and let the poster stand on its hidden architecture. Or he could put sixty-four percent on the board in red, next to the crystals, and let Mrs. Okonkwo see that he had measured his own shortfall. His father would say a result is a result. His father also said that about parking tickets.

He looked up the etymology of "yield" on his phone while the kettle hissed behind him, because it felt like the kind of thing a good poster would include and because he wanted to know if the word had always meant surrendering something. It had roots in paying, in giving over. The crystals sat in their lid, blue and geometric, holding their 4.1 grams with what he was willing to interpret as dignity. In the corner, his mother's jar of sourdough starter sat fermenting on the counter, bubbling its slow argument with the flour, which had been going for three years now and which nobody had ever once weighed.

Priya leaned on the table. "Sixty-four's not terrible," she said. "Maddie's volcano did nothing. Zero percent. It just sat there."

"That's not a real yield. That's a lawn ornament."

He picked up the red marker and, on a fresh index card, wrote Percent yield: 64%, then held it against the poster, moving it from the corner to the center and back to the corner, trying to decide whether it was a confession or the most honest sentence he owned.

"Center," Priya said, and pointed her spoon at it. "Definitely center."

The training manual sat open on the picnic table between James and Priya, its pages already soft from the humidity. They had two days to become peer educators, which meant two days to learn how to say words like condom and chlamydia to a circle of fifteen-year-olds without their voices going strange. Priya read aloud from the chapter on consent, stumbling over "enthusiastic and ongoing," and James understood, with a small cold shock, that he had never once said any of this out loud either.

The camp director, a phlegmatic woman named Ruth who had run the program for eleven summers, paired them for rehearsal because they were opposites. Priya talked too fast when she was nervous. James went quiet, which Ruth said was worse, because a quiet boy in front of a quiet room teaches nothing. So they drilled. Priya practiced slowing down until the word "contraception" stopped collapsing into a single syllable, and James practiced raising his hand mid-sentence, a trick Ruth taught him for signaling to a room that he intended to keep talking.

On Thursday they got the clinic chapter, a photocopy with a map of the county health office circled in green marker. Confidential, the pamphlet said. Low cost. No notification required for minors in their state. Priya highlighted the phone number. James made flashcards, and that evening, at the long table in the mess hall, he flipped through them while the kitchen staff ladled out dinner behind him.

He had volunteered for kitchen duty after supper, mostly to be useful, and while restocking the shelf for the cooks he found a stack of cans at the back, soup, left over from the staff meals. Out of boredom he turned one around and read the label. Sodium, nine hundred milligrams per serving, two and a half servings per can. He did the arithmetic twice on the paper sleeve of a salt shaker, then got out his phone and checked what the limit actually was. The World Health Organization, he read, recommended adults eat less than two grams of sodium a day, which was less than five grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure. One can of soup, then, was already more than a full day of it. He stood there holding the can, thinking of his grandfather's kitchen, the cans stacked in the cabinet above the stove, the way his grandfather salted everything before tasting it.

"Less than two grams of sodium," he said to Priya that night at the campfire, before he could lose his nerve. "That's less than five grams of salt, for a whole day. The WHO says it lowers blood pressure." She looked at him across the flames. "Your grandpa," she said, because he had told her, in one of the long walks between sessions, about the stroke scare in March. He nodded. "He gets through that before lunch." She didn't say anything comforting, which was why he liked her, and instead asked whether he had called the old man, and he said no, and she said maybe the talk and the call were the same problem, and he laughed even though it wasn't funny.

The next morning he called, crouched by the shower house where the signal reached. His grandfather was cheerful and deflecting in the way of men who had agreed to nothing. James walked him through the cans, the two grams, the five grams of salt, and his grandfather said he'd look into it, honey, in a tone James recognized as the same tone he himself used when his mother told him to floss. Still, when they hung up, something had moved. He had said a hard true thing to someone he loved. It didn't fix anything. But he had said it.

At the afternoon rehearsal, Ruth finally acceded to their request to practice in front of the whole group of trainees, eleven teenagers arranged in the amphitheater seats. James stood up, and the words came, steady and clear, his elocution better than he had any right to expect. Consent as a conversation. Contraception as a shared responsibility. The clinic's address, the green circled map, the sentence about confidentiality that he delivered slowly because it mattered most.

When he finished, a girl in the second row raised her hand and asked whether it was true that salt was bad for you, because her dad had said soup was healthy. James opened his mouth, and Priya beside him started to laugh, and he laughed too, because of course that was what they remembered, the cans, the arithmetic, the thing he hadn't even rehearsed.

"Tell me the number," the girl said. "For the salt. I'll write it on my arm."

Gabrielle's grandmother kept the key to the old Fiesta in a china cup on the hall shelf, between two thimbles, as though the car were something small and easily lost. On the first morning of half term Gabrielle held the key in her palm and followed her grandfather out to the drive, where he stood gesticulating at an empty stretch of kerb as if it had personally offended him.

"There," he said. "That's where you'll practise. Reverse in, stop within two car lengths, no touching the kerb." He set out two folding chairs on the pavement to stand for the cars in front and behind, then weighed them with bricks from the garden because, he said, the wind last Tuesday had carried one into the hedge and he wasn't chasing furniture across Hertfordshire twice.

Gabrielle had done thirty hours of lessons and one mock test, and she had reversed into bays until she could do it with her eyes half closed. Bays were kind. They had painted lines. This kerb had nothing painted on it at all. "I only ever practised bay parking," she said, easing the Fiesta forward past the chairs. "My instructor said the examiner picks. I don't even know what they can pick."

Her grandfather got in the passenger side and pulled the seatbelt across. "On the practical driving test in Great Britain," he said, "parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask you to do." He said it the way he recited seed packet instructions, flat and total, and she understood that he had looked it up, probably at four in the morning, probably more than once.

So it could be asked. That was the problem, and she turned the wheel and thought about it while the rear wheel kissed the kerb with a sound like a swallowed word. The chairs sat there, smug and bricked. On her fourth attempt she clipped the nearside one anyway, and her grandfather leaned out the window and repositioned it in silence, which was somehow worse than being told off.

The perspective she had brought from lessons was that a test was a test: rules fixed, examiner neutral, you performed and were judged. Her grandfather's perspective, which she had absorbed over years of watching him let people out at junctions and thank lorry drivers with a raised finger, was that driving was a conversation with strangers. She had thought these were two different things. Somewhere around her ninth attempt, when she stopped staring at the kerb and started watching the space itself, noticing how the Fiesta's nose swept like a sentence finding its punctuation, she began to suspect they were the same thing. The examiner was a stranger. You were being tested on the conversation.

By the afternoon she could do it. Not every time, but most times, and the misses were near misses, small and correctable. Her grandmother came out with sandwiches and stood at the gate in her cardigan, watching, and when Gabrielle finally left the chairs untouched and the wheels a decent hand's width from the kerb, her grandmother applauded with both hands, dropping half a sandwich into the flowerbed.

On the second morning they drove to the A road so she could practise merging, which her grandfather described as "joining the dance," and which Gabrielle described, through her teeth, as trying to step into a gallop from a standing start. The slip road was short. Lorries occupied the middle lane with a kind of ancient indifference. Twice she slowed too much and had to stop at the hatched lines, and twice her grandfather said nothing at all, which she had learned was his way of saying try again, and the third time she matched her speed to the traffic, signalled, and slid into a gap a lorry driver made smaller for her, then bigger, which was his way of saying well done.

The subterfuge came on the last day, when she found the folded paper in the Fiesta's door pocket: her grandfather's handwriting, a drawing of the test centre car park with the bays marked in blue and the road marked in red, annotated "she will be asked this" beside the bays. He had spent the week quietly certain the examiner would choose the bay park, the thing she already knew, and had drilled her in the parallel park anyway, in case he was wrong. She put the paper back.

At the test centre on Monday she sat in the waiting room with her licence in her hand, and a boy two chairs down was muttering "parallel park, parallel park, please let it be the parallel park" like a prayer. When the examiner called her name and led her to the car, he walked around to the passenger door, paused, and said, "We'll start with a bay park, if that's all right."

Gabrielle looked at the painted lines, blue in her mind, red on the tarmac, and heard herself say, "Actually, could we do the parallel park first?"

The examiner raised an eyebrow and made a small note on his clipboard. "Keen. Right then, pull up on the left when you're ready, somewhere safe and legal."

The letter from the art program arrived on a Tuesday, thin enough that Julia knew before opening it that it was a no. They wanted sketches, they had said, five pages from life, and she had sent portraits of her mother at the kitchen table, her brother asleep on the couch, the neighbor's dog tied to the porch rail. Somewhere between the envelope and the recycling bin, her mother rescued it and pinned it to the corkboard, which Julia pretended not to notice.

She decided to apply again, and to do it properly this time, which meant starting over rather than resubmitting the same smudged pages. Her old drawings had a soft, foggy look that she used to think of as atmosphere. Spread across the kitchen table now, they looked like they had been left out in the rain. The shadow under her brother's jaw had drifted down his neck. Her mother's cheekbone had a ghost of itself hovering an inch to the left.

Marcus came over on Thursday with a bag of chips and no plans, the way he had since they were nine. He leaned over the table while she was trying to rescue a portrait, one finger hovering above the paper, not touching. "Which grade did you use?" he asked.

"Grade? It's a pencil."

"They're graded." He picked up the yellow pencil by her elbow and turned it until she could see the letter stamped near the end. "Six B. The soft ones are marked with a B. The more clay in the core, the harder the pencil, and those are marked H. More clay makes a lighter mark. Less clay, more graphite, softer and darker." He set it down. "My dad drafts. I grew up around this stuff."

Julia looked at the pencil as though it had been sitting on her desk for years, which it had. "So everything I drew with this is going to keep smearing."

"Basically, yeah."

She spent Friday evening introspecting in a way she distrusted, lying on her bed cataloguing her own excuses, and decided that honesty was more useful than feeling sorry for herself. The truth was she had never thought about her materials at all. She had thought about faces, about likeness, about the version of her mother she wanted to keep. The paper and the graphite had been as invisible to her as water is to a fish.

Saturday she took the bus to the art store with twenty dollars of birthday money and stood in front of a wall of pencils like a wall of decisions. There were 4H and 2B and HB, whole alphabets of gray. She bought three: a hard one, a middle one, and a soft one, because she wanted to see for herself what the letters actually did. At home she tested them in the back of her notebook, three columns of strokes, and pressed her thumb across each one. The hard pencil left a pale line that barely smudged at all, nearly impermeable to her rubbing finger. The soft one bloomed into a gray smear at the lightest touch. She sat with the notebook open and thought about apportionment, how the same few ingredients, shifted a little one way or the other, made something fixed or something that gave. Her mother came through with laundry, glanced at the columns of strokes, and said nothing, but set a cup of tea down beside them.

The next portrait took two days instead of one afternoon. Julia built her mother's face out of the hard pencil first, pale scaffolding, the cheekbone exactly where it belonged, and only at the end went in with the soft one for the places that were truly dark: the window behind her, the shadow inside her collar. When she finished, she held the page flat and blew across it, and nothing moved. She carried it to the kitchen where Marcus was eating cereal over the sink, a habit she had given up correcting.

He put the bowl down and took the page in both hands. He looked at it for longer than he usually looked at anything.

"So you learned the letters," he said.

"I learned the letters." She took the page back before he could smudge it with his cereal fingers, then, catching herself, held it out again. "Go ahead. Try. Rub the cheekbone."

Marcus pressed his thumb to her mother's face and lifted it clean. Julia laughed, a short, surprised sound, and turned the page to the light.

"That part's a 4H," she said. "The collar's where you'll lose."

John locked the bathroom door because it was the only room in the house with a lock, and sat on the edge of the tub with his notes balanced on his knee. Tomorrow at the peer health training he had to stand in front of six other seniors and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the county clinic, and the coordinator had been clear: if you can't say it in plain words, you don't know it. So he said it to the mirror.

"Consent means everyone involved is choosing freely, and you can take it back," he said. "Contraception isn't one thing. Condoms, the pill, the IUD. They work differently and some protect against infections and some don't." He heard himself slip into the cadence of a morning announcement and stopped, started again, slower. At the clinic you could walk in, ask for a full panel, and results came back in a week; nobody called your house unless you asked them to.

His phone buzzed on the sink. A text from his mother: At CVS. Machine says 125 over 78. Is that bad?

He set down the notes. He knew blood pressure numbers were two things, a top and a bottom, and he knew 120 over 80 was famous the way 98.6 was famous, but he did not know what 125 over 78 meant. He typed it in and found the 2017 American guideline, the one everybody used now. Elevated, the page said, meant a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80. He read it twice to make sure he had the numbers in the right places, top against top, bottom against bottom. His mother's numbers sat inside that range like a coin in a slot.

"Elevated," he texted back. "Not high. It's the category under high."

Three dots appeared, then: Your father is truculent about the machine. Says it squeezed his arm wrong.

John smiled at that. His father distrusted anything free. But his mother's number did not portend anything in itself, as far as he could tell; it was a category, a label, the way "elevated" was a word that meant exactly what the guideline said it meant and nothing more. He was surprised by how much that helped. A word for the thing made the thing smaller.

He went back to his notes and found the same principle sitting there in his own handwriting. The peer health training gave them a heuristic: say the rule, then say what to do, then say where to go. Consent, contraception, clinic. It wasn't wisdom, exactly. It was a handle you could grab so the whole heavy subject didn't slip through your fingers in front of an audience.

Someone knocked. "John. It's Marcus." His brother's voice, fourteen and trying to sound casual. "Mom texted me some number. Is she okay?"

"She's fine. It's called elevated. It's not the high one."

A pause on the other side of the door. "What are you doing in there?"

"Practicing a thing for tomorrow." He hesitated with his hand on the lock. He'd been rehearsing for seniors, for people his own age, and the whole time there'd been a fourteen-year-old down the hall who thought the clinic was something that happened to other people. Marcus had come home from school in September with a question about condoms and their father had gone quiet in a way that ended the conversation, and John had let it end, which was the part he hadn't practiced saying out loud.

He opened the door. Marcus stood there holding his own phone, screen out, his mother's text enlarged. Behind him the hallway was empty, their father still at the pharmacy.

"Sit on the tub," John said. "I need the practice anyway."

"I'm not sitting on the tub."
