"Fine, stand." John picked up his notes. "Okay. Consent first. It means everyone's choosing, freely, and you can change your mind halfway through. That's not a technicality, it's the whole thing." He watched Marcus's face do the thing faces do when a brother is suddenly saying words their father won't say. "Then there's contraception, which is more than one thing. And then there's the clinic on Fourth Street, where you can get tested without anybody calling home. Do you want to hear that part?"

Marcus put the phone in his pocket. "Is the machine going to say Mom has a bad number?"

"It's going to say the same number it already said. Words don't change it." John tapped his notes against the sink edge. "Elevated. Sit down and I'll tell you the rest."

Marcus sat on the tub.

Rachel had wanted the junior medic slot at Camp Wanokip for one reason, which was that the infirmary had air conditioning, and by the second week of August she had stopped pretending otherwise. Nurse Okafor let her do real work anyway. On Tuesday she let Rachel wrap the cuff around a counselor's sunburned arm, watch the gauge fall, and call out the numbers.

"One twenty-six over eighty-two," Rachel said, reading the dial like a weather report.

"Which means what, exactly?" Nurse Okafor had her arms crossed, but her eyes were doing the teasing.

"It means the blood is going places at a certain amount of pressure, top number when the heart squeezes, bottom number when it rests." Rachel had read the manual twice under her blanket with a flashlight, which she considered a completely normal way to spend a camp evening.

"So if a person came in at, say, one hundred forty over ninety, day after day?"

"Too high," Rachel said. "The heart's working too hard, pushing against too much resistance. And you can move it with the boring stuff. Less salt, more vegetables, actual exercise. Not even heroic exercise. Walking."

Nurse Okafor smiled at "boring stuff" the way you smile at a student who has finally stopped performing and started saying true things. "Tell that to Dak."

Dak was the waterfront director, twenty-two, built like a canoe, and currently sitting on the infirmary cot with the wounded dignity of a man who had been told his blood pressure was creeping up. Rachel brought him his water and tried to allay his fears, though what came out was "It's not like you're dying, it's like you're a slightly overinflated pool toy," which did not allay anything. He threw a pillow at her.

The complication arrived on Wednesday, in the form of a phone call from her mother. Her mother ran a wellness collective back home and held opinions about blood pressure that involved celery juice and, more urgently, held opinions about Rachel's upcoming college physical in September. "They'll push a lot of tests on you," her mother said. "You don't need all of it at your age."

"Which tests?" Rachel asked, mostly to keep her voice level.

"All of them. Just say no politely."

That night the whole camp did the crepuscular thing they always did, drifting down to the lake in the last gray light for the no-electronics hour. Rachel found herself next to Dak on the dock, both of them dangling their feet in the water. "You doing okay?" he asked. "You have the face of a person arguing with somebody who isn't here."

Rachel told him about the physical, and about her mother, and about how at home her mother's way of thinking felt like the whole world and here Nurse Okafor's way felt like the whole world and they could not both be the whole world. She was careful not to make it a speech, because Dak was already lying back on the planks with his eyes shut.

"Here's a thing," Dak said, eyes still closed. "When I did my staff physical in June, they offered me an HIV test. I said, why, do you think I have something? And the doctor says, no, everybody gets it. Everybody aged thirteen to sixty-four, at least once, as part of routine care. It's a CDC recommendation. Routine. Like checking your height."

"Huh," Rachel said.

"Right? I thought it was some judgment about me, and it was just a box they tick for everyone. I almost said no out of pure pride." He sat up and squinted at her. "Your mom's not wrong that some things get pushed on people. She's just maybe wrong about which things."

Rachel sat with that, feet in the warm shallows, because the two pictures were refusing to collapse into one. Her mother was right that patients ought to ask questions; Nurse Okafor was right that the asking shouldn't stop at no. A test could be routine and a person could still want to understand it, and neither of those canceled the other. What stayed uncertain was what she would actually say in the exam room in September, and she was honest enough with herself to leave that open.

Thursday morning she took Dak's pressure again. One twenty-four over eighty-one. "Two points," he said, with the grandeur of a man announcing a championship. "That's my celery."

"That's you skipping the second salt packet at lunch," Rachel said, and wrote the numbers down.

He leaned over her shoulder to read the log, and tapped the empty line beneath it. "So what's the plan for the one in September? You going to tell your mom you're getting everything?"

Rachel clicked the pen twice, and did not answer. "Sleeve up," she said.

The guitar had belonged to Aaron's grandfather, and it came to him through his mother, who carried it into the band room on a Tuesday because he had no car and the case was too long for the bus. It smelled like the inside of a closet, and the strings were dull enough that his reflection in the brass bell of the Sousaphone looked back at him through a fog. He set it on a chair and unlatched the case the way you open something you're not sure you have permission to touch.

His grandfather had played, his mother said, though nobody in the family could say what or how well. The last time anyone remembered hearing it was a wedding fifteen years ago. Aaron had signed up for guitar as his fine arts credit because it was the class that didn't meet before eight in the morning, and because Mr. Reyes let students practice in the band room after school while he sorted sheet music and pretended not to listen.

The problem was the strings. Mr. Reyes had put a page on the board that first week, a diagram Aaron had copied without understanding, and when he pressed his fingers where the page said, the notes came out wrong, soured, like a door that doesn't shut all the way. Priya, who sat near him in class and had been playing since she was nine, leaned over his case one afternoon and frowned at the instrument itself rather than his hands.

"When did you tune it last?" she asked.

"Did I what it?"

She plucked the lowest string, the fat one, and let it wobble out its pitch. "It's not even close. You have to tune it before anything on that page will work." She pointed at the board, where the diagram still hung. "From the lowest string up, it's E, A, D, G, B, and then E again. That's standard tuning." She said it the way she'd tell him the room number for a final, quick, useful, already moving on to her own practice.

He didn't have a tuner. Priya had one, a little green clip, but she was leaving for a lesson, and he wanted, for reasons he couldn't have contextualized without sounding prettier than the truth, to do this part himself. The truth was smaller: he'd watched his grandfather's hands once, at that wedding, before the memory went soft around the edges, and the hands had turned the pegs without looking, the way you adjust a shower you've used for years.

Mr. Reyes kept a pitch pipe in the top drawer of the file cabinet, a thing like a flattened harmonica, and when Aaron asked, he handed it over without a speech. That was the deal with Reyes. He would answer what you asked and then get out of the way, which some students read as indifference and Aaron was beginning to read as respect, a kind of probity about where teaching stopped and your own ear began. Aaron blew into the pipe and got a reedy E, and blew again, and turned the fat string's peg until the two sounds stopped arguing.

The rest went slower. A for the second string, and he learned quickly that the pegs responded differently, one smooth, one gritty, one with a dead spot that needed a nudge past where he thought it should go. D, then G, and by then his fingertips hurt in a specific new way, a striped soreness across the pads. On the fifth string he turned the peg the wrong direction and the pitch climbed away from B, and he had to chase it back down, and this time he counted the turns so he'd know the way back. The thin string worried him most. He'd read enough forum posts at midnight to know it could snap, and he tightened it in small patient fractions until the pipe's high E and the string's high E sat together, not identical, but close enough that the wobble between them slowed like a swing losing momentum.

When all six were there, he played the chord from the page, the one that had sounded like a broken door, and it sounded like a room instead. Not a good room. The guitar had sat in an attic for a decade and its voice had dust in it. But the notes were the right notes, in the right order, and something in his chest went loose and quiet.

Priya found him there an hour later, still in the band room, playing the same four chords over and over because each repetition felt less like an accident. She listened from the doorway for a minute before she came in. "It's flat on the G," she said. "It went out while you were playing. Old guitars do that."

"So I tune it again?"

"So you tune it again. Every time, maybe forever. That's most of it, honestly." She said it without cruelty, the way you tell someone the commute is long. She sat down across from him and took out her own guitar, and for a while they both just tuned, the small clicking of pegs and the thin comparing of pitches filling the band room where the Sousaphone loomed in its corner like a dozing animal.

Aaron thought, while he turned the G back up, that he had spent the year assuming he was the kind of person who didn't stick with things, that this would go the way of the running app and the sourdough starter, and that his grandfather's guitar would end up back in the attic as evidence. He didn't know yet whether that was wrong. But he'd learned something that felt like it could be carried in the hands rather than the head: the instrument didn't hold its tuning on its own, and neither, apparently, did anyone. You came back, you found the E, and you worked up from the lowest string, listening for the wobble to slow.

His stomach growled. Priya laughed without looking up from her pegs, and Aaron checked the high E once more, then closed the case around the guitar, loosely, without snapping the latches all the way, and said, "Same time tomorrow?"

Savannah had chosen the bank because it had a parking lot with faded white lines and almost no traffic after four o'clock, which made it perfect for parallel parking practice and terrible for everything else. Her mother's Corolla sat between two rubber cones she'd borrowed from her uncle, and for the twentieth time she reversed, turned the wheel, straightened, and got out to measure the gap with her sneaker. Too far from the curb. She knelt down, looked at the distance the way her driving instructor had told her to, and tried to feel where the curb was instead of calculating it.

Inside the bank, in the waiting area by the mortgage desk, her mother was signing papers for a loan, which was why Savannah had the car and the whole afternoon. She was supposed to wait, but her phone buzzed with a message from Priya, who was in the same position she was: seventeen, off to McMaster in September, trying to find a room in Hamilton before the good ones disappeared. Priya had sent photographs of two leases she'd been emailed, side by side, and a single question mark.

Savannah sat on the stone ledge outside the bank doors and enlarged the first one. It was a dense document, clauses about guests and parking and damage, a header in the landlord's own font. The second was different. Its first page had a government crest, the words "standard form of lease," and a layout that looked official rather than homemade. She remembered something she'd read on a tenants' rights site in June, late at night, when the search for a room had started to feel like a second job. She scrolled back through her browser history until she found the page.

Ontario required most private residential landlords to use that government standard lease form for new leases. And if a landlord hadn't provided one, a tenant could ask for it in writing. She read the line twice, then looked at Priya's photographs again. The first lease, the homemade one, was for a basement room near Gage Park, cheap, close to campus, the exact kind of place Savannah wanted. The second, the standard one, was fifteen minutes farther out and forty dollars more a month.

She called Priya from the driver's seat, cones still flanking the Corolla. "The Gage Park one didn't use the standard form," she said. "That doesn't mean the landlord is bad. But you can request it in writing, and see what he does."

"So it's legal or it isn't?" Priya asked. Savannah said she thought it was more like a signal. A landlord who got annoyed by a written request was telling you something; a landlord who sent the form back the same week was telling you something too. Priya said she'd draft the email tonight, and Savannah, watching a man in a suit juggle a coffee and the door, said she had to go practice her merge before rush hour.

The on-ramp to the expressway was the part that frightened her, not because she doubted the car but because merging meant trusting strangers to make room. Her instructor had a phrase for it, "match the traffic," which sounded simple until she was at the bottom of the ramp with a transport truck filling her mirror. She accelerated, signalled, and slid into a gap a hatchback had opened for her, and the driver behind her, instead of honking, eased off with what she could only describe as patience. She had expected to be stigmatized as a learner, the white sticker on the back marking her out for contempt, and half the time she was. But not always, and the times she wasn't felt like data worth collecting.

She thought about the landlord while she drove, holding the lane, checking mirrors on a rhythm. Her father, a stoic about most things, had signed whatever was put in front of him his whole life and considered questions a form of ingratitude. Priya's mother, at the other extreme, distrusted every landlord on principle and would have called the homemade lease proof of bad faith. Savannah was trying to hold both views at once and end up somewhere she could actually live. The request in writing was neither trust nor accusation. It was a polite test, and she liked that it let the landlord answer it himself.

Back at the bank lot, the shadows had stretched across the cones. Her mother came out with her copy of the loan agreement folded into her purse, and Savannah reversed into the space between the cones on the first try, close enough to the curb that she could touch it if she leaned out the window. Her mother stood in front of the car with her arms crossed, and Savannah pulled forward an inch to straighten, then cut the engine.

"There's a girl in my program," her mother said, getting in. "Her daughter's a paralegal. She says never sign anything you didn't read twice." Savannah showed her the two leases on her phone, side by side, and pointed at the crest on the second one. "This one's the standard form," she said. "Ontario makes most landlords use it. If they don't, you can ask for it in writing." Her mother studied the screen for a long moment, then said, "Send that to Priya before she sends the deposit." "Already did," Savannah said, and eased out of the lot toward the on-ramp, where the evening traffic was beginning to build.

The envelope from SUNY Purchase sat on the table beside Leo's cold coffee, and under it, face down, was the flyer for Friday's open mic at the Root Cellar, twelve dollars at the door. He had forty-three dollars in his wallet, which was not enough for both the entry fee and the bus ticket his sister had texted him about that morning. Her message was still open on his phone: "Dad's deposition got moved to the 14th, so I'll be in the city overnight. You could crash on my floor, take the 6 a.m. back. Or not. I know money's tight." He read it three times, then turned the flyer over as if the other side might have gotten cheaper.

Across the room, the espresso machine hissed and a barista named Marcus, who wore a faded lunar-lander pin on his apron, argued cheerfully with a woman about a coupon from the mall next door. "Free travel mug for a ten-minute survey," she said, tapping the paper. "Can't beat free." Marcus laughed. "There ain't no such thing as a free lunch," he said, sliding her cup across the counter. "Where'd you get that, a fortune cookie?" "Robert Heinlein," Marcus said. "The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, 1966. He didn't invent it, but that book's the reason everybody says it now."

Leo had come here to do calculus homework, and the torpid warmth of the shop, all steam and sleepy afternoon light, had conspired with his worry until the problem set sat untouched. He copied one derivative, then set down his pencil. Ten minutes for a survey earned a mug, which was maybe eight dollars, which was most of a bus fare. But the ten minutes were the same ten minutes he'd promised to practicing the bridge of his song, the one he'd need if he actually played Friday. He'd been telling himself all week he'd practice tomorrow, and he could feel the plan calcifying into an excuse, tomorrow hardening into a shape he'd never have to act on.

He got in line. The woman with the coupon had gone, and Marcus was wiping the portafilter with the slow care of someone who took small work seriously. "Did you mean that," Leo asked, "about no free lunch?" Marcus shrugged. "I mean the book's good. It's about a moon colony that overthrows Earth. But the saying, yeah. Somebody always pays." He pulled Leo's Americano and, unprompted, nodded at the envelope. "College?" "Deposit's due May first. Three hundred dollars." It came out of him before he'd decided to say it, the way expensive facts do.

Marcus didn't offer him a job or a discount, which Leo half respected him for. He said only, "So what are you giving up to get the three hundred?" and went back to the grounds, their dark deposition settling at the bottom of the tamp like sediment in a riverbed. Leo carried his coffee to the table and sat with the question, which was more use to him than the calculus. The survey mug, the bus ticket, the open mic, the deposit: none of them were free, because each one consumed the same finite wallet, the same finite Friday, the same ten minutes he could only spend once.

He took out his phone and typed to his sister: "I can't come. Money's going to the deposit." He watched the words sit there. What he'd wanted, all along, was not the open mic exactly, but the version of himself who played it; and what he'd lose by skipping it was a night he could picture too clearly, his sister's floor, the early train, the city going by. He thought about adding that, then thought about how it would sound like asking her to talk him out of deciding, and he sent it plain.

Then, because ten minutes is also just ten minutes, he walked next door to the mall kiosk and took the survey anyway. The clipboard asked about laundry detergent and radio habits, and his answers were mostly honest, and at the end the kid behind the counter, maybe nineteen, handed him a travel mug in a plastic sleeve. "Free lunch," the kid said, grinning. "There ain't no such thing," Leo said, and the grin flickered, uncertain whether it had been corrected or complimented. "Robert Heinlein," Leo added. "You'd like it."

He carried the mug back to the coffee shop, where the afternoon crowd had thickened and Marcus was calling out names. His sister had replied with a single thumbs-up, and below it, in the same gray bubble, the address of a diner near her apartment and the words "Saturday, if the deposit clears." He set the mug on his envelope, took out the flyer, and folded it into his pocket instead of throwing it away, pressing it flat against his thigh. Then he picked up his pencil and worked the derivative, and after that the next one, while behind him the machine hissed on.

The community centre on Ashbury Road smelled of floor wax and instant coffee, and on Thursday nights it belonged to the/mock trial club, which was really just eleven teenagers, a folding table, and a man named Mr. Okafor who had agreed to referee without ever explaining why. Aidan arrived early because he had drawn the worst possible assignment: arguing both sides of a school dress-code case before the mock Supreme Court. Not one side, then someone else's side. Both. In the same night, in front of people who would notice every contradiction.

"You'll argue for the student at seven and the school at seven forty," Mr. Okafor had told him, checking his watch as though the schedule were a legal document. "The case is about a girl suspended for wearing an armband to school, same as the old one. You'll need the famous line somewhere, or you'll lose on style points alone."

"What famous line?" Aidan had asked, and Mr. Okafor had only smiled, which Aidan found less mysterious than infuriating.

So he had spent the week in the library with a photocopied case brief, and on Tuesday night he had found it, reading it twice because the first time it had seemed too simple to be the thing everyone quoted. In Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969, the Supreme Court had ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate. He copied it onto an index card in careful print, then turned the card over and wrote the school's counter-argument on the back, and felt a small, absurd foreboding, as though the two sides of one card might start fighting in his jacket pocket.

At seven, standing at the folding table with the card face-down in front of him, Aidan argued for the student. He was clumsy at first, saying "um" like a metronome, but when he reached for the line, something shifted. "In Tinker v. Des Moines, in 1969, this Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." Priya, playing a justice, stopped doodling. Aidan kept going, and for ten minutes he was genuinely enraptured by his own argument, gesturing at nothing, imagining the schoolhouse gate, the armband, the girl standing outside both.

At seven forty he turned the card over.

"The school's position," he began, and heard his own voice flatten. The counter-argument was harder, and not only because he'd rehearsed it less. He argued that the armband disrupted class, that a school is not a street corner, and the justices leaned in anyway, because a hard argument well made is more interesting than an easy one shouted. But midway through, Priya asked him a question he hadn't prepared for: "Do you believe what you're saying right now?"

The room went quiet in the specific way rooms do when everyone has been thinking the same thing and is grateful someone else said it. Aidan looked at the card, at its two sides, and understood for the first time why Mr. Okafor had given him both. "I believe it's arguable," he said. "I believe the Court found for the students seven to two in 1969, and I believe the school still loses here, but I didn't understand why until I had to make the school's case and feel where it bends." He set the card down face-up, both halves visible. "The disruption argument isn't nothing. It's just not enough at the schoolhouse gate."

He'd expected laughter, or worse, the polite silence reserved for people who crack in public. Instead Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard, and DeShawn, playing the sternest justice, said, "That's the first honest answer anyone's given all night," and then ruined it by adding, "Counsel is still over time, though. By a lot."

Afterward, folding chairs stacked and the lights half off, Priya caught him at the door. "So which one are you actually?" she asked. "The kid with the armband or the school?"

Aidan held up the index card, both sides showing, edges soft from his grip. "Ask me again when it's real," he said, and put it in his pocket, where the two arguments sat together, unresolved, all the way home.

Emile had agreed to meet Dara at the Saturday market because her mother kept a vegetable stall there and Dara could not leave it for long. He arrived with his economics textbook zipped into a backpack along with two granola bars, and found her weighing tomatoes for a woman in a sun hat, the scale's needle swinging, then settling. He had three days to learn how to explain why a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation, for a presentation he would give alone, in front of a class that included Dara, who already understood the material better than he did and had offered to practice with him anyway.

"You brought the graph?" she said, when the tomato woman had gone. He unrolled it on the wooden counter between a crate of radishes and a jar of tulips. The line climbed steeply, hung, then fell like something dropping off a ledge. Dara tapped the ledge. "Start there. What is that?"

He knew the numbers. He had memorized them on the bus that morning, the way he memorized French verbs, by rhythm rather than meaning. "Inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980," he said, "and it fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve raised rates sharply." The words came out in one breath, flat as a receipt.

Dara folded her arms. "Now say it like you know why it matters."

A man wanted two pounds of green beans. While she served him, Emile stared at the graph and tried to feel the difference between reciting and understanding. Around him the market did its ordinary commerce: a baker calling out prices, a kid negotiating over honey sticks, coins changing hands. Everything here cost money, and money, he was beginning to grasp, had a price of its own, though he could not yet say that sentence aloud without hearing how much he was imitating the textbook.

"Try me as a customer," Dara said when the beans were bagged. "Pretend I'm someone at the market who doesn't know anything."

"Excuse me, ma'am," Emile began, and hated the sound of it. "When borrowing money gets more expensive, people borrow less." He stopped. "But then what? I always lose the thread after the first step."

"Then what," Dara repeated. She wasn't going to fill it in for him. Her mother had raised her on the principle that you didn't hand someone a fish at a stall where fish were sold, and Emile suspected the principle extended to graphs.

He walked away from the stall, past the cheese vendor, and stood where he could see the whole market at once. His father had sequestered his savings account last year, moved it somewhere Emile couldn't touch it for school clothes, and Emile had been furious, though the money had lasted longer because of it. He turned that over. Scarcer, costlier, slower. The words weren't the mechanism, exactly, but they pointed at it, the way a sign pointed at a town rather than being the town. When he came back, a young couple was buying corn, and Dara counted their change with one hand while gesturing at him with the other to wait, and something in the ordinariness of the exchange steadied him.

"Okay," he said when they'd gone. "Here's my problem. I can give you the numbers, and I can give you the theory, but I can't connect them. It's like the graph is a mountain range and my explanation is a postcard of it."

"That's the most honest thing you've said all morning," Dara said. "Most people fake the connection. Don't fake it. Say the fact, say what you understand, and admit where you're guessing." She paused. "Though if your whole presentation is 'here are the numbers, the rest is fog,' Mr. Halvorsen will call it bathos. A big dramatic setup collapsing into nothing."

He laughed despite himself. "Fine. So what's germane? What actually belongs in my three minutes?"

"The fact belongs. The drop belongs. Whether you fully grasp the mechanism or not, that happened: fourteen point eight in March 1980, under three by 1983, after the Fed raised rates." She said it plainly, the way she'd said the price of beans. "Then give your one honest step, the costlier borrowing part, and stop. Let the graph carry the rest."

They ran it twice more. His delivery got steadier, and he could feel the small gain, but he also felt what it cost him: the admission, out loud, in front of the class he would face on Tuesday, that his understanding had a border, and that he could see where the border was but not beyond it. Dara packed up the unsold radishes as the market thinned. The afternoon light came in low and gold across the stalls, and somewhere behind them a vendor was already folding a canopy, the aluminum legs clacking together.

"You'll do fine," she said. "You're the only person in that class who'll admit what he doesn't know."

"That's a terrible strategy," Emile said, shouldering his backpack.

"It's the only one you've got," she said, and handed him a tomato, unasked, still warm from the sun.

Mr. Okafor had taped a sample ballot to the whiteboard on Monday, and by Wednesday it was still there, curling at the corners like a leaf deciding whether to fall. He would not tell them how to vote, he said, but he would not let them treat the election as weather, something that simply happened to the country. "You want to historicize it," he said, tapping the board with a knuckle. "Place it. Ask what came before, what forces arranged it. Then you walk in and pull a lever like you mean it." Mason had written the word in his notebook, historicize, and underlined it twice, though mostly he was thinking about the fact that in nine days he would be eighteen, and in eleven days he would vote.

He had registered in September at the DMV, a trip his grandfather had insisted on driving him to even though the office was four blocks from the school and the weather was still warm. In the car afterward, his grandfather had done the thing he always did at moments he considered ceremonial, turning his wedding ring with his thumb, a mannerism Mason had noticed since he was small and had never asked about. "Nobody in my family voted before 1965," his grandfather said at a red light. "Legally, I mean." He didn't say anything else, and Mason hadn't needed him to.

The morning of the election, Mason woke before his alarm. He ate cereal standing up. He took the sample ballot his teacher had photocopied, folded twice, and put it in his jacket pocket along with his driver's license, and he walked the six blocks to the community hall with his breath showing white in front of him and his stomach doing something complicated that was not quite fear.

The line moved slowly, and he spent it listening to two women behind him argue about a school levy in the polite, murderous way of neighbors. When his turn came, he gave his name to a poll worker with reading glasses on a beaded chain, a woman whose son had been in Mason's chemistry class last year. She ran her finger down the list. Ran it again. Flipped a page, then flipped it back, and Mason felt the paper-thin confidence of the morning begin to go out of him like heat from a cracked window.

"I don't see you here, honey," she said. "Are you sure you're at the right precinct?"

He was sure. He had checked twice. He gave his address, his birthday, the September date of the DMV visit, and she shook her head with real regret, and behind him the line shifted its weight, and Mason's face went hot. He thought of the folded sample ballot in his pocket, of the underlined word in his notebook, of his grandfather turning the ring in a stopped car. He was about to ask whether he could just fill something out, some form, when the woman raised a hand toward a younger poll worker at a side table.

"He can do a provisional ballot," the younger woman said.

"What's that mean," Mason asked, and heard how young his voice came out.

"It's under the Help America Vote Act of 2002," she said. "A voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot. It only counts once officials confirm your eligibility." She handed him a form on a clipboard. "You fill this out, your ballot goes in a special envelope, and if they confirm you're registered, it gets counted."

He filled out the form at the side table, his handwriting smaller and more careful than usual, and fed his ballot into its envelope, and the envelope into a folder, and then there was nothing left to do but thank them and walk out. He told no one at school. When Mr. Okafor asked the class, at the end of fourth period, who had voted that morning, Mason raised his hand, and it did not feel like a lie, exactly, but it did not feel entirely like the truth either, and he held both of those feelings at once without deciding between them, the way you hold two books you intend to read.

The twist came nine days later, in the same classroom, during the same period. Mr. Okafor was collecting essays when the front office called down, and a runner brought Mason a sealed envelope, county stationery, and everyone watched him open it because everyone always watches. The letter said his eligibility had been confirmed. His provisional ballot had been counted. The DMV clerk had simply failed to transmit his registration on time, an oversight, no one's malice, a snag in the nascent machinery of his civic life, now repaired.

That night his grandfather called. "So it counted," he said. "So your vote counted."

"It counted," Mason said. "It just counted late." He was quiet a moment, and then, because his grandfather would understand it in a way no one else would, he added, "The election was called before mine counted. It didn't matter."

"Everything matters," his grandfather said, and Mason heard the ring turn against the phone, a small metallic whisper, once, twice.

Eva had the museum map folded into her back pocket and fifteen minutes before the placement review session started, which was not enough time and was exactly the time she had. She took the escalator two steps at a time to the third floor, where the Hall of Human Biology kept its dim, blue-lit corridor, and found the mitochondria exhibit at the far end, past the plastic brain and the giant walk-in ear.

She had gotten the question wrong on Tuesday. On the practice exam, question forty-one had asked what happens in muscle cells when oxygen runs low, and she had written that lactate builds up as a waste product and shuts the cell down. Her mark came back with a red line through it and a note in the margin: reread fermentation. Daniel, who sat beside her in the review session and had gotten it right, had offered to explain, and she had said no thank you, which had come out colder than she meant. Now it was Saturday, and she was standing in front of a wall display with her phone in her hand, determined to disabuse herself of her own answer before Monday's exam.

The display was called Inside the Powerhouse. A transparent model of a cell the size of a car occupied the middle of the room, its mitochondria picked out in orange. Along the left wall ran a sequence of panels: glucose, glycolysis, pyruvate, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, ATP. She read them in order, resting her fingertips on the railing in front of each one. Glucose split into two molecules of pyruvate, yielding a small payout of ATP. If oxygen was plentiful, the pyruvate went into the mitochondria and the payout grew enormous. If oxygen ran low, the sequence stopped partway, and she stood at that panel for a long time, because the panel stopped partway too. A piece of the interactive screen had gone dark, a recalcitrant gray rectangle where the words about what happened next should have been.

"Are you here for the review session?" a voice asked. A girl of about ten stood beside her, holding a clipboard, a junior docent by her badge. Her badge said Priya.

"No," Eva said. "I'm here to fix my own head. Do you know what this panel says? The one that's out."

Priya looked at the dead rectangle and then at her clipboard. "It's been broken since Thursday. But I know the piece, I had to memorize the script." She read from her clipboard in a flat, rehearsed voice: "When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose."

"Say that again," Eva said. Priya said it again, slower, and Eva typed it into her phone, then deleted it, because typing it was not the same as having it. "So the lactate isn't the poison. It's the fix."

"It's the trade," Priya said, as though correcting a customer who had misread a price. "You get less ATP that way. Two per glucose. But you keep getting it."

Eva walked to the far wall, where a stationary bike sat in front of a heart-rate monitor, part of an exhibit on exertion. She pedaled hard for ninety seconds, watching her pulse climb and feeling the familiar burn arrive in her thighs, the same burn she had felt in August sprinting across her uncle's farm field to beat a storm to the barn. She had thought then that the burn was the moment her legs gave up. She pedaled and understood that it was the moment her cells improvised. Her legs had kept moving through the whole field, which meant the glycolysis had kept going, which meant the NAD+ had kept coming back, which meant the lactate had been on her side the entire time. She slowed the pedals. A woman waiting behind her with a toddler asked if she was done, and Eva got off, still breathing hard.

She took out her phone to text Daniel. She wrote, I was wrong about forty-one. When muscle cells run low on oxygen they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis keeps making 2 ATP per glucose. The lactate isn't what stops you. She looked at the message. It read like the docent's clipboard, flat and complete, and she decided that was fine, because completeness was what she had come for. She sent it.

Daniel replied almost immediately, and his reply was a voice message. She stood under the blue lights with the phone against her ear, sweat cooling on the back of her neck. "Hey," he said. "So first, that's the whole thing, you basically just recited the model answer, nice. Second, I have to tell you something. Professor Ayeni posted an announcement an hour ago. Monday's exam got moved to Friday. Some scheduling thing with the gymnasium." There was a pause with wind in it; he was outside somewhere. "So you spent your Saturday learning this for nothing, kind of."

Eva looked at the broken panel, the gray rectangle that had made her pedal a museum bicycle in front of a toddler to understand a sentence she could have read off a working screen. She thought about the denouement she had been picturing all week: the exam, question forty-one, her pen moving without hesitation, the small private vindication of it. That denouement was gone, or postponed, and the knowledge was still here, sitting in her legs and her phone and her memory, arriving five days early for a party that had been rescheduled.

She put the phone in her pocket and turned back toward the model cell. Priya was leading a family toward the giant ear, clipboard tucked under her arm. Eva caught up with them at the mouth of the walk-in cochlea and tapped the girl on the shoulder.

"Your script," Eva said. "The broken panel. Somebody should tell the front desk it worked anyway."

The scoreboard in left field had lost its middle digit, so the score read 4 instead of 14, and Victor thought that was as good a summary of the season as any. They were down five in the sixth. He stood in the on-deck circle twisting his bat when Danny Kohl, their third hitter, launched a double off the wall, and the whole dugout started hammering the bench like a drum line.

"That's three in a row for Kohl," Coach Renner said, mostly to himself, but loud enough. Victor heard him say to the assistant, "Get the ball to Kohl every time he's up. He's burning."

Victor was batting fourth. He had walked twice and singled once, and no one had hammered anything for him. When he came back to the bench after a groundout that moved Danny to third, Renner didn't look at him. He looked at Danny, who was spitting sunflower seeds into a paper cup and grinning.

"Next inning, if Kohl gets on, we bunt him over," Renner said. "Want Kohl swinging while he's hot."

"Coach, I'm four for seven the last two games," Victor said.

"And Kohl's hot tonight."

The word landed on Victor like a tag. Hot. As if Danny's body were a stove and the dial had been turned up by circumstance. Victor had read something once, late at night, phone light under his blanket because his roommate was asleep, a Wikipedia spiral that had started with coin flips. He tried to remember the details while he stood at second base in the top of the seventh, watching their left fielder take a bad route to a sinking line drive.

Between innings he found the page again, crouched by the bat rack. 1985. Three names: Gilovich, Vallone, Tversky. They had looked at basketball shooters and concluded that streaks were no more common than chance. There was a word for the belief, a word the study used, and Victor mouthed it to himself before he let anyone else hear it.

In the eighth they trailed by two. Danny led off with a walk, which did not portend anything, Victor told himself, though his hands were sweating anyway. Then Victor worked the count full and doubled into the left-center gap, and Danny scored. The dugout began hammering the bench again, and Victor, standing on second with his hands on his knees, realized they were hammering for him. For one turn of the order, he was the stove.

He led off the ninth with the score tied. On the third pitch he lined a single, and the first-base coach squeezed his shoulder. The next batter, a junior named Ellis, took three straight fastballs for strikes, and Victor stole second on the third one anyway, sliding in under the tag in a cloud of dust. When he stood and brushed himself off, Renner was signaling from the third-base box: bunt.

The idea was obvious. Ellis would make an out, Victor would take third, and Danny, three for four with the hot hand, would end it with one swing. The whole park could feel the plan assembling itself. Victor looked down at Danny in the on-deck circle, tapping his cleats with his bat, loose and happy and ready.

He called time and walked toward the third-base box.

"What are you doing," Renner said. Not a question.

"There was this study," Victor said. "Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone, Tversky. They looked at basketball shooters, and the streaks weren't any more common than chance. They called it the hot hand fallacy."

Renner's jaw moved the way it did when he chewed gum that had gone to rubber. "This is baseball, not basketball."

"I know. I'm saying maybe Danny's not hot. Maybe he's just a good hitter who's had four balls fall in."

"Maybe you're a kid who read something on his phone."

"Coach," Danny called from the circle, easy, unbothered. "I'll take it from here."

Renner looked at Victor for a long second, then put the bunt sign back up, sharper this time, an obsolescent gesture now that every kid on the field could read the whole alphabet of signs. Victor went back to second. He thought about how his father described jury duty once, how the affidavit he'd signed felt heavier than the testimony itself, a thing you had to stand behind. Whatever happened next, he had said his page out loud, in front of everybody.

Ellis bunted. Victor took third. The left fielder's dead scoreboard digit hung above them all like a held breath. Danny dug in, twisted his hips once, and the first pitch came in low and outside.

"Take," the catcher said, and Victor, leading off third, watched the ball sail past and heard the crowd begin to rise.

The laptop lab at Camp Wyacanna smelled of pine sap and hot plastic, and Abigail had claimed the corner station on the first day so she could see both the door and the lake. Her project for the final week was due in three days, and she had chosen the hardest option on the list: write a program that searched a sorted list, and then stand up in front of everyone and explain why anyone should care. She had until now written programs that did what she told them and nothing more, and the gap between that and explaining felt like the gap between swimming and teaching swimming.

Her first attempt walked through the list one item at a time, comparing, comparing, comparing. It worked. It was also, according to the camp's test data, slow in a way she could feel in her teeth, like chewing taffy. Rohan, who sat diagonally behind her and narrated his own debugging like a sports announcer, kept calling her program "the obedient one." She did not ask what he meant by that.

The trouble began with Marcus. Marcus had arrived second week, loud in the way of someone performing confidence, and he'd decided the final presentations should be a competition. Not graded, he said when the counselor raised an eyebrow. Just a race. Someone would hide a target word in a million-entry list, and two programs would hunt for it at the same time, in front of everyone, on the projector.

"A million," Marcus said. "My program checks every entry in order. Clean. Honest work."

"A million entries," Abigail said. "One at a time."

"That's the point."

Rohan spun his chair around. "You're going to sit there while your computer grinds through a million comparisons like some obstreperous toddler demanding every single thing in the house."

"I'm going to win," Marcus said.

That night Abigail stayed after lights-out in the lab, the one room the counselors didn't patrol because the windows faced the water. She drew on the whiteboard. A million items. Check the middle one first, she thought, because the list was sorted, and if the target came after the middle, then half the list was suddenly irrelevant. Not checked. Gone. Then the middle of what remained, then the middle of that. She wrote the numbers down in a shrinking column and kept crossing out halves until she was looking at a single circled digit. Twenty. She counted her crosses again. Twenty comparisons, and a million items reduced to one. She sat down on the floor with her back against the desk and stared at the column for a long time, because it looked like a magic trick and she wanted to find the seam where the trick cheated, and there wasn't one. She looked up "binary search" on her phone mostly to find out whether she'd invented it or just found it lying on the ground, the way you find a good stone.

The next morning she rebuilt her program. Middle, compare, throw away half. Middle, compare, throw away half. The code was shorter than her first version, which bothered her. In her experience things that worked better were supposed to cost more. She tested it on the camp's sample list and the answer arrived so fast the screen barely seemed to change, and she caught herself distrusting her own success, rerunning it four times as if speed were a mistake that repetition would correct.

The race was Thursday evening, after the bonfire got going and before the talent show collapsed into the usual argument about the sound system. Marcus had spent the week making his linear program look polished, and he was a connoisseur of presentation, Abigail had to admit that. He had transitions between slides. He had a countdown. When the counselor loaded the million-entry list onto the projector and picked a target word hidden somewhere in it, Marcus cracked his knuckles like a man about to lift something.

"On three," the counselor said. "One, two, three."

Marcus's program began. The projector showed a bar crawling across the list, and the crowd, mostly eleven-year-olds who had wandered over from the marshmallow line, cheered for it the way they'd cheer for anything moving. Abigail's program checked the middle entry. Then it checked the middle of the right half. The counter in the corner of her screen read two, then three, then four, and Marcus's bar was maybe a fifth of the way across his million.

At the count of twenty her screen went still and printed the target word. It was over before the marshmallow line had advanced a single camper. Marcus's bar kept crawling, out of some stubbornness or maybe just because nobody had told it to stop, and eventually the crowd's attention drifted back to the fire, and eventually he closed his laptop without the word being found. He didn't say anything to her. He said something to Rohan later that she half-heard from the picnic table, something about how the race wasn't really fair if you used a trick, and she turned it over while she ate.

The trick question was the one that kept her up. Because she had needed the list to be sorted for the halving to mean anything, and Marcus's stubborn crawl would have worked on any list at all, sorted or shuffled or upside down. His was the sturdier method and hers was the faster one, and she hadn't decided yet whether sturdier or faster counted for more, or whether the honest answer was that it depended on the list, which felt like cheating to say out loud. She practiced her explanation in the shower block with its permanent smell of chlorine, saying the number twenty out loud to the tile.

On Saturday she stood in front of everyone with the whiteboard behind her, the shrinking column still visible in blue marker. She told them about the million items and the twenty comparisons. Then she told them the part she was less sure of, that her way only worked because the data had been made orderly first, and that making it orderly cost something too, and that she hadn't finished deciding when that cost was worth paying.

"Twenty," said a small girl from the marshmallow line, holding up a foil-wrapped square of something that had begun as chocolate. "Out of a million?"

"Twenty," Abigail said. "Count them if you want."

The box had been under the bed in Gran's spare room for as long as Addison could remember, and she had never once been allowed to open it. Tonight Gran had said, almost offhandedly, that she could, which was how Addison knew something had changed, though she did not ask what.

"You're doing that college essay," Gran said from the doorway, hands folded over her cardigan. "The one about family. Take it, then. But read it carefully, not fast."

The box smelled of coal smoke and old paper. Inside were a christening gown gone brown at the hem, a ration book, and a bundle of letters tied with shoelace. Addison untied it on the bed while the light outside went crepuscular and the radiator ticked. The topmost letter was dated 1842, written in a hand so cramped she had to sound the words aloud. A man named Joseph Lockwood, her great-great-great-grandfather, wrote to his sister about shifts at the mill, about the dust that got into his lungs, about being turned off for asking his wage in full. She read it twice. She had expected soldiers or farmers in her family, people who turned up in textbooks. Joseph turned up nowhere.

She carried the letter downstairs. Gran was peeling potatoes at the sink, and the window behind her had gone to purple. Addison read a line aloud, about the foreman docking him a shilling, and Gran set the knife down.

"Your grandfather spent years on that lot," she said. "Before he got ill. He wanted to write it all down, our Joseph and the rest of them, and nobody would take it. Said the library wasn't interested in mill hands." She dried her hands slowly. "There's his study, you know where."

The study still smelled of him, pipe tobacco gone stale in the carpet. Addison found his notebooks first, then, behind them on the low shelf, a battered paperback with a spine cracked white. The Making of the English Working Class. 1963, said the title page, and E. P. Thompson. In the margin, in her grandfather's pencil, a line was underlined twice: he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from, and then in quotes, the enormous condescension of posterity. She did not know the word posterity at first, then she did: everyone who came after, everyone like her. She sat down on the floor with the book in her lap and the notebook open beside her and did not notice the room going dark.

Her grandfather's notes were the problem. In one notebook he had written that Joseph was out on strike in 1842, standing with the hands. In the other, later notebook, the claim had a question mark beside it, and a page reference to a newspaper of the time that listed Joseph Lockwood among the men who went back in on the third day. Addison went back and forth between the two notebooks, then to the letters, then to the book. The newspaper was a partial thing, she understood; its owner hated the strikers, and a list in such a paper could be wrong, or vindictive. But the first notebook rested on a story Joseph's daughter had told sixty years after the fact, which was partial too, the apportionment of blame smoothed by family love. She could not predicate Joseph's loyalty on either source alone, and she could not stop wanting to know it.

She carried both notebooks down to the kitchen. "Gran, which one is true? Was he out on strike or wasn't he?"

Gran looked at the pencil question mark for a long moment. "I never asked him," she said. "He'd sit there with his papers and I'd think, there's tea to be made. I never asked what he'd found." She tapped the page. "Maybe he couldn't decide either. That's why the question mark."

The potatoes were boiling over. Gran lifted the pan and Addison found herself holding both notebooks against her chest, the way you hold something you're afraid of being asked to put down. She thought about her grandfather, alone in this room, wanting to rescue a man no book had room for, and ending on a question mark anyway. She would write the essay with both versions in it. She would say what she could not settle.

"The enormous condescension of posterity," she said aloud, testing it.

"What's that, love?"

"Nothing. Something Grandad underlined." She set the notebooks on the table, side by side, question mark facing up, and reached for a plate.

Violet told herself she had taken the junior counselor job for the experience, and for most of June this was almost true. She liked the mornings at Lakeview Day Camp, the way the five-year-olds arrived with their backpacks still bobbing above their shoulders, the smell of sunscreen and cut grass outside the arts shed. She told her mother she was practically volunteering, since eight dollars an hour was hardly money at all. She did not mention that she had been keeping a tally in the back of her notebook since the first week, a column of hours with small sums beside it, because the tally was just for practice, the way one might practice budgeting.

In the third week of July, Deenie, who ran the oldest campers' group, wrenched her ankle on the dock steps and went home for the summer. The director, Ms. Amara, stood at the picnic table with her clipboard and asked who could cover Deenie's afternoons, the extended-care block that ran until six. Several hands went down again as fast as they had gone up. Violet raised hers and kept it there. By Friday she had worked the morning block, the afternoon block, and two extra days covering the front desk while the receptionist was out, and when she added the column in her notebook she counted fifty-one hours in one week.

She was not counting the money, she reminded herself. She was being useful, which was different. Rosa, her best friend at camp, had a theory about this. "You proselytize about not caring," Rosa said, peeling the label off her water bottle in one long strip. "You convert people to it. That's how much you care about not caring." Violet laughed and said Rosa should have been a lawyer, which was what Rosa's mother was and what Rosa was tired of hearing about.

The paycheck came on the second of August, a thin envelope with a stub inside. Violet read it in the supply closet where the extra life vests hung, because that was the only quiet place at two o'clock. The stub listed her regular hours at eight dollars. Then there was a second line, hours at twelve dollars an hour, eleven of them. Twelve was not a number she had earned anywhere. Eleven was a number she recognized, the amount past forty. She stood there doing arithmetic on the paint-spattered counter, and the total matched exactly, and she felt a small unearned glow, as though she had gotten away with something she had not even attempted.

She decided not to ask about it. If the camp wanted to overpay her, that was the camp's problem, and mentioning it might make someone realize a mistake and take the money back. She rehearsed several versions of this reasoning on the bus home and found all of them convincing. Rosa, when told, was less convinced. "You're being an apologist for your own greed," Rosa said, "and not even greed for money. Greed for being the girl who doesn't ask." Violet said that was the most convoluted compliment she had ever received, and also that Rosa should return the orange crayon she had borrowed in April.

But the twelve dollars sat in her mind the way a pulled thread sits in a sweater. On Monday she went to the office during nap block and found Ms. Amara laminating name tags. Violet put the stub on the desk, faceup, and tapped the second line. "I didn't work any senior hours," she said. "Why are eleven of my hours at twelve dollars?"

Ms. Amara looked at the stub, then at Violet, and something in her expression shifted, a loosening, as if she had been braced for a complaint and received a question instead. "That's not a mistake," she said. "It's the law. Non-exempt employees get one and a half times their regular rate for every hour past forty in a workweek. Eight times one and a half is twelve." She slid the stub back across the desk. "You crossed forty last week, so your last eleven hours paid at twelve. Most of your hours this summer won't, since you're usually under. But when you cover for someone, they can add up fast."

Violet said, mostly to the laminator, "I thought that was only for real jobs." Ms. Amara said the law did not distinguish, not in the way Violet meant, and turned the machine off between name tags. "Half the counselors never read their stubs," she added. "You read yours." She said it without particular praise, as a fact she had observed, and somehow that landed heavier than praise would have.

On the bus home, Violet took out her notebook and, next to her column of hours, wrote a second column, rate, and a third, earned, and filled them in for every week so far. The numbers were smaller than her old estimates, because her old estimates had quietly rounded up. She noticed this about herself and did not entirely know what to do with it, that her careful tally had been careful the way a funhouse mirror is careful. She was, she concluded, a person who liked to seem unconcerned with money while being extremely concerned with it, and she could admit that now without deciding yet whether to change it. Rosa would say this was progress. Rosa would also say the orange crayon thing again.

In August she signed up for two more of Deenie's afternoon blocks, telling Rosa it was for the experience. Rosa raised an eyebrow and said nothing sagacious, which in Rosa's mouth was practically a standing ovation. On the last Friday of the summer, Violet bought two ice creams with her own money from the truck by the lake, and handed one to Rosa, and said, "I'm only letting you think I'm generous. My hours past forty pay time and a half, and I checked the schedule." Rosa took the cone and bit the top off. "Fifty-one hours next week?" she asked, and Violet, watching the older campers tip their canoe in the shallows, said, "Fifty-two."

The basement smelled of dryer sheets and cold pizza, and Deng had pushed the folding table against the wall so two laptops could sit side by side under the single good lamp. He slid his chair back and pointed at his screen, where a line of red text refused to go away. "It won't compile. It keeps saying the field is not visible."

Loic leaned over. Deng's test code tried to print the value of a variable called count straight out of the class they had written together, something like System.out.println(searcher.count), and the compiler was treating it like a locked door. The declaration up in the class read private int count. Loic read the error three times before the shape of it settled. "It's marked private," he said slowly. "So it can only be read or changed by code inside that same class."

"Even my code? We're in the same project."

"Same project isn't the same class." Loic tapped the word on the screen. "That's what it means. It's not broken, it's doing exactly what it says."

Deng groaned and dropped his forehead onto his wrist. Their algorithms exam was Monday, and they had planned this night weeks ago: Loic would finally learn binary search well enough to explain it out loud, and Deng would pass the practice test he'd been failing. The pizza box near Loic's elbow held one cold slice with olives, which Deng had ordered deliberately because he called Loic's tastes epicurean, an accusation Loic had stopped contesting around tenth grade. Loic folded the slice in half and ate it anyway, because refusing cold pizza on principle was a richer man's game.

"Okay, forget the test for a second," Loic said. He pulled his own laptop closer and opened a blank file. "Explain linear search to me like I'm your grandmother."

Deng sat up, willing to be distracted from his broken code. "You walk the whole array from the start. Look at index zero. Is that your number? No. Index one? No. You keep going until you find it or you run out."

"So a million sorted numbers, worst case, a million checks."

"A million checks, yes. Because sorted doesn't help you if you start at the beginning like a coward." Deng grinned, then sobered. "Binary search is the part that uses the sortedness. You check the middle first."

Loic typed an array into the file, twenty numbers in order, and put a target near the end. He checked the middle element. It was too small; his target was bigger, so the target had to live in the right half, and the entire left half, ten elements, stopped existing for him in one comparison. He said this out loud, watching Deng nod, and then did it again with the remaining half, and again, until the middle of a two-element range was suddenly the number he wanted. Four checks. He sat back. "That's it? That's the whole thing?"

"That's the whole thing. Each check throws away half of what's left. Twenty numbers, four or five checks. A million, around twenty."

The proportion seemed to destabilize something Loic had assumed was fixed, that searching a bigger pile had to cost proportionally more. He had always thought of work as scaling with size, the way carrying more books cost more arms. He started drawing it in his notebook: a line for linear search climbing steadily like a staircase into the dark, and beneath it a nearly flat curve that crawled even as the numbers grew enormous. He was not a math person, or he had spent years saying so, and the flat curve made him suspicious of himself. Somewhere along the way he had decided he was the kind of student who understood things slowly and by hand, and here was a idea he had picked up in one sitting by cutting a list in half repeatedly. He didn't say any of this to Deng. He just kept drawing.

Meanwhile Deng had gone quiet, which for Deng meant progress. He had written a method inside the class itself, a small getCount method sitting right below the private field, and his test now called that instead of reaching into the field directly. The compiler accepted it without complaint. "So the test can ask the class for the number," Deng said, "but it can't just take it."

"Right. The class hands it over through a method, because the field is only for code inside that class." Loic watched Deng run the test and saw the green checkmark, and felt an odd small pride in someone else's screen, which he also did not announce.

"Okay," Deng said, turning the lamp so it lit Loic's notebook instead of his own face. "Your turn. Explain binary search to me like I'm the exam grader. No hands, no cut-up paper. Just words."

Loic put down the pen. He talked through the sorted array, the middle check, the discarded half, the discarded half of that, and he heard his own sentences become steady, the way a word repeated until it feels like yours. When he finished, one loose thread stayed: he could explain why halving beat walking, could even feel it, but he still couldn't say precisely how many checks a million numbers needed, only that it was around twenty, only that Deng had said so. That number sat in his mind unverified, borrowed.

"Again," Deng said, sliding his chair around to face him fully, "but this time tell me why the array has to be sorted first. Pretend I doubt you."

"You should doubt me," Loic said, and reached for the notebook to start a new page.

The canoe tipped on the second day, and by the third morning the whole camp knew that Priya had been the one holding it crooked. Nobody said so out loud. They just let the fact drift around the mess hall like the smell of oatmeal, and Priya ate her toast with her shoulders up around her ears. Juliette, who had been paired with her for the Friday paddling assessment, understood that she had two weeks to solve a problem she could not name politely: her bow paddler was terrible, and she would have to say so, eventually, to her face.

Their counselor, a college junior named Dana who was working the summer between what she called "semesters of crisis," had been furloughed from her actual internship and seemed to regard canoe instruction as a form of hospice care for her career. She taught by shrugging. When Juliette asked how to tell a partner she was doing something wrong, Dana said, "Specifically. And like she's a person," and then went back to reading a battered social psychology textbook she kept folded open on the dock.

Juliette was not naturally a confronter. Her mother sold real estate and could parametrize any human interaction into a spreadsheet of outcomes; her father believed honesty was a virtue best practiced on other people's children. Juliette had absorbed both positions without committing to either, which meant she mostly said "it's fine" in a voice that made it clear it was not fine, which Priya had surely noticed.

The book on the dock turned out to matter. Juliette, drying her feet beside it while Priya retrieved a dropped paddle, read the page it happened to be open to. In 1999, two researchers, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh, had found that people liked a partner more when that partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements. She read it twice, wondering whether Priya had been mirroring her all week, the copied laugh, the way she sat when Juliette sat, or whether it was the other way around and she was the copy.

"You're doing the thing," Priya said that evening, from the top bunk, in the dark.

"What thing."

"The mirror thing. There's a study. Some year in the nineties. Chartrand and Bargh. People like you more when you copy how they're sitting." A pause, then, more quietly: "Is that why you've been nice to me? Because you read the same page?"

Juliette lay still and considered lying, considered a hedonistic little fantasy in which she said yes and Priya laughed and the canoe became a boat that carried them both. "I read the page today," she said. "But I decided to pair with you before I read it. You don't have to believe that."

On Thursday, the last practice day, Priya put the canoe in the reeds twice. At lunch, out by the fire pit away from the others, Juliette made herself do it. "Your J-stroke is fine on flat water. The problem is when we turn, you switch sides a half second before I call it, so we're both on the same side and the boat walks into whatever's nearest. If you wait for the call, my steering can handle the rest." She heard her own voice, how specific it was, how it sounded almost like kindness, and how it was not quite kindness either, only information delivered at close range.

Priya turned her spork over in her hand. "You've been thinking about how to say that for days."

"Obviously."

"You could have just said I was bad."

"You're not bad. You're early." Priya almost smiled at that, and Juliette caught herself adjusting her posture to match the way Priya had drawn up one knee, and decided not to worry about which of them was doing the study and which was doing the finding. On Friday they came through the assessment channel upright, Priya waiting, with visible effort, for every call, and afterward she reached across the gunwale and splashed Juliette with the flat of her paddle. "Half a second," she said. "That's all I was borrowing."

The bus smelled of wet canvas and diesel, and the windows had gone pale with the kind of boreal light that arrives in March before the weather has agreed to change. Elijah sat in the fourth row from the back, a folded application on his knee, the words GIANT SANDWICH SHOP, NOW HIRING, FLEXIBLE HOURS showing through the crease. Tomorrow at four o'clock he would sit across a desk from someone whose name he did not yet know, and he would have to look that person in the eye.

"You're staring at the floor again," said Priya, who was sixteen like him and had worked at the library since she was fourteen. She held up her phone as a pretend camera. "Look here. Answer. Don't look away, don't look up like you're asking the ceiling for notes."

"I'm composing," Elijah said. "There's a difference."

"There isn't. Tell me about a time you showed responsibility."

He told her about the summer he'd mowed six lawns every week for his uncle, and he kept his eyes on hers for the whole first sentence, then dropped them for the second, then dragged them back. "Better," she said, and she didn't sound like she was lying, which he had learned to check for. "Slower. People trust slow."

Two rows ahead, Dennys turned around over the seatback. Dennys was seventeen and already worked at the deli counter of the Martindale Grocery, and he had a red apron folded in his backpack like a flag of a small country. "You applying at Giant Sandwich?" he said. "Good luck. Kenny up front at my place runs the slicer and he says it's the best station, you just stand there and the meat does the work. They'll probably start you on that if you get it."

"The slicer," Elijah said.

"The meat slicer, yeah. Kenny's seventeen. They gave him slicer shifts last month when the other guy quit." Dennys shrugged. "He says the blade's sharp as anything but you keep your fingers back and it's fine."

Priya was already typing. She read for a moment, frowning, then turned the screen so both boys could see it. "Under US federal law," she read, "workers aged sixteen and seventeen have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous." She scrolled. "There's a list. It's called the hazardous occupations orders. Slicers are on it. Power-driven meat-processing machines."

"So Kenny can work any shift they give him," Elijah said slowly, working it out, "any hours at all, but not that machine."

"Wait." Dennys's face had gone very still, the way it did in math class right before he understood something. "They've got him on it four days a week." He pulled out his own phone and started scrolling through his messages, his thumbs fast, his mouth pressed into a line. He didn't say anything for three stops. The bus filled and emptied around them; a kindergarten brother and sister argued over a granola bar; the driver adjudicated from the mirror with a single raised finger, and the arguing stopped.

The thing Elijah had not worked out, yet, was what he himself was supposed to do with the information. He could ask, tomorrow, whether the sandwich shop used a slicer, and he could ask it in a clear voice with steady eye contact, and the answer would tell him something about the place. Or he could say nothing and take the job and be careful, the way Kenny was careful, the way everyone was careful with things that were technically somebody else's problem. Priya made him rehearse his chronology, his short history of mowing lawns and watching a neighbor's cat and one volunteer Saturday at the food pantry, in order, oldest to newest, because "managers like a chronology," she said, "it shows you think in straight lines." He gave it to her twice. The second time he did not look away once.

Here is what Elijah did not know: three rows back, a girl named Ruth was listening. Ruth was seventeen, senior year, and she rode this bus because it was the bus, and she had her headphones in but no music playing, which was a habit she'd developed since starting her job. Tomorrow at four o'clock it would be Ruth behind the desk at Giant Sandwich, because the manager had left on short notice and Ruth, who had been there eight months, was the only one who could cover the interviews. She watched the boy in the fourth row practice his eye contact, watched him fail at it and fail again and then, on the third try, hold it, and she thought about how much harder it was to do than it looked, and how nobody ever taught you.

She also thought about the slicer. When she'd been hired, the owner had walked her past the back counter and said, "You'll learn the slicer eventually, everyone does," and she'd said okay, because she was sixteen then and did not yet know what she knew now. She had never been put on it, but the schedule for next week had a blank at the slicer station, and the blank had a small pencil note beside it that said NEW HIRE.

At the Martindale stop, Dennys stood up, then paused in the aisle. "I'm going to say something to my manager," he said, not quite to either of them. "Not to get anyone in trouble. Just so he knows. Because maybe he doesn't."

"That's the right thing," Priya said.

"Maybe," Dennys said. "Or maybe I get Kenny's hours and Kenny hates me. See you." He shouldered his backpack and the doors folded open and the boreal light came in cold and level through the gap where he'd been standing.

The next afternoon Elijah sat across the desk from a girl with a clipboard and a name tag that said RUTH, and she asked him to describe a time he'd shown responsibility, and he told her about the lawns, slowly, holding her eyes the whole way through. She wrote something down. Then she looked up.

"Can I ask you a question instead of the other way around?" she said. "What would you do if someone asked you to do something at work that you thought might not be allowed?"

Elijah thought of Dennys standing in the aisle, undecided and then decided, and of the pencil note he would never know existed.

"I'd ask first," he said. "Before I said yes or no."

Ruth set down her pen and looked at him for a long moment, the way the bus driver had looked at the mirror.

"The slicer," she said. "It's the slicer, isn't it."

Antoine arrived at the book club nine minutes late, holding his copy of The Great Gatsby with a paper napkin folded inside it as a bookmark, because he had promised his sister Priya he would say something today and he had spent the whole bus ride trying to figure out what. The meeting was in the back room of the community library, where six folding chairs circled a table scattered with orange peels and a plate of biscotti nobody touched. Beatriz, who ran the club and was maybe sixty, had already begun.

"We're on chapter three," she said. "The party at Gatsby's. Antoine, sit, sit."

He sat. Priya had told him last week, over dishes, that reading was not the same as noticing, and that if he only ever read for plot he would go through books the way most people went through their lives, which was to say asleep. She had lent him a paperback called Ways of Reading, its margins already dense with her handwriting, and she had said, "Pick one lens. One is enough to start." He had picked the one about power and money, because the other one, the one about women, had seemed harder, like a language he hadn't learned the grammar for. He was not sure the two were really separate, and that not-sureness was exactly what he wanted to say today, if he could say it.

Beatriz read the passage aloud, the one where Nick, drunk for only the second time in his life, rides in a car with a man named Owl Eyes and a driver who loses a wheel. Then she said, "There's a line earlier in the chapter I want on the table. Everyone, page sixty-two." There was a rustle of pages. "In The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, the narrator Nick Carraway says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.'"

"Pompous," said Marcus, a college sophomore home for the summer.

"Or insecure," said his mother, Ruth.

Antoine found the line and read it twice. Then he raised his hand, felt ridiculous, and put it down. "Priya gave me this book," he said, and held up Ways of Reading. "It says you can read a novel by asking who has money and who doesn't, and what the money does to them. So I tried it. Gatsby throws these enormous parties, and almost nobody who eats his food and drinks his liquor even knows him. They come, they take, they leave. That's the whole economy of the chapter."

"Good," said Beatriz. "Go on."

"But here's the thing I keep hitting." He turned to the napkin-marked page. "Nick says he's one of the few honest people he's ever known. But he's not honest, or not only. He hides things. He keeps quiet about Tom and Myrtle. He lets Gatsby lie to his face and doesn't say a word. So when he says he's honest, what's actually happening?" He looked around the table. "Maybe the claim of honesty is itself part of the social climbing. He's marking distance from the liars while taking their hospitality."

There was a pause, the good kind, where everyone was actually thinking.

"That's subterfuge," Ruth said slowly. "The narrator's whole pose. It underpins the whole book, if you're right."

"And it's not just the money lens," Antoine said, surprising himself. "Because the women, Jordan, Daisy, Myrtle, they're all being moved around like property between the men, and Nick judges them for lying while he lies. So the two lenses, the money one and the gender one, they're not really two. They're the same question. Who gets to claim innocence, and who pays for everyone else's appetite." He heard his own voice and winced at it, the phrase everyone else's appetite sounding borrowed from Priya's margins, which it was.

"Or," said Marcus, "he's a guy writing a memoir, and memoirs are flattering by nature, and there's no system under it at all."

"That's the part I can't settle," Antoine admitted. "I can't tell if Nick is a product of the machine or if the machine is his excuse. Maybe both. I'd rather say both than pretend I know."

Beatriz smiled at him the way teachers smile when they've decided to say something sharp. "You know," she said, reaching for the biscotti and finally taking one, "I've watched you, Antoine, arguing for a whole hour against a narrator who insists he's honest. You've been more relentless than anyone at this table." She bit the biscotti. "Would you say you're one of the few honest people you've ever known?"
