The room went quiet. Antoine laughed, then stopped laughing, because everyone was still watching him.

"I'll think about it," he said, and closed the book on the napkin.

Andrew had promised Mr. Okafor, before winter break, that he could explain binary search by the first robotics meeting of January, and Mr. Okafor had said, "Good, because the judges at regionals like to ask," which was how Andrew found himself on a Thursday night in Dev's basement with a laptop, a plate of cold pizza, and Dev's little sister Priya, who was eleven and had appointed herself the audience.

"Okay," Andrew said. "Pretend I'm thinking of a number between one and a hundred."

"Fifty-seven," Priya said immediately.

"That's not how the game works." He slid the laptop toward her anyway. "You guess, I tell you higher or lower, and you try to use each answer to cut the problem down."

She guessed fifty. Higher. She guessed seventy-five. Lower. Sixty-two. Lower. Fifty-nine. Lower. Fifty-eight. Lower. Then fifty-seven, and she drummed her heels against the leg of the beanbag chair like she'd won a marathon.

"Seven guesses," Andrew said, writing it down. "Now do it the dumb way. Guess one, then two, then three." She got to fifty-seven with a face of increasing disgust, and he wrote that number beside the first. "That's linear search. You just walk through everything in order. It always works, even if the list is a mess. But if the list is sorted, you can keep cutting it in half, and half again, and the guesses barely grow even when the numbers get huge." He showed her the two totals side by side, seven and fifty-seven, and for a hundred items it hardly mattered, but then he typed a number with a lot of zeros into a scratch file and watched her do the arithmetic.

"You're telling me a million items takes only twenty guesses." Dev said it from the couch, where he had been half-watching and half-dismantling a servo. "That's ridiculous."

"That's the point. It beats linear search because every comparison throws away half of what's left instead of one item. You have to pay for it, though. The list has to be sorted, and keeping it sorted costs you whenever you insert." Andrew pulled up his actual assignment, the Java file with the loop in it, and turned the laptop so both of them could see. The basement was finished on one side and bare cinder block on the other, the boreal corner where the furnace lived and where nobody put a rug, and Dev's dad kept the thermostat set to whatever temperature preserved the pipes and nothing else, so they had all claimed the couch-side.

"Who wrote Java, anyway?" Priya asked, because she was eleven and asked things like that. "Was it a computer?"

"James Gosling," Andrew said, and then, because he wasn't sure and didn't want to be sure and wrong, "hold on." He looked it up. Sun Microsystems, 1995. He sat back. "It's older than me. It's older than both of us."

Dev pointed a screwdriver at him. "You're coding in something older than you are and you didn't know."

"I code in C at school too, and that's from the seventies, I just never thought about Java being, like, a person's project that got released the year my parents got married." Andrew said it lightly, but something about the fact had snagged him. He had imagined languages arriving fully formed, the way the periodic table arrives, and instead someone named James had sat somewhere, possibly in a basement not unlike this one, and typed the first version of the thing that was now under his hands.

Priya wanted to see the search run, so he compiled it, and the printout of the probed indices scrolled past, then another with a missing target scrolling past to the last few, each one a clean halving. Priya watched the numbers collapse toward each other, ten million narrowing to five million narrowing to a single slot, and pronounced it mesmerizing, which made Dev laugh into his pizza. Andrew had to admit she wasn't wrong. There was something about the way the loop closed in, patient and inevitable, that he could watch longer than was reasonable.

Then he broke it. He changed less than to greater-than, one character, and ran it again, and the loop walked confidently in the wrong direction, probing down into the low end while the target sat up high, and returned not-found for a number that was plainly sitting in the array. "See, this is the part judges care about," he said, mostly to himself. "The idea is easy. The off-by-one and the flipped comparison, that's where it dies." He fixed it, broke it a different way, let the bounds cross so mid landed outside the list and the whole thing threw an exception Priya found even funnier than the wrong answer.

"Can you actually explain it, though?" Dev said. "Like out loud, to a person, not to a screen. You explained it to Priya by cheating. She's smart."

"I did not cheat."

"You used a game. Judges aren't eleven."

Andrew frowned at that, because it was fair. The number game was honest but it smuggled the idea in through fun, and he needed to know whether he could carry the idea without the smuggler. He stood up, faced the furnace end of the basement as if it were a judge's table, and talked: a sorted array, a low index, a high index, a middle, a comparison that discards half the remaining range, and a loop condition that stops when the range is empty. His voice did something weird on the second sentence, too fast, and he heard himself saying "efficiency" three times in a row like a word he was hiding behind.

"Slower," Dev said. "Also you said efficiency like it owes you money."

"There's a pragmatics to this, okay, how you say it matters as much as what you say." Andrew started over, slower, and this time when he got to why binary beat linear, he pointed at the two numbers still written on the napkin, seven and fifty-seven, and said "the gap only gets worse from there," and Priya, from the beanbag, whispered "million items, twenty guesses," at exactly the right moment, and Andrew laughed and said, "Right, exactly that," and felt the explanation click into place somewhere behind his sternum, or at least click into place enough, because he still wasn't sure he'd say it the same way twice, or that a judge would ask it the way he expected, or that the version in his head wouldn't shed some important clause under pressure. He decided he could live with that. He wrote James Gosling and 1995 on the napkin under the two numbers, for no reason he could defend, and folded all of it into his pocket.

"Again," Dev said, tossing him the screwdriver to hold like a microphone. "From the top, robot boy."

Andrew took it, squared his shoulders toward the furnace, and said, "A sorted array, a low index, a high index."

Kaylee arrived at Mr. Okafor's studio with the Mozart photocopied and no marks on it yet, which he noticed immediately, because he picked up the sheets, fanned them, and set them back down on the music stand as if weighing a fish.

"Exposition, development, recapitulation," he said. "Mark them by Thursday. I am not going to tell you where they are." He wanted her ready for the theory placement exam in September, and he had a way of framing every lesson as a dare, which Kaylee half resented and half relied on.

She played through the first movement of the sonata once, slowly, and put a pencil line where she thought the exposition ended. Then she erased it. Then she drew it two bars later and sat looking at it like it might confess something. The trouble was that the music kept seeming to end and then refusing to. Phrases closed themselves neatly and new ones opened in the same breath, and she could not tell which closure was the real one and which was just a way of pausing.

That evening she went to the community center, where her friend Jonah was rehearsing for the open mic on Friday. His little brother Theo, who was eleven and had written a melody on the center's ancient keyboard, played it for them twice. It wandered up, wandered down, and stopped on a note that left everyone's chest slightly tight.

"It doesn't sound finished," Theo said.

Jonah, who wanted his own set to go well and had limited patience for his brother's problems, said, "It sounds fine, Theo, it's just short." But Kaylee had been staring at Theo's hands, and she remembered the last two chords he had played. She asked him to play just the ending again, and then she asked him what note the melody was sitting on.

"It's on the sixth," Theo said. "I like the sixth."

"Try going down to the fifth first. Underneath. Then land where home is." She couldn't say it in proper terms, but she hummed what she meant, and when Theo played it, the last phrase settled, and Theo's face changed, and Jonah, from across the room, said, "Oh, that's finished, that's actually finished."

On the bus home Kaylee thought about it without meaning to. The chords Theo had played at the end, the fifth and then the home note, were the same thing she'd been circling with her pencil all afternoon. She looked it up on her phone in the narrow light, holding the fact up against the memory of Theo's hands: an authentic cadence, a V chord moving to the I chord, sounds final, which is why melodies usually end their last phrase with it. She did not understand why the V chord wanted the I chord, only that it did, the way water wants level, and she let the fact sit in her overnight, the way her mother said she metabolized new information, slowly and with snacks.

At Thursday's lesson she had marked the exposition where the whole thing came to a full stop in the new key, the V moving to a I that was final but in the wrong place, like a door locked shut in a stranger's house. The development she had marked at the point where everything went unstable, sequences tumbling through keys with no home at all. And the recapitulation she had marked where the opening theme returned, and this time, at the end, everything cadenced in the right key, V to I, the door locked in her own house, and the movement was over, actually over.

Mr. Okafor went through her markings with a red pen and changed one bar line, then changed it back. "You marked by feeling," he said. "Not by logos. You cannot tell me why the exposition ends there."

"No," Kaylee said. "I can tell you what it does. Theo's melody did the same thing, and it wasn't finished until the end. I don't know why the chords work. I just know when they're lying about being done."

Mr. Okafor considered this, tapping the red pen against the Mozart. "Half my college students can't say that much. All right. Next week, the second movement, and I want you to tell me where it lies."

Kaylee stuffed the photocopied sheets into her backpack, sedimentary now with erased lines and redrawn ones, layers of her own wrong guesses pressed under the right ones. At the door she paused.

"Can I bring a recording Friday? Theo's playing his melody at the open mic. It ends properly now, and he wants someone to hear it who knows why."

The library on Miller Street kept its computer lab in the basement, below the geology shelves, and Mathis had chosen the terminal in the corner because its screen faced the wall. He was sixteen and had told his mother he was going to look at colleges. This was not entirely a lie. He was looking at what colleges looked for, and one of the things they looked for, according to three different forums he'd read that week, was a portfolio. Two programs, at least, that did something. He had nine days before the application deadline for the summer intensive, and so far he had a file called BankAccount.java that would not compile and a notebook filling up with crossed-out ideas.

The plan was simple enough that he could say it out loud without embarrassment: a class that held a name and a balance, kept its fields private, and gave the rest of the world getters, polite little doors into the data. His older cousin Anselm, who did this for a living in another city, had sketched the shape of it on a napkin at Thanksgiving. Private fields, getters, a constructor to set things up. Anselm had said the word "constructor" and then gotten pulled away by pie, and Mathis had been left with the napkin and the word and no example.

He typed for an hour. The lab smelled like the cleaning solvent the janitor used, and the boy two terminals over was watching videos with his headphones turned up loud enough that Mathis could hear the percussion through them. At four o'clock a girl from his chemistry class, Dara, came down the stairs with a stack of books about volcanoes, settled at the table behind him, and did not look at his screen. He was grateful and also aware of her there, the way you're aware of the clock during an exam.

The problem arrived quietly. He wrote his constructor, wrote his getters, wrote a test in another file that created an account and printed the balance. Nothing printed. Or rather, something printed, but not what he'd written in the constructor. The balance came out as zero. The name came out as null, which the program displayed with a kind of blank indifference, as if the account belonged to no one and had never belonged to anyone. He checked the test. He checked the class. He put his notebook flat on the desk and copied both files onto it by hand, side by side, as though the error might be visible on paper the way it wasn't visible in the glare of the monitor. Dara looked over once, saw pages of words like public and static, and went back to her igneous rocks, the fused and glassy kinds that form when magma cools too fast to crystallize.

He tried things. He moved the test code. He renamed a variable. He closed the file and opened it again, which he knew was superstition but performed anyway, the way you restart a machine that isn't broken to reassure yourself that it could have been. The library's heat clicked on with a sound like a struck pipe. Outside the narrow window at street level, boots went by on the sidewalk, two pairs, unhurried.

It was Dara who found it, or half found it. She had come over to ask if he had a pen, and she stood behind his chair, and her eyes went where eyes go, to the middle of the screen. "Why does that one say void?" she asked. "None of the others do."

He looked where she was looking. The line was his constructor, the one that was supposed to set the name and the balance. In front of it, small and ordinary and fatal, he had typed void. He had done it because every other method in his files had void in front of it, and because his hands had learned the rhythm, and because nothing had told him otherwise. Anselm's napkin, he realized now, showed a constructor with no return type at all. He had assumed the napkin was sloppy, a cousin's shorthand. He found the napkin in the front pocket of his backpack, soft from handling, and smoothed it on the desk beside the keyboard. There it was. No void. No int, no String, nothing where a return type would go.

He didn't delete the word immediately. He sat with his finger over the backspace key and thought about what he had actually been doing all afternoon, which was carrying a rule from one place into another where it didn't apply. Then he erased the void, letter by letter, v-o-i-d, and ran the test.

The output appeared at the bottom of the screen, and it was exactly what he had typed into the constructor, the name and the balance, arriving in the world at last. Dara had leaned in without his noticing. "So that word was the whole problem?"

"Java's like that," he said. "Everything's exactly what it says, nothing more." He copied the corrected file to his flash drive, then, after a moment's thought, copied the broken version too, and titled it mistake.java, and the cursor blinked at the end of the name while he decided whether to keep it.

Alexa had told everyone she was only doing this for the grade, which was true except for the part where it wasn't. The Saturday halaqa at the mosque had opened its floor to questions, and a boy from the physics department, maybe nineteen, raised his hand and asked how the scholars could possibly rule on online banking when the Quran was revealed fourteen centuries before anyone held a phone. Alexa, sitting in the back with her notebook, thought: there is my debate topic, handed to me like a gift. She was scheduled to argue against Danish next week, in the community hall after Maghrib, on whether the prohibition on riba still applied to modern finance, and until this moment she had been planning to pad her case with statistics she did not quite trust.

Her grandfather, she remembered, used to transcribe verses from the Quran into a ledger he kept beside his prayer mat, copying slowly in blue ink because he said his hand had to slow down to the speed of his understanding. She had been eleven the summer she watched him do it, in a house that smelled of cardamom and newspaper. When she asked why he didn't just print the page, he laughed and said the printing was for reading, the copying was for thinking. She had thought that was a grandiose thing to say about a notebook. She thought about it now anyway.

The imam did not answer the physics boy directly. He said, "Sister Farida addressed this last year," and turned to a woman in a grey hijab near the window, and Alexa felt something in her chest go hot and small, because she had been about to raise her own hand, and now someone else would get her answer.

Sister Farida stood. She was a patent lawyer, Alexa knew, the kind of person who said "with respect" before disagreeing with you. "Online banking, cryonics, esports contracts," she said, ticking them off. "The texts don't directly answer these. That's precisely what ijtihad is for." Alexa wrote the word down, then underlined it, then felt foolish for underlining it.

Afterward she followed Sister Farida to the shoe racks near the entrance, where the whole conversation had to happen over the sound of coat zippers and someone's toddler negotiating for a biscuit. "Sorry," Alexa said, "the word you used. Could you spell it?" She felt her face doing the thing it did when she wanted to seem casual and did not succeed. Sister Farida spelled it, then said, "I can't teach it to you in five minutes. A qualified scholar spends years before anyone lets them exercise that kind of independent reasoning. The Quran, the hadith, the whole tradition, and then judgment." Alexa asked what happened if the scholar got it wrong, and Sister Farida smiled in a way that Alexa could not decode. "Then two qualified scholars disagree, and you choose whom to follow. It's not a plebiscite, Alexa. You don't vote on it." She put on her shoes and left before Alexa could ask how she had known her name.

In the library the next afternoon, Alexa found the shelf behind the children's section where the mosque kept its older books, the ones with cracked spines that nobody borrowed. She pulled down a volume on Islamic jurisprudence, sat on the carpet between the shelves, and read the relevant chapter twice with her finger under the line. Independent reasoning, exercised by a qualified scholar, applying the Quran and hadith to questions the texts do not directly answer. It was exactly what Sister Farida had said, which should have been satisfying. Instead she copied the definition into her notebook in blue ink, slowly, and understood for the first time why her grandfather had needed the copying and not the printing. She also understood, with a colder clarity, that she was not a qualified scholar, that Danish was not either, and that the debate she had been framing as a contest of evidence was actually a contest of borrowed authorities. Her opening paragraph, the one with the statistics, now looked to her like a costume.

The imam noticed the girl still in the library at four o'clock, cross-legged on the carpet with three books open around her, and recognized her as the one who had hovered at the shoe racks on Saturday looking wounded when Sister Farida had answered the banking question first. He had seen that expression before, on students who mistook being first for being right. He almost went over to tell her that the question she was chasing was older than she was, that he had wrestled with riba and modern finance for twenty years and still changed his mind every Ramadan. But she was writing something in blue ink, very slowly, and he had learned when a person was copying for thinking. He took his keys and locked the front door from the outside, leaving through the side entrance, and did not tell her the hall closed at four.

The debate, when it came, went nothing like her opening paragraph. Danish stood up with his graphs and his confident voice and called the prohibition an artifact of a barter economy, and Alexa stood up and heard herself say, "That's not actually a religious argument, that's a history argument wearing one." She laid out the texts on interest, then laid out ijtihad, then said the sentence she had practiced against her bedroom wall: "The honest answer is that applying a seventh-century text to a credit card is exactly the work the tradition built a whole discipline for, and I'm not qualified to do it, and neither is he, and the fact that we're up here anyway is a flaw in this format, not a proof of anything." There was a silence, and then Mrs. Haddad, who taught the Sunday school, started laughing, and after her the whole hall did, not unkindly.

She won on the scorecards, which the judges handed to her afterward with congratulations she did not want. Sister Farida had come, sitting in the last row, and Alexa found her by the tea urn afterward. "You gave away the win," Alexa said. "You told them you weren't qualified." Sister Farida poured two cups and handed one over. "I told them the truth and let them decide," she said. Alexa looked at the cup, at the steam, at the last rows of chairs being stacked by volunteers, and thought of the plebiscite line, and of her grandfather's ledger, and of the blank half page still left in her notebook. "There's more I got wrong," she said. "Can I read you my notes?"

The math club met on Thursdays in the back corner of the school library, at the two tables nearest the window where the afternoon light came in flat and gold across the scratched wood. Keira arrived early, as she usually did, and spread out her binder, the problem set from Tuesday still unfinished. The problem asked for the area enclosed between a line and a parabola, and she had gotten an answer she did not believe, because it was negative, and an area, she was fairly sure, could not be.

"I got forty-one over six," said Devon, dropping into the chair across from her and sliding his notebook over so she could see. His work was neat, almost architectural, each step ruled off from the next with a straight edge.

"I got the same number," Keira said. "Negative forty-one over six."

Devon frowned at her page, then at his. Priya came over from the shelves with a book on typography she had been carrying around for a week, set it down, and looked at both solutions. "You integrated the same things," she said. "Look. Same functions, same limits. He did parabola minus line. You did line minus parabola."

"Then which one is the area?" Keira asked. Nobody answered right away. Somewhere near the circulation desk a scanner beeped, twice, and the librarian murmured something to a freshman about a late fee, a small disbursement of quarters counted out onto the counter. Keira listened to the coins without looking up, her pencil resting on the margin where she had been doodling the two curves.

She had drawn them before she ever computed anything; that was how she liked to start, sketch first, numbers second. On her page the line cut through the parabola, and between the two crossing points the parabola rode above the line, a closed sliver of shaded region, thin at the ends and fat in the middle. She shaded it lightly with the side of her pencil, then held the page up so the others could see. "The parabola's the upper one," she said. "The whole way across, between where they cross. It's on top."

"So the area is the integral of the upper function minus the lower function," Priya said slowly, reading the picture as much as the symbols. "Over the interval where they're ordered that way. Parabola minus line. That's Devon's."

Keira looked at her own negative answer, then at Devon's positive one, and felt the two halves of her brain settle into their usual argument. The part of her that trusted procedure wanted a rule she could apply blindly, write once in her notes and never question: bigger minus smaller, done. The part of her that trusted the picture distrusted any rule that worked without looking, because a parabola and a line could cross again somewhere outside the interval, could trade places, and then a single memorized subtraction would fail her. The rule was not really about parabolas or lines at all, she realized. It was about which function was above which, over a specific stretch.

"Try it backwards," she said to Devon. "Draw your curves first. Don't compute anything, just draw."

Devon, who never drew anything if he could avoid it, took out a fresh sheet and sketched the parabola opening upward, then the line slicing through it. He shaded the sliver between the crossing points, his hand less certain than hers but the shape unmistakable. "It's the same picture," he said, sounding almost betrayed by his own arithmetic. "I just got lucky with the order."

"Not lucky," Priya said. "You did upper minus lower. You just didn't check that it was upper."

Keira tried a second problem, one she invented on the spot, where the line rode above a downward-opening parabola, and made herself find which was upper before she touched a single integral. Then a third where the two curves crossed inside her interval, just to see what would break, and something did break, the shaded region flipping sides halfway through, and she sat with that for a moment, her pencil still, the inchoate shape of a harder idea forming at the edge of her attention. She would have to split the interval, she thought, at the crossing point, and handle each piece separately. She was not sure yet. She wrote a question mark beside it instead of an answer.

She thought about how easily she could have imputed the difference between her answer and Devon's to carelessness, hers or his, some slipped sign or dropped term, and gone on to the next problem knowing nothing. Instead the wrongness had been the whole lesson. The sign had been telling her something true: that she had measured the region from underneath.

"Forty-one over six," she said, and wrote it at the bottom of the page with the units, square units, in small letters after the fraction. Then she turned the page over, drew two new curves crossing twice, and slid the sheet across the table to Devon. "Your turn. Don't compute yet. Shade it."

The restaurant smelled like burnt coffee and maple syrup, a combination Samuel would later associate with the entire summer he turned sixteen. He sat at the corner table of the Ridgeview Diner with his hands folded, the way his mother had told him to, while the manager, a reticent man named Delgado who spoke mostly in short declarative sentences, looked over his one-page application.

"You're sixteen," Delgado said. It wasn't a question, so Samuel didn't answer it. "Weekends, bussing tables, clearing plates, restocking. Seven twenty-five an hour." He said the number the way he said everything, flat, as though it had been posted on the wall for years, which in a sense it had.

Samuel had prepared a few things to say, mostly about his work ethic, but the number caught him off guard. It sounded small. It sounded like the price of two and a half milkshakes at the restaurant he was sitting in. He said yes anyway, because a job was a job, and because his friend Marcus had been teasing him for weeks about being the last of their group without one.

That evening Marcus came over, and they sat on the porch steps while the sprinklers hissed across the lawn. Marcus had started two weeks earlier at a burger place one town over, and he was still in the flush of it, showing Samuel his first paycheck like a winning lottery ticket. Then he paused, squinting at it. "Wait. Yours will be seven twenty-five? I make more than that. Like, more per hour."

"How much more?" Samuel asked.

"Enough that it's weird. We do the same stuff. You're not worse at carrying plates than I am at carrying trays." Marcus turned the stub over as though the explanation might be printed on the back. "It's not like you're worse at anything."

Samuel thought of his geometry teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, who had a habit of saying that before you solve a problem you have to agree on what kind of problem it is. Some things were exercises, some were theorems, and some were what he called lemmas, smaller results you needed first, the scaffolding under the real proof. Samuel had liked that idea, the notion that you could be honest about not yet knowing something, that uncertainty was a station you could work from rather than a failure.

He looked it up on his phone while Marcus ate the last of the pretzels. The federal minimum wage was $7.25 an hour, and it had been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, which meant it had been the same number since Samuel was in preschool. But many states and cities set a higher minimum, and Marcus's burger place sat just across the state line, in a state that had done exactly that. Samuel read the dates twice. He thought about 2009, about how his parents talked about that year, and about how a number could sit still for so long while everything around it moved.

"So it's not the boss being cheap," Marcus said, leaning over to see the screen. "It's the law. Different law here."

"Here it's the federal one. There it's the state one." Samuel turned the phone off and set it face down on the step, the way Mr. Okonkwo did when he wanted a class to think instead of read.

Marcus left after that, satisfied, but Samuel stayed on the steps until the sprinklers shut off. He found himself weighing something he couldn't quite name. Part of him thought he should quit before he started and apply across the line, where the same hours would add up to more, and part of him thought that was a cowardly way to think about the diner, about Delgado, about the town he'd grown up in. His grandfather had worked at the hardware store on Miller Road for forty-one years and had never once, as far as Samuel knew, compared his pay to anyone else's. Samuel admired that and also suspected it was a kind of surrender, a willingness to let habit subjugate ambition and call the result loyalty. He could not decide which interpretation was fair, or whether fairness had anything to do with it.

The next morning, a Saturday, he took the bus to the diner for his first shift. Delgado handed him a tan apron and a rag and pointed at table eleven, where a family of five had just left a wreckage of napkins and half-eaten pancakes. Samuel tied the apron, gathered the plates with the careful stacking motion he'd practiced in his mirror at home, and carried them toward the kitchen. Behind him he heard Delgado say, without looking up from the register, "Bus fourteen next. And smile at the door when you pass it."

Samuel adjusted his grip on the plates, caught his own reflection in the chrome panel by the pass-through window, and smiled.

The test streaks on parchment adumbrated the finished bars Hannah hoped for, faint hints of gloss that would either deepen into shine or dull into bloom, and she could not stop checking them against the side of the tray. Behind the folding table at the farmers' market, under a canopy the color of dry lavender, she held the bowl of melted chocolate at thirty-one degrees and waited the way Dara had taught her, which was to say not passively but with attention, watching for the moment the surface stopped looking wet and started looking alive.

"You're hovering," Dara said. She was restocking the truffle case and did not look up. "Hovering changes nothing. Either you seeded enough stable crystals or you didn't."

Hannah stirred anyway, slow figure eights, because her hands wanted something to do. She had been coming to this stall since the first Saturday in June, when she'd admitted to herself that the summer her mother had imagined, a hospital volunteering schedule and a head start on prerequisites, was not the summer she wanted at all. Dara had hired her on the condition that she learn tempering before she was allowed near a mold. "Snap is honesty," Dara had told her. "A bar that snaps clean tells you someone paid attention. A bendy bar tells you they didn't."

Theo appeared at four minutes to ten, before the market officially opened, carrying a cooler that looked older than either of them. He set it on the ground by the honey stall next door, where the keeper was arranging jars of a wildflower strain she described, to anyone who paused, as autochthonous to the valley, native to these hills and nowhere else. "Salvage operation," Theo said, lifting the cooler lid to show Hannah a brick of frozen soup wrapped in a grocery bag. "From the dorm kitchen. Everything got tossed at move-out, so I took it. Been in the freezer at my uncle's all month."

"Your uncle's freezer."

"Deep freeze. The big chest kind." He looked proud of this, the way he used to look proud of finishing a problem set an hour before it was due. "I figured I'd thaw it tonight and we'd eat it before my shift. Freezing kills everything anyway, right? It's like sterilizing."

Hannah kept stirring. She had spent the winter reading whatever she could find about food, first out of guilt about abandoning the medical track and then out of something that had stopped being guilt, and one of the things she'd read had stuck with her the way certain facts do, complete and portable, a stone in the pocket. "It doesn't kill them," she said. "Freezing food at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, which is zero Fahrenheit, stops bacteria from growing, but it doesn't kill most of them. Thawed food can spoil again."

"So it's fine and then it's not fine."

"It was never fine. It was paused." She said it and heard, with a small internal wince, how much it sounded like her mother, who had said a version of it about her deferral, about the year Hannah wanted to take before committing to anything. Everything is paused, nothing is decided, and meanwhile time spoils. Hannah had argued then that deciding too fast was its own kind of failure, that a choice made under pressure was a snapshot, not a portrait. She still believed it. She also, at ten in the morning at a folding table, with soup thawing in a cooler a meter away, felt the pull of the opposing claim, and could not say which one was truer.

Theo squatted by the cooler, hand resting on the lid. In his first-year philosophy seminar he had discovered nihilism and worn it like a jacket for about six weeks, claiming nothing mattered, not grades, not the deadening logistics of adulthood his father laid out for him over dinner. Then he'd spent a spring weekend caring for a friend's sourdough starter and quietly stopped making the claim. He looked at the soup the way he'd once looked at the starter. "The move-out fridge was unplugged for a day before I got there," he said. "Maybe two."

"Then don't eat it."

"It smells okay."

"You can't smell okay. Okay is invisible." She tapped the side of her bowl. The chocolate had thickened to the right working consistency, and Dara was watching now over the top of the truffle case, saying nothing, which Hannah understood as permission or as a test, probably both. She spooned a cap of chocolate onto parchment and watched it set in the breeze coming off the river. When she peeled it up and snapped it in half, the sound was clean, a bright small crack, and the broken edges showed a surface with a depth to it, like the shell of something that had decided what it was. Tempered. She held out the two halves, one to Theo and one to the honey keeper, who took hers with a nod of professional respect.

"It's the crystals," Hannah said, mostly to Theo, though she was careful not to lecture. "You have to get the right ones to form, and then they recruit the rest. It's order spreading through the whole batch." She was aware that she was talking about more than chocolate and also that she did not want to say so out loud, because saying so would make it a speech, and some things survive being said and some things don't, and she didn't yet know which kind of thing this was.

Theo ate his half slowly, which for Theo was remarkable. Then he closed the cooler, carried it past the compost bins near the port-a-johns, and came back with empty hands and the grocery bag gone. He stood at the end of the table while the ten o'clock bell rang and the first customers came down the row, a woman with a canvas bag already asking about the dark bars, and Hannah reached for a sheet of molds, and Theo picked up the tasting knife without being asked and began slicing samples, laying them out in a fan.

The restaurant smelled of burnt coffee and onions, and Zoe had chosen it because it was loud enough that no one would listen to her stumble through Portuguese. She spread the newspaper on the table between two water glasses, smoothing the fold flat with the heel of her hand. In forty minutes she would call her placement examiner, read a short article aloud, and summarize it in her own words. If she passed, she could register for the intermediate seminar in the spring instead of spending another semester in a room where they conjugated verbs she had already conquered in middle school.

The article was three paragraphs about a city council vote on bike lanes. Three paragraphs, and she was still on the first sentence, dragging her finger under each word like someone crossing a river stone by stone. "Depois," she read, "de, das, das discussões." She said it again, slower, as though the sentence might pity her and rearrange itself. The waitress came by twice. The second time she refilled the water and said, "You're doing homework on a Friday night," not unkindly, and Zoe said, "Something like that," and put her palm over the page so it wouldn't look like homework.

The problem was not the vocabulary. She could look up words; her phone was right there. The problem was time. When she read this way, every sentence cost her a minute, and by the time she reached the end she had already forgotten the beginning. She had tried to summarize the article twice on the ride over, and both times she had produced a list of fragments, like the turbid water at the bottom of a glass: when the vote happened, that a man named something had objected, that there was a number, three hundred or three thousand, she honestly could not have said which.

At the next booth, two college-aged guys were arguing about a study guide. "You skipped the whole chapter," one said. The other held up his highlighter like a piece of evidence. "I wasn't reading it, I was scanning it. Scanning is when you hunt for one detail, like a name or a number. I just needed the date." His friend rolled his eyes. "That's why you missed the point. Skimming gets you the general idea, fast. You skipped everything that mattered." Zoe's hand stopped moving over her page.

She turned the words over while the waitress set down a plate of fries she had ordered to justify the table. Skimming, reading quickly for the general idea. Scanning, hunting through the text for one specific detail. All semester she had been doing neither; she had been reading like a defendant signing a contract, terrified of missing a clause. But the examiner was not going to quiz her on clause eleven. The examiner wanted to know what the article was about.

She flipped the newspaper over, then back, as though the page itself were responsible for her method. Then she gave herself one pass, fast, no dictionary, letting the unfamiliar words blur past like telephone poles from a car window. Her eyes snagged on numbers, on the capital letters of names, on words she recognized: votação, ciclovias, orçamento. Vote, bike lanes, budget. When she reached the end she was breathing hard, which was ridiculous, because she was sitting in a restaurant eating fries. Still, something about the speed exhilarated her, the way letting go of the handlebars had when she was nine, the ground rushing by under a self she hadn't known she could trust.

Second pass. This time she scanned, deliberately, hunting for the one detail she had already forgotten, the figure that kept sliding between three hundred and three thousand. Her eyes moved in a pattern, rejecting whole lines, snagging only where a numeral stood out against the type. There it was: três mil, three thousand, the cost in some currency she would have to fudge as "the budget amount" if asked. She looked up at the ceiling and laughed once, quietly. She had spent half an hour on paragraph one and four minutes on the whole article.

The waitress collected the ketchup and said, "Whatever that was, it looked like a win." Zoe, warmed and reckless, explained: a test, a phone call, a summary in a language she had been studying for six years and still could not read like a normal person. The waitress said her nephew was bilingual, said it like a bromide, the kind of comforting thing people say about other people's struggles, and Zoe nodded and thanked her and privately disagreed. Bilingual was a place she had not arrived at. She was, at best, a competent tourist with a decent map.

At 7:40 she dialed. A recorded voice gave instructions in Portuguese, and she understood them, which felt like being handed a gift she hadn't paid for. She read the article aloud, tripping only twice, and then the examiner asked her to summarize it in her own words. Zoe heard herself say that the council had approved new bike lanes after a long debate, that a councilman had opposed the cost, and that the project would take a share of the annual budget, roughly three thousand, though she hedged on the unit and the examiner did not press.

There was a pause on the line, long enough that Zoe's stomach dropped. Then the voice said, in careful, accented English, "Your reading is very precise. Almost too precise. You read like someone who is afraid of the words. Next time, read like someone who is curious about them."

Zoe said she would. She hung up, sat back, and pushed the newspaper to the edge of the table. After four minutes of skimming she could say what the article meant; after forty minutes of crawling she could only recite it. So which one had she failed at, exactly, and which one counted? She picked up a cold fry, wrote the words "skimming" and "scanning" on the napkin so she wouldn't lose them, and then, hearing herself, laughed and turned the napkin over. "It's not a cheat sheet," she told the empty booth. "It's just the rules of the road."

She left the napkin on the table, face up, for the waitress to clear or the next Friday-night student to find.

Mrs. Okafor's studio smelled of rosin and the lemon polish she applied to her piano bench every Friday, as though preparing it for surgery. Juliette spread the score of Mozart's K. 332 across the music stand, a photocopy already bruised with three colors of pencil, none of which she trusted anymore.

"Again," said Mrs. Okafor, and played the opening eight bars. "Tell me where your first theme ends."

Juliette put her finger on the page and then took it off, as if the paper had asked for an acquittal she could not grant. "Measure twelve. Or nineteen. It keeps depending on which side I argue from."

"You sound pugnacious about it."

"I sound like a lawyer, is what I sound like." She leaned closer to the staves. The trouble was that Mozart, being Mozart, refused to stop singing. The tune at the beginning spilled onward so graciously that she could not point to the bar where it finished being itself and started being something else, and her markings kept sliding around like furniture in a dream.

Mrs. Okafor folded her hands. "Instead of hunting the end of the tune, hunt the change of key. In the exposition there's a passage that moves you from the home key to the second key. It's called the bridge."

Juliette wrote bridge? in the margin and played from measure twelve with her right hand alone, following the harmony under her left. Somewhere around measure twenty-two the music stopped being tuneful and got busy, scales and figures hurrying somewhere, and then, with a small click she could feel in her teeth, the notes settled into a new key. She sat back. "There. That's where it modulates. So the busier stuff before it, that's the bridge, which means the first theme has to end before the bridge starts, which means it was measure nineteen all along and my blue pencil was right and my red pencil owes my blue pencil an apology."

"Your pencils have a legal system now?"

"They've acclimated to the firm. It's very hierarchical."

They marked the exposition together after that, second theme bracketed in green, codetta in a color Juliette improvised by scribbling blue over red, which produced something like a bruise. When she got to the development, though, she slowed down. The development did what it wanted. It took her bridge material, her busy un-tuneful scales, and made them the main event, tumbling through keys she could not name, and she thought: so the passage that merely carries you from here to there becomes the whole conversation elsewhere. She did not say this out loud, because Mrs. Okafor had a policy about epiphanies announced in lesson time, but she marked a question mark next to it.

"The recapitulation," said Mrs. Okafor, "you'll find on your own for Thursday. And bring the Beethoven, the little one, op. 49."

"Is that a test?"

"It's a present. It's easier."

Juliette began gathering her pencils, and then stopped, because she had noticed something she had been noticing for three weeks and refusing to examine: Mrs. Okafor kept saying Thursday, and giving her extra repertoire, and mentioning, in the offhand voice of someone mentioning weather, that the conservatory audition deadline was in November. Juliette had said, at Christmas, in front of her mother, that she was going to study biology and keep the piano for herself, for pleasure, ungraded. Mrs. Okafor had said "of course." Now here was Beethoven arriving like a subpoena.

"Mrs. Okafor. Opus 49. The audition deadline."

"Mm," said Mrs. Okafor, polishing the fallboard with her sleeve, an elaborate innocence. "Lovly piece, opus 49."

"You think I should audition."

"I think you found the bridge in twenty minutes after hunting the theme's ending for a week. You find things. That's all I think." She closed the piano lid. "Whether you want to be found is a separate question, and not mine."

Juliette looked down at her score, at the bruise-colored codetta, at her question mark in the development. She was good at questions with answers, at expositions that modulated where the book said they would; what she was not good at yet was deciding things that stayed decided. On the empty staff paper beneath the last system she wrote, in very small letters, biology?, and beneath it, also small, november, and then, because the moment seemed to require honesty, she drew a fermata over both of them, a hold, unmeasured.

She closed the score. "For Thursday, then. The Beethoven."

"And the recapitulation."

"And the recapitulation," said Juliette, and at the door she turned back and pointed her blue pencil at the piano like a small pugnacious baton. "If the bridge shows up in the Beethoven disguised as a second theme, I'm calling you about it."

"I'd expect nothing less," said Mrs. Okafor, and lifted the lid again.

The fourth floor vending machine took Sadie's dollar and gave nothing back, which felt like the whole week in miniature. She had spent Tuesday in Mr. Okafor's seminar arguing about a pesticide called Kelvar with a boy named Dmitri, and she was still losing the argument in her head three days later, on the teal upholstered chair outside room 412, where she was supposed to be delivering a water pitcher.

Dmitri had leaned back and said the burden of proof lay with the people claiming harm, that you waited for evidence before you banned something, because bans cost jobs. Sadie had wanted to argue and found she couldn't, not cleanly, not the way she could argue about things she'd actually read. So she'd gone home and typed serious irreversible damage into the library search bar at midnight, and the phrase had surfaced a document she'd never heard of, and now she had it screenshotted on her phone like a stone in her pocket.

The water pitcher was for Mr. Ahmadi, who had a liver thing nobody on the floor said out loud and a daughter named Layla who came every evening at six with a canvas bag of hospital-inappropriate food. Sadie had learned the shift's geography in three weeks: which nurses wanted silence, which families wanted talking, which rooms you knocked on twice and which you passed quickly. The Ahmadi room was a talking room. Layla was maybe twenty-five, worked in county public health, and treated Sadie like a person rather than a polo shirt.

"You look like you're studying for something," Layla said today, catching her refilling the pitcher. "Or against something."

"A debate I already lost." Sadie set the pitcher down. "There's this pesticide they want to use near the river, and I said we should hold off, and this guy said, wait for proof it actually hurts people. And I didn't have an answer. I had a feeling and no answer."

Mr. Ahmadi turned his head toward the window. Layla smiled at him, then back at Sadie. "My whole job is that argument. Do you know the Rio Declaration?"

Sadie shook her head, feeling the screenshot grow warm in her pocket.

"Nineteen ninety-two, big UN environment meeting. Principle fifteen." Layla pulled a tab on her coffee lid, unhurried. "It says where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures. People call it the precautionary principle."

"That's a mouthful."

"It's a leash," Layla said. "It keeps 'we're not sure yet' from becoming 'never.'"

Sadie took out her phone and found the screenshot and held it up, and Layla laughed, short and surprised, and said, "You already had it. Why are you losing to this boy?"

Because, Sadie admitted, it felt like the principle cut both ways, and she said so, pulling the visitor chair closer. If you acted without certainty, you could ruin livelihoods over nothing; if you waited, you ruined a river you couldn't un-ruin. Irreversible was doing a lot of work in that sentence, and so was cost-effective, and she suspected Dmitri would grab both words and pull. Layla listened with her chin on her fist and offered nothing, which Sadie was beginning to understand was how Layla talked best.

"There was a case in my office," Layla said finally, quietly, glancing at her father. "A well near a plant. Kids with the same bloodwork, more or less. The company's experts said causality was equivocal, too many other explanations, no proof the plant did it. And they were right, technically. Proof takes years. The families had months." She straightened the blanket edge without seeming to notice she'd done it. "The county couldn't make the plant close on suspicion. But they could require testing the town had to pay for, and they did, and the testing came back worse than anyone guessed. Nobody was absolved, exactly. Everyone had done the defensible thing."

"And the kids?"

"Some of them are fine. It's not a story with a shape." Layla gathered her canvas bag, checking the time. "Tell your Dmitri the principle doesn't say who's right. It says who has to move first."

Sadie walked the empty pitcher back down the corridor, past the vending machine she now forgave, past a nurse dictating notes in a low monotone, and thought about the word defensible, which she hadn't used before tonight and which she disliked on contact. Outside room 409 an old woman waved her over to fix a window blind that had stuck halfway, admitting gray evening light at a crooked angle, and Sadie stood on a chair and worked the mechanism until it gave. The blind snapped down all the way, darker than the room needed, and the old woman said, "Oh, well, now I can't see the parking lot at all," and laughed, and Sadie stood there with her hand still on the cord, deciding whether to raise it again.

The group chat had forty-three unread messages by the time Naomi sat down at her kitchen table, and most of them were about Marcus. Someone had posted a screenshot of the school's new attendance system, which scanned faces in the hallway, and someone else had noticed that it had marked Marcus absent three days in a row, which was impossible, because Marcus was in her second period and had lent her a green highlighter only that morning. "The camera doesn't like me," Marcus had written, followed by the shrugging emoji, and then a wall of replies arguing about whether that was even possible.

Naomi typed, "It's a program. Programs don't like or dislike." She deleted it before sending. It sounded like something her father would say about the dishwasher.

"It's not that deep," Priya wrote. "So a computer glitches sometimes. Teachers make mistakes too."

"Yeah but teachers' mistakes are random," Marcus answered. "This thing's mistakes are all in one direction. Ask around. Who else is getting flagged?" Over the next hour, a pattern assembled itself out of scattered complaints: Marcus, who was Black; Ana, whose face the system seemed to read as male half the time; Jaylen, who wore a hoodie that flattened him into shadow. Not one of the flagged kids was white. Not one of them had thought to compare notes before.

Naomi scrolled back through the thread with her chin on her fist. In her civics class they had spent two weeks on the Constitution, and she had done her presentation on the Fourth Amendment, and she had felt virtuosic about it, standing at the front of the room with her index cards, laying out the logic of warrants and probable cause like a solved proof. She had not once, she realized now, connected any of it to the camera above the gym door.

Priya was still going. "Honestly who cares, I have nothing to hide. They can scan my boring face all day."

Naomi's thumbs hovered. She typed slowly. "Would you let me read your phone? Like all of it. Every text, every number you've called, how long you talked."

"That's different, you're a person."

"Okay, would you let a company you've never heard of read it?"

Priya sent the eye-roll emoji, but she didn't answer right away, and in the pause Theo jumped in with a link. "This actually happened," he wrote. "In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers."

"Not the calls?" Naomi asked, reading the article on her laptop while the chat blinked. "Just the records. Who you called and for how long."

"Millions of them," Theo confirmed. "Ordinary customers."

Priya came back online twenty minutes later. "Okay so I asked my mom and she said the government can't just do that, there are laws." Her next message took longer to appear, the typing indicator pulsing on and off. "But I looked it up and it happened anyway. So the laws and the doing are two different things."

Naomi leaned back and looked at the ceiling, which was her thinking posture, inherited from her mother. The scale of the leak felt tectonic to her, something enormous shifting beneath ordinary life without making a sound, and yet Priya's reaction had been a shrug until the shrugging got hard. Meanwhile the hallway camera was tiny, one bad system in one bad school, and it was ruining Marcus's attendance record in real time. Maybe that was the trick of it, she thought, that the enormous thing was easy to ignore and the small thing was fixable. She didn't type that. She wasn't sure it was true.

She opened a new message to Marcus directly. "Do you have the three absence emails?" He sent screenshots, timestamped, with the subject line ATTENDANCE ALERT in gray capitals. She forwarded them to the vice principal with a short paragraph asking whether the system had been tested across different skin tones, then copied the paragraph into the group chat so everyone could see what she'd asked and how. Theo immediately added that there were researchers who audited this kind of software professionally. Ana said her cousin had gotten a similar flag last year and nobody had believed her, and that seeing the pattern laid out in the thread made her feel less crazy, which was not a feeling Naomi had anticipated.

The vice principal replied the next morning: the vendor would be contacted, the flagged records held in suspense pending review, the attendance office instructed to accept manual corrections. It was not an apology and it was not a fix. Marcus reposted it with "small victories," and Priya, who had started the whole argument with "not that deep," wrote, "I still think most surveillance is boring people watching boring people. But I don't think the boring people all get watched the same."

Naomi read that twice. She wanted to tell Priya that she had just stated the entire problem in one sentence, but she suspected that saying so would make Priya retreat. Instead she wrote, "Meeting before school Monday, room 114, we're drafting what we want them to change. Bring the screenshots."

Twelve people clicked the little thumbs-up, including Marcus, including Ana, including Priya, last of all, at 11:42 that night.

The rink smelled like cold rubber and burnt coffee, and the party had taken over the benches behind the boards, where Loic's aunts had laid out a table of noodle boxes that were going lukewarm while everyone watched the screen above the skate rental counter. On the ice, his little cousin's skating lesson was winding down, but nobody was watching the ice. The big screen was showing the World Cup match, and the sound was off, which somehow made everyone louder.

"Forty-eight," said Théo, Loic's cousin, holding a fork like a gavel. "I'm telling you, this one has forty-eight teams. It's the first time ever."

"It's thirty-two," said Uncle Marcel. "It's always been thirty-two. You're inventing things." He reached across Loic for a spring roll. "More teams means worse teams. Dilution. Like adding water to good soup."

Loic had been quiet, working through his own disagreement with himself. He liked Uncle Marcel's argument; it had the shape of something true, a preference for excellence over inclusion. But he also remembered something Théo's numbers were brushing against, something about the tournament being different this time, bigger, stranger. He couldn't place where he'd learned it, which bothered him, because a fact you can't place is a fact you shouldn't use.

"You're both guessing," he said, and pulled out his phone.

"Look at this," Uncle Marcel said, gesturing at the screen with his fork. "The match is in Toronto. The next one, my friend at work says, is in Mexico City. How does a tournament travel like that? It's absurd. A proper tournament has one host, one crowd, one heartbeat."

Loic scrolled. The wifi at the rink was friable, thin as old ice, and the page loaded in pieces: first the year, 2026, then a headline, then the sentence he'd been half-remembering. He read it twice, feeling the small satisfaction of a thing settling into place.

"It's forty-eight," he said. "This World Cup, 2026. First one ever with forty-eight teams. And it's hosted by three countries." He looked up. "Canada, Mexico, and the United States. That's the whole thing. First with forty-eight, first with three hosts."

Théo put down his fork with the gravity of a judge. "I said forty-eight."

"You said forty-eight and invented a reason," Loic said. "Different crime."

The aunts laughed. Uncle Marcel waved him off, but he leaned in to see the screen, and Loic let him read it himself rather than disabusing him out loud, because a man who finds his own error keeps more dignity than one who is corrected in front of spring rolls.

"But Marcel has a point," Loic went on, surprising himself by saying it, since he'd spent most of the argument against him. "Sort of. I think." Everyone turned back to him, and he felt the pressure of having to sound surer than he was. "More teams probably means more bad matches early on. That's just arithmetic. But it also means more countries get to be in it, whole places that never qualified before, kids watching who've never seen their flag in a tournament. That's worth something. I don't know which thing matters more. Maybe they both do."

"That's not a position," Théo said. "That's a shrug with vocabulary."

"It's a position with an asterisk," Loic said. "I'm allowed the asterisk."

Down the glass, the birthday girl came off the ice, blades hissing on the last dry strip before the door, cheeks red as stop signs, helmet crooked. She barrelled into the row of coats and Loic caught her, mostly, one skate blade scraping his shin on the way past. On the screen above them, the muted crowd in Toronto rose as one, a wave of blue and green, and here in the rink the whole family rose with it, shouting at a television with no sound, and Uncle Marcel was shouting loudest of all.

"See," he said, pointing at the screen as the ball hit the net. "Forty-eight teams and still only one can win it. That part I like."

Loic's little cousin tugged his sleeve and asked him who he was cheering for, and he honestly did not know yet. "The host countries," he said. "All three. It's their party." She considered this, and skated a slow circle around the bench to show it was acceptable.

Behind the counter, the rental clerk turned the volume up, and the noise of the crowd came through at last, and it was louder than all of them.

The travel agency sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered shoe repair, and on the Tuesday of her spring break Kaitlyn arrived at nine with a laptop bag and a printed sheet of instructions from her geography teacher. Mrs. Okonjo had arranged the placement through a cousin who owned the agency, and the assignment was due Friday: study two countries the agency books trips to, and use their population pyramids to argue which would need more schools and which would need more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Kaitlyn wanted the argument to be good enough that Mrs. Okonjo would read it to the class instead of filing it.

The cousin, Ms. Adeyemi, put her at the desk by the window between the printer and the rack of brochures. "Kenya and Japan," she said. "We send a student group to Nakuru every summer and a retirees' tour to Kyoto in autumn. You can use the booking maps, but don't touch the till." Then she went to the counter to help a man who wanted to change a flight to Lagos.

Kaitlyn opened the pyramids first. Kenya's was a triangle, wide at the bottom, each bar for children longer than the bar above it. Japan's looked like a top spinning on a thin stem, the widest bars in the sixties and seventies. She wrote in her notebook that a country with a broad base is young, so its spending would run toward classrooms and teachers, and a country whose bulge sits near the top will build wards and hire caregivers. She underlined it, then stopped underlining, because the sentence felt like something copied rather than concluded.

She pulled up the agency's file of trip maps to see whether the argument changed depending on which part of each country you looked at. The Nakuru map had a shaded strip along the lake, riparian zones marked in green, but the flood-risk layer covered other streets too, blocks that sat well back from any water. That bothered her. She had assumed flooding meant living beside a river, and if that assumption was wrong, her pyramid argument might rest on the same kind of guess.

She clicked through the map's layer list. Underneath the flood shading was a layer labeled DEM, and she turned it on alone. The town appeared as a grid of tiny squares, each one carrying a number. She moved the cursor along a street three kilometres from the lake and watched the values drop, square by square, toward a low pocket where the numbers clustered in the thirties while the surrounding blocks read in the hundreds. The flood layer's shaded blocks sat exactly over that pocket.

"You found the elevation data," Ms. Adeyemi said, coming over with two cups of tea. She set one down at Kaitlyn's elbow.

"It's called a digital elevation model?" Kaitlyn asked, reading the layer's full name from the panel.

"That's the one. Every cell stores the ground height, and the software uses it to say where water will flow and collect." Ms. Adeyemi tapped the low pocket on the screen. "That street floods because it's a bowl, not because it's near anything." She went back to the counter, where a woman had begun asking about visa fees.

Kaitlyn sat with that for a while. The map had exculpated the river, in a way; the water's arrival at those far streets was no longer the river's doing but the ground's shape, gravity reading the landscape square by square. She thought about the etymology lesson from the term before, how "population" came from a word for a place being peopled, as though the people were a layer laid over the land the way the numbers were laid over the map. You could read a country stacked like that: elevation underneath, ages on top.

She went back to the pyramids with the same caution. She zoomed the Kenyan map to a district whose population data she found in a government table, and its base was even wider than the national one. In Japan she found a prefecture where the bars in the eighties exceeded the bars in the twenties by more than the national shape showed. So the answer was not simply Kenya schools, Japan nursing homes; it was which region, which decade. She wrote three paragraphs, then cut the third because it claimed more than her tables supported. What stayed uncertain she marked plainly: she could not say how fast migration would move young workers into the old prefectures, and no pyramid told her that.

At five Ms. Adeyemi checked the printer, found a test page Kaitlyn had run of the Nakuru map with the elevation layer on, and pinned it above the brochures for the summer bookings. "Useful," she said. "Families ask about the rain." Kaitlyn packed her laptop, folded the map into the side pocket of her bag, and paused at the door with it half open, looking back at the pin.

The first time Eva's grandfather lost the number game, he blamed the kitchen noise. The second time, he blamed his coffee. By the fourth time, he set down his mug, folded his hands, and said, "All right, Tinkerbell. What are you doing to me?" He was the one who had proposed the game, an old standby from his dispatch days: think of a whole number from 1 to 100, and the other person guesses, with only higher or lower for an answer. He had beaten her aunt with it for thirty years. Eva had simply started in the middle, at fifty, and then picked the middle of whatever remained. Higher, so sixty-five. Higher, so eighty-two. She never needed more than a handful of guesses, never fumbled, never once went back over ground she'd already covered. "You're cutting the field in half every time," he said slowly, tapping the table. "Every single time." He demanded a rematch after dinner and lost that one too.

That was over spring break. Now it was Monday, third period, Computer Science II, and Mr. Okafor had put a sorted list of a hundred names on the board with a single name circled. "Find Vasquez," he said. "Write me a function. You have the period." He sat back down at his desk, which was his way; he assigned and waited, and if you wanted help you had to come to him, which Eva never did because asking felt like admitting the problem had beaten her before she'd fought it.

She started the obvious way, looping from the first index and checking each name against Vasquez. It worked. She ran it and the counter said she had checked forty-one names. It worked, and it was slow, the way walking every block of a city to find one address works. Beside her, Dooriya was doing the same thing, chewing the end of her pen and muttering, "Forty-something, I bet. Watch, it'll be like fifty." Their friendship had a rhythm: Dooriya talked, Eva listened, and on Thursdays Dooriya saved her a seat at lunch without being asked, because she knew Eva's bus ran late on Thursdays.

Eva sat very still with her hands off the keyboard. The kitchen table came back to her, her grandfather's face going from smug to suspicious to delighted. Fifty, then the middle of the half, then the middle of that. She had never known what it was called. She had just known that it won.

She opened a new file and wrote it carefully: find the middle of the range, compare, and if the target is higher, keep the upper half; if lower, the lower half. She tracked it on paper first, drawing brackets around shrinking sections of the list, because she didn't trust herself with the boundaries yet, the off-by-one places where the halves met. The first version looped forever. The second skipped Vasquez entirely and landed on the name after it. On the third try the counter read six. Six comparisons. She turned her screen slightly toward Dooriya without a word.

"Six?" Dooriya leaned over. "Mine's at forty-one. What is that, some trick?"

"It's called binary search," Eva said. "It only works on sorted data."

"Why only sorted?"

Eva started to answer and stopped, because the honest reply was that she could feel the shape of it, the way halving only helped if higher and lower actually meant something, but she couldn't yet say it in a sentence she trusted. "I'll show you at lunch," she said. "I want to get the words right first." Dooriya nodded and copied down the middle-finding line, and when Mr. Okafor wandered past and glanced at Eva's counter, he looked at it for a long moment, then at her, and wrote a small check in his grade book without saying anything at all.

At lunch she laid it out for Dooriya using napkins, one hundred of nothing in her head, guessing games, higher, lower, keep halving. Dooriya caught on fast and then, characteristically, ran ahead. "It's like how my mom says the whole country's becoming a plutocracy, everything organized around money, but if the information were actually sorted, if people could see it in order, then finding anything would take, what, seven steps instead of a hundred?" Eva laughed and said that wasn't quite it, or maybe it was, she wasn't sure. She had been thinking about something smaller and closer: how her school liked to pathologize the way her grandfather slowed down after his stroke, the specialists with their labels, when what he needed was a game he could still win and a granddaughter who didn't rush him. And she had been thinking, too, about her aunt in her cosmopolitan apartment in Toronto, who sent postcards from three countries a year but lost the number game every Christmas. Two different women, two ways of moving through the world, and Eva somewhere between, still deciding what her own way would be.

"Do you think it always works?" Dooriya asked, stacking their trays. "Like, even if the list is a million names?"

"I think so," Eva said. "But I haven't tested a million of anything yet." She slid the napkin, still covered in her brackets, into the front pocket of her backpack, next to her phone, where her grandfather's last message was still unread: Rematch this weekend. Bring your little trick.

Lucas arrived at the farmers' market at seven with a folding table, a double boiler, and three kilograms of couverture chocolate he had bought with his last paycheck. He had secured the corner spot near the honey vendor by promising her ten percent of whatever he sold, and he set up the table under the one canvas awning that still had all its grommets. His plan was modest: tempered chocolate bark with pistachios and dried cherries, sold in paper sleeves for four dollars each. The night before, he had watched the same eleven-minute video four times, and the maxim from it had stuck in his head: the chocolate must be heated, cooled, and heated again just slightly, or it would never set with shine.

The morning was already warm. By nine the thermometer zip-tied to the market's information booth read 34 degrees Celsius, and the canvas over his table did little except make a patch of shade the color of weak tea. He melted the chocolate to forty-five degrees, poured two thirds of it onto the marble slab he had borrowed from his mother's kitchen, and worked it with a spatula, spreading and gathering, spreading and gathering, until it thickened and began to hold a ridge when he dragged the edge through. That part felt like something he could learn with his hands.

The seed method was what undid him. He returned the slab chocolate to the bowl and added the reserved third to bring the temperature down to thirty-one, but his thermometer had been sitting in the sun and read high, and by the time he trusted it, the bowl had cooled past the point of no return. A test streak on parchment dried dull and bent when he tried to break it. The second batch went the other direction: too warm, and the streak never set at all, staying wet under his fingertip like paint.

He was scraping the failed batch back into the boiler when Priya from the tamale stall came over with a plate. "Lunch leftovers," she said. "Half a plate of rice and whatever you want off it. My eyes were too big." She set it on his table, and they ate standing up, and then she left the remainder, wrapped in foil, next to his burner. "I'll be back around one," she said. "We'll finish it for dinner."

She did not come back at one. At two, Lucas noticed the foil packet still sitting on the table's sunny edge, warm as a stone from the grill. He thought about their old family rule at home, the one his father repeated, that food was fine as long as it smelled fine, and then he thought about the six hours the rice would have sat out by the time Priya returned for dinner. He pulled out his phone and searched, standing between his marble slab and the honey jars.

The result was from the USDA, plain as a road sign: refrigerate cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 32 degrees Celsius. Ninety Fahrenheit, the page said, for anyone who thought that way. He looked at the thermometer on the information booth, which still read 34, and looked at his own watch, which said the rice had been out since noon. He picked up the foil packet, walked it to Priya's cooler, and set it on the ice. When she wandered back at three with a bag of limes, he pointed at the cooler. "It's been over ninety all day," he said. "You've got one hour, not two. It went in at twelve fifty." She thanked him and did not argue, which he noted with some surprise.

The fact sat in his mind while he worked the third batch of chocolate. His father's maxim about smell was not exactly wrong, he decided, just built for a different world, a kitchen where the same hands cooked and ate. The USDA number was a rule for strangers and heat, a way of commodifying safety itself into something a vendor could quote at a market. It was not tangential to what he was doing with the chocolate either. Both were about temperature and time, about a narrow window in which a thing stayed good, and both were learned by ruining a batch.

The third batch behaved. He brought the chocolate down on the slab, seeded the bowl, and when he streaked a line of it on parchment, it set in under two minutes with a surface like a dark window. He broke off a corner and it snapped, a clean sound with no bend under it. He poured the rest onto parchment, scattered pistachios and cherries, and cut it into rough rectangles before it fully hardened, scoring lines that would break straight later.

Priya came by at closing with two dollars and a slice of watermelon. She took a sleeve of bark, broke a piece, and listened to it snap. "So you figured it out," she said. Lucas took the money, folded the table's legs, and put the last sleeve of chocolate in his own cooler, on top of the ice.

The video arrived during fourth period, passed from phone to phone like contraband: grainy footage of a fire at a food processing plant, a caption claiming it had happened that morning in a town two hours away, that the smoke was toxic, that everyone downwind should be evacuated. Rose watched it twice on Priya's cracked screen, feeling the particular jolt that such clips were designed to produce, the way three seconds of fire could desensitize you to the fact that somewhere real people might be running. Priya had already sent it to forty people in the marching band group chat. Rose told her to wait, and Priya said wait for what, and Rose didn't have an answer yet.

She had an answer of a different kind waiting in the computer lab. The class was doing a database unit, and Rose and her partner Marco had written a query that was supposed to list every customer in one table alongside their orders from another. When the results came up, half the rows were fine and the other half showed the word NULL, printed in gray, where the order information should have been. Marco leaned back and declared the database broken. "We broke it," he said. "Or the software broke it."

Rose stared at the gray words, then at their SQL, which had the phrase LEFT JOIN in it. She opened the unit's reference sheet, then a tutorial page, then ran the query both ways, once with LEFT JOIN and once with an INNER JOIN, and compared what appeared. With the inner join, the NULL rows vanished entirely; with the left join, they came back. She turned the screen toward Marco. "It's not broken," she said. "A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, and fills the right table's columns with NULL wherever there's no matching row." Marco frowned at the words as if they were personally insulting him, then counted the rows, then counted the customers, and the numbers agreed.

That evening, at the auxiliary campus library annex where the main building's renovation had chased everyone, Rose sat with the fire video open on her laptop. The idea that had worked on the NULL rows kept nagging at her: the thing wasn't broken, it was behaving according to a rule she hadn't known. So what rule governed a video like this? She remembered a segment from a media literacy assembly, half-attended, something about checking where an image had come from before trusting where it was going. She took a screenshot of the video's clearest frame, opened a reverse image search, and dropped it in.

The results stacked up quietly. The same frame appeared in a news article from four years ago, a fire in an entirely different province, with no toxic smoke and no evacuations. The caption in the viral post was a costume draped over old footage. Rose felt the jolt drain out of her and leave something colder behind, and also something like the small triumph of the NULL rows: not broken, just misunderstood. She screenshotted the article and its date and closed her laptop.

Priya was harder than the query. Rose found her before first period by the lockers, where the morning crowd thinned around them without quite leaving. "It's real fire," Priya said. "I saw it burn." Rose held out her phone with the search results, and Priya looked, and her face did something complicated, moving from defense to confusion to a flush that Rose recognized as embarrassment on behalf of the forty people in the band chat. "So I panicked everyone for nothing."
