"Falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic." She said it without checking her notes. "The point is that free speech doesn't protect that."

"Who wrote it?"

Laura opened her mouth and then stopped, because she suddenly wasn't sure she had ever known, or whether she had known and let it go the way you let go of a fact that's inconvenient to the sentence you're building. She flipped to the photocopy. "Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes. Nineteen nineteen. It's in the Schenck opinion itself."

"So the same man who wrote the theatre line wrote the opinion you're attacking Thursday." Marcus leaned back until the chair creaked. "Your strongest argument against the government side is a sentence the government side wrote."

She read the line again, the whole fact of it sitting there in Holmes's own words: free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic, written in 1919, in this very case. She had been wielding the fire line for years without ever asking whose hand it came from. In eighth grade she'd used it in a class discussion about a kid who got suspended for a parody account, and she'd felt so right, so adult, invoking the theatre. She hadn't known then that the words came from the opinion that sent men to prison for leaflets. Maybe it didn't change whether the words were true. Maybe it changed something else.

"Maybe it's both," she said. "The line is good. The application is terrible. He wrote a principle I agree with and then used it to uphold a conviction I think was wrong."

"That's not an argument, that's a headache."

"That's the argument." She was writing now, fast, the pen skipping. "Thursday I say: the theatre analogy came from the same pen that jailed Schenck, and that should make us careful with it. Tuesday I say: even Holmes thought there were limits, and the fire example still holds." She stopped. "Except that's not really careful. That's just convenient. I'm picking up the line when it helps and putting it down when it doesn't."

Marcus pulled the rubber band and let it go. "So pick. Which side do you actually believe?"

The radiator under the window ticked, the room's own stubborn homeostasis, holding its temperature against whatever was happening to hers. Outside, a security guard was pushing a cart of returns toward the front desk. Laura thought about being parsimonious with her principles, saving them up and spending them only where they'd buy the most, and how that wasn't the same as having principles at all. But she also thought that a person who could see both sides wasn't weaker than a person who saw one. She just hadn't figured out yet what seeing both sides was for.

"I don't know," she said. "Ask me Tuesday."

"Tuesday you're the government."

"Then ask me Thursday." She closed the legal pad and slid the photocopy of the opinion into her folder, the theatre line face down. "I want to get the dates exactly right in my notes before I say any of it out loud again."

Marcus stood and stretched. "The room's ours for twenty more minutes."

Laura opened the folder back up, found Holmes's sentence, and began, slowly, to copy it out by hand.

The club's check-in list had four hundred and twelve names on it, and Priya's new program was supposed to find any one of them in a heartbeat. Instead it found about one name in ten and reported "not found" for the rest, which was how Jade ended up spending her Saturday at her grandmother's kitchen table with a laptop, a plate of almond biscotti, and a growing suspicion that software hated her personally.

"Your grandmother says you look disaffected," her grandfather said, setting down his coffee. He had a way of repeating Gran's vocabulary back at her like borrowed tools. "Also that you've barely touched the biscotti, which is the more serious charge."

"The program's broken and I can't see why." She turned the laptop toward him. "It's a binary search. You check the middle of the list, and if the name you want comes before the middle, you throw away the whole second half, because it can't be there. Then you do it again on what's left." She drew a line splitting the screen in half with her finger. "Priya says it's supposed to be almost instant. On four hundred names, linear search would mean reading down the list one by one until you find the person, which could take ages. Binary search should take, like, nine steps."

Her grandfather chewed his biscotti with the patience of a man who had outlasted three separate decades of broken technology. "And it doesn't work."

"It finds some names. Adrian Ruiz, yes. Monica Tran, no, and she's definitely on the list, I've seen her sign it."

He didn't reach for the laptop, which she appreciated. Instead he got up, went to the hall shelf, and came back with the enormous dictionary he'd owned since before her mother was born. "Play a game with me. I've thought of a word. Find it."

"You can't just tell me?"

"Where's the sport in that."

She opened the dictionary to the middle. "Is your word before this page or after it?"

"After."

She let the first half fall flat against the table, five hundred pages gone in one soft slap. "Before or after?"

"Before."

Another half discarded. Within six flips she had narrowed the ocean to a single page, and there, between "vermilion" and "vernal," sat her grandfather's word, which turned out to be "vertigo." He looked so pleased that she suspected he'd chosen it for her benefit.

"So why," he said, spooning sugar into his coffee, "does your machine's version stumble when mine doesn't?"

She stared at the dictionary's gutter, at the words marching up the page in their fixed order, and felt something shift. "Because the dictionary's sorted." She said it slowly, testing the weight of it. "Every page is in order, so I always know which half to throw away." She pulled the laptop back and scrolled Priya's list, and there it was: Adrian Ruiz near the top, then someone named Alvarez after him, then Baker, then back to a whole run of A's, because three different club members had been typing names in as people arrived at the door, and none of them had re-sorted anything. The list was a pile, not an order. "Binary search works only on sorted data," she said, mostly to herself. "Our list was never sorted. It's checking the middle, throwing away the wrong half, and the name it's looking for is sitting in the trash."

"Congratulations. You've just discovered why librarians are superior to the rest of humanity." He raised his mug in salute. "Your grandmother maintains that alphabetizing is a moral act. I always thought she was externalizing. Now I see she was making a technical argument."

Jade was already half in her own world, re-sorting the list in the editor, watching four hundred scrambled names resolve into a clean procession of letters. She thought about how she'd explain it to Priya on Monday, and about how, in her head, two ideas had been living separately all week: the failure, which felt like chaos, and the algorithm, which felt like certainty. Now they were one thing. Not certainty exactly, because there were surely more ways for the program to be wrong, more assumptions she hadn't checked, a whole hidden stack of things she believed about her data without knowing she believed them. But she had caught one assumption, at least, and dragged it into the light.

She tested the fixed version on Monica Tran. Found, in nine steps.

"Gran," her grandfather called toward the living room, "the girl has achieved order. There's hope for the family yet."

"Then she can alphabetize the spice rack," Gran called back.

Jade laughed, typed a quick message to Priya, and reached for the last biscotti.

The blood pressure cuff hissed and tightened around Aiden's arm for the fourth time that morning, and for the fourth time the number on the trainer's tablet read something different. He was at a two-week health careers camp in the hills above the reservoir, in a cabin-turned-classroom where the walls were papered with anatomy posters left over from some earlier decade. He had signed up mostly because his mother wanted him to be doing something, and partly because the brochure had made auscultation look romantic, which he now understood was an affectation of the brochure and not of the actual work. The work was repetitive. The work was a matter of tiny differences.

His partner, Priya, took the next reading while Aiden sat still and tried not to clench. She was insouciant about the whole enterprise in a way he envied, sliding the cuff on as if it were a sweatband, chatting the whole time about the dining hall's soft serve. The instructor, Mr. Okonkwo, drifted between the pairs of them saying almost nothing, which Aiden had at first taken as neglect and now took as method. When Aiden asked how he was supposed to remember what counted as high, Mr. Okonkwo only said, "Look it up yourself, then tell me tomorrow," and moved on.

He looked it up that evening on the dock, phone held above his face, mosquitoes tracing slow orbits around the screen. He read the line twice to fix it: under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89. He said it aloud once, quietly, so Priya wouldn't hear and mock him. Systolic, the top number, was the squeeze; diastolic, the bottom, was the rest between squeezes. If either one fell in its range, that was the stage. He thought about his grandfather then, unexpectedly, the way a fact can summon a person.

His grandfather kept a home monitor on the kitchen table in a shoebox, next to the TV remote and a dish of peppermints. Aiden had watched him use it last Christmas, cuffing his own arm with the bored competence of long habit, writing the numbers in a spiral notebook with a pencil he licked first. Nobody in the family had ever said what the numbers meant. His grandfather had survived a lot and had decided, Aiden suspected, that the surviving was behind him, and that the notebook was mostly for show, something to burnish his image as a man who took care of himself without actually needing anyone to take care of him.

Aiden called him on Thursday night instead of waiting for the scheduled Sunday slot. He could hear the lake through the cabin's screened window and the campers playing cards two buildings over. His grandfather answered on the fifth ring, and Aiden asked him to read out the last few entries from the notebook. There was a long pause, the sound of a chair scraping, the shoebox opening. His grandfather read the numbers flatly, without commentary: 128 over 76. Then 134 over 79. Then 131 over 82. Then, two weeks back, 136 over 84.

Aiden did the arithmetic of it in his head while his grandfather waited. The first reading was fine, under both thresholds. The second, 134 over 79, sat inside the systolic range even though the diastolic was below it. The third and fourth hit both. "What are you getting at?" his grandfather asked, and Aiden heard something underneath the gruffness, maybe caution, maybe interest. He had planned, walking to the phone, to come at it sideways, to mention the camp and let the conversation drift toward checkups on its own. Facing the actual voice, he decided sideways was dishonest.

"I'm learning this at camp," he said. "Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means systolic 130 to 139 or diastolic 80 to 89." He heard his grandfather's breath change. "A couple of your numbers fall in that range. Both numbers, in the last one." He had thought about whether to say the word hypertension at all, and had decided his grandfather was a grown man who had been writing these figures for years and deserved the real term rather than a soft one.

"You going to diagnose me over the phone now," his grandfather said, but it wasn't quite a question, and it wasn't quite a joke either. He asked what camp was like, whether the food was any good, whether Aiden was keeping his room at home from becoming a disaster. Then, just before hanging up, he said he had a card somewhere with the clinic's number and he'd see about an appointment, maybe, no promises. Aiden said okay. He stood at the window afterward with the phone still warm in his hand, uncertain whether he had done the right thing or only the technically correct thing, whether the guideline told you what to do or only what to name.

On Sunday his grandfather called him first, before the scheduled slot. "I found the card," he said. "It was under the peppermints. I'm calling them tomorrow at nine." In the background, the pencil was already scratching something into the notebook.

Samuel spread the flashcards across the kitchen table like a man laying out evidence for a trial he was not sure he could win. Tomorrow at four he had to pass the peer health facilitator check, fifteen minutes in front of the coordinator, explaining consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the county clinic. Tonight the kitchen was his, his mother on shift until eleven, and the only witness was the dishwasher's low hum.

He started with consent, saying it out loud to the refrigerator. "Consent is a clear, freely given yes. Not silence, not maybe, not a yes you talked someone into." It sounded rehearsed, because it was. He had written the sentences on the bus, on his hand, on the back of a chemistry worksheet, until the words had lost their edges. That was the problem. He could recite them and not believe a single one in a specific situation, and Mrs. Okonkwo, the coordinator, would smell that hollowness the way a substitute teacher smells fear.

Nadia came in for cereal at nine, barefoot, fifteen, skeptical by constitution. "You're talking to the fridge again."

"I'm practicing. Ask me something. Anything. Hard questions."

She leaned on the counter, spoon in hand, and obliged. "Okay. If someone's on the pill, they don't need a condom, right?"

Samuel opened his mouth and then closed it, because the honest answer required a story, and the story was three weeks old. He had been at Duval's Pharmacy waiting for his mother's blood pressure medication when a girl from his grade, Marta, stood at the counter with a paper bag and a question she asked too quietly. "Does this, like, cover infections too? The birth control?" The pharmacist had shaken her head, kind and unhurried. "It prevents pregnancy. It doesn't protect against infections. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections." Marta had nodded, paid, and gone out into the March drizzle with her bag clutched like contraband, and Samuel had stood there realizing he'd had it wrong too, in some dim, unexamined way, assuming that one protection was protection.

"So?" Nadia said now, dragging him back. "Was I right?"

"No. That's the thing. The pill prevents pregnancy, but it doesn't protect against infections. Only condoms do both. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of STIs." He said it and heard the pharmacist's cadence in his own voice, borrowed but true.

"Then why doesn't everyone just use both?"

"Because people make tradeoffs. Because nobody taught them. Because it's awkward to talk about, and this whole thing I'm doing tomorrow is trying to make it less awkward." He heard his own earnestness and let it stand there, unfashionable and exposed.

There was a second voice in his head, older than the pharmacist's. His mother, the previous Sunday, chopping onions, when he'd told her about the facilitator program. "You're seventeen," she'd said. "What do you know to teach anybody?" Not an accusation exactly, more a genuine question, the kind she asked while doing something else so that he could pretend not to answer if he chose. And beneath it, unspoken, the whole grammar of how she'd been raised, in a house where such things were managed by silence and luck. He had not argued with her. He had thought about her cousin Adaeze, whose story the family told in fragments and never in full, and he had decided that silence was a tradition you could decline to inherit without despising the people who'd kept it. Still, he couldn't fully dismiss her point either. He was seventeen. Tomorrow he would stand in a church basement with a laminated diagram and more confidence than his experience could strictly support, and that gap was real.

"Okay," Nadia said, setting down her bowl. "Role-play me. I'll be some random person at your thing. Do the consent part."

He straightened. "Imagine you're with someone, and things are moving, and you're not sure if they want to keep going. What do you do?"

"I ask."

"How?"

"What do you mean, how? Do you want to? That's how."

"And if they say nothing?"

"Then I stop." She said it so plainly that he almost laughed, not at her but at the fifteen minutes of jargon he'd been rehearsing for a thing she'd compressed into four words. Except it wasn't that simple, and he knew it, and it was his job tomorrow to say why: that stopping can feel enormous in the moment, that people say yes to avoid disappointing, that consent can be withdrawn after it's given and the withdrawing must be honored the same as the first no.

"That's right," he said. "That's the whole center of it. Everything else is plumbing."

"What about the clinic stuff? Where do people even go?"

He pulled the county health department's printout from under a flashcard, a page he'd annotated in three colors like scripture requiring its own hermeneutics. "Here. Testing is free, you can walk in, and it's confidential, which means they don't tell your parents. You can call ahead, or just show up." He traced the hours with his finger. "Results take about a week. If something shows up, most of it's treatable."

Nadia studied the page with an interest she tried to disguise. "Is it scary? The test?"

"I haven't done it," he admitted. "So I don't know. I shouldn't pretend I do." He slid the page toward her. "But I'm going to find out, before summer. Then I can say it from the inside."

The dishwasher clicked off, leaving the kitchen quieter than he'd noticed it being. His mother would be home in twenty minutes, tired, penurious with her energy at that hour, saving her words for the morning. He gathered the flashcards into a stack, then stopped, and left the clinic page out on the table where she would see it, face up, when she came in.

Nadia took her bowl to the sink. "You'll pass," she said. "Even though you talk to appliances."

"Thanks," Samuel said, and turned the flashcards facedown.

The lab had been left open for exam review, and Jessica had claimed the corner bench by the window because nobody else wanted the stool with the wobbleg leg. Mr. Okafor had posted one final problem on the board: a stretch of DNA to be transcribed into RNA and then translated, letter by letter, into amino acids. It was due at the end of the period. She copied the sequence into her notebook, ATGCCGATTAG, and began building the RNA strand beneath it, checking each letter against the pairing rules she had memorized so many times they had started to feel like arithmetic.

She had gotten four letters in when Marisol dropped onto the stool across from her, notebook already open. "Yours has to be right," Marisol said. "Mine keeps coming out as gibberish on the translator chart. I don't even know if I did the first part correctly."

"Show me," Jessica said, and turned her own notebook face down, the way she always did when she wasn't sure, a habit that fooled people into thinking she was confident.

Marisol's page read DNA: GATTACA, and beneath it RNA: CTAATGT. Jessica stared at it. Something was off, but not where Marisol thought. "You did the complement backwards," she said slowly. "You just wrote the same letters in reverse order, kind of. It's supposed to be the opposite letters. Adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine." She tapped the first letter. "So across from G you want a C, which you have, but across from the A's you want T's, and across from T's you want A's."

Marisol rewrote it, and Jessica watched the new strand take shape: CTAATGT again, then CTAA, then Marisol stopped, frowning at the third letter, which she had written as a T. "Wait. The fourth one. In DNA it's an A. Am I supposed to put T in the RNA?"

This was the moment Jessica had been dreading, because her own notebook, still face down, contained three T's in her RNA strand, and a cold suspicion was forming in her. She had studied the unit twice. She had drawn the diagrams. And somewhere in her memory a single word sat stubbornly unattached. She flipped her notebook over and compared. "Hold on," she said. "I wrote T's too. But there's something about RNA that's different. One letter changes."

Marisol leaned across the bench. "Different how? You're the one who got an A on the last quiz."

"Uracil," Jessica said, mostly to herself, and then said it again with more certainty, because the word had finally located its partner. "In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine. It pairs with adenine. So anywhere you'd put a T, you put a U instead." She looked at Marisol to see whether this landed as revelation or as more noise, and Marisol was already erasing, muttering, "So all my T's are wrong. Fantastic."

They rebuilt both strands together, letter by letter, Jessica reading the rules aloud and Marisol checking her work, and Jessica felt the strange double pleasure of teaching something she had learned approximately ninety seconds ago. "It's like the cell keeps two alphabets," she said. "Almost the same, one letter apart, and you have to know which one you're reading before you can copy anything." She didn't say the rest of what she was thinking, which was that she still couldn't explain why the cell bothered with two alphabets, or what the letters actually were, chemically, only how they behaved toward each other, and that this felt like reciting a law in a language she couldn't yet speak. Her father called that kind of knowledge logos without understanding, words accurate on the surface and empty underneath, and she had argued with him about it at dinner once, insisting that saying the right words was how understanding started. He had asked her whether a parrot that said "two plus two is four" knew arithmetic, and she had called him facetious and gone to her room.

Marisol finished translating her corrected strand and sat back. "Okay. Amino acids done. If I fail this exam anyway, you have to indemnify me. Emotional damages."

"I'll pay you in flashcards," Jessica said. "That's all I've got."

Mr. Okafor came by on his way to the front, glanced at Marisol's corrected page, and slid a strip of paper beside it: a new DNA sequence, twice as long, and beneath it the single instruction "translate." No DNA strand given for the RNA, no intermediate step. Marisol looked at Jessica. Jessica looked at the board, where the original problem still ended in a flourish of A's, and realized she had spent forty minutes learning to copy DNA into RNA, and now the paper was asking for the part she had practiced least.

"Okay," she said, and pulled the chart of codons closer. "You read, I'll write."

The tournament had thirty-two schools in it and one empty chorus room behind the cafeteria, and Mya had been promised both. Her debate rounds were on the second floor, the one-act rehearsals were wherever she could find walls, and her partner, Dev, had handed her a battered binder before the bus left with the words "you're the director now" and an expression that suggested he had just converted his obligations into an annuity, paying himself out over time in free afternoons.

She had compartmentalized, in theory. Rounds until noon, rehearsal at noon, lunch eaten while walking. In practice the compartments leaked. During her second cross-examination she caught herself thinking about whether Jonah should enter left or right, and she asked a question about trade deficits that her opponent answered in a tone of genuine confusion, since it had nothing to do with her case.

At noon she herded four actors into the chorus room, where the risers made a shallow stage. They were doing the scene where the sister returns after seven years, and it kept going wrong in a way Mya couldn't name. Jonah, playing the brother, would cross toward Priya, playing the sister, and Priya would end up behind him, half invisible to the imaginary audience, her big line delivered to the back of his shoulder.

"Move when he moves," Mya said. "Just, like, drift."

Priya drifted. Jonah crossed faster. She ended up in the same pocket of invisibility, only now she looked like she was hiding on purpose, which was a different and worse choice.

"I feel like furniture," Priya said. "Furniture with lines."

Mya stood on a riser and looked at the shape they made, the two of them lumped on one side of the stage like a pile of coats. She had spent three years of debate learning that positioning was argument, that where you stood determined what the judges could see, and it occurred to her, slowly and with some embarrassment, that a stage worked the same way and nobody had ever needed to tell her. She got the binder out. Between a page on "spike marks" and a page on "cheating out" there was a paragraph with a word underlined twice in pencil by some previous director whose name was water-damaged into illegibility.

"It's called countering," Mya said. "When one actor crosses, the other one shifts to balance the stage, so the audience can still see both."

"Shift where?" Jonah asked.

"Wherever isn't behind you. Opposite direction, kind of."

They ran it again. Jonah crossed toward Priya with his speech about the money, and Priya took two quiet steps downstage and to the side, and suddenly there were two people on the stage instead of one person and a shadow. The line she'd been muffling all morning landed flat and clean: "You can't buy back a year, Marcus." Mya, standing on the riser with her phone out to time the scene, forgot to start the timer.

She texted Dev between rounds, sitting on the floor outside the auditorium with her laptop open to a case she was supposed to be reordering.

The countering thing worked. Priya stopped being a coat rack. Also I think I'm going to lose round three, I spent all of prep writing "DOWNSTAGE LEFT" on notecards. Do not say I told you so. You may think it very loudly.

His reply came during her opponent's first speech, a single thumbs-up, which she felt was obdurate in its cheerfulness, though she had to admit she'd trained him to be that way about her.

In round four she argued that certainty was a luxury of people who hadn't read the evidence, and she meant it more than she usually did. Directing had made debate feel suddenly transparent, both of them just ways of deciding where people should stand so the audience could see them. But that wasn't quite right either, and she couldn't have said which one had gotten clearer. She won the round on a 2-1 and the judge's reason made sense only in the way that judges' reasons sometimes did.

The final rehearsal was at five, in the actual black box theater, borrowed for twenty minutes because a teacher had liked her when she'd asked nicely. The actors ran the scene with the real lights, and Priya's counter was so smooth now that Mya almost didn't see it happen, Jonah crossing, Priya answering, the two of them keeping the stage balanced between them like a scale that wanted to stay level.

When they finished, nobody said anything for a second. Priya was still standing in her spot, breathing like someone who'd just landed something, and Jonah was looking at Mya with his eyebrows up, waiting.

"Once more," Mya said, and climbed off the stage to watch from the back of the house, where the audience would be.

The basement smelled like dryer sheets and cold pizza, and Marcus's laptop sat open on the pool table because the actual desk was buried under model airplane parts. Jaxon pulled a folding chair up beside him and unfolded his notebook to the page where he'd copied the assignment: build a class in Java, keep the fields private, write getter methods, write tests. He had wanted this for weeks, ever since Marcus had shown him a program that tracked every guitar pedal he owned, and Jaxon had understood, with a small clean shock, that software was something a person could just make.

"Private fields first," Marcus said, tapping the screen. "That's the whole religion of it. Nobody reaches in and grabs your data. They have to knock." He typed `private String playerName;` and `private int score;` and then, beneath them, the getters, small polite doors into the class: `public String getPlayerName() { return playerName; }`. Jaxon copied the shape of it into his notebook, not the words exactly but the architecture, the idea that a thing could hold its facts close and still let you look.

He built his own class on the second laptop, a `Song` class, because he wanted a program that remembered what he'd been learning on guitar. Title and artist private, getters below, and then a test that created a `Song`, called the getters, and checked what came back. It ran. Green bar. He leaned back and let himself feel it for exactly four seconds before Marcus said, "Now make it useful. Add a constructor so you can't build a song with nothing in it."

So Jaxon wrote `public Song(String title, String artist)` and set the fields inside it, and then ran the test again, and the green bar was gone. The compiler refused to compile his old test, and the error pointed at the line where the test did `new Song()`, empty parentheses, no arguments, and said it couldn't find that constructor. Jaxon read it three times. "I didn't delete anything," he said. "It's right there. The class. I just added a constructor."

"Then it should work," Marcus said, in the tone of somebody reciting a maxim he didn't fully trust: when in doubt, blame the machine. He took the laptop, scrolled, gave it back. "Nope, that's real."

Jaxon sat with it. Before he'd written any constructor, `new Song()` had worked; he had run that test himself, watched it pass. After he added one constructor with parameters, the empty version stopped existing. He said it out loud slowly, testing it: "If a class defines no constructor at all, the compiler adds a default no-argument one. But once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added." It was like the compiler had been holding the door open for him out of courtesy, and the moment he built his own door, courtesy withdrew. He wasn't sure yet whether that felt like a trap or like being taken seriously.

"Message Deja," Marcus said. "She broke her whole project over this last month and she'll pretend she didn't." Jaxon texted her, and while they waited he fixed the test the honest way, giving `new Song()` real arguments, real title, real artist. His phone buzzed with her reply: "lol welcome. my old test broke the second i added a constructor with parameters. i sat there for an hour thinking my laptop was moribund. it was fine. i was the problem. you have to write the no-arg one yourself now if you still want it." Jaxon read it twice, then typed back, "But you don't have to want it. That's the part I like."

Because he did like it, and he could admit that it was a strange thing to like. His father's whole approach to problems was to get in there and fix them with his hands, wires and wrenches, no layers between you and the thing; Marcus's approach was to paste the error into a search box and interpolate an answer from whatever strangers had said. Jaxon was discovering he wanted both, the grease-under-the-fingernails reading of the error line by line and the borrowed experience of somebody who'd already been stuck here. Maybe a considered position was just knowing when to do which, though he was honest enough with himself not to be sure he'd know when that was.

He ran the test again. Green bar. Marcus peered over, mock solemn, and said, "Your getters work. Your fields are locked up like a museum. I'm proud of you and I want royalties." Jaxon laughed and started typing a second test, because one green bar was a fact and two was starting to be a pattern, and at the top of the file he wrote a comment for his future self: this is the one that bit you.

The skate park sat behind the middle school like a bowl carved out of the afternoon, and James had been standing at the top of the quarter pipe for ten minutes without dropping in. He was not afraid of the drop itself. What bothered him was his physics worksheet, folded into his back pocket, which he had taken out four times already. His tutor had said the words to him last night, separate the velocity into components, and James had nodded the way you nod when the words mean nothing yet. Below him, his friend Ravi was carving the shallow end with his arms loose, tracing long curves on the concrete, and James watched the board leave the coping and fall, and fall, and land, and thought: everything here is falling. The only question is what it does while it falls.

"Are you skating or doing your taxes?" Ravi called up.

"Homework," James said. He sat down on the coping and unfolded the worksheet against his knee. A ball launched at twelve meters per second at thirty degrees, and the problem wanted the range. "I keep setting it up as one motion. One speed, one angle, one straight push. And I keep getting answers that are wrong."

Ravi skated over, kicked his board up into his hand, and climbed the ramp to sit beside him. He read the problem upside down. "So split it."

"I don't know what that means." James said it flatly, without embarrassment, because Ravi had watched him fail a math test in eighth grade and had lent him notes ever since. "He said something about the horizontal part and the vertical part being separate. I wrote it down and then I lost the sentence."

Below them the drinking fountain by the chain-link fence was running, because some kid had jammed the button with a pebble, and the water rose in a silver rope and bent over itself and fell. Ravi noticed it first. He pointed with his chin. "Doesn't that look like your graph?"

It did, in a way James could not immediately name. He stared at the water while it held its shape, the same shape, rising less and less steeply, hanging for an instant, then steepening downward, and the word arrived before the reasoning did: parabola. The graph from algebra class, y equals x squared, drawn in water. He took out his phone and searched, mostly to prove himself wrong.

Ravi leaned over to read the screen while the wheels of somebody's board rattled across the far side of the bowl. He read aloud, half to himself, the way he read everything. "Galileo showed that the path of a projectile, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola. Two New Sciences, published in 1638." He scrolled. "That's a real book. He was old when he wrote it." It seemed strange to Ravi that a shape could have a lineage, that some old man watching cannonballs had handed this curve down through almost four centuries to a kid on a quarter pipe, and he said so, and James only half heard him.

Because something had come apart in James's mind, the way the water had come apart in the air, into a sideways piece and a falling piece. The horizontal motion had no reason to change; nothing pushed against it if you ignored the air, which felt like cheating until he considered that the air was extrinsic, a local annoyance, not part of what the ball was doing. The vertical motion was just falling, the falling he already knew. Two clean straight things crossed over each other, and where they crossed, the curve appeared, the same curve as the fountain. He took out a pencil, drew the axes on the back of the worksheet, split twelve into its sideways part and its upward part, and the numbers came out obedient for the first time all week. He did not trust it entirely. He still did not understand why the world would keep those two motions separate, only that it seemed to, and that a man dead for centuries had said it did.

"Drop in with me," Ravi said, standing, stamping his board down onto the coping beside James's sneakers. "Then throw something."

James folded the worksheet into his pocket and set his board on the metal edge. He looked down the curve of the ramp, at the water still arcing silver over the drain across the park, and wondered whether he would feel the separation, the sideways push and the fall, or whether it would only ever be one motion from inside. He pushed off.

Ravi watched him drop in, low and committed, and when James shot out the far side and flung the board up into the air, both of them tracked it against the sky.

"Parabola," Ravi called out, catching it as it came down.

The paper was due in nine days, and Ava had spread it across her grandmother's dining room table like a field surgeon laying out instruments: the draft, the sources, the teacher's comments sheet with its red marginalia, and her laptop balanced on a stack of National Geographics from 1984. Mrs. Perrine had written "Footnotes need work. See me" on page six, which was the kind of note that cauterized all her confidence in a single stroke, leaving nothing but the sore awareness that she did not know what she didn't know.

"You're biting that pencil like it owes you money," her grandmother said, setting down a mug of tea that Ava hadn't asked for and would drink anyway.

"It's the citations. She marked half of them wrong and I don't know why. I did exactly what the guide in the library said."

Her grandmother disappeared into the study and returned cradling a fat orange book with a cracked spine, dust fanning off it in the lamplight. "Your grandfather's. Chicago Manual of Style. He footnoted everything, even letters to the editor. Swore by it." She set it down with the ceremony of someone delivering a family relic, and Ava, charmed despite herself, opened it to the chapter on notes.

There it was, an example with the word ibid. marching down the page after a full citation, ibid., ibid., ibid., a little stutter of Latin that looked efficient and scholarly and exactly like what she had done. She had used it eleven times in her paper on the Peloponnesian War, because it saved her typing Thucydides over and over, and because it looked the way footnotes were supposed to look, the way they looked in her grandfather's generation.

"Grandpa used this?" she asked.

"Underlined the whole section. He said an oligarchy of editors in Chicago decided how the rest of us should cite, and he'd be damned if he'd argue with them." Her grandmother laughed at the memory, then squinted at the page. "Is that what's wrong? You didn't use the ibid.?"

"I did use it. That might be what's wrong."

She pulled the laptop closer and searched, half to defend herself and half to prove the manual right, because it would have been a nice thing, to have inherited a correct grandfather. What she found instead sat there on the screen while her grandmother read over her shoulder. The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, had begun discouraging ibid. in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title. She read it twice, and something in her chest performed a small, complicated maneuver that was half relief and half loss.

"So my way is outdated," she said slowly. "Not wrong, exactly. Outdated."

"Seventeen editions," her grandmother said. "That book of his is the fourteenth." She touched the orange spine the way you'd touch a photograph of someone gone. "He'd have called that specious, you know. Changing a perfectly good Latin word because some committee got restless. He liked things that stayed put."

Ava laughed, a real one that surprised her. "He sounds like half the guys in Thucydides, honestly. Complaining that Athens isn't what it was while Athens sails off without them." She was already scrolling back through her draft, finding the eleven ibids., deciding which ones would become Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 3.82 and which ones could just go, because half of them, she could see now, had been propping up sentences she hadn't actually earned. That was the uncomfortable part. The ibids. had let her hide, a little, behind the look of rigor. Shortening each citation meant naming, every single time, exactly what she was leaning on.

She began to type. The room went quiet except for the keys and the tick of the kitchen clock, and after a while her grandmother pulled out the other chair and sat down across from her with a crossword, not helping, just present. Twice Ava started to ask whether she should really trust a 2017 rule over fifty years of her grandfather's practice, and twice she decided the question answered itself, which did not stop it from circling back. She kept working anyway. Certainty about the rule didn't require certainty about everything, and maybe, she thought, deleting the last ibid., that was the whole difference between a draft and an argument: you committed to what you could verify and you were honest about the rest.

"Tea's gone cold," her grandmother said around midnight, standing, collecting the mug. She paused at the door with the orange manual under her arm, and Ava looked up from her bibliography, twenty-three entries now, alphabetized, formatted, repeatable by anyone who cared to check.

"Keep the book anyway," her grandmother said. "The old rules are in there too, if you ever need to know how he thought."

Ava set it on the table beside her laptop, spine cracked to the chapter on notes, and went back to typing Thucydides one more time.

Andrew arrived at the community art studio on the first Tuesday of October with a cardboard box of drawings he had made over three years, and the box was heavier than it looked. He set it on the long table near the window, where the afternoon light fell across the scarred wood in pale rectangles, and began lifting out the pieces one at a time. There were charcoal hands, a watercolor of the drainage ditch behind his house, four pen-and-ink moths pinned to imagined boards. The studio smelled of turpentine and old coffee, and someone's radio was playing low in the back room.

The portfolio course met twice a week for six sessions, and the teacher, a quiet woman named Ruth who wore paint under her fingernails the way other people wore rings, had said on the first day that they would each build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme. Ten, she had repeated, holding up both hands with the fingers spread. And with it, an artist's statement. Andrew had written the number in the margin of his notebook and underlined it twice.

His problem was the theme. Everything he had made was competent and nothing was connected. Priya, the girl across the table who worked in ink and spoke in short, definite sentences, suggested water, since two of his drawings involved rain. His mother, when he described the assignment at dinner, suggested family. Neither felt right, and he spent the second session pushing drawings around the table like a man trying to solve a puzzle with pieces from different boxes.

It was Priya who broke first. On the Thursday of the third week she slid a single sheet toward Ruth, a paragraph of careful cursive, and Ruth read it and passed it back with a small smile. "This is good," Ruth said, "but you keep calling yourself 'the artist.' The statement is written in the first person by the artist. Say 'I.'" Priya looked down at the page, at the phrase the artist chose to render, and began crossing out words with her pen. Andrew, watching from across the table, felt something shift in his understanding of the assignment, though he could not yet say what.

That night he sat at his desk at home and tried to write his own statement, and the same instinct took him. The artist explores themes of containment, he typed, and stopped. It sounded like a wall text from a museum, like a voice announcing him from a distance. He deleted it and tried again. I explore, he wrote, and the sentence immediately felt more exposed, more like a confession than a description. He closed the laptop and went to bed without finishing.

On Saturday he found his theme by accident. He had taken the bus to the studio early, before anyone else arrived, and was sorting through the box again when he noticed how many of his drawings were of things held inside other things: moths under glass, a fish in the drainage ditch's concrete channel, his grandmother's hands folded one inside the other in the last drawing he had made of her. He laid six pieces along the window ledge and saw the thread he had been sewing without knowing it. Containment, he wrote in his notebook. Places that hold things.

Ruth arrived while he was counting. "How many?" she asked, counting with her eyes. "Six that work," he said. "I need ten." She nodded and said the four he made next would be better than the six he already had, because now he would be making them on purpose. He thought about arguing, about defending the older pieces, but she was already moving on to the kiln room, and he let it go.

He worked through the next two sessions making four new pieces, and Priya stood over his shoulder once and said, "The moth one is scathing, in a quiet way." He wasn't sure that was what he meant, but he didn't dislike it. When Marcus, the oldest student in the class, told him the theme was brilliant in a voice that wanted complimenting back, Andrew only said thanks, because he had learned that year to recognize a sycophant and to give him nothing to feed on.

On the last Tuesday, Ruth read his statement aloud to herself while the class packed up. She paused at one line, where Andrew had written I am drawn to containers because I cannot decide whether they protect what is inside them or disenfranchise it from the world outside, and she read it twice. "That's the true sentence," she said. "The whole portfolio is the argument around that sentence, and you don't have to win it." Andrew looked at his ten pieces lined up on the wall, the moths and the ditch and his grandmother's folded hands, and then at the page in Ruth's hand where every sentence began with I.

He picked up his pencil and added, at the bottom of the statement, one more line: I still don't know. Then he carried the box to the window, where the light was already thinning, and began to photograph each piece in order.

The problem had followed Naomi home from robotics, and now it sat at the dinner table beside her, unnoticed by everyone else. Across the table her brother Theo was telling their parents about his group project, laughing a little as he described how his lab partner had mislabeled an entire data set and nobody had said anything until the grade came back. "We didn't want to make it weird," Theo said, spooning more rice. "So we all just let it ride."

Naomi put down her fork. "That's exactly what happened with us." She told them about Marisol, who had built the drive-train mount off spec twice, and how the whole team had praised her effort in the meeting afterward and said nothing about the spec. Then the mount failed the drop test on Thursday, in front of the judges, and Marisol had stood there red-faced while everyone pretended it was bad luck. "I said it was the plywood," Naomi said. "It wasn't the plywood."

Her mother tilted her head. "So why didn't anyone tell her?"

"Because she's my friend," Naomi said, and heard how thin it sounded the moment she said it. "Because she works harder than anyone and it felt like kicking her."

Theo, who was seventeen minutes older than Naomi and never let her forget it, was quiet for once. He pushed edamame around his plate. Their father launched into one of his garrulous stories about a colleague who had been "brutally honest" at work and made enemies for a decade, a story that circled the airport without landing, and Naomi stopped listening halfway through. She was thinking about Priya, the team captain, who had stayed after the meeting last week and said, quietly, "Somebody has to talk to her before regionals," and then looked at Naomi and left it there.

After dinner she went up to her room and called Priya. "I'll do it," Naomi said. "But I don't know how to say it without it being either nothing or cruel." Priya said she'd been reading something her mom left on the coffee table, a book from 2017 called Radical Candor, and that the whole idea was that good feedback meant caring personally about someone and challenging them directly, both at once, not one or the other. "That's it," Naomi said slowly. "That's the part I kept missing. I thought I had to choose."

She thought about it while she drafted a message and deleted it, then drafted again. Her old instinct, the nice one, would have produced some version of "the mount was so close, you tried so hard," which would instantiate exactly the silence that had already cost them one competition. The other extreme, the one her father's colleague practiced, was just an insult wearing a virtue costume. Somewhere between silence and insult there was a narrow path, and she couldn't quite see it, only feel where it wasn't.

Saturday morning she found Marisol in the shop before anyone else arrived, already sanding the new mount. Naomi's hands were cold. "Can I show you something before you cut that?" She laid the old mount on the bench next to the drawings. "See where the holes are a quarter inch off the spec line? That's what failed Thursday. Not the plywood, like I said. I lied about that, and I'm sorry." Marisol's jaw went tight, and Naomi kept going because stopping now would be its own kind of lie. "I'm telling you because you're the best builder we have and we need you at regionals, and because I should have said something three weeks ago instead of letting you walk into the drop test."

Marisol looked at the holes for a long time. Then she picked up the drawing and held it against the failed mount, and Naomi watched her see it, the small drift she must have measured around without noticing. "Why didn't anyone say anything," Marisol said, not quite a question. "I don't know," Naomi said. "I think we thought we were being kind." Marisol snorted, and marked the drawing with a pencil, twice. "Okay," she said. "Next time tell me the day I do it, not the day it breaks."

They cut the new mount together, both of them checking the spec line out loud before each pass of the saw, an arrangement so obvious in hindsight that Naomi almost laughed. It wasn't fixed, exactly; she could still feel a thin place in the air between them, and she didn't know whether it would close or harden by regionals. But when Marisol clamped the piece down and said "measure it again, and I mean actually say the number this time," Naomi read the dial and said, "Quarter inch on the line," and Marisol nodded once, like it was a kind of thanks.

The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and paper. Landon took a number from the dispenser, 47, and sat down beside his grandfather, who had already taken off his hat and set it on his knee like a small patient animal. The light above the tellers read 41. On the table in front of them lay two printed leases, one for an apartment on Gladstone Avenue and one for a unit above a laundromat on Weston Road. Landon had spread them out with the pages overlapping, a spreadsheet on his phone weighted on top.

He was here to open a student account, but the appointment was at eleven and it was ten forty, and his grandfather had said, "Might as well use the time," so here they were, using the time. Landon worked a pencil down the margin of the first lease. Rent, nine hundred and fifty. Utilities, hydro not included, water included. He wrote "hydro?" and underlined it twice.

"That one's a year lease," his grandfather said, tapping the Gladstone pages. "The other one's only eight months. Ends in April."

"That's worse, isn't it? Then I have to sign again and they can change things."

His grandfather tilted his hand back and forth, a gesture that meant neither yes nor no. In Ontario, he said, when a fixed-term lease ends, you don't have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month automatically, on the same terms. Landon stopped writing.

"Automatically?"

"Automatically. Same terms. You just keep paying and keep living there."

Landon looked at the eight-month lease with new attention. It was not a trap; it was a door that stayed open. He pulled the phone spreadsheet closer and started a second column beside the first, dividing the leases into what they cost per month and what they cost per month if the month-to-month part went on past the term. The numbers did not transmute into anything simpler. They stayed stubborn and particular.

Number 44 was called. A woman at the counter argued about a hold on a cheque, her voice carrying across the carpet. Landon's grandfather leaned over the second lease, the one above the laundromat, and read aloud in a murmur: "Tenant responsible for own utilities, all." "All" meant hydro, water, and heat, and heat above a laundromat in January was not a small thing, though the rent was sixty dollars less. Landon remembered his mother saying that a cheap apartment with utilities excluded was a peccadillo that could turn into a crisis by February, and he had not known what the word meant then and had looked it up, a small sin, a minor fault. He wrote "heat?? call" in the margin.

"So the eight-month one," he said slowly, "if I don't sign anything new, it just keeps going. Same rent, same everything."

"Same terms," his grandfather said. "That's what I said to Mrs. Okafor, when her landlord kept pushing papers at her. She didn't sign, and nothing happened. Nothing bad, I mean. She's still there."

"So a landlord pushing a new one-year lease isn't pushing something I need."

"You can sign if you want. Some people like the certainty. But you don't have to." His grandfather put his hat back on, then took it off again, a small restless cycle.

Landon added a third row to the spreadsheet: deposit, first and last month's rent, which both leases wanted, which meant the real cost of moving in was not the monthly cost at all. He had twelve thousand saved from two summers at the garden centre and a season of birthday cheques he had never spent, and the numbers in front of him were the first honest accounting of what independence actually charged. It was not a seismic realization, nothing so dramatic; it was arithmetic. But arithmetic, done properly, had its own weight. He underlined the total for the Gladstone apartment, one thousand and forty if hydro ran ninety a month, and the laundromat unit, nine hundred and ninety if heat and water together came in under a hundred and forty, which he did not know, and could not know from a bank chair.

That was the part that stayed uncertain. He could compare the leases line by line, but the utilities were guesses, and the guesses were the difference between them. He wrote both totals, circled neither, and turned the pencil over and over between his fingers.

"Forty-seven," the light said.

He gathered the pages, squaring their edges against the table. At the new-accounts desk a young banker named Priya asked for his student letter and his identification, and slid a form toward him with a pen chained to a clipboard. While she keyed his information into the computer, he laid the leases out again on the counter, because the surface was wider than the table had been.

"Moving out?" Priya asked, glancing at the pages.

"Comparing two places. One's eight months, one's a year. I'm trying to work out the real monthly cost with utilities, but the eight-month one I don't have to resign when it ends, it just goes month to month on the same terms, so the term doesn't really matter for the math."

"That's right," she said, stamping his form. "People get worried about that for no reason."

His grandfather stood, hat in hand, and looked at the two circled-and-uncircled totals upside down. "Which one?" he said.

Landon picked up the Gladstone lease, then set it back down and picked up the other one, the laundromat, with its unknown heat. He folded it once, along the line where he had written "call," and put it in his jacket pocket inside his grandfather's envelope of birthday money. "I'm going to ask them what last winter cost," he said, and shook Priya's hand across the counter.

Samuel's mother pulled into the far corner of the grocery store lot at seven on a Sunday, where the asphalt sloped gently toward the cart corrals and the only other car was a bakery van with its back doors open. She had chosen the hour deliberately, and she said so twice on the drive over, the way she said most things twice when she was nervous. "Empty lot, Samuel. Best we'll get." He didn't answer, because he was watching the slope. His father, who had driven trucks for eleven years before the office job, used to say that a parking lot is never flat, and Samuel had begun to internalize that, the way he had begun to internalize the feel of the steering wheel going lock to lock without looking at his hands.

What his mother wanted, though she framed it as a gift to him, was her Tuesday evenings back. Every week she drove his aunt Ruth to physical therapy forty minutes away, and every week she came home with a headache and a complaint about the headlights on the parkway. If Samuel passed his test on Thursday, he could share the driving, and she could close her eyes in the passenger seat for once. He knew this because she had mentioned it three times since the test was scheduled, always at the end, always casually, as if it were a footnote rather than the headline.

They set up two shopping carts as the car he would park behind, and a folded umbrella stood in for the one in front. "Pull up even with the cart," his mother said, reading from the state manual on her lap, "then turn the wheel all the way and back up till you're at forty-five degrees." Her voice had the careful flatness of someone reciting something she did not fully understand. Samuel did it twice, badly, clipping the umbrella with the rear tire, then once, well enough that neither of them said anything for a moment.

The trouble was the slope. The lot tilted toward the curb that ran along the cart corral, and each time he finished the park and lifted his foot off the brake, the car eased forward on its own, a slow deliberate drift, and he had to press down again. "It's just gravity," his mother said, which was the kind of statement that explained nothing and somehow still helped. On his fourth attempt he brought the car to rest exactly where he wanted it, close to the curb, front end neatly in, and sat there with the engine idling and his hands still on the wheel, feeling something that was almost competence.

"Which way are your wheels pointing?" his mother asked. She was looking at the manual again, but he had the sense she was testing him rather than reading. He looked down through the windshield as if he could see them, which of course he couldn't. The car faced downhill. There was a curb a foot to his right. He thought about his father's trucks, about wheel chocks, about the way heavy things behaved when you stopped holding them.

"Toward the curb," he said. "If the wheels are toward the curb and the brakes fail, the car rolls into the curb. Not into traffic." He heard his own voice say it and realized he had never actually said it aloud before; he had read it once in the manual, weeks ago, half-asleep, and it had sat in him since, waiting. His mother lowered the booklet and looked at the front wheel, tilted her head, and turned the page to check. "That's it," she said. "Exactly that." He turned the wheel to make it true, and felt the small click of the position settle, and the car sat there against the slope like it had made a decision.

Afterward they drove to the highway, because the test included a merge and the merge frightened him more than any parking maneuver. His mother's plan was the on-ramp by the mall, three lanes, moderate traffic. The trouble with merging, as far as Samuel could tell, was that other drivers were capricious; the same man who slowed to let you in on Tuesday would accelerate to close a gap on Wednesday, and there was no way to know in advance which version of him you were getting. On the ramp he checked the mirror, the blind spot, the mirror again, and a blue hatchback let him in with a small forgiving dip of its headlights, and he was on the highway, doing sixty, his mother saying "good, good, stay in this lane."

He did it four more times, looping off at the next exit and back around, and by the third loop the fear had rearranged itself into something more like attention. He wasn't calm, exactly, but he was no longer guessing. You watched the traffic and made a judgment and committed to it, and if the judgment was wrong you adjusted, and the adjusting was the actual skill, not the judgment. That was not in the manual. His father had a taped index card above his old desk that read, in handwriting Samuel had never been able to date, "Slow is smooth and smooth is fast," and Samuel had always found it a little smug, the kind of epigram that sounds wiser than it is, but somewhere on the fourth loop he thought he understood what it was trying to say and forgave it.

On the drive back to the lot he parked between the two carts one last time, on the slope, close to the curb, and turned the front wheels toward it without being asked. His mother watched him do it and closed the manual. "Tuesday," she said. "Aunt Ruth's appointment is at four. You'd drive there, I'd drive back." He nodded, and left the wheels where they were, and put on the handbrake, and they sat in the idling car in the empty corner of the lot while the bakery van pulled away and the first Sunday shoppers began to arrive.

The kitchen table still had flour on it from her mother's baking, so Ella spread her physics worksheet on top of a tea towel. It was Sunday evening, two days before the exam, and the problem on the page showed two parallel plates, 0.02 metres apart, connected to a 100 volt supply. Find the electric field strength at a point between them.

She worked it in pencil. Voltage divided by distance; that much she remembered from the board at school, though Mr. Okafor had written it in a hurry at the end of the period and someone had asked a question she hadn't caught. She set out 100 divided by 2, because the problem also said, in smaller print, 2 centimetres. The answer came out as 50. She wrote it in the box, looked at it, and felt the particular unease of a number that seemed too polite to be true.

Her brother Daniel came in and opened the fridge, which he did whenever he wanted an audience. He was nineteen and a self-declared raconteur, currently between jobs and generous with stories about them. "You look like the equation bit you," he said, pulling out the milk.

"It's this plates question. I got fifty, but Priya texted me something completely different and she's never wrong." Ella turned her phone so he could see. Priya's message read: it should be in the thousands, check your units.

Daniel drank from the carton, which their mother had told him about a hundred times. "Units," he repeated. "That's your whole problem in life, honestly. You read the first number and stop."

She almost threw the tea towel at him. Instead she sat still for a moment and did what her maths teacher had once suggested, which was to introspect before rewriting anything: look at the steps, not the answer. The problem said 0.02 metres. She had used the 2 centimetres line underneath, the helpful conversion someone had printed for convenience, and divided by 2 instead of 0.02. Centimetres were not metres. The gap in her working sat there like a stone in a riverbed, obvious once the water dropped.

She rubbed out the 50 and divided again. 100 divided by 0.02 came out as 5,000. The field between the plates was 5,000 volts per metre, not fifty of anything. Her hundredfold error had come from the unconverted unit, a hundred centimetres hiding inside every metre. She wrote the correct line in pen this time and texted Priya back: got it, five thousand, thanks.

"Five thousand," she said aloud, mostly to the answer. "That's a lot of volts per metre for something the size of a matchbox."

Daniel leaned over her shoulder. "So if the plates were further apart, same battery, the field would be weaker? Like spreading the same hundred volts thinner?"

She hadn't thought of it that way, and she turned it over while he watched, wanting to be sure before she agreed. "Same hundred volts, bigger gap, fewer volts per metre. Yes." It was strange to her that the battery's push and the space it crossed were two separate things, one fixed and the other chosen, and that the field lived in the division between them. She still couldn't picture what the field actually was, only what it did, and she wrote a small question mark in the margin beside the word field, to ask Mr. Okafor on Tuesday.

Their mother came in from the garden with mud on her wrists, complaining that the allotment's lower patch had flooded again, alluvial soil, she said, lovely when it drains and a swamp when it doesn't. She washed her hands at the sink and glanced at the worksheet drying on the towel. "Sorted?" she asked.

"Sorted," Ella said. "Except the part I can't see." She put the question mark in the margin, then took it out again, then put it back, and left the pen lying open beside it.

The library smelled of radiator dust and old glue, and Grayson had claimed the table by the window where the afternoon light came in flat and gray. He spread out a sheet of graph paper he had drawn himself, a parabola copied carefully from the textbook: y equals x squared, running from zero to one, a shallow curve hugging the bottom of the page and then climbing. His calculus test was in four days, and he still did not believe what the book claimed about it. He had underlined the sentence twice and then, feeling ridiculous, underlined it a third time. The area under that curve, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, was exactly one third.

He counted the little squares under the curve. Whole ones first, then the broken ones at the edge, guessing at halves and quarters, tallying in the margin the way his grandfather had taught him two summers ago. His grandfather kept a jar of pencil stubs on the workbench and believed every hard thing could be softened by counting. "Count the squares," the old man had said, showing Grayson how to estimate the paint needed for a crooked wall, the seed for a garden bed. "Count them and then trust your counting." Grayson's tally came to about thirty-four squares, and since the full unit square held a hundred, that was close enough to a third to sting. He had hoped, in some part of himself, that the counting would disagree.

Behind him, two chairs scraped. Priya and Marcus from his class settled at the next table with their review packets, and Priya immediately leaned over his shoulder.

"Is that graph paper? For calculus?"

"Estimating," Grayson said. "Squares under the curve. My grandfather's method."

Marcus picked up the sheet, tilting it toward the window. "That's the most perspicacious thing I've seen all week, and also the slowest. You know the integral does this in one line."

"That's the problem," Grayson said. "It does it in one line and I don't believe it. One line feels like a trick. Counting feels like looking."

Priya sat down across from him, uninvited, which was how she did most things. "So look, then count, then argue with yourself. That's what my sister says college is." She pulled his textbook over and found the antiderivative rules, then turned the page to the section on parametrized curves. "Also, you're going to need this next chapter. When you parametrize a curve, you describe it with a variable instead of y versus x. It's the same curve wearing different clothes."

Grayson copied the integral onto his own paper, the long S-shape of it, the x squared sitting inside, the limits 0 and 1 written small at top and bottom. He worked it through the rule the book gave, arrived at one third, wrote it, and sat back. Then he counted his squares again, more carefully, correcting a tally mark he had doubled. Thirty-three squares and a scrap. One third of a hundred. The two methods had arrived at the same number from opposite directions, one by chopping the world into pieces and adding them up, one by a rule that fell out of symbols like water down a pipe.

"Except the integral is exact," Marcus said, watching his face. "Your squares are you squinting."

"Exact how, though," Grayson said. "I followed the rule and got the answer the book wanted. If I'd gotten something else, I'd have gone back and found my mistake. So did I find out it's one third, or did I find out that I can follow a recipe?" He tapped the graph paper. "My grandfather counted squares on walls for fifty years and his paint never ran short. He trusted the pieces. I want to trust the pieces and the recipe. I just don't know yet what I'm allowed to trust."

Priya had stopped writing her own review. She was quiet for a moment, which was rare enough that Marcus looked up too. "My mom does that," she said. "Physics. She says the curve never touches its asymptote but you still build the whole plane around it." She slid the graph paper back toward him. "Maybe exact isn't the point. Maybe the counting is how you keep yourself honest while the symbols do the fast part."

The radiator ticked. Somewhere behind the shelves a cart of returned books rolled and stopped. Grayson took out a clean sheet and drew the parabola again, but this time he shaded the region beneath it lightly with the side of his pencil, the whole curving wedge of it, and wrote one third beside it in his grandfather's stubby-pencil script, small and square. He would call the old man tonight and tell him the squares had been right, nearly right, right enough. Then, under that, he wrote the integral too, and between the two, nothing, a blank space where the argument between them lived. He looked at the page for a long moment, then folded it in half and put it in his backpack, outer pocket, where he could reach it on the bus.

"Same table tomorrow?" Priya asked, gathering her things as the lights along the ceiling began their warning flicker.

"Bring graph paper," Grayson said. "I want to count the squares under one more curve."

Rosalie set the double boiler on the stove before her mother left for the late shift, and by seven the kitchen smelled like a candy shop, which was exactly the problem. She was trying to smell nothing at all. The recipe she'd found online, printed and annotated in her looping hand, said chocolate was chemistry before it was cooking, and chemistry did not care how charming the kitchen smelled. She had a thermometer, a marble slab borrowed from Mrs. Okafor next door, and three hundred grams of dark couverture she had bought with her tutoring money after her father said, gently, that this particular obsession could wait until she was earning.

It could not wait, because Sana's birthday was Saturday, and Sana had announced, in the cafeteria, with the casual cruelty of a best friend, that she was tired of store-bought things. "Anyone can buy a box," she had said. "You're the one who's always going on about process." Rosalie had not gone on about process, exactly, but she had once spent forty minutes explaining why she'd redone a lab three times, so the accusation had landed somewhere near truth.

The first batch seized in the bowl, turning from silk to gravel while she stirred. The second she scorched, misreading the thermometer in the steam. By the third she had learned to be patient with the melt, dragging the spatula slowly, waiting for the temperature to climb like a fever that had to peak. Then came the part the forums argued about: the seeding, the tabling, the arguments about method that people would expatiate on for thousands of words, each convinced their way was the only one. Rosalie had read four of these essays and closed her laptop, because the arguing was the opposite of helpful. What she needed was one true thing to hold onto, and she'd found it buried in a comment thread: properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.

That was her test, she decided. Not shine, not the snap, not the folklore. Shrinkage. If the chocolate pulled away from the plastic mould as it hardened, it was real; if it clung, she had failed and would have to begin again with the last of her couverture, which was not enough for a full batch.

She poured the third batch into the moulds, tapped out the bubbles, and slid them into the cool pantry. Then she sat on the kitchen floor with her phone, texting Sana about nothing, about the history quiz, about whether Mr. Iyer would actually collect the outlines he'd assigned, because waiting for chocolate was like waiting for anything: better done while pretending to do something else.

When she checked, forty minutes later, one mould had released. She turned it over, tapped it once, and a bar dropped into her palm with a sound like a knuckle cracking, clean and bright, its surface gleaming even under the pantry's dull bulb. The other mould held fast. She turned it, tapped, tapped harder, and nothing moved; the chocolate was dull where it met the plastic, and when she finally pried a piece out with a knife, it bent rather than snapped and left a smear on the plastic like evidence of a crime. She stood at the counter holding both pieces, one perfect and one ruined, from the same bowl, poured minutes apart, and understood that she had not actually failed or succeeded. She had half succeeded, which was somehow more instructive and more infuriating.

She thought about her father's taxonomy of worthwhile pursuits, the unspoken one: practical things at the top, uncertain things at the bottom, and her chocolate somewhere in the basement beside her abandoned violin and the summer she'd spent learning to juggle. He wasn't cruel about it. He just asked, each time, whether it would lead anywhere, and she never had an answer that satisfied him, because the honest answer was that she didn't make things to arrive somewhere. She made them to find out whether she could. But sitting on the kitchen floor now, she could see his side of it too, could see why a man who worked two jobs might look at a marble slab on loan from a neighbor and see a grandiose production built around a birthday gift, when a card would have done. Both views were true at once, and she could not resolve them, and she found, testing the feeling the way she'd test a temperature, that she didn't entirely want to.

She had maybe a hundred and fifty grams left. Not enough for a full batch of moulds, but enough for one careful attempt, if she was exact. She washed the marble slab, melted the remaining chocolate with the failed pieces stirred back in, and worked it across the cool stone with the spatula, watching for the moment the gloss began to thicken, when the fluid turned fudgy at the edges. Her arms ached. It was past eleven. She brought it back to temperature, poured it into the one clean mould, and set it in the pantry with the discipline of someone who had already learned what impatience cost.

At midnight she turned the mould over and tapped. For a second nothing happened, and she felt the whole evening tilt toward ruin. Then the bar slid free, glossy and whole, and shrank slightly in her palm, smaller than the cavity that had held it, as though it had decided to release itself.

She texted Sana a photo of the bar with no caption, then wrapped it in parchment paper and set it on the counter for morning, next to a note for her father that said only, "Try one. They snap."

Katherine had the practice exam open on the kitchen table and her phone propped against the sugar bowl, replaying the video from the museum field trip. On the screen, a docent in a dour grey uniform held a sealed tube above a beaker of ice water while a cluster of eleventh graders leaned in. The gas inside the tube was brown, the brown of weak tea left steeping too long, and as the tube sank into the ice it began, unmistakably, to pale.

"Rewind it again?" her brother Danny asked, dragging his chair closer with a screech. He had a cold and had been assigned to the kitchen table for quarantine purposes, and he had opinions about everything on her screen.

"You've seen it four times."

"It looks like the tube's emptying. Where does it go?"

"Nowhere. That's the whole point." She said it with more confidence than she had. On Saturday, standing in front of that actual tube with condensation fogging the glass, she had felt something assemble itself in her head, the same click she got when a sentence in an essay finally found its shape. The brown gas was nitrogen dioxide. The colourless stuff it turned into was dinitrogen tetroxide. The reaction between them gave off heat. Cold water pushed it one way, and warm water pushed it back, because when she had watched the docent move the tube into a bath of hot water, the brown had flooded back, deeper than before.

The practice question was the problem. It described a sealed tube of the same gas and asked what happened when it was cooled. Katherine had written, in her first attempt on Sunday, that the mixture would turn darker brown. She had reasoned that cooling slowed everything down, so whatever was happening would simply be less of it, paler by dilution of effort. Mr. Okafor had marked it wrong with a single red slash and written "come see me," and she had not come see him, because she wanted to work it out herself first, which was either discipline or pride and she suspected both.

"Okay," she said, pulling a fresh sheet toward her. "Watch. I'm going to do it out loud so you can catch me if I'm being stupid."

"You're always being stupid," Danny said, but he said it around a spoonful of cereal, which softened it.

"The forward reaction, brown to colourless, gives off heat." She drew two boxes and an arrow, then a second arrow curving back. "So heat is like a product. If I cool the tube down, I'm pulling heat out, and the system makes more of it." She paused. It sounded too tidy, like one of those essay arguments that worked only because she wanted it to. "But that's the thing I got wrong before. I thought cold meant everything slows."

"So which is it?"

She looked at the video, frozen on the pale tube in the ice bath. The evidence was right there, stubborn and uninterested in her reasoning. The tube had gone pale in the cold and dark when it was warmed, which meant cooling pushed toward the colourless side. "It's both, kind of. The molecules slow down, but the balance shifts too, and the shift wins for the colour." She wrote it out: cooled, paler; warmed, darker brown. Then, underneath, the part Mr. Okafor would actually be grading: the system responds to the change by shifting to counteract it.

"That's a dialectic," Danny said, with the authority of a fourteen-year-old who had learned the word two weeks ago in English and deployed it hourly.

"That is not what that word means."

"It's two opposite things fighting and the answer comes out of the fight."

She opened her mouth to correct him and then closed it, because he wasn't entirely wrong, and she hated that. What she liked about the principle was that it wasn't a formula, it was a way of holding two facts in tension: the reaction is exothermic, and the temperature changed, and the answer lives between them.
