She let him have it, partly because she was tired of arguing with him and partly because a small, ungenerous part of her wanted to watch the ball drop short so she could be right in peace. He fired. The ball climbed, a lazy, towering path that seemed to promise everything, hung for a moment at the top, and then came down and struck the ground at almost exactly the same tile. Marcus walked over and stood on the spot. He walked back and stood where the first ball had landed. He put a pebble on each mark and looked at her.

"Same place," he said. "That's broken. The launcher's broken."

Annabelle crouched at the two pebbles and measured the gap between them with her hand, which came to about the width of her palm, close enough that a windy day or a careless read could account for it. In her notebook she had been separating each launch into horizontal and vertical components, the method Mr. Okafor had drilled until it felt less like math and more like a filing system, a taxonomy of motion where sideways and up-down lived in separate drawers and never touched. She had trusted the drawers without ever wondering what they meant together. Now she looked at the two pebbles and felt the drawers sliding open at once.

"Thirty and sixty," she said slowly. "They add up to ninety." She said it again to hear it outside her head, then fired the launcher herself at forty-five to have a third mark, which landed past both pebbles, and she stood over the three points in the fading light not saying anything, because she did not yet want to predicate an answer on two measurements and a hunch. Marcus asked her what ninety had to do with anything, and she said she didn't know yet, exactly, only that the numbers were not a coincidence, and he pulled his sweatshirt around himself and waited, which for Marcus was a kind of apology.

While she fired the two angles a second and third time to see if the pebbles kept agreeing, she found herself thinking about last spring, when she had dropped the idea of tutoring at the writing center in order to take a second science elective. She had told herself then that physics was the practical choice, that she preferred problems with answers, though the truer reason was that the boy who ran the writing center had once laughed at a poem of hers in front of the whole table, and she had never decided whether leaving was cowardice or hygiene. She still hadn't decided. The balls kept landing on the same tile, and the question kept not resolving, and she let both of those things simply be true.

She packed the launcher while Marcus retrieved the last yellow ball from under the slide. At the gate he stopped and turned the dial back and forth between thirty and sixty, and she saw something shift in his face, the same shift she had felt at the pebbles.

"Do it again," he said. "From thirty. I want to watch it this time."

The projection screen in room 214 had a yellow stain in its lower corner, shaped like a small country, and while the rest of the class shuffled worksheets Carson kept looking at it, comparing it to the wound in the painting behind it. Ms. Okoye had put up Kahlo's self-portrait with the thorn necklace, the hummingbird dead at her throat, and had said only, "Formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Take twenty minutes, then we talk." No further instruction. Carson wanted the twenty minutes to produce something worth saying out loud, which was a different want from wanting to understand the painting, though he couldn't yet explain the difference.

He began the way the worksheet told him to: palette, balance, focal points. The background was vegetal, a wall of leaves so green it felt pressurized, closing in on the figure from both sides. The foreground was flesh and blood, the warm brown of her skin against the cool dark animals. He wrote that the green transmute line and crossed it out. Wrote again: the greens transmute the background from setting into pressure. That was better. The colour stopped being scenery and became something acting on her body.

Across the room, Priya was writing fast, which usually meant she had landed on an argument. When the timer went off she put her pen down and raised her hand before Ms. Okoye could even ask. "Kahlo is a Surrealist," Priya said, standing halfway. "The dead hummingbird, the thorn vine, the monkey staring out. It's dream logic. Breton called her work a ribbon around a bomb."

"That's a real quote," said Marcus from the back, not standing, not raising his hand. "But she rejected the label. Kahlo said she didn't paint dreams, she painted her own reality. So calling her a Surrealist is exactly what she said not to do."

"She can't just opt out of her own movement."

"It's not her movement if she said no to it."

Ms. Okoye folded her arms, which Carson had learned was her way of handing the room to them, and he understood suddenly that the fight was his problem now, because he had spent the twenty minutes with the painting in a way neither of them quite had. He raised his hand. "Can I read my notes?"

"Please," said Ms. Okoye.

He stood, paper shaking slightly in his hand, and worked through it aloud. The composition first: the figure dead centre, frontal, symmetrical almost to the millimetre, everything in the background paired, two leaves, two butterflies, two eyes of the cat. Surrealism, at least as he understood it from the Dali prints in the hallway, leaned on rupture and drift, things placed where they shouldn't be. This painting insisted on order. The strangeness wasn't in the arrangement; it was in the stakes. Then the colour: how the littoral quality of the light, that pale haze where sea meets land, softened the leaves so the violence of the thorns arriving at her neck felt almost quiet, which made it worse, not better. Then the symbols, which he said he couldn't fully read. "The hummingbird is dead and it's black and it hangs where a pendant would go. I know it means something. I can't tell you what."

"So it's Surrealist," Priya said, softer now, like she was testing whether the word still fit.

"I think it's an amalgam," Carson said. "It takes Surrealist objects, the bird, the thorns, the monkey, but it refuses the Surrealist composition. And Breton's quote actually works both ways, if you let it. A ribbon around a bomb. The ribbon is the symmetry and the soft light. The bomb is what's underneath. Breton meant it as praise for a movement she then rejected, but the description might still be true even if the label isn't." He heard himself say might and decided to leave it there instead of smoothing it over. "I don't know which part of the painting to trust more, the calm or the wound. That's honest. That's where I am."

Marcus was nodding slowly, not in agreement exactly, more like someone recalibrating. Priya had pulled her worksheet back toward her and was drawing a line through her opening sentence.

Ms. Okoye said nothing for a moment, then clicked to the next slide, a Kahlo painting of a hospital bed floating in a void. "Same method," she said. "Twenty minutes."

Carson sat down and read his own last line again. Then he picked up his pen, turned the paper over, and wrote at the top of the blank side: a ribbon around a bomb, and under it, twice, the words trust and wound, waiting to see which one the new painting argued for.

The line outside the community centre had begun to form before six, when the sky over the car park was still the grey of an unwashed window, and Charlie stationed herself near the door with a clipboard she was not entirely sure she needed. Her job was simple: greet voters, direct them to the correct table, and keep the queue moving. She was sixteen, three years too young to vote, and had taken the volunteer shift anyway because her mother had said that watching democracy was the next best thing to practising it, and because Charlie wanted, with a fierceness she did not fully understand, to know what she would be walking into when her turn finally came.

Priya arrived at half past seven, slipping through the doors with a canvas bag of pastries for the volunteers, though she lingered by Charlie's table instead of leaving. Priya's family had moved here three autumns ago, and she still spoke about politics the way other people spoke about weather, as something that changed your plans whether you liked it or not. "Back home," she said, peeling the foil off a pastry, "we're having an election too. The prime minister called it early. She has to, if she loses the confidence of parliament." Charlie filed that phrase away, confidence of parliament, the way she filed formulas before a test, without yet knowing where it fit.

Marcos came at nine with his grandmother, a small woman in a green coat who voted first and then waited on a folding chair by the noticeboard, reading every poster twice. Marcos had lived here for two years and still kept a photograph of the presidential palace in his pencil case, which Charlie knew because he had shown it to the whole class in September. He drifted over to Priya and Charlie during a lull, and somehow, in the way of conversations between people standing too long in one place, they began to argue about which system was better, parliamentary or presidential, each of them defending the country they knew.

"You can get rid of our leader in weeks," Priya said. "If parliament decides it doesn't have confidence in her, she's finished. A vote, and she's out." Marcos folded his arms. "That's chaos. Our president serves the full term. The whole country votes for the president directly, separately from the congress, on a fixed day, for a fixed number of years. You can't just kick her out because congress disagrees with her." He said it with the flat certainty of someone reciting gravity. Priya opened her mouth to object, then closed it, which for Priya was remarkable.

Charlie had been half listening, mesmerized by the rhythm of the queue, the shuffling feet, the soft clatter of the stamp at table two, and the argument pulled her back like a hand on her sleeve. "So wait," she said slowly, turning the clipboard over in her hands. "The difference isn't who votes. It's whether the leader's job depends on keeping the parliament happy." She looked from one to the other. "Priya's prime minister can be removed if parliament turns on her. Marcos's president can't be, not just for that. The president is elected separately, for a fixed term, and stays even when the legislature hates her." Marcos nodded; Priya, after a moment, nodded too.

"It means our elections are about everything at once," Priya said. "Party, leader, platform, all in one vote. Yours are two separate votes." "And ours means the president doesn't have to panic every time congress gets bellicose," Marcos said, glancing toward his grandmother, who had overheard the word and raised an eyebrow at him. Charlie laughed despite herself. The same fact seemed to open in two directions at once: one system made a leader accountable day by day, the other made her stable year by year, and she could not see how a country got to have both.

The presiding officer leaned out of the back room and called that a ballot box at table four had jammed, and that it had to be cleared before the noon rush or they would lose an hour of voting, and would Charlie bring the spare seal and the logbook. She went, and Priya and Marcos came with her, and for ten minutes the three of them knelt on the linoleum under the fluorescent lights, coaxing the mechanism loose while the officer recorded each step, and Marcos's grandmother offered, from her folding chair, the observation that in her village they had once counted votes by lamplight because the power had failed, and nobody had thought to complain. The box gave way at last with a click, the seal went on, and the first voters of the noon rush were already filing in.

At eight that evening, when the doors were locked and the counting began, Charlie sat on the stage steps between Priya and Marcos, watching the officers open the boxes under the pool of lamplight as though excavating a stratum of the day, layer after layer of folded paper, each one a private decision now becoming a public number. Priya leaned against the wall with her phone in her lap, waiting for news from home, where the counting had already begun. Marcos had his phone open to the palace photograph again. "I still think ours is better," he said quietly. "I still think ours is," Priya said, and neither of them sounded angry anymore. Charlie said nothing, because she had not decided; she only knew that in three years she would walk through these doors herself, and that she would be thinking, all the way to the booth, about what exactly her one vote was choosing. The officer called out the first total, and all three of them leaned forward to hear it.

The whiteboard behind pit table fourteen had two words on it in his own handwriting, O(log n), circled twice, and Mathis could no longer remember which of the three energy drinks had been responsible for writing it. What he remembered was the problem: the robot's autonomous routine had to look up a motor power value in a sorted table of sensor readings, and at the last practice it had stalled for the full thirty seconds, wheel jerking, doing nothing. The table had a thousand and twenty-four rows. He had been checking them one by one.

"Team, huddle," said Priya, spinning a marker between her fingers. "Counselor wants our algorithm choice before the qualifier round. What's the scribble?"

Mathis looked at the circle. Two days ago it had meant something obvious, and now the obviousness had drained out of it like heat from a Thermos. "It's the other way to search," he said slowly, testing each word as he said it. "If the list is sorted, you don't start at the top. You look at the middle, decide which half your answer is in, throw the other half away, and do it again."

"Waste half the table every time?" Dev said. "That sounds worse."

"Smaller waste, fewer times." He picked up the marker and drew a bar, split it, split the remaining half again. His hand kept going until the slivers were thinner than the marker. Somewhere in the back of his mind a question surfaced, the kind he liked: how few cuts would it actually take? He wrote 10 beside the last sliver, then scratched it out, then wrote it again.

He had been doing it the slow way for three competitions, he realized. Not because the slow way was good, but because the slow way came first, and habits calcify around whatever you happened to build at two in the morning. He'd been the one who wrote the lookup code, so he'd defended the lookup code, and nobody had pushed back hard enough to crack it.

"Before we vote," said the counselor, Ms. Okafor, leaning over the table with her clipboard, "somebody explain the notation. The whole room should hear it."

Priya pointed at Mathis. "He wrote it."

Mathis felt his ears go warm. But the question was fair, and he had asked it of himself in the shower that morning, and half an answer was already sitting there. "The way we do it now is called linear search. Programmers describe it as O(n), which means its work grows in step with the list. Double the rows, double the looking." He tapped the circle. "Binary search is O(log n), which means its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size. The list can get huge and the work barely moves."

"What's a logarithm," said Dev, flatly.

"A thing I'm going to relearn at eleven p.m. tonight," Mathis said, and Ms. Okafor laughed into her clipboard.

The vote was four to one, Dev voting no on principle. Then came the part nobody put on the highlight reel: Mathis wrote the function in twelve minutes and it looped forever on the practice rig, the cursor of the debug display frozen between two rows, and he sat with his chin in his hands while the ceiling fans pushed the turbid air of the gymnasium around, air that smelled like solder and Gatorade and the specific genus of panic that only arrives when your own code stares back at you. Priya found it, not him. "Your middle rounds down," she said, "so when you're down to two rows, the middle is the first one, and you keep cutting to the same half forever." He changed one character, a less-than to a less-than-or-equal, and the robot ran the routine in a time so short the display had to be refreshed to show it.

In the queue for the qualifier, Dev knocked his shoulder against Mathis's. "So if the table was a million rows."

"Twenty cuts. Roughly."

"A million rows, twenty looks."

"That's the shape of it."

Dev shook his head like a person refusing to believe in a magic trick he had just watched up close. The queue moved forward, and their robot sat on the field mat with its claw folded, and Mathis thought about how he still couldn't say, exactly, why halving a list led to logarithms rather than something else, only that it did, the way water finds the low corner of a tray. The announcer called their team number.

"Drive team, you're up in ninety seconds," Priya said, and held out the controller.

Claire had requisitioned the gym for every afternoon that week, and the slip of paper from the main office, signed in the vice principal's cramped hand, felt like the first real proof that she was directing anything at all. The one-act was hers: she had chosen it, cut it, cast it, and now six classmates in sneakers stood on the taped rectangle she had measured out as the stage, waiting for her to tell them where to go. The performance was Friday night, in front of parents and the drama club and Mr. Halvorsen, who had handed her the script in September with the casual cruelty of a person who had never had to learn anything new.

"Okay," she said, standing where the audience would sit, in the bleachers' shadow. "Dev, when Nadia says her line about the letter, I want you to cross left. Just walk left, and it'll read as you leaving the conversation before you actually leave."

Dev crossed to the right.

"No, left," Claire said. "My left. Other way."

He stopped in the middle of the stage with his arms slightly out, a boy stranded between two directions that both claimed to be true. "That is left," he said. "You're facing me. Your left is over there."

Nadia, who had done two musicals at the community theater, sat down on an imaginary chair and began unlacing her shoe. "Stage left and stage right are from the actor's point of view," she said, not looking up. "Facing the audience. So they're backwards from yours."

Claire stood very still. In her notebook she had written an entire page of blocking, every entrance and cross and turn, using left and right the way she used them in the hallway, the way anyone facing forward used them. Three days of planning, and all of it was a mirror image of what she had meant. "Okay," she said again, because the word bought her a second. "So when I say left, you assume I mean stage left. Which is the actor's left. Which is my right."

"Welcome to theater," Nadia said, and re-laced her shoe.

The reversal was not just a mistake to be corrected; it kept unfolding in Claire's head like a proof she couldn't stop. She was the one facing the actors, so her language had to turn around, had to describe the world from inside someone else's body facing the opposite way. Directing, apparently, meant speaking from a position she did not occupy. She flipped her notebook page by page, rewriting every direction, and the actors ran the scene twice more while she learned to say "right" and point left, her arm crossing her body like a fencer's parry.

By Thursday the blocking held, but the scene had gone dead, and Claire knew it was her fault. She had been so afraid of a wrong turn that she had stopped the actors every ten seconds, and Dev, who had been excited in September, had gone disaffected, delivering his lines at the floor with the flatness of a kid serving detention. His elocution was perfect, that was the bitter part, every consonant crisp and every pause placed, and it meant nothing because he had stopped caring whether anyone believed him.

"Run it once without me stopping you," she said. "Whatever happens, keep going. Even if you fall off the stage."

They ran it. Dev moved through her blocking exactly as written, precise and lifeless, and Nadia watched him with something that was not quite pity. At the line about the letter, Dev crossed stage left as instructed, and then, halfway across, he stopped and turned back toward Nadia, inventing a hesitation Claire had never asked for, holding the letter above her head so Claire couldn't take it. It was good. It was better than anything in her notebook.

"Keep that," she called, and felt the peculiar doubled sensation again, giving an instruction she could only verify from the actor's side of the room.

Afterward, while the others gathered their bags, Dev hung back. "So tomorrow," he said, "when you say left, which left do you mean?"

"Stage left," she said. "Yours. I've been living on your side of the stage all week, more or less." She believed it, too, though she suspected that under pressure tomorrow she would point and trust her arm over her mouth, and she could not honestly say which side of the mirror she would end up directing from.

Friday night the gym filled. The taped stage sat beneath the far basket, and Claire stood where she had stood all week, out front, facing her actors. The house lights dimmed, the recorded music started, and Dev walked on from stage right, paused, and crossed to stage left, his own hesitation intact, the letter lifted high.

From behind her, in the dark, she heard a parent whisper, "Why does he keep going the wrong way?"

The basement smelled like dryer sheets and old carpet, and Dev's laptop sat on a folding table between a deflated air mattress and a box of holiday lights nobody had ever strung. Hannah had agreed to come over because the first CS assignment was due Monday and she had told herself, all through orientation week, that she would not be the person who started behind. Dev had claimed the class would be easy. Dev had also claimed the basement was ventilated.

"So the class is called Student," Hannah said, typing. "Private fields. Name and age. That's the whole spec, plus getters." She wrote the fields first, the way the slides did, then started the constructor. Her fingers knew roughly where the keys were, which was more than she could say for the syntax. Around them, Dev's younger brother was playing something loud upstairs, a soundtrack of distant explosions that the floor transmitted faithfully.

"Private means nobody outside can touch the fields directly," Dev said, scrolling his phone. "You have to go through the getters. Encapsulation. The professor spent forty minutes on it." Dev had a way of prognosticating about courses,declaring which would be blowoffs and which would ruin everyone's lives, on evidence no stronger than a syllabus. So far his record was mixed.

Hannah typed the constructor. She gave the parameters the same names as the fields, because that seemed tidy, and she wrote name = name; and age = age; and felt the small satisfaction of lines that looked like they meant something. She wrote the getters, wrote a main method that made a Student and printed the name, and ran it.

The output said null.

She stared at it. She ran it again, as though the program might have been distracted the first time. Null again. She checked the print statement, then the getter, then the constructor, reading each line out loud in the flat voice of someone who suspects she is being tricked but can't locate the trick. "Student s = new Student. Hannah, eighteen. s.getName. It prints null." She looked over at Dev, who had set the phone down with the reluctance of someone closing a good article.

"Wait," Hannah said. She highlighted the constructor's parameter. "It's called name. And the field is called name." She copied the line into the chat window where she'd been keeping notes for herself, stared at name = name, and understood, slowly and with a certain indignation, that the two names on either side of the equals sign were the same name, that she had assigned the parameter to itself, and that the field had never been involved at all. "It's just handing the parameter back to itself. The field never gets anything." Dev leaned in and nodded slowly, the nod of a person who had definitely done this exact thing and had never once mentioned it.

"So how do you even tell them apart," Hannah said, mostly to the room. She scrolled, found nothing in her notes, then tried the thing she'd half noticed in one of the lecture slides, the word this with a dot in front of the left-hand name. "this," she said, typing it. "This. What, this name? This one here?" She wrote this.name = name; ran it again, and the output said Hannah, plain and correct, and she sat back and let out a breath she hadn't fully admitted to holding. "Okay. So this-dot means the object's own field. When the parameter has the same name." Dev said, "Huh," in the tone of a man observing weather.

She fixed age the same way and then, because she didn't trust anything anymore, wrote a second test that changed nothing and printed both values, then a third that made a second Student with different values and printed both students, to make sure the first one's fields hadn't somehow leaked into the second's. They hadn't. She pushed the laptop back a few inches, the way you push back a chessboard after a game that went better than expected but that you did not entirely understand.

Dev, who had spent the last ten minutes as a detractor of nothing so much as his own unopened assignment, opened his laptop and began copying her constructor line for line. Hannah watched him do it and thought about asking whether he wanted to know why it worked or whether the line was enough. Upstairs, something exploded, and then it got quiet, and she never asked.

Nolan locked the bathroom door and turned the fan on so his mother would hear white noise and not words. In the mirror, his mouth looked like it belonged to someone else, someone who could stand in front of a sophomore health class on Thursday and say things out loud.

"Consent," he said, and the word came out flat, like a tax form.

The student wellness office had chosen him because he'd written a paper on reproductive health that Ms. Adeyemi called "unusually clear." That was the whole qualification. Sixteen, clear, and now expected to explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the county clinic to students who were mostly fourteen and terrified of their own bodies. Priya, the other peer educator, wanted the job for her college applications, which she admitted without embarrassment. "I'm going to monetize everything I do from now on," she'd said at lunch, stacking her volunteer hours like inventory. "The clinics, the food bank, this. It all goes in the spreadsheet." Nolan had laughed, but privately he thought his own reason was thinner. He'd volunteered because Priya had, and because saying no would have meant admitting he didn't understand any of it himself.

He tried again. "Consent means everyone involved actually wants to be there, and can say no without it costing them something." Better. Priya had coached him on that phrasing at her kitchen table, tapping the Formica on each clause. She wanted the presentation to be good, really good, not spreadsheet-good, though she would never separate the two wants in public.

The hard part was the contraception section. He had a stack of notecards on the sink ledge, and the flashcards he'd made from the clinic's pamphlets. The pill, the shot, the implant, the ring, the condom. He was sorting them by how well he could explain each one when he remembered the pharmacy in September, standing behind his cousin Dana at the counter while she picked up her prescription. Dana was nineteen and treated him like a person, not a kid, which was the only reason he'd gone along. The pharmacist, an older woman with reading glasses on a chain, slid the bag across, and Dana asked, casually, the way you'd ask about a refill date, "So does this cover me for infections too? Like, everything?"

"No," the pharmacist said. "Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections. For anything else, you'd need condoms as well, or you'd need testing."

Dana had nodded like she'd already known, but afterward, in the parking lot, she'd been quiet, then said, "I didn't know that. I genuinely didn't." She'd looked at the bag in her hand as if it had shrunk. Dana's whole want that fall had been to get her life orderly after a bad breakup, prescriptions and budgets and a planner with color-coded tabs, and Nolan had watched the pharmacist's one sentence put a crack in the order, a fact she'd have to build around.

Now he laid the notecards out along the edge of the tub. The pill. The shot. The implant. The ring. The condom, alone at the end, holding its extra job. He felt the strange satisfaction of a pattern clicking into place, and then the discomfort underneath it, because the pattern meant that everything Dana had arranged for herself was impermeable to one category of risk, and the one method that addressed it was the one people negotiated in the moment, with another person, where consent lived. The two halves of his presentation were not two halves. They touched.

He practiced that section with the shower running behind him. "There's a thing people get wrong," he said to the mirror, to the sophomore he imagined there, hunched and half-listening. "The pill prevents pregnancy. It doesn't protect against infections. Condoms are the only common method that does both." He said it three times until it stopped sounding like a recitation and started sounding like something he might actually say to someone he cared about, the way the pharmacist had said it to Dana, without judgment, without a lecture about why or how, just the fact, laid down like a rail to travel on.

The testing part was easier to rehearse. The county clinic on Harmon Street, walk-ins on Tuesday afternoons, no parental notification for STI testing, results by phone in a week. He'd written the address on the board in his notebook four times so it would live in his hand and not just his head.

A knock rattled the door. "Nolan, you've been in there forty minutes," his mother said.

"Practicing," he called back.

"For what?"

He looked at the notecards, at the condom card standing apart from the others, at his own face deciding how much of the truth to give her. "For a thing at school," he said, and picked up the cards, squared them, and slid them into his back pocket, all but one, which had fallen behind the towel bar, the word CLINIC showing in the gap. He left it there for the moment and washed his hands.

He dried them on the towel and, reaching back for the dropped card, knocked it farther down behind the bar instead, so that only its edge showed, pale against the plaster, like something the wall had half swallowed and might yet give back.

Simon's eighteenth birthday had arrived in March with a summons folded into an envelope marked OFFICIAL, and by June he was sitting in the assembly room of the county courthouse with seventy strangers, holding a slip of paper that read Juror 44. He had wanted this, in a way he found slightly embarrassing to admit. Voting had felt abstract, a lever pulled once, but a jury was power you could feel in your hands, and he intended to feel it.

The room smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax. Two rows ahead of him a girl was reading a phone with a Union Jack sticker on the case, and when the overhead speaker crackled and went silent again, she turned around as if the silence had given her permission. "You waiting for the civil panel too?" she asked. "I'm Priya. My aunt's in Manchester. I'm only here because my number came up."

They talked to pass the time. Somewhere in the middle of complaining about the delays, Priya mentioned her aunt, and then, almost as gossip, said, "In 2022 the United Kingdom had three prime ministers in one year, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, and Rishi Sunak, and none of them faced a general election. The governing party just changed its leader, twice."

Simon set down the paper. "That can't be right," he said. "The people didn't vote for Truss or Sunak at all?"

"Not a single ballot," Priya said. "My aunt voted for the party, and the party decided the rest on its own."

He began to ruminate on this, the way he did in the back of civics class, turning the fact over while the room hummed around them. Here he was, Juror 44, in a building whose entire architecture said power comes from the people, in stalls and booths and panels. And across an ocean, a head of government had been swapped out twice in twelve months without the public being asked. It seemed, at first glance, like a theft.

"It's more efficient," Priya said when he said so. "When a leader fails, they're gone in weeks. Your way, you're stuck for four years."

"Efficient for whom?" Simon said. "The party. Not the voters." He was thinking of impeachment, the only mechanism he knew for removing a president, how it demanded a trial, a vote, a public reckoning, how slow and clumsy and, in the end, how rarely it worked. A system that removed leaders quickly but privately versus a system that removed them almost never but in the open. He said some of this out loud, less certain by the sentence.

An hour later a bailiff called the civil panel, forty names, and both of theirs were among them. The courtroom was smaller than Simon expected, wood-paneled, a judge already seated. The case involved a disputed contract and an injunction one company had filed against the other, and the judge told the panel that the injunction was the urgent part, that the ancillary claims would follow in due course. Jurors were questioned one at a time. Simon watched Priya take the chair, answer plainly, and be kept.

Then his own name. The attorney for one side, a woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, asked the panel a general question: whether anyone believed that decisions made without full public scrutiny could ever be legitimate. Simon felt the morning's argument rise in him like a tide. He could give the safe answer and sit in that chair for three weeks. Or he could say what he had actually worked out, that the British way traded accountability for speed and the American way traded speed for accountability, and that he genuinely could not rank them, that both seemed to him half of something.

He said it. The attorney with the glasses looked at him for a long moment, conferred briefly with her colleague, and said, "Thank you, Juror 44, you're excused." In the hallway Priya was waiting by the water fountain, still a juror, annoyed that he'd been let go before her. "You talked your way out of it," she said.

"I talked my way into it," Simon said. "Just not into the chair." He held up the folded summons, which told him, in small print, that his service was complete for twelve months. It was the strangest feeling, being satisfied and dismissed in the same breath. Outside, on the courthouse steps, Priya's aunt was double-parked with the hazard lights on, honking once through the open window.

"You'll have to tell me who won," Simon said.

"Only if you look up who Truss's replacement was," Priya said, and got in the car.

Lea spread the printed graph across the picnic table in her backyard, weighting two corners with her mother's terra cotta pots because the August wind kept lifting the paper like something trying to escape. The graph was the Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record, a century squashed into one axis, and it climbed in a long diagonal sawtooth that her textbook had assigned along with three questions she could not answer. She had a stack of index cards, a mug of coffee gone lukewarm, and forty-eight hours before her first college placement exam, which would decide whether she started in the introductory environmental science course or tested into the one her brother had called the real one.

The diagonal she understood. More carbon dioxide, decade over decade, an upward trend a child could read. What she could not account for were the small zigzags riding on top of it, dozens of them, evenly spaced, sawing up and down like a heartbeat drawn by someone with an unsteady hand. She had assumed they were measurement noise, the instrument's small errors, until she wrote that on an index card, looked at it, and felt the wrongness of it. Errors did not repeat so regularly. Errors did not line up year after year like stitches.

Her neighbor Marcus came through the gap in the fence without knocking, the way he had since they were nine, holding a bottle of root beer and his own copy of the same graph. "Placement exam?" he asked, and she nodded at the table. He sat on the bench across from her, shook the bottle without thinking, then set it down carefully when he saw the paper.

"These wiggles," Lea said, tapping the sawtooth with her pen. "I wrote down that they're measurement errors, and now I think that's stupid, but I don't know what else they are." Marcus leaned over the graph. The wind moved the paper under the pots, and the shadow of the elm above them flickered across the carbon dioxide line like a second, smaller graph.

Marcus was quiet long enough that she thought he was stalling. He was the kind of student who liked to adjudicate between competing guesses out loud, weighing each one before committing, and she watched him do it now. "Either it's the instrument," he said, "or something on Earth is doing it. Something that changes every year." He turned the pen over in his fingers. "So. What happens to trees each season?"

Lea looked up, not at him but at the elm, at the whole backyard going gold at its edges. The question seemed too simple to be the key, and then it wasn't. She thought of every leaf on every tree in the Northern Hemisphere, the maple dropping its brown coins onto the patio stones, the forests she had flown over once on the way to her grandmother's, and she pulled the graph closer and turned it sideways as if the angle might help. "They grow," she said slowly. "In spring and summer. And then in autumn and winter the leaves die and fall off and decay." She traced one zigzag with her finger, down and up, down and up. "So all those plants, that whole half of the planet, take in carbon dioxide when they're growing, and then put it back out when the leaves die."

"Which would pull the line down every summer," Marcus said, "and let it climb back every winter."

"And it would look exactly like this." She said it and then sat back, half disbelieving that the explanation had come out of her own mouth, out of a backyard and a question about trees. It was strange to think of the graph as a record not just of smokestacks and traffic but of sentience in the loose, green, seasonal sense, every leaf on Earth inhaling in unison, and stranger still that a number measured on a volcano in Hawaii could register her own elm dropping its leaves each October. She did not say any of this aloud. She wrote it on a fresh index card, both sides, and then crossed out her earlier card about measurement errors and let it lie face down on the table.

There was still the diagonal underneath, the part that did not zigzag back down to where it started, and that part she could not fix with a question about trees, and she was honest enough with herself to leave it that way for now, an open debt. She knew the trend, knew the wiggles, and did not yet know everything the two together meant. She took one pot off the corner of the graph so the wind lifted the edge again, and smoothed it flat with her palm. "Ask me another one," she said. "I think I'm getting this."

The party was in Dara's backyard, which meant paper lanterns on the fence and a playlist someone's older brother had codified into three hours of songs no one admitted to loving. Brooklyn arrived holding a Tupperware of brownies and a laptop bag, because the robotics notebook was due at midnight and the presentation was Monday, and she had promised herself she would not leave Dara's without telling Marcus what she actually thought about his code.

The trouble had started Tuesday, when Marcus had pushed his motor-control loop to the shared repository and Brooklyn had found, within four minutes, a sign error that would send the arm smashing downward instead of lifting. She had said nothing. She had said nothing on Wednesday too, and on Thursday, when Priya asked whether anyone had checked Marcus's section, Brooklyn had looked at the table and said it looked fine. That was the word she kept returning to, fine, sitting in her mouth like a coin.

"Brooklyn, you're at a party," Priya said now, handing her a cup of punch. "Why do you have the laptop out?"

"Because at midnight the notebook locks. And somebody has to tell him his loop is wrong before it's in the submitted version forever."

"So tell him."

"It's not that simple."

"It's exactly that simple. You've made a whole philosophy out of it."

Brooklyn had, a little. Her mother's approach, inherited from a family that praised everything, held that kindness meant never letting someone feel small. Her physics teacher's approach, which she distrusted and admired, held that precision was a form of respect and feelings could be sorted later. Somewhere between the two was a position she couldn't quite reach, and midnight was coming.

Marcus was by the fence, teaching a sophomore how to fold a napkin into a swan, badly, with enormous confidence. She watched him fail three times, laughing each time, and thought about how easily he shrugged off napkin mistakes and how she had no idea what he did with code mistakes, because in four months of building the robot together, no one on the team had ever admitted one out loud. Not once. It was a strange thing to notice at a birthday party, with lantern light on the grass and someone's terrible karaoke starting up by the garage, a small cold foreboding under the cake and the noise.

She found Priya again by the drink table. "That article you sent me. The team research one."

"Edmondson? You read it?"

"Twice. She called it psychological safety," Brooklyn said. "In 1999. A team's shared belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake."

"And we don't have it."

"Marcus broke a servo in October and blamed the manufacturer. Priya, I hid a wiring error for two days in November. Nobody in our group has ever said the words 'I messed up' to anybody else."

"So you're going to break the streak."

"I'm going to try not to break Marcus instead." She took a brownie from her own Tupperware for courage, which was a canny move in the sense that it bought her ninety seconds of chewing instead of talking.

She caught Marcus alone by the beanbag toss. "Can I show you something before midnight? It's about the loop."

He set down his beanbags. "Is it bad?"

"It's one line. Line two-forty. You're subtracting where you meant to add, so the arm goes down when the sensor says up. I tested it in simulation, that's how I found it, not by staring at your code being smarter than you."

He looked at the grass. "Why didn't you say something Tuesday?"

Because she had been afraid of this exact face. "I was a coward," she said. "I told myself I was being nice. But nice would have been telling you in time to fix it calmly instead of at a birthday party at eleven p.m."

He laughed at that, a real one, surprised out of him. "Okay. Line two-forty." They sat on the picnic table with the laptop between them, and he fixed it in one minute, and then he said, quietly, "I broke that servo myself, you know. Dropped it on the shop floor."

"I hid a wiring error in November," she said. "For two days."

"You're kidding."

"Priya knows. Now you do. It's apparently that kind of night." The lanterns buzzed faintly overhead; somewhere behind them, the karaoke had reached a high note it should not have attempted, and they both winced and laughed.

At 11:58 they committed the notebook, and Marcus raised his cup of punch and said, "To fine," and Brooklyn understood that he had heard her use the word on Thursday and had known, even then, that it was a lie. They didn't resolve anything larger. The team would have to learn this again on Monday, and probably after that, and Priya was already yelling at them to come inside for cake before someone ate the corner piece with the frosting rose.

Brooklyn closed the laptop and followed him toward the lights, leaving the last brownie on the picnic table for whoever found it.

Luca had not expected the robotics track at Camp Winnowick to contain homework, and he told anyone who would listen that signing up for Java in July was like volunteering to convalesce at a dentist's office. His counselor, Priya, had only smiled and said the laptop lab had air conditioning, which in a camp where mosquitos were practically endemic counted as a luxury resort.

The project was simple on paper: build a class called SongList with private fields and getter methods, then test it. Priya handed out cards with the requirements and then sat in the corner, refusing to answer questions, which made her, in Dara's words, "an autocrat of the silent variety." Dara was the girl at the terminal next to Luca's, twelve years old, allergic to being wrong, and the fastest typist in the cabin.

"Private means private," Dara announced on the second morning, scrolling through Luca's screen without asking. "Your songs are hidden. Nobody can touch them. It's like a vault."

"A vault with a door you built," Luca said, because he had learned the getter methods by then, the little public methods named getSongs and getSize that handed the vault's contents out to anyone who asked. His test class called getSongs forty times an hour. Everything worked. He had a list of eleven campfire songs stored in his SongList object, and the test printed them all, and he felt the specific smugness of a sixteen-year-old whose code compiles on the first try.

Then came the twist, though at first it looked like a catastrophe. On Thursday afternoon Dara borrowed his SongList class for her own project, a game where a grumpy camp director confiscates songs from campers. Her Confiscator class called getSongs, and somewhere in her code she called clear on whatever came back, the way you'd empty a bin. When Luca reopened his test afterward, his SongList, his private, protected, carefully encapsulated SongList, printed zero songs. Eleven songs, gone. He stared at the empty output like a man who'd locked his house and come home to find the furniture on the lawn.

"That's your bug," Dara said, when he accused her. "Your vault. Your door."

"It's private," Luca said. "I typed the word private. It's right there."

They fought about it for a full ten minutes, politely at first and then with escalating accusations involving each other's mothers and formatting habits, until Priya finally drifted over, looked at two lines of code, and said only, "Interesting. What did getSongs actually hand back?" Then she wandered away again, which was her version of teaching.

Luca sat with the question. He wrote a tiny experiment: he made a SongList, called getSongs, added a song to the thing it returned, and printed the list again. The original SongList had grown by one. He ran it twice more, then leaned back so fast his chair squeaked. The getter wasn't handing out a copy of his list. It was handing out the list itself, the actual object, the same one living behind the word private. His vault door opened directly onto the vault. Dara's Confiscator hadn't broken in; he'd handed it the key and called it hospitality.

"So it's not really private at all," he said out loud, to no one.

"It's private the way my diary is private when I read it aloud at dinner," Dara said, which was generous of her, since it was her code that had emptied his list.

Luca rewrote the getter that evening while the rest of the cabin was at the campfire. Instead of returning the list directly, he built a new list in the getter, put the same songs into it, and returned that. Now Dara's Confiscator could clear its little heart out; it would only be emptying the copy. He tested it by letting her game confiscate everything twice, and his original still printed all eleven songs, stubborn as a raccoon in a trash can. He made her run her whole project again, and when the final line of his test printed "11 songs remaining," he stood up and did a small, shameful victory dance that Dara filmed.

There was a piece he still couldn't quite settle, and he was honest about it at the talent show the next night, when Priya asked what he'd learned. "Copies are safer," he said, holding the microphone like a man accepting an award. "But if my list were huge, I'd be copying it every time somebody asked to look. I don't know which is worse yet." He shrugged. "Ask me in September."

"What I learned," Dara called from the third row, "is that Luca's vault had a revolving door."

"It had a door that led directly to the vault," Luca corrected. "There's a difference, and it cost me eleven songs." He sat down to applause from people who had no idea what he was talking about, and Priya, in the back, raised her cup of bug juice to him.

The mosque on Saturday afternoons smelled of carpet cleaner and burnt coffee, and Lucas had claimed the corner by the bulletin board because it had the one working outlet for his phone. He was trying to watch the sunset time like it might change on him, 7:42, then 7:41 the next day, as if the sun were mocking him. In two weeks his father would be in Karachi for his grandmother's surgery, and Lucas would run the family iftar alone, the whole thing, from the moment the adhan app chimed until the last glass of tea.

The problem was that his father did everything by feel. Dates appeared, warm, at exactly the right second; the water pitchers were cold; the samosas came out of the oven when Auntie Yasmin was already seated. Nobody had ever written it down. When Lucas asked his father for the order of things, his father waved a hand and said, "You'll see, it's not complicated," which was the kind of thing adults said when something was actually very complicated and they had forgotten why.

His cousin Mariam found him at the mosque, dropped onto the bench beside him with her hijab still pinned crooked from volleyball. "You look like you're doing taxes," she said. He showed her the note on his phone, the schedule he'd built with buffers and contingencies, and she read it twice. "You've got the dates at the end," she said. "With dessert."

"Dates are dessert."

"No, they're first. First thing, the second the sun sets." She said it lightly, the way she said everything, but Lucas felt the floor tilt a little. He had eaten iftar at that table for seventeen years and could not have said what came first. He'd assumed, all this time, he was watching his father's preferences rather than a practice, and the distinction suddenly mattered. "You break the fast with a date," Mariam said. "The Prophet did it that way, so everybody does." She shrugged, as if to say this was the least interesting fact in the world, and asked if he'd saved her a spot for the community dinner.

That night Lucas called his grandmother in Karachi, ostensibly to ask about her flights, really to check. She was already three questions ahead of him. "Tell your father the Ajwa dates are behind the rice jars, not in the fridge, he always thinks I hide them." Then, softer, "You're doing it this year?" A pause in which he understood she already knew and had perhaps even suggested it, that this might be a quiet detente between her and his father, an end to the annual argument about who was crumbling under the load of hosting. "Don't aggrandize it," she said. "It's a meal, not a performance. Feed people on time and everything else forgives you."

He spent the following week at the mosque kitchen, where the volunteer aunties staged the community iftar and tolerated him because he washed dishes without being asked. He timed everything. He learned that the sunset call wasn't a suggestion, that two hundred people would reach for dates in the same instant, and that the volunteers who had them ready looked calm while the ones who hadn't looked like the building was on fire. On Thursday he got it wrong himself, distracted by a tangential argument about whose biryani recipe the kitchen used, and the dates were still in the store room when the adhan sounded. He watched Uncle Farooq stand in the doorway holding an empty bowl, saying nothing, which was worse than shouting.

Afterward, drying sheet pans, Lucas made a second list. Not the schedule with its buffers, but a short one. Dates on the plate before the sky turns. Water poured. Everything else is negotiable. It occurred to him that his father's feel and his own list weren't rivals the way he'd assumed; the list was just feel, written down by someone who needed it written. What he couldn't decide was whether leading the meal meant keeping order or giving it away, whether his grandmother's "it's a meal, not a performance" was wisdom or an instruction to make himself invisible. He texted Mariam. She replied with a single thumbs up, which settled nothing.

On the night, his father called from the Karachi airport at 6:15 and talked for nine minutes about the taxi, and Lucas let him, because saying goodbye is its own errand. At 7:38 he set the plate of dates in the center of the table, the ones from behind the rice jars, and stood with the water pitcher sweating against his palm. Auntie Yasmin was mid-story about a neighbor's wedding. The sky through the window went from orange to a thin, pressed gray.

The app chimed. His little cousin reached for the plate before the sound finished.

"Wait," Lucas said, but he was smiling when he said it, and he put the first date in her hand.

The laminated card had eleven bullet points on it, and James had read it so many times that the words had started to feel like weather, something that happened to him rather than something he said. He was nineteen days into his job as a junior counselor at Camp Wanoka, and the health director, Rhonda, had decided that the oldest campers, the fifteen and sixteen year olds, would get a session on consent, contraception and testing, and that James would lead it. He was eighteen. He had learned what a dental dam was on Tuesday.

His first attempt had gone badly in a way he was still turning over. He had stood in front of seventeen teenagers in the craft shed, recited the bullet points in the flat elocution of a boy reading a fire safety poster, and watched their faces close one by one, like shop doors at the end of a street. A girl named Priya had finally said, "Do you actually know anything, or did they just hand you a card?" He had said the honest thing, which was the card, and she had laughed, and the laugh had been worse than the silence.

He practiced after that in the empty boathouse, saying it out loud to the lake. Consent is ongoing and it can be withdrawn. Contraception reduces risk but nothing eliminates it except abstinence, and if you say abstinence like a threat nobody hears the rest. He found that if he admitted what he did not know, the sentences opened up instead of closing. This felt like a discovery he could not quite put into words, so he kept saying it to the lake.

The problem came to find him on Thursday, at the picnic table behind the infirmary, where a camper named Dominic was pretending to rearrange a first aid kit that Rhonda had already arranged. Dominic was sixteen and phlegmatic by nature, slow to alarm, which made it stranger that his hands would not stay still. He asked whether the clinic in town would call his mother. He said a girl from his school, in June, and he did not finish the sentence. He said, "They'd need a form. Everything needs a form. My mom signed a form so I could go on the sail trip."

James did not know. This was the part he would later understand as the real beginning, the moment when the card ran out. He walked Dominic to the infirmary and stood beside him while Rhonda called the county clinic, and he listened to her side of the conversation, which was mostly nodding sounds. When she hung up she said it plainly, without ceremony: all fifty states and Washington, DC, allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age. She said Dominic was over any minimum age here, and that no one at the clinic would call his mother, and that she would drive him herself on her supply run Friday morning.

Dominic looked at James then, not at Rhonda, and James understood that Dominic needed to hear it twice, from someone closer to his own age, from someone who would be there Saturday and Sunday and the week after. So James said it again, all fifty states and DC, no parent's permission, some states set a minimum age, and heard the sentence become true in his own mouth. They arranged to meet at the dock at eight. Dominic shook his hand, formally, like a man closing a deal, and went to find his bunkmates.

The session on Saturday went better than the one in the craft shed, though not because James had become smooth. He told the seventeen campers about Dominic, with permission, with the details sanded off, and he told them the law the way Rhonda had said it, and he asked them what they thought consent actually required of a person, and he let the silence sit until Priya said, "Asking, and meaning it when they answer," which was better than any bullet point. The campers argued about whether sixteen was old enough for any of it, and a boy named Felix said his older brother had gotten tested and it had taken twenty minutes, and James realized he was barely talking anymore, and that this was the job.

Friday morning, though, the dock at eight had been empty. Dominic had not come. Rhonda made the supply run alone, and when James found him later, shooting baskets on the cracked court behind the mess hall, Dominic said his mother had surprised him with a visit day, and she was here, right now, in the parking lot, unloading a cooler of sandwiches, and he could not do it this week. He would do it after camp, he said. He said it looking at the ball in his hands.

James wanted to argue and found he could not, because the law gave Dominic the right to decide, and deciding included deciding not yet, and that was the same principle he had been teaching, turned around and pointed at him like a joke with no punchline. He said he would sit with Dominic on the bus home if Dominic wanted, and talk about which clinic was near his house. Dominic said okay, and banked the ball off the backboard, and it rolled to the fence and stopped there in the long grass, and neither of them went to get it.

John stood at the bathroom mirror with his phone balanced against the soap dish, rehearsing. He had volunteered, somewhat against his own expectations, to run the consent workshop for the freshman health seminar, and tomorrow afternoon three separate classrooms of younger students would look at him while he tried to explain things that a nurse practitioner had explained to him only two weeks ago.

The bathroom was the only room in the house with a lock his mother respected, so it had become his rehearsal space. He pressed record on the voice memo app, faced himself, and said, "Consent is a yes you can say out loud, and it has to be a yes you could change." He stopped. The sentence sounded like a poster. He tried again. "If someone is asleep, they can't say yes. If someone says yes because they're scared of what happens if they say no, that isn't a yes either." Better, but his voice in the recording was flat, and he wondered whether the flatness came from the bathroom's acoustics or from him.

His younger sister, Ruth, knocked twice and said through the door that she needed to pee. He told her to wait four minutes. She said, "You've been in there since dinner," and then, quieter, "Is this about that clinic thing?"

He opened the door. Ruth stood in the hallway in her soccer shorts, and behind her, holding two mugs of tea as though they portended some long and terrible conversation, was his mother. "Nurse Alvarez called back," his mother said. "About the peer health program. She wants to know if you'd also cover the testing part tomorrow."

John let them both into the bathroom, which was absurd, but it was where his notes were: the clinic pamphlet on the edge of the tub, the index card with the phone number, the printed schedule of drop-in hours. He sat on the closed toilet lid. Ruth leaned against the sink. His mother remained standing, truculent in the way she got when she felt she'd been maneuvered.

"You went to the clinic yourself?" Ruth said. "You said you were at Devin's."

"I was at the clinic," John said. "Then I was at Devin's. I got tested." He said it plainly because saying it plainly was the whole thing he was trying to learn. "I felt completely fine, so I figured I didn't need to, and then at the appointment the nurse told me that chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so a test is the only reliable way to know whether you have one. Feeling fine doesn't prove anything. That's actually the one fact I'm sure I'll get right tomorrow."

Ruth pulled the pamphlet from the tub and read it. "So you could have something right now and not know it."

"That's what testing is for," he said. "It's not a punishment. It's fifteen minutes and it's free, and the nurse was nicer to me than my dentist ever is."

His mother set the mugs down on the shelf where his father's shaving foam used to live. "You didn't tell us you were going."

"Because it would have become a whole family summit," John said. "Like this one." He picked up the index card and turned it over. On the back he had written his outline for the workshop, the sequence he'd built out of the nurse's practical heuristic: name the thing, describe the action, give the next concrete step. Say what consent is. Say what contraception does and where to get it. Say where the clinic is, that it's confidential, that you don't need a parent, and that the test is the only way to know, because the infections usually show nothing.

"You're doing this tomorrow," his mother said. It was half a question.

"Three periods," John said. "Ms. Okafor signed off."

Ruth handed back the pamphlet. "You're going to stand in front of freshmen and talk about this. You, who threw up before the eighth grade spelling bee."

"I know," John said.

"What if someone asks you something you can't answer?"

He looked at the card. There were gaps in it, real ones. He could explain consent as a principle and still not know what to say to a kid whose girlfriend said yes out of habit, or whose parents had taught him something entirely different, or who believed, with total certainty, that a person who looked healthy was healthy. He could give the clinic's address and still not know how a sixteen-year-old without a car was supposed to get there on a Tuesday afternoon. "Then I'll say I don't know," he said. "And I'll write it down and ask Nurse Alvarez."

His mother finally sat on the edge of the tub. "I'm not angry," she said. "I was going to be angry. I had it prepared. But you went, and you came back, and now you're teaching it, and I don't know what to do with a son who does the sensible thing without telling me."

"Be annoyed quietly," Ruth said. "I need to pee."

After she left, his mother stood, kissed the top of his head, which she hadn't done since he was eleven, and carried both untouched mugs of tea back down the hall. John locked the door, looked at himself in the mirror, and started recording again. "Consent is a yes you can say out loud," he told his reflection, "and it has to be a yes you could change. And if you've had sex, get tested, because feeling fine isn't proof of anything. The clinic's on Fenwick Street. Drop-in hours are Tuesdays." He stopped the recording and played it back. His voice sounded less flat than before. He pressed record and started over.

The camp's health lodge smelled like sunscreen and grape bubblegum, and Rachel had volunteered there mostly to escape the dining hall dishes, so it was a kind of cosmic joke that the first thing Nurse Padma taught her was a machine. "Systolic over diastolic," Padma said, fastening the cuff around a counselor's tanned arm. "Top number, bottom number. Top is when the heart pushes, bottom is when it rests." Rachel wrote it on her forearm in pen, which Padma pretended not to notice.

The want came later, on a Tuesday, when Joanie from Cabin 4 tripped over a canoe and opened her knee. While Padma stitched, she asked Rachel to take Joanie's pressure, and the little screen blinked up 148 over 92, numbers that meant nothing to Rachel until Padma's eyebrows did something complicated. "That's high," Padma said. "For a kid." Rachel felt her stomach drop as if she'd been the one to bleed.

Joanie, being Joanie, was delighted to have a medical condition. She narrated it to the whole cabin that night, lying on her bunk with her knee elevated on a pillow like a queen's foot. "My blood pressure," she announced, "is famous." The other girls were less impressed, because Joanie also claimed to be allergic to mosquitoes, thunder, and the crepuscular hour between dinner and campfire, which she said made her "spiritually itchy." Rachel liked her anyway. Joanie was honest in a way that had no filter, an idiosyncrasy that made her terrible at cards and good at friendship.

Rachel, meanwhile, had spent the evening doing arithmetic she barely understood. If high pressure meant something bad, and Joanie had it, then something bad was happening, and Rachel had watched the numbers happen without stopping them. She found Padma by the supply shelf, restocking gauze. "Is Joanie sick?" she asked. "Like, actually?"

Padma didn't answer right away, which Rachel had learned meant the answer was a question. "What do you think happens to your body when you're nervous?" Rachel considered this. She thought of the paddling test she'd failed in June, how her hands had shaken so badly the paddle knocked her own hat off, twice, in front of everyone. "Everything gets loud," she said. "Fast. Like the heart's sprinting." Padma snapped the gauze box shut. "Take her pressure tomorrow morning," she said. "Before she's awake enough to perform for anyone."

So at seven the next morning, Rachel sat on the edge of Joanie's bunk with the cuff and the machine and a sense of mission she usually reserved for capturing the flag. Joanie, hair flat on one side, stuck out her arm without opening her eyes. The machine hummed, tightened, and released. 118 over 74. Rachel took it twice more because she didn't believe herself. Both times, normal.

She carried the numbers to the lodge like a relay baton. "Yesterday it was 148 over 92," she said, "in here, when she was bleeding and scared. This morning it's normal. So the machine isn't wrong. Something about the moment is." Padma smiled in the small way that meant Rachel had arrived somewhere on her own. "There's a name for it," Padma said. "White coat hypertension." She was already unscrewing a pen. "When it reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home. It's why we sometimes send people home with a cuff, or have them wear a monitor that checks all day, before anyone decides anything."

Rachel practiced saying it out loud on the walk to the lake, enjoying the weight of it. White coat hypertension. She imagined the blood pressure machine as a shy animal that only got startled around doctors, which was not the mechanism, she was fairly sure, but which made her laugh anyway. She tried explaining it to her co-CIT Marcus, who was mopping the boathouse. "So the number is true and also a lie," Marcus said, wringing the mop. "That's the most medical thing I've ever heard." "It's true in the moment," Rachel said. "It's just not the whole truth. You'd have to see her on an ordinary day to know her ordinary number."

That was the part she turned over for the rest of the week, because it seemed bigger than blood. A single reading, a single bad afternoon, a single failed paddling test: none of them told you what a person was, only what a person was right then. She wasn't sure how far the idea stretched, and she liked not being sure. On Friday she cuffed Joanie one last time by the campfire, partly for science and mostly for show. "Normal," Rachel reported. Joanie sighed, deeply disappointed. "So I'm not dying." "You're not dying." "Then at least tell me I'm allergic to the blood pressure machine," Joanie said, and held out her arm again.

Gabrielle had been dreading the parallel parking more than the examiners, more than the roundabouts, more than anything on the syllabus, and so it was parallel parking she practised first, in her grandmother's gravel drive, between two plastic bins dragged out of the garage to stand in for parked cars. Her grandmother sat on the garden wall with a flask of tea, calling distances the way a coxswain calls a stroke. "More lock," she said. "No, more than that." Gabrielle turned the wheel and felt the nearside wheel kiss the kerb with a sound like a struck match.

She stopped the engine and put her forehead on the rim of the wheel. "That's it, isn't it. If I touch the kerb in the test, I've failed."

"Who told you that?"

"Everyone. It's all over the forums. Touch the kerb and you're done."

Her grandmother poured a second cup and said nothing, which was not her usual mode. She was a woman who gesticulated when she described so much as a supermarket queue, so the stillness meant something. "Look it up," she said at last. "Properly, not on a forum."

Gabrielle found the answer that evening at the kitchen table, her phone propped against the sugar bowl while her grandmother sliced plums for a crumble. On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passed with no more than fifteen driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults. She read it twice, then a third time, because the words refused to arrange themselves into the doom she'd been carrying around. "Fifteen," she said aloud. "You're allowed fifteen faults." Touching the kerb gently, according to a footnote in some official guidance she found afterwards, could count as one fault, a driving fault, the minor kind, and she still had fourteen left in the bank. The vast superstructure of terror she'd built on one grazed wheel was, apparently, a tower built on air. There were, of course, the other kinds, the serious and dangerous faults, each one fatal to the result on its own, and she could not quite see the border between a fault that was minor and a fault that was serious, and that unseen border unsettled her more than the number soothed her.

"So it's not one strike and out," her grandmother said, laying plums in a fan.

"It's fifteen strikes and out. And then some strikes count as the whole game."

Her grandmother laughed, a short bark that startled the cat. "That's very British. Generous and merciless at the same time."

The next problem was the merge, and it could not be solved in a gravel drive between two bins. The nearest motorway was forty minutes away, and for the first two of those forty minutes Gabrielle's grandmother rode with her hands folded in her lap, silent as a nun, before observing that silence in a passenger was not in any way calming and that Gabrielle's shoulders had risen nearly to her ears. They stopped at a lay-by and swapped the radio to a station neither of them liked, because it turned out that familiar music made her grandmother want to conduct, and conducting involved gesticulation, and a gesticulating passenger at seventy miles an hour was its own category of dangerous fault. The subterfuge with the radio worked: her grandmother settled, Gabrielle's shoulders descended, and at the next junction they watched a lorry bear down while a space opened beside it like a decision being made for her. She pressed the accelerator, slotted in, and heard her grandmother exhale a word she pretended not to hear.

They drove to the coast and back. On the way home, in the last light, they argued gently about the test itself, or rather about what it was for. Gabrielle had begun to think of the fifteen faults as a kind of grace, a system that assumed learners would err and still deserved to drive; her grandmother thought it assumed nothing so generous, only that examiners needed a scale and errors needed counting. "It's not forgiveness, love, it's arithmetic," she said. Gabrielle wasn't sure she agreed, and said so, and neither of them conceded, and somehow the disagreement was the pleasantest part of the whole day. She held both ideas in her hands the way she'd learned to hold the wheel at ten and two, not choosing yet.

On the morning of the test she parked between the examiner's cones without touching anything at all, not the kerb, not the bins of her imagination, nothing, and she used perhaps two of her fifteen faults on the roundabout near the industrial estate, and the examiner, a dry man with a clipboard, told her at the end that she had passed. She drove home alone, legally, for the first time, turned into her grandmother's road with the windows down, and executed, out of pure celebration, the most beautiful parallel park of her life in front of the garden wall. The nearside wheel kissed the kerb with a sound like a struck match.

Her grandmother, watching from the window, raised her flask in a slow salute. "Fault number one," she called through the glass.

Savannah had circled the block twice before she let herself stop behind the silver sedan on Milberry Street, four car lengths of open curb beside it, the bank's brass doors waiting half a block down. Her road test was in six days. Her instructor, a stoic man named Ruiz who had spoken maybe forty sentences across four lessons, had said exactly one of them about parking, and she had been chewing on it since: "You back in from alongside the car in front, wheel toward the curb first, then away." She had nodded at the time without really seeing it, the way she nodded in calculus when a proof ended and everyone else looked satisfied.

She pulled alongside the sedan, checked her mirror, and reversed with the wheel turned toward the curb. The Honda crept in, nose still jutting toward the street, and stopped at an angle so obvious that a woman walking a terrier gave the car a wide, deliberate arc on the sidewalk. Savannah straightened, pulled out, and tried again without turning the wheel back. Same result: a diagonal, a wedge of car that belonged to no lane at all.

The third time, halfway into the space, she turned the wheel away from the curb, and the rear of the car swung so the nose came around, and suddenly she was level, close enough to the sedan that she could read the expired registration sticker. She sat with her hands on the wheel, breathing, then pulled forward and back until the tires kissed the curb. It had not felt like a trick. It had felt like two motions that needed each other, and she had only ever done the first one.

She was still sitting there when her phone buzzed. Her mother, from inside the bank: Are you coming in or not? Savannah locked the car and walked the half block, and it was only at the doors that she realized she had not thought about the parking once on the way, which was either progress or the beginning of forgetting.

Inside, the branch smelled like carpet cleaner and warm paper. Her mother was already at a teller's window with the deposit slip, and Savannah took the number for her own appointment, opening her first account with the eleven hundred dollars she had made lifeguarding. The clerk, a young guy with a lanyard, asked if she wanted overdraft protection, and her mother leaned over and said, "Tell her what that actually costs," and the guy, to his credit, did. Savannah listened to the fee schedule and thought about how the brochure in the lobby had made it sound like a kindness, a little umbrella held over you, and how the small print was where the umbrella got billed out from under you. She declined it. Her mother said nothing, which from her was applause.

On the walk back to the car, her mother asked how the parking had gone, and Savannah said, "I figured out the second turn." Her mother, who had failed her own test twice at eighteen and never let anyone in the family mention it, as though a failed test were something that could stigmatize a person for life, just nodded. Then, at the corner, she said, "Take the highway home."

"You said the merge scares you."

"It does. That's why."

The on-ramp rose in a long curve, and Savannah checked her mirror, then her blind spot, then the mirror again, the way Ruiz had shown her, looking for a gap she could walk the car into. A truck sat in the right lane like a verdict. Behind it, a space opened, and she pressed the accelerator and moved into it at the speed of traffic, and no one honked, and no one died, and the ordinary grace of that surprised her. Her mother's hand was flat on her knee, not gripping, just resting there, which was as close as she came to saying anything.

They rode in the flow of cars, and Savannah held her lane and thought, without wanting to, about how the parking and the merge were almost opposite instructions. In one you slowed down and gave ground and let the geometry work; in the other you committed, speed as a form of politeness. She could not yet say whether a good driver was someone who knew which situation demanded which, or someone who could feel the moment when one turned into the other. Probably the test next week would not ask her that. Probably the test would ask her to park between cones on a quiet street, and the cones would not care what she understood.

Her exit came up. She signaled early, checked the mirror, eased down the ramp with the wheel turned toward the curb of her own street waiting three lights ahead, and her mother said, "Same spot in front of the house. Show me again."

The community centre on Delmore Street smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and the room the mock court used had a water stain on the ceiling shaped, according to everyone who studied it, like either Ohio or a dog. Aidan had been assigned Tinker v. State of Ohio, a fictional case, but the packet Mrs. Okoye had photocopied included a page of real precedent, and at the top of that page, underlined twice by some previous student, was Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969.

He was supposed to argue both sides. That was the whole exercise. Eighteen minutes for the student who had been suspended after giving an angry speech on the courthouse steps, a speech that ended with the words "they should burn it down," and then, after a break for water and nerves, eighteen minutes against him. Aidan sat in a plastic chair with his notes on his lap and felt the peculiar foreboding of a person who suspects he will lose an argument with himself.

Priya, who had drawn the judging panel, leaned over the folding table that served as the bench. "Ready? Petitioner first. That's you, arguing the school can't punish the speech."

Aidan stood. His first draft had been all feeling, the kind of speech that had enraptured him when he wrote it at midnight, all righteousness and quotation marks, and he could see now why it would fail. So he started with the precedent instead. "Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969," he said, and heard his voice steady the way it did when he stopped performing.
