"It held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action." He paused. "That's the test. It's called the imminent lawless action test."

"What's 'imminent' mean, exactly?" asked Marcus from the panel, chewing his pen.

"Like, now. Not someday. Not in theory." Aidan looked down at the facts he had invented and then been assigned to defend. "My client said 'they should burn it down.' He said it to forty people who were already leaving. Nobody had a match. The crowd was thinning out. Whatever he was advocating, it wasn't likely to produce anything that afternoon, because everybody was going home to dinner."

Priya scribbled something. It might have been "going home to dinner." It might have been a grocery list. That was the terror of the mock bench.

The break was three minutes. Aidan drank his water and then had to stand in front of the same chairs and take it all back, which felt, in a visceral and embarrassing way, like stepping on his own foot. "The state's position," he began, "is that this wasn't abstract advocacy. He named the building. He stood on its own steps. It was directed at inciting lawless action, and he had a crowd." He heard the words come out and recognized, with some horror, that he half believed them, or at least could believe them, the way you can believe a song in a language you don't speak.

"Half of them were walking away," Priya said, not unkindly.

"Walking away isn't the same as no likelihood," Aidan said. "That's my argument. It's not a great argument." He looked at the water stain, at Ohio or the dog. "Honestly, if you're asking me what I actually think, the Brandenburg test protects him, because 'should burn it down' is the kind of thing people say when they're angry, and the whole point of the test is that you can't punish angry words unless they're aimed at making something happen right then and likely to. But I'm supposed to be the state right now, so I'll keep going if you want."

Marcus lowered his pen. "Is that allowed? Arguing badly on purpose?"

"He's not arguing badly," Priya said. "He's arguing a side he doesn't hold. That's different." She shuffled her papers, and Aidan understood that she was granting him something, though he couldn't have named it. "Finish the rebuttal. You have four minutes."

He finished. He sat down with his heart going and his notes out of order, and Marcus leaned across the table and slid him the last of the coffee, which was cold and had a thumbprint in the lid. "You argued against yourself and won," Marcus said. "Or lost. Honestly, man, I can't tell which, and I was judging."

"That makes two of us," Aidan said, and drank the coffee anyway.

Emile had promised his uncle he would run the tomato stall until noon, and he had promised the economics club he would come to Thursday's meeting with something to say about inflation. Both promises felt manageable at seven in the morning, when the market was cool and the baskets were full, and less so by nine, when Mrs. Okafor arrived and began, as she did every Saturday, to complain that his prices had gone up again.

"Two years ago these were a dollar fifty," she said, holding a Cherokee Purple up to the light like evidence in a trial.

"Fuel went up. The feed for the cover crop went up. My uncle says he's not making more, he's just keeping pace." Emile weighed the tomatoes without meeting her eye, because this was the exact argument he could not win, or even follow, and it was the reason he had nothing to say on Thursday.

"You're in that club at school, aren't you," Mrs. Okafor said. It wasn't a question. "The one where they argue about money. My grandson joined it, then quit. He said all they did was fight about the Federal Reserve."

At that moment Marcus came down the aisle carrying two coffees and a bag of peaches, wearing his club T-shirt with the supply curve printed on the back, which was how he dressed on Saturdays the way other people wore jerseys. He had been Emile's first friend at the school and the reason Emile had joined the club at all. He set one coffee on the crate beside the scale and said, "I heard that from three aisles away. Are you fighting about interest rates with a customer?"

"She started it," Emile said.

Mrs. Okafor paid for her tomatoes, exact change, and told Marcus that inflation was the government's fault and that someone ought to do something about it, and then she moved on to the honey stall, and the conversation was somehow his now.

Marcus leaned against the table and began his speech about Thursday's meeting, which Emile had missed for a dentist appointment. A sophomore named Priya had argued that if inflation rose one percentage point, the central bank only needed to raise its interest rate by one percentage point to answer it, a matching move, symmetrical and tidy. "And you know what Dev said to her?"

"I don't."

"He said that's exactly wrong. There's a thing called the Taylor rule, and it says when inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than that."

"More," Emile repeated. He thought of Mrs. Okafor's tomatoes, of his uncle recalculating prices every month, matching every increase and never getting ahead. "So it has to overshoot."

"That's the rule. I looked it up last night." Marcus bit into a peach with the satisfaction of someone who had stayed up past midnight for a principle.

Emile tried to hold both pictures at once: the club's clean diagram of a rate on a graph, and his uncle at the kitchen table sequestering receipts in a shoebox, doing the grim arithmetic of a small farm that borrowed money every spring. The rule made a strange kind of sense to him, the way it refused symmetry, and yet he could feel something in it that he couldn't yet name, some gap between the sentence Dev had quoted and the market stall they were standing at, where every rise in a price had a person behind it holding the fruit.

"Here's what I don't get," Emile said. "The rule says raise more than inflation. Fine. But somebody's loan gets more expensive when they do that. Some farmer's line of credit. Maybe my uncle's."

Marcus looked at him for a long moment, and Emile watched his friend arrive at the recognition that this was germane, that the meeting's argument and the stall's ledger were about the same thing, though neither of them had the language to connect them fully. "Priya would say that's not the point of the model."

"Priya's parents own the hardware store on Route 9," Emile said. "She knows exactly whose loans those are."

They were quiet while a woman with a stroller bought a basket of Romas and Emile made change, and the change itself felt like part of the argument, coins passing hand to hand, every transaction a small negotiation over what a dollar was worth this month versus last month. He understood now what he would say on Thursday: that he accepted the rule as stated, that raising by more than the rise was the only position he could defend, and that he still couldn't say what the right amount more was, or who paid for the overshoot. The uncertainty wasn't a hole in his argument. It was the argument.

"You'll come Thursday?" Marcus said, crumpling the peach bag.

"I'll come. I'll even wear the shirt."

"No you won't. You hate the shirt." Marcus grinned and pushed off the table, and Emile stacked the empty baskets, one inside another, and watched him go down the aisle toward the honey stall, where Mrs. Okafor was still holding forth.

The basement smelled of damp carpet and microwave popcorn, and Deshad's laptop balanced on a milk crate between them. Loic had come over because the computer science placement exam was on Saturday, and because Deshad's mother made better snacks than anyone else's mother, though he would not have admitted the second reason in the vernacular of their friend group, where you showed up for the material and pretended the food was incidental.

"I don't get why it matters," Deshad said, scrolling through practice problems. "You look for the thing until you find the thing. That's a search. Done."

Loic pulled the laptop toward himself. "Say the list is sorted. A thousand names, alphabetical. You could start at the top and check every one." He typed a small demonstration, a loop crawling down an array, and watched the counter tick up: one, fourteen, ninety-two. "That's a linear search. But watch." He rewrote it, halved the range, halved it again. "Binary search. You jump straight to the middle, see which half your target is in, throw away the other half. Ten guesses, max, for a thousand items."

Deshad leaned back against the couch and ate a cold kernel of popcorn with the concentration of an epicurean sampling something rare. "Okay. That's actually satisfying. Like tearing a phone book in half."

Deshad's little sister Nia came halfway down the stairs, wrapped in a blanket, and stood there without saying anything. She had a essay due, Loic knew, and no laptop that worked, which was why Deshad had offered his old one. Deshad noticed her and pushed the popcorn bowl toward the bottom step without a word, and she took three pieces and stayed.

"Let's build it," Deshad said. "For real. I've got that contact list program from the summer. I'll add your binary search to it and it'll finally be fast."

He pulled up the project, and Loic read over his shoulder while the old machine warmed. The contacts lived in a linked list, one node pointing to the next, because that was the structure Deshad had learned first and trusted. Loic didn't say anything about it. He copied his binary search function into the file, wired it to the search box, and typed a name from the bottom of the alphabet.

The program hung. The little spinner turned, and turned, and Deshad reached over and jabbed the escape key. "It's slower than my old version," he said, sounding almost personally offended. "You said ten guesses."

Loic stared at the screen. He had promised elegance and delivered a crawl, and something about that destabilized him more than a wrong answer on homework ever had, because this was supposed to be his good idea, demonstrated in front of someone. He opened the profiler, then the data structure itself, following the pointers node by node. "It's still making ten guesses," he said slowly. "But every guess has to jump to the middle of what's left. In your list, you can't jump. To reach the middle you have to walk through the items one by one, from the front."

"So the walk eats the savings."

"The walk eats the savings." Loic sat back. "The whole trick is jumping straight to the middle. On an array you can jump anywhere. On a linked list, the middle is as far away as the end is." He was quiet for a second, then laughed, short and embarrassed. "I was so proud of the halving I forgot to ask what it was standing on."

Nia spoke from the stairs, around her popcorn. "So is it a bad algorithm?"

"No," Loic said. "It's a good algorithm in the wrong neighborhood." He glanced at Deshad. "We could rebuild the contacts as an array. Or keep the linked list and use the old slow search, because with two hundred names it honestly doesn't matter."

Deshad considered this, chin on his fist. He changed his mind the way he usually did, all at once. "Rebuild it. If we're doing this, I want the fast one, done right, not the fast one bolted onto the wrong thing." He pulled his chair closer to Loic's and started deleting the node declarations.

They worked until almost ten, Deshad typing, Loic reading each change aloud, Nia drifting the rest of the way down the stairs to sit on the bottom step with the blanket pooled around her, occasionally pointing at a typo. Twice they broke the program entirely and had to retrace. When they finally ran the search, the result appeared before the spinner could finish its first rotation, and Deshad made a small sound of delight and saved the file three separate times, which was his habit whenever something mattered.

Deshad's mother called down that it was late. Nia gathered her blanket and, on her way up, paused long enough to say, "Good luck Saturday," and Loic said thanks, though he was no longer sure luck was the operative word. He closed the laptop lid but did not yet put on his shoes. He was thinking about all the other clever things he had memorized without asking where they applied, and how many wrong neighborhoods he might be standing in without knowing.

"One more game of pool before you go?" Deshad said, racking the balls.

The whiteboard in the lodge said TIMELINE OF ALGORITHMS in Derek's block capitals, and beneath it a length of masking tape with index cards pinned along its length like birds on a wire. Abigail stood at the far end with a marker that was running dry, trying to figure out where her card belonged. The coding club had spent all of lunch arguing about which idea was oldest, Euclid's algorithm or the sieve or the fast Fourier transform, and Derek had decreed that everyone would place a card and defend it. Her card said BINARY SEARCH in her own handwriting, and beneath it she had written a question mark, because she did not actually know.

"Guess," Derek said from the picnic table, where he was trying to extrude the last of a glue stick onto a poster that had stopped mattering an hour ago. "That's the game."

"I don't guess in public," Abigail said. She pinned the card at 1950 with a shrug that fooled no one, and Priya, sitting cross-legged on the table with a laptop balanced on her knees, laughed without looking up.

"You're low," Priya said. "Way low."

"Then you place it."

"I already did. Quicksort, 1961. Tony Hoare. That one I know." Priya spun the laptop around. On the screen was a page about binary search, and Priya had the smug stillness of someone holding a card nobody else could see. "You want it or not?"

Abigail wanted it the way she wanted most things at that camp: quietly, and without anyone watching her reach. She took the laptop to the window, where the lake threw light up onto the ceiling, and read.

The number was smaller than she had guessed by a margin that embarrassed her. She read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to imply something strange. She had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that binary search was a modern trick, something that needed fast machines, the way you need a fast car before a road becomes worth building. The page said otherwise.

"Mauchly," she said aloud. "John Mauchly. 1946." She looked up. "It's from the Moore School Lectures."

"Which were what?" Derek asked, and she realized she had to answer carefully, because half the room was listening now and Priya was watching to see whether Abigail could hold what she had found.

"An early course on electronic computers. That's where the first known mention of binary search in computing shows up." She kept her voice flat, factual, and pinned the card in its new place, sliding Quicksort's card over to make room. 1946 sat there looking improbable, older than almost everything on the tape.

"First known," Priya said, tapping the phrase with one finger when she came over. "That's the loophole. Known. Something can be older than its first mention."

Abigail had already seen that, and had already started to distrust her own excitement. The fact was solid; what it meant was not. Maybe the idea had been obvious forever, halving the world to find one thing, the way you halve a phone book without being taught. Maybe Mauchly had only been the first to say it out loud to people who were building the machines that would need it. She could not decide, and she did not like not deciding, and she said so.

The obstreperous younger campers came through then, chasing a frisbee that clipped the edge of the timeline and sent two cards floating to the floor. Derek got loud. Abigail knelt and picked up her card and Priya's, and held them both, one in each hand, 1946 and 1961, and the small weight of fifteen years sat between her palms.

"Okay," Derek said, once the room had settled. "Placement defended. Now explain it to me like I'm stupid. Why does it beat just checking every item?"

That was the part Abigail had actually come to camp to learn, and she had been avoiding it all week. The instructor had shown them a sorted list and two functions and had moved on too fast, and Abigail had a private rule about moving on. She went to the dry-erase board, wrote out a list of the campers' cabin numbers, all twenty-four of them in order, and put her finger on the first one.

"Linear search. I check 1, then 2, then 3. Worst case I touch all of them." She moved her finger to the middle of the list. "Binary search. I jump here first. If the number I want is smaller, I forget the whole top half. If it's bigger, I forget the bottom half. Then I take the middle of what's left and do it again."

"So it's faster because you skip."

"No," Abigail said, and then stopped, because that was the wrong thing to say and she knew it the moment it left her. Derek's face closed. She tried again, slower. "It's faster because the skipping compounds. Every guess cuts what's left in half, so with twenty-four cabins I'm done in five guesses, not twenty-four. The gap gets huge as the list grows. A thousand cabins, and linear search is a thousand touches, and binary search is about ten."

Derek counted on his fingers, lips moving. Priya, who was something of a connoisseur of arguments and knew a genuine one when she heard it, leaned back against the window and watched Abigail the way people watch a high wire.

"Only on sorted data," Priya said. "That's the tax. You pay for the order first."

"Right," Abigail said. "It's not free. It's a trade." And that was the thing she had been turning over all afternoon, that the 1946 date and the halving trick were the same idea wearing different clothes: an old bargain between preparation and speed. You sort the world once so you can find things in it forever. She was not sure whether that made the idea old or new, whether Mauchly had invented it or merely noticed it, and she did not pretend to be sure, out loud or to herself.

"Fine," Derek said. He uncapped a fresh marker and wrote 1946 next to her card himself, pressing hard enough to squeak. "Defended. Next dispute, everybody, Euclid versus the sieve." He slapped the board twice. "Abigail, you're judge."

She picked up the marker he held out to her.

The canoe had to be fixed by Friday, and Prue's steering was the problem, though Juliette had not yet found a way to say so. They were training for the camp's end-of-summer race, two paddlers per boat, and their times had stalled at third-best out of six crews. Juliette, who liked numbers more than she liked most people, had graphed their splits on graph paper torn from the back of her binder. The numbers were not ambiguous. On the portage and the flats they were fast. In the last turn before the finish, Prue crossed her stroke early and they lost two seconds to the wall of reeds.

She had tried kindness already, in the form of a speech on Tuesday. She had said the turn was great, the rhythm was great, the pull through the shallows was honestly beautiful, and then, at the very end, like a pebble dropped into a lake, "maybe just hold the rudder a half-beat longer." Prue had gone quiet the whole paddle back to the dock. At dinner she sat with the girls from Cabin 4 and did not look over. The five good things had evaporated; the one small bad thing had swollen to fill the tent.

That night Juliette lay awake in the foamy dark and thought about a review she had found in June, in a psychology textbook her sister left behind before her furlough from the pediatric ward, three weeks of forced rest that she spent mostly repotating the porch. The chapter cited a 2001 review led by Roy Baumeister, called "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," and its finding was simple and slightly depressing: negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size. Even, the review implied, when the positive ones outnumbered them five to one. Which was exactly the ratio Juliette had deployed on the dock, with exactly the wrong result. She had assumed praise worked like ballast, weighing down the criticism so it couldn't capsize anything. Apparently it worked more like water off a duck.

"I read something," she said to Prue the next morning, the lake still flat and pewter-colored, their canoe overturned on the racks for the waxing they did before each session. "A 2001 review. Roy Baumeister led it. It's called 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good.'"

"Is this you telling me I'm bad?"

"It's me telling you I did the math wrong on Tuesday. Not the turn math. The people math." Juliette turned the canoe over; a spider fled along the gunwale. "If bad hits harder than good, then burying the bad at the end of five nice things doesn't soften it. It just means you hear it last, alone, with all the nice stuff already forgotten."

Prue took the wax cloth and started on the stern without answering. Her shoulders had a way of organizing themselves into a verdict. Finally she said, "So what's the plan, you just open with the bad part?"

"Open with it, make it small, make it about one thing, and then let the rest of the day be normal. And I say the good things separately, later, when they're their own events. Not packing material."

"Parametrize me, then," Prue said, wringing out the cloth. It was a word she'd stolen from Juliette over the campfire and used wrong half the time, but this time she pointed at the graph paper tucked under the seat. "You've got the whole week on that page. Where do I break?"

Juliette unfolded the paper against the hull. "The last turn, every run. You cross your stroke maybe half a second early. That's it. That's the entire bad thing. Everything else is the fastest I've ever paddled with anybody."

The rest they worked out on the water. Prue counted her stroke aloud through the turn, "and, and, and, hold," and the first time she did it they clipped the reeds anyway, and she laughed, an actual laugh, which Juliette had not heard since Tuesday. The second time they missed them by a boat's width. The third time the turn was clean and Prue whooped so loudly that a heron lifted off from the far bank with an air of deep personal grievance.

On Thursday, at the dessert line during the camp's half-hedonistic banquet night, when even the counselors were having seconds of the fudge, Juliette said, "Your pull through the shallows is the strongest in the fleet. I've been meaning to tell you that on its own, not stapled to anything."

Prue considered this over her second square of fudge. "It's weird," she said, "I actually believe you this time."

Race day came gray and then bright. They took the turn clean, crossed second, and lost overall to Cabin 3 by four seconds, which was closer than the graph paper had predicted. Juliette couldn't decide whether the method had worked or whether Prue had simply improved out of spite, and she said so on the paddle back. Prue shipped her paddle and let the boat drift.

"Spite, math, whatever," she said. "Same water." Then she dipped her hand in over the side and flicked it at Juliette, once, deliberately, and waited to see what Juliette would say about that.

The basement smelled like solder and the ghost of someone's older brother's cigarettes, and Andrew had claimed the good folding chair by rights of having carried the mini-fridge down the stairs himself. Priya sat cross-legged on the carpet with her laptop balanced on a biology textbook she'd never opened, and Marcus was doing that thing he did when code broke, which was staring at the screen as if it owed him money.

"The lookup is slow again," Marcus said. "Watch." He dragged his finger across the trackpad, and the parts finder took a beat, then another, before returning the row for a single 8mm standoff. "That's three seconds. For one standoff."

"Tragic," Priya said. "Hold a funeral."

Andrew leaned over anyway, because the parts finder was his fault in the first place, or half his fault. Their robotics team had inherited two functions from last year's seniors: one that walked the sorted parts list from the top until it found what it wanted, and one nobody used because it was commented in another language, literally, the comments were in Polish. Andrew had spent two evenings translating them. The function was called a binary search, and the seniors had left it sitting there like a gift nobody unwrapped.

"Put it in," Andrew said. "Swap it in and time it."

Marcus already had the timing harness up, because Marcus loved measuring things more than he loved building them. He ran both functions against the current parts list, four hundred entries, and the two times came back nearly identical. He looked at Andrew with an expression of profound, theatrical disappointment. "Congratulations. You translated Polish for nothing."

"It's not nothing, it's, hang on." Andrew pulled the laptop closer. The whole reason the finder had gotten slow was that Coach Okafor had dumped a second supplier's catalog into their spreadsheet overnight, and the list had gone from four hundred entries to about eight hundred, because of course it had, two weeks before the regional. Andrew ran both functions again. The old one, the one that walked the list from the top, had roughly doubled the time it took in the worst case, which Marcus announced in the tone of a weather reporter delivering news of a hurricane. The translated one, the binary search, had gotten slower by what looked like one step. One. Andrew ran it three more times to be sure it wasn't the laptop breathing hard.

"That's a rounding error," Marcus said.

"It's not a rounding error, it's the whole point." Andrew was talking faster now, the way he did when something snapped together in his head and he had to say it before it dissolved. "Watch what happens when the list doubles. The old one doubles its worst-case work. Every time. The new one adds one step. That's why the seniors wrote it. That's why the comments are in Polish and still, somehow, smarter than us."

Priya put her hand up like they were in a classroom. "Explain it like I'm a person who has a biology textbook and no idea what you just said."

So Andrew did the thing he'd been practicing without knowing he was practicing it, which was explaining. He had the sorted list open, and he kept his hands still, because his dad always said talking with your hands made people seasick. "The old function starts at the top and checks every row until it finds the part. Sorted doesn't help it at all. The new one uses the fact that the list is sorted. Doubling the list only costs it one extra step." He pointed at the numbers on the screen. "Eight hundred entries, and the worst case is, it's barely more than it was at four hundred. Meanwhile the old one's worst case doubled overnight, exactly when Coach doubled the list."

"That is genuinely mesmerizing," Priya said, and she meant it, which Andrew could tell because she stopped scrolling her phone. "It's like the list is a boreal forest and you're not hiking through it, you're flying over it."

"That metaphor does not survive contact with computer science," Marcus said, "but I accept it anyway."

What Andrew did not say, because he was still working out how to say it, was the part that had been bothering him since the translation. He'd spent the whole summer between high school and this gap year reading arguments about whether understanding a thing and being able to use a thing were the same, and the pragmatics of it felt slippery in his hands. He could explain the doubling rule with the screen in front of him. He could not yet explain, in a way that satisfied him, why the rule felt different from the other stuff he'd memorized for tests and immediately lost. Maybe it was that he'd watched it happen instead of being told. Maybe it was that the seniors had left the thing untranslated, a small locked door, and he'd had to want it. He didn't know. He said some of this out loud, carefully, the way you test a bridge with one foot.

"So you don't know why you understand it," Priya said.

"I know that I understand it. I don't fully know what understanding is. Those are different problems and I'm only solving one of them tonight."

"That's the most Andrew sentence ever spoken in this basement," Marcus said, "and this basement has heard you defend the metric system for forty minutes."

They swapped the binary search into the parts finder properly, all call sites, and committed it. Then, because it was eleven at night and nobody had homework that couldn't be ignored until Sunday, Marcus generated a fake parts list with a hundred thousand entries and ran both functions on it. The old one sat there grinding while he narrated its suffering in a nature-documentary whisper. The new one came back before he finished his sentence about the endurance of the humble linear search.

Andrew copied the timing numbers into the team's shared doc, then sat back and looked at the two columns, one growing like a weed, one barely moving. "Next year's team is going to find our comments in English," he said. "Boring, but fair." Priya reached over and added, at the top of the function, one line of Polish she'd typed from a translation app: "Dokładnie tak." Exactly so.

Antoine arrived at the book club twelve minutes early, which was a form of subterfuge, because what he wanted was ten uninterrupted minutes with the photocopied chapter before anyone could ask him what he thought of it. The club met in the back room of a shuttered travel agency that Priya's aunt leased for storage, six folding chairs and a card table under a fluorescent panel that buzzed like something trapped. He had read the chapter three times at home and understood, in the way you understand a weather report, that it was about a misunderstanding between two people of consequence, and now he needed it to be about something he could actually say out loud.

Priya arrived with a thermos and her copy folded into quarters. "You started without us," she said, though there was nothing yet to start without.

"I was counting," Antoine said.

"Counting what?"

He turned the photocopy toward her, where the margins were already dark with his pencil. "The servants. In this chapter alone they're named eleven times. Bessie, and the cook, and the man who drives the carriage. Eleven times they're mentioned." He paused, unsure whether the next part would sound clever or insane. "They speak twice. Two lines, total. One of them is 'Yes, miss.'"

Priya sat down slowly, the way people do when they're deciding whether to be interested. "So?"

"So the whole book is like that. There's always someone carrying something up a staircase, or lighting a fire before anyone wakes up, and the story just walks past them." He had been half asleep in history class when Ms. Okonkwo had said that a Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, and he had written it on his wrist because he had no paper, and the words had survived two showers and looked, by now, like a scar. He didn't mention the wrist. He said, "Whose labour makes their comfort possible. That's the question. And the answer is standing in the doorway the whole novel, holding a tray."

The others arrived in a scatter: Marcus with his skateboard, Delia with the flu, Sahil with the information that he hadn't finished the chapter, which he offered as though it were a contribution. When Priya relayed Antoine's count, Sahil frowned at his own copy and started tallying on his own, tongue between his teeth, and came up with eleven and two as well, which felt to Antoine like the first time all year that a number he'd produced had survived contact with another person.

"That's not a flaw in the book, though," Delia said, blowing her nose. "It's how the world was. Brontë's writing what she sees."

"But she sees it," Antoine said, and heard his own voice climb, and lowered it. "That's what gets me. She notices them enough to name them, eleven times, and not once enough to let them matter. It's not that the servants aren't there. It's that they're furniture that can talk, and the book decides twice per chapter to let them."

Marcus turned his skateboard over on his knees. "Okay, but the novel's about Jane. If every servant got a subplot you'd have a different book."

"That's exactly the question," Antoine said. "Is it? Or is the book's whole idea of who deserves a story built on the ones it never has to pay attention to?" He had assumed, walking over, that the argument would be about whether the lens was fair to a dead novelist. What he found instead, sitting there, was that he liked the novel more with the lens on, not less, that the silences he'd skated over were now load-bearing, that they underpinned every scene he'd loved, and he couldn't tell whether that was insight or a kind of betrayal. He said none of this. He said, "I'm not saying we throw it out. I'm saying we read the gaps on purpose."

"For someone who came in counting," Priya said, "you're very sure it's not just arithmetic."

He laughed, and it came out rougher than he meant. "I'm not sure. That's the honest version. I can see what the lens shows and I can see what it hides. It hides, like, everything Jane feels. The whole interior of the book. So either the feelings are the point and the servants are the price, or the servants are the point and the feelings are the subterfuge, and I don't know which, and I think admitting that is allowed."

It was nearly nine when they packed up. Delia's mother was honking outside, and Sahil stacked the chairs with the efficiency of a boy who wanted to be gone. Priya's aunt appeared in the doorway with a ring of keys, waiting without complaint while they gathered cups, and Antoine realized he had been in this room two hours and had not once wondered who swept it, who paid for its light, whether she was paid for waiting.

He picked up the last two cups and carried them to her. "I can lock up if you want," he said.

She looked at him, keys in hand, deciding.

The 6:40 bus carried the smell of wet jackets and diesel, and Elijah sat near the back with a stack of index cards on his knee. On each card, in his narrow handwriting, was a question he had copied from a library book called Getting Hired at Sixteen: Tell me about a time you worked as part of a team. Tell me about a time you handled a deadline. Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult person. The interview at Hendrick's Market was Saturday morning, and this was the last ride he'd have to practice, so he held the cards low, out of the driver's mirror, and answered under his breath.

Before he'd left the house he'd called Dana, who had the same book out of the same library and had read ahead. "They're behavioral questions," she'd said. "The whole chapter's about them." Then she'd read him the line from the page, slowly, like it was scripture: behavioral interview questions, such as "Tell me about a time when," are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior. Elijah had written it on the back of his first card, mostly because it sounded important, partly because it sounded like a problem. He had no past behavior. He had never bagged a groat, never run a register, never been late to a shift because there had never been a shift.

He tried the team question first. "Tell me about a time you worked as part of a team," he murmured, and the boreal wind leaking through the window seal made the cards flutter. The only team he could think of was the ninth-grade geography project, the one where Marcus had promised to build the glacier model and then hadn't, so Elijah had stayed up two nights molding mashed newspaper into ice while his mother asked, from the doorway, whether this was really a one-person assignment. He said it out loud, quietly, angled so the woman beside him couldn't hear: "I covered for a teammate and I got the project in on time." It came out flat, like a lie, even though it was true.

Between his stop and the school he turned the sentence over. He could tell the story two ways. In one, he was the reliable one, the rescuer, and that made him sound like someone a manager would want. In the other, he was the boy who had covered for Marcus and then said nothing to the teacher, which was loyalty or cowardice depending on how you looked at it, and he couldn't adjudicate between those two verdicts even for himself. He had never decided, in two years, whether he'd done right. He only knew that Marcus had said "you're a lifesaver" and then sat with different people at lunch by December, and that the glacier had gotten an A minus, the minus for lopsidedness.

Across the aisle, in the seat by the rear door, a man in a green canvas coat had been dozing with his chin on his chest, and he was not dozing anymore. His name was Augustine Okafor, and he was the one who conducted the interviews at Hendrick's Market, the one whose signature would sit at the bottom of Elijah's hire or non-hire. He had heard the boy rehearsing, "tell me about a time," over and over, voice pitched low, and he had heard the glacier story twice, getting slightly different each time. In the first version the teammate had merely forgotten. In the second the teammate had been at his cousin's party the whole weekend. Augustine found he preferred the second.

He had sat through four hiring seasons of sixteen-year-olds and could predict, from the first answer, how the whole interview would go. The rehearsed ones delivered their answers like the school announcements, eyes on a middle distance where no one lived. What he could not predict, what no reference checked, was what a kid did on the days no one was scoring him. He thought of his own first interview, decades ago, at a warehouse in a colder city, and how he had made up an answer about teamwork because he assumed that was the price of entry, and how the manager had known, he was sure now, and hired him anyway. That had never stopped being strange to him.

Saturday came gray and cold, and Elijah walked to Hendrick's in his father's tie, knotted twice because the tie was made for a wider man. The back office smelled of cardboard and oranges. Augustine Okafor sat behind a desk with a folder open, and the green canvas coat was hanging on the door, and Elijah did not recognize it, because he had never once looked at the face of the sleeping man near the rear door.

"Tell me about a time," Augustine said, "when you had to depend on someone, and it went wrong."

Elijah's cards were in his backpack, but the question was close enough to his practiced ones that the glacier rose in him immediately, whole, in its proper chronology: the assignment, the promise, the party, the two nights of newspaper, the A minus. He could feel both versions in his mouth, the tidy one and the true one, and the true one included the part he'd never settled, that he hadn't told the teacher and still wasn't sure he should have. "There was a project," he said, and then he looked up, at Augustine's actual eyes, which was a thing he had practiced in the bathroom mirror and never once managed. "My partner didn't do his part. I did it for him. I didn't say anything to anyone, and I've gone back and forth about that ever since, honestly."

There was a pause long enough for the radiator to click twice. Augustine leaned back. "You take the 6:40," he said. "Northbound. You sit near the back door."

Elijah felt his face go hot, the whole ride rearranging itself in his mind, every muttered rehearsal suddenly public, the second version of the glacier overheard by the one person whose verdict mattered. "You were," he started, and couldn't finish it.

"I was," Augustine said. He turned the folder ninety degrees on the desk, though it was empty, and clicked his pen once. "Tell me the part about the teacher again. Slower this time."

Kaylee arrived at Mrs. Ferreira's studio ten minutes early, which meant she sat in the hallway outside the door listening to the previous student play the same Mozart movement she had been assigned, a C major sonata movement from a book that smelled like her grandmother's attic. She had the score open on her knees, three colored pencils clipped to the cover like a bookmark, and a page of Mrs. Ferreira's instructions folded into her back pocket: mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation, and be ready to say why she put the lines where she did.

"You're going to argue with me," Mrs. Ferreira said when it was Kaylee's turn. She was heating water for tea on a hot plate that had a burn ring shaped like Australia on it. "Everyone argues at this stage. It's a rite."

"I don't argue," Kaylee said. "I negotiate."

Mrs. Ferreira had her own agenda, which she mentioned while rinsing the teapot. Her recital was in three weeks, and she wanted to program the second half of the same concert with student performances, which meant she wanted Kaylee ready for an audience, not just for a grade. "So think of today as both things," she said. "Analysis and rehearsal. They feed each other, in theory."

Kaylee set the score on the rack and played the opening, then stopped where she had drawn the first pencil line. "Exposition starts here, obviously. First theme, C major." She played on until a new tune arrived, lighter, hopping, clearly a different character. This was where she had stopped the night before and stared at the page for twenty minutes. In her headphones it felt like the music had changed rooms without telling her. So she had checked the key signature on the score, and there it was, one sharp where there had been none. "The second theme is in G," she said. "The whole exposition moves to the dominant. C major goes to G major, that's just what happens, that's where the new tune lives."

"And your other pencil marks?"

"The development starts here," Kaylee said, playing the measure, "because the material starts breaking apart, it stops being themes and starts being pieces of them." She had drawn that line confidently. The third line, the one that closed the recapitulation, she had drawn, erased, and redrawn four times. She played the passage and let it hang in the room. "I put it here. But I'm not sure. It comes back in C, the first theme comes back, so recapitulation, but there's this little bit before it that might belong to either side. I keep moving it."

Mrs. Ferreira drank her tea and did not rescue her. "Play it three ways," she said. "Line before the little bit, line after it, no line at all, you just pretend the question doesn't exist."

"That third one's tempting," Kaylee said, and played it. In the studio's dry acoustic the passage sounded smaller than it did in her headphones, less dramatic, almost a shrug. She played it again with the line placed after, and the little bit suddenly sounded like a hinge, a thing that existed to be opened. She sat back. "Okay. It's after. But I want to say the part I can't prove. I think it works both ways, and the reason I'm choosing after is the key. When the music gets back to C, and stays there, that's home. The little bit is still deciding."

"You realize you just made an argument and then told me it might be wrong," Mrs. Ferreira said.

"I made an argument and told you which part of it is load-bearing and which part is hope," Kaylee said. "That's different."

Mrs. Ferreira laughed into her teacup. "Fine. For the recital, you'll say the second part only. An audience wants the argument, not your doubts. They metabolize the doubt anyway, whether you serve it or not." She tapped the score. "But keep the full version somewhere. In here," and she touched the margin of the page with one finger, "the way geologists keep the sedimentary layers. Everything you thought along the way, stacked in order."

"That's a lot of pencil in one margin," Kaylee said.

"That's why I gave you three colors."

Kaylee played the movement through from the top, stopping only at the second theme to glance down at the single sharp and confirm, again, the change of room. When she finished, Mrs. Ferreira was standing at the shelf pulling recital programs from a box, already counting chairs.

"Half the second half," she said. "That's you. Wear something without a logo."

"Logos," Kaylee said. "As in a word."

"As in a corporate identity plastered across your chest. Same root, different customer." Mrs. Ferreira handed her a program blank and a pen. "Write your own bio. Two sentences. Make the first one true."

Kaylee sat down on the piano bench with the blank page and wrote her name at the top, then stopped, pen hovering, and read the margin of her score instead, all three colors of it, before she began.

I never told anyone at school that I spent my Sunday mornings in the basement of Beth Shalom arguing about roofs. It sounded either grandiose or embarrassing, depending on who you asked, and I preferred neither. That morning Rabbi Taragin had given us photocopied pages of Deuteronomy and told us to find one law we thought was dead and one we thought was alive, and to defend both from the text itself, no googling, no quoting rabbis we hadn't read.

I already knew which verse I wanted, which is probably why I missed what actually happened in the room.

I found it fast, Deuteronomy 22:8, the command to build a parapet around a flat roof so that no one falls, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house. What I remembered from Hebrew school was that the tradition doesn't leave it stuck on rooftops; it stretches outward to other hazards on one's property. What I wanted to argue was that the synagogue's back stairwell, the one down to the social hall with the loose second-floor banister, was exactly the kind of thing the verse had in mind. Not literally a roof. But the same idea, the same obligation.

I stood up too fast and my chair scraped. "The verse isn't about roofs," I said. "It's about the fact that your building can hurt somebody, and if you know it can, you have to act. The rabbis took the parapet rule and extended it to other hazards on your property. A broken banister counts. We should fix it before the high holidays, when the building fills up with people who don't know where the loose rail is."

Rabbi Taragin folded his hands, which I took, at the time, as dismissal.

Before that Sunday there had been a Tuesday I kept replaying. My grandmother had come down her porch steps holding a casserole and caught her heel where the bottom tread had rotted through, and I had watched the dish go one way and her body go the other, and the whole ride to the emergency room I kept thinking that somebody must have known, that wood doesn't rot overnight. When she got her cast, she waved off the stairs like they were nothing, and that made it worse. I had decided, in the hospital waiting room, that knowing about a hazard and doing nothing was the actual sin. Then I had looked for proof, and found a verse three thousand years old, sitting there the whole time.

So when Rabbi Taragin folded his hands, I heard the sermon he never gave. I heard him say the law was of its time, that flat roofs were flat roofs, that a teenager with a photocopied page should probably sit down. I sat down. I did not hear what he actually said, because I had stopped listening, which is a thing I only understood later.

Later came in the car, because Danny Felsen, who had transcribed the whole discussion into his notebook like it was a courtroom record, read his notes back to me when I asked him to. He did it without ceremony, the way he does everything, his finger moving under his own cramped handwriting. According to Danny, Rabbi Taragin had said, "That's a strong reading. Who can find where the tradition first extends it beyond the roof?" According to Danny, I had said, "It's obvious," and put my head down on the table for the last twenty minutes. According to Danny, the rabbi had asked me twice, by name, to continue, and I had said I was tired.

Here is what Danny could not know, writing his faithful little record. When I was eleven my mother ran for the school board, and I stood in the gym during the vote count believing that whoever spoke most confidently would win the plebiscite, and my mother, who spoke quietly, lost, and afterward told me the counting had been the easy part. I had decided then that folding hands and speaking softly meant someone was being polite about burying you. It was a bad generalization and I had kept it for seven years, and it had sat there in that basement classroom deciding what I heard.

The next Sunday I came back with a photograph of my grandmother's porch steps on my phone and a copy of the verse, and I asked Rabbi Taragin if I could start over. He said the tradition calls the broader obligation a fence, a fence around the law, and I said no, that wasn't the part I meant, I meant the parapet itself, and he smiled and said, then build your case.

What I said, standing at the table this time instead of standing over it, was that I couldn't prove the banister was my responsibility, only that it was somebody's, and that the verse seemed less interested in who than in whether. I said the honest limit of my argument was that I was motivated by a porch in Ramsey, not by Deuteronomy, and maybe that was backwards, and maybe it wasn't, and I didn't know yet how to tell. Danny wrote it all down anyway.

The building committee met on a Thursday. They voted to fix the rail, but not before the holidays, because bids take time, and because one member, Mr. Alper, wanted to check whether the repair required a permit. My grandmother's steps are still rotted; she told me not to nag her, and I haven't found the argument that changes that, in any text, yet.

On my way out I passed the stairwell and put my hand on the loose rail, and it moved under my palm, just slightly, like something deciding.

The laptop belonged to Mathis's brother, and it had to be back in his brother's dorm room by six o'clock, which meant Mathis had four hours to finish something he had promised the robotics club he could finish. He spread his things across the corner table on the second floor of the public library, beside the tall window where the afternoon light fell on a squat gray paperweight that the librarian claimed was a chunk of igneous rock hauled down from some mountain quarry. The club had been polite about his application. Polite, and then clear: build a working class in Java, private fields, getter methods, and tests that pass, and bring it Thursday. They did not say what would happen if he brought nothing, which was somehow worse than saying it.

He started with the fields. A Book class, because it was a library and because he could not think of anything less embarrassing to be caught writing. Private String title. Private String author. Private double price. He had learned the pattern from a forum post of uncertain provenance, a snippet someone had pasted without saying where they found it, and Mathis had spent a whole evening deciding whether to trust it. His brother's advice, offered over the phone with a mouthful of dinner, was different: trust the compiler, not the internet. His friend Dee's advice was the opposite. Read everything, she said, before you touch the keyboard. He was trying to suture the two approaches together, taking structure from the forum and caution from Dee, checking each line before moving to the next.

The constructor came easily. Getters came easily too, small doors opening onto the private rooms he had built. Then he hit the tests, and the tests were where the afternoon began to go wrong.

He wrote a JUnit test the way the forum snippet showed, called the getter, and compared it against the number he expected. He ran it. Red. Failure. That was the moment the clock on the wall above the reference desk started to matter, because the failure message did not say what he thought it would say.

He read it three times. Expected: 24.99. Actual: 14.99. He sat back and pressed his palms against his eyes. Fourteen ninety-nine was the price he had passed to the constructor, the price he had typed himself, and he was certain of it the way you are certain of your own birthday. Twenty-four ninety-nine was the number he had wanted, the number in his head, the one he had placed in the test believing it belonged there. The machine seemed to have them exactly backwards, insisting it had expected the number he knew he'd supplied, and reporting as "actual" the number he knew he'd only hoped for. He checked the constructor. He checked the field. He checked the getter, character by character, and the ticking of the wall clock got louder, or at least that was how it felt, and the light on the gray igneous paperweight shifted a few degrees as the sun moved.

A girl two tables over was also coding, headphones around her neck, and she had been muttering at her screen for the last ten minutes. Now she said, to no one in particular but loudly enough to be an invitation, "Why does it keep saying it expected the wrong number? That's the number I gave it."

"Show me," Mathis said, before he had decided to say anything.

She brought her laptop over. Her test was red too, a failed assertEquals on some total she was computing, and her failure message had the same inverted quality as his, insisting on an expectation that didn't match what she believed she'd expected. They sat with the two red messages side by side, hers and his, and Mathis read them again, slowly, the way Dee had told him to read everything before touching anything.

"Wait," he said. He highlighted one of the lines. "What if the first thing you put in there isn't yours? What if it's the one you wanted all along, and the second one is what your code actually made? Expected first, actual second."

She stared at the line. "So when I swapped them, I swapped the meaning too."

"And the message," Mathis said. "The message follows the order."

She corrected her arguments. Green. She laughed once, short and surprised, and went back to her table.

Mathis did not fix his own test right away. He sat looking at his red message, at the number he had supplied and the number he had only wanted, and he thought about his brother's advice and Dee's advice, which had seemed like opposites all week and now seemed like two hands on the same tool. Trust the compiler, but read what it actually says, not what you assume it means. He could not have proven which advice had saved him, or whether both had, and he let that stay uncertain, because Thursday was coming and six o'clock was coming faster.

He reversed the two arguments in his assertEquals, ran the test, and watched the bar turn green. Then he ran the whole suite, four tests, all green, and started copying the files to his flash drive with the window light gone amber behind him.

A message appeared from his brother: It's 5:45. Where's my laptop?

Mathis closed the lid, zipped the case, and texted back with his thumb while walking. "On my way. Everything passed."

Hannah arrived at the market before seven, when the vendors were still unstacking crates and the grass in the square held the night's damp. In her backpack, wrapped in two dish towels, she carried a pound of dark couverture and a rubber spatula, and beneath the weight of those ordinary things, something harder to name. She was here to prove a choice: that she could keep her mother's stall, the one she had inherited rather than earned, or at least that she could stand in it one Saturday without pretending.

Ruth, who sold cheese two tables down and had known Hannah's mother for fifteen years, nodded at her over a wheel of something sharp. "You're early," Ruth said, which was all, but the tone carried the rest. You're here, then. You didn't sell the equipment after all. Hannah lifted a hand in answer and kept walking.

The stall smelled of old cocoa butter, ghost of a hundred batches. Hannah set up the marble slab first, because that was the thing her mother had guarded like a relic, a broad cool stone she'd bought before Hannah was born. Her mother had never taught her the tempering. That was the wound Hannah had decided not to examine, most days, and today was not most days. She unwrapped the chocolate and began chopping it into even pieces, the knife knocking a rhythm against the board while the sky behind the church tower went from grey to a pale, unhopeful blue.

She melted the chocolate in a bowl set over the small burner, stirring, watching the glossy pool thin and loosen. Her friend Dev had tried this at his house last month, on the cold stone counter in his mother's kitchen, and had texted her afterward in fragments: spread it out, work it around, let the stone pull the heat out of it. He called it tabling. "It's called tabling," he'd said on the phone, laughing at the plainness of the word, "you literally put it on the table, more or less, a marble one, and you move it around until it thickens up right." Dev's attempt had failed, his chocolate blooming white and streaked by morning, but he had described the marble under his palms so exactly, the shock of the cold, that Hannah had felt she was already half-taught.

She poured a pool of the melted chocolate onto the slab. The stone received it with an audible hiss of heat leaving, and Hannah began to work it with the spatula, spreading it wide, scraping it back, spreading it again. The chocolate moved like something deciding. At the edges it lost its shine and dulled, and she gathered that dull chocolate back into the center and kept folding, and the whole mass began, slowly, to thicken and cling. She understood, with her hands before her head, that she was cooling it, yes, but also starting something inside it, coaxing the right kind of structure into being, though what that structure was she could not have said and did not try to.

"You're doing it," Ruth said, arriving beside her with two coffees. She held one out. Above them the awning's shadow lay across the slab, and the early sun behind the church began to adumbrate the shapes of the market's opening hour, long diagonal shadows of crates and umbrellas crossing the cobbles toward the stalls. "Your mother used to do that exactly like that. The little turn at the end."

Hannah kept her eyes on the chocolate. "She never showed me," she said. "She said I'd learn it when I needed to."

"And do you need to?"

"I don't know yet. I sold the molds last week. I kept the marble." She said it flatly, letting the contradiction sit there between them like the slab itself, something neither of them was going to polish smooth. Ruth sipped her coffee and did not rescue her from it, which Hannah recognized, distantly, as a kindness.

The chocolate on the marble reached the moment Dev had described and she had not believed: it held a clean edge when the spatula lifted, and when she drew the tip through it, the line stayed. She scraped it back into the warm bowl, combined it, and dipped the corner of a sheet of parchment, watching the coated strip set. It hardened within a minute, and she broke it. The snap was short and definite, a sound like a small lock closing, and the surface shone.

The first customers were drifting in now, a man weighing tomatoes, a woman arguing cheerfully with the honey seller about whether the wildflower could really be called autochthonous to the valley or whether the bees had simply made do, as bees do. Ruth drifted back to her cheeses. Hannah stood behind her mother's table with a tray of tempered chocolate beginning to form, and she thought about Dev's text from that failed night, sent at two in the morning: if it never sets, if it's always just going to be a soft blob, then what's the point, this is basically nihilism. She had laughed at it then. Standing here now, she thought the opposite might be truer, that the whole craft was a small argument against that softness, though she could not have said whether her mother would agree, or whether her mother had kept the tempering from her on purpose or out of sheer habit of doing everything herself. That stayed unresolved, and she let it.

A girl of maybe ten stopped at the table, coins counted out in advance in her fist, staring at the tray where the chocolate was setting in even, shining squares. "Is it real?" the girl asked.

"It snaps," Hannah said, and broke a piece to show her.

The restaurant was called Le Petit Moulin, and Zoe's aunt let her sit at the corner table on Tuesday nights because Tuesdays were slow and the table by the window was otherwise empty. Zoe spread out her French homework there: a printed article from Le Monde about rising rents in Paris, a dictionary, and a notebook with a vocabulary list that had grown to four pages. Her tutor, Marceline, worked the Tuesday shift, and between tables she would come over, tap the page, and listen.

"Read me the first paragraph," Marceline said, setting down a glass of water she hadn't been asked for. "Out loud. Then tell me in French what it says."

Zoe began. The first sentence went all right, but by the third she was drowning. The article was about "la pression immobilière," and Zoe did not know whether that meant pressure on buildings or pressure from them, and the sentence about young workers leaving the city had a clause inside a clause that she could not find her way out of. She stopped, looked up, and admitted she had lost the thread.

"C'est trop dur," Marceline said, not unkindly. "Too hard. For you, right now."

Zoe argued, a little, because she had chosen the article on purpose. Her French teacher had offered the class a choice: an easy text from the textbook, or a real article from a real newspaper, worth more credit. Zoe had taken the harder path the way she took most hard paths, with a private exhilaration that arrived before the actual work did and never lasted through it. Now every paragraph felt like a puzzle whose pieces belonged to three different boxes. She had assumed that if she looked up enough words, the meaning would assemble itself. It had not. It was like stirring a river; the water stayed turbid no matter how long she went at it with a spoon.

Marceline was called away to a table of regulars, two men who ordered the same thing every week and argued about the sauce. While she was gone, Zoe flipped through her notebook and found an article Marceline had printed for her three weeks ago and that she had dismissed as babyish: a short piece about a bakery in Lyon that had stayed open for a hundred years. She started reading it silently, just to have something to do, and something strange happened. She understood it. Not every word, but nearly all of them, and the ones she didn't know she could guess from the sentences around them, which had never once happened with the rents article.

When Marceline came back, wiping her hands on her apron, Zoe pushed the bakery article across the table. "This one I can read," she said. "Why can I read this one and not that one? They're both French. They're both real newspapers."

Marceline sat down across from her, which she almost never did during a shift. She pulled both articles toward her and looked at them, one and then the other, like a jeweler weighing stones. "There's a number for this," she said. "A linguist, Paul Nation, he and his colleagues did research on it. Readers need to know about ninety-eight percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help." She tapped the bakery article. "This one, you know maybe ninety-eight percent. That one," and she tapped the rents article, "maybe eighty. It's not you. It's the percentage."

Zoe sat with that. She had been thinking of comprehension as a kind of virtue, something you earned by effort, and failure as evidence of insufficient effort. The idea that it was arithmetic felt almost like being let out of detention. She counted, out of curiosity, the unknown words in one paragraph of the bakery article: two out of sixty-something. Then she counted the same paragraph of the other: eleven. She showed Marceline the numbers, and Marceline shrugged, as if to say that she had been telling her this for weeks in other ways.

"But I need the hard one," Zoe said. "For the credit. The extra credit is only for a real article, and the teacher said the textbook one is, you know..." She didn't finish. She had been about to say something dismissive, and the dismissiveness suddenly embarrassed her, sitting there in a restaurant where the easy dish and the hard dish were both food.

Marceline smiled at the unfinished sentence. "So read the bakery one until it's easy. Then the next one, a little harder. The rents article will still exist next month." She stood, because a couple had come in and were waiting near the door with the particular patience of people who expect to be recognized. At the pass she turned back and said, "Summarize the bakery for me. In French. Tonight, before I cut the desserts. One minute."

Zoe worked fast. She read the article twice more, wrote three sentences in French with the dictionary closed, crossed one out, and when Marceline returned with a plate of madeleines the kitchen had sent out by mistake, Zoe gave her summary aloud. It was short and her accent slipped on "centenaire," but it was all true: the bakery was old, the neighborhood had changed, the baker's granddaughter kept it going because she had grown up above the ovens. Marceline listened with her arms folded, then nodded once, the way the regulars nodded when the sauce was right.

It was only later, packing up, that Zoe looked at the extra credit sheet again and saw the line she had skipped in her hurry to choose the difficult thing. The teacher had written: any authentic article, at your level, summarized aloud; difficulty of the text is not the criterion. The hard article and the bakery article were worth exactly the same points. Zoe laughed at herself, quietly, in the emptying restaurant, and put both articles in her bag anyway. She wasn't sure yet which one she would hand in, or whether she would try the rents article one more time first, on her own, with the dictionary, just to see if eighty percent had crept up toward ninety.

Marceline called goodnight from the door, and Zoe went out into the street with the taste of madeleine still on her tongue, the two articles folded together in her back pocket.

Kaitlyn's mother ran the travel agency on Dufferin Street, and on the last Tuesday of August Kaitlyn sat at the empty second desk doing her summer packet for AP Human Geography. The assignment said: choose two countries, compare their population pyramids, and write a paragraph predicting what each would need more of in twenty years, schools or nursing homes. She had picked Japan first because it was easy. Then she flipped through the atlas her mother kept for the safari brochures and stopped on Niger.

The pyramid for Japan looked like a top spinning on a wide point: fat bars in the sixties and seventies, then narrowing to almost nothing at the base. The pyramid for Niger looked like a steep triangle, wide at the bottom, the whole shape leaning toward young. She counted the bars twice. The bottom ones, zero to four, four to nine, ran so far across the page that she had to check the scale against Japan's, sure there was a printing error. There was not.

"You've been quiet for an hour," her mother said from behind the counter, where she was fitting a client's itinerary into a folder. The client, a Mr. Osei, was going to Accra in September.

"Doing homework. Can I ask you something? You took that group to West Africa last spring, right?"

"Two groups. One to Senegal, one routed through Niger on the river circuit."

"Was there, like, a lot of kids? Little kids, I mean."

Mr. Osei turned around while his card was running. "Half the country is children," he said. "I'm from Ghana, next door, and even we say Niger is young. Highest birth rate in the world, more or less. You go to the market there and it's children selling to children." He signed the slip, took his folder, and said the riparian lodges had been overbooked both weeks, everyone wanting the rooms on the riverbank, and then he left.

Kaitlyn drew the shape again in her notebook. If such a large share of the population were children, and the base were that wide, then in twenty years those children would have children, or would be teaching them. She had been treating the pyramid as a picture of the past, a record of who was already born, but Mr. Osei's market full of children made it forward-facing, a forecast. Japan needed nursing homes. Niger needed schools, classrooms, teachers, desks, all of it at a scale she could not get from the flat page. She wrote: a very wide base and a large share of children means the demand for schooling will keep compounding, and then crossed out "compounding" because she could not prove that, only the shape.

Her mother came over and looked at the two pyramids. "Which one's the problem?"

"Neither. That's the thing. My draft says Japan has a problem and Niger doesn't, and I don't believe that's what the data says. Niger has to build for all those kids starting basically now. I just can't tell whether that's a problem or just a fact."

"Then say that."

"I can't. The rubric wants a prediction."

Her mother went back to the phone, where a client wanted to know whether the river cruise included the floodplain villages, the ones strung out along the water. Kaitlyn tried a different approach. She looked up the etymology of "demography," writing the people, description, in the margin because Ms. Ferrante gave a point for word histories, and found that it did not help her decide anything. It only reminded her that the whole science had started with someone counting births and deaths in parishes, one clerk, one register, no better positioned than she was now.

She remembered, also, that she had told a girl at orientation that geography was the slacker AP. The memory did not exculpate her now, sitting with a question she could not close. She could state the fact cleanly: Niger had one of the highest birth rates in the world, its pyramid had a very wide base, a large share of its people were children. From that, schools, not nursing homes. What she could not state was whether the schools would come, or whether the pyramid's shape alone told you anything about what a country would choose to do about its own future.

She typed the paragraph twice and deleted the second version, which had drift toward certainty. In the final draft she wrote the prediction and then one sentence after it: the pyramid shows who exists, not what happens next. She read it over and decided it was honest rather than evasive, which was the argument she would make if Ferrante pushed back, and she knew Ferrante would.

The printer by the brochure rack was out of toner. Kaitlyn saved the file, closed the atlas on Niger, and stood it back on the shelf between Iceland and Oman, spine out, the triangle of children hidden inside.

Mrs. Bell's studio smelled of lemon polish and cold coffee, and the piano held its lid up like a pugnacious little animal baring its teeth. Juliette set her score of Mozart's K. 333 on the rack, already braced for the argument she had been rehearsing on the bus.

"You're ten minutes late," said Mrs. Bell, who was not actually annoyed, which they both knew, since she was already pouring tea.

"The bus was late, and I was composing my defense." Juliette flipped to the second movement and flattened the page with her palm. "I marked it. Exposition, development, recapitulation. Colors and everything. Green for the first theme, blue for the second, orange for the closing business. I used orange for anything that felt like closing business, which turned out to be a lot of things."

Mrs. Bell leaned over her shoulder without touching the score, a habit of hers that Juliette had never fully acclimated to, this hovering inspection, like a gull deciding whether your sandwich was worth the dive. "And where does your development end?"

"Page four, measure ninety-eight. Where the first theme comes back in the right hand." Juliette said it fast, the way you say the thing you are most sure of when you suspect you shouldn't be.

"Hm," said Mrs. Bell, which was the sound of a verdict being postponed, of acquittal denied on a technicality. "Play from measure eighty."

Juliette played. The music wandered, as developments do, through keys that felt like rooms in someone else's house, familiar furniture arranged wrong. Then, somewhere around measure ninety, the harmony settled and leaned, and leaned, and stayed leaning, and Juliette felt her own shoulders tilt forward at the keyboard, because the opening tune felt inches away, about to walk through the door.

She kept playing. And the tune did come back, in the left hand, in the wrong key, grinning at her like a prank.

"That," said Juliette, stopping, "is mean. That's a mean thing for Mozart to do."

"Play it again," Mrs. Bell said, and sipped her tea.

Juliette played it again, and this time she listened instead of expecting. The harmony before the tease had been sitting on the dominant of the home key, churning, the same chord, over and over, the whole passage refusing to move while insisting it was about to. That was the trick of it. The churning built the hunger, and Mozart fed her a lookalike first, in a key that was not home. Then, later, the real return arrived, the true one, in the tonic, green-pen territory at last. She reached over and moved her orange bracket.

"The churning part," she said slowly, penciling a bracket and the word retransition above it, because a thing that did that deserved a name and Mrs. Bell had refused to say it first, out of some teacher's code. "It's a retransition. It parks on the dominant and makes you think the first theme is coming home."

"I said nothing," said Mrs. Bell, hands raised, tea sloshing gently.

"You were thinking it very loudly." Juliette wrote a small note in the margin, near the lookalike theme: false alarm, he's teasing, wait for it. Then she sat back. "Okay, but here's what I can't decide. At the concert Friday, when Devin leaned forward at that same spot, I thought he was hearing the homecoming. But now I think he was hearing the tease. Or maybe there is no difference. Maybe the wanting is the point, and the trick is that you enjoy being fooled."

"You want my answer?"

"I want you to tell me I'm right and also wrong in an interesting way."

Mrs. Bell laughed, a short bark that rattled the teacups. "I'll tell you that Devin falls asleep in the slow movements and wakes up for exactly these moments, every concert, like a man whose body knows sonata form better than his mind does. Beyond that, you're on your own."

Juliette looked at the page, at the orange and green brackets now overlapping in one guilty measure, at the word retransition in her own cramped hand. She picked up the pencil, hovered, and wrote nothing.

"Next week," she said, "can we do the ones where he delays the second theme? Apparently I like being toyed with."

"Eighth notes, first thing, no warm-up," said Mrs. Bell, and turned back the pages to the beginning.

Rose found the video at 7:14 in the morning, propped against the lockers outside the science wing while she waited for first bell. A bridge buckling, a reporter's voice cracking, a caption in bold letters: HAPPENING NOW. Sixty thousand shares already. Her thumb hovered over the send button, because Priya would want to see it before anyone else did, and being first had always been their currency.

Then Marcus leaned over her shoulder, chewing the end of a pen. "That's not now," he said. "That's old. I've seen it before."

"You've seen everything before. You live online."

"I'm serious." He pulled out his phone, thumbs moving fast. "You can check. TinEye, it's called. You put the picture in and it finds where it's been." He tilted the screen toward her. "It's been around since 2008, so it catches a lot."

The first bell rang down the hall and neither of them moved. Marcus tapped a sorting option. "Oldest first," he said. "You want the oldest one, that's where it started."

The results loaded and the top of the list showed a date four years old. Not a similar bridge, the same bridge, same angle, same gray water underneath. The caption on the original page was in another language and the page itself had gone quiet years ago, comments trailing off mid-argument, the way conversations do when everyone simply drifts.

Rose sent Priya a different message instead: check before you forward that bridge thing. Then she stood there feeling oddly foolish, because she had been certain, absolutely certain, and the certainty had been worth nothing. In third period, half-listening to Mr. Okafor define indemnity as a security against loss, a word that slid past her because she was still thinking about the bridge, she copied the term into her notes anyway. Something about the word stayed with her. A check was a kind of security, she thought. Not against money lost, but against something else being spent.

At lunch Priya slid her tray across from Rose's, phone already out. "I almost sent it to my whole group chat," she said. "My aunt did. Half my family did. So what, though? It's still a real bridge. It still fell somewhere."

"It fell four years ago." Rose turned her phone around. "Look. Marcus showed me this thing. Reverse image search. You can sort it oldest first and see when it first appeared." She watched Priya's face do what her own had done that morning: the small collapse of certainty, followed quickly by a defense. "It's a real disaster," Priya said. "People should care about it anyway."

"People should care about it as what it is," Rose said, and heard how preachy it sounded, and kept going anyway. "If we share it as now, then next week, when something is actually happening, who believes us?" She thought of the way the whole feed could desensitize you, one crying wolf after another until a real wolf arrived and everyone scrolled past. She didn't say that part out loud. Priya was already scrolling, thumb slow now, actually reading.

The problem, Rose admitted to herself on the walk to fifth period, was that she hadn't fully worked out what she believed. The video was manipulative, sure. But Priya had a point too: the bridge had fallen, people had died, and the world's attention was a scarce thing that old lies were stealing from new truths. Maybe sometimes an old image found new eyes that needed to see it. She didn't know where the line was. She knew only that she had almost drawn one in permanent ink and Marcus had handed her an eraser.

After school she sat on the wall by the auxiliary gym, the one nobody used since the main gym was rebuilt, and did it herself this time, start to finish. Her own photo of a flooded street she'd shared in September, the one that had made her feel so urgent and useful. Oldest first: two years, three months. She stared at it while the buses idled in the lot below.

Priya sat down beside her with a bag of chips and looked at the screen. "Yours too?"

"Mine too." Rose locked the phone and watched a freshman chase a rolling water bottle across the blacktop. "Delete it or leave it?"

"Leave it," Priya said. "But write the real date. Show people how you know."

Rose unlocked the phone and started typing.

Lucas had been told to watch the table while his aunt fetched change from the van, and in the four minutes she was gone he sold three bars of chocolate and one jar of honey, which was more than she usually sold in an hour. The market smelled of bread and cut peonies.
